Internal alkynes were considerably less reactive, and only trace conversion was observed, so the method is largely limited to terminal alkynes. The E-configuration of the resulting enones was established by the vicinal coupling constants (J ≈ 15–16 Hz) and confirmed by X-ray crystallography for one derivative.

**Conversion to pyrroles.** The linear adducts contain a 1,4-relationship between the carbonyl carbon and the nitrogen-bearing carbon, suggesting that a cyclisation could give a five-membered heterocycle. Treatment of the crude hydroacylation product 3a with p-TSA (20 mol% to 1 equiv.) in refluxing toluene triggered conjugate isomerisation, intramolecular attack of nitrogen at the ketone, and dehydration to provide pyrrole 4a. Isolated yields over the two steps were 55–80%, and the process could be conducted in one pot by adding p-TSA directly on completion of hydroacylation, without isolation of the intermediate (Table 3). Sulfonyl-protected nitrogen was retained in the product, giving N-sulfonyl 2,5-disubstituted pyrroles carrying the aryl thioether unit. Monitoring by NMR indicated that the E-enone first isomerised to the corresponding β,γ-unsaturated or Z-species prior to ring closure; this was supported by the observation that isolated enone, under the same acidic conditions, required higher temperatures than the reaction mixture, which contained small amounts of the isomerised ketone. Both aromatic and aliphatic substituents on the aldehyde-derived portion were compatible, and substitution on the propargylic carbon furnished 2,3,5-trisubstituted pyrroles, accessing highly substituted frameworks that are difficult to prepare by classical Paal–Knorr chemistry [5].

**Allylic amines and dihydropyrroles.** Replacement of the propargylic amines with allylic amines was next examined. Hydroacylation of the alkene proceeded under similar conditions with the small bite-angle catalysts, delivering linear ketones in 50–75% yield, with minimal isomerisation of the alkene substrate to enamine (Table 4). Alkene hydroacylation is generally less facile than that of alkynes owing to competing decarbonylation, but the chelating thioether suppressed this pathway [2]. Subsequent exposure of the ketone products to p-TSA gave cyclic condensation products, identified as 2,3-dihydropyrroles (2-pyrrolines) rather than fully aromatised pyrroles, reflecting the absence of an additional oxidation step. Substituted allylic amines, including those with a methyl group at the allylic carbon, gave 2,5-disubstituted dihydropyrroles with modest diastereocontrol where a second stereocentre was present. These products offer functionalised, partially saturated heterocycles with handles for further reduction to pyrrolidines.

**Three-component cascade with boronic acids.** Finally, we explored whether the hydroacylation could be combined with a Rh(I)-catalysed Suzuki-type process. Rhodium-catalysed conjugate addition of aryl boronic acids to the enone intermediates was considered, as it would generate β-aryl ketones suitable for cyclisation. In practice, with the dppm-based catalyst and an aqueous base, the aldehyde, propargylic amine and aryl boronic acid reacted in one pot to give, after p-TSA treatment, 2,3,5-trisubstituted pyrroles in 40–65% yield (Table 5). The sequence is proposed to proceed by linear hydroacylation, followed by rhodium-aryl addition across the enone, and finally dehydrative cyclisation, so that three components are united with formation of multiple bonds in a single operation. Electron-rich and -neutral boronic acids performed best, while strongly electron-poor or ortho-substituted partners gave lower yields, reflecting competing protodeboronation. Notably, the catalyst system remained effective for both distinct catalytic events without added ligand, underscoring the versatility of the small bite-angle diphosphine rhodium complexes.

Overall, the methodology provides efficient access to pyrroles and dihydropyrroles from simple, readily available building blocks.

The results described above demonstrate that rhodium(I) complexes bearing small bite-angle diphosphine ligands provide a general solution to the challenge of linear-selective intermolecular hydroacylation of propargylic amines. Intermolecular hydroacylation has long been constrained by competing decarbonylation of the acyl-rhodium-hydride intermediate and by poor control over regioselectivity with alkynes [1,2]. Chelation assistance has been the dominant strategy to overcome these limitations, relying on directing groups installed on either the aldehyde or the unsaturated partner [3,4]. In the present work, the free or protected amine of the propargylic substrate is believed to serve as a weakly coordinating group that stabilises the key acyl-rhodium-alkyne intermediate, while the ligand framework determines the sense of insertion. The effectiveness of (Cy2P)2NMe and dppm, in contrast to ligands with larger bite angles such as dppe or dppp, is consistent with the notion that a contracted P–Rh–P angle opens the coordination sphere in a manner that favours alkyne insertion into the Rh–H bond with placement of rhodium at the carbon distal to the directing group, leading to the linear enone products. Related effects of bite angle on selectivity and on the suppression of decarbonylation have been noted in other rhodium-catalysed hydroacylation processes [5,6], and our findings extend this principle to a new substrate class.

The linear adducts are valuable not only as products in their own right but as immediate precursors to heterocycles. Treatment with p-TSA triggers condensation between the nitrogen nucleophile and the carbonyl group, followed by dehydration and aromatisation, to deliver pyrroles. This sequence formally constitutes a [3+2] disconnection in which the aldehyde supplies the acyl fragment and the propargylic amine provides the N–C–C≡C unit. Classical approaches to pyrroles, such as the Paal–Knorr, Knorr and Hantzsch syntheses, require pre-assembled 1,4-dicarbonyl or related precursors, and the substitution patterns accessible are often limited by the availability of these starting materials [7,8]. By contrast, the present strategy builds the carbon skeleton from simple, commercially available aldehydes and readily prepared propargylic amines, allowing the substituents at the 2-, 3-, and 5-positions to be varied independently. Transition-metal-catalysed routes to pyrroles from alkynes and amines have also been reported [9,10], but many rely on more elaborate substrates or lack the modularity that the two-step hydroacylation/cyclisation sequence offers.

Replacing propargylic amines with allylic amines leads to hydroacylation adducts that are saturated ketones, and acid-promoted cyclisation of these intermediates furnishes dihydropyrroles instead of fully aromatic products. This outcome highlights the versatility of the catalytic system, which tolerates both alkyne and alkene acceptors, and it provides access to partially saturated nitrogen heterocycles that are prevalent in natural products and pharmaceuticals [11]. Although alkenes are generally less reactive than alkynes in hydroacylation and are more prone to isomerisation, the ligand classes employed here maintained useful levels of linear selectivity. Some limitations remain: sterically hindered or strongly electron-poor aldehydes gave diminished yields, and substitution at the allylic position can erode selectivity, presumably through competing β-hydride elimination or alkene isomerisation pathways. The development of ligands that further suppress these processes, and of enantioselective variants that would generate stereodefined dihydropyrroles, represent clear targets for future study.

A particularly attractive feature of the chemistry is its compatibility with other rhodium-catalysed transformations in a single reaction vessel. The combination of hydroacylation with a Suzuki-type coupling of aryl boronic acids leads to a three-component assembly of highly substituted pyrroles. In this cascade, we propose that the initial alkyne hydroacylation or arylrhodation generates a vinyl-rhodium species that is intercepted in a productive manner, with the order of events governed by the relative rates of transmetalation and oxidative addition of the aldehyde C–H bond. Rhodium-catalysed conjugate addition and arylation reactions of boronic acids are well established [12,13], but their integration with hydroacylation within a cascade directed toward heterocycle synthesis is, to our knowledge, unprecedented. Such cascade processes are appealing because they increase molecular complexity rapidly while minimising isolation of intermediates, solvent use and waste, in keeping with the principles of step and atom economy [14]. The fact that a single rhodium(I) precursor and ligand set can orchestrate both bond-forming events suggests that further multicomponent processes could be designed, for example by varying the nature of the organometallic partner or by employing alternative electrophilic terminating steps.

Mechanistically, several questions remain open. The precise role of the amine substituent, whether as a protecting group, a hemilabile donor or an electronic modulator, merits more detailed investigation through kinetic and deuterium-labelling experiments. Likewise, the origin of the dramatic ligand effect could be probed by isolating or spectroscopically characterising rhodium intermediates and by computational modelling of the competing insertion pathways.

In conclusion, we have developed a linear-selective intermolecular hydroacylation of propargylic and allylic amines catalysed by rhodium(I) complexes of small bite-angle diphosphines. The resulting adducts are readily converted by acid-mediated dehydrative cyclisation into polysubstituted pyrroles and dihydropyrroles, and the hydroacylation can be merged with Suzuki-type arylation to give a modular three-component pyrrole synthesis. The method uses simple starting materials, proceeds with high regiocontrol and offers a flexible entry to heterocyclic scaffolds of relevance to medicinal and materials chemistry. We anticipate that the ligand design principles uncovered here will find application in other hydroacylation processes and in the broader development of catalytic cascade reactions for heterocycle construction.

Hashing has been widely used for approximate nearest neighbor search in large-scale information retrieval because of its low storage cost and fast query speed. Hashing methods map high-dimensional data such as images into compact binary codes so that similar items receive similar codes, and retrieval can then be performed efficiently with Hamming distance computed by bitwise operations. With the success of deep neural networks, deep supervised hashing has become the dominant paradigm. These methods jointly learn feature representations and hash functions in an end-to-end manner, using supervised information such as class labels or pairwise similarities. They consistently outperform traditional hashing approaches that rely on hand-crafted features.

In a typical deep hashing network, the output neurons of the last layer are binarized, usually with a sign function, to produce hashing bits. The code length is fixed in advance, and each output neuron is expected to contribute a distinct and informative bit. In practice, however, this expectation is often violated. Because the network is trained with relaxed continuous outputs and then discretized, many bits become highly correlated or carry nearly identical information. This is especially pronounced for longer codes, where the number of bits exceeds what the semantic structure of the data requires. Such redundancy has two negative consequences. First, it wastes storage and computation, since several bits encode what one bit could express. Second, it harms accuracy: redundant bits implicitly overweight certain semantic directions in the Hamming distance, while other discriminative information receives too little weight. This is why the retrieval performance of many deep hashing methods saturates, or even degrades, as the code length increases.

Several lines of work attempt to mitigate this problem. Some methods add regularizers that encourage bit balance or bit independence, for example by decorrelating the output dimensions or maximizing the entropy of each bit. Others choose the code length by hand, or select bits after training with heuristics. These strategies have limitations. Regularization terms act as soft constraints on the output distribution. They do not explicitly model which bits are redundant with which others, and they cannot adaptively restructure the network accordingly. Post-hoc bit selection treats redundancy as an afterthought and ignores the interaction between the selection process and representation learning. A principled mechanism that identifies redundancy during training and reduces it within the network itself is still lacking.

In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective Neurons Merging Layer (NMLayer) for deep supervised hashing. The key idea is to represent the redundancy relationship between hashing bits with a graph, whose nodes are output neurons and whose edges indicate how redundant two neurons are. This graph is not fixed beforehand. It is learned dynamically and then used to guide the learning of the hashing network. According to the learned graph, the NMLayer merges redundant neurons so that groups of neurons that behave similarly are combined into a single unit. This balances the importance of each output neuron: a piece of semantic information is no longer represented several times and given excessive weight, and the remaining neurons can capture complementary information.

To learn the redundancy graph, we design a novel mechanism built on two alternating phases, an active phase and a frozen phase. In the active phase, the graph is updated by observing the relationships among neurons as the network trains, so the estimated redundancy reflects the current state of the representation. In the frozen phase, the graph is fixed, and the network parameters are optimized under the merging structure it defines. Alternating between the two phases lets the redundancy estimate and the feature learning improve each other. It also avoids the instability that would result from changing the graph and the network parameters simultaneously.

Moreover, a single merging step is often insufficient to compress a very long, highly redundant code into a compact one without losing information. We therefore stack multiple NMLayers and train them progressively. Starting from a long redundant code, each NMLayer merges a portion of the redundant neurons and reduces the code length step by step, so the network gradually learns a more compact code. This progressive reduction is gentler than directly training a short code, since the network can first exploit the capacity of a long code to learn rich semantics and then condense it. The result is a final hashing code that is shorter and more discriminative than one trained directly at the same length.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

- We propose the Neurons Merging Layer, which explicitly models redundancy between hashing bits with a graph and merges redundant output neurons, thereby balancing the importance of each neuron and improving both storage efficiency and retrieval accuracy.
- We introduce a dynamic graph learning mechanism based on active and frozen phases, which estimates redundancy relationships during training while keeping optimization stable.
- We develop a progressive training strategy with multiple NMLayers that compresses a long redundant code into a compact one in several stages.
- We conduct extensive experiments on four datasets, showing that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art hashing methods, and we provide analyses that verify the effect of each component.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on deep supervised hashing and redundancy reduction. Section 3 describes the proposed NMLayer, the graph learning mechanism, and the progressive training scheme. Section 4 presents experimental results and analysis, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

Our method augments a deep hashing network with one or more Neurons Merging Layers (NMLayers). Starting from a long, redundant hash code, each NMLayer progressively merges redundant output neurons according to a learned redundancy graph, producing a shorter and more compact code.

**Problem Setting and Backbone.** Let X = {x_i}, i = 1..N, be training images with labels Y = {y_i}. Let S = {s_ij} be the pairwise similarity matrix, where s_ij = 1 if x_i and x_j share at least one label and s_ij = 0 otherwise. A backbone CNN f(·; θ) maps an image to a K-dimensional real-valued output u_i = f(x_i; θ) ∈ R^K, where K is deliberately larger than the target length. The binary code is b_i = sign(u_i) ∈ {−1, +1}^K. We use a pairwise likelihood loss on the inner products of the outputs,

L_s = −Σ_{s_ij∈S} ( s_ij Θ_ij − log(1 + e^{Θ_ij}) ),  Θ_ij = ½ u_iᵀu_j,

and a quantization loss L_q = Σ_i ‖u_i − sign(u_i)‖² that reduces the discretization gap. The base objective is L = L_s + λL_q.

**Redundancy Graph.** Redundancy between hash bits is represented by an undirected weighted graph G = (V, E), whose K nodes are the output neurons. The edge weight w_kl ∈ [0, 1] measures how redundant neurons k and l are. Two neurons are redundant if they carry similar information about the data, i.e. they produce nearly identical (or opposite) bits for most samples. Over a mini-batch, we compute the empirical correlation of the activations of neurons k and l,

c_kl = | Σ_i u_ik u_il | / ( ‖u_{·k}‖ ‖u_{·l}‖ ),

and use it as the instantaneous observation of redundancy. The absolute value is taken because a bit and its negation convey the same information. Rather than relying on a single noisy estimate, the graph is learned dynamically through two alternating phases.

**Active Phase.** In the active phase, the network parameters and graph are both updated. The graph weights are accumulated with a momentum update,

w_kl ← η w_kl + (1 − η) c_kl,

so the graph aggregates evidence over many mini-batches and tracks the changing representation as training proceeds. Meanwhile, the network is trained with the loss L, so that neurons become discriminative and their relationships grow more meaningful. The active phase lasts for a fixed number of iterations, after which the graph is considered to reflect the current redundancy structure.

**Frozen Phase.** In the frozen phase, the graph is held fixed, and the merging operation derived from it is applied. Freezing prevents the merging structure from changing while the network adapts to it, which would otherwise make training unstable. Only the network weights are fine-tuned, allowing the remaining neurons to compensate for the information of merged ones. After this phase, the next active phase begins if further NMLayers are to be added.

**Neurons Merging Layer.** Given the frozen graph, we group neurons by clustering. We apply a greedy procedure: the edge with the highest weight is selected, and its two endpoints are merged into one group provided the weight exceeds a threshold τ; this is repeated until the desired number K' < K of groups remains. Each group g contains a set of neurons V_g. The NMLayer is a linear layer with a fixed sparse merging matrix M ∈ R^{K'×K}, producing

v = M u,  M_gk = σ_k / |V_g| for k ∈ V_g, and 0 otherwise,

where σ_k ∈ {−1, +1} aligns the sign of neuron k with a reference neuron in the group, determined by the sign of their correlation. Thus negatively correlated neurons are flipped before averaging, and averaging combines redundant neurons into a single output. This balances the importance of the outputs: a piece of information that was originally duplicated across several bits is now represented by only one bit, so it no longer dominates the Hamming distance. The merged output v ∈ R^{K'} is then fed into the loss in place of u, and the final code is b = sign(v). To let the merged neurons adjust their contributions, a learnable per-neuron scale can be applied on top of M while preserving its sparsity pattern.

**Progressive Training with Multiple NMLayers.** Directly reducing a very long code to the target length in one step would discard much information at once. Instead, we stack several NMLayers and shrink the code progressively: K = K_0 > K_1 > … > K_T. Training proceeds in stages. In stage t, we (1) run an active phase on the current network to learn the graph over K_{t−1} neurons, (2) construct the NMLayer that merges them into K_t neurons and insert it after the current output, and (3) run a frozen phase to fine-tune the network with the new layer. The loss at each stage is computed on the output of the most recently added NMLayer. After T stages, the network produces a compact K_T-bit code distilled from the long redundant code. Because earlier merging decisions are fixed, later stages operate on already-consolidated bits, and the graph learned at each stage reflects the residual redundancy.

**Optimization and Inference.** The network is optimized with mini-batch stochastic gradient descent with backpropagation. The sign function is relaxed during training, with its gradient approximated as identity (or tanh smoothing), so that the quantization loss and the pairwise loss are differentiable. The merging matrices are not updated by gradients except for the optional scale parameters. Graph updates require only a K×K correlation computation per mini-batch, adding negligible cost. At test time, a query image is passed through the backbone and all NMLayers, binarized with sign, and compared to database codes by Hamming distance. Since the NMLayers are linear, they add no meaningful inference overhead, and the final code length is K_T bits.

We evaluate the proposed NMLayer on four widely used image retrieval benchmarks and compare it with state-of-the-art shallow and deep hashing methods. Retrieval quality is measured by mean average precision (mAP) at several code lengths, along with precision-recall curves and precision@top-k curves. Unless stated otherwise, all numbers are averaged over five runs with different random seeds.

**Comparison with state-of-the-art methods.** Table 1 reports mAP for code lengths of 12, 24, 32, and 48 bits. Our method achieves the best mAP in nearly all settings across the four datasets. On CIFAR-10, NMLayer improves over the strongest competing deep hashing baseline by 1.8, 2.1, 2.4, and 2.2 points at 12, 24, 32, and 48 bits respectively. The gains are larger on the more challenging multi-label datasets such as NUS-WIDE and MS-COCO, where average improvements of 2–4 points are observed. Shallow methods with hand-crafted or pretrained features (e.g., ITQ, KSH, SDH) are clearly inferior to deep methods, confirming the benefit of end-to-end representation learning. Pairwise-based deep methods (e.g., DPSH, HashNet) and pointwise or proxy-based methods (e.g., DCH, CSQ) perform competitively at longer codes, but their performance saturates or even declines as the code length grows, which is consistent with increased redundancy among bits. In contrast, our method continues to improve or remains stable with longer codes, because the merging process removes redundant bits rather than keeping them.

The precision-recall and precision@top-k curves lead to the same conclusion. At 32 bits, our method yields higher precision at all recall levels and maintains higher precision as the number of retrieved samples increases, indicating that the learned compact codes preserve semantic neighborhoods better than the baselines' codes.

**Effect of progressive compression.** A central claim is that a compact code learned from a long redundant code is better than a code of the same length trained directly. We therefore compare (i) training a network directly with K bits, (ii) training with a long code (e.g., 96 bits) and truncating or selecting K bits, and (iii) our progressive NMLayer scheme, which starts from the long code and merges down to K bits. Direct training is consistently worse than ours, by about 2 points mAP on CIFAR-10 at 24 bits. Truncation or selection of bits performs worst, as it discards information carried by the removed neurons without compensation. The progressive scheme gives the best results, supporting the idea that a redundant code gives optimization more freedom early on, and merging then consolidates it into a compact code.

**Ablation study.** We examine the main components in Table 2. Removing the NMLayer and using the long code directly leads to lower mAP and higher storage cost. Replacing the learned redundancy graph with a fixed graph built from initial bit correlations reduces mAP by about 1.5 points, and a random merging graph reduces it further, showing that the quality of the learned relationship matters. Disabling the active/frozen phase mechanism, so that the graph is updated continuously, makes the graph unstable and lowers accuracy; the alternation of active phases (where the graph is learned) and frozen phases (where the network is trained under a fixed graph) yields a more reliable redundancy estimate. Using a single NMLayer to go from the long code directly to the target length is also inferior to using multiple NMLayers progressively, with the gap widening for larger compression ratios. Performance generally increases up to two or three stacked layers and then plateaus, so we use this range as a compromise between accuracy and training cost.

**Analysis of redundancy.** To verify that the method reduces redundancy, we measure the average absolute correlation between pairs of hash bits on the test set. Baseline codes show noticeably higher correlation, which grows with code length. After merging, the correlation among bits decreases substantially, and bit balance, measured by the proportion of +1 and −1 values per bit, becomes closer to uniform. We also compute the variance of per-bit contribution to the Hamming distance; merged codes exhibit a more even distribution, matching the stated goal of balancing the importance of output neurons. Visualization of the learned graph shows that strongly connected neurons correspond to bits with highly correlated activations, and that edges become sparser as training proceeds through successive phases.

**Sensitivity and efficiency.** We vary the initial long-code length and the merging ratio. Accuracy improves as the initial length increases from 1× to about 3× the target length and then saturates, while training time increases moderately. The method is not sensitive to the phase lengths within a reasonable range; extreme values (very short active phases) give noisy graphs and slightly lower mAP. At inference, the NMLayer is absorbed into the final layer's weights, so the extra cost is zero, and the final code has exactly the target length, giving the same storage and Hamming-search cost as the baselines. Training overhead is about 20–30% relative to single-stage training.

**Generality.** Plugging the NMLayer into different backbones and loss functions (pairwise and classification-based) consistently increases mAP by 1–3 points, suggesting that it is complementary to existing hashing objectives and not tied to a particular network design.

This paper addressed the redundancy between hashing bits in deep supervised hashing, a problem that becomes prominent when a network's output neurons are discretized into binary codes. We proposed the Neurons Merging Layer (NMLayer), which represents the redundancy relationship between output neurons as a graph and uses that graph to merge redundant neurons. The graph is learned dynamically through an alternation of active and frozen phases. Several NMLayers can be stacked and trained progressively, so that a long, redundant code is gradually condensed into a compact one. Experiments on four datasets showed that the method outperforms the state-of-the-art hashing methods we compared against.

**Discussion**

Several observations follow from our results and design.

First, redundancy among hashing bits is a real and measurable source of inefficiency. Conventional deep hashing treats every output neuron as equally valuable and relies on the loss function to make the bits discriminative and weakly correlated. In practice, such penalties act only indirectly and are further weakened by the quantization step, so some bits end up carrying near-duplicate or weakly informative information. The NMLayer addresses this by acting on the structure of the network rather than only on the loss. Because merging is guided by a learned graph, the model decides which bits are redundant from the training dynamics instead of from a fixed heuristic. This is why we expect the benefit to be most visible at short code lengths, where each bit must carry more information, and when starting from a long code that contains considerable overlap.

Second, the active and frozen phases play complementary roles. In the active phase, the relationship between neurons can adapt as the representation evolves. In the frozen phase, the relationship is held fixed so that the network can adjust to the merged structure and be optimized stably. Without such separation, a graph estimated from rapidly changing features would be noisy, and merging decisions made on it could be unreliable. We view this alternation as a general way to couple structure learning with parameter learning, and it may be useful beyond hashing.

Third, progressive training with multiple NMLayers provides a smoother path to compact codes than training a short code directly. Learning a short code from scratch forces the network to settle quickly on a small set of bits, which may be a poor local solution. Starting with a longer code gives the network more capacity to discover useful distinctions, and successive merges then remove redundancy step by step while retaining the most informative combinations. The cost is additional training stages and a few extra hyperparameters, such as the number of merging layers and the schedule of code lengths.

**Limitations**

Our approach has limitations. The graph is built from pairwise relationships between neurons, so it may not capture higher-order dependencies among groups of bits. The merging operation also assumes that redundant neurons can be combined without losing important information, which may not hold when two bits are correlated on the training set but separate classes in rarer cases. The progressive scheme requires choosing the intermediate code lengths, and we selected these empirically rather than through a principled criterion. The extra training stages increase training time compared with a single-stage network, although the final model has no extra retrieval cost, since the merged code is compact and queries are answered with ordinary Hamming distance computation. Finally, our evaluation focused on four benchmark datasets of moderate scale with label supervision. We have not studied very large-scale collections, weak or noisy labels, or cross-modal retrieval, where the structure of redundancy could differ.

**Future Work**

Several directions follow naturally. The redundancy graph could be extended to model group-level or conditional relationships, for instance with hypergraphs or attention-based affinities. The merging schedule could be learned automatically, so the network determines both how much to compress and where to do it, perhaps guided by a budget on storage or retrieval time. The NMLayer could also be combined with unsupervised or semi-supervised hashing, where the absence of labels makes redundancy even more harmful, and with cross-modal hashing, where bits must remain aligned across modalities. Finally, the idea of merging neurons according to a learned relationship graph may apply to other compact representation problems, such as network pruning, feature selection, and product quantization.

**Conclusion**

We presented the Neurons Merging Layer, a simple and effective module for reducing redundancy in deep supervised hashing. By learning a neuron-relationship graph through active and frozen phases, merging redundant neurons accordingly, and stacking multiple layers in a progressive scheme, the method turns long redundant codes into compact and more discriminative ones. Experiments on four datasets confirm consistent gains over state-of-the-art methods. We hope this work encourages further study of structural, rather than purely loss-based, approaches to producing efficient binary codes for large-scale retrieval.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, heterogeneous autoimmune disease characterized by the production of autoantibodies and immune-complex deposition, which can involve virtually any organ system. It predominantly affects women of childbearing age, and its incidence and prevalence vary substantially across ethnic groups and geographic regions [1,2]. Reported prevalence is higher in people of Asian, African, and Hispanic ancestry than in those of European ancestry, and disease in these populations is often more severe, with more frequent renal involvement and greater damage accrual [3,4]. In China, the estimated prevalence of SLE is among the highest in the world, at approximately 30 to 70 per 100,000 people, implying that more than one million Chinese people may be living with the disease [5,6].

SLE is associated with an increased risk of death compared with the general population. Standardized mortality ratios reported in cohorts from Europe, North America, and Asia typically range from 2 to 5, with the greatest excess observed in young patients and in those with renal disease [7,8]. Survival has improved markedly over the past six decades. Five-year survival was below 50% in the 1950s, rose to approximately 80–90% in the 1970s and 1980s, and exceeds 90% in many contemporary series [9,10]. This improvement is generally attributed to earlier diagnosis, including recognition of milder disease, more effective use of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents, better management of lupus nephritis, improved dialysis and transplantation services, and advances in the prevention and treatment of infection and of comorbid conditions [10,11]. Nonetheless, several reports suggest that the gains in survival have plateaued since the 1990s, and that mortality in SLE remains clearly higher than expected [12,13].

The causes of death in SLE have also changed over time. A bimodal pattern of mortality was described in early studies, in which early deaths were attributed to active lupus and infection, and late deaths to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [14]. In Western cohorts, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, and infection now account for a large proportion of deaths, whereas death from active disease, particularly renal failure, has declined [8,15]. Comparatively little is known about whether this pattern applies in Asian populations. Studies from Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand suggest that infection and active lupus remain leading causes of death, whereas cardiovascular death appears less common [16–18]. Differences in genetic background, disease phenotype, treatment practices, health care access, and the prevalence of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis may all contribute to such variation [4,19].

Despite the very large population of patients, long-term prognosis of SLE in China has not been well summarized. Systematic registries and national surveillance of SLE only began to develop in recent years, and most available information comes from single-center hospital cohorts of varying size, design, and period. Many of these reports were published in Chinese-language journals and are not easily accessible to international readers, and they are rarely captured by the search strategies of previous meta-analyses, which have focused on English-language literature [9,20]. Consequently, existing global estimates of SLE survival and mortality draw on limited data from mainland China, even though the Chinese population accounts for a substantial fraction of all patients with SLE worldwide. Individual Chinese studies report heterogeneous survival rates, in part because of differences in referral patterns, severity of disease at enrollment, calendar period, and duration of follow-up. Pooling these data can offer more precise and generalizable estimates.

Likewise, data on the causes of death in Chinese patients with SLE are scattered across case series and cohort studies, many of which are small and use different classification schemes. Understanding the distribution of causes of death is of practical importance, because it can identify targets for intervention and guide the allocation of clinical resources. For example, if infection is the dominant cause of death, strategies such as vaccination, prophylaxis, judicious use of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, and early detection of opportunistic infection may be prioritized. If cardiovascular disease is relatively uncommon in this population, or is likely to become more important as survival lengthens, preventive strategies would need to be adapted accordingly [21]. Comparing the causes of death in China with those reported elsewhere may also shed light on the influence of ethnicity, environment, and treatment approach on lupus outcomes.

Given these gaps, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies published in English and Chinese. Our first objective was to estimate the pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates of Chinese patients with SLE from cohort studies, and to compare them with estimates from other Asia-Pacific and Western populations. Our second objective was to describe the distribution of causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE by synthesizing cohort studies and case series, and to explore how this distribution differs from that reported in other regions. We hope that these findings will provide a more complete picture of the contemporary prognosis of SLE in China and will inform clinical practice and future research.

This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines [2]. Because the analysis used only published data, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.

**Search strategy**

We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WANFANG, and SINOMED from database inception to December 2013. English and non-English (Chinese) articles were eligible. The principal search terms were "systemic lupus erythematosus" or "SLE", combined with "follow-up", "prognosis", "survival", "mortality", "death", and "China" or "Chinese". Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms were combined with Boolean operators, and the strategy was adapted to the indexing system of each database. Additional studies were identified by consulting clinical experts, screening the reference lists of selected papers and relevant reviews, and searching related Chinese textbooks of rheumatology and internal medicine.

**Eligibility criteria**

For the survival analysis, we included cohort studies that enrolled Chinese patients with SLE diagnosed according to the American College of Rheumatology classification criteria [3,4] or the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria [5], and that reported survival rates at 5 and/or 10 years, or provided data allowing their calculation (number of patients, number of deaths, and follow-up duration). Studies from mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan were considered. For the death-cause analysis, both cohort studies and case series were eligible if they reported the number of deaths and the distribution of causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE. We excluded studies restricted to special subpopulations (e.g., pediatric-onset only, pregnancy-only, or single-organ involvement such as lupus nephritis alone) when these would bias survival estimates, case reports, reviews, conference abstracts without sufficient data, and studies with fewer than 10 deaths for cause analysis. When several publications reported on overlapping populations from the same center, the report with the largest sample or longest follow-up was retained.

**Study selection and data extraction**

Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed full texts of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. Two authors independently extracted data using a predesigned chart covering: (1) study characteristics (first author, publication year, region, setting, design, recruitment period, and follow-up duration); (2) clinical data (sample size, sex ratio, age at onset, disease duration, diagnostic criteria, and treatment); (3) analytic data (number of deaths, 5- and 10-year survival rates and confidence intervals, standardized mortality ratios where available, and the numbers of deaths attributed to each cause); and (4) study quality indicators. Causes of death were harmonized into categories: infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy (neuropsychiatric lupus), cardiovascular disease, pulmonary involvement (including pulmonary hemorrhage and pulmonary hypertension), hematologic involvement, gastrointestinal involvement, malignancy, and others. Where original authors used different labels, categories were assigned by consensus based on the descriptions provided.

**Quality assessment**

Methodological quality of cohort studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale [6], evaluating representativeness of the cohort, ascertainment of outcome, adequacy and completeness of follow-up, and comparability. For case series, we used items adapted from quality criteria for case series [7], including clear definition of the population, consecutive enrollment, explicit criteria for attributing cause of death, and the source of death information (medical records, death certificates, or autopsy). Quality scores were used descriptively and in sensitivity analyses rather than as exclusion criteria.

**Statistical analysis**

Survival rates at 5 and 10 years were pooled as proportions. Because proportions near 1 produce skewed distributions and unstable variance, rates were transformed using the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation before pooling and back-transformed for presentation [8]. When studies reported survival only as a Kaplan–Meier curve, rates were read from the curve at the specified time points. Likewise, the proportion of deaths attributable to each cause was pooled from the number of deaths with that cause divided by the total number of observed deaths in each study.

All pooled analyses were performed using both random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) [9] and fixed-effects (inverse variance) models, and results from both are reported to allow assessment of robustness. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values above 50% considered substantial [10]. Sources of heterogeneity were explored by sensitivity analysis, in which each study was omitted in turn to evaluate its influence on the pooled estimates, and by restricting analyses to higher-quality studies. For the death-cause analysis, we additionally performed prespecified subgroup comparisons by region (mainland China versus Hong Kong/Taiwan) and by period of observation (before versus after 2000), where data permitted.

Potential publication bias was examined by visual inspection of funnel plots and by Egger's regression test [11], with P < 0.10 indicating possible asymmetry. Given the small number of survival studies, these tests were interpreted cautiously. The pooled survival rates were qualitatively compared with those reported from other Asia-Pacific countries and from Western cohorts identified in prior publications. All tests were two-sided, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant unless otherwise stated. Analyses were conducted using Stata (version 12.0; StataCorp, College Station, TX) and Review Manager (version 5.2; The Cochrane Collaboration).

A total of 2,846 records were initially identified through database searching (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, WANFANG, and SINOMED), and an additional 37 records were obtained through expert consultation, reference lists, and textbooks. After removal of duplicates and screening of titles and abstracts, 214 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Five cohort studies met the criteria for survival analysis [1–5], and 36 studies (cohort studies and case series) were suitable for death-cause analysis [6–41]. The main reasons for exclusion were lack of survival data, insufficient follow-up information, overlapping patient populations, and absence of specified causes of death.

**Characteristics of included studies**

The five survival studies comprised 4,469 Chinese patients with SLE and 380 observed deaths. They were conducted in mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan, and patient disease onset ranged from 1995 to 2013. Sample sizes ranged from several hundred to more than 1,500 patients. All studies were hospital-based or registry-based cohorts, and the majority of patients were women. Study quality assessment indicated generally adequate representativeness and outcome ascertainment, although loss to follow-up was incompletely reported in two cohorts. The 36 death-cause studies included 2,179 observed deaths derived from more than 20,000 patients with SLE. These were mostly single-center series published in Chinese-language journals, covering periods from the 1980s to the 2010s.

**Pooled survival rates**

The overall pooled 5-year survival rate after disease onset was 94% (95% CI, 92%–96%) under the random-effects model, and the fixed-effects estimate was similar. The pooled 10-year survival rate was 89% (95% CI, 85%–92%) under the random-effects model, with a comparable fixed-effects result. Heterogeneity was moderate for the 5-year estimate and more pronounced for the 10-year estimate, probably reflecting differences in region, period of recruitment, and care setting. Survival in the cohorts from more recent decades tended to be higher than in earlier cohorts, although the small number of studies precluded formal meta-regression.

**Publication bias and sensitivity analysis**

Funnel plots for the survival analyses were approximately symmetrical, and Egger regression tests did not suggest significant publication bias (P > 0.05 for both 5- and 10-year survival), although the small number of studies limited the power of these tests. In sensitivity analyses, sequential omission of each study did not materially change the pooled estimates; the 5-year survival rate remained between 93% and 95%, and the 10-year rate between 87% and 91%. Exclusion of the study contributing the greatest heterogeneity reduced the I² value but did not alter the overall conclusions. Results were consistent between the random-effects and fixed-effects models.

**Causes of death**

Among the 2,179 deaths, infection was the leading cause, accounting for 33.2% (95% CI, 29.6%–36.9%) of deaths. Renal involvement, mainly end-stage renal disease or renal failure due to lupus nephritis, was the second most common cause (18.7%; 95% CI, 15.8%–21.8%). Lupus encephalopathy, including neuropsychiatric lupus and related central nervous system complications, accounted for 13.8% (95% CI, 11.0%–16.9%), and cardiovascular disease for 11.5% (95% CI, 8.9%–14.4%). Together these four categories represented approximately 77% of all deaths. Other causes, including pulmonary involvement (such as pulmonary hemorrhage, interstitial lung disease, and pulmonary hypertension), gastrointestinal complications, hematologic involvement, malignancy, and unspecified causes, each accounted for a smaller proportion, generally less than 6%.

Within the infection category, pulmonary infection was the most frequently reported site, followed by septicemia and central nervous system infection. Bacterial pathogens predominated, but fungal, tuberculous, and opportunistic infections such as those caused by Pneumocystis and cytomegalovirus were also reported in a considerable minority of cases. Heterogeneity in the proportions of death causes was substantial across the case series, particularly for infection and renal involvement, and the fixed-effects and random-effects estimates differed modestly for these categories.

**Subgroup and temporal observations**

When studies were grouped by period of death, the proportion of deaths due to infection remained high across decades, whereas the proportion attributed to renal failure appeared lower in more recent series. The proportion of cardiovascular deaths was somewhat higher in studies with longer follow-up, but remained lower than that typically reported in Western cohorts. Studies reporting deaths within the first 5 years of disease more often cited infection, lupus encephalopathy, and active lupus nephritis, whereas later deaths included relatively more cardiovascular and malignancy-related causes, though data for stratified analysis were limited. Funnel plots and Egger tests for the main death-cause proportions did not show significant asymmetry, and sensitivity analyses excluding small series (fewer than 30 deaths) yielded estimates within 2 percentage points of the primary results.

**Comparison with Asia-Pacific data**

The pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates were similar to those reported in other Asia-Pacific cohorts [42–44]. Compared with these and with Western populations, the Chinese series showed a relatively higher proportion of deaths from infection and lupus encephalopathy and a lower proportion from cardiovascular disease [45,46].

This systematic review integrates the available cohort evidence on long-term survival of Chinese patients with SLE and summarizes the causes of death reported across 36 studies. The pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates after disease onset were 94% and 89%, respectively, for patients diagnosed between 1995 and 2013. These figures are comparable with those from other Asia-Pacific countries and approach those reported in North American and European cohorts in recent decades [1–3]. The leading causes of death were infection (33.2%), renal involvement (18.7%), lupus encephalopathy (13.8%), and cardiovascular disease (11.5%). Compared with Western series, this distribution shows a higher proportion of deaths from infection and neuropsychiatric lupus and a lower proportion from cardiovascular disease.

The survival of SLE has improved markedly since the 1950s, when 5-year survival was below 50% [4]. This improvement is attributed to earlier diagnosis, detection of milder disease, wider use of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, better dialysis and transplantation, and improved management of infection and hypertension [2,5]. Our pooled estimates suggest that Chinese patients have shared in these gains. The 10-year survival of 89% is similar to that reported in Korea, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore, although some of these cohorts reported modestly lower or higher values depending on era, referral pattern, and disease severity [6–8]. Because most of our included cohorts were drawn from tertiary centers, there may be some selection toward more severe disease, which could underestimate survival in the broader community. Conversely, patients followed in large academic centers may receive better care than those in smaller hospitals, and losses to follow-up could bias survival upward. The true population-level survival is therefore uncertain, and the direction of net bias cannot be determined from the available data.

The predominance of infection as a cause of death is consistent with findings from Asian and Latin American cohorts, in which infection accounts for a large share of early mortality [6,9]. Several factors may explain the higher proportion in China. Active lupus, particularly lupus nephritis, is commonly treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and cytotoxic agents such as cyclophosphamide, which predispose patients to bacterial, fungal, and opportunistic infections, including tuberculosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia [10]. Tuberculosis remains endemic in China, and delayed recognition of infection in immunosuppressed patients may worsen outcomes. Moreover, infection may be difficult to distinguish from disease flare, leading to delayed or inappropriate therapy. These observations support rigorous infection screening, vaccination, prophylaxis where indicated, and minimization of glucocorticoid exposure.

Lupus encephalopathy accounted for nearly 14% of deaths, a proportion higher than generally reported in Western cohorts. This may reflect ethnic differences in disease expression, since Asian patients are reported to have more severe renal and neuropsychiatric manifestations [11], as well as differences in terminology, because "lupus encephalopathy" in Chinese literature may include a wide spectrum of central nervous system events, some of which may be infectious or related to treatment. Variation in diagnostic criteria and limited autopsy confirmation make attribution of death uncertain.

Cardiovascular disease was a less frequent cause of death (11.5%) than in Western cohorts, where it dominates late mortality [3,12]. Several explanations are plausible. Chinese patients with SLE may have a lower background burden of atherosclerotic disease, and ethnicity-related differences in lipid profile and obesity may contribute. In addition, the cohorts studied had relatively short follow-up, so patients may not have survived long enough to develop accelerated atherosclerosis, which typically emerges after many years of disease. Early deaths from infection and active disease may act as competing risks, reducing the observed cardiovascular share. As survival improves, cardiovascular mortality may rise in China, and attention to traditional risk factors will become increasingly important [12].

Renal involvement remained a major cause of death, in line with global data. Although renal survival has improved with induction therapy using cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate, delayed biopsy, limited access to care, and treatment-related complications may still contribute to mortality in some regions [13].

This study has several limitations. Only five studies met criteria for survival analysis, and the number of patients and deaths was modest relative to the large Chinese SLE population. Heterogeneity existed in calendar periods, centers, inclusion criteria, and follow-up duration, and we could not stratify by sex, age at onset, nephritis, or treatment. Death-cause analysis relied on case series and cohorts of varying quality, often without standardized definitions or autopsy data, and proportions of causes are not mortality rates; they cannot be used to compare absolute risk with other populations. Hospital-based reports may overrepresent patients dying in hospital from acute complications. Publication bias is possible despite funnel plot and Egger testing, which have limited power with few studies. Finally, we could not calculate standardized mortality ratios because comparable general-population data were generally unavailable.

In conclusion, long-term survival of Chinese patients with SLE is similar to that in other Asia-Pacific regions, with pooled 5- and 10-year survival of 94% and 89%. Infection, renal disease, lupus encephalopathy, and cardiovascular disease are the main causes of death, with relatively more infection and neuropsychiatric deaths and fewer cardiovascular deaths than in Western populations. These differences may reflect ethnicity, more aggressive immunosuppression, and limited follow-up duration. Priorities for improving outcomes include prevention and early treatment of infection, careful use of immunosuppressants, timely management of nephritis and neuropsychiatric disease, and long-term cardiovascular risk monitoring. Large, prospective, nationally representative cohorts with standardized cause-of-death ascertainment are needed to refine these estimates and guide care.

Composite resins have become the material of choice for direct restorations in anterior and posterior teeth, owing to their esthetic properties, adhesive capability, and conservative cavity preparation requirements [1,2]. Despite continuous improvements in filler technology and monomer chemistry, the clinical longevity of resin-based restorations remains limited, with fracture, marginal degradation, and secondary caries identified as the principal causes of failure [3,4]. These failures are closely linked to the extent of polymerization achieved at placement and to the ability of the material to resist degradation in the oral environment over time.

**Polymerization, radiant exposure, and material properties**

Light-activated composite resins undergo free-radical polymerization initiated by photosensitizers, most commonly camphorquinone, in the presence of an amine co-initiator [5]. The degree of conversion (DC), defined as the percentage of aliphatic carbon–carbon double bonds converted into single bonds, is a key determinant of the physical, mechanical, and biological behavior of the polymer network. Incomplete conversion is associated with reduced stiffness and strength, greater water uptake, and increased elution of unreacted monomers, with potential consequences for biocompatibility and durability [6,7].

The energy delivered to the material, expressed as radiant exposure (J/cm²) and calculated as the product of irradiance and exposure time, is the principal clinical variable controlling the amount of photons available to activate the initiator system [8]. Although manufacturers typically recommend 20–40 s exposure at approximately 400–1000 mW/cm², the literature offers no consensus regarding the minimum radiant exposure required for adequate properties. Values ranging from approximately 6 to 24 J/cm² have been proposed, depending on the composite shade, translucency, filler content, increment thickness, and the property being evaluated [9–11]. Furthermore, the reciprocity between irradiance and exposure time is not absolute, since high irradiance with short exposure can alter network formation, increase polymerization stress, and yield a less homogeneous polymer [12]. The development of high-output light-curing units and of reduced-time protocols has made the question of minimum radiant exposure increasingly relevant to clinical practice.

**Filler technology**

Composite resins are commonly classified according to filler particle size and distribution. Micro-hybrid composites contain a blend of particles of different dimensions, generally in the range of 0.4–1 µm, providing high filler loading and good mechanical properties [13]. Nanofilled composites incorporate discrete nanometric particles and nanoclusters, improving polish retention and esthetics while maintaining acceptable strength [14]. These differences in filler size, load, and silane coupling influence light scattering and penetration, the mobility of the monomer, and the filler–matrix interface, and consequently may alter both the response to radiant exposure and the susceptibility to degradation [15]. Comparative information on how these two classes respond to different energy levels, particularly in the long term, remains scarce.

**Aging and hydrolytic degradation**

In the oral cavity, restorations are subjected to water, enzymes, temperature fluctuations, masticatory loading, and exposure to radiation from ambient and therapeutic sources. Water diffuses into the polymer network, causing plasticization, swelling, hydrolysis of ester bonds in the matrix, and degradation of the filler–matrix interface, along with leaching of unreacted components [16,17]. Water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) are therefore widely used as indicators of network integrity and of the hydrolytic stability of composites [18]. Because these processes occur over years, laboratory studies rely on accelerated aging protocols such as thermocycling, prolonged water storage, and artificial weathering with ultraviolet (UV) light and condensation [19]. UV-accelerated aging combines photo-oxidative and hydrothermal stresses that may promote chain scission, additional crosslinking, surface cracking, and filler debonding, and it has been used to simulate long-term changes in color and mechanical behavior [20,21]. However, the effects of such aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of composites cured with different radiant exposures have not been thoroughly investigated.

**Rationale and objective**

Most studies on radiant exposure examine properties immediately or shortly after polymerization, while aging studies usually employ a single curing protocol. As a consequence, it remains unclear whether a deficiency in initial energy delivery persists, is attenuated, or is exacerbated after prolonged aging, and whether initially superior properties obtained with higher radiant exposure are maintained over time. Additionally, it is uncertain whether the relation between radiant exposure and hydrolytic degradation differs between micro-hybrid and nanofilled materials. Clarifying these questions may help establish evidence-based curing recommendations that favor long-term clinical performance.

Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of radiant exposure (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and UV-accelerated aging (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 h) on the degree of conversion, flexural strength, modulus, water sorption, and solubility of a micro-hybrid and a nanofilled composite resin. The null hypotheses tested were that neither radiant exposure nor accelerated aging time would significantly affect these properties, and that the response would not differ between the two composite resins.

**Experimental design**

Two commercial light-cured resin composites were investigated: a nanofilled composite (Filtek Supreme, shade A2B, 3M ESPE, St. Paul, MN, USA) and a micro-hybrid composite (Filtek Z250, shade A2, 3M ESPE). The study followed a 3 × 4 factorial design for each material, with radiant exposure (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and UV accelerated aging time (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 h) as the independent variables. The response variables were degree of conversion (DC), flexural strength (FS), flexural modulus (M), water sorption (WS), and solubility (WL). Specimens were randomly allocated to the experimental groups (n = 10 per group for FS and M, n = 5 for DC, and n = 10 for WS and WL). Sample size was based on previous studies using similar protocols [1,2].

**Light-curing and radiant exposure**

A quartz-tungsten-halogen/LED unit (specify model) was used for photoactivation. Irradiance was measured before each specimen-preparation session using a calibrated radiometer and verified with a spectrometer-based power meter placed at the specimen surface distance. The irradiance was approximately 600 mW/cm². Radiant exposure (J/cm²) was calculated as the product of irradiance (W/cm²) and exposure time (s). The three radiant exposures were obtained by varying the exposure time: 6 s (3.75 J/cm²), 15 s (9 J/cm²), and 40 s (24 J/cm²). The tip of the light guide was positioned in contact with the Mylar strip covering the specimen. For bar-shaped specimens, the tip was applied in overlapping sections to cover the entire length, and each section received the nominal exposure [3].

**Specimen preparation**

Bar-shaped specimens (25 × 2 × 2 mm) for FS and M were fabricated in a stainless-steel split mold in accordance with ISO 4049 [4]. The composite was inserted in a single increment, covered with a polyester strip and a glass slide to extrude excess material, and light-cured as described above. Disc-shaped specimens (6 mm diameter × 1 mm thickness) for WS, WL, and DC were prepared in a similar manner. After removal from the molds, specimens were examined and any with visible voids or flaws were discarded. All specimens were stored dry in light-proof containers at 37 °C for 24 h before aging or testing.

**UV accelerated aging**

Specimens were subjected to accelerated aging in a UV weathering chamber (e.g., QUV, Q-Lab) in accordance with ASTM G154 [5]. Cycles consisted of 8 h of UV exposure at 60 °C using UVB-313 lamps, followed by 4 h of condensation at 50 °C. Specimens were placed with the irradiated surface facing the lamps, and their positions were rotated periodically to ensure uniform exposure. Aging durations were 500, 1000, and 1500 h. Control specimens (0 h) were not exposed to the chamber and were stored dry at 37 °C. After aging, specimens were kept in dry conditions until testing, except for WS and WL analyses.

**Degree of conversion**

DC was determined by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with attenuated total reflectance (FTIR-ATR). Spectra of uncured material were obtained by placing a small amount of composite on the diamond crystal. Spectra of cured specimens were collected from the top surface of the discs at 32 scans and 4 cm⁻¹ resolution over 400–4000 cm⁻¹. DC was calculated from the ratio of the aliphatic C=C absorbance peak (1638 cm⁻¹) to the internal reference aromatic C=C peak (1608 cm⁻¹) in cured and uncured states [6]:

DC (%) = [1 − (R_cured / R_uncured)] × 100,

where R is the ratio of the aliphatic to aromatic peak intensities. For aged groups, DC was measured after the corresponding aging period, as an index of the residual unsaturation and structural change of the aged network.

**Flexural strength and modulus**

Flexural strength and flexural modulus were assessed by a three-point bending test in a universal testing machine (e.g., EMIC DL 2000) with a 20 mm span and a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min until fracture. Specimen dimensions were measured with a digital caliper (0.01 mm accuracy). FS (MPa) was calculated as

FS = 3Fl / 2bh²,

where F is the maximum load (N), l the span (mm), b the specimen width (mm), and h its height (mm). Flexural modulus (GPa) was calculated from the slope of the linear elastic portion of the load–displacement curve:

M = F₁l³ / 4bh³d,

where F₁ is the load at a point in the linear region and d the corresponding deflection [4]. Tests were performed at room temperature.

**Water sorption and solubility**

WS and WL were evaluated according to ISO 4049 [4]. Discs were placed in a desiccator containing silica gel at 37 °C and weighed daily on an analytical balance (0.0001 g precision) until a constant mass (m₁) was achieved. Diameter and thickness were measured to calculate volume (V). Specimens were then immersed in distilled water at 37 °C for 7 days, blotted dry, and weighed (m₂). They were then reconditioned in the desiccator until constant mass (m₃). WS and WL (µg/mm³) were calculated as:

WS = (m₂ − m₃)/V;  WL = (m₁ − m₃)/V.

The test was conducted on specimens of each aging time and radiant exposure.

**Statistical analysis**

Data were checked for normality (Shapiro–Wilk) and homogeneity of variances (Levene). For each composite and each response variable, two-way ANOVA was used with radiant exposure and aging time as factors, including their interaction. Pairwise comparisons were conducted with Tukey's post hoc test. All analyses were performed at a significance level of α = 0.05 using standard statistical software.

**Degree of conversion**

Two-way ANOVA showed that radiant exposure, accelerated aging time, and their interaction significantly affected DC for both the micro-hybrid (Filtek Z250) and the nanofilled (Filtek Supreme) composite (p<0.05). In the non-aged groups (0 h), DC increased progressively with radiant exposure. Specimens cured at 3.75 J/cm² had significantly lower DC than those cured at 9 and 24 J/cm² (p<0.05) for both materials. For Z250, DC rose from approximately 52% at 3.75 J/cm² to approximately 60% at 24 J/cm². For Filtek Supreme, DC rose from approximately 48% to approximately 57% over the same range. The difference between 9 and 24 J/cm² was smaller and reached significance only for the nanofilled material.

After UV aging (500, 1000, and 1500 h), the relationship between DC and radiant exposure was lost. Within each aging period, DC values did not differ consistently among radiant exposures (p>0.05). Aging produced a general increase in DC relative to the 0 h condition, which was most evident in specimens cured at the lowest radiant exposure. As a result, the initial differences among radiant exposure groups were reduced or eliminated. DC then remained stable or changed only slightly between 500 and 1500 h. Across aging periods, Filtek Supreme tended to show lower DC than Z250, although this difference was not significant in all conditions.

**Flexural strength**

FS was significantly influenced by radiant exposure, aging time, and their interaction for both composites (p<0.05). In the non-aged condition, FS was lowest at 3.75 J/cm² and increased at higher radiant exposures. Z250 showed values of roughly 110–140 MPa, and Filtek Supreme showed slightly lower values. Increases from 3.75 to 9 J/cm² were significant for both materials, whereas the further increase to 24 J/cm² was significant only for Z250.

Aging had a marked effect on FS. After 500 h of UV aging, FS decreased significantly relative to baseline in most groups (p<0.05). Further aging to 1000 and 1500 h produced additional reductions, and the lowest values were generally observed at 1500 h. The effect of radiant exposure on FS became inconsistent after aging. In several aged groups, specimens cured at 3.75 J/cm² performed similarly to those cured at 24 J/cm² (p>0.05). The reduction in FS caused by aging was more pronounced for Filtek Supreme in the high-exposure groups. At 1500 h, the two materials showed similar FS values in most radiant exposure conditions.

**Flexural modulus**

The modulus (M) followed a trend similar to that of DC. In the non-aged groups, M increased significantly with radiant exposure for both composites (p<0.05). Z250 exhibited higher modulus values than Filtek Supreme at all radiant exposures, with values of approximately 8–11 GPa and 6–9 GPa, respectively. Increasing radiant exposure from 3.75 to 24 J/cm² raised the modulus by roughly 20–30% in both materials.

Accelerated aging significantly altered the modulus (p<0.05), and the correlation between radiant exposure and modulus was no longer observed in aged specimens. After 500 h, modulus values in the low-exposure groups were similar to, or slightly higher than, those of the high-exposure groups. For longer aging times (1000 and 1500 h), values decreased moderately and were statistically similar across radiant exposures. The interaction between radiant exposure and aging time was significant, indicating that the influence of radiant exposure depended on aging duration.

**Water sorption**

WS was not significantly affected by radiant exposure for either composite (p>0.05). Mean values at 3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm² were statistically similar within each aging condition. Aging time, however, had a significant effect (p<0.001). WS was highest in non-aged specimens, approximately 25–35 µg/mm³, and decreased progressively with aging. The lowest values occurred after 1000 and 1500 h, with no significant difference between these two periods. Filtek Supreme exhibited slightly higher WS than Z250 in the non-aged condition, but this difference became less apparent after aging. The interaction between radiant exposure and aging was not significant (p>0.05).

**Solubility**

WL values were low for both composites and were similarly unaffected by radiant exposure (p>0.05). Aging time significantly reduced WL (p<0.001). Non-aged specimens showed the highest solubility, and aged groups showed significantly lower values, in some cases approaching zero or slightly negative values. Negative values reflect a mass after the desorption cycle that was higher than the initial conditioned mass. The reduction was observed after 500 h and was only slightly greater at later time points. No significant differences were found between materials in most aged conditions.

**Summary of main effects**

The ANOVA results are summarized as follows. For DC, FS, and M, radiant exposure, aging time, and their interaction were significant. For WS and WL, only aging time had a significant effect. Radiant exposure was therefore a determinant of initial polymerization outcomes and mechanical behavior in non-aged specimens. Its effect was attenuated or eliminated after UV aging, and it had no detectable influence on water-related properties under any condition. In contrast, aging time was a significant factor for every property evaluated, with an increase in DC and decreases in FS, M, WS, and WL.

**Influence of radiant exposure on polymerization and mechanical behavior**

The present study shows that radiant exposure governs the initial polymerization state of both composites, but that this influence is largely overridden once the materials undergo prolonged UV aging. In the non-aged groups, the degree of conversion (DC) and modulus increased with radiant exposure, consistent with the dose-dependent nature of photopolymerization, in which the number of photons absorbed by camphorquinone determines the radical concentration and, ultimately, the extent of monomer conversion [1,2]. At low radiant exposure (3.75 J/cm²), restricted radical generation and early vitrification likely limited mobility of the pendant methacrylate groups and residual monomers, producing a looser network with lower stiffness [3]. Higher exposures delay vitrification and allow additional conversion, which accounts for the improved modulus. The magnitude of the effect differed between materials, which is plausibly related to differences in filler load, filler morphology, and resin composition. The nanofilled composite (Filtek Supreme) contains nanoclusters and discrete nanoparticles that increase the filler surface area and may scatter light differently from the micro-hybrid composite (Filtek Z250), affecting light penetration and the efficiency of energy absorption [4,5]. The monomer systems also differ: Z250 relies on Bis-GMA, UDMA, and Bis-EMA, whereas Supreme includes TEGDMA and Bis-GMA with a different balance of flexibility and viscosity, so that the radiant exposure required to approach a conversion plateau is not identical [6].

Flexural strength was less consistently related to radiant exposure than DC or modulus. This is not unexpected, since strength depends not only on crosslink density but also on filler–matrix interfacial quality, the flaw population, and the stress distribution within the specimen [7]. A modest increase in conversion may therefore raise stiffness without producing a proportional rise in strength, particularly if polymerization stress and microdefects increase concurrently at high exposures. These findings suggest that the relationship between radiant exposure and mechanical properties is nonlinear, with diminishing returns beyond a material-specific threshold. Clinically, this supports the view that no single universal minimum radiant exposure can be defined; rather, the requirement depends on composite formulation, shade, and thickness [2,8].

**Effect of UV accelerated aging**

Accelerated aging significantly changed all measured properties, and the absence of a correlation between radiant exposure and DC or modulus after aging indicates that aging-related processes dominated over initial curing differences. Several mechanisms may explain this. First, UV radiation and the associated humidity and temperature cycling can cause continued post-cure in poorly converted specimens, thereby equalizing differences among groups, while simultaneously inducing chain scission and oxidation in the polymer network [9]. Second, water uptake plasticizes the matrix, leaches unreacted monomers and oligomers, and may hydrolyze the silane coupling agent at the filler–matrix interface, reducing load transfer [10,11]. The net outcome is the convergence of properties irrespective of the initial radiant exposure, which suggests that early differences in network structure are partly transient under aggressive environmental conditions. A limitation of interpreting DC after aging is that spectroscopic changes may reflect both residual double-bond consumption and oxidative modification of the matrix, so the measure is not purely a conversion index in aged specimens.

The reductions in water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) after aging were unexpected at first glance, as degradation is generally expected to increase both. Possible explanations include additional crosslinking from UV-induced post-polymerization, which reduces free volume and hydrophilic sites, and prior leaching of soluble components during the aging protocol so that less soluble material remained available for extraction in the subsequent test [12]. Surface densification or the loss of hydrophilic species during aging may also have contributed. Nevertheless, a lower WS and WL does not necessarily indicate improved long-term stability, because the mechanical properties simultaneously declined, indicating that the network was altered in ways not captured by gravimetric tests alone. The lack of an effect of radiant exposure on WS and WL implies that these properties are controlled mainly by resin composition and filler content, in agreement with earlier reports that hydrophilicity of monomers such as TEGDMA and UDMA is the primary determinant of water uptake [13,14].

**Clinical implications and limitations**

From a clinical perspective, the results suggest that increasing radiant exposure can improve initial stiffness and conversion, but that this benefit may not be preserved in the long term if the restoration is subjected to degrading conditions. Therefore, adequate curing should be regarded as necessary but not sufficient for durable restorations; resistance to hydrolytic and photo-oxidative degradation depends on formulation and on the stability of the filler–matrix interface. Both composites tested here showed sensitivity to aging, indicating that the nanofilled and micro-hybrid architectures offer no clear protection against it.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The study was performed in vitro using only two composites from one manufacturer and a single shade, which restricts generalization. UV accelerated aging does not fully reproduce the oral environment, where masticatory loading, enzymatic activity, pH variation, and thermal cycling act together, and UV exposure is minimal. Radiant exposure was varied under controlled laboratory conditions, whereas clinical delivery is affected by distance, angulation, and increment thickness. Finally, DC was measured under defined conditions, and depth-dependent gradients were not evaluated. Future work should include different compositions, depth-resolved conversion, and combined chemical and mechanical aging methods.

**Conclusions**

Increasing radiant exposure improved the degree of conversion and modulus of both composites in the absence of aging, but did not influence water sorption or solubility. UV accelerated aging significantly altered physico-chemical and mechanical properties and eliminated the correlation between radiant exposure and DC or modulus.
