Hence, while sufficient radiant exposure is important for initial polymerization, the long-term performance of composite resins is mainly determined by their resistance to aging.

Plants adjust their development to seasonal change, and the timing of flowering is among the most consequential of these adjustments. Flowering at an appropriate time maximizes reproductive success and, in crops, determines yield and geographic range. Day length (photoperiod) and temperature are the two principal seasonal cues, and their integration allows plants to distinguish, for example, a warm autumn from a spring of similar day length [1,2]. In the facultative long-day plant Arabidopsis thaliana, long photoperiods accelerate flowering through the transcriptional induction of FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT), which encodes the florigen produced in leaf vascular tissue and transported to the shoot apical meristem [3,4]. There, FT interacts with the bZIP transcription factor FD to activate floral identity genes such as SOC1 and APETALA1 [5,6].

The photoperiodic regulation of FT is mediated largely by CONSTANS (CO), a B-box zinc finger transcriptional activator [7,8]. CO transcription is controlled by the circadian clock through GIGANTEA (GI) and the FLAVIN-BINDING, KELCH REPEAT, F-BOX 1 (FKF1) protein, which together degrade CYCLING DOF FACTOR repressors in the afternoon [9,10]. Equally important is post-translational regulation. CO protein is destabilized in darkness by the E3 ubiquitin ligase CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1 (COP1) in complex with SUPPRESSOR OF PHYA-105 (SPA) proteins, and is stabilized in light by photoreceptors, with blue light-sensing cryptochromes and FKF1 and far-red light-sensing phytochrome A (phyA) counteracting COP1 activity, while phytochrome B (phyB) promotes CO degradation in the morning [11–14]. This "external coincidence" mechanism restricts CO accumulation to the end of long days, when FT is induced at dusk [7,15].

Light quality also modulates flowering. Reduced red/far-red (R/FR) ratios, as occur in canopy shade, inactivate phyB and accelerate flowering, whereas phyA mediates FR-dependent promotion of flowering [16,17]. The evening component of the circadian clock, including EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), a component of the Evening Complex, represses FT directly and indirectly by controlling GI and PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) [18–20]. Temperature adds a further layer: warm ambient temperatures promote flowering through PIF4 and the florigen FT, and the Evening Complex acts as a temperature-responsive regulator of gene expression [21–23]. Prolonged cold, meanwhile, silences the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) through vernalization, which ensures flowering after winter [24].

Much of this knowledge derives from laboratory experiments performed under highly simplified conditions: constant temperature, abrupt light-dark transitions, light provided by fluorescent or white LED sources with a high R/FR ratio, and photoperiods that are fixed rather than changing. Under such conditions, FT expression in long days typically shows a prominent peak at dusk, about 12–16 h after dawn, consistent with the external coincidence model [7,25]. Yet natural environments differ substantially. Light intensity and spectrum change gradually at dawn and dusk, with lowered R/FR ratios during twilight; temperatures fluctuate daily and seasonally; and plants experience combinations of cues that are rarely reproduced in growth chambers [26,27]. Studies in the field have shown that gene expression, including that of flowering genes, can differ strikingly from laboratory patterns, and that laboratory-derived models can fail to predict flowering time in nature [28–30]. For instance, FT expression in field-grown Arabidopsis and in rice has been reported to show profiles and levels that cannot be explained by laboratory responses to single environmental variables [29,31]. These observations highlight a gap between mechanistic understanding gained in controlled environments and the regulation operating in natural seasons.

Closing this gap requires both characterizing molecular responses in natural environments and identifying which environmental parameters are sufficient to reproduce them under controlled conditions. Field experiments, although informative, are difficult to replicate and genetically dissect because many variables change simultaneously. If key parameters can be identified and incorporated into laboratory conditions, it would be possible to apply the full power of Arabidopsis genetics and molecular biology to seasonal responses [32].

Here we examined FT expression in Arabidopsis grown outdoors in natural long days in spring and found that FT peaks in the morning, in addition to a smaller dusk peak, a pattern distinct from that seen under standard laboratory long days. We then asked which environmental features account for this difference. We found that supplementing growth conditions with a R/FR ratio similar to that of open fields, together with a daily temperature oscillation, is sufficient to reproduce both the morning FT expression and the flowering time observed in nature. Using these adjusted conditions, we analyzed the contributions of light signaling components and show that phyA and ELF3 are important for morning FT induction. Finally, we show that these conditions stabilize CO protein in the morning, suggesting that morning CO accumulation is a critical mechanism underlying photoperiodic flowering in nature. Our results demonstrate that modest refinements of standard growth conditions can reveal regulatory mechanisms relevant to natural environments and provide a framework for studying seasonal responses in the laboratory.

Plant materials and growth conditions

Arabidopsis thaliana accession Columbia-0 (Col-0) was used as the wild type. The mutants and transgenic lines used were phyA-211, elf3-4, co-10, ft-10, and pFT::GUS, as well as lines expressing CO under its native promoter (pCO::HA-CO) in the co-10 background [1-4]. Seeds were surface sterilized, stratified at 4°C in the dark for 3 days, and sown on half-strength Murashige and Skoog medium containing 0.8% agar and 1% sucrose, or on soil as indicated. Plants were grown in controlled-environment chambers (Percival) under long days (16 h light/8 h dark).

Standard laboratory conditions (LD) consisted of constant 22°C and white fluorescent light of approximately 100 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ with a red/far-red (R:FR) ratio of about 6-7. Adjusted conditions (termed "natural-like" long days, NLD) used white light supplemented with far-red LEDs to reduce the R:FR ratio to about 1.0-1.2, matching open-field measurements, and a daily temperature oscillation that tracked field measurements (minimum 12°C before dawn, maximum 22°C in the afternoon, with gradual ramping). Photon flux density was kept equal between conditions. Light spectra were measured with a spectroradiometer (Apogee SS-110) at plant height, and temperature was verified with data loggers placed at rosette level.

Field sampling

Plants of Col-0 were grown outdoors at the field site in spring (March-May) after germination in the greenhouse and transfer outdoors at the seedling stage. Aerial parts of 10-15 plants were pooled per sample and harvested every 4 h over 24 h on selected days with day lengths of approximately 12-15 h. Samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen. Light intensity, R:FR ratio, and air temperature were recorded concurrently with a quantum sensor, spectroradiometer, and temperature logger. Three biological replicates were collected from independent days or independent plant pools.

Flowering time measurement

Flowering time was scored as the number of rosette leaves at bolting and as days to bolting (first visible inflorescence of 1 cm). At least 15 plants per genotype and condition were scored in each of three independent experiments. Plants were randomized within chambers and rotated weekly to minimize positional effects. Statistical differences were evaluated by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test or Student's t-test as appropriate (P < 0.05).

RNA extraction and quantitative RT-PCR

Seedlings (10-day-old unless noted) were harvested at the indicated Zeitgeber times (ZT) and frozen in liquid nitrogen. Total RNA was extracted using a Plant RNeasy kit (Qiagen) with on-column DNase I treatment. One microgram of RNA was reverse transcribed with oligo(dT) and SuperScript III (Invitrogen). Quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix on a CFX96 real-time system (Bio-Rad). Transcript levels of FT, CO, GI, PIF4, and clock genes were normalized to PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 2A SUBUNIT A3 (PP2AA3) or ISOPENTENYL PYROPHOSPHATE:DIMETHYLALLYL PYROPHOSPHATE ISOMERASE 2 (IPP2) [5]. Relative expression was calculated by the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 1. Each experiment included three biological replicates with technical triplicates.

Histochemical GUS staining

Seedlings carrying pFT::GUS were fixed in 90% acetone, washed, and incubated in X-Gluc solution (1 mM X-Gluc, 50 mM sodium phosphate pH 7.0, 0.5 mM potassium ferricyanide/ferrocyanide, 0.1% Triton X-100) at 37°C for a fixed duration, cleared in 70% ethanol, and imaged with a stereomicroscope.

Protein extraction and immunoblot analysis

Seedlings were harvested at the indicated time points and ground in liquid nitrogen. Total proteins were extracted in buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.1% Nonidet P-40, 1 mM PMSF, 50 µM MG132, and a protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). Extracts were cleared by centrifugation at 14,000 g for 10 min at 4°C. Equal amounts of protein were separated by 8% SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes, and probed with anti-HA-peroxidase (Roche, 3F10) for HA-CO. Anti-actin or Ponceau S staining served as loading controls. Signals were detected by chemiluminescence and quantified with ImageJ. For protein stability assays, seedlings were treated with 100 µM cycloheximide, and samples were collected at the indicated times after treatment. Half-lives were estimated by fitting an exponential decay curve to band intensities from three independent experiments.

Light and temperature treatment experiments

To dissect the contributions of individual factors, plants were grown under four combinations: standard R:FR with constant temperature, low R:FR with constant temperature, standard R:FR with temperature oscillation, and low R:FR with temperature oscillation. Temperature oscillation profiles were applied in the same chambers with programmed ramping. For phyA and ELF3 analyses, wild type, phyA-211, and elf3-4 were grown in parallel under LD and NLD, and FT and CO protein levels were assessed over a 24 h time course sampled every 4 h.

Data analysis and reproducibility

Time-course data are presented as mean ± standard deviation of at least three biological replicates. Diel expression peaks were compared by two-way ANOVA with genotype/condition and time as factors. Rhythmicity and peak phase were estimated using JTK_CYCLE or cosinor fitting where noted [6]. All experiments were repeated at least twice with consistent results, and representative data are shown. Analyses and plotting were performed in R (version 4.2) and GraphPad Prism.

FT expression peaks in the morning in natural spring conditions

To examine FT regulation in nature, we sampled wild-type Col-0 plants grown outdoors in Hokkaido-like spring long days (approximately 14–15 h of daylight) and measured FT transcript levels across the day. FT expression showed a pronounced peak in the morning, shortly after dawn, with a smaller and more variable increase near dusk. This contrasts with the evening-dominant peak typically observed in laboratory long days at constant 22°C with white fluorescent light [1,2]. The morning peak was reproducible across several days with different weather, although its amplitude varied with temperature and cloud cover. FT expression was also detectable in the morning in plants sampled in early spring, when day length was shorter than 13 h, indicating that the morning peak was not simply a consequence of long photoperiod.

Light quality and temperature cycles reproduce the natural FT pattern

We next asked which environmental parameters distinguish natural from laboratory conditions. Measurements of the light spectrum at the field site showed a red/far-red (R/FR) ratio of approximately 1.0–1.2, whereas our standard chambers provided R/FR ratios above 5 because of the red-rich fluorescent sources. Daily temperatures in the field also fluctuated, typically from about 10°C at dawn to 20°C in the afternoon.

We tested these factors individually and in combination. Lowering the R/FR ratio to approximately 1.0 by supplementing far-red light increased FT expression in the morning but did not eliminate the evening peak. Applying a daily temperature oscillation (12°C at night rising to 22°C during the day) without altering R/FR had a modest effect on FT. Combining the two treatments, which we refer to as the adjusted natural long-day (NLD) condition, produced a FT profile with a dominant morning peak and a diurnal waveform closely resembling that in the field. The morning FT level under NLD was several-fold higher than under standard long days, whereas the evening peak was reduced. Principal component analysis of the transcript time courses placed NLD samples closer to field samples than to any single-factor treatment, indicating that the factors act synergistically.

Flowering time under adjusted conditions matches nature

We then compared flowering behavior. Col-0 plants flowered with approximately 14 leaves under NLD, similar to plants sown in the field in spring, and earlier than plants grown under standard long days at constant temperature, which produced more rosette leaves. Mutants lacking FT (ft-10) were strongly delayed under both conditions, confirming that FT is the major determinant of flowering under NLD. Thus, modest adjustments to R/FR and temperature are sufficient to reproduce both the molecular and phenotypic features of natural long-day flowering.

phyA and ELF3 are required for morning FT expression under NLD

We next investigated light signaling components. In standard long days, phyB and the cryptochromes are key regulators of FT [3,4]. Under NLD, the phyB mutant showed elevated FT overall, consistent with its role as a repressor, but the morning peak was still observed. By contrast, the phyA mutant lost most of the morning FT expression and flowered later under NLD, whereas its phenotype was weak under standard conditions. This indicates that low R/FR conditions enhance the contribution of phyA, which perceives far-red light and promotes CO function [5,6].

The elf3 mutant displayed high FT expression throughout the day, with loss of the diurnal pattern, and flowered early under both conditions. However, the effect of elf3 on morning FT was greater under NLD. Because ELF3 is a component of the evening complex that represses PIF4 and other targets, and its activity is temperature sensitive [7,8], we examined whether temperature cycles contributed. In the elf3 mutant, the response to temperature oscillation was reduced, supporting a role for ELF3 in integrating light and temperature inputs to FT. The phyA elf3 double mutant resembled elf3, suggesting that ELF3 acts downstream of or in parallel to phyA in controlling morning FT.

NLD stabilizes CO protein in the morning

Because CO is the main activator of FT, we asked whether the morning FT peak reflected CO regulation. CO transcript patterns were similar between standard and NLD conditions, with expression rising during the day. In contrast, CO protein, assessed in plants expressing a tagged CO under its native promoter, accumulated in the morning under NLD but was barely detectable at that time under standard conditions, where CO accumulated mainly toward the end of the day. Treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 increased morning CO under standard conditions, indicating that CO is normally degraded at this time, but had less effect under NLD, consistent with stabilization.

CO stabilization depended on phyA: morning CO protein was reduced in the phyA mutant under NLD, whereas it was elevated in elf3. Levels of the E3 ubiquitin ligase COP1 target interactions were consistent with this pattern, as the FKF1-dependent evening CO accumulation was maintained in all genotypes [9]. Finally, the co mutant showed almost no morning FT under NLD, and overexpression of CO partially restored morning FT in phyA, demonstrating that CO acts downstream of phyA. Together, these data show that natural-like R/FR and temperature cycles stabilize CO in the morning through phyA and ELF3, thereby driving morning FT expression and early flowering.

The results presented here show that the diurnal pattern of FT expression in natural long days differs substantially from that observed under standard laboratory conditions. In the field during spring, FT peaks in the morning, whereas in the laboratory it is typically dominated by a peak around dusk [1,2]. Importantly, modifying two environmental parameters, the red/far-red (R/FR) light ratio and daily temperature oscillation, was sufficient to reproduce both the morning FT expression and the flowering time observed outdoors. This suggests that the complexity of natural environments can, at least for this trait, be reduced to a small number of experimentally tractable cues, and that laboratory conditions have emphasized a regulatory mode that is only part of the plant's natural response.

**Light quality and temperature as determinants of morning FT expression**

Standard laboratory light sources, particularly white fluorescent tubes and many LED systems, have a high R/FR ratio compared with sunlight at open-field sites, where the ratio is lower, especially near dawn and dusk and under canopy shade [3]. Lowering the R/FR ratio is known to accelerate flowering and to enhance FT expression through phytochrome-dependent mechanisms, but previous work focused largely on shade avoidance and on the dusk-phased FT peak [4,5]. Our results indicate that a natural-like R/FR ratio, combined with temperature cycles, shifts the activity of the photoperiod pathway toward the morning. Temperature is a well-established modulator of FT, acting through PIF4, the evening complex, and chromatin-based mechanisms [6,7]. Constant temperatures used in most laboratory experiments conceal the interaction between thermal cycles and light signaling. The additive or synergistic effect of the two cues suggests that integration occurs at shared nodes, likely including ELF3 and CO.

**Roles of phyA and ELF3**

Under the adjusted conditions, phyA and ELF3 were important for morning FT expression. PhyA perceives far-red-enriched light and is known to stabilize CO protein by suppressing its degradation by the COP1–SPA complex [8,9]. In standard conditions, phyA contributes mainly to the promotion of flowering at the end of the day, when FR is relatively enriched. Our data extend this role: with a lower R/FR ratio, phyA activity in the morning becomes sufficient to support FT activation. ELF3, a component of the evening complex, represses FT directly and indirectly through PIF4 and GI [10,11]. Its temperature-dependent function, and its interaction with phytochrome B, suggest that ELF3 activity is shaped by both light quality and temperature cycles, so that the evening complex's repressive influence on morning FT is altered under natural-like conditions. The requirement of both components indicates that morning FT expression is not the product of a single pathway but arises from convergence of light and temperature signaling on the regulation of CO and FT.

**CO protein stabilization as a central mechanism**

A major finding is that the adjusted conditions stabilize CO protein in the morning. Because CO is regulated post-translationally, with degradation in darkness by COP1 and in the morning through phyB-mediated mechanisms, CO accumulation is largely confined to the late afternoon under laboratory conditions [8,12]. Stabilization of CO in the morning, enabled by FR-enriched light through phyA and cryptochromes, provides a plausible explanation for the shift in FT timing. CO transcript levels are not themselves sufficient to explain FT output, consistent with previous work showing that protein stability is the principal determinant of CO activity [8,13]. We therefore propose that extension of the window of CO activity into the morning is a critical feature of photoperiodic flowering in nature, and may allow plants to measure day length more robustly under fluctuating conditions. Further experiments, such as measuring CO–chromatin association at the FT promoter and testing mutants in COP1, SPA, and FKF1, will help clarify how these inputs are integrated.

**Implications for laboratory studies and seasonal biology**

These findings have methodological implications. Mutant phenotypes, regulatory interactions, and the relative importance of signaling components may differ depending on growth conditions. Genes that appear to play minor roles in standard conditions, such as phyA, may be more important in natural settings, while the apparent roles of others may be overestimated. Modeling efforts that predict flowering from laboratory data may also need to be recalibrated with realistic light and temperature inputs [14]. The adjusted conditions provide a practical, reproducible bridge between field and laboratory, allowing mechanistic dissection of seasonal responses with the genetic tools available in Arabidopsis. The approach should be extendable to other seasonal traits and species, including crops, where light quality and temperature fluctuations are likewise important.

**Limitations and future directions**

Our simulated conditions do not recreate all aspects of natural environments. Light intensity, spectral changes in blue and UV-B wavelengths, humidity, soil conditions, and year-to-year variation in temperature were not addressed, and the field data represent a limited number of sites and seasons. Other factors such as vernalization, ambient temperature memory, and the age-dependent pathway likely modulate FT in nature [15]. Future work should test additional seasons and natural accessions, and examine how the morning FT peak interacts with FLC-mediated regulation.

**Conclusion**

Expression of FT in natural long days peaks in the morning, and this pattern, along with natural flowering time, can be reproduced in the laboratory by adjusting the R/FR ratio and introducing daily temperature oscillation. Under these conditions phyA and ELF3 are key regulators, and stabilization of CO protein in the morning is likely a critical mechanism. Refining standard growth conditions to approximate nature more closely thus offers a powerful strategy for understanding how plants interpret seasonal cues.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in image recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing, largely because multilayered neural networks can acquire hierarchical representations of input patterns [1], [2]. Among these models, the Deep Belief Network (DBN) is a representative generative architecture in which Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are stacked and pre-trained layer by layer in an unsupervised manner [3], [4]. The greedy layer-wise pre-training provides good initial parameters for subsequent supervised fine-tuning and alleviates difficulties such as vanishing gradients and poor local minima in deep networks [4], [5]. The RBM, a two-layer stochastic network with visible and hidden neurons, is trained efficiently with contrastive divergence (CD) [6], and DBNs built on it have shown strong performance on benchmarks such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 [3], [7].

Despite these advantages, the performance of RBMs and DBNs depends strongly on the network structure, namely the number of hidden neurons in each RBM and the number of layers in the DBN. These quantities are usually fixed in advance by trial and error, grid search, or the experience of the designer [8]. If the network is too small, it cannot represent the distribution of the input space; if it is too large, it suffers from overfitting, redundant neurons, and unnecessary computational cost. Because a conventional RBM or DBN cannot change its structure during learning, the designer must train many candidate models, which is expensive for large data sets. Methods such as random search and Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters [9], [10] reduce this burden, but they still treat the structure as an external setting rather than as something the model itself acquires from data.

Adaptive structure learning has long been studied for neural networks. Constructive approaches such as cascade correlation [11] grow a network by adding units, whereas pruning approaches such as optimal brain damage [12] remove unimportant connections from a large network. For energy-based models, several works have proposed adding or removing hidden units of RBMs according to training progress [13], [14], and nonparametric formulations have been explored as well [15]. However, most of these studies address only a single RBM, and the determination of an appropriate depth for a DBN has received comparatively little attention. Since the representational power of a DBN is closely related to its depth, a mechanism that decides when a new layer is required is of considerable importance.

In our previous research, we proposed an adaptive structural learning method of RBM, which we call Adaptive RBM [16]. This method monitors the energy-based learning state during training and automatically generates a new hidden neuron when the existing neurons are insufficient to represent the input patterns, detected through the fluctuation of the network parameters. Neurons that are found to be unnecessary are removed by a neuron annihilation procedure. As a result, the model can discover a suitable number of hidden neurons according to the complexity of the input space, without requiring prior knowledge. Experimental results indicated that the Adaptive RBM achieved higher generalization capability than a conventional RBM with a fixed number of hidden neurons on several benchmark data sets [16].

A further issue is the interpretability and sparseness of trained networks. Deep models are often regarded as black boxes, and extracting explicit knowledge from a trained network requires that its structure be compact and its connections sparse [17], [18]. Regularization approaches, including weight decay and L1 penalties, are common ways to encourage sparsity [19]. The Learning Forgetting method [20] is another approach, in which weights that make little contribution are gradually decayed so that only essential connections remain, thereby producing a skeletal structure suitable for rule extraction. We then developed a hybrid method that combines the Adaptive RBM with Learning Forgetting, which reduced redundant connections while maintaining the ability to represent the input data [21]. Nevertheless, this hybrid method was limited to a single RBM and did not address how multiple RBMs should be stacked into a deep architecture.

In this paper, we propose an adaptive learning method of DBN that determines the optimal number of layers during learning by means of a layer generation algorithm. The proposed method first trains an Adaptive RBM on the input data. When the trained RBM cannot sufficiently represent the data, as judged by the remaining reconstruction error or the energy-based criterion on the hidden representation, a new RBM is generated and stacked on top of the current network, using the hidden activations of the lower layer as its input. Layer generation continues until no further improvement is obtained, so that the depth of the DBN is decided automatically from the data rather than predefined. Because each layer also adjusts its own number of hidden neurons and, with the Learning Forgetting method, its own sparse connections, the resulting DBN is expected to have a compact structure with moderate computational cost and good model stability.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. First, we present a layer generation algorithm that extends the adaptive structural learning of RBM to a DBN with a self-organized depth. Second, we integrate the algorithm with the neuron generation and annihilation mechanism and the Learning Forgetting method, so that the numbers of neurons, weights, and layers are all determined adaptively. Third, we evaluate the proposed model on benchmark data sets and compare it with conventional DBNs having fixed structures, examining classification accuracy, network size, and the effect of the generated layers.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the RBM, the DBN, and the adaptive structural learning method with Learning Forgetting. Section 3 describes the proposed layer generation algorithm. Section 4 presents the experimental settings and results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future work.

The proposed method builds on the adaptive structural learning of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and extends it to the Deep Belief Network (DBN) by adding a layer generation mechanism. The method has three components: (1) adaptive RBM learning, which adjusts the number of hidden neurons during training; (2) the Learning Forgetting method, which sparsifies the trained weights; and (3) the layer generation algorithm, which stacks new RBMs on the existing network until no further improvement is obtained.

**1. Restricted Boltzmann Machine**

An RBM is an undirected bipartite graphical model with a visible layer v ∈ {0,1}^I and a hidden layer h ∈ {0,1}^J. Its energy function is

E(v,h) = −Σ_i b_i v_i − Σ_j c_j h_j − Σ_{i,j} v_i W_ij h_j,

where b_i and c_j are the visible and hidden biases and W_ij is the connection weight. The joint distribution is p(v,h) = exp(−E(v,h))/Z, where Z is the partition function. Because of the bipartite structure, the conditional distributions factorize:

p(h_j=1|v) = σ(c_j + Σ_i W_ij v_i),  p(v_i=1|h) = σ(b_i + Σ_j W_ij h_j),

with σ the logistic sigmoid. Parameters are trained by approximately maximizing the log-likelihood with contrastive divergence (CD) [1]. For one training pattern, the updates are ΔW_ij = η(⟨v_i h_j⟩_data − ⟨v_i h_j⟩_recon), with analogous rules for the biases, where η is the learning rate.

**2. Adaptive structural learning of RBM**

In a standard RBM, the number of hidden neurons is fixed beforehand. Our adaptive method monitors the training state and changes the number of hidden neurons during learning, following the neuron generation and annihilation scheme [2]. The monitored quantity is the variance of the weight-update magnitude, which indicates whether the current capacity is sufficient.

*Neuron generation.* Let the training error be the mean squared reconstruction error, and let its change over a fixed window of epochs be tracked. If the error stops decreasing while it remains above a tolerance, the network is judged to have insufficient representational capacity. A new hidden neuron is then inserted. Its weights are initialized with small random values, and its bias is set to zero. Insertion is repeated at most once per monitoring window, so that the effect of each new neuron can be observed before another is added.

*Neuron annihilation.* After the generation phase, the activation probability of each hidden neuron is averaged over the training set. Neurons whose average activation is persistently close to zero or close to one contribute little information, because their outputs are almost independent of the input. Such neurons are removed together with their connections. This step prevents overgrowth and keeps the computational cost low.

The resulting procedure ends when the reconstruction error falls below a predefined threshold or the maximum number of epochs is reached. The number of hidden neurons is thus determined by the input space rather than set manually.

**3. Learning Forgetting method**

The explicit extraction of knowledge from a trained network requires sparse connectivity. We therefore apply the Learning Forgetting method [3] to the trained RBM, as in our previous work. A penalty term that drives weights toward zero is added to the learning objective, which yields the update

ΔW_ij = η(⟨v_i h_j⟩_data − ⟨v_i h_j⟩_recon) − κ·sgn(W_ij),

where κ is the forgetting coefficient. Weights that are not consistently supported by the data decay to zero, whereas weights carrying essential regularities are maintained. After this phase, weights with absolute value below a small threshold are pruned. Neurons left with no connections are removed. The result is a compact RBM whose remaining connections can be inspected as explicit features.

**4. Deep Belief Network**

A DBN is constructed by stacking RBMs and training greedily layer by layer [4]. The first RBM is trained on the input data. The hidden activation probabilities of the trained RBM are then used as the visible data of the next RBM, and the procedure is repeated. After pre-training, the stack is used either as a feature extractor for a classifier or fine-tuned with supervised learning. In a traditional DBN the number of layers and the number of neurons in each layer must be specified in advance.

**5. Layer generation algorithm**

The proposed algorithm determines the number of layers automatically. It operates as follows.

1. Train the first RBM with the adaptive structural learning method (Section 2), followed by the Learning Forgetting method (Section 3).
2. Evaluate the current top layer. The evaluation criterion is the reconstruction error of the RBM on the training data for the unsupervised case, and the classification error of a supervised output layer attached to the top hidden layer for the labeled case.
3. If the criterion exceeds the tolerance, and the previous layer addition improved it by more than a minimum margin δ, generate a new RBM. Its visible layer has as many neurons as the current top hidden layer, and its hidden layer starts with a small number of neurons.
4. Train the new RBM on the hidden activations of the layer below, again using adaptive structural learning and forgetting.
5. Repeat steps 2–4. Terminate when the criterion falls below the tolerance, or when adding a layer no longer yields an improvement of at least δ. The last added layer is then discarded if it degraded performance.

By this process the depth of the network grows only as far as the data requires. Because each new RBM can itself add or remove hidden neurons, both the width of each layer and the overall depth adapt to the complexity of the input space. A theoretical motivation is that adding a layer to a DBN can increase a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood provided the new layer is properly initialized [4]; the stopping rule approximates the point at which this gain vanishes.

**6. Experimental setting**

We evaluate the method on benchmark data sets, including MNIST [5] and CIFAR-10 [6], measuring classification accuracy, the final number of layers and neurons, and the sparsity of the trained weights. The proposed model is compared with a DBN with a fixed structure trained with CD, and with an adaptive RBM without layer generation. Hyperparameters, including the learning rate η, the forgetting coefficient κ, the monitoring window, and the threshold δ, are chosen on a validation subset. Each experiment is repeated with different random seeds, and the mean and standard deviation are reported.

We evaluated the proposed adaptive DBN on three benchmark data sets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and a UCI-style tabular set used in earlier studies of adaptive RBM [1]. We compared it with a conventional DBN with a fixed structure, the adaptive RBM without layer generation, and the adaptive RBM combined with the Learning Forgetting method [2]. All models were trained with contrastive divergence (CD-1) and fine-tuned with supervised back-propagation. Results are averaged over five runs with different random seeds. Unless noted otherwise, values are reported as mean ± standard deviation.

**Neuron generation and annihilation behavior in a single RBM**

We first examined how the adaptive RBM changed its hidden layer during training on MNIST. Starting from 10 hidden neurons, the network generated neurons rapidly during the early epochs, when the training error was high. The number of hidden neurons then stabilized as the error decreased. After convergence the first RBM held 187 ± 9 hidden neurons. The neuron annihilation step removed 14% of the generated neurons on average. This result indicates that the generation step tends to overshoot slightly and that the annihilation step corrects the overshoot. A fixed RBM with 500 hidden neurons reached a similar reconstruction error (0.0121 versus 0.0126 for the adaptive RBM) while using about 2.7 times as many hidden units.

**Layer generation**

We then evaluated the layer generation algorithm. A new RBM layer was stacked when the energy-based reconstruction error of the current top layer stopped improving despite further neuron generation. On MNIST the algorithm produced 3.4 ± 0.5 hidden layers on average, with the typical configuration 784-187-95-48-… . Layer sizes decreased monotonically in all runs, consistent with hierarchical abstraction of input features. On CIFAR-10, which has a more complex input space, the algorithm generated 4.6 ± 0.7 layers. On the tabular data it generated only 2.0 ± 0.0 layers. The number of layers therefore adapted to the complexity of the input space without manual specification.

**Classification performance**

Table 1 summarizes the test accuracy of the compared methods.

| Method | MNIST | CIFAR-10 | Tabular |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed DBN (3 layers) | 98.1 ± 0.1 | 61.3 ± 0.6 | 93.4 ± 0.5 |
| Adaptive RBM (single layer) | 97.6 ± 0.2 | 57.9 ± 0.8 | 93.9 ± 0.4 |
| Adaptive RBM + Forgetting | 97.5 ± 0.2 | 57.6 ± 0.9 | 93.8 ± 0.4 |
| Proposed adaptive DBN | 98.3 ± 0.1 | 64.8 ± 0.5 | 94.2 ± 0.3 |

The proposed adaptive DBN achieved the highest accuracy on all three data sets. The improvement over the fixed DBN was small on MNIST (+0.2 points) and larger on CIFAR-10 (+3.5 points), where deeper representations were beneficial. A paired t-test over the five runs showed that the CIFAR-10 improvement was significant (p < 0.01). The MNIST improvement was not significant (p = 0.08). The single-layer adaptive RBM performed worse than the multilayer models on the image data sets. On the tabular data it outperformed the fixed DBN, which suggests that the fixed DBN was over-parameterized for the simple input space.

**Network size and computational cost**

Table 2 reports the total number of parameters and training time relative to the fixed DBN.

| Data set | Parameters (proposed / fixed) | Training time (proposed / fixed) |
|---|---|---|
| MNIST | 0.31 | 0.74 |
| CIFAR-10 | 0.52 | 1.18 |
| Tabular | 0.12 | 0.43 |

The proposed model used between 12% and 52% of the parameters of the fixed DBN. Training time was lower on MNIST and the tabular data. On CIFAR-10 it was 18% higher, because many neurons and layers had to be generated during training. This overhead is incurred once, and the resulting compact network reduces inference cost. The fixed DBN also required a grid search over layer count and layer width. This search was not included in its training time. The total cost of the fixed DBN, including the search, was therefore considerably higher than that of the proposed method.

**Effect of the Learning Forgetting method and sparsity**

We next examined the sparsity of the trained networks. Applying Learning Forgetting to the adaptive DBN raised the proportion of weights with magnitude below 0.01 from 22% to 71% on MNIST, with a loss in accuracy of only 0.1 points. In the same setting, the fixed DBN with forgetting reached 58% sparsity and lost 0.4 points. The sparse structure of the adaptive DBN made the connections between hidden neurons and input pixels easier to inspect. Visualization of the first-layer weights showed localized stroke-like detectors, while second- and third-layer neurons responded to combinations of these strokes. The result supports the use of the adaptive DBN for extracting explicit knowledge from trained networks, although we did not quantify interpretability beyond sparsity and visual inspection.

**Stability across runs**

The standard deviations of accuracy for the proposed model were equal to or smaller than those of the baselines on every data set. The final layer count varied by at most one layer among runs. The generated structure was thus reasonably reproducible, even though neuron generation depends on random initialization and mini-batch order. Sensitivity analysis showed that the thresholds controlling neuron and layer generation affected the final structure moderately. Changing the layer generation threshold by ±50% altered the mean layer count on MNIST between 2.8 and 4.0, while accuracy varied by less than 0.3 points.

**Summary**

The adaptive DBN determined suitable numbers of neurons and layers automatically. It improved accuracy over fixed-structure DBNs, especially on the more complex data, and it produced considerably smaller and sparser networks.

The experimental results indicate that the proposed adaptive learning method of DBN, which combines the adaptive structural learning of RBM with a layer generation algorithm, can determine a suitable network structure from the input data without manual design. Conventional RBM and DBN models require the numbers of hidden neurons and layers to be fixed before training, and these hyperparameters are usually tuned by trial and error or by grid search [1], [2]. In contrast, our method monitors the training state of each RBM and allocates new hidden neurons by a neuron generation mechanism when the network cannot represent the input space. It removes redundant neurons by a neuron annihilation mechanism, and it stacks a new RBM layer when the representational ability of the current top layer saturates. The resulting structures were compact compared with fixed, over-parameterized networks, while classification accuracy on the benchmark data sets was comparable to or higher than that of standard DBNs and other published results.

Several observations deserve discussion. First, the neuron generation and annihilation mechanisms were effective in controlling the capacity of each layer. When a layer was too small, the monitored variance of the training error remained large and neurons were added until the error stabilized. When a layer was larger than necessary, neurons contributing little to the reconstruction were removed. This behavior is consistent with the idea that the optimal number of hidden neurons depends on the complexity of the data distribution rather than on the dimensionality of the input alone [3]. Second, the layer generation algorithm showed that depth is also data dependent. For simple data sets, few layers were sufficient, and additional layers brought no meaningful improvement. For more complex data sets, deeper hierarchies were generated automatically and gave better discrimination. Because a new layer is added only when the preceding layer no longer improves the representation, the method avoids both an unnecessarily deep model and an under-fitted shallow one, which helps to balance computational cost and model stability.

Third, the hybrid approach with the Learning Forgetting method, developed in our previous research [4], is relevant to the problem of extracting explicit knowledge from trained networks. Forgetting drives weak connections toward zero and yields a sparse structure in which the remaining connections are more interpretable. Interpretability matters when a trained DBN is to be used in applications that require explanations, and a sparse, compact network is also easier to analyze and cheaper to execute. Although we did not conduct a full rule-extraction study in this paper, the sparsity observed in the trained weights suggests that such extraction would be more tractable than for dense networks of fixed size.

Despite these positive results, there are limitations. The method introduces its own parameters, such as the thresholds that trigger neuron generation, annihilation, and layer generation. Although these were less sensitive than the structural hyperparameters they replace, they still influence the final structure, and an automatic way of setting them would make the method more autonomous. In addition, the adaptive procedure increases training time per epoch compared with a fixed network, because the network state must be monitored and the structure modified during learning. The total cost can be lower than that of an exhaustive search over architectures, but a systematic comparison of computational cost was beyond the scope of this study. Furthermore, our evaluation was limited to a small number of benchmark data sets and mainly to classification tasks. Whether the same behavior holds for larger, high-dimensional, or noisy data, such as natural images or time-series data, remains to be verified. Finally, the layer generation criterion is based on a greedy, layer-wise decision. A globally optimal depth is not guaranteed, and fine-tuning of the whole network after the structure is fixed may be necessary to reach the best performance [5].

Several directions for future work follow. One is to combine the proposed method with other deep architectures, such as convolutional networks or deep Boltzmann machines, so that adaptive structure determination can be applied to image and sequence data. Another is to investigate the theoretical basis of the generation and annihilation criteria, for example in terms of the free energy or the likelihood bound of the model, which could give principled thresholds. A third is to use the sparse trained networks for explicit knowledge extraction and to evaluate the quality of the extracted rules quantitatively. Finally, incremental or online learning settings, in which the input distribution changes over time, are a natural application of a model that can modify its own structure.

In conclusion, we proposed an adaptive learning method of DBN that determines the optimal number of hidden neurons, weights, and layers during learning. By extending the adaptive structural learning of RBM, together with the Learning Forgetting method, to a layer generation algorithm, the model builds a deep architecture that fits the input space without prior specification of its structure. Experiments on benchmark data sets showed that the method obtains compact and sparse networks with competitive recognition performance, and that the depth of the network adapts to the complexity of the data. These findings suggest that adaptive structure learning is a promising approach to reducing the cost of model design, improving model stability, and facilitating the interpretation of deep networks, and we expect that further development along the lines described above will broaden its applicability.

Hip fracture is among the most serious consequences of osteoporosis in the elderly and is associated with high mortality, long-term disability, loss of independence, and a considerable economic burden on health systems [1,2]. Because of population ageing, the global incidence of hip fracture is projected to rise substantially over the coming decades [3]. Roughly one fifth of patients die within a year of the fracture, and many survivors never regain their pre-fracture mobility [4]. Reliable, patient-specific identification of individuals at high risk is therefore essential, so that preventive pharmacological or lifestyle interventions can be targeted and the costs of surgical treatment and rehabilitation reduced.

**Clinical assessment of fracture risk**

Clinical assessment still relies largely on areal bone mineral density (aBMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), usually expressed as a T-score at the proximal femur or lumbar spine [5]. Although low aBMD is a well-established risk factor, it explains only part of fracture risk. A large proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores lie above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. DXA is a two-dimensional projection technique. It cannot resolve the three-dimensional geometry, the cortical–trabecular distribution, or the spatial heterogeneity of density that govern the mechanical response of the femur. Tools such as FRAX improve prediction by adding clinical risk factors, but they do not account for the mechanical competence of an individual's bone or for the loading conditions that cause fracture [7].

**Image-based finite element analysis**

Finite element analysis (FEA) based on quantitative computed tomography (QCT) has emerged as a promising alternative. In this approach, patient-specific geometry is reconstructed from CT data, and heterogeneous material properties are assigned to each element through empirical relationships between CT attenuation (Hounsfield units), apparent density, and elastic modulus [8,9]. Such models have been validated against ex vivo mechanical tests, where they predict femoral strength and fracture location with reasonable accuracy [10,11]. QCT-based FEA has also been shown to discriminate fractured from non-fractured subjects better than aBMD alone in prospective and retrospective cohorts [12,13]. Fracture risk indicators (FRI), usually defined as the ratio of the local stress or strain to the failure strength or strain of bone, provide a spatially resolved measure of the likelihood of failure and allow the probable site of fracture initiation to be identified [14].

**Loading configurations and the femoral neck**

The femoral neck is the principal site of hip fracture because of its slender geometry, thin cortex, and high load transmission. The outcome of an analysis depends heavily on the loading configuration. The single-legged stance represents physiological loading during walking and standing, in which the joint reaction force produces compression and bending, with tensile stresses at the superior neck and compressive stresses at the inferior neck [15]. By contrast, a sideways fall onto the greater trochanter is the dominant cause of hip fracture in the elderly, and more than 90% of hip fractures are associated with falls [16]. The loading direction in a fall reverses the stress pattern in the neck and may induce high stress on the superior cortex, which is thin and fragile with age [17]. Several studies have simulated both configurations, and some have suggested that fracture risk may be underestimated if only stance loading is considered [18,19]. However, comparative evaluation of the FRI distribution for stance and fall configurations under identical load magnitudes has received limited attention, particularly in vivo.

**Bilateral variation and the choice of hip**

Another unresolved issue is the choice of hip to be examined. In clinical practice, DXA or QCT scanning is normally performed on a single hip, often selected arbitrarily or by convention, on the assumption that left and right femurs are sufficiently symmetrical to be interchangeable [20]. However, asymmetry in the proximal femur has been reported in geometry, density, and cortical thickness, and may result from limb dominance, habitual loading, pathology, or natural variation [21,22]. Bilateral differences in aBMD of several percent are common, and in some individuals they alter the diagnostic classification [23]. Given that FEA is highly sensitive to geometry and spatial density distribution, even modest asymmetries could produce meaningful differences in computed stress and FRI fields. Previous FE studies have mostly modelled a single femur per subject, or used small samples, so the extent to which bilateral differences influence predicted fracture risk, and whether they differ between men and women, is poorly understood. This question matters because women have lower peak bone mass, undergo accelerated postmenopausal bone loss, and suffer the majority of hip fractures [24].

**Aim and scope of the present study**

The present work therefore examines the variation of fall-induced hip fracture risk between the right and left femurs using QCT-based FEA. Models of both femurs of thirty anonymous subjects were generated, and FRI was evaluated at the superior and inferior aspects of the femoral neck under single-legged stance and sideways fall configurations with equal load magnitude. The specific objectives were: (i) to compare FRI distributions between the two loading configurations and identify the likely site of fracture initiation; (ii) to quantify the left–right variability of FRI and test its statistical significance; and (iii) to compare the bilateral FRI of men and women. By clarifying the need for bilateral assessment, this preliminary study aims to contribute to more accurate, patient-specific hip fracture prediction and, consequently, to more effective preventive strategies for the geriatric population.

**Subject data and image acquisition**

Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) datasets of the proximal femora of thirty anonymous patients (both left and right sides) were retrieved retrospectively from a clinical image repository. The cohort included both men and women, and all personal identifiers were removed before analysis. Scans were acquired with a calibrated clinical CT scanner at a slice thickness of 1 mm and an in-plane resolution of approximately 0.8–1.0 mm. A calibration phantom was included in the field of view so that Hounsfield units (HU) could be converted to equivalent bone mineral density [1,2]. Patients with prior hip surgery, implants, or visible pathological lesions were excluded. Each dataset was handled with the same image-processing and modelling workflow so that any difference between sides could not be attributed to procedural variation.

**Geometry reconstruction and meshing**

The proximal femur was segmented in medical image-processing software using intensity thresholding followed by manual correction to separate the femoral head from the acetabulum and to remove soft tissue and the pelvis. Cortical and trabecular bone were not segmented separately, and the femur was treated as a single continuous domain with spatially varying material properties [3]. A triangulated surface was generated, smoothed to remove stair-step artefacts, and used to build a volumetric mesh of ten-node quadratic tetrahedral elements. A mesh convergence study on one representative femur showed that an average element edge length of about 2 mm kept the change in peak principal strain below 5%, and this size was adopted for all models [4]. Left and right femurs were meshed with identical parameters.

**Material property assignment**

The HU values were converted to equivalent K₂HPO₄ density and then to apparent density (ρ_app) by linear calibration. Young's modulus was assigned to each element from empirical density–modulus relationships of the power-law form E = aρ^b, with separate coefficients for cortical and trabecular regimes [5,6]. Values were mapped element by element, with a limited number of discrete material bins to keep the computation tractable. Poisson's ratio was set to 0.3 throughout. Bone was modelled as isotropic and linear elastic, which is acceptable for estimating the onset of failure at physiological loads [7]. Ultimate stress and strain thresholds were defined as density-dependent, with distinct tensile and compressive limits to reflect the asymmetric strength of bone [8].

**Loading and boundary conditions**

Two loading configurations were simulated for every femur, namely single-legged stance and sideways fall.

*Single-legged stance.* The femur was oriented anatomically, with the shaft axis inclined at about 7° to the vertical in the frontal plane. A joint contact force was applied to the femoral head, and an abductor force was applied to the greater trochanter [9]. The distal end of the shaft was fully constrained.

*Sideways fall.* The femur was rotated so that the shaft was inclined at about 30° to the horizontal and the neck was internally rotated by about 15°, following previous fall models [10,11]. The impact force was applied to the greater trochanter, and the femoral head was restrained by constraining its superior surface in the loading direction, with the distal end constrained to resist rigid-body motion.

To ensure that any difference in the fracture risk indicator (FRI) came from the bone's geometry and density distribution and not from different loading, the same load magnitude was applied to every model and both configurations. The load was scaled to a value equivalent to a typical body weight multiple, and the same load direction relative to the femoral axis was used for the left and right sides. Where the left femur was mirrored for setup, mirroring was applied consistently.

**Finite element analysis and fracture risk indicator**

All simulations were run as static linear analyses in a commercial finite element solver. The FRI was defined at each node or element as the ratio of the computed local stress or strain to the corresponding density-dependent failure limit, with the tensile ratio used where the principal stress was tensile and the compressive ratio used where it was compressive [12]. FRI values of 1 or more indicate predicted local failure. Distributions were extracted over the femoral neck, which is the weakest region of the proximal femur. Nodal values were sampled on defined paths along the superior and inferior surfaces of the neck, from the head-neck junction to the intertrochanteric region, using the same anatomical landmarks in all femurs. Peak and mean FRI along each path were recorded, and the percentage difference between the configurations was calculated as |FRI_fall − FRI_stance|/FRI_stance × 100 for each aspect.

**Left–right comparison and statistical analysis**

For each subject, the FRI distributions of the left and right femurs were compared under both loading configurations, with the difference expressed in absolute and percentage terms. Paired-sample t-tests were used to test whether the mean FRI differed between left and right femurs, with subjects serving as their own controls. The normality of paired differences was checked with the Shapiro–Wilk test. The significance threshold was set at p ≤ 0.05, and tests were two-tailed. Subjects were subsequently grouped by sex, and mean FRI values were compared between men and women for each side and load case. Because of the small subgroup sizes, these comparisons were treated as descriptive. Analyses were performed in standard statistical software.

**Assumptions and limitations of the modelling approach**

Isotropic linear elastic behaviour, a static load, and the omission of muscle forces other than the abductor were simplifying assumptions applied equally to all models [7,9]. The aim was a comparison between sides within the same subject, and not an absolute prediction of fracture load, so these assumptions affect both sides in the same way.

**Model characteristics and validation**

The finite element models of the 60 femora (30 left, 30 right) were generated from QCT datasets with a mean element count of approximately 2.1 × 10⁵ tetrahedral elements after the mesh convergence check. Density-based material mapping yielded a heterogeneous elastic modulus distribution in every model. The mean peak von Mises strain differed by less than 3% between the two finest mesh densities, so the selected mesh was considered adequate. The predicted strain patterns agreed qualitatively with those reported in earlier image-based studies [1,2]. Highest values were concentrated in the femoral neck in both loading configurations, and the load transfer paths matched the known trabecular architecture.

**Fracture risk indicator distribution in single-legged stance**

In the single-legged stance configuration, the fracture risk indicator (FRI), defined as the ratio of the computed equivalent strain to the yield strain of the local bone, was highest at the inferior (medial) aspect of the femoral neck in nearly all models. The inferior surface was under compression. The mean FRI there was 0.41 ± 0.09 for the left femora and 0.43 ± 0.11 for the right. The superior surface was under lower tensile strain, with a mean FRI of 0.17 ± 0.05 (left) and 0.18 ± 0.06 (right). No FRI exceeded unity in this configuration under the applied load, so no model was predicted to fracture in normal stance. The FRI was highest in the subcapital to mid-cervical region and fell steadily toward the intertrochanteric region.

**Fracture risk indicator distribution in sideways fall**

Under the sideways fall configuration, the strain distribution shifted markedly. The peak FRI moved to the superolateral aspect of the femoral neck, where the mean value was 0.68 ± 0.17 (left) and 0.71 ± 0.19 (right). The inferior aspect showed lower values of 0.48 ± 0.12 and 0.50 ± 0.13, respectively. Compared with single-legged stance, the FRI at the superior surface was 64–74% higher, whereas the increase at the inferior surface was only 14–19%. Thus the superior neck was consistently the most critical location in a fall. In six femora (10%), the local FRI at the superior neck exceeded 0.9, indicating that fracture initiation was imminent at the applied load. Four of those six belonged to female subjects.

**Left–right differences**

The FRI differed between the contralateral femora of nearly every subject. The absolute inter-limb difference at the superior neck in sideways fall ranged from 1% to 38% of the larger value, with a mean of 13.6%. Differences at the inferior surface were smaller (mean 6.2%). In 11 of 30 subjects, the difference at the superior neck exceeded 15%. In 7 subjects, the side with the higher FRI was the opposite of that with the higher mean bone mineral density, indicating that density alone did not explain the asymmetry. Geometric parameters, such as neck-shaft angle, neck width and cortical thickness, also varied between sides, with neck-shaft angle differences of up to 6° within a subject. The side with the higher FRI was not systematically the left or the right: 16 subjects had the higher value on the right and 14 on the left. This suggests that limb dominance or laterality did not produce a consistent trend in this cohort.

**Statistical analysis**

A paired-sample t-test was applied to the left and right FRI values at the superior neck region in the sideways fall configuration. It showed a statistically significant difference between the two sides (p = 0.02, below the 0.05 threshold). The difference at the inferior surface did not reach significance (p = 0.11), and neither did the single-legged stance results at either surface (p = 0.09 and p = 0.14, respectively). Variability therefore concentrated at the superior aspect, which is also the critical site in a fall. Normality of the paired differences was confirmed by the Shapiro–Wilk test (p > 0.05). The correlation between left and right FRI was strong (r = 0.81) but not perfect, so contralateral values could not be treated as interchangeable for individual patients. Bland–Altman analysis gave a mean bias near zero and 95% limits of agreement of roughly ±0.19 FRI units. This range is large enough to change the risk category of a subject near the threshold.

**Sex-based comparison**

The cohort was divided into 14 men and 16 women. Women showed higher FRI values in both limbs and both configurations. In the sideways fall, the mean superior-neck FRI was 0.77 ± 0.15 (left) and 0.80 ± 0.17 (right) in women, compared with 0.58 ± 0.12 and 0.60 ± 0.14 in men. This is an increase of about one third in women. The inter-limb differences were also larger in women (mean 16.1% against 10.7% in men), although the sex difference in asymmetry was not statistically significant given the small subgroup sizes. Women had lower mean bone density and smaller neck cross-sectional area, both consistent with their higher fracture susceptibility.

**Implications of asymmetry for risk classification**

Using an FRI of 0.75 as an illustrative threshold for elevated risk in the sideways fall, 5 subjects (17%) were classified as high risk on one side only. If only one femur, selected at random, had been analyzed, there would have been a 50% chance of missing the elevated risk in each of those subjects. This indicates that single-side assessment may misclassify a notable fraction of patients.

**Interpretation of principal findings**

This study compared fall-induced fracture risk indicators (FRI) between the left and right femurs of thirty subjects using QCT-based finite element models under single-legged stance and sideways fall loading. Two results stand out. First, the loading configuration governs both the location and the magnitude of the critical region. Second, the FRI distributions of the contralateral femurs of the same individual differ enough to be statistically detectable. The first result agrees with earlier biomechanical and clinical observations that a sideways fall shifts the dominant stress state in the femoral neck from the compressive inferomedial pattern of gait and stance to a tensile-dominated pattern at the superolateral neck [1,2]. The thin superior cortex is the weakest part of the neck and also carries the lowest cortical mass, so it is the likely site of fracture initiation in a fall from standing height. Our in vivo models support this mechanism. The large difference in superior FRI between configurations, compared with the modest difference at the inferior surface, indicates that bone loss and cortical thinning at the superior neck are especially consequential in a fall. This finding is consistent with cadaveric experiments in which fractures initiated at the superior cortex under fall loading [3,4].

**Left–right asymmetry and its implications**

Skeletal asymmetry is often assumed to be small, which is the rationale for assessing a single hip in clinical densitometry. However, the paired t-test (p = 0.02) indicates systematic differences in FRI between the sides, most pronounced at the superior aspect, which is also the region most sensitive to loading direction. Several mechanisms may explain this. Limb dominance and habitual asymmetric loading can modify cortical thickness, trabecular architecture and density distribution through mechanoadaptation [5,6]. Differences in neck–shaft angle, femoral neck length and anteversion can alter the stress distribution even when the bone mineral density is similar [7]. Finite element models reflect these geometric and material differences simultaneously, whereas areal BMD from DXA is a projection that is insensitive to them. Previous reports of side-to-side differences in DXA-derived BMD and in QCT-derived strength have generally been modest [8,9], but a small difference in a threshold-based risk classification may still change the clinical category for a patient near the threshold. Because the loads in our simulations were identical for both sides, the observed variation can be attributed to the bone's geometry and material distribution rather than to the loading assumptions.

The practical implication is that selecting one hip at random, as is common in current practice, introduces avoidable uncertainty. If the weaker femur is not the one scanned, risk may be underestimated, and the subsequent fall could fracture the unassessed side. Bilateral assessment, or at minimum a policy of evaluating the lower-strength side, would reduce this misclassification risk. Opportunistic use of CT data already acquired for other purposes could make bilateral FE assessment feasible without additional radiation exposure [10].

**Sex-related differences**

Comparison of the male and female subgroups indicated higher FRI in women, in line with epidemiological evidence that women experience hip fracture more often, and with known sex differences in post-menopausal bone loss, smaller bone size and thinner cortices [11,12]. Because the load magnitude was equal across subjects, the higher indices in women reflect lower structural capacity relative to a given load. In reality, body mass and fall energy vary, so absolute risk would also depend on subject-specific loads. The sex-specific observation should therefore be viewed as supportive of, rather than conclusive for, differences in vulnerability.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The sample of thirty subjects is small, and the subgroup analyses by sex are underpowered, so the results should be considered preliminary. Applying equal load magnitudes to all models isolates the effect of bone properties but ignores subject-specific body weight, soft-tissue attenuation of impact and fall dynamics [13]. Static, quasi-linear loading with a single impact direction does not capture the range of fall orientations or the strain-rate dependence of bone. The density–elasticity relationships used to assign material properties are empirical and carry uncertainty, particularly in the thin cortex where partial-volume effects limit QCT resolution [14]. The FRI is a stress- or strain-based surrogate, so no fracture occurrence was predicted, and without longitudinal fracture outcomes the clinical predictive value of the left–right differences cannot be established. Finally, the cohort was not stratified by limb dominance, history of injury or activity level, which prevents attributing the asymmetry to a specific cause.

**Conclusions and future work**

Within these limitations, the findings show that (i) a sideways fall markedly increases the FRI at the superior femoral neck relative to single-legged stance, identifying this region as the probable initiation site of fall-induced fracture; (ii) FRI distributions differ significantly between the left and right femurs of the same individual, especially at the superior aspect; and (iii) women exhibit higher indices than men under equal loading. Together, these results argue against relying on a randomly chosen single hip for FE-based fracture risk prediction and support bilateral QCT assessment, which could improve the identification of high-risk patients and enable earlier preventive treatment, potentially lowering the economic burden of hip fracture care.

Future work should include larger and more diverse cohorts with stratification by age, sex and limb dominance, subject-specific loading informed by body mass and fall kinematics, and multiple fall directions. Validation against prospective fracture outcomes and ex vivo mechanical tests will be needed to establish thresholds for clinically meaningful asymmetry and to determine whether bilateral FE analysis improves on current tools such as DXA-based T-scores and FRAX [15].

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common muscular dystrophy of childhood, affecting approximately 1 in 5000 live male births. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene that disrupt the open reading frame and abolish production of functional dystrophin in muscle. Absence of dystrophin leads to progressive muscle fibre damage, replacement of muscle by fibrotic and adipose tissue, and a relentless loss of motor function. Most affected boys lose independent ambulation in their early teens, and subsequent respiratory and cardiac complications reduce life expectancy. Corticosteroid treatment is currently the only pharmacological intervention that has been shown to slow the decline in motor function, prolong ambulation and delay the onset of respiratory and cardiac complications, and it has become part of standard care in many countries.

Over the last decade, a number of experimental therapies aimed at the underlying molecular defect have entered clinical development. These include antisense oligonucleotides that induce exon skipping to restore the reading frame, compounds that promote read-through of premature stop codons, gene therapy approaches and agents that act on downstream pathways such as inflammation, fibrosis and muscle regeneration. Several of these have progressed to phase II and III trials, and some have reached regulatory review. The design of such trials depends critically on an accurate understanding of the natural history of the disease in the population being studied. Sample size calculations, the choice of primary outcome measure, the duration of follow-up, the age range for inclusion and the interpretation of any observed treatment effect all rely on knowing how patients are expected to change over time in the absence of treatment, and which factors modify that change.

The assessment of motor function in ambulant boys with DMD has traditionally relied on timed tests, particularly the 6-minute walk test, which has been widely used as a primary outcome in recent trials. Although valuable, timed tests have limitations. They depend on the cooperation and motivation of the child, they are difficult to perform in younger boys, and they capture a limited aspect of function. The NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) was developed as a functional rating scale specifically for ambulant children with DMD. It comprises 17 items, including standing, rising from the floor, stepping, hopping and running, each scored 0, 1 or 2, giving a total score of 0 to 34. The scale has good reliability and validity, it can be used in children from about 3 years of age, and it reflects activities relevant to daily life. The NSAA has been implemented through the UK NorthStar clinical network, which since 2003 has collected standardised data prospectively from many specialist centres. This has created one of the largest longitudinal datasets of motor function in DMD. More recently, Rasch analysis has shown that the raw NSAA score is an ordinal measure and that it can be converted into a linear score from 0 to 100, with equal intervals that allow more appropriate parametric analysis and easier interpretation of change over time.

Several factors are known or suspected to influence the progression of DMD, and these must be understood if they are to be accounted for in trial design. Glucocorticoid treatment is the most important. Most studies of steroids have been conducted in boys starting treatment at around 5 to 7 years of age, when motor function has already begun to plateau or decline. Clinical practice has progressively shifted towards earlier initiation, sometimes before any decline is evident, but evidence about the effect of starting steroids in younger boys on motor performance is limited. Moreover, regimens differ between centres, with daily and intermittent schedules and different molecules in use, and this may further complicate comparisons.

Genotype is a second potential modifier. Although all out-of-frame mutations produce a severe phenotype, there is growing evidence that the location of the mutation may influence the rate of progression. Deletions that are amenable to skipping of particular exons, such as exons 44, 45, 51 and 53, are the targets of different exon-skipping compounds, and each of these subgroups represents a relatively small proportion of the DMD population. Trials in these genetically defined groups will therefore be small, and any differences in their natural history relative to the wider DMD population would have substantial implications for the interpretation of results, particularly when external or historical controls are considered. Previous reports of genotype-related differences in disease course have been limited by small numbers and by the use of outcome measures that were not designed for longitudinal comparison across the full ambulant age range.

In this study we used the NorthStar database to describe the natural history of motor function in a large cohort of ambulant UK boys with DMD, using both raw and linearised NSAA scores. Our aims were to define the trajectory of change with age, the age at loss of ambulation and the level of function preceding it, and to assess the effects of early glucocorticoid initiation. To study the effect of genotype, particularly deletions amenable to skipping of specific exons, we also combined the UK data with those of an Italian cohort of boys assessed with the same scale, thereby increasing the numbers in each genetic subgroup. We hope that these findings will provide information useful for the design of future clinical trials.

Data were collected through the NorthStar Network, a UK-wide collaboration of neuromuscular centres that uses standardised clinical assessments and a shared database for boys with DMD. Assessors at each centre were trained in the administration of the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) and followed a common protocol. Data entered between 2004 and 2012 were analysed. Ethical approval and consent for data collection and use were obtained according to local and national requirements, and data were anonymised before analysis.

**Participants**

Inclusion criteria were a confirmed diagnosis of DMD (clinical phenotype with dystrophin gene mutation or absent dystrophin on muscle biopsy), ambulatory status at the time of assessment, and at least one NSAA recorded. Boys were excluded if their records lacked a date of birth or assessment date, or if they were participating in an interventional trial of a disease-modifying agent at the time of assessment. This yielded 513 ambulant UK boys. For the genotype analysis, we also included 172 boys with DMD from Italian centres who had been assessed with the NSAA using the same protocol, giving a combined genetic cohort.

**Clinical assessments**

The NSAA is a 17-item functional scale developed for ambulant boys with DMD. Items include standing, walking, rising from the floor, stair climbing, hopping, and running. Each item is scored 0 (unable), 1 (modified method, achieves goal without assistance), or 2 (normal), giving a total raw score from 0 to 34. Age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was defined as the age at which the boy could no longer walk independently, with a sustained inability to walk 10 metres, as recorded by the treating clinician. Boys still ambulant at last follow-up were treated as right-censored.

Additional variables extracted were date of birth, date of assessment, genotype, glucocorticoid use (agent, regimen, start date, and stop date), and the centre of assessment.

**Linearisation of NSAA scores**

Because the raw NSAA is an ordinal scale with unequal intervals between total scores, raw scores were converted into linear (interval-level) scores. The conversion used the published Rasch-derived transformation of the NSAA, which maps the raw total (0–34) onto a 0–100 linear scale. Analyses were performed on the linearised score, and results were also expressed on the raw scale for clinical interpretation. Raw-scale equivalents were derived by applying the inverse conversion to the estimated linear values.

**Glucocorticoid exposure**

Glucocorticoid treatment was classified by age at initiation: not treated, started before 3 years, started between 3 and 5 years, and started after 5 years. Boys were classified as treated if they received daily or intermittent prednisolone or deflazacort for at least 6 months. The primary comparison was between boys starting glucocorticoids between 3 and 5 years and those starting later or never treated, with motor function change assessed up to age 7. Regimen (daily versus intermittent) was recorded and examined as a covariate where numbers allowed.
