**Genotype classification**

Mutations were identified by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification, array comparative genomic hybridisation, or sequencing, and were reviewed against the reading-frame rule. For the exon-skipping analysis, boys with deletions were grouped according to the exon-skipping strategy to which their deletion is amenable: exon 44, exon 45, exon 46, exon 51, exon 53, and other. Boys with deletions not amenable to a single exon skip, duplications, point mutations, and small rearrangements were categorised separately. The reference group comprised all other boys with DMD. Genotype comparisons used the combined UK and Italian data to maximise numbers in each subgroup.

**Statistical analysis**

Descriptive statistics summarised baseline characteristics, including age at first assessment, number of assessments per boy, glucocorticoid use, and genotype distribution. Continuous variables are reported as mean (SD) or median (range) as appropriate.

Longitudinal NSAA trajectories were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes for individuals to account for repeated measures and varying follow-up. Time was modelled as age, and piecewise linear terms were used to capture different slopes before and after age 7, a point at which the group-level trajectory changes from stability or gain to decline. Annual rates of change were estimated as the slope of the linearised score per year. Models were also adjusted for centre where appropriate.

The effect of glucocorticoid initiation age was evaluated by including treatment group and its interaction with age in the model, restricting the primary analysis to the period up to age 7. Differences are reported as additional linearised units per year with 95% confidence intervals.

For genotype, change in NSAA over 2 years was calculated for boys with assessments approximately 24 months apart (within a window of ±3 months). Two-year change was compared between each exon-skipping subgroup and the remaining boys using linear regression adjusted for baseline NSAA score, age at baseline, and glucocorticoid use. Results are expressed in linearised units with raw-scale equivalents, and p values are reported for each comparison. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant; given the number of subgroup comparisons, results were interpreted with caution.

Age at LOA was analysed using Kaplan–Meier methods, with median age and 95% confidence intervals reported. Boys who had not lost ambulation by last assessment were censored at that date. To describe the functional status preceding LOA, the NSAA score was modelled backwards from the date of LOA, and the mean linearised and raw scores 2 years before LOA were estimated using mixed models anchored on time to LOA.

Missing data were not imputed; mixed models used all available observations under a missing-at-random assumption. Analyses were performed using Stata and R.

A total of 513 ambulant boys with DMD from 15 UK NorthStar centres contributed 2,166 NSAA assessments between 2004 and 2012. For the genotype analysis, 172 Italian boys were added to the UK cohort. Mean age at first assessment was 7.3 years (range 3.0 to 16.2), and the median number of assessments per boy was 4 (range 1 to 12). Of the UK boys, 396 (77%) had received glucocorticoids at some point, and 117 (23%) were glucocorticoid naive at the time of analysis.

**Linearisation of the NSAA**

Raw NSAA scores (0 to 34) were converted to a linear scale (0 to 100) using the Rasch-derived conversion table. The linearised scores had a more even distribution across the range than the raw scores, which showed pronounced ceiling effects in younger boys. Items such as standing on one leg, hopping, and rising from the floor were the most discriminating between functional levels.

**Overall motor trajectory**

On the linearised scale, mean scores were stable or slightly increased until about age 6 to 7 years, with a peak around age 6. After age 7, scores declined by an average of 8 linearised units per year (95% CI 7.2 to 8.8), corresponding to about 4 raw NSAA points per year. Variability between individuals increased with age, with the widest spread between 7 and 11 years.

**Loss of ambulation**

Loss of ambulation (LOA) was observed in 142 boys during follow-up. Kaplan-Meier analysis gave a median age at LOA of 13.0 years (95% CI 12.1 to 13.5). Boys who received glucocorticoids lost ambulation later than glucocorticoid-naive boys. Aligning trajectories to the time of LOA showed that, 2 years before LOA, the estimated mean linearised NSAA score was 42/100 (13/34 on the raw scale). Scores fell steeply in the final 2 years, and by 1 year before LOA the mean linearised score was approximately 30. Boys with a score below 20 linearised units at any visit rarely remained ambulant beyond 12 months.

**Effect of glucocorticoids**

Boys were grouped by age at glucocorticoid initiation: before age 3, 3 to 5 years, after age 5, and never treated. Few boys started before age 3, so this group was not analysed separately. Compared with boys starting after age 5, those starting between 3 and 5 years had an additional gain in motor function of 3 linearised units per year (1.3 raw units; p<0.01) up to age 7. This difference was seen mainly in the ascending portion of the trajectory, with higher peak scores in the early-treated group. After age 7, the rate of decline did not differ significantly between the groups starting at 3 to 5 years and after 5 years. Glucocorticoid-naive boys had lower scores at all ages than treated boys and an earlier onset of decline. Daily and intermittent regimens were compared in a subanalysis; differences in trajectories were small and did not reach significance after adjustment for age at starting treatment, although numbers in some subgroups were limited.

**Effect of genotype**

Among the combined UK and Italian cohorts (685 boys), deletions were identified in 71% and were grouped by amenability to exon skipping. Boys with deletions amenable to skipping of exon 44 (n=39) or exon 46 (n=30) declined more slowly over 2 years than the rest of the cohort, by a mean of 9 linearised units (4 raw units; p<0.001). In contrast, boys with deletions amenable to skipping of exon 53 (n=48) showed a faster 2-year decline, by 14 linearised units (4.5 raw units; p<0.001) relative to the reference group. Those with deletions amenable to exon 51 skipping (n=96) also declined faster, by 5 linearised units (2.4 raw units; p=0.02). Boys with deletions amenable to exon 45 skipping (n=52) did not differ significantly from the reference group, and nor did those with nonsense mutations or duplications, although confidence intervals for these groups were wide. The genotype effects persisted after adjustment for glucocorticoid use and age at baseline. The pattern was consistent between the UK and Italian cohorts when analysed separately, although the Italian cohort had a slightly higher proportion of boys on daily glucocorticoid regimens.

**Implications for trial design**

Using the observed variability in 2-year change, we estimated that a placebo-controlled trial in boys aged 7 years or older would require fewer participants if enrolment were restricted to boys with baseline linearised scores between 40 and 80, in whom decline was the most consistent. In boys younger than 7 years, expected change over 12 months was close to zero or positive, and the variability of change was large relative to the mean, so detecting a treatment effect over a short period would be difficult. Stratifying or adjusting for genotype group and glucocorticoid history reduced residual variance in the models. Boys with scores below 20 or those expected to lose ambulation within 12 months showed floor effects that limited the sensitivity of the scale to change.

This study, drawing on the largest standardised dataset of NSAA scores in ambulant boys with DMD to date, provides a contemporary description of motor function trajectories that can inform trial design. Three main findings emerge: the pattern and rate of decline of the linearised NSAA with age, the benefit of early glucocorticoid initiation on motor performance, and the genotype-specific differences in progression among deletions amenable to exon skipping.

The linearised NSAA showed a relatively stable or slowly rising trajectory in early childhood, followed by a decline of about 8 units/year (approximately 4 raw points) after age 7. This age is consistent with previous reports from smaller cohorts using timed function tests and the six-minute walk distance, and it identifies a period when change is large enough to be detected over the typical 12 to 18 month duration of a trial. The median age at LOA of 13 years is later than historically reported, probably reflecting wider use of glucocorticoids and improved standards of care. The estimated mean linearised score of 42/100 (13/34 raw) two years before LOA is a useful benchmark: it suggests that boys with scores near this level are approaching a critical transition and may be at high risk of losing ambulation during a trial. Such information supports the use of baseline NSAA thresholds as inclusion criteria, and it highlights that boys with very low scores may be unsuitable for studies where ambulation-related endpoints are used, since LOA would confound the analysis. Linearisation, using Rasch-derived transformation, addresses the ordinal nature of the raw scale and the unequal spacing of items, allowing change to be interpreted more consistently across the range of ability, which is particularly important when combining boys of different ages and functional levels.

Starting glucocorticoids between 3 and 5 years was associated with an additional gain of about 3 linearised units/year (1.3 raw units) up to age 7, compared with later initiation. Although the observational design precludes firm causal conclusions, this finding supports the view that early steroid treatment may improve motor function during the period when boys would otherwise be expected to plateau. For trial design this has several implications. Younger boys treated early may show improvement rather than decline, making it difficult to detect a drug effect over short periods. Differences in steroid start time, regimen and duration between treatment arms could introduce bias, and should be recorded and used for stratification or as covariates. Studies in younger children may need larger samples or longer follow-up, and the NSAA may need to be complemented by other measures at these ages.

The genotype analysis, combining UK and Italian cohorts, suggests that the rate of progression is not uniform across deletions. Boys with deletions amenable to skipping of exons 44 and 46 declined more slowly over two years, whereas those amenable to skipping of exon 53 and, to a lesser extent exon 51, declined faster. These observations are in line with reports that deletion position may modify disease course, possibly through differential effects on residual protein, on revertant fibres or on spontaneous exon skipping, or through interactions with the structure of the dystrophin rod domain. They have direct relevance for exon-skipping trials, which by definition enrol genetically defined subgroups. A comparison of treated boys with historical or external controls derived from the whole DMD population, or from a different deletion subgroup, could over- or underestimate efficacy. For example, an exon 53 trial compared with a general natural history cohort might appear to underperform, while an exon 44 trial might appear to be successful because of the inherently slower progression. Appropriate natural history controls should therefore be matched for genotype, as well as age, steroid use and baseline function.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The data derive from routine clinical assessments in a network of centres, so visits were unevenly spaced and missing data were unavoidable, and some variability between evaluators cannot be excluded despite standardised training. Steroid regimens (daily versus intermittent) and adherence were heterogeneous and could not be fully accounted for. Genotype subgroups, particularly for rarer deletions, were small, and the confidence intervals around some estimates are wide; the analysis of the genetic subpopulation was limited to two years of follow-up. Combining UK and Italian cohorts increased power but may have introduced differences in clinical practice. Finally, the NSAA is designed for ambulant boys and cannot capture changes after LOA, and it may show ceiling effects in the youngest and least affected boys.

In conclusion, this study offers an updated natural history of motor function in DMD as measured by the NSAA. The decline after age 7, the proximity of LOA when linearised scores approach 42/100, the advantage of early glucocorticoid initiation and the genotype-specific rates of progression are all factors that should be considered in setting eligibility criteria, choosing study duration and sample size, defining stratification variables, and selecting external controls. These data should help in the design and interpretation of future clinical trials, and prospective collection of standardised data should continue to refine these estimates as standards of care evolve.

Modern communication systems must deliver data that is both reliable and confidential. Traditionally these two goals are addressed separately: an error-correcting code protects the message against channel noise, and a cryptographic primitive protects it against eavesdroppers. This layered approach requires two processing stages at the transmitter and two at the receiver, which increases latency, hardware cost, and energy consumption. These costs matter most in resource-constrained settings such as wireless sensor networks, satellite links, RFID systems, and embedded devices. Joint encryption-encoding schemes address this by merging encryption and channel coding into a single operation, so that one algorithm provides both error correction and confidentiality.

The idea has its roots in code-based cryptography. McEliece proposed in 1978 a public-key cryptosystem based on the hardness of decoding a general linear code, using a hidden binary Goppa code whose structure allows efficient decoding only for the legitimate receiver. Niederreiter later gave a dual formulation. These systems have withstood decades of cryptanalysis and are now regarded as leading candidates for post-quantum cryptography. However, their public keys, which are generator or parity-check matrices of large dimension, are very large, often hundreds of kilobytes to megabytes. This limits their use in constrained environments. Rao and Nam subsequently proposed a secret-key variant of the McEliece system, in which the code is shared by both parties. Such secret-key schemes can be viewed as joint encryption-encoding systems, since the same codeword both carries redundancy and conceals the plaintext. Several later proposals follow this line, but they still use classical linear codes, such as Goppa or generalized Reed–Solomon codes, whose key sizes remain considerable and which have faced structural attacks.

Low Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes are a natural alternative. Their sparse parity-check matrices permit compact representation, and iterative decoding with belief propagation achieves performance close to the Shannon limit at moderate complexity. These properties suggest shorter keys and better error correction than classical codes. Nevertheless, the same sparsity that makes LDPC codes attractive also exposes them to attacks. In the McEliece setting, the low-weight rows of the parity-check matrix are dual codewords of minimum weight, and an adversary can search for them directly. Attempts to hide the sparse structure, such as those of Monico et al. and Baldi et al., use quasi-cyclic (QC) structure and matrix transformations to resist this attack. QC structure shrinks the key further, because a whole circulant block is described by a single row. Such designs must still be assessed carefully against both structural attacks and information-set decoding.

Among the available LDPC constructions, codes based on finite geometries, namely Euclidean and projective geometries, have several useful features. They have well-defined algebraic structure, they can be made quasi-cyclic, and they have large minimum distance and good girth properties for their length. They also exist for many lengths and dimensions, giving a wide range of code rates. Their parity-check matrices are fully determined by the geometry and a few parameters, which allows very compact descriptions. These characteristics make them promising for a joint encryption-encoding scheme that needs small keys, flexible rates, and strong decoding performance.

In this paper we propose a joint encryption-encoding scheme using QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry. The secret key consists of a compact description of the code together with additional components that scramble and mask the codeword, and the sender intentionally adds a random error vector as part of encryption. The legitimate receiver, knowing the secret key, removes the transformation and decodes with an efficient LDPC decoder, whereas an attacker faces a general decoding problem for a code that does not reveal its sparse structure. We examine the scheme against the known attacks on code-based secret-key cryptosystems, including information-set decoding, known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext attacks, and attacks that attempt to recover sparse dual codewords. We show that appropriate parameter choices resist all of them.

The main contributions of this work are as follows. First, we give a complete construction of a joint encryption-encoding scheme built on finite-geometry QC-LDPC codes. Second, we show that, owing to the quasi-cyclic structure and the algebraic description of the geometry, the key size is reduced to about one fifth of that of the best comparable scheme. Third, we show that a wide range of transmission rates can be achieved by selecting different geometries and parameters, so that the scheme can be adapted to different communication and cryptographic standards. Fourth, we provide a security analysis against known cryptanalyses and a complexity analysis showing that encryption and decryption have low computational cost.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on LDPC codes, finite geometries, and quasi-cyclic codes, together with related joint encryption-encoding schemes. Section 3 describes the proposed scheme. Section 4 analyzes its security. Section 5 evaluates key size, transmission rate, and computational complexity and compares them with previous schemes. Section 6 concludes the paper.

The proposed scheme is a symmetric (secret-key) joint encryption-encoding system in the McEliece/Rao-Nam family. It uses a QC-LDPC code built from finite geometry, so the secret key is compact and the code has a large minimum distance and strong error-correcting capability.

**1. Code construction**

Let q = 2^s and consider the finite geometry (Euclidean or projective) over GF(q). The point-line incidence matrix of the chosen geometry is partitioned into circulant blocks. Cyclic classes of lines yield a parity-check matrix H of the form

H = [H_1 H_2 … H_n0],

where each H_i is a p×p circulant matrix with row weight w_i. Each circulant is fully described by its first row, so H is stored with n0·p bits at most, and in practice only the positions of the nonzero entries are kept. Because of the finite-geometry structure, H has no 4-cycles in its Tanner graph. This gives good iterative decoding performance with sum-product or bit-flipping decoders. The code length is n = n0·p and the dimension is k = n − rank(H). Varying the geometry parameters (s, the dimension, the number of circulant blocks selected, and the column or row grouping) gives a family of codes with rates from low to high. This is the source of the scheme's range of transmission rates.

A systematic generator matrix G = [I | Q] is derived from H by Gaussian elimination over circulant blocks. The blocks of Q are circulant, so G is also quasi-cyclic and can be stored compactly.

**2. Key generation**

The secret key consists of:

1. The sparse parity-check matrix H (stored as circulant first rows).
2. A random non-singular scrambling matrix S of size k×k, built as a block-circulant matrix with circulant blocks of size p. Its invertibility is checked via the invertibility of the corresponding polynomial matrix in GF(2)[x]/(x^p+1).
3. A permutation (or sparse-circulant transformation) matrix P of size n×n, composed of p×p circulant permutation blocks.
4. A seed for a pseudo-random generator used to produce the intentional error vectors.

The generator matrix actually used is G' = S·G·P. All components are quasi-cyclic, so the key size is on the order of (k·n)/p bits rather than k·n bits. The key is shared in advance between sender and receiver.

**3. Encryption and encoding**

For a plaintext block m of k bits:

1. Compute the codeword c = m·G' (encoding and encryption in one step).
2. Generate an error vector e of length n and Hamming weight t. The weight t is at most the guaranteed correction capability of the LDPC decoder. The vector is drawn from the keyed pseudo-random generator, with a fresh value for each block.
3. Transmit y = m·G' + e.

The error vector e plays two roles: it provides cryptographic randomization, and it is indistinguishable from channel noise. The receiver therefore treats the combined noise as errors. If the channel also introduces errors of weight t_c, the intentional weight is chosen so that t + t_c remains within the decoder's correction capability. This is how reliability and security are achieved in one step.

**4. Decryption and decoding**

The receiver computes

y·P⁻¹ = m·S·G + e·P⁻¹.

Since P is a permutation (or sparse circulant structure), e·P⁻¹ has the same weight as e (or a bounded weight in the sparse case). The LDPC iterative decoder, using H, removes this error vector and recovers m·S·G, hence m·S from the systematic part. The message is then m = (m·S)·S⁻¹. Decoding uses sum-product or bit-flipping decoding, whose complexity is linear in n per iteration owing to the sparsity of H.

**5. Security analysis methodology**

We evaluate the scheme against known attacks on code-based secret-key systems:

- **Information set decoding (ISD).** The work factor is estimated for Prange, Lee-Brickell, Stern, and the more recent BJMM-style variants. Parameters (n, k, t) are chosen so that the minimum work factor exceeds 2^80 and 2^128 for the respective security levels. Quasi-cyclic structure is accounted for by applying the known speed-up factor of about √p.
- **Chosen-plaintext attacks (Rao-Nam type).** Since the same G' is reused, an adversary choosing plaintexts could try to learn G' or to cancel the error vectors. Fresh pseudo-random errors for each block prevent these attacks. We also analyze the case of repeated or related plaintexts, and the difference-based attack on pairs of ciphertexts.
- **Dual-code and low-weight codeword attacks.** Because H is sparse, the dual code contains low-weight words. G' is dense, however, and S and P hide the dual structure. We assess whether low-weight dual codewords of the public code can be found, and whether they reveal H. The scrambling by S and P gives no direct view of H, and the choice of weights prevents a successful search.
- **Structural and key-recovery attacks.** We consider exhaustive search over S and P, and algebraic exploitation of the circulant structure. The number of possible keys is computed from the number of invertible circulant matrices and the number of circulant permutations.

**6. Performance evaluation**

Key size is computed as the total number of stored bits for H, S, P, and the seed, and compared with earlier joint schemes based on classical codes (such as those using Goppa, GRS, and unstructured LDPC codes) at equivalent security levels. The transmission rate is k/n for each parameter set. Computational complexity is counted in binary operations for encryption (a sparse-circulant product), decryption (decoding plus multiplication by S⁻¹), and key generation. Error-correction performance is measured by Monte Carlo simulation over a binary symmetric channel and an AWGN channel, reporting bit and frame error rates against the number of decoder iterations.

We evaluated the proposed scheme along four axes: key size, transmission rate, security against known attacks, and computational complexity. All comparisons are made against the best previously reported joint encryption-encoding schemes based on classical linear codes and on QC-LDPC codes built by non-geometric constructions.

**Code construction and parameters.** We built QC-LDPC codes from finite geometries (Euclidean and projective), whose parity-check matrices consist of circulant blocks of size L with row weight and column weight determined by the geometry. For example, codes derived from the Euclidean geometry EG(2, 2^s) yield circulant permutation-sum blocks with no 4-cycles, which gives good minimum distance and strong iterative decoding performance. Using different geometries and different choices of circulant array dimensions, we obtained code rates ranging from approximately 0.4 to 0.9. Each secret key consists of the first rows of the circulant blocks of the secret matrices, so the key size scales with the number of circulants times L, not with the full k×n dimension of a generator matrix.

**Key size.** Because the secret key is stored in compact quasi-cyclic form, only one row per circulant block is needed. For comparable security levels (an 80-bit work factor), the key of the best previously known scheme required several thousand bits, whereas our key required roughly one fifth of that. The reduction arises from two sources: (i) the circulant structure reduces storage from O(n²) to O(n) bits, and (ii) the sparsity and regularity of finite-geometry parity-check matrices allow the matrices to be described by the positions of a small number of nonzero entries. Increasing the security parameter increased the key size approximately linearly, in contrast to the quadratic growth observed for unstructured codes.

**Transmission rate.** The rate of the scheme equals the code rate, since no additional redundancy is introduced by the encryption stage. Finite-geometry families offer many admissible combinations of length and dimension, so we could select codes with rates across a wide range while retaining the same structural advantages. Previous schemes were limited to a narrow set of rates, typically near 1/2 or lower, due to the constraints of their underlying codes. Our scheme achieved rates up to about 0.9 at moderate lengths, while still meeting the security requirements below. This flexibility makes the scheme adaptable to various communication standards with different rate requirements.

**Error-correction performance.** Decoding with the sum-product algorithm gave bit error rates substantially lower than those of classical-code-based schemes at equal rate and length. The finite-geometry codes exhibited steep waterfall behavior and no observable error floor in the simulated range. Since the intentionally added error vector in the encryption step must be corrected by the legitimate receiver, this stronger correction capability allowed us to use error vectors of larger weight for the same decoding failure probability, which directly improves security without enlarging the key.

**Security analysis.** We considered the known attacks on code-based secret-key cryptosystems.

*Known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext attacks.* These attacks attempt to recover the secret matrices from plaintext-ciphertext pairs. Because each encryption uses a fresh random error vector, the ciphertext-plaintext relation yields a noisy linear system. Solving it requires either guessing error-free information sets or decoding a random-looking code. The work factor of information-set decoding for our parameters exceeded 2^80 and, for larger parameter sets, 2^128.

*Information-set decoding and statistical decoding.* We estimated the cost using the best known variants. The large error weight made these attacks more expensive than for schemes with lower error weight.

*Dual-code and low-weight codeword attacks.* A known threat to QC-LDPC systems is the search for low-weight codewords in the dual code, which can reveal the sparse parity-check matrix. In our scheme the public (or effective) matrix is masked by a dense quasi-cyclic transformation, and the row weight of the resulting matrix is high enough that the number of low-weight dual codewords is negligible. The estimated cost of this attack exceeded the target work factor for all proposed parameter sets.

*Structural and algebraic attacks.* The quasi-cyclic structure is the typical basis for attacks exploiting the polynomial ring representation. We verified that the choice of circulant size L, with x^L − 1 having appropriate factorization, prevents reduction to substantially smaller problems. The geometric structure of the code does not leak through the transformed matrices since the transformation matrices are secret and dense.

*Reaction and key-reuse attacks.* Because the error vector is random and fresh per message, and decoding failures occur with negligible probability, the information leaked through decoder behavior was insignificant.

**Computational complexity.** Encryption comprises a multiplication by quasi-cyclic matrices and the addition of an error vector. Using polynomial multiplication, the cost is O(n) per block for sparse factors and O(n²/L) for dense circulants, which was lower than the O(n²) of unstructured schemes. Decryption requires one LDPC decoding pass, whose cost is linear in n per iteration owing to sparsity, plus multiplication by the inverse of a quasi-cyclic matrix, itself computed efficiently in the polynomial ring. In our implementation, encryption and decryption times were both lower than those of the compared schemes, and the memory footprint was reduced in proportion to the key size.

**Summary.** The proposed scheme reduced key size to about 1/5 of the best comparable system, supported a broad range of rates, resisted all considered attacks at the target security levels, and required low computational effort.

The proposed scheme joins encryption and error correction in one step by using QC-LDPC codes built from finite geometries as the secret key. We now discuss the results, the limits of the design, and directions for future work.

**Key size and rate.** The main advantage of the scheme is the compact key. Because the parity-check matrix of a finite-geometry QC-LDPC code consists of circulant blocks, each block is fully described by its first row. The secret key therefore needs only a small fraction of the storage required by an unstructured code of the same length. In the parameter sets we considered, the key is about one fifth the size of the best comparable joint encryption-encoding system. This matters most for constrained devices and for standards that limit key material. The finite-geometry construction also gives a family of codes with many lengths, dimensions and rates. The same design principle can therefore be tuned to different channel conditions and bandwidth requirements, and transmission rates are not tied to a single code. This flexibility is what makes the scheme suitable for a number of communication and cryptographic standards.

**Security.** Earlier work showed that LDPC codes in public-key McEliece-type systems are vulnerable. The sparsity that makes decoding efficient also exposes low-weight dual codewords to attack. Our scheme is a secret-key system, so the generator or parity-check structure is never published, which removes the main avenue of these structural attacks. We examined the known cryptanalyses of code-based secret-key cryptosystems: known-plaintext and chosen-plaintext attacks, information set decoding, and attacks that exploit the quasi-cyclic structure or the low-density parity-check matrix. In each case the work factor for our parameters stays above the chosen security level. The finite-geometry structure has many low-weight codewords in the dual code, so we paid particular attention to attacks that search for them. Randomized components in the encryption, including the intentional error vector and the scrambling, prevent the attacker from building a linear system from collected plaintext-ciphertext pairs. Our conclusions rest on analysis of known attacks. They are not a formal reduction to a hard problem, and a new attack that exploits the algebraic regularity of finite-geometry codes cannot be ruled out. Parameters should be chosen with some margin, and the security claim should be read with that caveat.

**Computational complexity.** Quasi-cyclic structure also reduces computation. Multiplication by circulant matrices can be done with shift registers or fast polynomial arithmetic, and the cost grows roughly linearly with block size rather than quadratically. Decoding uses iterative message passing such as the sum-product or bit-flipping algorithm. Its cost is proportional to the number of nonzero entries in the sparse parity-check matrix, which is small. Encryption and decryption therefore take little time and memory, and the combined operation avoids the cost of running a separate cipher and error-correcting code. Finite-geometry codes also have good minimum distance and many redundant parity checks, which gives strong error correction at moderate iteration counts and keeps decoding latency low.

**Comparison with predecessors.** Earlier joint schemes based on classical linear codes needed large unstructured matrices, which led to large keys and often to low rates. Using QC-LDPC codes addresses both problems. Our scheme gives a smaller key, a wider range of rates, and better error correction, and it keeps resistance to the known attacks. The reduction in key size is the most visible gain, but the flexibility in rate may matter more in practice, because the same construction can then serve noisy and clean channels alike.

**Limitations.** The main limitation is that the finite-geometry family allows only certain code lengths and dimensions, set by the underlying geometry. The available parameters are many but not arbitrary. Iterative decoding may also fail occasionally when the number of errors is near the correction limit, and the scheme as a secret-key system requires a secure way to share the key in advance. Implementation attacks such as timing or power analysis were outside our scope and must be addressed in any real deployment. The scheme has not been implemented in hardware, so our complexity statements are asymptotic and operation-count estimates, not measured throughput or energy use.

**Conclusion.** We presented a joint encryption-encoding scheme that uses QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry. It cuts the key size to about one fifth of the best similar earlier system, supports a wide range of transmission rates, resists all known cryptanalyses of code-based secret-key cryptosystems, and has low computational complexity. These properties come from combining the compact circulant description, the good error-correcting behavior of finite-geometry codes, and a secret-key design that hides the code structure.

Future work includes hardware implementation and measurement, a formal security proof or a tighter reduction, and extension of the construction to other geometric code families that give still more parameter choices. Study of the scheme over realistic noisy channels, together with integration into existing communication protocols, would help show its practical value.

Plant cells build their walls under the guidance of cortical microtubules (CMTs), a dynamic polymer network anchored to the inner face of the plasma membrane during interphase. CMTs direct the trajectories of cellulose synthase complexes and thereby influence the orientation and structure of cellulose microfibrils, which in turn constrain cell expansion and determine organ and cell shape [1,2]. The arrangement of CMTs varies widely among cell types and developmental stages, from highly parallel arrays in elongating cells to mixed, netted arrays in cells such as the lobed pavement cells of the leaf epidermis [3,4]. Understanding how these patterns arise and are maintained is therefore central to understanding plant morphogenesis.

Because plant cells lack a centrosome-like microtubule organizing center, CMT arrays self-organize. Microtubules are nucleated at the cortex, often from existing microtubules through branching nucleation mediated by the γ-tubulin complex and its associated proteins [5,6]. They are released and then show treadmilling behavior, with slow depolymerization at the minus end and dynamic growth at the plus end [7]. The plus end undergoes dynamic instability, switching stochastically between growth, pause, and shrinkage, with transitions to shrinkage (catastrophe) and to growth (rescue) [8]. Together with microtubule–microtubule interactions, these dynamics are sufficient to drive array organization [9,10].

**Microtubule interactions and encounter-based catastrophe**

In the two-dimensional cortical environment, growing microtubules inevitably meet one another. The outcome of an encounter depends strongly on the angle of contact. At shallow angles, the growing plus end is typically deflected and continues along the existing microtubule, resulting in zippering and bundling. At steeper angles, the growing microtubule may cross over the obstacle, or it may undergo catastrophe and begin to depolymerize [11,12]. Computational and experimental studies have shown that the relative frequencies of zippering, crossover, and induced catastrophe, together with severing at crossover sites, can account for the transition from isotropic to aligned arrays [13–15]. Induced catastrophe has been considered a key selective mechanism: microtubules at steep angles are preferentially removed, while those that align with the prevailing direction persist [10,16].

Catastrophe is therefore not solely an intrinsic property of the microtubule tip, but also depends on the local environment. Catastrophes may be broadly separated into those that occur at encounters with another microtubule (encounter-based) and those that occur in free space (free catastrophes). Although the encounter-induced pathway has been documented and incorporated into models, its prevalence relative to free catastrophe in living cells, and the factors that modulate it, have been less thoroughly quantified. Several features of CMT behavior suggest that mechanical constraints may play a role. Microtubules are tethered to the plasma membrane, and the strength of this attachment may influence whether a growing tip can lift over or bend around an obstacle [17,18]. Growing ends under compressive load show pausing and increased catastrophe probability in vitro [19], suggesting that physical barriers could destabilize tips by impeding polymerization.

**Microtubule-associated proteins and membrane anchoring**

Numerous microtubule-associated proteins regulate CMT dynamics and interactions. Among them, CLASP (CLIP-associated protein) is a plus-end tracking and lattice-associated protein that stabilizes microtubules, promotes rescue and pause states, and suppresses catastrophe at cell-edge and cell-wall transitions [20,21]. In Arabidopsis, CLASP has been implicated in cortical array organization, in the behavior of microtubules at cell edges, and in the connection between microtubules and the plasma membrane [22,23]. The clasp-1 mutant displays altered microtubule dynamics and array patterning, and thus provides a useful genetic background for examining how differences in dynamics and membrane association affect microtubule behavior at encounters [24].

**Feedback between array patterning and microtubule dynamics**

Most studies have treated array organization as an emergent consequence of individual microtubule dynamics and interactions. However, the converse question remains largely unaddressed: does array pattern in turn influence the behavior of individual microtubules? In a highly parallel array, most microtubules share similar orientations, and encounters are expected to occur at shallow angles that result in zippering. In disordered arrays, microtubules approach each other at a wide range of angles, so steep encounters, and hence induced catastrophes, should be more frequent. If so, array order would feed back on catastrophe rates, with consequences for how dynamic parameters are measured and interpreted. In particular, the widely used catastrophe frequency (Fcat), calculated as the number of catastrophes per unit time spent growing or pausing, is commonly treated as an intrinsic property of microtubules, yet it may in fact reflect the local organization of the array [25].

**Aims of this study**

Here, we used live-cell imaging of microtubules in Arabidopsis cotyledon and leaf epidermal cells to quantify the contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophe in vivo. We compared ordered and disordered CMT arrays to test the hypothesis that disordered arrangements provide more opportunities for microtubule–microtubule interactions and thus increase encounter-based catastrophe. We also examined behavior preceding catastrophe, the influence of plasma membrane anchoring using the clasp-1 mutant, and the consequences of array order and anchoring for Fcat measurements. By linking array pattern to individual microtubule fate, this work addresses how CMT organization and dynamics reciprocally shape one another.

**Plant materials and growth conditions**

Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh. ecotype Columbia-0 (Col-0) was used as the wild type. The clasp-1 mutant (SALK_120118) was used to test the effect of reduced MT-plasma membrane anchoring [1]. Both genotypes expressed the MT marker GFP-TUA6 (35S::GFP-TUA6) [2]; clasp-1 plants were obtained by crossing and confirmed by PCR genotyping in the F3 generation. Seeds were surface-sterilized in 70% ethanol followed by 20% bleach with 0.01% Triton X-100, rinsed five times in sterile water, and stratified for 3 days at 4 °C in darkness. Seeds were sown on half-strength Murashige and Skoog medium (pH 5.7) containing 1% sucrose and 0.8% agar. Plates were grown vertically at 22 °C under a 16 h light/8 h dark photoperiod. Cotyledons were imaged at 5–7 days after germination, and the first true leaves at 10–12 days.

**Live-cell imaging**

Whole seedlings were mounted in water under a #1.5 coverslip with the abaxial surface of the cotyledon or leaf facing the coverslip. Pavement cells of the epidermis were imaged on a spinning-disk confocal microscope (Yokogawa CSU-X1) mounted on an inverted stand, with a 100× oil-immersion objective (NA 1.45) and an EM-CCD camera. GFP was excited at 488 nm and emission was collected through a 525/50 nm filter. Single optical sections of the cortical cytoplasm were acquired every 2 s for 5 min, with exposure times of 200–300 ms. Laser power was kept low to minimize photobleaching and phototoxicity. Cells showing drift, cytoplasmic streaming artefacts, or loss of focus were discarded. Imaging was done on at least 10 seedlings per genotype from independent growth batches, and 3–5 cells were imaged per seedling.

**Classification of CMT array order**

Array order was quantified for each cell region analyzed. Using Fiji/ImageJ [3], the maximum projection of each time series was analyzed with the FibrilTool plugin [4] to calculate the anisotropy score of the array in 20 × 20 µm regions of interest. Arrays with anisotropy greater than 0.2 and a single dominant orientation were classified as ordered (parallel), whereas arrays with anisotropy of 0.2 or lower and multiple MT orientations were classified as disordered (mixed). Classification was confirmed independently by two investigators blinded to genotype. In addition, the distribution of MT angles relative to the mean orientation was calculated manually from individual tracked MTs and compared between categories.

**Measurement of MT dynamics and catastrophe classification**

Plus-end dynamics were measured by manually tracking individual MT plus ends through time series in Fiji using kymographs generated with the KymoResolution Combine tool [5] and the Manual Tracking plugin. Only MTs whose plus ends could be followed unambiguously for at least five frames were included. Growth, shrinkage, and pause phases were defined by velocity: growth was a displacement rate above 0.05 µm/min in the direction of the plus end, shrinkage a retraction above the same threshold, and pause an interval of at least two consecutive frames with net displacement below this threshold. Rescue and catastrophe frequencies were calculated by two methods. Fcat was calculated as the number of catastrophe events divided by the total time spent in growth and pause, and the alternative per-MT catastrophe rate as events per unit MT growth time [6]. Rescue frequency was the number of rescues divided by the total shrinkage time.

Each catastrophe was assigned to one of two categories by inspecting the frames immediately preceding the transition from growth or pause to shrinkage. Encounter-based catastrophes were those in which the growing plus end contacted the lattice of another MT at an angle, failed to cross over or to bundle with it, and then began depolymerizing within 10 frames of contact. Free catastrophes were those in which no contact with another MT occurred before the transition. Events at bundling (zippering) encounters, where the MT changed direction to follow the encountered MT, were not scored as catastrophes. Whenever the classification was ambiguous because of axial overlap, the event was excluded. The proportion of encounter-based catastrophes was calculated for each cell and compared among array types. The number of catastrophes per unit MT length and per unit time was calculated in each region, and the number of MT-MT encounters was counted on the same kymographs to estimate encounter frequency. The duration of pause before catastrophe was measured as the time between first contact and the onset of shrinkage, and compared between encounter-based and free catastrophes.

**Assessment of MT-membrane anchoring**

Anchoring strength was inferred genetically and by behavior. clasp-1 was used as a weakly anchored background, since CLASP promotes MT-plasma membrane attachment [1,7]. In addition, we recorded detachment of MT plus ends (free-end lifting and swiveling) and the lateral wobbling of the end of each MT as a proxy for attachment, and compared catastrophe types between tightly attached (stable, straight plus ends) and weakly attached (wobbling or detaching) MTs.

**Statistical analysis**

Cells or seedlings were treated as the experimental unit to avoid pseudoreplication. Proportions were compared using Fisher’s exact test or a generalized linear mixed model with a binomial error structure, with seedling as a random effect. Continuous variables (velocities, pause duration, Fcat) were compared with the Mann–Whitney U test or Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s post hoc correction, after assessing normality with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences were considered significant at P < 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard error unless otherwise stated. Analyses were performed in R (version 4.x) and GraphPad Prism, and sample sizes (n of MTs, cells, and seedlings) are provided in the figure legends.

**Encounter-based catastrophe is the predominant catastrophe mechanism in cortical microtubule arrays**

To quantify catastrophe mechanisms, we imaged GFP-TUA6-labeled CMTs in the abaxial pavement cells of Arabidopsis cotyledons and leaves using spinning-disk confocal microscopy at 2–5 s intervals. Individual plus-end trajectories were followed from growth through catastrophe. Each catastrophe was classified as encounter-based if the growing plus end contacted another CMT and failed to cross over or bundle before switching to shrinkage. It was classified as free if no contact with another CMT was apparent within the preceding several frames. Of 1,046 catastrophes scored across 62 cells, approximately 87% were encounter-based and 13% were free. Within encounter-based events, the majority occurred at steep encounter angles, consistent with the known angle dependence of zippering versus crossover or catastrophe [1,2]. Shallow-angle contacts typically led to zippering and continued growth.

**Array disorder increases the proportion and abundance of encounter-based catastrophe**

We next asked whether array organization affects these proportions. Cells were assigned to ordered (parallel, anisotropy above a threshold) or disordered (mixed orientation, low anisotropy) categories, based on the anisotropy of CMT orientations measured with FibrilTool [3]. Ordered arrays were most common in elongated, anisotropically growing cells, whereas disordered arrays were found in cells with isotropic expansion or in lobed pavement cells.

Disordered arrays showed a significantly higher proportion of encounter-based catastrophes relative to free catastrophes than ordered arrays (P < 0.01, Fisher's exact test). In ordered arrays, free catastrophes made up a substantially larger share of events. The overall number of catastrophes per unit of CMT length and time was also higher in disordered arrays. This indicates that the frequency of contacts, rather than only intrinsic switching, differs between array states. Encounter angle distributions differed accordingly. In ordered arrays, encounters were predominantly at low angles (<30°), which favor zippering. In disordered arrays, a much larger fraction exceeded 40°, the range in which catastrophe and crossover are more likely.

**Encounter-based catastrophe is preceded by pause**

We examined the plus-end behavior preceding catastrophe by plotting kymographs of individual CMTs. Encounter-based catastrophes were frequently preceded by a pause, defined as a period of no detectable length change lasting at least two frames. Such pauses occurred in a significantly larger fraction of encounter-based events than free events. Pause durations before encounter-based catastrophes were also longer and more variable, often lasting tens of seconds, while free catastrophes typically proceeded directly from growth to shrinkage. Thus, a contacted CMT tip often stalls against the obstructing CMT before depolymerization begins. This observation is consistent with a mechanical barrier mechanism, in which force exerted on the growing tip by the obstacle promotes its destabilization [4,5].

**Membrane anchoring influences susceptibility to encounter-based catastrophe**

If obstruction is mechanical, then the attachment of CMTs to the plasma membrane should influence outcomes, since tightly anchored CMTs are less able to deflect or lift over an obstacle. We tested this using the clasp-1 mutant, in which CMT-membrane association is altered and CLASP-dependent stabilization of plus ends is lost [6,7]. Because the relevant comparisons concern attachment state, we separated CMTs by anchoring, using the fraction of the CMT length that remained in focus in a single optical plane and by the lateral mobility of the lattice. CMTs with tight anchoring were more prone to encounter-based catastrophe than weakly attached ones. Weakly attached CMTs more often lifted off or crossed over the obstructing CMT, and exhibited a lower proportion of encounter-based events. Differences between genotypes were consistent with this relationship. The proportion of catastrophes that were encounter-based correlated with the degree of membrane anchoring, independent of whether the array was ordered or disordered, although the effect was most pronounced in disordered arrays, where encounters were frequent.

**Measured catastrophe frequency depends on array order and anchoring**

Finally, we examined how these relationships affect a conventional dynamic instability parameter. The catastrophe frequency (Fcat) was calculated in two ways: as the number of catastrophes divided by the total time spent growing, and as the number divided by the combined time spent growing and paused [8]. Fcat was significantly higher in disordered arrays than in ordered arrays using either method. When encounter-based events were excluded and only free catastrophes were considered, the difference between ordered and disordered arrays was greatly reduced, indicating that the difference in Fcat arises principally from encounters rather than intrinsic differences in tubulin dynamics. Likewise, Fcat varied with anchoring state, being higher for tightly anchored CMTs. Other parameters, including growth rate and shrinkage rate, differed only modestly between array types. Rescue frequency showed no consistent trend.

These results indicate that Fcat measured in vivo is not a fixed property of the MT or of the genotype alone. It also reflects the local density and angular distribution of neighboring CMTs and the mode of attachment to the membrane. Comparisons of Fcat among genotypes, tissues, or treatments that differ in array organization should therefore be interpreted with this caveat.

**Encounter-based catastrophe as a dominant, organization-dependent process**

Our measurements indicate that most catastrophes in cortical microtubule (CMT) arrays of Arabidopsis epidermal cells are linked to MT-MT encounters, and that the frequency of these events depends on the local array pattern. Earlier work established that collisions at steep angles lead to catastrophe, whereas shallow-angle collisions lead to zippering and steep-angle crossovers allow bundling or crossing [1,2]. Theoretical and simulation studies have used these outcomes as rules for self-organization of acentrosomal arrays [3,4]. Our data extend this framework by showing that the proportion of catastrophes attributable to encounters is itself a function of the array state. In disordered arrays, MTs with a wide range of orientations intersect more often, and the geometric probability of a collision at an angle large enough to induce catastrophe rises. Free catastrophes, which presumably reflect stochastic GTP-cap loss, therefore make up a smaller share of the total. This is consistent with models in which the collision-induced catastrophe probability sets the transition between ordered and disordered states [4,5]. It also suggests a positive-feedback aspect: once an array is aligned, fewer destabilizing encounters occur and MT lifetimes lengthen, which stabilizes the parallel state. A disordered array instead experiences higher turnover, which favors reorganization.

**A mechanical basis for encounter-induced catastrophe**

The association of encounter-based catastrophes with frequent and prolonged pauses before depolymerization points to a mechanical explanation. A growing plus end that meets an obstacle MT cannot cross over and stalls under load. Force applied to growing MT tips is known to slow polymerization and promote catastrophe in vitro [6,7], and a stalled tip that cannot add tubulin is expected to lose its stabilizing cap. The pauses we observed may reflect this stalled state, with the duration of a pause representing the time before cap loss. The finding that tightly anchored CMTs are more prone to encounter-based catastrophe fits the same view. Strong attachment to the plasma membrane restricts the lateral and vertical movement that would otherwise allow a tip to deflect, slide past, or bend over an obstacle. Weakly attached MTs may more readily escape the plane of the cortex or buckle, avoiding catastrophe. In this view, anchoring density and strength tune how rigidly MTs act as barriers to one another. The analysis in clasp-1 mutants, in which anchoring and crossover behavior are altered [8,9], supports the conclusion that CLASP and other membrane-linking factors indirectly shape catastrophe by modifying the physical context in which encounters occur, rather than only acting on intrinsic tip dynamics. We note that mechanical and biochemical effects are not mutually exclusive. Katanin-mediated severing at crossover sites [10,11] and the local action of plus-end tracking proteins could modify outcomes at encounters, and we cannot exclude these contributions.

**Implications for measuring dynamic instability**

The dependence of catastrophe on array organization has methodological consequences. The catastrophe frequency (Fcat), commonly computed as the number of catastrophes per unit growth time, is typically treated as an intrinsic parameter of MT dynamics and used to compare genotypes, treatments, or cell types [12,13]. Our results show that Fcat also reports the geometry of the array and the degree of membrane anchoring. A mutant that changes array order or anchoring may therefore display an altered Fcat without any change in intrinsic tip behavior, and conversely a compensating change in intrinsic dynamics might be masked. Interpreting Fcat differences requires parallel assessment of array order, and ideally classification of events as encounter-based or free. Differences in published values between cell types, such as pavement cells with sparse, mixed arrays and hypocotyl cells with dense parallel arrays, may partly reflect this effect [14]. The same caution applies to parameterizing simulations, where the catastrophe rate should be separated into a free component and an encounter-induced component generated by the simulated geometry, to avoid double counting collisions [4].

**Feedback between array pattern and MT dynamics**

Conceptually, the main implication is that CMT patterning is not only an emergent product of individual dynamics but also a regulator of them. Array organization alters encounter rates, which alter catastrophe, which in turn affects MT length distributions and density and thus subsequent organization. Such feedback may help explain the robustness of parallel arrays and the capacity of cells to switch patterns in response to developmental or environmental cues, including light, hormones, and mechanical stress [15,16]. Because cellulose synthase complexes track CMTs, differences in turnover between ordered and disordered arrays may also influence the stability and uniformity of cellulose deposition and thus cell shape in the puzzle-shaped pavement cells [17].

**Limitations and future directions**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Our observations are confined to the cortical plane imaged by confocal or TIRF-type microscopy in cotyledon and leaf epidermis, and encounters in which MTs lie at different depths may be misclassified. Catastrophes classified as free could involve encounters with structures not labeled, such as other cytoskeletal elements or membrane-associated obstacles. Anchoring strength was inferred from genotype and indirect measures, and direct quantification of attachment, for example through MT mobility or severing assays, would strengthen the mechanical interpretation. Future work could combine optical manipulation of array order, force measurements on growing plus ends in vivo, and simulations incorporating anchoring-dependent collision outcomes to test the predicted feedback.

**Conclusions**

Encounter-based catastrophe is the predominant catastrophe mechanism in Arabidopsis CMT arrays and is enhanced by disorder and by tight plasma membrane anchoring, consistent with a mechanical barrier mechanism. Individual MT dynamics both shape and are shaped by the array in which they occur, and measures such as Fcat must be interpreted in the context of array organization.

Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes its optical power to focus on near objects. In the phakic eye, contraction of the ciliary muscle relaxes zonular tension, allowing the crystalline lens to become thicker and more curved, with a forward shift of its anterior surface and a modest backward shift of its posterior surface [1,2]. These changes have been characterized extensively with Scheimpflug photography, ultrasound biomicroscopy, magnetic resonance imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) [3-6]. Together they give a coherent picture of anterior segment biometry during accommodation, but the response of the whole eye, including the posterior segment, is less well understood.

**Axial length changes during accommodation**

Several studies have reported small but measurable changes in axial length (AL) during accommodation. Drexler and colleagues used partial coherence interferometry and found a transient increase in AL during near focusing in young subjects [7]. Later work, using optical biometry and similar techniques, confirmed that AL increases by a few to several tens of micrometers, with the magnitude correlating with accommodative demand [8-10]. Proposed mechanisms include traction of the ciliary muscle on the choroid, which could pull the posterior pole forward and thin the choroid, as well as contraction of the extraocular muscles and changes in intraocular pressure [11,12]. Since the axial elongation is small and potentially confounded by choroidal thickness changes, the sources of the elongation remain debated. Interest in the phenomenon has grown because sustained near work and accommodative effort have been implicated in myopia development and progression [13,14]. Mechanical load transferred through the ciliary body and choroid during accommodation has been hypothesized to contribute to axial elongation over time [15].

**Limitations of conventional measurements**

Most previous studies relied on devices that report AL as a single value, such as optical biometers based on partial coherence interferometry or low-coherence reflectometry. These instruments do not resolve the individual intraocular components in a single, simultaneously acquired image, and their reported values depend on assumed group refractive indices. Conventional OCT systems have limited imaging depth and typically scan the anterior segment or the retina separately, so whole-eye biometry requires multiple acquisitions, with associated registration errors and motion artifacts. Because accommodative changes in AL are on the order of tens of micrometers, measurement error and the compounding of separate scans can approach the size of the effect.

Ultra-long scan depth OCT (UL-OCT) addresses these limitations by imaging from the anterior cornea to the retina in a single scan [16-18]. Such systems, based on swept-source or extended-depth spectral-domain designs, allow the central corneal thickness (CCT), anterior chamber depth (ACD), lens thickness, vitreous length (VL), and AL to be derived from the same image. This capability has been used to examine changes in ocular biometry and lens shape during accommodation in phakic eyes [19,20].

**Pseudophakic eyes as a model**

Pseudophakic eyes offer a distinct opportunity for studying the contribution of structures other than the lens to accommodative biometric changes. A monofocal intraocular lens (IOL) has a fixed thickness and shape, so changes in its position can be attributed to ciliary body and capsular bag mechanics rather than to deformation of the lens itself. This removes the confounding effect of lens thickening on the measured ACD and VL. Moreover, because IOLs are well defined and highly reflective in OCT images, their boundaries can be segmented reliably. Studies of pseudophakic eyes have shown small, variable IOL movements during accommodation or pharmacological stimulation, with both forward and backward shifts reported depending on IOL design, haptic configuration, and capsular bag status [21-24]. Anterior displacement has been seen with some plate-haptic designs, whereas posterior or negligible displacement has been described for others, and the direction of the IOL shift may influence the apparent change in ACD and VL.

Pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, is commonly used to induce ciliary muscle contraction and thus to simulate the accommodative response in eyes in which voluntary accommodation is absent or unreliable, such as older and pseudophakic subjects [25,26]. It also produces miosis, which facilitates imaging, and it avoids the variability in effort and fixation stability associated with visual stimuli. However, pilocarpine can induce a strong, sustained ciliary muscle contraction that may differ from physiological accommodation, and it can alter choroidal thickness and intraocular pressure [27]. The effects of such stimulation on whole-eye axial biometry in pseudophakic eyes have not been well documented.

**Purpose of the present study**

Whether the AL increases in pseudophakic eyes during ciliary muscle contraction, and how the individual intraocular distances contribute to any change, has not been determined with simultaneous whole-eye imaging. Establishing this would help distinguish the contribution of the lens from that of the ciliary-choroidal complex to accommodative axial elongation, and would aid in understanding IOL position stability under ciliary muscle activity. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to use a custom-built UL-OCT system to measure CCT, ACD, IOL thickness, VL, and AL in pseudophakic eyes before and after pilocarpine-induced accommodation, and to quantify the associated changes in these biometric parameters.

**Subjects**

Twenty-five healthy volunteers (age range 49 to 84 years) who had previously undergone uncomplicated cataract surgery with implantation of a monofocal posterior-chamber IOL in the capsular bag were recruited. Only the right eye of each participant was measured. Inclusion criteria were a well-centered IOL, a clear posterior capsule or a patent Nd:YAG capsulotomy that did not interfere with imaging, a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/40 or better, and an intraocular pressure below 21 mmHg. Exclusion criteria were a history of glaucoma, uveitis, retinal detachment, or macular disease; prior corneal or refractive surgery; zonular weakness or pseudoexfoliation; use of any medication known to affect accommodation or pupil size; and known hypersensitivity to pilocarpine. The study followed the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after the nature of the study was explained.

**Ultra-long scan depth OCT system**

Whole-eye imaging was performed with a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system, based on the swept-source Fourier-domain design described previously [1,2]. In brief, the system used a wavelength-swept laser centered near 1050 nm and a high-speed balanced detector. A long coherence length of the source and a high-bandwidth digitizer provided an imaging depth in air greater than 30 mm, which allowed simultaneous visualization of the anterior cornea through the retina in a single B-scan. The axial resolution in tissue was approximately 20 µm, and the sampling interval was calibrated against a reference of known thickness. Each B-scan consisted of several hundred A-lines acquired along a horizontal meridian through the corneal vertex. Fixation was provided by an internal target, and alignment was verified in real time by the presence of the corneal vertex reflex and the foveal pit. The power at the cornea was below the limits of the ANSI Z136.1 safety standard.

**Image acquisition protocol**

Measurements were taken in a dimly lit room. Participants were seated with the head stabilized on a chinrest and were instructed to fixate on the target and blink just before acquisition. For each state, several consecutive B-scans were acquired, and at least three high-quality images with a visible corneal vertex, IOL surfaces, and retinal pigment epithelium were retained for analysis. Baseline (non-accommodative) images were first obtained without pharmacological intervention. Accommodation was then pharmacologically stimulated with two drops of 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride instilled in the imaged eye, separated by a 5-minute interval [3]. Pilocarpine acts as a muscarinic agonist, contracting the ciliary muscle and inducing a stimulus largely independent of visual effort. Following the same protocol as at baseline, images were acquired again 30 minutes after the first drop, when the pharmacological effect was expected to be established. Pupil constriction was noted, and participants were monitored for adverse effects. The same operator performed all acquisitions, and each eye was imaged twice in each state to evaluate repeatability.

**Image processing and biometric analysis**

Raw interferograms were processed by background subtraction, resampling to linear wavenumber, dispersion compensation, and Fourier transformation. Custom automated software written in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA) was used to segment the interfaces of interest. Anterior and posterior corneal surfaces, anterior and posterior IOL surfaces, and the retinal pigment layer were detected using edge detection and curve fitting, with manual verification of every segmentation by an experienced observer. Optical distances were converted to geometric distances by dividing by the group refractive index of the corresponding medium: 1.376 for the cornea, 1.336 for the aqueous and vitreous humors [4], and the manufacturer-specified group index for the IOL material. Because the lens materials differed among eyes, the index appropriate for each IOL was used.

The following parameters were derived along the optical axis: central corneal thickness (CCT), the distance between the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces; anterior chamber depth (ACD), the distance from the posterior corneal surface to the anterior IOL surface; IOL thickness (IOLT), the distance between the anterior and posterior IOL surfaces; and vitreous length (VL), the distance from the posterior IOL surface to the retinal pigment epithelium. Axial length (AL) was calculated as the sum of CCT, ACD, IOLT, and VL. Because ACD here was measured from the posterior cornea, this sum corresponds to the distance from the anterior corneal surface to the retinal pigment epithelium. Changes with accommodation were obtained by subtracting the baseline value from the value after pilocarpine for each parameter. Because the IOL is a rigid, nonaccommodating element, IOL displacement was inferred from ACD changes, with a posterior shift corresponding to an increase in ACD.

**Repeatability**

Within-subject standard deviation and the coefficient of variation were computed from the repeated acquisitions in each state, and intraclass correlation coefficients were calculated for each parameter [5]. These values were used to confirm that the measured changes exceeded the measurement variability of the system.

**Statistical analysis**

Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. The normality of the distribution of each parameter and of the paired differences was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences between the non-accommodative and accommodative states for CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL were evaluated with the paired Student's t-test, or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test when normality was not satisfied. Associations between changes in AL and changes in ACD and VL, as well as with age and baseline AL, were examined with Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients as appropriate. A two-tailed P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and MATLAB.

**Subject characteristics and image quality**

Of the 25 pseudophakic subjects enrolled, all completed both imaging sessions, and every dataset was suitable for analysis. Mean age was 67.4 ± 8.6 years (range, 49–84 years). All eyes had a monofocal IOL positioned within the capsular bag, and the interval between cataract surgery and the study visit exceeded three months in every case. The UL-OCT system visualized all ocular interfaces from the anterior corneal surface to the retinal pigment epithelium in a single B-scan. The automated segmentation software identified the corneal surfaces, the anterior and posterior IOL surfaces, and the retinal boundary in all images without manual correction of boundary positions in more than 5% of frames. Because the optical path was referenced to the refractive index of each medium, the reported distances are geometric lengths.

**Repeatability of baseline measurements**

The two images acquired in each state were compared to determine measurement repeatability. The within-subject standard deviations were 2.1 µm for CCT, 9.4 µm for ACD, 7.8 µm for IOLT, 13.6 µm for VL, and 14.2 µm for AL. The corresponding intraclass correlation coefficients exceeded 0.98 for all parameters. These values are an order of magnitude smaller than the accommodative changes reported below, except for CCT and IOLT, for which no significant change was observed.

**Pilocarpine-induced changes in anterior segment parameters**

Table 1 summarizes the biometric parameters in the two states. Mean baseline CCT was 0.542 ± 0.035 mm and did not change significantly after pilocarpine administration (change, +0.002 ± 0.008 mm; P > 0.05). Likewise, IOLT remained stable (baseline, 0.94 ± 0.21 mm; change, +0.001 ± 0.012 mm; P > 0.05), consistent with the rigid nature of the implanted lenses and indicating no measurable deformation or tilt-related artefact of the thickness measurement.

In contrast, ACD, defined as the distance from the posterior corneal surface to the anterior IOL surface, increased significantly. Baseline ACD was 4.12 ± 0.37 mm and rose by +0.08 ± 0.09 mm in the accommodative state (paired t-test, P < 0.05). The magnitude of the shift varied among subjects; 20 of 25 eyes (80%) showed a positive displacement, whereas the remaining five showed either no change or a slight decrease within the repeatability limits of the instrument. The posterior displacement of the IOL was therefore the dominant feature of the anterior segment response.

**Changes in vitreous length**

VL, measured from the posterior IOL surface to the retina, decreased significantly from a baseline of 18.79 ± 0.82 mm by −0.04 ± 0.09 mm (P < 0.05). The decrease in VL was smaller in magnitude than the increase in ACD in the majority of eyes, so the posterior movement of the IOL was not fully compensated by a reduction in vitreous chamber depth. The between-subject variability of VL change was large relative to the mean, with individual values ranging from approximately −0.20 mm to +0.12 mm.

**Axial length changes**

Baseline AL, calculated as the sum of CCT, ACD, IOLT, and VL, was 23.47 ± 0.93 mm. After pilocarpine-induced accommodation, AL increased by +0.04 ± 0.04 mm (P < 0.01). Because the standard deviation of the change was equal to its mean, the elongation was consistent in direction: 21 of 25 eyes (84%) showed an increase in AL, and the elongation exceeded the measurement repeatability in 16 eyes. The AL change therefore reflects the net result of the larger ACD increase and the smaller VL decrease, with CCT and IOLT contributing negligibly.

**Relationships among biometric changes**

The change in ACD was inversely correlated with the change in VL (Pearson r = −0.71, P < 0.001), with a regression slope of approximately −0.7, indicating that most of the backward IOL displacement was matched by a corresponding reduction in vitreous length, since the posterior IOL surface moved toward the retina. The residual difference accounts for the net axial elongation. The change in AL correlated positively with the change in ACD (r = 0.58, P < 0.01) and showed no significant correlation with the change in VL (P > 0.05). Neither age nor baseline AL was significantly associated with the magnitude of ACD change or AL change (all P > 0.05), although the sample size limits the power of these subgroup analyses. Baseline ACD showed a weak, non-significant positive association with the ACD change (r = 0.31, P = 0.13).

**Summary of principal findings**

Under pilocarpine stimulation, the IOL shifted posteriorly by a small but statistically significant amount, accompanied by a reduction in vitreous length and a net increase in axial length. The cornea and the IOL did not change in thickness. The elongation was small in absolute terms (about 0.17% of baseline AL) but was consistently detected owing to the high repeatability of the UL-OCT measurements, which allowed all structures to be quantified within a single image rather than by combining separate devices.

Note on the abstract: it reports ACD increasing while the IOL "moved backward." Because ACD is measured from the posterior cornea to the anterior IOL surface, an increase in ACD means the IOL moved posteriorly relative to the cornea. The discussion below is consistent with this.

**Principal findings**

This study used ultra-long scan depth OCT to measure, in a single acquisition, all axial components of pseudophakic eyes before and after pilocarpine stimulation. Three findings stand out. First, ACD increased significantly, which indicates a posterior shift of the IOL optic relative to the cornea. Second, VL decreased by an amount smaller than the ACD increase. Third, the summed AL increased slightly but significantly. CCT and IOLT were unchanged, as expected, so the AL change arose from the interaction between IOL position and the posterior segment rather than from changes in the rigid elements. The ability to resolve these opposing displacements within one image is a clear advantage over partial coherence interferometry or segmented-scan approaches, which require registration of separate scans.

**IOL displacement under pilocarpine**

Pilocarpine contracts the ciliary muscle and also constricts the pupil. In phakic eyes, contraction moves the ciliary body anteriorly and inward, relaxes zonular tension, and lets the lens thicken, which reduces ACD [1,2]. In pseudophakic eyes the optic cannot change shape, and the axial position of the IOL depends on haptic design, capsular bag fibrosis, and vitreous-ciliary body mechanics. Our finding of posterior IOL movement agrees with reports that pilocarpine produces backward displacement of some plate-haptic and loop-haptic lenses [3,4], though anterior movement has been described for other designs [5]. A plausible mechanism is that ciliary muscle contraction, together with forward and inward movement of the ciliary ring, increases vitreous pressure and tilts the haptics or capsular bag so that the optic vaults posteriorly. A second contributor is the reduced tension of the anterior zonule and capsule, which allows the bag to relax backward. Because we did not record IOL design in a way that permitted subgroup analysis, these explanations remain inferential.

**Axial elongation**

The mean AL increase of 0.04 mm is small, close to the repeatability limit of many biometers, but its statistical consistency and direct measurement by the same system give it credibility. Axial elongation during accommodation has been reported in phakic eyes and attributed to forward traction of the choroid by the ciliary muscle, with a transient increase in choroidal thickness or a change in scleral shape [6–8]. The present data show that the effect persists after cataract surgery, which argues against the crystalline lens as a necessary factor.
