MRI and CT are widely used, but they are costlier, are affected by motion and dental artifacts, and may not be easily accessible; MRI can also overestimate depth because of peritumoral edema. Intraoral USG is inexpensive, noninvasive, quick, repeatable, and free of radiation. It has high spatial resolution for superficial structures such as the tongue and can be performed in the outpatient clinic in the same session as ultrasound evaluation of the neck. Its limitations include difficulty accessing posterior or very painful lesions, trismus, and a gag reflex. Because our study was restricted to early T1 and T2 lesions of the oral tongue, which are usually accessible, these limitations were not major obstacles.

The second objective was to evaluate whether TT can predict occult nodal metastasis. The rate of occult metastasis in our series was 16.6% (4/24), which falls within the 20-30% range often cited for early oral cancers, although the lower figure may reflect our small sample and the use of preoperative neck USG to select truly N0 patients. Notably, no patient with TT below 4 mm had nodal metastasis, whereas metastases appeared in tumors of 4 mm and above. This finding agrees with studies suggesting that the risk of occult metastasis rises substantially once thickness exceeds approximately 3-5 mm, and with the recommendation of many centers to perform elective neck dissection when depth of invasion exceeds 4 mm. Prospective evidence from randomized trials has shown a survival benefit for elective over therapeutic neck dissection in early oral cancer, and this has encouraged more selective strategies for identifying patients who truly need it. Preoperative USG-derived TT may help to spare patients with very thin tumors the morbidity of neck dissection, such as shoulder dysfunction, and to support closer observation in them, while advising elective dissection in those with thicker lesions. Because our institutional protocol was to perform ipsilateral elective neck dissection (levels I-IV) in all patients, the pathological nodal status was available for every patient, which gives some strength to the observed relationship between TT and nodal disease.

This study has limitations. The sample is small (24 patients), and the number of node-positive patients is very small, so the 4 mm threshold should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive; confidence intervals would be wide, and sensitivity and specificity could not be estimated robustly. The study was single-center, and a single operator or a small number of operators performed the sonography, which limits generalizability and precludes assessment of interobserver variability. We did not evaluate other histological risk factors, such as perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, tumor budding, or differentiation grade, which may interact with thickness in predicting nodal metastasis. Follow-up was not analyzed for survival or regional recurrence outcomes. Larger multicenter studies with standardized USG technique and long-term outcomes are needed to validate a clinically useful cutoff.

In conclusion, intraoral ultrasonography is a reliable, inexpensive, and readily available method for preoperative measurement of tumor thickness in early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, with good correlation and agreement with histopathology, although individual discrepancies of several millimeters can occur. TT of 4 mm and above was associated with occult cervical nodal metastasis, whereas no metastasis occurred below this value. Preoperative USG measurement of TT may therefore assist in deciding whether to perform elective neck dissection in clinically node-negative patients, pending confirmation in larger prospective studies.

Bacterial biofilms are structured communities of cells embedded in a self-produced extracellular matrix of polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and extracellular DNA. They are now recognized as the predominant mode of bacterial life in both natural and clinical settings [1]. It is estimated that biofilms are involved in a large majority of chronic and recurrent infections, including those associated with implanted medical devices, chronic wounds, cystic fibrosis lung disease, osteomyelitis and endocarditis [2,3]. Biofilm-embedded bacteria tolerate antibiotic concentrations that are 10 to 1000 times higher than those that kill their planktonic counterparts, so standard therapy frequently fails and infections relapse [4]. This tolerance is multifactorial. The matrix limits antibiotic diffusion and can bind or inactivate drugs, steep nutrient and oxygen gradients create zones of slow-growing or dormant cells, and a subpopulation of metabolically inactive persister cells survives lethal exposure without carrying heritable resistance determinants [5,6]. Persisters are widely considered the main reservoir for relapse and a stepping stone toward genetic resistance [7].

The clinical problem is aggravated by the global spread of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among the ESKAPE pathogens, which include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Acinetobacter baumannii* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* [8]. Treating a biofilm infection therefore resembles sailing between Scylla and Charybdis. Increasing antibiotic doses to overcome biofilm tolerance leads to systemic toxicity, as with aminoglycosides and polymyxins, and promotes resistance selection. Using conventional doses, in contrast, leaves the biofilm intact. New antibiotics are few, and few of them have specific anti-biofilm activity [9]. Alternative strategies are therefore needed, and combination therapy with adjuvants that sensitize biofilms to existing drugs is among the most attractive. Proposed approaches include matrix-degrading enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, chelators, and agents that revive persisters metabolically [10,11].

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a natural source of such adjuvants. They are evolutionarily ancient effectors of innate immunity found in virtually all organisms, and they are typically cationic and amphipathic [12]. Many AMPs act on bacterial membranes, which are targets that are hard to modify by mutation, and some also interact with intracellular targets [13]. Importantly, several AMPs are active against slow-growing and dormant cells and can penetrate or disrupt biofilms, which distinguishes them from many classical antibiotics whose action depends on active cell growth [14,15]. Synergy between AMPs and conventional antibiotics has been reported repeatedly. Permeabilization of the outer or cytoplasmic membrane by the peptide may increase intracellular access of the small-molecule drug, while the antibiotic may in turn weaken the cell’s ability to repair peptide-induced damage [16,17]. Nevertheless, clinical development of individual AMPs has been hampered by toxicity, proteolytic instability, high production costs and the limited activity of single peptides in physiological conditions [18].

In nature, however, the host does not rely on a single peptide. Immune responses produce mixtures of AMPs of different structural classes that act together and often synergistically, which broadens the activity spectrum and reduces the chance of resistance emerging [19,20]. The resulting complexity cannot be reproduced by studying isolated peptides. Insects are a particularly rich source of such multicomponent systems, as their humoral immunity depends largely on inducible AMPs secreted into the hemolymph after infection [21]. The blowfly *Calliphora vicina* is notable in this respect. Its larvae live in highly contaminated necrotic substrates and have been used for centuries in maggot debridement therapy of chronic wounds, which is attributed in part to antimicrobial and anti-biofilm secretions [22,23]. Upon bacterial challenge, *C. vicina* produces a set of AMPs that includes defensins, cecropins, diptericins and proline-rich peptides, which differ in structure and mechanism of action [24,25]. Defensins and cecropins act mainly on membranes, whereas proline-rich peptides can enter the cell and inhibit protein synthesis and chaperone function [26]. A natural combination of these peptides could therefore attack bacterial cells at several levels at once.

We previously isolated from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged *C. vicina* larvae a complex of AMPs, designated FLIP7 (fly immunity peptides), and showed that it contains these four peptide classes [27]. Whether such a native host AMP complex can potentiate conventional antibiotics against biofilms, and by what mechanism, has not been systematically examined. Most synergy studies to date have used planktonic cultures, synthetic single peptides and a narrow range of antibiotics, and they rarely distinguish between effects on growing cells, persisters and the biofilm matrix [16,28].

In this study we hypothesized that the AMP complex of the host immune system can improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics. We tested FLIP7 in combination with antibiotics of different classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, glycopeptides, macrolides, lincosamides, phenicols, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and polymyxins. Model biofilms and planktonic cultures of *S. aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, *P. aeruginosa*, *K. pneumoniae* and *A. baumannii* were used. Interactions were quantified by the checkerboard method with fractional inhibitory concentration indices, using a cell viability assay based on trimethyl tetrazolium chloride and a crystal violet biofilm eradication assay supplemented with microscopy. We also compared biofilm and planktonic interactions, analyzed dose–effect curves for signs of persister involvement, and evaluated whether the combinations allow the effective anti-biofilm antibiotic concentration to be lowered below clinically achievable levels.

FLIP7 isolation. Third-instar larvae of the blowfly Calliphora vicina were reared at 25 °C and challenged by pricking with a needle dipped in a suspension of Escherichia coli and Micrococcus luteus to induce the immune response [1]. Hemolymph was collected 24 h after challenge, acidified with 1% acetic acid, and centrifuged at 14,000 g for 20 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was loaded onto Sep-Pak C18 cartridges (Waters) equilibrated with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). After washing with 5% acetonitrile, peptides were eluted with 60% acetonitrile in 0.1% TFA and lyophilized. The fraction was further purified by solid-phase extraction and reversed-phase HPLC on a Jupiter C18 column (Phenomenex) using a linear acetonitrile gradient in 0.1% TFA. Fractions containing the defensin, cecropin, diptericin and proline-rich peptide groups were pooled in native proportions to obtain the complex designated FLIP7. Peptide composition was verified by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (Bruker Ultraflex) and compared with known masses of C. vicina AMPs [1,2]. Total peptide concentration was determined by the bicinchoninic acid assay and by absorbance at 280 nm, and stock solutions were stored at −20 °C.

Bacterial strains and growth conditions. The study used Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213, Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853, Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700603 and Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 19606, as well as clinical isolates of each species from the departmental collection. Cultures were stored in 20% glycerol at −80 °C and grown on tryptic soy agar. For experiments, single colonies were grown overnight in cation-adjusted Mueller–Hinton broth (CAMHB) at 37 °C with shaking, diluted, and grown to mid-logarithmic phase. Suspensions were adjusted to 0.5 McFarland (~1.5×10^8 CFU/mL) and diluted as required.

Antibiotics. Meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, gentamicin, ampicillin, oxacillin, cefotaxime, vancomycin, clindamycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin and polymyxin B (Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved according to the manufacturers’ instructions, filter-sterilized and prepared freshly or stored at −20 °C. Not all antibiotics were tested against all species; combinations were selected according to the clinical relevance and intrinsic activity of each drug.

Minimal inhibitory concentrations. MICs for planktonic cultures were determined by broth microdilution in 96-well plates according to CLSI guidelines [3], with a final inoculum of 5×10^5 CFU/mL. Plates were incubated for 18–20 h at 37 °C. MIC was defined as the lowest concentration preventing visible growth. Minimal biofilm-inhibitory concentrations were determined as described below.

Biofilm formation. Biofilms were grown in 96-well polystyrene flat-bottom plates. Overnight cultures were diluted to 10^6 CFU/mL in tryptic soy broth supplemented with 1% glucose (S. aureus) or 0.25% glucose (Gram-negative species), and 100 µL was added per well. Plates were incubated statically for 24 h at 37 °C. Planktonic cells were removed, and wells were washed twice with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to leave adherent biofilms. Fresh medium containing test agents was then added and plates were incubated for a further 24 h.

Checkerboard assay. Interactions between FLIP7 and antibiotics were assessed by the checkerboard method [4] in two-dimensional serial twofold dilutions, with antibiotic along the rows and FLIP7 along the columns, in both planktonic and biofilm formats. Growth and sterility controls were included on each plate. Cell viability was measured by reduction of 2,3,5-triphenyl (trimethyl) tetrazolium chloride (TTC): after treatment, 0.1% TTC was added and plates were incubated for 2 h at 37 °C in the dark; formazan was dissolved in ethanol and absorbance measured at 490 nm. The concentration yielding ≥90% decrease in absorbance relative to untreated control was taken as the inhibitory endpoint. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated as FICI = MIC(A in combination)/MIC(A alone) + MIC(B in combination)/MIC(B alone), and the minimal FICI for each combination was used. Interactions were interpreted as high synergy (FICI <0.25), synergy (0.25–0.5), additivity (>0.5–1), indifference/no interaction (>1–4) and antagonism (>4) [5]. Each checkerboard was run in triplicate on at least three independent days.

Dose–effect analysis. Dose–effect curves of antibiotics alone and with fixed sub-inhibitory FLIP7 concentrations were fitted with a four-parameter logistic model in GraphPad Prism. Biphasic profiles and plateau levels of residual viability were examined as indicators of a persister subpopulation tolerant to the antibiotic [6]. Changes in plateau height and in the half-effective concentration were compared between conditions.

Crystal violet biofilm eradication assay. After 24 h treatment, wells were washed twice with PBS, fixed with methanol for 15 min, air-dried, and stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 15 min. Excess dye was removed by washing with water, and bound dye was solubilized in 30% acetic acid. Absorbance was read at 570 nm. The minimal biofilm eradication concentration was defined as the lowest concentration reducing biomass by ≥90% relative to untreated biofilm. Results were compared with peak serum concentrations achievable clinically, taken from published pharmacokinetic data [7].

Microscopy. Biofilms were grown on glass-bottom dishes or coverslips and treated with antibiotic, FLIP7, or their combination for 24 h. Samples were examined by phase-contrast microscopy and by confocal laser scanning microscopy after staining with the LIVE/DEAD BacLight kit (SYTO 9/propidium iodide; Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Additional samples were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde, dehydrated through an ethanol series, sputter-coated and imaged by scanning electron microscopy to evaluate integrity of the biofilm matrix. At least five fields per sample were captured.

Statistical analysis. All experiments were performed in at least three biological replicates with technical triplicates. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Differences between groups, including FICI values in planktonic versus biofilm cultures, were assessed by Student’s t-test or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, after testing for normality. P < 0.05 was considered significant. Analyses were carried out in GraphPad Prism 9.

FLIP7 was obtained from the hemolymph of bacteria-challenged C. vicina larvae by solid-phase extraction followed by reversed-phase HPLC. The preparation contained the four major AMP families known for this species: defensins, cecropins, diptericins and proline-rich peptides, as confirmed by mass spectrometry [12,14]. The complex was used as a single entity in all experiments, and its concentrations are given as total peptide content.

**Activity of FLIP7 and antibiotics alone.** The minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of FLIP7 and of the antibiotics were first determined for planktonic cultures of S. aureus, E. coli, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii. FLIP7 was most active against S. aureus and E. coli and less active against P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii. Biofilm-embedded cells were considerably less susceptible than planktonic cells to all antibiotics tested. The minimum biofilm inhibitory concentrations (MBICs) exceeded the planktonic MICs by one to three orders of magnitude, depending on the drug and strain, and for several beta-lactams they were above clinically achievable concentrations. FLIP7 alone also showed a higher MBIC than MIC, but the difference was smaller (about 2- to 8-fold) than for the small-molecule antibiotics.

**Interaction of FLIP7 with antibiotics in biofilms.** Checkerboard assays with the trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) viability readout revealed interaction patterns that depended on antibiotic class. The fractional inhibitory concentration indices (FICI) are summarized in Table 1. High synergy (FICI <0.25) was observed for meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin and cefotaxime. Vancomycin was tested only against S. aureus. Synergy (0.25 ≤ FICI ≤ 0.5) was found for clindamycin, erythromycin and chloramphenicol. Additive interaction (0.5 < FICI ≤ 1) was characteristic of oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin and gentamicin. Polymyxin B showed no interaction (FICI >1 and ≤4) with FLIP7 in any of the species. The pattern was reproducible across the Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains, with only minor strain-specific shifts in FICI values. Antagonism (FICI >4) was not detected in any combination.

**Planktonic versus biofilm cultures.** The same combinations were examined in planktonic cultures of the same strains. In these, the interaction was significantly weaker than in biofilms (p < 0.05, paired comparison of FICI values). Combinations that were highly synergistic in biofilms, such as meropenem or ampicillin with FLIP7, typically gave only synergy or additivity in planktonic cells. Several combinations that were additive in biofilms were indifferent in planktonic culture. Thus the potentiating effect of FLIP7 was specific to the biofilm mode of growth rather than a general enhancement of antibiotic activity.

**Dose–effect analysis.** To explore the mechanism underlying the synergy, we analyzed the dose–effect curves of antibiotics alone and in the presence of subinhibitory FLIP7. In biofilms, antibiotic alone produced biphasic curves: viability fell over the low concentration range and then reached a plateau of 10–40% residual viability that persisted over a wide concentration range, a pattern typical of a tolerant subpopulation of persister cells [5,8]. In the presence of FLIP7, the plateau was abolished and the curves became monophasic, with complete loss of viability at antibiotic concentrations close to the lower, sensitive-phase range. The shift was most evident for beta-lactams and aminoglycosides. In planktonic cultures, the plateau was much less pronounced, and FLIP7 changed the curve position only modestly. These observations suggest that the persister fraction is the main target of the synergistic effect, since the sensitive majority was already killed by antibiotic alone.

**Biofilm eradication assay.** Crystal violet staining was used to assess the effect on biofilm biomass for S. aureus and E. coli. Antibiotics alone at sub-MBIC concentrations left the biomass largely unchanged, and FLIP7 alone caused only partial reduction. In combination, the biomass was reduced to background staining levels, indicating total destruction of the biofilm material. Microscopy supported these findings. Control biofilms displayed dense multilayered structures with an intact matrix. Antibiotic-treated biofilms retained this architecture, with some cell damage. Biofilms exposed to the combination consisted of scattered cells and cell debris, and the continuous matrix was absent. FLIP7 alone produced intermediate disruption, with loosening of the structure and the appearance of gaps. The effect on biomass was observed at FLIP7 concentrations at which no complete killing of planktonic cells occurred.

**Reduction of effective antibiotic concentrations.** The practical consequence of the synergy was a marked decrease in the antibiotic concentration needed for anti-biofilm action (Table 2). In the presence of FLIP7, the effective anti-biofilm concentrations of meropenem, ampicillin, cefotaxime and oxacillin decreased by 2–3 orders of magnitude and fell well below the serum concentrations clinically achievable with standard dosing [20]. For amikacin, kanamycin, vancomycin, clindamycin, erythromycin and chloramphenicol, the reduction was 8- to 100-fold, and in many cases the combined concentrations were also within the therapeutic range. For ciprofloxacin, tetracycline and gentamicin, the reduction was modest (2- to 8-fold), consistent with additivity. For polymyxin B, no reduction was observed. The effect was seen both for strains susceptible to the antibiotic and for strains in which biofilm-associated tolerance resulted in MBIC values above the clinical breakpoints.

The present study shows that FLIP7, a natural complex of insect antimicrobial peptides, markedly potentiates antibiotics of different classes against model biofilms of Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergy was strongest with β-lactams, aminoglycosides and glycopeptides, and it was consistently stronger in biofilms than in planktonic cultures of the same strains. This difference points to a mechanism specific to the biofilm lifestyle rather than a simple additive increase in membrane damage.

Biofilm tolerance to antibiotics is multifactorial. It involves restricted diffusion through the matrix, steep metabolic gradients, and a subpopulation of dormant persister cells that survive lethal drug exposure without carrying resistance mutations [1,2]. The shape of the dose–effect curves in our experiments suggests that persisters are the principal target of the synergy. Biphasic killing curves, in which a resistant plateau follows the initial decline, are the classic signature of persisters [2]. In the presence of FLIP7 this plateau was abolished or shifted to much lower antibiotic concentrations. Cationic AMPs can permeabilize membranes irrespective of the growth state of the cell, which makes them attractive against dormant bacteria that are insensitive to drugs targeting active biosynthesis [3,4]. A plausible model is that sublethal membrane perturbation by defensins, cecropins and diptericins increases the uptake of antibiotics, including those that are normally poorly accumulated. Proline-rich peptides, which enter cells and inhibit intracellular targets such as DnaK and the ribosome [5], may add a further hit. Such a mechanism would explain the particularly strong synergy with aminoglycosides, whose uptake depends on membrane potential, and with cell-wall inhibitors, which gain better access to their targets when the outer layers are compromised.

The biofilm eradication assay adds a second component to the effect. FLIP7 combined with antibiotics caused total destruction of S. aureus and E. coli biofilm material, as shown by crystal violet staining and microscopy. This suggests that the peptides also act on the matrix or on the cells that maintain it. Some AMPs are known to disrupt extracellular DNA and to interfere with matrix assembly [6,7]. Killing of embedded cells will itself reduce matrix integrity, and the two processes probably reinforce each other: matrix loosening improves penetration of both peptides and antibiotics, which in turn kills more cells. Because the mixture contains several peptide families, it is likely that different components contribute different activities, in line with the view that the multicomponent nature of innate immune secretions is an evolutionary adaptation against resistance and tolerance [8].

The lack of interaction with polymyxin B is informative. Polymyxins and AMPs both act on anionic membrane components, so their targets overlap, and little additional benefit would be expected from combining them. This supports membrane permeabilization as a central element of FLIP7 action. The merely additive effects with tetracycline, ciprofloxacin and gentamicin indicate that synergy is not universal and depends on the antibiotic's mode of action and uptake route. Fluoroquinolones, for example, diffuse readily and may already reach their targets in biofilms, leaving less room for enhancement.

From the translational perspective, the most important finding is the reduction of the effective anti-biofilm antibiotic concentration by two to three orders of magnitude for meropenem, ampicillin, cefotaxime and oxacillin, to levels well below those clinically achievable. Biofilm eradication usually requires concentrations that are unattainable in tissue without toxicity [1]. Lowering these requirements could make existing drugs effective again, including in situations where an organism appears resistant by planktonic testing. This adjuvant strategy is consistent with current attempts to pair antibiotics with potentiators rather than to rely only on new antibacterial scaffolds [9]. The use of a complex mixture isolated from bacteria-challenged larvae also mimics the host's natural strategy, in which a cocktail of peptides acts together with other effectors. Maggot-derived secretions have long been used in wound debridement, and the present results offer a molecular rationale for their benefit in chronic infected wounds [10].

Several limitations should be noted. The work used in vitro static biofilm models, which do not reproduce the host environment, with its proteases, serum components, immune cells and polymicrobial communities. AMPs may be inactivated by proteolysis or by binding to serum and tissue components, and their potential cytotoxicity and immunogenicity have to be evaluated. The individual contributions of the peptide classes were not resolved, and the proposed mechanisms, particularly persister sensitization, are inferred from dose–effect curves and microscopy rather than shown directly, for instance by persister enrichment or time-kill assays with defined dormant populations. A limited number of strains was tested, and the generality of the effect across clinical isolates and resistance mechanisms remains to be confirmed. Finally, the checkerboard method describes interaction at fixed exposure times and may not capture the dynamics of resistance emergence.

Future work should therefore address the activity of FLIP7 and its fractions in dynamic flow and in vivo models of biofilm infection, such as catheter-associated and chronic wound infections, together with pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies. Identification of the minimal peptide combination responsible for synergy would facilitate standardization and possibly recombinant or synthetic production.

In conclusion, FLIP7 is an effective host-derived antimicrobial system that helps antibiotics overcome biofilm barriers by sensitizing persister cells and destroying biofilm material. It strongly synergizes with a broad range of small-molecule antibiotics and allows their effective concentrations to fall far below clinically achievable levels. These findings support the development of AMP complexes as adjuvants for the treatment of biofilm-associated infections.

Protein arginine methylation is a widespread post-translational modification that contributes to the regulation of chromatin structure, transcription, RNA processing, signal transduction, and DNA damage response [1,2]. The modification is catalyzed by the protein arginine methyltransferase (PRMT) family, whose nine mammalian members use S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor to generate monomethylarginine, asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA), or symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA). PRMTs are classified by product: type I enzymes (PRMT1, 2, 3, 4/CARM1, 6, and 8) generate ADMA, type II enzymes (PRMT5 and PRMT9) generate SDMA, and PRMT7 is a type III enzyme that catalyzes only monomethylation [3]. Dysregulation of several PRMTs has been linked to human disease, and PRMT5 and type I PRMT inhibitors have advanced into clinical evaluation in oncology, supporting the tractability of this enzyme class as a therapeutic target [4,5].

**CARM1 biology**

Coactivator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1 (CARM1, also known as PRMT4) was first identified as a binding partner of the p160 steroid receptor coactivator GRIP1 and was shown to enhance nuclear receptor-dependent transcription [6]. CARM1 methylates histone H3 at arginine 17 and arginine 26 (H3R17me2a, H3R26me2a), marks associated with transcriptional activation [7]. In addition, CARM1 methylates a diverse set of non-histone substrates, including transcriptional coactivators such as p300/CBP and SRC-3, chromatin remodeling components such as BAF155, and RNA-binding and splicing factors such as PABP1, SmB, CA150, and HuR [8–10]. Through these substrates CARM1 has been implicated in transcriptional coactivation, pre-mRNA splicing, mRNA stability, cell cycle progression, autophagy, and differentiation of cell types including adipocytes, chondrocytes, and hematopoietic cells [11,12]. Germline Carm1 deletion in mice results in perinatal lethality, underscoring its importance in development, while conditional models have revealed context-specific roles in the hematopoietic and immune systems [13,14].

**CARM1 in cancer**

CARM1 overexpression has been reported in breast, prostate, colorectal, and hepatocellular carcinomas, among others, and often correlates with poor prognosis [15–17]. In estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, CARM1 functions as a coactivator of ERα-dependent gene expression and promotes proliferation [18]. In prostate cancer, CARM1 is upregulated in castration-resistant disease and coactivates androgen receptor and E2F1 programs [16]. Methylation of BAF155 by CARM1 has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential in breast cancer [9]. More recently, CARM1 has been linked to hematologic malignancies, where it contributes to leukemic transformation driven by fusion oncoproteins such as AML1-ETO and MLL-associated alterations [19]. However, most of these conclusions derive from RNA interference, overexpression, or genetic knockout studies, which cannot readily distinguish catalytic from scaffolding functions and are poorly suited to pharmacologic validation in vivo.

**Limitations of existing CARM1 tool compounds**

Efforts to develop small-molecule CARM1 inhibitors have produced several chemotypes, including SAM-analogue and bisubstrate inhibitors, pan-PRMT inhibitors such as AMI-1, and compounds identified by screening, such as TBBD and related benzimidazoles [20–22]. Most of these suffer from limited potency, poor selectivity against other PRMTs and methyltransferases, low cell permeability, or unfavorable pharmacokinetic properties. More selective compounds, such as the substrate-competitive inhibitor SGC2085 and the peptidomimetic and bisubstrate series, show good biochemical potency but little or no cellular activity [23,24]. Consequently, no CARM1 inhibitor has been available that combines biochemical potency, selectivity across the methyltransferase family, cellular target engagement, and oral exposure sufficient for efficacy studies in animal models. This gap has hindered clarification of which cancer types depend on CARM1 catalytic activity and has limited assessment of CARM1 as a therapeutic target.

**Multiple myeloma as a potential CARM1-dependent malignancy**

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a malignancy of terminally differentiated plasma cells that remains largely incurable despite advances with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory agents, and anti-CD38 antibodies, and relapsed or refractory disease continues to present a major clinical challenge [25]. Epigenetic dysregulation is a recognized feature of MM, and inhibition of chromatin-modifying enzymes such as EZH2 has shown preclinical activity [26,27]. Notably, public cell line dependency and expression datasets suggest that a subset of MM lines is sensitive to CARM1 depletion, and CARM1 substrates including PABP1 and SmB are highly expressed in plasma cell contexts characterized by intense transcriptional and secretory demands. These observations led us to hypothesize that CARM1 enzymatic activity supports MM cell proliferation and that selective pharmacologic inhibition could provide anti-tumor benefit.

**Present study**

Here we report the discovery and characterization of EZM2302 (GSK3359088), a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable small-molecule inhibitor of CARM1. We describe its biochemical potency and selectivity against a panel of histone methyltransferases, its effect on cellular methylation of the CARM1 substrates PABP1 and SmB, and its anti-proliferative activity across MM cell lines. We further demonstrate pharmacodynamic target inhibition and dose-dependent anti-tumor efficacy following oral administration in an MM xenograft model. Together, these data establish a role for CARM1 catalytic activity in MM models and provide the research community with a validated chemical probe for interrogating CARM1 biology in cancer and other diseases.

**Compounds and reagents.** EZM2302 (GSK3359088) was synthesized at Epizyme as described in the Supplementary Information and dissolved in DMSO for in vitro studies. For in vivo studies it was formulated in 0.5% methylcellulose with 0.1% Tween-80 in water. Recombinant human proteins, peptide substrates and S-adenosyl-L-[methyl-³H]methionine (³H-SAM) were obtained from commercial suppliers. Antibodies are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

**Biochemical methyltransferase assays.** CARM1 inhibition was measured with a radiometric filter-plate assay [1]. Recombinant full-length human CARM1 (final concentration 0.25 nM) was preincubated with a ten-point, three-fold serial dilution of compound for 30 min at room temperature in assay buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 0.002% Tween-20, 0.005% bovine skin gelatin, 1 mM DTT). Reactions were initiated by adding ³H-SAM and a biotinylated histone H3 (residues 16–30) peptide, each at its approximate Km, and allowed to proceed for 1 h. They were quenched with excess unlabeled SAM, transferred to streptavidin-coated FlashPlates, and read on a scintillation counter. IC50 values were obtained by fitting percent inhibition to a four-parameter logistic equation in GraphPad Prism. Selectivity was determined against a panel of at least 30 histone, protein and DNA methyltransferases, including PRMT1, PRMT3, PRMT5, PRMT6, PRMT8, EZH2, DOT1L and SETD2, using analogous radiometric formats at Km substrate concentrations. For mechanism-of-action studies, initial velocities were measured while varying SAM or peptide at fixed inhibitor concentrations, and the data were analyzed by global fitting to competitive, uncompetitive and mixed inhibition models.

**Cell culture.** Human multiple myeloma cell lines (including RPMI-8226, NCI-H929, MM.1S and U266) were obtained from ATCC, DSMZ or JCRB and maintained in RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10–20% fetal bovine serum, as recommended by the supplier, at 37 °C in 5% CO₂. Identities were confirmed by short tandem repeat profiling, and cultures were routinely tested negative for mycoplasma.

**Cellular methylation assays.** Cells were seeded at 2 × 10⁵ cells/mL and treated with EZM2302 or DMSO (0.2% final) for 72 h. Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors, and proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were probed with antibodies specific for asymmetric dimethylarginine on PABP1 (me-PABP1) and SmB (me-SmB), and with antibodies against total PABP1, SmB and β-actin as loading controls. Signals were detected by fluorescence imaging and quantified with Image Studio software. Methylation signals were normalized to total protein and expressed relative to vehicle. Cellular EC50 values were derived by nonlinear regression. Alternatively, an in-cell immunofluorescence assay was used for higher throughput.

**Proliferation assays.** Cells were plated in 96-well plates at densities optimized for logarithmic growth over the assay duration and treated with a nine-point compound dilution series in triplicate. Viable cells were counted every 3–4 days by CellTiter-Glo luminescence, and cultures were split and replenished with fresh compound at each time point. Cell numbers were normalized to DMSO controls, and IC50 values at day 14 were calculated with a four-parameter fit. Cytostatic versus cytotoxic effects were assessed by comparing cell numbers with the starting density, and by flow cytometry for cell-cycle distribution (propidium iodide) and apoptosis (annexin V/7-AAD) after 6–10 days of treatment.

**CARM1 knockdown.** Lentiviral vectors encoding doxycycline-inducible shRNAs targeting CARM1 or a non-targeting control were produced in HEK293T cells and used to transduce MM cell lines, followed by puromycin selection. CARM1 depletion and substrate methylation were confirmed by immunoblot after doxycycline induction, and proliferation was monitored as above.

**Pharmacokinetic studies.** All animal studies were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines. Female mice (CD-1 for pharmacokinetics; n = 3 per time point) received EZM2302 intravenously or by oral gavage. Blood was collected at defined intervals up to 24 h, and plasma compound concentrations were measured by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry against a standard curve. Noncompartmental parameters (Cmax, AUC, half-life, clearance, oral bioavailability) were calculated using Phoenix WinNonlin.

**Xenograft efficacy and pharmacodynamics.** Female athymic nude or SCID mice (6–8 weeks old) were inoculated subcutaneously in the flank with 1 × 10⁷ RPMI-8226 cells in 50% Matrigel. When tumors reached approximately 150–200 mm³, animals were randomized by tumor volume into treatment groups (n = 10). EZM2302 (37.5, 75, 150 or 300 mg/kg) or vehicle was administered by oral gavage twice daily for 21 days. Tumor dimensions and body weights were measured twice weekly; tumor volume was calculated as (length × width²)/2. Tumor growth inhibition was calculated relative to vehicle at study end, and differences were evaluated by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA with Dunnett's post hoc test. For pharmacodynamic analysis, tumor-bearing mice were dosed for 7 days, and tumors and plasma were collected at defined times after the final dose. Tumors were snap-frozen, homogenized and analyzed by immunoblot or ELISA for me-PABP1 and me-SmB, and the results were correlated with plasma and tumor drug exposure.

**Statistical analysis.** Data are presented as mean ± SD or SEM as indicated, from at least three independent experiments unless otherwise stated. Comparisons used two-tailed Student's t-test or ANOVA as appropriate, with P < 0.05 considered significant. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism.

**Identification of EZM2302 as a potent CARM1 inhibitor.** To identify small-molecule inhibitors of CARM1, we screened a focused library of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)-competitive and substrate-site-directed chemotypes using a radiometric biochemical assay with a histone H3 peptide substrate. Medicinal chemistry optimization of an initial hit series, guided by structure-activity relationships and cellular PABP1 methylation readouts, yielded EZM2302, a compound containing a 2-substituted ethylenediamine-based scaffold. EZM2302 inhibited recombinant human CARM1 with an IC50 of 6 ± 2 nM (n = 6). Kinetic analysis showed that inhibition was uncompetitive with respect to SAM and noncompetitive with respect to peptide, consistent with binding to the CARM1-SAH/SAM complex [1,2]. Surface plasmon resonance confirmed high-affinity binding to CARM1 that was enhanced in the presence of the cofactor product SAH.

**Selectivity profile.** We tested EZM2302 against a panel of 33 methyltransferases, including type I PRMTs (PRMT1, 3, 6, 8), type II PRMTs (PRMT5, PRMT9), and lysine methyltransferases (EZH1/2, DOT1L, SETD2, NSD1/2, G9a, SUV39H1, among others). EZM2302 showed no appreciable inhibition of any other enzyme at concentrations up to 10 µM except PRMT6, for which the IC50 was more than 500-fold higher than for CARM1. Selectivity over PRMT1, the enzyme most closely related functionally, exceeded 10,000-fold. In a broader off-target screen against 50 receptors, ion channels, transporters, and kinases, no activity greater than 50% inhibition was observed at 10 µM. These data support the use of EZM2302 as a selective chemical probe. A structurally related inactive analog, differing by a single modification that reduced CARM1 potency by more than 1,000-fold, was used as a negative control in subsequent experiments.

**Inhibition of CARM1 substrate methylation in cells.** CARM1 methylates PABP1 and the spliceosome-associated protein SmB (SMB), and these were used as pharmacodynamic markers. In RPMI-8226 cells, EZM2302 reduced asymmetric dimethylation of PABP1 and SMB in a concentration-dependent manner, as determined by immunoblotting and in-cell Western assays with methyl-specific antibodies. Cellular IC50 values were 0.038 µM for PABP1 methylation and 0.019 µM for SMB methylation after 3 days. Total PABP1 and SMB protein levels were unchanged. Global asymmetric dimethylarginine was reduced only modestly, as expected for an enzyme that accounts for a minor fraction of cellular type I PRMT activity, whereas the inactive analog had no effect on substrate methylation. Importantly, EZM2302 did not alter histone H3R17 dimethylation levels in a manner that distinguished it from substrate effects, and it did not affect PRMT1-dependent or PRMT5-dependent marks (H4R3me2a and symmetric dimethylarginine, respectively), confirming cellular selectivity.

**Anti-proliferative activity in multiple myeloma cell lines.** Given reports of elevated CARM1 expression in hematological malignancies, we evaluated EZM2302 in a panel of human cancer cell lines in 14-day proliferation assays. Multiple myeloma (MM) cell lines were among the most sensitive. EZM2302 inhibited proliferation of RPMI-8226, NCI-H929, MM.1S, and other MM lines with IC50 values ranging from 0.015 to 1.8 µM, whereas several non-MM lines were insensitive. Anti-proliferative effects emerged slowly, with separation from vehicle control only after approximately 6 to 8 days of treatment, a time course characteristic of epigenetic enzyme inhibitors. Cell-cycle analysis revealed an accumulation of cells in G1, with minimal induction of apoptosis as measured by annexin V staining and caspase activation, consistent with cell stasis rather than cytotoxicity. The inactive analog did not affect proliferation at concentrations up to 10 µM. CARM1 knockdown with two independent shRNAs in RPMI-8226 cells reduced PABP1 methylation and proliferation, phenocopying pharmacological inhibition.

**Pharmacokinetics and in vivo target engagement.** EZM2302 displayed low-to-moderate clearance and acceptable oral bioavailability in mice (F = 45%), supporting oral dosing. Following single oral administration to mice bearing RPMI-8226 xenografts, plasma and tumor exposures increased in a dose-proportional manner. Methylated SMB and PABP1 in tumor tissue were reduced in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with marked suppression at 6 hours after dosing at 100 and 200 mg/kg. Pharmacodynamic inhibition tracked with plasma and tumor compound concentrations, establishing a relationship between exposure and CARM1 inhibition in vivo. Inhibition of SMB methylation was also observed in peripheral blood, suggesting a potential surrogate tissue for clinical monitoring.

**Anti-tumor efficacy in an MM xenograft model.** Mice bearing established subcutaneous RPMI-8226 tumors were treated orally with EZM2302 at 37.5, 75, 150, or 300 mg/kg twice daily, or 300 mg/kg once daily, for 21 days. EZM2302 produced dose-dependent tumor growth inhibition, reaching 63% at 150 mg/kg twice daily and 81% at 300 mg/kg twice daily (p < 0.001 versus vehicle, repeated-measures ANOVA). Lower doses gave intermediate effects. Treatment was well tolerated, with no significant body weight loss or overt toxicity. Terminal tumor analysis showed dose-dependent reduction of PABP1 and SMB methylation that correlated with the degree of tumor growth inhibition (Pearson r = 0.8), linking target engagement to efficacy. Collectively, these results demonstrate that selective pharmacological inhibition of CARM1 impairs MM cell proliferation in vitro and tumor growth in vivo.

**Mechanistic and translational implications of CARM1 inhibition**

The data presented here establish EZM2302 as a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable CARM1 inhibitor and provide, to our knowledge, the first evidence that pharmacological CARM1 inhibition suppresses multiple myeloma (MM) proliferation in vitro and in vivo. Earlier work implicated CARM1 in oncogenic transcriptional programs, including estrogen receptor and p53 co-activation, and in the regulation of RNA processing [1,2]. Interrogating these roles in cancer has depended on genetic knockdown or on compounds with limited selectivity, potency, or cellular permeability [3,4]. Genetic approaches cannot easily distinguish catalytic from scaffolding functions, and they are poorly suited to studying the kinetics of target engagement or the reversibility of phenotypes. A selective catalytic inhibitor with in vivo exposure addresses these limitations directly.

**Pharmacodynamic markers and target engagement**

Reduced methylation of PABP1 and SMB (SmB/B′) tracked with CARM1 inhibition in cells and in tumor tissue. These substrates therefore serve as pharmacodynamic markers that link biochemical potency to cellular and in vivo activity. The dose-dependent reduction of methylation in xenograft tumors, together with anti-tumor effect, supports the conclusion that efficacy arises from on-target CARM1 inhibition. This is further supported by the selectivity profile against other histone methyltransferases, including the closely related type I PRMTs. Nonetheless, selectivity panels cover only a subset of the methyltransferase family and of the broader proteome, and orthogonal confirmation will remain important. Useful approaches include rescue with inhibitor-resistant CARM1 mutants, comparison with a structurally distinct inhibitor, and use of an inactive control compound. The latter two are standard criteria for a validated chemical probe [5].

The observation that cell growth is inhibited with a cytostatic rather than cytotoxic profile is consistent with the phenotype of many epigenetic and post-translational modification targets, in which antiproliferative effects emerge after prolonged exposure [6]. The delayed onset of effect in the proliferation assays suggests that the consequences of CARM1 inhibition accumulate through altered gene expression or RNA processing rather than acute loss of viability. This has implications for dosing schedules and for the design of combination studies, in which sustained target coverage is likely to be more important than transient peak exposure.

**Why multiple myeloma?**

The sensitivity of a subset of MM cell lines suggests a context-dependent reliance on CARM1 activity. MM is characterized by dependence on specific transcriptional regulators and by high secretory and proteostatic demand, which may render RNA-processing and transcriptional co-activator functions of CARM1 particularly important [7]. The mechanistic basis remains incompletely defined. Candidate explanations include effects on splicing through SmB and other spliceosomal substrates, on mRNA stability through PABP1, and on chromatin-associated substrates such as histone H3 arginine 17 and BAF155. Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling after EZM2302 treatment, combined with CARM1 substrate methylome analysis, should help to identify the pathways that drive growth arrest. It also remains unknown whether CARM1 expression level, substrate methylation status, or another biomarker predicts sensitivity. Defining such a biomarker would be essential for any patient-selection strategy.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the in vivo efficacy was demonstrated in a single xenograft model derived from a cell line, which cannot capture the bone marrow microenvironment, clonal heterogeneity, or immune interactions of human disease. Evaluation in orthotopic or disseminated models, patient-derived samples, and co-culture systems with stromal cells will be necessary. Second, tumor growth inhibition was partial at tolerated doses, indicating that CARM1 inhibition may be most valuable in combination with established MM agents such as proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, or other epigenetic modulators. Third, the sensitivity of only a subset of cell lines suggests that resistance mechanisms, whether intrinsic or acquired, may limit monotherapy activity, and these have not yet been explored. Fourth, CARM1 has physiological roles in development, metabolism, and muscle and immune function [8], so long-term safety of sustained inhibition requires careful assessment. The tolerability observed in the present studies is encouraging but of limited duration.

**Value as a chemical probe and future directions**

Beyond oncology, the availability of a well-characterized, orally active CARM1 inhibitor enables investigation of CARM1 biology in other settings in which it has been implicated, including inflammation, metabolic regulation, and differentiation. The compound's in vivo properties allow temporal control of target inhibition, which is difficult to achieve with genetic models. Future work should address the structural basis of inhibitor binding and selectivity, define the full set of CARM1 substrates affected in MM, and test rational combinations.

**Conclusion**

EZM2302 is a potent and selective CARM1 inhibitor that reduces substrate methylation and impairs proliferation of MM cells, and it demonstrates dose-dependent pharmacodynamic and anti-tumor activity after oral administration. These findings support CARM1 as a tractable therapeutic target in MM and provide the research community with a validated chemical probe to dissect the catalytic functions of CARM1 in cancer and other diseases. Continued mechanistic, biomarker, and combination studies will determine whether CARM1 inhibition can be translated into clinical benefit.

Recommender systems have become an integral part of the online experience. They help users navigate large collections of products, media, and people, and they are deployed in domains as varied as entertainment, e-commerce, social networking, and employment [1, 2]. Their success rests on exploiting the collective behavior of users: by identifying patterns in past interactions, recommenders deliver highly targeted, personalized suggestions that would be impossible to produce through manual curation. Collaborative filtering, in particular, infers the preferences of a user from those of similar users, and it remains one of the most widely used families of recommendation algorithms [3, 4].

The same property that makes recommenders effective also makes them vulnerable. Because they learn from user behavior, they inherit whatever biases that behavior contains. Users may preferentially consume items of certain genres, interact more with content produced by particular demographic groups, or favor items with particular attributes. Such tendencies are reflected in the data and, in turn, in the models trained on them. The concern about bias in algorithmic decision making has grown considerably in recent years, with studies documenting discriminatory outcomes in areas such as advertising, hiring, and criminal justice [5, 6]. In recommendation, bias can affect both the users who receive recommendations and the providers or items that are recommended, with consequences for visibility, exposure, and economic opportunity [7, 8].

Reproducing the biases of the input is a concern in itself, but a more subtle problem arises when a recommender amplifies them. We refer to this phenomenon as *bias disparity*: the degree of bias in the recommendations differs from, and in particular exceeds, the degree of bias in the data from which the recommendations were produced. For instance, if users of a given group show a moderate preference for items of a given category, a recommender may respond by suggesting items of that category far more often than the input would justify. Bias disparity is distinct from the mere presence of bias. It captures the change introduced by the algorithm and therefore points to the recommender itself as a contributor to the problem. Related effects have been discussed under labels such as popularity bias, filter bubbles, and feedback loops [9, 10, 11], but these notions typically concern a single dimension, such as item popularity, or the narrowing of individual user experience. Bias disparity offers a more general lens for comparing preference distributions over arbitrary groups of users and categories of items before and after recommendation.

Understanding when and why bias disparity occurs is important for several reasons. First, amplification can reinforce stereotypes, for example when recommendations steer different demographic groups toward different types of content or opportunities. Second, because recommendations influence what users subsequently consume, amplified bias may feed back into the data used for future training, creating a cycle in which the bias grows over time [12, 13]. Third, a practitioner who wishes to mitigate the problem needs to know which properties of the data and which algorithmic choices make amplification more likely. Studying these questions on real data is difficult, since the underlying distribution of preferences cannot be controlled and the long-term effects of recommendations cannot be observed without deploying the system. Synthetic data, in contrast, permit systematic variation of the input conditions and simulation of the feedback process.

In this short paper, we present a preliminary experimental study of bias disparity based on synthetic data. We generate preference data in which we control the group structure of users and items, the strength of the bias within each group, and the relative sizes of the groups. We then apply standard collaborative filtering algorithms and measure how the bias in the recommendations compares with the bias in the input. This design allows us to identify the conditions under which a recommender exhibits bias disparity, and to examine how the effect depends on factors such as the initial level of bias and the representation of groups in the data. We further simulate the long-term effect of recommendations by iteratively adding recommended items to the user profiles and retraining, thereby observing how data bias evolves when users act on the recommendations they receive.

Beyond characterizing the problem, we consider a simple mitigation strategy. Specifically, we study a re-ranking algorithm that post-processes the recommendation lists so that the bias in the output is brought closer to that of the input. Post-processing approaches are attractive because they are independent of the underlying recommendation model and can be applied to existing systems without retraining [14, 15]. We evaluate the extent to which re-ranking reduces bias disparity and the cost it incurs in recommendation quality. Finally, we complement the synthetic analysis with observations on real data, examining whether the patterns identified in controlled settings are visible in commonly used recommendation datasets.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows. We formalize bias disparity as a measure of the change in preference bias between input and output of a recommender. We present an experimental study on synthetic data that reveals conditions leading to amplification and illustrates its long-term dynamics. We evaluate a simple re-ranking approach for reducing bias disparity. We also report preliminary observations on real data. Although preliminary, these results offer a first step toward a systematic understanding of how recommenders transform the biases present in user behavior.

We study bias disparity in collaborative filtering recommenders through controlled experiments on synthetic data, followed by an analysis of real data. We first formalize the notion of bias and bias disparity, then describe the data generation process, the recommendation algorithms, the long-term feedback simulation, and the re-ranking procedure.

**Problem Formulation and Definitions**

Let U be a set of users and I a set of items. Users are partitioned into groups according to a categorical attribute (e.g., gender), denoted by G = {g_1, ..., g_k}, and items are partitioned into categories (e.g., genre), denoted by C = {c_1, ..., c_m}. In the experiments we consider two user groups (a majority and a minority, or two balanced groups) and two item categories, which allows for a clear interpretation of the results while retaining the essential dynamics.

We define the *preference ratio* of a group g for a category c in a set of user-item interactions as the fraction of interactions of g that involve items of c. Bias is measured relative to the category's share in the catalog. Let P(c) be the fraction of items belonging to category c. The input bias of group g toward category c is

B_in(g, c) = [ Σ_{u∈g} Σ_{i∈c} r(u,i) / Σ_{u∈g} Σ_{i∈I} r(u,i) ] / P(c),

where r(u,i)=1 if u has interacted with i. A value above one indicates that the group over-consumes the category relative to its catalog presence. The output bias B_out(g, c) is computed identically but over the top-n recommendation lists produced by the recommender, so that r(u,i)=1 if i appears in u's list. Bias disparity is then the relative change

BD(g, c) = (B_out(g, c) − B_in(g, c)) / B_in(g, c).

A positive value indicates that the recommender amplifies the bias present in the input, and a negative value indicates attenuation.

**Synthetic Data Generation**

We generate a user-item interaction matrix with controllable group sizes, category sizes, and preference strengths. Each user is assigned to a group, and each item to a category. For each group-category pair, we specify a preference probability p(g, c) that controls the likelihood that a user in g interacts with a given item in c. Interactions are sampled as independent Bernoulli trials with these probabilities, scaled to obtain a target density. By varying p we create different levels of input bias, ranging from none (identical preferences across groups) to strong, in which one group strongly prefers one category.

We examine several experimental dimensions: (i) the relative size of the groups, from balanced to highly skewed; (ii) the relative size of the categories in the catalog; (iii) the strength of the group preferences; and (iv) the matrix density. For each configuration we generate multiple random instances (ten in our setup) and report averages, which mitigates sampling variance. To avoid the trivial case in which all users are identical, we also add item popularity heterogeneity by drawing item-specific multipliers from a long-tailed distribution, reflecting the popularity skew typical of real systems [1].

**Recommendation Algorithms**

We consider representative collaborative filtering approaches. The first is a user-based k-nearest-neighbor method [2], which scores items by the similarity-weighted interactions of the most similar users, using cosine similarity. The second is an item-based neighborhood method [3]. The third is a matrix factorization model optimized for implicit feedback, such as weighted regularized matrix factorization [4] or Bayesian personalized ranking [5]. As a non-personalized baseline, we use a most-popular recommender, which helps separate the effect of popularity from that of personalization. Hyperparameters (neighborhood size, number of latent factors, regularization) are fixed to reasonable defaults across configurations, since our aim is to compare conditions rather than to tune accuracy. For each user, the top-n unseen items (n=10 in our default setting) form the recommendation list, from which B_out is computed.

**Long-Term Effect of Recommendations**

To study how recommendations influence data bias over time, we simulate an iterative feedback loop, in the spirit of prior analyses of feedback effects in recommenders [6]. At each iteration, the recommender is trained on the current interaction matrix and produces top-n lists. Each user then "consumes" a recommended item with a probability determined by the underlying preference p(g, c) of the user's group for the item's category, so that users accept recommendations they would plausibly like and reject others. Accepted items are added to the interaction matrix, and the model is retrained. We repeat this process for a fixed number of iterations and record B_in and B_out at each step. This allows us to determine whether bias disparity compounds over time, converges to a stable level, or dissipates, and how this depends on the initial conditions.

**Bias Disparity Mitigation**

We evaluate a simple post-processing re-ranking algorithm, in the spirit of fairness-aware re-ranking approaches [7]. For each user, the recommender produces a candidate list of size larger than n (e.g., 2n–5n) with predicted scores. The re-ranker then selects n items from the candidates so as to keep the category distribution of the group's aggregate recommendations close to the input bias of that group. Concretely, it greedily replaces items from over-represented categories with the highest-scoring candidates from under-represented categories until the group-level output bias approaches B_in(g, c) within a tolerance. We assess the trade-off between bias disparity reduction and recommendation quality, measured by precision@n and recall@n on held-out interactions, with a random 80/20 split per user.

**Analysis on Real Data**

To complement the synthetic study, we examine real data, using the MovieLens dataset [8] with user gender as the group attribute and movie genre as the item category, and, where applicable, a second dataset with comparable attributes. We compute B_in from the observed ratings (treated as implicit interactions), train the same recommenders, and compute B_out and BD for each group-genre pair. Because the real data have uncontrolled characteristics, this analysis is descriptive: we report the pairs where bias is amplified or attenuated and compare the patterns with those seen in the synthetic experiments, without drawing causal conclusions.

**Evaluation Protocol**

All synthetic results are averages over repeated random draws, and we report variability across runs. Unless stated otherwise, we vary one factor at a time while holding the others at default values, enabling attribution of changes in bias disparity to specific data properties.

We first examine synthetic data, where the input bias is controlled, and then turn to the effect of re-ranking and to observations on real data. Bias disparity is defined as the relative change between the bias of a group of users toward an item category in the input data and the bias of the corresponding recommendations. Positive values indicate amplification, and negative values indicate attenuation. All synthetic results are averaged over 10 runs with different random seeds, and variation across runs was small (standard deviation below 0.02 in all reported settings).

**Bias disparity under varying conditions.** We generated data with two user groups (M and F) and two item categories (A and B), and varied the preference of each group toward category A. When the input bias was balanced, the recommendations of a user-based collaborative filtering algorithm [1] remained close to balanced, with disparity near zero. As the input bias moved away from balance, disparity became nonzero and its direction depended on the group. For the group whose preference was already skewed toward a category, recommendations were skewed more strongly, so the majority preference was amplified. For example, when group F selected category A in 70% of its interactions, the recommendations to F contained category A at a rate corresponding to a positive disparity of roughly 0.15–0.25, depending on the algorithm. The opposite group showed a smaller but consistent shift in the opposite direction, which indicates that recommenders can reinforce stereotypical preferences.

The magnitude of disparity was sensitive to the popularity structure of the items. When the more popular items were concentrated in one category, bias toward that category was amplified for both groups, including the group whose input preference for it was weaker. This effect was strongest for algorithms that rely heavily on item popularity. A non-personalized popularity baseline produced the largest disparities, and matrix factorization [2] produced intermediate values. Neighborhood-based methods followed the input bias most closely, though they still amplified it for strongly skewed groups. Increasing the density of the rating matrix reduced disparity for all methods, and sparse settings produced the most pronounced amplification. This is consistent with the view that limited evidence leads models to fall back on dominant patterns in the data [3].

The relative sizes of the groups also mattered. When one group was much larger than the other, recommendations to the smaller group drifted toward the preferences of the larger group. The smaller group's bias was therefore attenuated, and its disparity was negative when its preference differed from that of the majority. Hence disparity affects minority groups in a different way, since their distinct preferences are not reflected in their recommendations.

**Long-term effects.** To study the feedback loop between recommendations and data, we simulated repeated rounds in which users were shown top-k recommendations, accepted a fraction of them, and the accepted items were added to the training data before retraining. Over successive iterations, the bias in the data moved steadily in the direction of the initial amplification. After 20 iterations, groups with an initial bias of 0.7 toward a category reached 0.8–0.9 in the data, depending on the acceptance rate. Higher acceptance rates accelerated this drift. The process did not oscillate, and it flattened as the data approached saturation. The initially unbiased setting remained stable, while even a mild initial bias (0.55) led to a measurable increase over time. These results suggest that a small amplification at a single step can accumulate into a considerable shift in the data, which is consistent with earlier reports of feedback effects in recommendation [4].

**Bias disparity reduction through re-ranking.** We evaluated a simple post-processing re-ranking algorithm that reorders each user's recommendation list so that the proportion of items from each category matches the group's input bias, while retaining the original scores as far as possible. We compare it with the unmodified lists in terms of bias disparity and recommendation quality, measured by precision at k.

Re-ranking reduced the absolute bias disparity to near zero in most settings, with remaining values below 0.05. This outcome is expected, as the procedure targets the quantity directly. The cost in accuracy was modest: precision at k fell by 2–6% relative to the original lists, with larger losses when the original disparity was large, since more items had to be replaced. In the long-term simulation, applying re-ranking at every iteration largely stopped the drift. The bias in the data remained within a few percentage points of its initial value over 20 iterations. This indicates that correcting disparity at each step can prevent the gradual change in the data, although re-ranking only matches the existing bias and does not reduce the input bias itself.

**Observations on real data.** We also computed bias disparity on a movie rating dataset [5], using gender as the user attribute and movie genre as the item category. In the input data, male and female users showed different preferences across genres. For example, female users had a higher proportion of ratings in romance, and male users had a higher proportion in action and sci-fi. The recommendations produced by the algorithms generally followed these patterns, and for many genre–group pairs the disparity was positive for the group already inclined toward the genre. The strongest amplification occurred for genres with few ratings, where small differences in the input became large differences in the output. Several genres showed negative disparity for the underrepresented group, and this matches the group-size effect observed in the synthetic experiments. Because the real data have unknown and uncontrolled structure, these observations should be read as illustrative rather than conclusive.

**Summary.** The experiments show that bias disparity depends on the input bias, item popularity, data density, and group size. Recommendations tend to amplify existing preferences, this amplification accumulates through feedback, and a simple re-ranking step can control it at a small cost in accuracy.

The experiments reported here show that recommendation algorithms do not merely reflect the biases present in their input data; under certain conditions they change them. Using synthetic data with controlled group structure, we found that bias disparity depends on the interaction of several factors: the degree of preference bias in the input, the relative sizes of the user and item groups, and the way the recommendation algorithm aggregates information from similar users. These findings are preliminary, but they suggest a number of lessons about how bias propagates through collaborative filtering pipelines.

**Interpretation of findings.** The main observation is that bias disparity is not uniform across groups. When one user group has a stronger preference for a particular item category than the rest of the population, the recommender tends to amplify this preference for the group, particularly when the item category is small or the neighborhood of similar users is dominated by like-minded users. This is consistent with the intuition that neighborhood-based and latent-factor methods concentrate on dominant patterns in the data, and that minority patterns or moderate preferences are smoothed toward the majority signal [1,2]. Conversely, in some configurations the recommender reduced the initial bias, which shows that amplification is not an inevitable property of collaborative filtering but a function of data characteristics. This distinction matters because it implies that auditing for bias disparity must be done per group and per category, rather than relying on aggregate indicators.

The long-term simulations indicate that the effects compound. When recommendations are fed back into the data as new interactions, even a modest initial disparity can grow across iterations, producing feedback loops similar to those described in work on popularity bias and filter bubbles [3,4]. In such cases, the data a system collects becomes progressively less representative of users' underlying preferences, because exposure is shaped by earlier recommendations. This has implications beyond fairness in a single recommendation round: biased data degrade the training signal for future models, and may homogenize the experience of users who belong to particular groups.

**Mitigation.** The simple re-ranking algorithm we considered reduced bias disparity in the recommendation lists by adjusting the ordering of candidate items so that the distribution of item categories more closely matched that of the input data. It did so at a moderate cost in measured accuracy, a trade-off commonly reported for fairness-aware post-processing methods [5]. Re-ranking has practical advantages: it is independent of the underlying model, easy to deploy, and interpretable. However, it addresses the symptom rather than the cause. It does not alter the model's internal representation, and it presupposes that matching the input distribution is the desired target, which is a normative choice. In some applications one might instead want to match a population-level target or an equal-exposure criterion, and the appropriate reference distribution should be decided with domain knowledge and stakeholder input.

**Observations on real data.** Our analysis of real datasets showed that bias is present in the input data in ways that resemble the synthetic settings, with distinct user groups exhibiting different preferences toward item categories. Because the real-data analysis is limited, we regard it as indicative rather than conclusive. Real data contain confounding factors, such as item availability, presentation effects, and prior recommendations, which make it difficult to attribute observed differences to user preference alone. Nevertheless, the presence of measurable preference differences suggests that the mechanisms studied synthetically are relevant in practice.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be noted. First, the synthetic data are simplified: group memberships are discrete, preferences are generated from simple probabilistic models, and users are assumed to act on recommendations in a straightforward manner. Real users have richer and more dynamic behavior, and their responses to recommendations may moderate or intensify feedback effects. Second, we evaluated a small set of algorithms, so we cannot claim that our conclusions generalize to modern deep learning or sequence-based recommenders. Third, our bias measure focuses on the distribution of item categories for user groups, which captures one notion of bias; other notions, such as exposure of individual items, error disparity, or intersectional effects, were not examined. Finally, the re-ranking evaluation considered a single strategy and a limited set of accuracy metrics, without user studies to determine how changes in recommendation lists are perceived.

**Future work.** Several directions follow naturally. A more systematic exploration of the parameter space, including overlapping groups, continuous attributes, and heterogeneous user activity levels, would clarify which conditions are most prone to amplification. Theoretical analysis could explain why certain algorithms amplify bias and could provide guarantees for mitigation. In-processing approaches, which incorporate bias constraints into model training, should be compared with post-processing to understand the accuracy and fairness trade-offs more fully [5]. Longitudinal experiments with models of user choice that account for exposure and position effects would give a more faithful picture of feedback loops. Finally, validating the findings on larger real datasets, ideally with interventional or A/B data, would help separate user preference from system influence.

**Conclusion.** We presented a preliminary study of bias disparity in recommender systems, examining when recommendations amplify or attenuate biases in the input data and how this evolves over repeated interactions. Our results show that bias disparity is conditional on group structure and data characteristics, that it can accumulate over time, and that a simple re-ranking approach can reduce it at a modest cost in accuracy. These results argue for routine monitoring of bias disparity in deployed recommenders and for treating the choice of fairness target as an explicit design decision. Although further work is required to establish generality, the study provides a basis for more comprehensive investigations of how recommendation algorithms shape, and are shaped by, the data on which they depend.

Pursuit-evasion games have been studied for decades, motivated by applications such as search and rescue, surveillance, security, wildlife monitoring, and human-robot interaction. In the classical formulation, one or more pursuers attempt to capture an evader, while the evader tries to avoid capture indefinitely. The answer to whether capture is possible depends on the relative motion capabilities of the players, their sensing, and the geometry of the environment. Much of the literature assumes that both players are holonomic point or disk agents. Real mobile robots, however, are frequently subject to kinematic constraints that limit their maneuverability. In this paper we study how such a constraint affects the outcome of a pursuit-evasion game.

We consider a differential drive robot (DDR) pursuing an omnidirectional evader in a bounded convex environment. Both players are unit disks with the same maximum speed. The evader can instantaneously change its velocity in any direction, whereas the DDR can change its heading only at a bounded angular rate. The DDR wins if it collides with the evader, and the evader wins if it avoids collision forever. At first glance the DDR appears to be at a severe disadvantage. With equal speeds and no turning limitation, a single pursuer in a convex region can capture the evader, but an evader that can instantly change direction can exploit a pursuer's turning delay, for instance by moving tangentially to the pursuer's turning circle. We show that, despite this limitation, the DDR can still guarantee capture.

**Related Work**

The study of pursuit-evasion originates in differential games [1], where the lion-and-man problem [2] and its variants established that capture depends delicately on the speed ratio, the environment, and the information available. In bounded convex domains, a single pursuer with speed at least that of the evader can capture it in finite time under mild conditions [3], while in unbounded or non-convex environments multiple pursuers may be needed [4]. Visibility-based pursuit-evasion [5], in which pursuers must detect an evader with a limited field of view, and graph-based variants such as cops and robbers [6] have produced a substantial body of complementary results. Cooperative strategies using multiple pursuers, including those based on Voronoi partitions [7] and sweeping or encirclement [8], have been extensively analyzed.

Pursuit with nonholonomic constraints has received comparatively less attention. The classical homicidal chauffeur problem [1] considers a slower but agile evader against a faster pursuer with a minimum turning radius, and it characterizes the capture region through a barrier surface.
