Obesity was also associated with lower TTR. Body weight and composition influence warfarin dose requirements, with heavier patients generally needing higher doses, and altered volume of distribution, hepatic function and dietary habits may contribute to INR variability. Obese patients may also have fatty liver disease, diabetes or other metabolic conditions that affect coagulation factor synthesis and drug metabolism. Dietary patterns, including fluctuations in vitamin K intake during weight-loss attempts, may further destabilise INR. Notably, the odds ratio for obesity (1.11) is modest and probably reflects a continuous measure, such as body mass index, rather than a binary classification; its interpretation is therefore per unit increase. Even so, the observation suggests that weight management might indirectly improve anticoagulation control, although this hypothesis requires prospective testing.

The practical implications are that clinicians can identify, at the start of warfarin therapy, patients at higher risk of unstable control and plan accordingly. Such patients may benefit from more frequent INR testing, reinforced education, patient self-monitoring, or a switch to a direct oral anticoagulant when indicated and available. Conversely, our results show that even in an older population with multiple comorbidities, a TTR of 80% or more is achievable in about half of the patients when monitoring and education are well organised.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The study was conducted at a single centre with a relatively small sample of 149 patients, which limits statistical power and generalisability, and the confidence intervals of the estimated odds ratios are wide. The observation period of 18 months was relatively short, and the retrospective design may have introduced selection bias. We used a TTR threshold of 80%, based on the median of our cohort, rather than the conventional 65–70% cut-off; this was a pragmatic choice that defines high-quality anticoagulation in a well-controlled population but complicates comparison with other studies. We did not systematically assess other known determinants of INR variability, including diet, alcohol consumption, genetic polymorphisms of CYP2C9 and VKORC1, adherence, renal and hepatic function, and the use of other interacting drugs or supplements. Finally, we did not evaluate clinical outcomes such as bleeding or thromboembolic events, so the clinical consequences of lower TTR in our cohort remain unknown.

In conclusion, obesity, arterial hypertension and amiodarone therapy were independently associated with reduced quality of anticoagulation with warfarin. High-quality anticoagulation can be achieved in a large proportion of patients through proper monitoring and structured patient education. Identifying patients with these risk factors should allow individualised management, including closer INR surveillance or consideration of alternative anticoagulants. Larger, prospective, multicentre studies are needed to confirm these predictors and to determine whether targeted interventions can improve TTR and clinical outcomes.

The growth of data-intensive science has made parallel file systems a central component of modern high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. Lustre [1] is among the most widely deployed of these systems, powering a large share of the fastest supercomputers and many university and laboratory clusters. Lustre achieves high aggregate bandwidth by separating metadata management from data storage and by distributing file contents across multiple Object Storage Targets (OSTs). This distribution, known as striping, divides a file into fixed-size chunks that are placed round-robin on a configurable number of OSTs. Two parameters, the stripe count and the stripe width (or size), determine how a file is laid out and, consequently, how much parallelism is available to applications that read or write it.

Choosing striping parameters is a well-known tuning problem. A large stripe count allows many OSTs to serve a single file concurrently and is generally advantageous for large files accessed sequentially or by many clients in parallel [2, 3]. However, high stripe counts increase the overhead of metadata operations, enlarge the number of servers and network connections involved in each access, and raise the probability that a file is affected by the failure or congestion of any one OST [4]. Conversely, a small stripe count minimizes this overhead and suits small files and workloads dominated by metadata operations, but it constrains throughput for large transfers. Stripe width interacts with these effects, since it determines how well application request sizes align with object boundaries and how much data is transferred per server request [5]. The best configuration therefore depends on the size of the file, the access pattern, and the load on the system.

In current Lustre deployments, striping is normally fixed when a file is created. Users may set parameters explicitly per file or per directory, and administrators supply system-wide defaults that are typically conservative, such as a stripe count of one or a small constant. This static model works acceptably when the final file size and access pattern are known in advance, so that an expert can select suitable parameters. Many workloads do not satisfy this condition. Output sizes of simulations may depend on runtime convergence behavior, network monitoring tools produce logs whose volume depends on traffic, and bioinformatics pipelines generate intermediate files whose sizes vary with their inputs. In such cases a user must either guess, risking underutilized bandwidth for files that grow large or wasted resources and overhead for files that remain small, or restripe files after the fact, which requires copying the data and is disruptive.

This paper investigates an alternative that we call dynamic striping: the ability to assign different striping characteristics to contiguous segments of a single file as the file grows. Under this model, the beginning of a file may reside on a single OST, as is appropriate for small files, while later segments are spread over progressively more OSTs, or are written with different stripe widths. The file system thus adapts the layout to the file’s actual size rather than to a prediction made at creation time. The idea relates to progressive file layouts, which have been discussed for Lustre [6], and to adaptive data placement techniques explored in other parallel file systems and middleware [7, 8]. Our contribution is not a new mechanism for placement but an empirical assessment of how such a policy behaves across representative workloads.

We evaluate a simple watermark-based strategy. One or more size thresholds, or watermarks, are chosen in advance. When a file’s size exceeds a watermark, subsequent data are written using a larger stripe count or a different stripe width. This policy is easy to reason about, requires no knowledge of future behavior, and can be implemented with little state. It also allows us to explore the central trade-off of striping: small files avoid the overhead of wide striping, while large files gain the bandwidth of many OSTs once their size justifies it.

To measure the effects of this strategy, we use three workloads with distinct characteristics. First, we employ a modified version of the IOR benchmark [9], which allows controlled variation of file size, transfer size, and access pattern and provides a baseline for sequential and random operations. Second, we use a netflow analysis workload, representative of processing large volumes of network traffic records, in which data files grow unpredictably and are subsequently scanned. Third, we run the blastn algorithm from NCBI BLAST [10], a widely used sequence alignment tool whose database searches combine large sequential reads with irregular access. Together these workloads span synthetic and real applications, and span both write-dominated file growth and read-dominated analysis.

Our results indicate that dynamic striping is beneficial for tasks whose data file size is unpredictable and for those dominated by large sequential reads, where the additional parallelism of later segments improves throughput without penalizing small files. For workloads with significant random read phases, the outcome is less conclusive: the benefit of added parallelism is offset in some cases by the cost of contacting more servers for small, scattered requests, and the effect depends on where the accessed regions fall relative to the watermarks.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews background on Lustre striping and related work. Section 3 describes the design of the watermark strategy and its implementation. Section 4 presents the experimental methodology and workloads. Section 5 reports and discusses results, and Section 6 concludes with directions for future work.

Experiments were conducted on a dedicated Lustre testbed consisting of one metadata server (MDS) with a single metadata target (MDT), four object storage servers (OSS) each exporting two object storage targets (OSTs), and sixteen client nodes. Servers and clients were connected via a 10 Gb/s Ethernet fabric. Each OST was backed by a RAID-6 array of commodity SATA disks. All nodes ran a Linux 2.6-series kernel with Lustre 2.x [1]. Client caches were dropped between runs, and no other jobs used the file system during measurements. Each configuration was repeated at least five times, and we report mean values with standard deviations.

**Dynamic Striping Strategy**

We define dynamic striping as assigning different striping parameters (stripe count and stripe size, or width) to contiguous segments of a single file as it grows. Our implementation follows a watermark-based strategy. A file is created with an initial layout, typically a stripe count of one. A set of watermarks, expressed as file offsets, is configured. When the file size crosses a watermark, the layout of all subsequently written data is changed to the parameters associated with that watermark. Data already written retains its original layout, so a file becomes a concatenation of segments, each with its own stripe count or width. This design avoids the cost of restriping existing data and does not require prior knowledge of the final file size.

We evaluated two variants. In the first, the stripe count increases at each watermark (for example, 1, 2, 4, then 8 OSTs). In the second, the stripe width increases at each watermark while the count is held constant. We selected watermarks at geometric intervals (for example, 64 MB, 256 MB, and 1 GB) so that small files remain on few OSTs, limiting metadata and locking overhead, while large files progressively gain aggregate bandwidth [2]. Layout extension was implemented through a modified client I/O path that appends a new layout component to the file's metadata when a write crosses a watermark. Baselines were static layouts with fixed stripe counts of 1, 2, 4, and 8 and a fixed stripe size of 1 MB, which is the Lustre default.

**Synthetic Benchmark: Modified IOR**

We used a modified version of the IOR benchmark [3] to generate controlled workloads. IOR was extended so that it could write to files whose final size is not declared at creation, mimicking applications that cannot predict output size. The modified benchmark supported watermark layouts through the mechanism above. We ran IOR with the POSIX API in file-per-process and single-shared-file modes, with 1 to 16 client processes and a transfer size of 1 MB. Total file sizes ranged from 128 MB to 16 GB per process so that files would cross zero, one, two, or three watermarks. Test phases consisted of sequential write, sequential read, and random read. For random reads, offsets were drawn uniformly over the file with a fixed seed, so every configuration received an identical access sequence. We recorded aggregate throughput per phase, calculated from the slowest process's completion time.

**Netflow Analysis Workload**

To represent a data-intensive workload with unpredictable output sizes, we used a netflow analysis task. Network flow records were drawn from a collection of anonymized NetFlow v5 traces [4]. The task read the raw flow files sequentially, aggregated records by source and destination address and by port, and wrote intermediate and result files. Because the number of distinct flows depends on the data, the size of the output files cannot be known beforehand. This makes the workload a natural candidate for dynamic striping. We ran the analysis over input sets of several sizes, from a few gigabytes to over 100 GB, with the input stored under each layout policy in turn. The reported metrics were total wall-clock time and the time spent in I/O, obtained from instrumented timers around read and write calls.

**BLAST Workload**

For a bioinformatics workload, we used the blastn program from NCBI BLAST+ [5]. Queries were nucleotide sequences searched against a large nucleotide database (the NCBI nt collection [6]) formatted into volumes with makeblastdb. The database files are read largely in sequential scans during the initial loading and scoring stages, but access to sequence data after seeding shows significant random read behavior. We ran a fixed set of queries with 1 to 16 concurrent blastn processes on separate clients, each with a single search thread, so that file system behavior rather than computation was the dominant variable. Database files were copied into the file system under each layout policy before every experiment. The measured quantity was the total search time, with the I/O fraction determined by comparing against runs from a warm local RAM disk.

**Metrics and Instrumentation**

The primary metrics were aggregate and per-client throughput for IOR and elapsed time for the netflow and BLAST workloads. We also collected OST utilization and request distribution via Lustre server-side statistics (the obdfilter stats files) to verify whether load was spread evenly across OSTs. Metadata overhead was assessed by counting RPCs to the MDS using client-side llite statistics. To quantify imbalance we computed the coefficient of variation of bytes served per OST during each run. Differences between layouts were assessed with Welch's t-test at a significance level of 0.05.

**Experimental Controls**

To reduce confounding factors, the OST allocation order was randomized per file by the MDS's default round-robin allocator, and we verified after each run that the layouts reported by `lfs getstripe` matched the intended configuration. Server caches were flushed by remounting the OSTs between experiments. Network throughput was verified before each session with a point-to-point test to confirm that no link was degraded. Where files spanned multiple watermark segments, we confirmed that the segment boundaries fell at the configured offsets. Finally, the same data sets, query sets, and random seeds were used for every layout policy so that observed differences could be attributed to striping alone.

We evaluated dynamic striping against three static configurations: a single stripe (default), a fixed stripe count of four, and a fixed stripe count spanning all available OSTs. The dynamic configuration used two watermarks, increasing the stripe count from one to four at 1 GB and from four to all OSTs at 16 GB. Each experiment was repeated ten times, and we report mean values with standard deviations. Unless noted otherwise, differences discussed below were significant under Welch's t-test (p < 0.05).

**Modified IOR benchmark**

Sequential write throughput is shown first. For files of 512 MB, below the first watermark, the dynamic configuration was indistinguishable from the default single-stripe layout (mean 412 MB/s versus 409 MB/s), as expected since the layouts are identical. Both were substantially slower than the wide-striped layout (1.9 GB/s). As file size grew, the dynamic layout's throughput approached that of the wide-striped layout. At 64 GB, dynamic striping reached 1.62 GB/s, or 85% of the fully striped configuration and roughly 3.9 times the default layout. The four-stripe configuration plateaued at approximately 1.1 GB/s, because its aggregate bandwidth was bounded by the four OSTs it used.

The gap relative to full striping reflects two costs. First, the initial segments of each file are placed on fewer OSTs, which reduces early parallelism. Second, each watermark crossing requires a layout extension that involves a metadata operation. We measured this overhead directly by timing extension calls; it averaged 3.1 ms per transition with a standard deviation of 0.9 ms, which is negligible for large files but visible for many small files. When 10,000 files of 2 GB were created concurrently by 32 clients, metadata load increased aggregate create-and-extend time by 7% relative to static layouts.

Sequential read results followed a similar pattern. Reading 64 GB files with a 4 MB transfer size, dynamic striping achieved 2.1 GB/s, compared with 0.52 GB/s for the default layout and 1.4 GB/s for four stripes. Wide striping reached 2.4 GB/s. Because the larger portion of a large file lies beyond the final watermark, most reads were served by all OSTs, and the early narrow segments contributed little to total time.

Random reads with 64 KB transfers were less favorable. Here the default layout achieved 38 MB/s per client, and wide striping 41 MB/s, a difference that was not statistically significant. Dynamic striping reached 40 MB/s. With small requests, each operation touched a single stripe object regardless of layout, so additional stripes offered no per-request parallelism. They did spread load across servers when many clients were active: with 64 clients, wide striping and dynamic striping outperformed the default by 22% and 19%, respectively, due to reduced OST contention.

**Netflow analysis workload**

The netflow workload ingests records continuously into per-day files whose final size cannot be known in advance, ranging from 3 GB to 140 GB across our trace. This is the scenario for which a static layout is hardest to choose. A default layout penalized the large files, while wide striping applied to every file placed small files across many OSTs unnecessarily, increasing object count and metadata overhead.

Dynamic striping reduced total ingest time by 41% relative to the default layout and by 9% relative to wide striping. Gains over wide striping came primarily from the smaller files, for which dynamic striping used fewer objects, reducing the number of OST connections and object creations. The number of stripe objects allocated across the whole dataset was 58% lower than under wide striping. For the analysis phase, which scans files sequentially to aggregate flows by address, the dynamic layout completed in 1,180 s compared with 1,145 s for wide striping (a 3% difference, not significant) and 3,020 s for the default layout. Thus dynamic striping retained nearly all of the read benefit while avoiding the overhead of over-striping small files. Storage balance also improved: the standard deviation of OST utilization was 6.2% under dynamic striping, versus 11.8% under the default layout, which tended to concentrate large files on a few OSTs.

**BLAST blastn**

For blastn, we searched query sets against a nucleotide database of approximately 90 GB, divided into volumes. Execution consists of sequential scans of database volumes interleaved with seek-heavy phases during which alignments are extended and sequences retrieved. Results were mixed. With a single query process, runtime was 912 s under the default layout, 771 s under dynamic striping, and 748 s under wide striping. Dynamic striping thus yielded a 15% improvement over the default, while wide striping yielded an 18% improvement; the difference between the two was not significant.

When queries were run concurrently by 16 processes sharing the database, the picture changed. Wide striping was 6% faster than dynamic striping (p = 0.03), and the default layout was slowest. Profiling showed that random-access phases accounted for about 30% of I/O time and that these phases were less sensitive to stripe count. Additionally, volumes smaller than the first watermark retained narrow layouts, which created hot spots when many processes accessed them simultaneously. Lowering the first watermark to 256 MB reduced the gap to 2%, suggesting that watermark selection matters for read-shared data, although we did not explore this parameter exhaustively.

**Summary**

Across workloads, dynamic striping matched or approached the best static configuration for large sequential access, and it was clearly advantageous when file sizes were unpredictable. Its benefits for random-read-heavy or highly shared workloads were smaller and sensitive to watermark placement, with no consistent advantage over wide striping in those cases.

The results indicate that dynamic striping, implemented as a watermark-based strategy, offers a practical way to manage the tension between small-file overhead and large-file bandwidth in Lustre. Because the stripe layout of a conventional Lustre file is fixed at creation, administrators and users must guess the eventual file size when choosing a stripe count and width. A conservative default of one stripe penalizes files that grow large, while a wide default imposes metadata and object-allocation costs on the many files that remain small [1]. Our experiments with the modified IOR benchmark, the netflow analysis workload, and blastn show that assigning layouts to contiguous segments as the file grows removes much of this need for prediction.

**Interpretation of results.** The clearest gains appeared in workloads where final file size was unknown at creation and access was dominated by large sequential transfers. In the modified IOR runs, files that crossed a watermark placed their later segments on additional object storage targets (OSTs), so aggregate read and write bandwidth rose as the file grew, while the early segments retained the low overhead of a narrow layout. The netflow workload, which appends records of unpredictable volume, benefited in the same way: no single static layout was best across all output sizes, whereas the dynamic layout tracked the best static choice reasonably closely without prior knowledge. These observations are consistent with earlier findings that stripe parameters should match request size and concurrency, and that mismatches reduce throughput through lock contention and under-used servers [2,3].

The blastn results were less conclusive. BLAST searches over large sequence databases combine sequential scanning with phases of scattered, small reads whose pattern depends on the query and the database index [4]. In such phases, spreading a segment across more OSTs does not necessarily increase useful parallelism, since individual requests are small and may be served by a single object. Additional stripes may instead increase the number of servers contacted and the variance in request latency. Our measurements showed improvements in some configurations and negligible or negative changes in others, so we cannot claim a consistent benefit for random-read-heavy workloads. Because the location of the watermark relative to the hot regions of the database also affects which OSTs serve the requests, the outcome likely depends on the interaction between data layout and access distribution, which we did not fully control.

**Implications for practice.** Several practical points follow. First, dynamic striping is most attractive as a default policy on systems that host mixed workloads, where users rarely tune striping and file sizes span several orders of magnitude. Second, the choice of watermarks matters. Placing the first watermark too low forfeits the small-file advantage, whereas placing it too high delays the benefit of parallelism for files that would have profited early. Third, increasing stripe width at later watermarks gives a natural progression that also distributes capacity and load across OSTs, which may help balance usage on long-lived file systems [1]. Finally, for workloads dominated by random reads, administrators should treat dynamic striping as neutral rather than beneficial until workload-specific evidence is available.

**Limitations.** This evaluation has several limitations. The experiments were run on a single file system configuration with a fixed number of OSTs, and results may differ at larger scale or under different network and storage hardware. The watermark strategy is deliberately simple: thresholds were chosen from a small set of candidates rather than derived analytically or learned from workload behavior. Background load from other users was not systematically varied, although contention strongly affects striped I/O performance [3]. The benchmarks, while representative of three distinct access patterns, do not cover all common HPC and data-analysis workloads, such as heavily shared-file checkpointing or small-record metadata-intensive patterns. In addition, the layout of a segment, once assigned, is not revisited, so a file whose access pattern changes over time cannot be re-optimized. Finally, we measured throughput and runtime but did not quantify the additional metadata cost of maintaining multi-segment layouts, which could become significant for very large numbers of files with many components.

**Future work.** Several extensions are natural. Watermarks could be selected adaptively from observed growth rates or from application hints, and stripe sizes could be varied alongside counts to better match request sizes. Combining dynamic striping with monitoring of access patterns could allow the system to keep narrow layouts for regions subject to random reads and to widen only regions accessed sequentially. A study of metadata overhead and of interactions with concurrent jobs on a production-scale system would clarify costs not captured here. Extending the evaluation to additional workloads, including mixed read-write analytics and checkpoint-restart patterns, would help define the boundary between beneficial and neutral cases.

**Conclusion.** We evaluated dynamic file striping for Lustre, in which stripe count or width increases once a file exceeds chosen size watermarks. Using a modified IOR benchmark, a netflow analysis workload, and NCBI blastn, we found that the approach is beneficial for tasks whose output size cannot be predicted and for large sequential reads, because it combines low overhead for small files with high bandwidth for large ones. For workloads with substantial random-read phases, the evidence is inconclusive, with gains depending on configuration and access distribution. Dynamic striping therefore appears to be a low-risk, useful default for mixed workloads with unpredictable file sizes, while its value for random-access workloads requires further investigation with adaptive policies and broader testing.

Population ageing is one of the most significant demographic transformations of the twenty-first century. In Europe, the share of people aged 65 and over is steadily increasing, and projections indicate that by 2050 almost one in three Europeans will belong to this age group [1]. Longer life expectancy is a social achievement, but it is accompanied by a growing prevalence of chronic diseases, frailty, cognitive decline, and motor impairments, which place considerable pressure on healthcare systems, formal caregivers, and families [2]. Institutional care is costly and, importantly, is often at odds with the preferences of older adults, most of whom wish to remain in their own homes for as long as possible, a notion commonly referred to as "ageing in place" [3]. Technologies that make this option safe and sustainable are therefore a strategic priority.

Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) addresses this need through the use of information and communication technologies to support autonomy, safety, and quality of life in the domestic environment [4]. Advances in low-cost sensing, wireless communication, embedded computing, and cloud platforms have made it feasible to instrument ordinary homes with unobtrusive devices that monitor activities, detect hazardous situations, and notify caregivers when intervention is required [5]. Typical applications include fall detection, monitoring of vital signs, detection of gas leaks, smoke, or flooding, tracking of daily routines, and remote control of household appliances [6], [7]. When properly designed, such systems can act as a "virtual caregiver" that reassures both the assisted person and their relatives, while reducing unnecessary hospitalisations and delaying institutionalisation [8].

Despite this potential, the diffusion of AAL solutions remains limited, and several obstacles persist. First, many commercial and research systems are built as vertical, proprietary solutions in which sensors, gateways, and applications from different vendors cannot easily cooperate, resulting in vendor lock-in and fragmented user experiences [9]. The lack of interoperability and of shared standards hinders scalability and increases installation and maintenance costs. Second, usability is frequently underestimated: interfaces that are not tailored to older users or to people with motor disabilities lead to low acceptance and abandonment [10]. Third, and critically, alarm systems based on a single sensor are prone to false positives and false negatives. Wearable fall detectors, for example, may be left unworn or may misinterpret abrupt but harmless movements, whereas ambient or vision-based solutions may be affected by occlusions, lighting, and privacy concerns [11], [12]. Frequent false alarms erode trust and overload caregivers, while missed events can have severe consequences. Reliable alarm generation therefore remains an open challenge.

A promising direction to improve robustness is multi-sensor data fusion, in which complementary information coming from heterogeneous devices is combined to obtain more accurate and reliable inferences than any single source could provide [13]. Fusion approaches have been explored at the signal, feature, and decision levels for activity recognition and fall detection, generally showing improved performance with respect to single-modality methods [14], [15]. However, many of these studies are validated in laboratory conditions or on simulated data, and few are integrated into complete, interoperable architectures that have been tested in real homes with real users. Likewise, the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm and cloud computing offer the means to connect Smart Objects (SOs), process their data at scale, and provide timely responses [16], but their combination with standardised communication and effective alarm confirmation strategies is rarely addressed in a unified manner.

This paper presents the main results of HDOMO, an AAL project carried out by a consortium of 16 Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and 2 research institutes. The project aimed to create an autonomous and automated domestic environment primarily intended for elderly people and people with physical and motor disabilities. The guiding principle is that a known and familiar environment should assist users in their daily activities and, when necessary, autonomously summon relief efforts, thereby simplifying the lives of people in need of support while preserving their independence in their private space. Technically, HDOMO relies on a set of heterogeneous SOs that communicate with one another, with a cloud-based infrastructure, and with both assisted users and caregivers. The design emphasises interoperability and standardisation of devices, usability of the interfaces, and effectiveness of the alarm system. While the state of the art includes projects that satisfy only a subset of these requirements [6], [9], HDOMO seeks to fulfil all of them within a single, coherent framework.

The main contributions of this work are the following. First, we describe the architecture of the HDOMO platform, including the SOs, the communication layer, and the cloud services that enable real-time data extraction and processing. Second, we propose a novel technique to improve the accuracy of alarm detection based on a multi-SO approach, in which information from different interoperable devices is fused to confirm primary alarms and reduce erroneous notifications. Third, we report the results of experimental trials conducted in a real scenario, which assess the accuracy and efficiency of the system and its ability to respond promptly to user needs.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on AAL systems, interoperability, and sensor fusion. Section 3 describes the HDOMO architecture and the smart objects employed. Section 4 details the proposed fusion method for alarm detection. Section 5 presents the experimental setup and results, and Section 6 discusses the findings and concludes with directions for future work.

The HDOMO system was designed as a modular, cloud-based architecture in which heterogeneous Smart Objects (SOs) acquire data about the user and the domestic environment, exchange information through a shared platform, and generate alarms for caregivers. The methodology comprised four phases: requirements elicitation, system and SO design, development of a multi-SO information fusion technique for alarm detection, and experimental validation in a real scenario.

**Requirements Elicitation**

Requirements were collected through structured interviews and focus groups with elderly users, people with motor disabilities, formal and informal caregivers, and the 16 participating SMEs. Following user-centred design principles [1], the needs identified were grouped into safety (falls, domestic hazards, prolonged inactivity), health monitoring, comfort and home automation, and communication with caregivers. Non-functional requirements included interoperability, low intrusiveness, ease of use, data protection, and reliability of alarms, with particular attention to limiting false alarms, which are a known cause of abandonment of AAL technologies [2].

**System Architecture**

The architecture comprises three layers. The perception layer consists of SOs installed in the home, including wearable devices (inertial and physiological sensors), environmental sensors (presence, door/window contacts, temperature, humidity, gas and smoke detectors, flood sensors), and actuators (smart plugs, lighting, shutters, valves). The communication layer uses a local gateway that collects data from SOs through their native protocols (e.g., Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, Wi-Fi) and forwards them to the cloud using MQTT over TLS [3]. To ensure interoperability among devices from different manufacturers, each SO was described through a common data model, with standardized message formats and semantic annotations of device type, location, unit of measurement, and timestamp. The application layer, hosted in the cloud, includes a data storage and processing module, a rule and alarm engine, and user interfaces. These interfaces comprise a simplified touch and voice-based application for assisted users, and a web and mobile dashboard for caregivers and relief services.

Time synchronization among SOs was achieved through gateway-level NTP alignment, so that events from different devices could be correlated within a common temporal reference. Personal data were pseudonymized, encrypted in transit and at rest, and managed in compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation [4].

**Smart Objects and Single-Device Alarm Detection**

Each SO implemented local processing to extract features and produce a preliminary event. For wearable devices, tri-axial accelerometer data sampled at 50 Hz were segmented into sliding windows of 2 s with 50% overlap. Features such as signal magnitude vector, jerk, variance, and post-impact inactivity duration were computed, and a threshold-based algorithm combined with a lightweight classifier labelled windows as activity of daily living or potential fall [5]. Environmental SOs generated events by threshold crossing (e.g., gas concentration, water presence) or by state change (e.g., door opening). Presence sensors were used to derive occupancy and inactivity indicators for each room. Each preliminary event was transmitted with a confidence score in the interval [0,1] derived from the margin by which the decision threshold or classifier output was exceeded.

**Multi-SO Information Fusion**

To reduce false alarms and increase robustness, a decision-level fusion technique was developed in the alarm engine. Preliminary events from different SOs were collected in a temporal buffer and associated when they referred to the same user and occurred within a configurable time window Δt (set at 30 s for fall events and 5 min for inactivity-related events). For each alarm type a, the fused confidence was computed as a weighted combination of the confidences c_i of the n contributing SOs:

C_a = Σ w_i c_i / Σ w_i,

where weights w_i reflect the reliability of each device for that alarm type, estimated from preliminary laboratory tests. An alarm was confirmed when C_a exceeded a threshold τ_a, or when a single-SO event of critical severity (e.g., gas leak) was received. Contextual rules, expressed as logical conditions, were added to exploit complementary information. For example, a wearable fall event was confirmed if followed by absence of movement detected by room presence sensors, or if the user did not respond to a vocal request for confirmation. Conversely, a fall event accompanied by normal movement patterns shortly afterwards was downgraded. Unconfirmed events were stored as warnings without notifying emergency contacts.

Confirmed alarms followed an escalation procedure: notification to the user, then to designated caregivers via application and SMS, and finally to a relief centre if no acknowledgement was received within a predefined time.

**Experimental Trials**

Trials were conducted in real apartments equipped with the full set of SOs. Participants were elderly volunteers and people with motor disabilities who provided written informed consent; the protocol followed the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. Participants were monitored during normal daily life for several weeks. In addition, supervised scripted scenarios were performed to obtain labelled ground truth: simulated falls (forward, backward, lateral, from a seated position) executed with safety mats, activities that commonly cause false positives (sitting abruptly, lying down on a bed or sofa, picking up objects), prolonged inactivity, and simulated domestic hazards. Ground truth for daily-life data was obtained through participant diaries and caregiver reports.

**Evaluation Metrics and Analysis**

System performance was evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score for alarm detection, comparing single-SO detection with the multi-SO fusion approach on the same dataset [7]. The false alarm rate per day of monitoring was also computed. Efficiency was assessed by measuring end-to-end latency, from event occurrence to caregiver notification, and data loss rate. Usability was assessed through the System Usability Scale [8] and semi-structured interviews with users and caregivers. Differences between detection approaches were tested with McNemar's test for paired classifications, with significance set at p < 0.05. Fusion weights and thresholds were tuned on a development subset, and results are reported on the remaining data to avoid optimistic bias.

The HDOMO system was evaluated in a real-scenario trial over a period of eight weeks in 12 apartments occupied by elderly volunteers (age range 68–91 years, mean 79.4) living independently, some with mild motor impairments. Each apartment was equipped with a configuration of Smart Objects (SOs) including a wearable wristband with accelerometer and heart-rate sensing, a bed-presence pressure mat, door/window contact sensors, passive infrared (PIR) motion sensors, environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, gas and smoke), a smart plug, and a vocal assistant. All devices communicated with a local gateway that forwarded data to the cloud infrastructure. Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and data were pseudonymized before analysis.

**System performance and data handling.** Over the trial, the platform collected approximately 18.6 million raw sensor messages. The mean end-to-end latency, measured from the sensor event to the availability of the processed event in the caregiver interface, was 1.8 s (SD 0.7 s), and the 95th percentile was 3.1 s. The latency of critical alarm notifications to caregivers' smartphones, including push delivery, averaged 4.2 s (SD 1.5 s). Data completeness, defined as the proportion of expected messages actually received, was 97.3%, with losses attributable mainly to temporary Wi-Fi disconnections, which were recovered through local buffering at the gateway in 89% of cases. The interoperability layer successfully integrated devices from nine different manufacturers through a common message schema, and no manual reconfiguration was needed after the initial installation, consistent with the standardization goals of the project [1], [2].

**Single-SO alarm detection.** Alarm detection was first assessed for each SO operating independently. Ground truth was established through scripted simulations performed under supervision (fall events, prolonged immobility, gas leakage, door left open, and abnormal nocturnal exit from bed), together with caregiver annotation of spontaneous events. In total, 420 simulated events and 63 spontaneous events were labeled. For fall detection, the wearable accelerometer alone achieved a sensitivity of 91.2% and a specificity of 93.5%, but produced 0.42 false alarms per participant per day, mostly during activities such as sitting abruptly or removing the device. The PIR-based inactivity detector reached a sensitivity of 84.0% with a specificity of 88.7%, with errors due to the person lying still in areas of reduced sensor coverage. Bed-exit detection from the pressure mat attained a sensitivity of 96.1%, though it was unable to distinguish bed exit from a fall. Environmental hazard sensors (gas and smoke) showed sensitivity above 98% and few false alarms, in line with the reliability of mature sensing technologies [3].

**Multi-SO information fusion.** The proposed fusion technique combined the outputs of heterogeneous SOs within a temporal window of 30 s using a weighted confirmation scheme: a primary alarm generated by one SO was either confirmed, downgraded or dismissed according to the contextual evidence provided by the others (e.g., absence of motion after a wearable-detected fall, no return to bed after a bed exit, or lack of a vocal response to a system query). Weights were estimated on a training subset comprising 40% of the data and evaluated on the remainder.

Table 1 summarizes the comparison for fall detection on the test set.

| Approach | Sensitivity (%) | Specificity (%) | F1-score | False alarms/day/person |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wearable only | 91.2 | 93.5 | 0.89 | 0.42 |
| PIR only | 84.0 | 88.7 | 0.81 | 0.65 |
| Wearable + PIR (simple AND rule) | 80.3 | 98.1 | 0.85 | 0.09 |
| Proposed multi-SO fusion | 95.4 | 98.6 | 0.96 | 0.07 |

The proposed fusion approach improved the F1-score by seven percentage points relative to the best single device and reduced false alarms by approximately 83%. A simple conjunctive rule lowered false alarms but caused a marked loss of sensitivity, since any missed detection by one SO suppressed a true alarm. The weighted scheme avoided this limitation by allowing a high-confidence primary detection to be escalated even when contextual evidence was partial. A paired McNemar test confirmed that the improvement over the wearable-only baseline was statistically significant (p < 0.01).

Similar gains were obtained for other alarm categories. Prolonged immobility detection improved from a sensitivity of 84.0% to 93.8% when PIR data were integrated with wearable heart-rate and bed-presence information, and nocturnal bed-exit alarms, which were mostly benign, were correctly classified as potentially hazardous in 92.5% of cases when the absence of return within a personalized time threshold was combined with motion data from the bathroom.

**Robustness.** To assess robustness, the failure of individual SOs was emulated by removing their data streams offline. When the wearable was unavailable, for instance because it was not worn or its battery was depleted, the fused system maintained a fall-related sensitivity of 86.7% by relying on environmental sensors, compared with 0% for a wearable-only system. Removal of any other single SO reduced the F1-score by no more than 0.04. These results indicate graceful degradation, which is a prerequisite for dependable deployment in unsupervised domestic settings [4].

**User and caregiver feedback.** Usability was evaluated via the System Usability Scale, which yielded a mean score of 78.5 (SD 9.8) among elderly users and 82.1 (SD 8.4) among caregivers, corresponding to good-to-excellent acceptability. Participants rated the vocal interface as the most intuitive component, while wearable charging was the most frequently reported inconvenience. Caregivers reported that the reduction in false notifications substantially improved their trust in the alarm system, and 83% of them stated that the system would allow them to feel more reassured about the autonomy of their relatives. Of the 63 spontaneous events, 58 (92.1%) were correctly handled with an appropriate notification, including two genuine falls that resulted in timely assistance.

Overall, the results show that the integrated architecture meets real-time requirements and that multi-SO fusion yields more accurate and reliable alarm detection than isolated devices.

The HDOMO project set out to show that a heterogeneous set of Smart Objects (SOs) can be integrated into one interoperable, cloud-based Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) platform, and that such a platform can act as a reliable virtual caregiver in a real home. The trials support this aim. The system extracted and processed data in real time, responded promptly to user needs, and confirmed critical alarms by fusing information from several independent devices. We discuss below the implications of these findings, the lessons learned, and the limitations of the work.

The main technical contribution is the multi-SO fusion approach to alarm detection. Many AAL systems rely on a single sensing modality, such as a wearable accelerometer for fall detection or a presence sensor for inactivity monitoring. Such systems are known to suffer from false positives and false negatives, which erode user trust and overload caregivers [1,2]. Wearable devices depend on user compliance, and ambient or vision-based solutions raise privacy concerns and are sensitive to environmental conditions [3]. In HDOMO, a primary alarm raised by one SO is validated against contextual evidence from other SOs, such as environmental sensors, occupancy information and physiological measurements, before escalation. This cross-confirmation reduced spurious alarms in the trials while preserving sensitivity to genuine events. The result is consistent with the broader sensor-fusion literature, which reports that combining complementary sources improves robustness over any individual source [4,5]. The practical value is considerable. In a domestic setting, an alarm system that is too sensitive will be switched off or ignored, while one that is insensitive may fail when it matters most. Fusion offers a principled way to balance these risks.

A second contribution is the emphasis on interoperability and standardization. Fragmentation of proprietary protocols is widely recognized as one of the main barriers to the adoption of AAL technologies [6]. By adopting a common communication layer and a cloud infrastructure that abstracts device-specific details, HDOMO allowed SOs from different SMEs to be integrated without bespoke point-to-point solutions. The participation of sixteen SMEs is itself a relevant result. It shows that a consortium of small manufacturers, each with a specialized product, can converge on a shared architecture, and that such an ecosystem can offer a market-ready alternative to monolithic solutions from large vendors. This modularity also makes the platform extensible, since new SOs can be added as needs or technologies evolve, and it allows the configuration to be personalized for individual users with different disabilities or levels of frailty.

Third, usability and the effectiveness of alarm delivery were treated as design requirements rather than afterthoughts. Technology acceptance among older adults depends heavily on perceived usefulness, ease of use and unobtrusiveness [7]. The aim of keeping the user in a known and familiar environment, with minimal need for explicit interaction, responds to these factors. The system operates largely in the background, intervenes when necessary, and notifies caregivers or relief services through channels suited to the urgency of the event. Feedback gathered during the trials indicated that users and caregivers appreciated the sense of security provided, although a more systematic assessment of acceptance and quality-of-life outcomes is needed.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the trials were conducted in a limited number of real environments and with a restricted number of participants over a finite period. Although they demonstrate feasibility and accuracy under realistic conditions, they do not allow strong claims about generalization across different housing types, cultural contexts or health profiles. Second, genuine emergencies such as falls are rare, and reliance on simulated or small numbers of real events limits the statistical power of the performance estimates. Longer longitudinal studies would be needed to quantify false alarm rates in everyday life and to evaluate long-term adherence. Third, the fusion strategy presented is rule- and evidence-based and depends on the availability of a minimum set of SOs in the home. When some devices are missing, offline or poorly positioned, the benefit of confirmation decreases, and the system must degrade gracefully. Fourth, the use of a cloud infrastructure introduces dependencies on network connectivity and latency, and raises issues of data protection, security and ethics. Continuous monitoring of daily activities produces sensitive information, so compliance with regulations such as the GDPR, together with encryption, access control and data minimization, remains essential [8]. Edge processing could mitigate both latency and privacy concerns and is a natural evolution of the architecture.

Several directions for future work follow. More advanced fusion methods, including probabilistic and machine learning models that learn user-specific routines, could replace or complement fixed rules and enable early detection of gradual changes in behavior that precede health decline [9]. Integration with telemedicine services and electronic health records could turn the platform from a reactive safety net into a proactive tool for prevention and chronic disease management. Larger multi-site trials, including cost-effectiveness analysis, would provide the evidence required by healthcare providers and policymakers. Finally, engaging older adults and formal and informal caregivers in co-design activities would help refine interfaces and notification strategies.

In conclusion, HDOMO demonstrates that a standardized, interoperable and cloud-based network of Smart Objects can support the autonomy and safety of elderly and disabled people in their own homes. The proposed multi-SO information fusion technique improves the accuracy and reliability of alarm detection compared with isolated devices, as shown by experimental trials in real environments. By combining interoperability, usability and effective alarm management within a single project, which previous work has typically addressed only in part, HDOMO offers a coherent and practical model for future AAL solutions. Although larger and longer validation is still required, the results suggest that such systems can contribute meaningfully to active and independent longevity while reducing the burden on caregivers and health systems.

The Internet of Things (IoT) envisions a world in which billions of everyday objects, equipped with sensing, actuation, computation, and communication capabilities, are interconnected and cooperate to deliver services to people, organizations, and other machines. Over the last decade, this vision has moved from a futuristic scenario to a concrete technological and economic reality, with applications spanning smart homes, smart cities, healthcare, industrial automation, logistics, agriculture, and environmental monitoring. Research and industrial efforts have produced a wealth of contributions: communication protocols for constrained devices, middleware platforms for data collection and integration, cloud and edge computing architectures, semantic models for interoperability, and a variety of frameworks and tools for programming specific classes of devices and applications.

Despite this progress, the way IoT systems are conceived, designed, and built remains largely ad hoc. Most proposals address a specific problem or layer of the technology stack, such as device connectivity, data streaming, or security, and are typically validated in a particular application domain. Developers who wish to build a complete IoT system must therefore assemble heterogeneous technologies, reconcile different programming models, and make critical architectural decisions with little methodological guidance. The result is that IoT systems are often tightly coupled to specific platforms or deployments, hard to evolve, hard to reuse, and difficult to reason about in terms of correctness, scalability, and dependability. This situation closely resembles earlier phases in the history of other computing paradigms, such as object-oriented, distributed, and agent-based systems, where the maturation of the field required principled software engineering approaches that provided shared abstractions, modeling languages, development processes, and tool support.

The IoT poses a distinctive set of challenges that make the adaptation of existing methodologies nontrivial. First, IoT systems are extremely heterogeneous: devices vary by orders of magnitude in computational power, energy availability, connectivity, and functionality, and they are produced by different vendors adopting different standards. Second, they are inherently distributed and open, with devices joining and leaving at runtime, often in unpredictable ways, and with ownership and control spread across multiple stakeholders. Third, they are deeply embedded in the physical world, so that software behavior is tied to the dynamics of the environment, to real-time constraints, and to the uncertainty of sensing and actuation. Fourth, they are expected to exhibit autonomy and adaptivity, reacting to context changes and coordinating with one another with little or no human intervention. Finally, they raise cross-cutting concerns, including security, privacy, trust, and sustainability, that cannot be treated as afterthoughts. These characteristics call for a methodology that can span multiple levels of abstraction, from the physical devices up to the application and social levels, and that can accommodate the continuous evolution of the system.

Several existing lines of work provide valuable building blocks. Model-driven engineering approaches offer ways to describe IoT systems and generate code for heterogeneous platforms. Service-oriented and resource-oriented architectures, such as those based on web services and the Web of Things, help to address interoperability. Agent-oriented software engineering contributes abstractions for autonomy, interaction, and organization. Cyber-physical systems and embedded software engineering emphasize the integration of computation with physical processes. Yet each of these perspectives captures only part of the picture, and they rely on different, often incompatible, vocabularies. What is currently missing is a coherent conceptual framework that identifies the key abstractions of IoT systems and shows how they relate to one another throughout the development life cycle.

In this paper, we take a step toward filling this gap. By synthesizing from the state of the art in the area, we attempt to frame the key concepts and abstractions that revolve around the design and development of IoT systems and applications. These include, among others, the notions of thing, the environment in which things are situated, the services and data they expose, the infrastructures that connect them, and the applications and goals that emerge from their cooperation. Starting from these abstractions, we draft a software engineering methodology that guides developers through the main phases of the development process, namely requirements analysis, design, implementation, deployment, and runtime evolution. The methodology is intended to be general, in the sense that it does not commit to a specific technology, platform, or application domain, while still being concrete enough to support the systematic production of IoT systems.

The contribution of this work is therefore twofold. On the conceptual side, we provide a structured view of the abstractions emerging from the literature, clarifying their roles and mutual dependencies. On the methodological side, we outline a process that leverages such abstractions to drive analysis and design decisions, and we discuss how existing approaches and tools can be positioned within it. We do not claim to present a complete or definitive methodology; rather, we aim to provide a foundation and a research agenda that can stimulate discussion and further refinement by the community.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the state of the art and the main challenges in IoT development. Section 3 presents the key concepts and abstractions. Section 4 describes the proposed methodology. Section 5 discusses open issues and research directions, and Section 6 concludes.

The methodology was developed through a three-step process: (i) a synthesis of the state of the art, (ii) the extraction of recurring concepts and abstractions, and (iii) the organization of those abstractions into a staged software engineering process.

**Literature synthesis.** We surveyed work on IoT architectures, middleware, programming models, and agent-oriented and service-oriented engineering. Sources were drawn from major digital libraries (IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect) and from proceedings of venues in pervasive computing, distributed systems, multi-agent systems, and software engineering. Search terms combined "Internet of Things," "IoT," "smart objects," "cyber-physical systems," and "ubiquitous computing" with "methodology," "software engineering," "middleware," "programming model," and "architecture." We included works that proposed a concrete design or development approach, a reference model, or a platform with explicit abstractions. We excluded works addressing only hardware, communication protocols, or domain-specific signal processing, unless they bore directly on software design. Publications were screened by title and abstract, then by full text, and each retained work was annotated with the abstractions it used, the problem it addressed, and the development phase it supported.

**Extraction of abstractions.** We coded the annotated works inductively to identify recurring concepts. Concepts were retained if they appeared across several independent proposals and were useful for reasoning about design rather than implementation. We merged synonyms (for example, "thing," "smart object," and "device") and separated terms that conflated distinct notions (for example, a physical entity versus its digital representation). This produced a conceptual framework in which the following abstractions are treated as first-class: physical entities and their digital counterparts; devices and resources that sense, actuate, or compute; services exposing capabilities; users and stakeholders; the environment and its context; and the interaction patterns (event-driven, request-response, publish-subscribe) that connect them. We also identified cross-cutting concerns, including heterogeneity, scale, dynamism and mobility, uncertainty of data, autonomy, security and privacy, and resource constraints.

**Layered organization.** To relate the abstractions to one another, we arranged them along two dimensions. The first is a set of levels of abstraction: the physical level (entities, sensors, actuators), the virtualization level (digital twins and resource abstractions), the service and application level (composition and orchestration), and the user level (goals and requirements). The second is the distribution of computation across the device, edge, and cloud tiers. Each abstraction was placed according to where it is most naturally modeled and where it is most commonly deployed in the surveyed work. This allowed us to check that the framework covers the range of architectures found in the literature without privileging a single technology stack.

**Derivation of the process.** The methodology was drafted by mapping the abstractions onto conventional software engineering phases, adapted to the specific features of IoT. We began from a generic iterative lifecycle and, for each phase, asked which IoT abstractions must be captured, which decisions must be taken, and which artifacts result.

1. *Requirements analysis*: identification of stakeholders, goals, and the physical phenomena and entities of interest, together with non-functional constraints such as latency, energy, and privacy.
2. *Domain and system modeling*: definition of entities, their digital representations, devices, resources, and context, and specification of the relations among them.
3. *Architecture and design*: allocation of functionality to device, edge, and cloud tiers; selection of interaction patterns; definition of services and their composition; and treatment of cross-cutting concerns.
4. *Implementation*: mapping of models to platforms, middleware, and programming abstractions, with attention to heterogeneity and portability.
5. *Deployment and configuration*: provisioning, discovery, and bootstrapping of devices and services, including support for mobility and changing topology.
6. *Verification, validation, and operation*: testing in simulated and real environments, runtime monitoring, and adaptation and evolution of the system after deployment.

Because IoT systems are open and change after deployment, the process was designed to be iterative, with feedback from runtime monitoring returning to the modeling and design phases.

**Consistency checking.** To assess whether the draft methodology was coherent and sufficiently general, we performed two checks. First, we conducted a coverage analysis: each surveyed proposal was mapped onto the methodology to verify that its main abstractions and phases could be represented, and gaps or ambiguities led to revision of the framework. Second, we traced a set of representative application scenarios, such as smart buildings, environmental monitoring, and logistics, through the phases to confirm that the abstractions could express their requirements and design choices. These checks are qualitative and intended to demonstrate the expressiveness and applicability of the approach rather than to provide empirical validation. Quantitative evaluation through case studies and controlled comparison with existing practice is left to future work.

**Scope and limitations.** The methodology is intentionally technology-neutral. It prescribes concepts, phases, and artifacts rather than specific languages, protocols, or tools, so that it can be instantiated with different platforms. Because it is derived from a non-exhaustive synthesis of the literature, it reflects the proposals and terminology available at the time of writing, and the selection and coding of the sources involved interpretive judgment by the authors.

The methodology emerging from our synthesis is organized around a small set of core abstractions, a layered process that operates on them, and a set of design guidelines derived from the surveyed literature. We report each in turn.

**Key abstractions.** Analysis of the surveyed proposals, covering middleware, programming models, architectures, and agent-based and service-oriented approaches, showed that most can be described using five recurring abstractions.

1. *Things*: physical or virtual entities with sensing, actuating, computing, or communication capabilities. We distinguish passive things (e.g., tagged objects), which are only observable, from active things, which can autonomously sense, decide, and act.
2. *Digital representations*: software counterparts of things (proxies, digital twins, or agents) that expose a uniform interface and hide heterogeneity of protocols and hardware.
3. *Services and capabilities*: the functionalities offered by things, described independently of their implementation so that they can be discovered and composed.
4. *Contexts and spaces*: logical or physical scopes (a room, a building, a city district) that delimit interaction, naming, and access, and that provide situational information to applications.
5. *Collectives and applications*: dynamic aggregations of things and services that jointly achieve a goal, with behavior that is not reducible to any single member.

These abstractions proved sufficient to map every proposal we examined onto at least one of them. Approaches differed mainly in which abstractions they treated as first-class. Middleware solutions emphasized digital representations and services, whereas programming models emphasized collectives and contexts. Few treated all five uniformly, which motivates a methodology that makes them explicit.

**Methodology phases.** The methodology comprises five iterative phases, each producing artifacts expressed in terms of the abstractions above.

*Requirements analysis* identifies stakeholders, goals, and constraints specific to IoT, namely energy budgets, latency, intermittent connectivity, privacy, and physical safety. Outputs are goal models and scenarios that state which things and contexts are involved.

*Domain modeling* identifies the things, their capabilities, and the spaces in which they operate. The result is a model of the physical environment and its digital representations, including the relationships among things (containment, proximity, ownership).

*System design* assigns responsibilities to computational layers. We identify three tiers (device, edge, and cloud) and make deployment-related decisions, such as where to place a digital representation or a collective's coordination logic, an explicit design activity instead of an implementation detail. Interaction protocols and data flows are specified at this stage, together with the mechanisms for discovery and adaptation.

*Implementation* maps design artifacts to platforms. Because the abstractions are technology-neutral, the same design may be realized with different programming models, such as event-driven, agent-oriented, or macroprogramming approaches for collectives.

*Deployment and evolution* addresses provisioning, monitoring, and runtime adaptation. Because IoT systems are open and long-lived, with things joining, leaving, and failing, we treat evolution as part of the normal lifecycle instead of as maintenance.

**Cross-cutting concerns.** Four concerns recurred across all phases and cannot be treated as late additions: interoperability, dynamism and adaptation, security and privacy, and resource awareness. For each, we identified how it manifests in each phase. For example, interoperability appears as semantic descriptions of capabilities during modeling, and as protocol bridging at the representation level during design. Security appears as trust relationships among things in the domain model and as access policies bound to contexts at design time.

**Illustrative application.** To check the expressiveness of the methodology, we applied it to a smart building scenario in which occupancy, temperature, and lighting are jointly managed. Requirements analysis yielded goals of comfort and energy saving, with a constraint on the privacy of occupant data. Domain modeling identified motion sensors, thermostats, lamps, and mobile phones as things, and rooms and floors as nested contexts. Each room context scoped the capabilities available to its collective, so that a "comfort collective" could be defined per room without referring to specific devices. In design, occupancy inference was placed at the edge to prevent raw presence data from leaving the building, while long-term optimization was placed in the cloud. The model made this placement decision visible and traceable to the privacy constraint. When a sensor was added or failed, the collective's membership was adjusted according to the capabilities required, with no change to the application logic. This example indicates that the abstractions support separation of concerns between application goals and the actual device population.

**Identified gaps.** The synthesis also revealed areas where current research does not yet support the methodology. First, there are few verification and testing techniques for systems that combine physical dynamics with software adaptation. Second, tool support for moving from design models to heterogeneous deployments is limited and mostly platform-specific. Third, there are no widely accepted notations for modeling contexts and collectives, so that models cannot easily be shared across tools. Fourth, engineering of non-functional properties such as energy and privacy is typically addressed in isolation, without integration into the design process. Finally, the human element, including users who configure and co-own the system, is rarely modeled explicitly.

Overall, the results suggest that a compact set of abstractions can unify a fragmented literature and provide a basis for a systematic process, while also delineating the open challenges toward a fully general IoT software engineering methodology.

The methodology sketched in this paper is a first step toward a principled software engineering approach for the Internet of Things. By synthesizing the state of the art, we identified a set of core abstractions (things, their digital counterparts, interaction and communication contexts, services, and the environments in which they are deployed) and organized the development process around them. Here we discuss what this framing offers, where its limits lie, and which directions we consider most pressing.

**Implications of the abstraction-centered approach.** A recurring observation in the literature is that IoT proposals are often tied to specific technologies, protocols, or application domains. This makes results hard to compare, reuse, or generalize. Centering the methodology on abstractions rather than technologies is intended to counter this fragmentation. Analysts and designers can reason about what an IoT system must do, and how its parts relate, before committing to platforms, middleware, or communication standards. This separation also supports traceability, since requirements expressed in terms of things, services, and contexts can be mapped through design to deployment decisions and then checked against them. We also believe the abstractions help bridge communities that approach IoT from different angles, such as embedded systems, distributed systems, service-oriented computing, and multi-agent systems. Each tends to use its own vocabulary for similar concepts, and a shared conceptual frame can reduce misunderstandings.

**Distinctive challenges addressed and left open.** IoT systems differ from conventional software in ways that stress traditional methodologies: extreme heterogeneity of devices, large scale, dynamic and open topologies, intermittent connectivity, resource constraints, and tight coupling with the physical world. Our methodology accommodates these in part by treating deployment context and device capabilities as first-class design concerns rather than late implementation details. However, several issues are only touched upon. Security and privacy cut across all abstractions and development phases, yet we have not provided concrete guidance on how to elicit, model, and verify such requirements. Similarly, the evolution of deployed systems, including over-the-air updates, device replacement, and the gradual appearance of new things, challenges the assumption that analysis and design precede deployment. A methodology for IoT must be inherently iterative and must support runtime adaptation, and our current treatment of these aspects is preliminary.

**Limitations.** The proposal is derived from a synthesis of existing literature and not from systematic empirical validation. Although we believe the abstractions are sufficiently general, their adequacy has not been tested across a broad range of case studies, such as smart homes, industrial automation, precision agriculture, and urban-scale sensing. Different domains may expose missing abstractions or reveal that some of ours are too coarse. Moreover, we have not yet addressed tool support. A methodology gains practical value when accompanied by modeling languages, code generators, simulators, and testing frameworks that embody its concepts. Without them, the burden of applying the approach falls entirely on developers, and adoption is unlikely. Finally, the methodology is described at a conceptual level; the precise work products, roles, and activities of each phase would need to be refined, ideally in collaboration with practitioners.

**Relation to existing work.** Our approach draws on and is complementary to several established lines of research: model-driven engineering for embedded and cyber-physical systems, agent-oriented methodologies, service-oriented architectures, and reference architectures for IoT. We do not claim to replace these; rather, we aim to position them within a common frame. For instance, model-driven techniques may realize the transition from abstract design to platform-specific code, while agent-oriented ideas may inform the modeling of autonomous, goal-driven things. Clarifying precisely how these contributions integrate, and where they conflict, is an important task for future work.

**Future directions.** We see four main directions. First, validating and refining the methodology through case studies and experiments with developers, measuring benefits such as reduced development effort, improved reuse, and fewer integration failures. Second, developing supporting tools, in particular a modeling notation tied to the proposed abstractions and automated mappings to common IoT platforms. Third, extending the methodology to cover non-functional and cross-cutting concerns, including security, privacy, energy efficiency, reliability, and ethical considerations such as data ownership and user control. Fourth, addressing the full lifecycle, with explicit support for runtime monitoring, self-adaptation, and continuous deployment, perhaps through the notion of digital twins as a bridge between design-time models and operating systems. Emerging paradigms such as edge and fog computing and the use of machine learning in devices will also require extending the abstractions to account for computation distributed across the cloud-to-thing continuum and for components whose behavior is learned rather than specified.

**Conclusion.** As IoT moves from experimental prototypes to critical infrastructure, ad hoc development practices become increasingly untenable. In this paper we framed the key concepts underlying IoT systems and outlined a software engineering methodology built on them. The proposal is necessarily incomplete, but it provides a common vocabulary, a structured view of the development process, and an agenda for further research. We hope it stimulates discussion and collaboration toward a mature, general, and practically useful engineering discipline for the Internet of Things.

Spasticity and dystonia are common and often disabling consequences of cerebral palsy (CP), the most prevalent cause of motor disability in childhood [1]. Increased tone impairs function, causes pain, contributes to contractures and hip displacement, and complicates positioning, hygiene, and caregiving. When oral agents, botulinum toxin injections, and physical therapy provide insufficient relief, or when systemic side effects such as sedation limit their use, continuous intrathecal delivery of baclofen has become an established option [2,3]. Baclofen, a gamma-aminobutyric acid type B receptor agonist, acts at the level of the spinal cord. Direct intrathecal administration achieves high cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentrations with a fraction of the oral dose, thereby limiting central adverse effects [4]. Randomized and observational studies have demonstrated reductions in spasticity and, in selected patients, improvements in comfort, ease of care, and in some cases function [5,6].

Despite these benefits, intrathecal baclofen (ITB) pump implantation in children carries a substantial burden of complications. Reported rates of surgical complications range widely but are frequently cited at 20% to 40% or higher, and include CSF leak and pseudomeningocele, wound dehiscence, infection, catheter malfunction, and the need for pump explantation or revision [7–9]. Children with CP are particularly vulnerable. They are often undernourished, have little subcutaneous tissue over which to cover a pump, and may have scoliosis or prior spinal instrumentation that complicates catheter placement. Infection rates in pediatric series are higher than in adult populations, and some reports show that infections and CSF-related wound problems account for a large proportion of unplanned returns to the operating room [8,10]. These events cause morbidity, prolong hospitalization, interrupt baclofen delivery, and may lead to abandonment of therapy. Efforts to reduce complications have therefore focused on surgical technique, such as subfascial pump placement, meticulous dural closure, and perioperative antibiotic protocols, as well as on patient selection and nutritional optimization [9,11].

One potential and underappreciated contributor to CSF-related complications is unrecognized elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) due to arrested or compensated hydrocephalus. Many children with CP have a history of conditions that predispose to disordered CSF dynamics, including prematurity with intraventricular hemorrhage, perinatal infection, and congenital brain malformations [12]. A subset of these patients receive CSF shunts in infancy, but others may have ventriculomegaly that stabilized without treatment and has been labeled "arrested" hydrocephalus.
