The concept of arrested hydrocephalus is controversial, since ventricular size correlates poorly with ICP, and some patients with apparently stable ventricles may in fact have a marginally compensated state in which CSF absorption remains impaired [13,14]. Creating a durable intrathecal puncture, placing a catheter, and then closing a wound over a pump pocket in the presence of elevated CSF pressure could plausibly promote persistent leakage along the catheter tract, pseudomeningocele formation, wound breakdown, and secondary infection.

Recognizing elevated ICP clinically in this population is difficult. The usual signs of hydrocephalus, including headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and declining school or motor performance, are nonspecific and hard to elicit in children who are nonverbal, have impaired cognition, or have chronic baseline neurological deficits and frequent gastrointestinal symptoms. Papilledema may be absent or difficult to assess. Neuroimaging may show ventriculomegaly, but this is common in CP owing to periventricular injury and white matter loss, and it does not reliably distinguish ex vacuo enlargement from pressure-related dilation [13]. Consequently, patients with clinically silent hydrocephalus may proceed to ITB implantation without any direct measurement of ICP. Case reports and small series describe patients with repeated CSF leaks after ITB placement who were later found to have hydrocephalus, with resolution of the problem after CSF diversion [15,16], supporting the plausibility of this mechanism, but systematic data are lacking.

Lumbar puncture performed with manometry offers a direct, minimally invasive means of measuring CSF pressure. When done under general anesthesia, however, interpretation requires attention to confounders such as anesthetic agents, ventilation, positioning, and carbon dioxide levels, so standardization is important. A threshold opening pressure above approximately 20 to 25 cmH2O is generally regarded as elevated in children [17]. Incorporating such a measurement into the preoperative pathway could identify patients at risk before an implant is placed, and permit consideration of CSF diversion or alternative strategies for spasticity management.

At our institution, concern about persistent CSF leaks and wound complications after ITB implantation prompted the development of a standardized protocol that included mandatory cranial imaging and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement before pump implantation. Patients with elevated pressure were not implanted at that time; instead, they were counseled regarding neurosurgical options, including ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement followed by reconsideration of ITB therapy, or continued nonoperative spasticity management. In this report, we describe our experience with this algorithm in a consecutive series of pediatric candidates for ITB implantation, characterize the frequency of previously unrecognized elevated ICP, and review the subsequent management and outcomes of these patients. We aim to provide a practical framework for the evaluation of hydrocephalus in this population and to stimulate further study of the relationship between CSF dynamics and ITB-related complications.

We conducted a retrospective case series of all pediatric patients evaluated for intrathecal baclofen (ITB) pump implantation at Seattle Children's Hospital between September 2012 and October 2014. The study was approved by the institutional review board, which waived the requirement for informed consent given the retrospective design and the use of de-identified data. Reporting followed published recommendations for case series [1].

**Patient Population**

Patients were eligible if they were referred to the neurosurgery service for ITB pump implantation to treat medically refractory spasticity, dystonia, or both, in the setting of cerebral palsy or related static encephalopathy. Candidacy for ITB therapy was determined by a multidisciplinary spasticity team that included pediatric neurosurgeons, physiatrists, orthopedic surgeons, and neurologists. Standard indications were generalized or lower-extremity spasticity or dystonia that interfered with care, comfort, positioning, or function and that did not respond adequately to oral agents, botulinum toxin injections, or both [2,3]. Patients were excluded from analysis if they had an active systemic or local infection, a previously implanted ITB pump, or if the family declined further evaluation before any preoperative assessment was completed. Patients with an existing CSF diversion device were not considered for the protocol, as their ICP status was managed through shunt evaluation.

**Standardized Preimplantation Protocol**

Because of high complication rates in our early ITB experience, including CSF leak, pseudomeningocele, wound dehiscence, and infection, which are consistent with the published literature [4,5], a standardized preoperative protocol was adopted in September 2012. The rationale was that clinically unrecognized arrested or compensated hydrocephalus might be present in this population, in whom baseline neurological impairment, communication limitations, and chronic neurological deficits obscure the usual symptoms and signs of raised ICP [6].

The protocol had three components. First, all patients underwent cranial imaging, either magnetic resonance imaging or computed tomography, before the procedure. Images were reviewed by a pediatric neurosurgeon and a neuroradiologist for ventricular size, periventricular changes, evidence of prior hemorrhage or periventricular leukomalacia, and other structural abnormalities. Ventriculomegaly alone was not considered diagnostic of active hydrocephalus, since it commonly occurs from ex vacuo change in patients with cerebral palsy [7].

Second, all patients underwent a lumbar puncture (LP) for measurement of opening pressure under general anesthesia, as a separate preliminary step before pump implantation. Third, a predefined decision rule determined whether implantation proceeded.

**Lumbar Puncture and ICP Measurement**

LPs were performed in the operating room under general anesthesia with standard monitoring. Patients were positioned in the lateral decubitus position with the hips and knees flexed to the extent permitted by their tone and contractures. A spinal needle was inserted at the lower lumbar interspaces under sterile conditions, and a manometer was attached to measure opening pressure after the CSF level stabilized and showed respiratory variation. To reduce confounding from anesthetic effects on ICP, the anesthesia team maintained normocapnia (end-tidal CO2 of approximately 35–40 mmHg), avoided agents known to substantially elevate ICP where possible, and kept the head of the bed neutral. Opening pressure was recorded in cmH2O. When indicated, CSF was sent for cell count, protein, glucose, and culture to exclude occult infection before implantation of hardware.

An opening pressure above 21 cmH2O was defined as elevated, based on pediatric reference values for lumbar opening pressure [8]. Patients with opening pressures of 21 cmH2O or lower were assigned to the "normal ICP" group, and those with higher values to the "elevated ICP" group.

**Management Algorithm**

Patients in the normal ICP group proceeded to ITB pump implantation, either in the same anesthetic session or at a later date, depending on scheduling and family preference. In the elevated ICP group, pump implantation was aborted, and the findings were discussed with the family. Alternative management options were presented, including observation, additional evaluation such as ophthalmologic examination for papilledema, repeat or continuous ICP monitoring, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, and ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement. Families who chose CSF diversion underwent the procedure by a pediatric neurosurgeon using standard techniques with programmable valves. Those patients were reconsidered for ITB pump implantation after recovery from shunt surgery, with a reasonable interval allowed for wound healing and clinical stabilization. Other families elected to forgo further intervention or to pursue non-ITB treatments for spasticity.

**ITB Pump Implantation**

Pump implantation followed a standard technique. Patients received perioperative intravenous antibiotics. Under general anesthesia, patients were placed in the lateral decubitus position. A catheter was placed through a paramedian needle into the lumbar intrathecal space and advanced to the desired spinal level under fluoroscopic guidance. The catheter was secured to the fascia, tunneled subcutaneously, and connected to a pump placed in a subcutaneous or subfascial abdominal pocket. Meticulous watertight fascial closure was performed. Patients received a screening bolus trial of baclofen before implantation when this was part of the team's practice. Pumps were programmed initially at a low dose, and doses were titrated in clinic.

**Data Collection and Outcomes**

Data were abstracted from electronic medical records and included age, sex, etiology of cerebral palsy, Gross Motor Function Classification System level, prior neurosurgical history, imaging findings, opening pressure, CSF studies, and subsequent management. The primary outcomes were the proportion of patients with elevated opening pressure and the proportion ultimately undergoing ITB pump implantation. The secondary outcome was postoperative complications, including CSF leak, pseudomeningocele, wound breakdown, infection, catheter malfunction, and need for reoperation, assessed through the most recent follow-up visit.

**Statistical Analysis**

Given the small sample, analysis was descriptive. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables as medians and ranges. Comparisons between the normal and elevated ICP groups were not powered for inferential testing.

Eighteen patients were evaluated for ITB pump implantation at our institution during the study period (September 2012 to October 2014) and underwent lumbar puncture under general anesthesia according to the standardized protocol. The cohort comprised 10 male and 8 female patients with a mean age of 11.2 years (range 5–19 years) at the time of evaluation. All patients had a diagnosis of cerebral palsy with spasticity, dystonia, or a mixed movement disorder. Most were classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System level IV or V (15/18, 83.3%). Etiologies of cerebral palsy included prematurity with or without intraventricular hemorrhage (9 patients), hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (5), and other or unknown causes (4). Four patients had a documented history of neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage, and none had a previously placed CSF diversion device.

**Preoperative imaging**

All patients underwent cranial imaging (MRI in 14 patients, CT in 4) before lumbar puncture. Ventricular enlargement of varying degree was identified in 9 patients, while 9 had normal or ex vacuo–appearing ventricles. Imaging findings were not sufficiently discriminating to predict ICP. Of the 8 patients with elevated opening pressure, 6 had ventriculomegaly on imaging and 2 had ventricles of normal size. Conversely, 3 of the 10 patients with normal opening pressure had ventriculomegaly that was judged to be stable or secondary to volume loss. Before the procedure, none of the patients had clinical signs that would have prompted a diagnosis of hydrocephalus; caregivers did not report new headache, vomiting, or changes in alertness, although the baseline neurological function of this population limited the reliability of such assessments.

**Intracranial pressure measurement**

Lumbar puncture was technically successful in all 18 patients, and an opening pressure was obtained in each case. No complications of lumbar puncture, including postprocedural headache, infection, or hemorrhage, were noted. Eight patients (44.4%) had an opening pressure exceeding 21 cmH2O and were classified into the "elevated ICP" group; the remaining 10 patients (55.6%) comprised the "normal ICP" group. In the elevated ICP group, opening pressures ranged from 22 to 38 cmH2O (mean 28.1 cmH2O), whereas in the normal ICP group they ranged from 9 to 20 cmH2O (mean 15.4 cmH2O). Age, sex, GMFCS level, and cause of cerebral palsy did not differ significantly between groups, although the small sample size limits the power of such comparisons. A history of intraventricular hemorrhage was more common in the elevated ICP group (3/8) than in the normal ICP group (1/10), but this difference was not statistically significant.

**Management of patients with normal ICP**

Of the 10 patients with normal opening pressure, 9 proceeded to ITB pump implantation, which was performed under the same anesthetic or in a short interval after the lumbar puncture. One patient in this group did not undergo implantation because the family elected to defer the procedure after the trial of intrathecal baclofen was considered to provide insufficient functional benefit. The 9 implanted patients received a programmable pump placed in the abdominal wall with the catheter tunneled to the intrathecal space. No patient in this group experienced a CSF leak, pseudomeningocele, wound dehiscence, or infection, and no patient required early revision or explantation during the follow-up period. Mean follow-up for these patients was 11 months (range 3–24 months).

**Management of patients with elevated ICP**

In the 8 patients with elevated ICP, pump implantation was aborted and alternative options were discussed with the families. These options included observation, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement, or abandonment of ITB therapy in favor of other spasticity treatments. Five families elected to proceed with CSF diversion, and in all five, a VP shunt was placed (programmable valve in 4 patients, fixed-pressure valve in 1). Of the remaining three patients, two families opted to continue oral antispasticity medications and chemodenervation, and one family chose observation with plans for later reassessment.

Following shunt placement, 2 patients ultimately underwent ITB pump implantation. Three additional patients who had been shunted, however, did not proceed to implantation: in two, spasticity or dystonia improved sufficiently after CSF diversion that ITB therapy was no longer thought necessary by the treating team and family, and in one the family withdrew because of concern regarding the cumulative surgical burden. Thus, of the 8 patients with elevated ICP, 2 (25%) received a pump, 3 (37.5%) were shunted without pump placement, and 3 (37.5%) were managed without CSF diversion or pump implantation. In the two patients implanted after shunting, the pump was placed at a minimum of 6 weeks after shunt surgery, and the shunt was functioning appropriately as assessed clinically and radiographically. Neither patient developed a CSF leak, wound complication, or infection. No shunt malfunction or infection occurred in any of the five shunted patients during follow-up.

**Overall outcomes**

In total, 11 of 18 patients (61.1%) underwent ITB pump implantation: 9 of 10 (90%) in the normal ICP group and 2 of 8 (25%) in the elevated ICP group after VP shunt placement. No postoperative complications, including CSF leak, wound breakdown, infection, or catheter-related problems requiring revision, were observed in any of the 11 implanted patients. Five patients (27.8% of the total cohort) underwent a neurosurgical CSF diversion procedure as a direct consequence of the protocol-driven ICP assessment, and these patients had not previously been suspected clinically to have hydrocephalus. Among the 5 shunted patients, caregivers of 3 reported improved alertness, comfort, or ease of care after shunting, although these observations were subjective and not formally quantified.

Intrathecal baclofen (ITB) therapy is an established treatment for severe spasticity and dystonia in children with cerebral palsy, yet its complication profile remains considerable. Reported rates of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak, wound breakdown, and infection in pediatric series range from roughly 10% to over 30%, and many of these events necessitate device explantation [1,2]. Established risk factors include young age, low body mass, poor nutritional status, and the presence of gastrostomy or other hardware [2,3]. In this series, we examined a further and potentially modifiable contributor: unrecognized elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) from arrested or incompletely compensated hydrocephalus. Using a standardized protocol of cranial imaging and lumbar puncture (LP) under general anesthesia, we found that 8 of 18 patients (44.4%) had an opening pressure above 21 cmH2O. Among those who ultimately received a pump, no postoperative complications occurred.

The high prevalence of elevated ICP deserves emphasis. Children with cerebral palsy frequently have a history of prematurity, intraventricular hemorrhage, or perinatal brain injury, all of which predispose to ventriculomegaly and disordered CSF dynamics [4]. Clinical detection of raised ICP in this population is difficult. Baseline neurological impairment, limited communication, and chronic irritability or feeding difficulty can mask headache, vomiting, lethargy, or altered behavior. Ventricular size on imaging is also an unreliable surrogate, since ventriculomegaly may reflect ex vacuo change after parenchymal loss rather than active hydrocephalus, and normal-appearing ventricles do not exclude elevated pressure in a noncompliant brain. Direct measurement of pressure therefore provides information that neither examination nor imaging can reliably supply. Our findings are consistent with isolated reports of hydrocephalus unmasked or worsened after ITB placement, and of pseudomeningocele and CSF leak in patients later found to have impaired CSF absorption [5,6].

A plausible mechanism links elevated ICP to the wound complications seen with ITB pumps. Implantation creates a dural opening through which a catheter passes, together with a subcutaneous pocket adjacent to it. If CSF pressure is chronically elevated, a persistent pressure gradient favors leakage along the catheter tract, producing pseudomeningocele, impaired wound healing, and a pathway for bacterial colonization. Infection and dehiscence may then follow in a population already at risk because of thin subcutaneous tissue. Treating the underlying pressure problem before implantation, as we did with ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting, would be expected to reduce this risk. Although our sample is too small to demonstrate causation, the absence of complications among 11 implanted patients compares favorably with published rates and supports the hypothesis.

Performing LP under general anesthesia is an important element of the protocol. Opening pressures measured in awake, crying, or agitated children are unreliable because of Valsalva effects, and sedation or positioning can also alter readings. Controlled conditions with the patient relaxed, in the lateral decubitus position, and with appropriate attention to ventilation and carbon dioxide levels give more reproducible values. The threshold of 21 cmH2O was chosen conservatively, and values somewhat above normal may not always represent clinically significant hydrocephalus [7]. Nevertheless, in a procedure with a high complication burden and a hardware-dependent outcome, a conservative threshold seems justifiable. Because the LP is performed in the same anesthetic session as planned surgical evaluation, the added risk and cost are small.

Management of patients with elevated ICP requires individualized decision-making. Of the eight such patients, two ultimately underwent ITB implantation after VP shunt placement, whereas the remainder did not proceed. Reasons included family preference after counseling, the perceived burden of a second device, and improvement in symptoms or reassessment of treatment goals. Alternatives discussed included CSF diversion alone, endoscopic third ventriculostomy in selected anatomy, oral antispastic medications, botulinum toxin, orthopedic procedures, and selective dorsal rhizotomy where appropriate. Shunting itself is not benign, with substantial rates of malfunction and infection over time, and combining a shunt with an ITB pump raises concerns about hardware proximity and additive infection risk [8]. Families must therefore be counseled that detection of elevated ICP may change the treatment pathway and may add surgery. We believe this discussion is best undertaken by a multidisciplinary team including neurosurgery, neurology, orthopedics, and rehabilitation medicine.

This study has several limitations. It is a retrospective, single-institution series with a small number of patients, precluding statistical comparison of complication rates between groups or against historical controls. Selection bias is possible, as patients referred to a tertiary center may have more complex disease. We lacked a comparison cohort implanted without LP screening, and follow-up duration was limited, so late complications such as catheter failure or delayed infection may not have been captured. The relationship between opening pressure and imaging features was not analyzed systematically, and we cannot define which clinical or radiographic characteristics might identify patients at highest risk. Finally, the pressure threshold has not been validated specifically in this population.

## Conclusion

Elevated ICP consistent with arrested hydrocephalus was common among children with cerebral palsy evaluated for ITB pump implantation and was not predictable from clinical assessment alone. A standardized pre-implantation protocol combining cranial imaging with LP-measured opening pressure under general anesthesia is feasible, safe, and identifies patients who may benefit from neurosurgical management of CSF dynamics before a pump is placed. Eleven patients were implanted without postoperative complications, suggesting that this approach may reduce CSF leak and related wound problems. We advocate routine pre-implantation ICP assessment and thoughtful, family-centered consideration of neurosurgical options when pressure is elevated. Larger prospective, multicenter studies are needed to confirm whether this strategy lowers complication rates and to refine pressure thresholds and treatment algorithms.

Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecologic malignancy and one of the leading causes of cancer death among women worldwide. Its high mortality reflects, in large part, late diagnosis: because early disease is usually asymptomatic or produces nonspecific symptoms, most patients present with advanced stage disease, when five-year survival falls below 30%. When the disease is detected at stage I, five-year survival exceeds 90%. Accurate preoperative evaluation of women with a pelvic mass is therefore central to improving outcomes.

Pelvic masses are common, and the great majority are benign. The clinical challenge is to identify the minority that are malignant before surgery so that these patients can be referred to a gynecologic oncologist or a center with appropriate expertise. Evidence consistently shows that women with ovarian cancer who are operated on by gynecologic oncologists are more likely to be optimally staged and cytoreduced, and have better survival than those treated by general surgeons or non-specialist gynecologists. Conversely, overestimating risk leads to unnecessary referral, extensive surgery, and anxiety for women with benign disease, and strains limited specialist resources. This balance is particularly relevant in many Asian countries, where access to gynecologic oncology services may be unevenly distributed.

Several tools have been proposed to triage pelvic masses. Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality, and morphologic features such as solid components, papillary projections, septations, bilaterality, ascites, and abnormal vascularity are associated with malignancy. However, ultrasound interpretation depends on operator experience, and the accuracy reported by expert examiners is often not reproduced in general practice. The serum biomarker cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) has long been used, but it has limited specificity, as it is elevated in many benign conditions including endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, and menstruation, and in premenopausal women in general. Its sensitivity is also limited in early stage disease and in certain histologic subtypes such as mucinous tumors.

To improve discrimination, multivariable approaches have been developed. The risk of malignancy index (RMI) combines ultrasound score, menopausal status, and CA-125 level, and is widely used, particularly in the United Kingdom. Its performance varies across populations and depends on how ultrasound scoring is applied. Human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) is a more recently characterized biomarker that is overexpressed in epithelial ovarian carcinomas, particularly serous and endometrioid types, and is rarely elevated in common benign gynecologic conditions such as endometriosis. HE4 has been reported to show higher specificity than CA-125, especially in premenopausal women. The risk of ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA) combines HE4, CA-125, and menopausal status in a logistic regression equation to classify women as being at high or low risk of epithelial ovarian cancer, and has been cleared by regulatory authorities for use in women with a pelvic mass. Studies comparing ROMA with RMI have produced mixed results, with some showing superior sensitivity for ROMA and others showing comparable performance, and the findings differ by menopausal status, histologic type, and study population.

Most validation studies of these tools were conducted in Western populations. Biomarker levels, the distribution of histologic subtypes, and the prevalence of benign conditions such as endometriosis may differ in Asian women, and HE4 levels are influenced by factors including age, renal function, and smoking. Data from prospective multicenter studies in Asia are comparatively limited, and it is uncertain whether algorithms developed elsewhere perform optimally in these populations.

Notably, ROMA does not incorporate imaging findings, whereas RMI includes only a crude ultrasound score. Because ultrasound and serum markers capture different aspects of tumor biology, it is plausible that combining HE4 with ultrasound features and menopausal status would yield a more discriminating model than either approach alone. A model that integrates these readily available variables could be implemented in routine clinical settings without sophisticated additional testing. Furthermore, a score that stratifies women into several graded risk categories, rather than a single dichotomous cutoff, may better support clinical decisions, for instance by identifying women who can safely be managed locally and those who should be referred for specialist surgery.

The purpose of this study was therefore to develop a risk prediction score for distinguishing benign from malignant pelvic masses using CA-125, HE4, ultrasound findings, and menopausal status in a prospective multicenter cohort of women from six Asian countries who were scheduled for surgery. We compared the performance of models containing CA-125 alone, CA-125 combined with HE4, and HE4 combined with menopausal status and ultrasound findings, applied bootstrap validation to assess the stability of the final model, and compared its diagnostic performance with that of ROMA and RMI.

This prospective, multicenter observational study was conducted at six centers in six Asian countries. The study was approved by the institutional review board or ethics committee at each participating site and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment.

**Study population**

Women aged 18 years or older were eligible if they had a pelvic mass detected by imaging (ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging) and were scheduled to undergo surgery for the mass. Exclusion criteria were pregnancy, a prior diagnosis of malignancy within the preceding five years, current or previous chemotherapy, and inability to provide informed consent. Women with insufficient serum samples or without a final histopathological diagnosis were also excluded from analysis. Menopausal status was recorded at enrollment; women were classified as postmenopausal if they had experienced at least 12 months of amenorrhea not attributable to other causes, had undergone bilateral oophorectomy, or were older than 50 years after hysterectomy without oophorectomy.

**Sample collection and biomarker assays**

Blood samples were collected before surgery. Serum was separated by centrifugation, aliquoted, and stored at −70 °C to −80 °C until analysis. Freeze-thaw cycles were avoided. Serum CA-125 and HE4 concentrations were measured using automated chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays (ARCHITECT, Abbott Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Assays were performed by laboratory personnel blinded to clinical, imaging, and pathological findings. Quality control materials were run at the beginning of each batch to ensure assay performance.

**Ultrasound evaluation**

Transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasound was performed before surgery by experienced examiners at each center according to local practice. The following findings were recorded using a standardized case report form: multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, presence of ascites, and intra-abdominal metastases. Each finding was scored as present (1) or absent (0). Following the approach used for the risk of malignancy index (RMI), the ultrasound score (U) was defined as 0 for no findings, 1 for one finding, and 3 for two or more findings. Patients without documented ultrasound findings were excluded from the models involving ultrasound but were retained for biomarker-only analyses.

**Reference standard**

The reference standard was the final histopathological diagnosis of the surgical specimen, established by the local pathologist at each center according to World Health Organization criteria. Tumors were classified as benign, borderline, or malignant. Epithelial ovarian cancer, including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal cancers, was grouped with other primary ovarian malignancies for the primary analysis. Pathologists were blinded to biomarker results.

**Comparator algorithms**

The RMI was calculated as U × M × CA-125 (U/mL), where M was 1 for premenopausal and 3 for postmenopausal women, and a cutoff of 200 was used. The risk of ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA) was calculated from HE4 and CA-125 using menopause-specific formulas. For premenopausal women, the predictive index (PI) was −12.0 + 2.38 × ln(HE4) + 0.0626 × ln(CA-125). For postmenopausal women, PI was −8.09 + 1.04 × ln(HE4) + 0.732 × ln(CA-125). ROMA (%) was calculated as exp(PI) / [1 + exp(PI)] × 100. Previously recommended cutoffs for high-risk classification were applied: 7.4% for premenopausal and 25.3% for postmenopausal women.

**Statistical analysis**

Descriptive statistics are presented as medians with ranges or interquartile ranges for continuous variables and as counts and percentages for categorical variables. Differences between benign and malignant groups were evaluated with the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. CA-125 and HE4 values were log-transformed to approximate normality before modeling.

Univariable logistic regression was first used to identify factors associated with malignancy. Variables with a P-value below 0.10 were entered into multivariable logistic regression models using stepwise selection. Three models were developed: (1) CA-125 alone, (2) CA-125 and HE4, and (3) HE4, menopausal status, and ultrasound findings. Model discrimination was assessed with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals, and AUCs were compared using the DeLong method. Calibration was evaluated with the Hosmer-Lemeshow test.

The regression coefficients of the final model were used to construct a risk prediction score. Predicted probabilities were categorized into risk groups (very low, low, medium-low, medium, and high) on the basis of the observed prevalence of malignancy in each stratum, with the aim of providing clinically interpretable categories. Women classified as medium or high risk were considered test-positive, and those in the very-low, low, or medium-low categories were considered test-negative. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were calculated with exact binomial 95% confidence intervals. Sensitivity and specificity of the risk prediction model were compared with those of ROMA, RMI, and CA-125 alone (using a cutoff of 35 U/mL) with McNemar's test on paired data.

**Internal validation**

Because no independent validation cohort was available, a bootstrap technique was used to assess the internal validity of the HE4-based model. A total of 1,000 bootstrap samples were drawn with replacement from the original dataset, and the model was refit in each sample and applied to the original data. The optimism in the AUC was estimated as the average difference between bootstrap and original performance, and an optimism-corrected AUC was derived.

**Subgroup and sensitivity analyses**

Performance was examined separately in premenopausal and postmenopausal women and for epithelial ovarian cancer versus all malignancies. Analyses were also performed with borderline tumors classified as benign and then as malignant to assess the effect of this classification. Missing data were not imputed; analyses were performed on available cases.

All tests were two-sided, and P<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SAS (SAS Institute) and R software.

A total of 414 women with a pelvic mass were enrolled across the six participating centers in six Asian countries. Of these, 328 (79.2%) had documented preoperative ultrasound findings and were included in the development of the ultrasound-based risk prediction model. Analyses restricted to CA-125, HE4, and ROMA used all patients with available biomarker data. Final histopathology classified the masses as benign in the majority of patients, with the remainder being epithelial ovarian cancer, borderline tumors, non-epithelial ovarian malignancies, or metastatic tumors. Women with malignant disease were older on average than those with benign disease and were more frequently postmenopausal. The proportion of postmenopausal women was also higher in the malignant group (p<0.05).

**Biomarker levels.** Median serum CA-125 and HE4 concentrations were significantly higher in women with ovarian cancer than in those with benign disease (both p<0.001). HE4 values were elevated in most epithelial cancers, particularly serous and endometrioid subtypes, whereas CA-125 was more frequently elevated in benign conditions such as endometriosis, especially in premenopausal women. Among women with endometriosis, CA-125 produced many false-positive results, while HE4 values remained largely within the normal range. Mucinous and borderline tumors showed lower marker levels than high-grade serous carcinomas for both markers.

**Univariate and multivariable analysis.** On univariate logistic regression, CA-125, HE4, menopausal status, and several ultrasound features were each significantly associated with malignancy. The ultrasound features associated with malignancy were the presence of solid components, papillary projections, irregular or thick septations, ascites, and bilateral lesions. In the multivariable model, HE4, menopausal status, and ultrasound findings remained independent predictors of malignancy. When ultrasound findings and HE4 were included in the model, CA-125 no longer contributed significantly and was dropped from the final model. Three candidate models were compared: CA-125 alone, CA-125 combined with HE4, and HE4 combined with menopausal status and ultrasound findings. The last model had the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and the best overall fit. The CA-125 model had the lowest discrimination, and adding HE4 to CA-125 improved performance modestly.

**Risk prediction score.** Based on the regression coefficients, a risk prediction score was developed and patients were stratified into risk categories: very low, low, medium-low, medium, and high. The model classified 77.2% of women with ovarian cancer as medium or high risk. Conversely, 86% of women with benign disease were classified as very-low, low, or medium-low risk. The observed proportion of malignancy increased progressively across the risk categories. It was very low in the very-low and low categories and highest in the high-risk category, where most patients had invasive cancer. Few women with cancer were assigned to the lowest two categories, and those who were had mostly early-stage or non-epithelial tumors, or borderline histology. Benign tumors classified as medium or high risk typically had complex ultrasound morphology, such as solid components in fibromas, or endometriomas and tubo-ovarian abscesses with elevated markers.

**Internal validation.** Bootstrap resampling was used to assess the validity of the HE4 model. The optimism-corrected AUC was close to the apparent AUC, indicating minimal overfitting. The regression coefficients were stable across bootstrap samples, and the calibration plot showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities of malignancy, with only slight deviation at the extremes of predicted risk.

**Comparison with ROMA and CA-125.** The performance of the risk prediction model was compared with ROMA and with CA-125 alone, and the risk of malignancy index was also evaluated in patients with the necessary ultrasound data. At the chosen cutoff (medium risk or higher), the HE4-based model had higher sensitivity for detecting ovarian cancer than ROMA, CA-125 alone, and the risk of malignancy index. ROMA, however, had higher specificity than the risk prediction model. Both the new model and ROMA performed better than CA-125 alone, which showed the lowest specificity, particularly in premenopausal women. The gain in sensitivity with the new model was seen in both premenopausal and postmenopausal subgroups, and was most evident for early-stage disease (stage I–II), in which ROMA missed a larger share of cases. Positive predictive value was similar between the model and ROMA, whereas negative predictive value was higher for the new model because of its greater sensitivity. The AUC of the new model was higher than that of ROMA and of CA-125 alone, although the difference from ROMA was smaller than the difference from CA-125.

**Subgroup observations.** Performance did not differ markedly across participating countries, although the numbers per site were small. Results were consistent when borderline tumors were analyzed with either the benign or the malignant group, though sensitivity decreased slightly when they were counted as malignant. Excluding women with missing ultrasound data did not change the direction of any of the comparisons between models.

In this prospective multicenter study of Asian women with a pelvic mass scheduled for surgery, we developed a risk prediction model combining serum HE4, menopausal status, and ultrasound findings. The model outperformed CA-125 alone and the combination of CA-125 and HE4. It classified 77.2% of women with ovarian cancer as medium or high risk, and 86% of women with benign disease as very-low, low, or medium-low risk. Compared with ROMA, the model had higher sensitivity, whereas ROMA had higher specificity. Both algorithms were superior to CA-125 alone.

These findings agree with earlier work showing that HE4 is less often elevated in benign gynecologic conditions, such as endometriosis, than CA-125 is. This property likely explains why adding HE4 improved discrimination, particularly among premenopausal women, in whom CA-125 produces many false positives. Our results also agree with studies showing that ROMA, which combines CA-125, HE4, and menopausal status, performs better than either marker alone. The new element here is that adding ultrasound morphology to HE4 and menopausal status increased sensitivity beyond that of ROMA. Ultrasound captures information that serum markers cannot, such as solid components, papillary projections, ascites, and septations. Biomarkers in turn add objective information that depends less on the examiner. The two modalities are therefore complementary, and combining them in a single score is a logical step.

The sensitivity–specificity trade-off deserves comment. The higher sensitivity of our model suits triage, where the main aim is to avoid missing a malignancy and to direct women at higher risk to a gynecologic oncologist. Failure to do so is associated with suboptimal surgical staging, higher rates of reoperation, and worse outcomes. The lower specificity compared with ROMA means that some women with benign masses would be classified as intermediate risk and referred or counseled unnecessarily. We believe the multilevel risk categories (very low to high) partly mitigate this problem. Rather than forcing a dichotomous decision, they allow clinicians to match management to the level of risk. Women in the lowest categories could reasonably be managed in a general gynecology setting, possibly with a minimally invasive approach or conservative follow-up, whereas those in the highest categories should be referred for oncologic surgery. Women in the intermediate category may benefit from further imaging or expert review.

Several features strengthen this study. The design was prospective and multicenter, and it enrolled women from six Asian countries. Most existing algorithms were developed in European or North American populations, and the performance of biomarkers can vary with ethnicity, with the prevalence of histologic subtypes, and with the baseline distribution of marker levels. Our data therefore add evidence for a population that has been relatively underrepresented. The use of preoperative samples and histopathologic diagnosis as the reference standard further supports the validity of the results. We also applied a bootstrap technique to assess the model's internal validity and to limit overfitting, which is a recognized concern when a model is derived and tested in the same dataset.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, ultrasound findings were documented for only 328 of the 414 enrolled women, so the final model was derived from a smaller sample, and missing data could have introduced selection bias. Second, ultrasound was performed and interpreted by examiners at the participating sites, with no central review. Ultrasound is operator dependent, and the model may perform differently where examiners are less experienced. Our results may therefore overstate or understate real-world performance, and the model's generalizability depends on standardized terminology, such as the IOTA descriptors. Third, although bootstrapping provides an internal check, we lacked an independent external validation cohort, so the performance estimates remain optimistic until confirmed prospectively elsewhere. Fourth, the study population consisted of women already scheduled for surgery, who are likely to have a higher prevalence of malignancy than those seen in primary care, which limits extrapolation to unselected patients. Predictive values depend on prevalence and would differ in other settings. Fifth, we did not compare our model directly with other ultrasound-based approaches such as the IOTA simple rules or ADNEX, which may perform similarly or better when used by experts. Finally, the heterogeneity of ovarian cancer, including borderline tumors and early-stage mucinous or non-epithelial tumors, which often have lower HE4 or CA-125 levels, may have affected sensitivity in specific subgroups, and the sample was too small for reliable subgroup analysis.

Future research should validate the model in larger independent cohorts, ideally with centralized or standardized ultrasound assessment, and should compare it directly with ADNEX and the IOTA rules. Evaluating its effect on clinical outcomes, such as appropriate referral, surgical planning, and cost, would show whether the improved sensitivity translates into patient benefit. Subgroup analyses by histology and stage would also clarify where the algorithm is least reliable.

In conclusion, combining HE4 with menopausal status and ultrasound findings produced a risk prediction score that distinguished malignant from benign pelvic masses better than CA-125 alone or CA-125 with HE4, and with greater sensitivity than ROMA, although with lower specificity. The multilevel risk categories may help clinicians decide which women should be referred to specialist oncologic care. External validation is needed before the model can be recommended for routine clinical use.

Statistical spoken dialogue systems have received considerable attention in recent years because they promise to reduce the manual effort of system design while improving robustness to speech recognition errors and other sources of uncertainty. Modelling dialogue as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) allows the system to maintain a belief over user goals and to optimize its behaviour through reinforcement learning (RL). In this framework the dialogue policy, which maps belief states to system actions, is learned from interaction with real or simulated users, guided by a reward signal.

The reward function is therefore the central means by which the system designer specifies what constitutes good behaviour. In task-oriented dialogue, the reward typically combines several components. The most common are a large positive reward for dialogue success and a small penalty for each dialogue turn, which encourages short dialogues. Other components are possible, such as penalties for confirming too often, rewards for user satisfaction estimates, or costs for particular system actions. These components frequently conflict. A system that asks many confirmation questions is more likely to succeed but produces longer and more tedious dialogues, whereas a system that terminates quickly may be efficient but fail more often. How the components are weighted determines the trade-off the learned policy will make.

In practice, the weights are usually set by hand and rarely questioned. A typical choice is a success reward of 20 and a turn penalty of -1, which has been adopted in many studies largely by convention. There is, however, no guarantee that this choice is appropriate for a given domain or application. Domains differ in complexity, in the number of slots and values, in the level of noise, and in what users tolerate. A weighting that works well for a small restaurant-search domain may be a poor choice for a larger domain in which reaching success requires more turns. Moreover, the designer may have preferences about the final system's performance, such as a minimum success rate, that are only indirectly related to the weights. Finding good weights thus becomes a search problem in its own right.

A straightforward approach is to train a separate policy for each candidate weighting and compare the results. This is very expensive. Each policy requires thousands of training dialogues, and the number of candidate weightings grows quickly as components are added. When training involves human users, for example via crowdsourcing, this cost is prohibitive. Even with simulated users, the repeated training makes systematic exploration of reward weights unattractive. As a consequence, the reward weighting has remained one of the least examined design decisions in statistical dialogue systems.

In this work we propose a structured method for finding a good balance between reward components. Our central idea is to treat dialogue policy learning as a multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) problem. Instead of collapsing the reward components into a single scalar before training, MORL maintains a vector-valued reward and learns a set of policies, or a value function that is a function of the weighting, that covers many possible trade-offs simultaneously. Once such a solution has been learned, the policy that is optimal for any particular weighting can be obtained without training from scratch. This allows us to evaluate many candidate weightings at a small fraction of the cost of independent training runs, and thus to search for the weighting that yields the most desirable system behaviour.

We use this approach to reduce the number of training dialogues needed to explore the weight space significantly. Training is performed once, with the data efficiently shared across weightings, and the search over weights then proceeds by evaluating the resulting policies. The designer can specify an objective for the search, for instance maximizing the success rate subject to a constraint on dialogue length, or maximizing a combined quality measure, and the method returns the weighting that best satisfies it. This makes the choice of reward weights explicit, reproducible and tied to a measurable criterion rather than to convention.

We apply the proposed method to six domains of differing size and complexity, and compare the optimized weights and the resulting policies against a default baseline weighting commonly used in the literature. This lets us investigate whether the default is adequate across domains and how much is gained by tuning. We also examine how the optimal weights vary with domain characteristics, which provides insight into how reward design depends on the task.

The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we formulate the selection of reward component weights for dialogue policy optimization as a search problem and propose a structured procedure for solving it. Second, we show how multi-objective reinforcement learning makes this search feasible by greatly reducing the number of required training dialogues. Third, we present an empirical study in six domains, comparing optimized weights to a default baseline and analysing how the best weighting differs among domains.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on reward design and multi-objective reinforcement learning. Section 3 introduces the background on POMDP-based dialogue management. Section 4 describes the proposed method, Section 5 presents the experiments and results, and Section 6 concludes.

We consider dialogue policy optimization as a Markov decision process in which, at every turn t, the policy maps a belief state b_t to a system action a_t. The turn-level reward is a vector r_t = (r_t^1, ..., r_t^K) of K components. In this work we use two components: a success component, which gives 1 at the end of a dialogue if it was successful and 0 otherwise, and a length component, which gives −1 for each turn. The scalar reward used in conventional training is the weighted sum r_t = w^T r_t, with w = (w_1, ..., w_K). Because the success reward is defined only at the end of the dialogue, we fix its weight to 1 and vary only the turn penalty weight w_2 = −λ, with λ ≥ 0. The default baseline corresponds to a success reward of 20 and a turn penalty of −1, i.e., λ = 1/20 after normalization. The goal is to find the λ that yields the best-balanced policy for a given domain.

**Reward-weight search**

A naive approach would train a separate policy for each candidate weight vector and evaluate each of them. This is expensive, since each policy requires thousands of dialogues. We therefore adopt multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), which learns a set of policies covering many weightings in a single training run, so the training data is shared across candidate weights.

**Multi-objective policy learning**

We use a multi-objective variant of Q-learning in which the value function is vector-valued: Q(b, a) = E[Σ_t γ^t r_t | b_0 = b, a_0 = a] ∈ R^K. For any fixed weight vector w, the scalarized value is Q_w(b, a) = w^T Q(b, a). Following the idea of linear scalarization with a convex coverage set, we maintain the vector-valued function approximator and, at decision time, act greedily with respect to Q_w, i.e., a_t = argmax_a w^T Q(b_t, a). Thus one trained model yields a policy for any w without retraining.

Because belief states are continuous, we use a Gaussian process (GP) approximation as in GP-SARSA. We model each reward component with its own GP sharing the same kernel over belief-action pairs. The kernel is the sum of a belief kernel (a Gaussian kernel) and a discrete-action kernel (delta). Using the linearity of the GP posterior, the posterior mean of the weighted return is the weighted sum of the component posterior means, which allows exact scalarization at action-selection time.

For exploration during training, we sample a weight vector w from a distribution over the admissible range of λ at the start of each dialogue and follow an ε-greedy policy with respect to Q_w. Because the return vector is observed regardless of the sampled w, every dialogue provides training information for all weightings. This is off-policy with respect to weights, and we correct for it by using the vector-valued update only with the greedy successor action under the same w within the dialogue, keeping w constant throughout the dialogue. Training continues for a fixed budget of dialogues.

**Evaluation of candidate weights**

After training, we extract a policy π_λ for each λ in a grid, e.g., λ ∈ {0, 0.01, ..., 0.2}. Each policy is evaluated with a simulated user over N test dialogues, yielding its average success rate S(λ) and average dialogue length L(λ). These pairs trace an empirical Pareto front between success and length. The front shows the trade-off explicitly: low turn penalties produce longer, more successful dialogues, while high penalties produce short but less successful ones.

To select a single weighting we need a criterion that is independent of the weighting used in training, since otherwise the evaluation would favor the policy trained for that specific weighting. We therefore define a target utility U(S, L) = S·R − L, with R being a fixed success reward, chosen to reflect the desired operating point of the system. In practice, we select the λ whose policy maximizes this utility on a held-out set of dialogues. Alternatively, a minimum success-rate constraint can be imposed (e.g., S ≥ 0.9), and the λ with the shortest average length is chosen among the feasible ones. We report results under the constraint-based criterion.

**Experimental setup**

We apply the method to six domains from a spoken dialogue system framework: information-seeking tasks for finding restaurants, hotels, laptops, TVs, and similar entities, which differ in the number of slots and database sizes and hence in complexity. For each domain we train one MORL model for 5,000 dialogues. The dialogue state tracker is a rule-based belief tracker, and the dialogue manager's action set comprises the standard summary actions (e.g., request, confirm, inform, select, bye). The user is an agenda-based simulator with a semantic error rate of 15%, producing noisy semantic inputs through an error model. A dialogue is successful if the system offers an entity matching the user's constraints and provides all requested information.

As a comparison we train baseline policies with the default fixed weighting using standard GP-SARSA on the same number of dialogues and the same settings. To measure the savings in training data, we additionally train single-objective policies for each λ in the grid and compare them with the MORL-derived policies for the same weights at several training budgets.

Each experiment is repeated for multiple random seeds, and we report mean success rate, mean length, and the utility together with 95% confidence intervals. Final policies are tested on 1,000 dialogues per seed and weighting. Differences between the optimized and baseline weights are assessed with a two-sided t-test.

We first examine whether multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) can replace repeated single-objective training, and then report the optimized weights found for each domain and how they compare with the default baseline.

**Efficiency of the MORL-based search.** We compared the proposed approach with a conventional grid search in which a separate policy is trained from scratch for every candidate weighting. Both approaches used the same simulated user and the same number of training dialogues per policy. With MORL, a single training run yields a policy set that covers the entire range of weightings, so each candidate weighting can be evaluated without retraining. In our experiments the MORL approach reached a stable estimate of the best weighting after roughly 4,000 training dialogues. The grid search needed several times more dialogues, because every point on the grid required its own training run. The policies retrieved from the MORL model for a given weighting performed close to policies trained directly for that weighting. The gap in average return was small, within the confidence intervals after about 3,000 dialogues, and it shrank further with more training data. This indicates that sharing experience across weightings does not noticeably degrade policy quality, while the number of required dialogues falls substantially.

**Effect of the weighting on policy behavior.** Varying the weight of the turn penalty relative to the success reward produced the expected trade-off. When the turn penalty was large, policies ended dialogues early. They reached shorter average lengths, but success rates dropped, mainly because the system committed to a database entry before collecting enough constraints from the user. When the penalty was small, policies asked more clarifying questions and confirmed more information. This raised success rates but lengthened dialogues. The relationship was not linear. Over a broad middle range of weights, success rate changed little while dialogue length continued to fall. Beyond a domain-specific threshold, success decreased sharply. This pattern shows that a good balance usually lies just before the success rate begins to degrade, and that the default weighting is not necessarily located there.

**Optimized weights across six domains.** We ran the search in six domains of differing size and complexity. The optimal weighting differed between domains. Domains with few searchable slots and small databases preferred relatively larger turn penalties. In these domains the system can identify the correct entity after few turns, and extra turns add cost without improving success. Domains with more slots or larger databases preferred smaller turn penalties. In them, additional turns improved the chance of finding an entity that matched the user's needs. A single fixed weighting therefore cannot be optimal for every domain, which supports searching for weights per domain.

**Comparison with the default baseline.** The baseline used the standard configuration, with a fixed per-turn penalty and a large reward for success. Policies trained with the optimized weights were compared with baseline policies on the same criteria: success rate, average dialogue length, and average reward measured under a common evaluation function. In all six domains the optimized policies matched or exceeded the baseline on the common evaluation function. The gains came mostly from shorter dialogues, with success rates changing little. In four domains, dialogue length decreased significantly (p < 0.05) while success rates stayed within the confidence interval of the baseline. In the remaining two domains the improvement was smaller. In one of these the default weighting was already near the optimum found by the search, and in the other the reward curve was flat over a wide range of weights. Even in these cases the search did not produce a worse policy, so applying it carries little risk.

**Robustness.** We checked the sensitivity of the results to random initialization by repeating the MORL training with different seeds. The selected weights varied only slightly between runs, usually by one neighboring grid point, and the resulting policies had statistically indistinguishable performance. The reward curve around the optimum was generally flat, so small deviations from the optimal weighting caused only small losses. This suggests that a coarse search suffices in practice, which further lowers the cost of the approach.

**Evaluation with different user behavior.** To test whether the optimized weights depend on the particular simulated user, we repeated the evaluation with simulated users of different error rates. Under higher error rates, the optimal weighting shifted toward smaller turn penalties, as more turns were needed to recover from misunderstandings. The optimized policies nevertheless remained at least as good as the baseline across all tested conditions, with the largest benefit in low-noise settings where the baseline wastes turns on unnecessary confirmations.

**Summary.** The results show three main findings. First, MORL substantially reduces the number of training dialogues needed to search over reward weightings, without a meaningful loss in policy quality. Second, the best weighting is domain dependent, so a single default is suboptimal in general. Third, policies trained with the optimized weights outperformed the default baseline or matched it in every domain, mainly by shortening dialogues while maintaining success rates.

In this work we addressed a problem that is often treated informally in the dialogue policy optimization literature: how to weight the components of a reward function. Most statistical dialogue systems use a reward that combines a large positive term for dialogue success with a small per-turn penalty, and the relative size of these terms is typically fixed once, by intuition or by convention, and then carried across domains. We proposed a structured alternative. Instead of training a new policy for every candidate weighting, which would be prohibitively expensive, we formulated the problem as multi-objective reinforcement learning. A single multi-objective learner is trained to cover a range of weightings simultaneously, and the resulting policies can then be evaluated for any candidate weight vector. This makes a search over reward component weights feasible with a number of training dialogues that is a fraction of what repeated single-objective training would require.

We applied the method to six domains and compared the weights found by the search with a default baseline. The main observation is that the default weighting is not consistently the best choice. Across domains, the optimized weights led to policies that performed better with respect to the chosen evaluation criterion, or reached comparable performance with shorter dialogues. The size of the gain varied with the domain. In domains with a small number of slots and a simple task structure, the default was already close to a good balance and the differences were modest. In larger and more complex domains, where the trade-off between completing the task and keeping the dialogue short is sharper, the optimal weighting departed more clearly from the default. This supports the view that the reward balance should be treated as a domain-dependent hyperparameter rather than a universal constant.

Several points deserve discussion. First, the notion of an "optimal" weighting is only meaningful relative to an external criterion. The reward weights define what the policy optimizes, but the quality of a dialogue system is judged by something else, such as task success rate at a given average length, or user satisfaction. Our search therefore requires that this criterion be specified beforehand. We used an objective measure that can be computed in simulation, which makes the procedure automatic and reproducible, but it is only a proxy for what real users value. A weighting that is optimal for a simulated user may not be optimal for human users, whose tolerance for long dialogues and whose reaction to errors can differ markedly. Incorporating human judgments, for example through a small number of user trials used to select among the candidate policies, is a natural extension.

Second, the efficiency of the method depends on the quality of the multi-objective learner. Policies obtained for a given weight vector through the multi-objective approach are approximations, and their quality depends on how well the weight space is covered during training and on how well the value function generalizes across weights. We observed that the approximation was sufficient to rank candidate weightings reliably, which is what the search needs. Nevertheless, a final policy trained from scratch with the selected weights may still be advisable once the search is complete, and this is inexpensive compared with the search itself.

Third, our study considered a reward made of two components, success and length. This is the most common case and has an intuitive interpretation, but real systems may include further components, such as penalties for confirmations, for repeated requests, or for violating dialogue conventions. The multi-objective formulation extends in principle to any number of components, but the search space grows, and the cost of exploring it grows with it. More sophisticated search strategies, such as Bayesian optimization over the weight space, could mitigate this. It is also unclear whether the weights found would remain stable when more components are added, since the components may interact.

Fourth, the results were obtained with a particular learning algorithm and a particular set of simulated environments. Although the six domains differ in size and complexity, they are all slot-filling information-seeking tasks. Whether the same conclusions hold for other dialogue types, such as negotiation, tutoring or open-domain conversation, where the objectives are less clearly defined, remains to be tested. Likewise, the sensitivity of the findings to the noise level of the input channel deserves study, since the best balance between success and length may change when recognition errors are frequent and more confirmation turns are needed.

In conclusion, we have presented a practical method for balancing the components of a dialogue reward by means of multi-objective reinforcement learning. The method replaces ad hoc choice of reward weights with a systematic search whose cost is kept low by sharing learning across weightings. Experiments on six domains showed that the commonly used default weighting can be improved upon, and that the best weights differ between domains. We believe the approach is useful both as a tool for system designers who need to tune rewards for a new domain and as a step toward treating reward design as an explicit, optimizable part of dialogue system development. Future work should evaluate the selected policies with real users, extend the search to more than two reward components, and investigate whether reward weights can be transferred between related domains to reduce the search effort even further.

The rapid development of information and communication technologies has changed the conditions in which modern education operates. Universities and schools are expected to prepare graduates who can work with large volumes of information, collaborate in digital environments and keep learning throughout life. In this context, cloud technologies are among the most promising directions for modernizing the educational process. They give users access to software, storage and computing resources through the Internet, without installing programs on a local computer or maintaining expensive hardware. For education, this means that teaching materials, tools for creating and processing data, and platforms for communication and assessment can be reached from any device, at any time and from any place.

Interest in cloud technologies in education is supported by national and international strategies for digitalizing society. Documents on the development of the information society, the modernization of higher education and the creation of a common European educational space all stress the need for open, flexible and accessible learning environments. Cloud services meet many of these requirements. They are usually inexpensive or free, they are updated automatically, they allow joint work on one document or project, and they scale easily as the number of users grows. They also support the shift from a reproductive model of teaching to one that stresses independent inquiry, project work and the development of students' digital competence.

Geography is a particularly suitable subject for these technologies. It studies natural and social phenomena at different spatial scales, and it relies on maps, statistical data, satellite images, graphs, diagrams and other visual material. Students must learn to read and build spatial models, analyze the dynamics of demographic and economic processes, compare territories and see how global and local phenomena are connected. Traditional teaching tools such as printed atlases, wall maps and textbooks are often not enough to show the changing character of these processes or to let students work actively with data. Interactive maps, online visualization of statistics, augmented reality, electronic quizzes and graphic editors can fill this gap. They make abstract material concrete, increase motivation and allow students to move from passive reception of information to its active investigation.

Researchers have studied the use of cloud technologies in education from several angles. Work on cloud-oriented learning environments has covered their architecture, the models of their deployment and the ways they change the roles of teacher and student. Other studies concern general-purpose office and communication suites, learning management systems and services for collaborative work. Geography education has its own literature on geographic information systems, virtual globes and web mapping. However, specialized online services that address concrete tasks of geographical education remain much less systematized. Teachers often learn about such services by chance, lack information on their capabilities and limitations, and have few methodological recommendations for including them in the curriculum. As a result, many useful tools are used rarely or without a clear didactic purpose.

The problem is made sharper by the diversity of available products. Services differ in functionality, language support, cost, technical requirements, the quality of their content and the degree of control the teacher has over the learning process. Some, such as Gapminder and the statistical resources of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA), provide data and visualizations for analyzing global development. Others, such as Settera Online and Click-that-hood, serve to learn and test knowledge of political and physical maps or of urban territory. Some tools, such as HP Reveal, add augmented reality to learning materials, while MOZAIK education offers interactive three-dimensional content. Graphic editors such as Canva and Paint Instant help students and teachers to create infographics, posters and illustrations. Choosing among them requires a clear understanding of their advantages and disadvantages from economic, technical, technological and didactic points of view.

The aim of this article is to substantiate the feasibility of using cloud technologies in teaching geography to students of higher school and to present a selection of online services that can contribute to the effective acquisition of geographical knowledge. To reach this aim, we address the following tasks: to clarify the essence and educational potential of cloud technologies; to describe the functional capabilities of the selected services; to generalize their advantages and disadvantages according to economic, technical, technological and didactic criteria; and to illustrate, with visual examples, how they can be applied in learning activities.

The novelty of the study lies in the systematic review of a group of specialized, mostly freely available services within a single framework of analysis oriented to the needs of geographical education. The practical value lies in the possibility of using the results when planning lectures, practical classes and independent work, and when developing electronic courses. In the longer term, the services considered may become part of virtual information and educational environments that are linked first into a common national and then a global educational space, which would widen access to quality geographical education and support the integration of educational systems.

The study was designed as an analytical and descriptive review of cloud-based services that can support geography teaching in higher education. It combined a theoretical analysis of the pedagogical literature with a practical evaluation of selected online tools. The work proceeded in four stages: identification of candidate services, formulation of evaluation criteria, hands-on testing, and generalization of the results.

**Selection of services.** At the first stage, we searched for cloud technologies applicable to teaching geography. We used academic databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, and national electronic libraries), the catalogues of educational applications, and the professional recommendations of geography teachers and university lecturers. Search terms included "cloud technologies in education," "online services for geography teaching," "interactive maps for learning," "data visualization in education," and "augmented reality in education," together with their equivalents in the national language. We included services that met the following conditions: (1) they run in a web browser or as a mobile application, without complex local installation; (2) a free version or a free educational plan is available; (3) their functions relate directly to the content of geographical disciplines, such as statistical analysis, cartography, toponymy, regional studies, and visualization; (4) they were stable and regularly updated at the time of the study. Services that required costly licenses, or that were designed exclusively for professional GIS work, were excluded. Ten services were selected: Gapminder, DESA (the United Nations statistical resources), two further online resources for working with maps and geographic data, HP Reveal, MOZAIK education, Settera Online, Click-that-hood, Canva, and Paint Instant.

**Evaluation criteria.** At the second stage, we developed a set of criteria grouped into four categories.
1. *Economic:* cost of use, availability of a free version, and absence of hidden expenses for the institution or the student.
2. *Technical:* hardware and software requirements, platform independence, need for registration, interface language, stability under limited internet bandwidth, and compatibility with mobile devices.
3. *Technological:* the ability to create, store, and export content, collaboration and sharing options, integration with other platforms and learning management systems, and the possibility of embedding results into presentations or websites.
4. *Didactic:* correspondence to the curriculum content, the potential for visualization and interactivity, support for independent and group work, opportunities for self-assessment and knowledge control, and the capacity to develop spatial thinking, analytical skills, and digital competence.

Each service was described according to these categories, and its advantages and limitations were recorded in a comparative table.

**Practical testing.** At the third stage, each service was tested by the authors in the role of both instructor and student. Testing was conducted on desktop computers and on mobile devices running different operating systems, using several popular browsers. For each tool, we modelled typical learning tasks:
- analyzing demographic and socio-economic indicators over time and comparing countries with Gapminder and the DESA databases;
- working with thematic maps and geographic data using the corresponding online map resources;
- creating augmented-reality content for a lecture, a field trip, or a laboratory class with HP Reveal;
- using MOZAIK education for interactive multimedia learning materials;
- memorizing toponyms and the political map through Settera Online and Click-that-hood;
- designing infographics, posters, and presentations with Canva;
- producing simple sketches, schemes, and map annotations with Paint Instant.

During testing we documented the sequence of operations, the time required to master the tool, difficulties encountered, and the quality of the final product. Screenshots were captured to provide visual examples of application and are included in the article as illustrations.

**Analytical methods.** The theoretical part of the research used analysis and synthesis of scientific sources on the implementation of cloud computing in education, comparison of the characteristics of the services, classification of the tools by their predominant didactic function (data visualization, cartographic training, augmented reality, content creation, and knowledge testing), and generalization of the results to formulate conclusions. A systematic approach was applied to consider the services as elements of a potential virtual information and educational environment. Qualitative content analysis was used to interpret the functionality and user documentation of each service. Because the study was exploratory and based on expert evaluation, no statistical hypothesis testing was undertaken, and the assessments were formulated descriptively rather than as numerical scores.

**Generalization and validation.** At the final stage, the results of the individual evaluations were compared and discussed by the authors to reduce subjectivity. Discrepancies were resolved by repeated testing of the problematic functions. The conclusions on advantages and disadvantages were then summarized by criterion category, and recommendations were made for use of the services in lectures, practical classes, independent work, and distance learning. The prospects for combining these tools into integrated virtual educational environments, which could be linked at national and later global levels, were considered on the basis of their interoperability and the openness of their formats.

**Limitations.** The evaluation reflects the state of the services at the time of the study. Cloud products change quickly in features, pricing policy, and availability, so some characteristics may become outdated. The assessment was carried out by the authors and has not yet been supported by a large-scale pedagogical experiment with students, which is planned as a subsequent stage of research.
