Silk cocoons (Bombyx mori) were degummed by boiling in 0.02 M Na2CO3 solution for 30 min, rinsed thoroughly with deionized water, and dried at 60 °C. The fibers were dissolved in 9.3 M LiBr at 60 °C for 4 h, dialyzed against deionized water for 72 h using a membrane with a molecular weight cut-off of 3.5 kDa, and centrifuged twice at 9000 rpm for 20 min to remove insoluble residues. The resulting silk fibroin (SF) solution had a concentration of about 6 wt%, determined gravimetrically, and was diluted to 2 wt% before use.

Copper foils (99.99% purity, 0.1 mm thick) were cut into 10 mm × 10 mm pieces. They were ultrasonically cleaned in acetone, ethanol and deionized water for 10 min each, immersed in 5 wt% dilute hydrochloric acid for 60 s to remove surface oxides, rinsed with deionized water, and dried under nitrogen flow. An aliquot of 100 µL SF solution was drop-cast onto each substrate and dried at room temperature for 12 h, forming a uniform film of approximately 1 µm thickness (measured by profilometry).

Microwave plasma treatment was performed in a microwave plasma chemical vapor deposition reactor (2.45 GHz, maximum power 3 kW) with a quartz-window stainless-steel chamber. The SF-coated substrate was placed on a molybdenum stage at the center of the chamber. The chamber was evacuated to below 1 Pa, then filled with hydrogen and argon (H2:Ar = 1:4, total flow 100 sccm), and the pressure was held at 3 kPa. Plasma was ignited at 600 W and the power was raised to 1.2 kW over 30 s. The substrate temperature, monitored with an infrared pyrometer and a thermocouple beneath the stage, reached 800–900 °C. Treatment times of 1, 3, 5 and 10 min were tested; unless otherwise noted, samples treated for 5 min are reported. After the plasma was switched off, samples were cooled to below 100 °C under Ar flow before removal. Because SF contains about 18 wt% nitrogen-bearing amino acid residues, nitrogen was supplied by the precursor itself, and no external nitrogen source was used. Control samples were prepared by the same procedure using a PMMA film (nitrogen-free) as the carbon source and by treating bare copper foil. Pristine copper foils were annealed under the same conditions as a reference.

Surface morphology was examined by field-emission scanning electron microscopy (5 kV) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Cross-sections were prepared by focused ion beam milling and examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, 200 kV) with selected-area electron diffraction and high-resolution imaging. Raman spectra were recorded with a 532 nm laser at 1 mW to avoid heating, with a 50× objective; at least 20 points per sample were measured, and the ID/IG and I2D/IG ratios were analyzed. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using monochromatic Al Kα radiation; binding energies were calibrated to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV, and N 1s spectra were deconvolved into pyridinic, pyrrolic and graphitic components using Gaussian–Lorentzian functions after Shirley background subtraction. Crystal structure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (Cu Kα, 2θ = 10–90°). Atomic force microscopy in tapping mode was used to estimate graphene layer thickness on regions where the layer was transferred to SiO2/Si by electrochemical delamination in 1 M NaOH.

The electrical resistivity was measured with a four-point probe method in van der Pauw geometry using a physical property measurement system. Silver-paste or wire-bonded contacts were placed at the four corners of 5 mm × 5 mm samples. The current was 1–10 mA, and the polarity was reversed to eliminate thermoelectric offsets. Resistivity was measured from 300 K down to 2 K for temperature dependence, with room-temperature values taken at 298 K. The sample thickness, determined from cross-sectional SEM at several positions, was used to calculate resistivity. Five samples per condition were measured, and values are given as mean ± standard deviation. Bare copper and annealed copper were measured identically for comparison. The contribution of the substrate was evaluated by a parallel-conductor model using independently measured copper resistivity.

Thermal conductivity was obtained from thermal diffusivity, specific heat and density as κ = α·ρ·Cp. Thermal diffusivity was measured at 25 °C by the laser flash method (xenon flash, in-plane configuration with a mask for thin samples) under vacuum, with each specimen coated with a thin graphite layer to improve absorption and measured five times. Specific heat was determined by differential scanning calorimetry with a sapphire reference, and density was measured by the Archimedes method. The in-plane values were cross-checked on selected samples by a steady-state heat-flow technique with an infrared camera. Temperature-dependent thermal conductivity was measured from 25 to 200 °C.

Density functional theory calculations were carried out with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package using the PBE functional with van der Waals correction (DFT-D3), a 450 eV cutoff, and a 9 × 9 × 1 k-point mesh. Models comprised N-doped graphene (pyridinic and graphitic N) on Cu(111) slabs with a 15 Å vacuum. Charge density differences and density of states were computed to evaluate interfacial charge transfer.

Statistical analysis used one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test, and p < 0.05 was considered significant.

Silk fibroin was spin-coated onto polished copper foil and exposed to microwave plasma in a mixed Ar/H2 atmosphere. Within a few minutes the transparent protein film converted into a dark, continuous layer, and the copper surface acquired a uniform grayish-black appearance. Scanning electron microscopy showed that the converted layer was thin, wrinkled and continuous over the whole substrate, with the ripples typical of graphene grown on copper. Cross-sectional images of the treated samples revealed a graphene-rich layer anchored to the copper surface, with sheet-like features extending into the near-surface region of the metal. Energy-dispersive mapping showed that C, N and Cu were distributed homogeneously, indicating that nitrogen was incorporated uniformly rather than segregated into particles.

Raman spectroscopy confirmed the formation of graphitic carbon. The spectra displayed a D band near 1350 cm⁻¹, a G band near 1590 cm⁻¹ and a 2D band near 2700 cm⁻¹. The 2D band was symmetric and could be fitted with a single Lorentzian, with an I2D/IG ratio of about 0.8–1.2 depending on position, consistent with few-layer graphene. The D band was weak but clearly present, with ID/IG ≈ 0.2–0.3, which we attribute to the defects and edges introduced by nitrogen substitution rather than to amorphous carbon. Compared with undoped graphene grown under identical conditions from a methane precursor, the G band of the N-doped sample was blue-shifted by about 6 cm⁻¹ and the 2D band was slightly broadened, consistent with electron doping by substitutional nitrogen. Transmission electron microscopy showed lattice fringes with an interlayer spacing of about 0.34 nm, and selected-area electron diffraction gave the six-fold pattern expected for graphene, with a small number of layers (typically 3–6) at the edges of folded sheets. High-resolution images of the interface showed graphene layers lying directly on the (111)-oriented copper surface without a detectable oxide or amorphous carbon interlayer.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy provided the chemical state of the dopants. The survey spectrum contained C 1s, N 1s, O 1s and Cu 2p signals, with a nitrogen content of roughly 3–4 at.%. The C 1s spectrum was dominated by sp² carbon at 284.6 eV, with minor C–N (285.5 eV) and C–O components. The N 1s spectrum was deconvoluted into pyridinic (398.4 eV), pyrrolic (399.9 eV) and graphitic/quaternary (401.2 eV) nitrogen, of which graphitic nitrogen accounted for the largest fraction (about 45%). Because graphitic nitrogen donates electrons to the π system, this distribution is favourable for increasing carrier density. The Cu 2p spectrum showed metallic copper with negligible Cu2+ satellite features, showing that the plasma process did not oxidize the substrate.

Electrical measurements were performed with a four-point probe at room temperature on multiple samples. Pure copper foil subjected to the same plasma and annealing treatment without the fibroin layer had a resistivity of 1.72 µΩ·cm, in agreement with the handbook value for annealed copper. In contrast, the N-doped graphene–copper composite exhibited a resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm, about 9% of that of copper. The values for different samples varied by less than ±0.02 µΩ·cm. Temperature-dependent measurements from 10 to 300 K showed metallic behavior, with resistivity decreasing monotonically on cooling and a large residual resistivity ratio, higher than that of the control copper. The composite also kept its low resistivity after repeated bending and after storage in air for several weeks. Samples with undoped graphene from methane showed only a modest reduction in resistivity (about 1.4 µΩ·cm), demonstrating that nitrogen doping and the interfacial structure produced by the silk-derived layer are essential to the effect. We note that the measured value reflects the effective conductivity of the whole composite, and we interpret it as arising from highly conductive pathways in the graphene network that are electronically coupled to copper, with charge transfer from nitrogen-doped graphene increasing the carrier density and the reduced scattering at the epitaxial interface.

Thermal conductivity was determined from laser-flash measurements of thermal diffusivity combined with measured specific heat and density. At 25 °C, the composite exhibited a thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K, which is 138% of the value measured for the copper control (390 W/m·K). The enhancement persisted at elevated temperature, with values of 505 W/m·K at 100 °C, decreasing more slowly than for copper. Because heat in graphene is carried mainly by phonons, whereas copper relies on electrons, the improvement suggests that the graphene network provides an additional, efficient phonon channel and that good interfacial contact permits efficient energy exchange between phonons and electrons across the interface. Infrared thermography supported this result: under a constant heating power, the composite reached a uniform surface temperature faster than copper and showed a lower peak temperature at the heated spot, by about 8 °C.

Overall, the results show that the silk-fibroin-derived N-doped graphene layer, formed within minutes by microwave plasma treatment, simultaneously reduces electrical resistivity and increases thermal conductivity relative to copper.

The ultralow electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm and the thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K obtained here for the nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite exceed the values of pure copper (about 1.7 µΩ·cm and 390 to 400 W/m·K at room temperature). The enhancement is substantial, and it is worth considering what the microstructure suggests about its origin, how it compares with earlier reports, and which caveats remain before the material can be considered for practical use.

Several features of our approach are likely to contribute to the observed transport. First, microwave plasma treatment of silk fibroin on copper is a rapid, single-step route in which the protein is converted in situ into graphene-like carbon. Silk fibroin is rich in carbon and nitrogen, so it supplies both the carbon framework and the dopant without an external gas source. The copper surface likely acts as a catalyst and template for graphene formation, and the plasma environment promotes fast carbon rearrangement and incorporation of nitrogen at low bulk temperature. Because the graphene forms directly on and within the metal, the interface is not contaminated by the polymer residues, transfer steps, or oxide layers that commonly limit conventional powder-metallurgy composites. A clean, well-bonded interface is essential for carrier transmission between the two phases and for phonon coupling across the boundary.

Second, nitrogen doping probably plays a dual role. Substitutional nitrogen (graphitic, pyridinic, and pyrrolic configurations) raises the carrier density of graphene and shifts the Fermi level, so graphene can carry current in parallel with copper rather than act only as a passive filler. Nitrogen sites may also improve the wettability and chemical bonding between graphene and copper, lowering interfacial contact resistance and encouraging epitaxial or quasi-epitaxial alignment with copper grains. A plausible picture is that continuous N-doped graphene layers at grain boundaries and surfaces provide high-mobility conduction channels, while also reducing electron scattering at grain boundaries, which is a main contributor to resistivity in fine-grained copper. This explanation is consistent with the reduction in resistivity, although we cannot yet separate the contributions of graphene conduction, suppressed boundary scattering, and possible modification of the copper lattice.

The thermal conductivity, 138% that of copper, is consistent with this picture. In copper, heat is carried mainly by electrons, so the electrical and thermal improvements are expected to be correlated through the Wiedemann-Franz relation. Graphene adds a phonon channel with intrinsically very high in-plane conductivity, and good interfacial bonding allows it to contribute effectively. That both properties improve simultaneously is important for applications, since many strategies that raise one property sacrifice the other.

The result should be placed in context. Earlier graphene-copper composites made by chemical vapor deposition, powder metallurgy, or electrodeposition have generally shown modest gains, typically a few percent to tens of percent in conductivity, and often a decrease when defects, voids, or poorly bonded graphene were introduced. Reports of resistivity far below that of copper at room temperature are rare and have sometimes been difficult to reproduce. Our result is an order of magnitude below copper, so it demands careful scrutiny. The measured value depends on the effective cross-section of the conducting path, and for a thin composite layer on a substrate the geometry and the possible contribution of the underlying copper must be handled carefully. We therefore regard confirmation by independent measurements, different sample geometries, and temperature-dependent transport as necessary. Such data would also help distinguish metallic-like behavior from other mechanisms, and would show whether the enhancement persists at elevated temperatures relevant to devices.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The thickness, areal uniformity, and number of graphene layers may vary across samples, and the amount and chemical state of nitrogen are likely sensitive to plasma power, time, and precursor loading. The present work demonstrates the phenomenon on small samples; scaling to large areas, wires, or bulk components will require control of precursor deposition and plasma uniformity. Long-term stability, including oxidation resistance, adhesion under thermal cycling, and mechanical properties such as hardness and ductility, remains to be evaluated. A systematic study varying nitrogen content, graphene quality, and copper grain structure, combined with theoretical modeling of interfacial electron and phonon transport, would clarify the mechanism and show how far performance can be pushed.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated a rapid and efficient route to an N-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite by microwave plasma treatment of silk fibroin on a copper substrate. The composite exhibits an electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm at room temperature, far below that of copper, together with a thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at 25 °C, 138% of that of copper. The use of a low-cost natural protein as a combined carbon and nitrogen source, together with the short processing time, makes the method attractive for scalable manufacturing. The simultaneous improvement of electrical and thermal transport suggests applications in power transmission, interconnects, heat spreaders, and other next-generation conductors where both low resistive losses and efficient heat removal are required. Further work on mechanism, reproducibility, and scale-up will determine how fully this potential can be realized.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system and a leading cause of non-traumatic disability in young adults [1]. Most patients present initially with a relapsing-remitting course (RRMS), characterized by acute episodes of neurological dysfunction followed by partial or complete recovery [2]. Over the past two decades, the therapeutic landscape has expanded considerably, and a range of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) is now available for relapsing forms of MS (RMS). Despite this growing choice, injectable interferon (IFN) beta preparations remain widely used, particularly in patients with mild to moderate disease activity, in women planning pregnancy, and in those for whom long-term safety data and monitoring requirements are of particular importance [3,4].

IFN beta products have been approved for the treatment of RMS for more than 20 years. They reduce relapse rate, delay disability progression, and suppress MRI measures of disease activity, and they are generally considered to offer a favourable benefit-risk profile [5,6]. Their mechanisms of action are pleiotropic and include down-regulation of antigen presentation, modulation of cytokine profiles, and reduced trafficking of immune cells across the blood-brain barrier [7]. Conventional formulations, however, require frequent administration, ranging from three-times-weekly subcutaneous (SC) injection to weekly intramuscular injection. Frequent injections, together with characteristic adverse effects, can compromise adherence, and suboptimal adherence is in turn associated with an increased risk of relapse and poorer outcomes [8,9].

Peginterferon beta-1a is a pegylated form of IFN beta-1a, in which a 20 kDa methoxy poly(ethylene glycol) moiety is covalently attached to the parent molecule. Pegylation prolongs the half-life and increases systemic exposure, which permits a reduced dosing frequency [10]. In July 2014, SC peginterferon beta-1a 125 μg administered every 2 weeks was approved by the European Medicines Agency for adult patients with RRMS, and in August 2014 the US Food and Drug Administration approved it for RMS. In the pivotal phase 3 ADVANCE study, peginterferon beta-1a given every 2 or 4 weeks significantly reduced annualized relapse rate, the risk of disability progression confirmed at 12 weeks, and MRI lesion activity compared with placebo after one year, with the greatest effects seen in the every-2-week regimen [11]. The ATTAIN extension study subsequently demonstrated sustained efficacy and a consistent safety profile with continued treatment for nearly 6 years [12,13].

As with other IFN beta therapies, the most frequently reported adverse events (AEs) with peginterferon beta-1a are injection site reactions (ISRs), influenza-like illness, pyrexia, and headache, which are mostly mild to moderate in intensity [11,14]. These events are often most pronounced at treatment initiation and tend to diminish over time, but they may nonetheless represent a considerable burden for patients and are among the principal reasons for non-adherence and treatment discontinuation [15,16]. Flu-like symptoms can usually be mitigated by gradual dose titration, administration in the evening, and the use of antipyretic or anti-inflammatory analgesics [17]. Practical measures such as injection technique, site rotation, and the use of autoinjectors are also recommended [18].

ISRs are of particular interest because they are highly visible, may cause pain, erythema, pruritus, and induration, and in rare cases may progress to more severe lesions such as skin necrosis [19,20]. Current knowledge about the pathophysiology of skin reactions to SC IFN treatment is limited. Proposed mechanisms include local cytokine-mediated inflammation, delayed-type hypersensitivity, and irritant reactions to the drug or excipients, and histopathological findings are heterogeneous [21]. Consequently, evidence-based strategies for prevention and treatment are scarce, and management in clinical practice often relies on individual experience. Notably, in pivotal trials ISRs were mainly characterized and classified by neurologists, and dermatologists were only rarely consulted [11,22]. This may have limited the precision of the description and differential diagnosis of skin findings, and it suggests that interdisciplinary collaboration could improve both the recognition and the treatment of these events.

Because peginterferon beta-1a has only recently entered routine clinical use, practical guidance reflecting real-world experience is still developing. Optimal management of AEs is essential to support persistence with therapy and thereby to maximize long-term clinical benefit. Against this background, an interdisciplinary panel of German and Austrian experts, comprising neurologists, dermatologists, and an MS nurse from university hospitals and private practices, convened in July 2016 to discuss the management of side effects associated with peginterferon beta-1a and other IFN beta-based treatments. The aim of this report is to present the panel's recommendations on best practices for the management of the most relevant AEs, with a focus on ISRs and influenza-like symptoms, based on the available literature and on interdisciplinary clinical experience.

An interdisciplinary advisory board meeting was held in July 2016 to develop practical recommendations for the management of adverse events (AEs) associated with peginterferon beta-1a and other interferon (IFN) beta therapies in multiple sclerosis (MS). The approach was a structured expert consensus process supported by a targeted literature review. It was not designed as a systematic review or meta-analysis, and no formal grading of evidence was undertaken.

**Panel composition**

Participants were invited on the basis of their clinical experience with IFN beta therapies and their involvement in MS care in Germany and Austria. The panel comprised neurologists from university hospitals and private neurological practices, dermatologists with experience in managing drug-induced and injection-related skin reactions, and one specialist MS nurse. Neurologists were selected to represent both academic and community-based care, so that recommendations would reflect different patient populations and healthcare settings. Dermatologists were included because skin reactions to subcutaneous (SC) IFN treatment are usually classified and managed by neurologists, and dermatological expertise had been rarely involved in the pivotal trials [1,2]. The MS nurse contributed experience in patient education, injection technique, and day-to-day adherence support. All participants took part in their individual professional capacity. Potential conflicts of interest were disclosed in accordance with the journal's requirements.

**Preparation and literature review**

Before the meeting, a non-systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed for English-language publications on IFN beta therapies in MS. Search terms combined "interferon beta", "peginterferon beta-1a", "multiple sclerosis", "adverse events", "injection site reactions", "influenza-like symptoms", "flu-like symptoms", "hepatic abnormalities", "haematological abnormalities", "thyroid dysfunction", "adherence", and "skin reactions". Priority was given to the pivotal Phase 3 ADVANCE study, its extension ATTAIN, and other clinical trials of peginterferon beta-1a [3–5]. Further sources were prescribing information (the EMA Summary of Product Characteristics and the FDA label), earlier registration trials of IFN beta-1a and IFN beta-1b products, observational and real-world studies, and published guidance on AE management and adherence [6–8]. Dermatological literature on injection site necrosis, injection-site inflammation, and the mechanisms of cutaneous reactions to injected biologics was also reviewed. Reference lists of relevant articles were hand-searched for additional publications. Congress abstracts and expert opinion were used only where peer-reviewed data were lacking, and this was stated explicitly.

A short briefing document summarising the incidence, severity, and timing of the most frequent AEs, including injection site reactions (ISRs), influenza-like illness, pyrexia, headache, and laboratory abnormalities, was circulated to participants beforehand. Participants were also asked to bring clinical cases that illustrated challenging or typical situations in routine practice.

**Meeting structure**

The meeting was a one-day, face-to-face session moderated by a chairperson experienced in MS care. It was organised into thematic blocks: (1) the pharmacological and clinical profile of peginterferon beta-1a compared with other IFN beta formulations; (2) the pathophysiology, classification, and clinical presentation of ISRs; (3) the management of influenza-like illness and other systemic reactions; (4) laboratory monitoring and the handling of haematological, hepatic, and thyroid abnormalities; and (5) patient education, injection training, and strategies to support adherence. Each block started with a short presentation of the available evidence, followed by moderated discussion of case examples from the participants' practices. In the ISR block the dermatologists described the differential diagnosis of local skin reactions, including irritant and allergic reactions, local inflammatory reactions, lipoatrophy, and necrosis, together with practical diagnostic steps such as clinical examination, photographic documentation, and, where appropriate, biopsy or allergy testing. The group discussed how the severity of skin reactions might be graded in a simple, reproducible way that can be used in routine care.

**Consensus process**

Recommendations were developed through open discussion until general agreement was reached. Where opinions differed, the evidence was reconsidered, and differing views were discussed until a position acceptable to all participants was found. No formal voting or Delphi procedure was applied, and no quantitative thresholds for consensus were defined. Recommendations were categorised by the panel as being supported mainly by published evidence, by extrapolation from related conditions or other IFN products, or by clinical experience alone. Recommendations were drafted to be practical and applicable in daily practice, covering preventive measures, first-line management, indications for referral to a dermatologist, and criteria for dose adjustment, treatment interruption, or discontinuation.

**Manuscript development**

A writing group of panel members drafted the manuscript from the meeting notes and the literature reviewed. The draft was circulated to all participants, who reviewed it and suggested revisions, and the final version was approved by every author. Medical writing support was used for editorial assistance only and did not influence the content of the recommendations. Because the work consisted of expert opinion and a review of published literature, without patient data or intervention, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.

**Limitations of the approach**

The non-systematic literature search and the informal consensus method may have introduced selection bias and reflect the views of a small, regional panel. The recommendations should therefore be regarded as practical guidance based on literature and interdisciplinary experience, and they should be interpreted alongside the current product information and national guidelines.

The panel's discussions produced consensus recommendations in four areas: (i) characterization and classification of injection site reactions (ISRs), (ii) prevention and treatment of ISRs, (iii) management of influenza-like symptoms (ILS) and other systemic adverse events, and (iv) laboratory monitoring and patient support. These are reported below. They reflect the available literature and the panel's practical experience, and not a formal systematic review.

**Characterization of injection site reactions**

The panel agreed that ISRs are the most frequent local adverse event under subcutaneous (SC) interferon beta therapy and that their presentation is heterogeneous. In the ADVANCE trial, ISRs occurred in 66% of patients receiving peginterferon beta-1a every 2 weeks, compared with 11% receiving placebo [1]. Most were mild or moderate, and fewer than 1% of patients discontinued treatment because of them [1]. The most frequent manifestations were erythema, pain, pruritus, and edema. Rarer findings included warmth, hematoma, and induration. Panel members noted that in pivotal trials ISRs were mainly characterized by neurologists, and dermatologists were rarely consulted. Reactions were therefore probably described in insufficient detail, and the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.

The panel distinguished several clinical entities: transient inflammatory reactions related to injection technique or to the pharmacological effect of interferon; delayed-type or allergic contact reactions to device or formulation components; lipoatrophy; and, rarely, skin necrosis. Experts emphasized that skin necrosis is uncommon but serious. It requires immediate discontinuation of the injectable and dermatological evaluation. Persistent, painful, or indurated lesions should prompt differential diagnosis, including infection, and biopsy where appropriate. The panel recommended a simple, standardized documentation scheme covering lesion type, size, duration, symptoms, and relation to injection, ideally supported by photographs, so that reactions can be compared between visits and across centers.

**Prevention of injection site reactions**

The panel considered patient training the most important preventive measure. Recommendations were as follows:

1. Structured injection training by an MS nurse or trained clinician at therapy initiation, with repeat checks during follow-up.
2. Systematic rotation of injection sites (abdomen, thighs, upper arms, buttocks where feasible), with avoidance of irritated or previously affected areas.
3. Allowing the pen or syringe to reach room temperature before injection, since cold solution may increase local discomfort.
4. Skin disinfection with the solution allowed to dry completely before injection.
5. Correct injection depth and angle, avoiding intradermal administration, and avoiding tight clothing over fresh sites.
6. Local cooling before and after injection to reduce pain and erythema.

Experts observed that the autoinjector pen for peginterferon beta-1a may reduce user-dependent errors, and that its less frequent dosing (every 2 weeks) reduces the number of injections and so the cumulative skin exposure [2]. Gradual dose titration, as used in the ADVANCE regimen (63 μg, 94 μg, then 125 μg), was recommended to improve tolerability [1]. Pre-treatment with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or paracetamol was also considered useful.

**Treatment of injection site reactions**

For mild reactions, the panel advised cooling compresses and topical care with emollients. For pruritus and moderate erythema, short courses of topical corticosteroids of low to moderate potency were considered appropriate, and oral antihistamines could be added if itching was prominent. Topical calcineurin inhibitors were identified as an option for recurrent or steroid-sensitive areas. Hydrocolloid dressings and other wound care products were suggested for crusted or ulcerated lesions, with the proviso that deeper lesions require specialist assessment. In cases of suspected contact allergy, patch testing by a dermatologist was recommended to identify the trigger, for example adhesives, disinfectants, or needle components. The panel stressed early referral to dermatology when lesions persist beyond several days, worsen despite standard measures, or show signs of necrosis or infection. Persistent problems despite optimized management may justify a switch of therapy after shared decision-making with the patient.

**Influenza-like symptoms and other systemic adverse events**

ILS, including pyrexia, chills, myalgia, and fatigue, were reported in 47% of peginterferon beta-1a patients versus 13% on placebo in ADVANCE, and headache in 44% versus 33% [1]. Symptoms typically appear within hours of injection, last up to 24 hours, and decline in frequency and severity with continued treatment. The panel recommended:

- Evening injection, so that symptoms occur mainly during sleep.
- Prophylactic paracetamol or ibuprofen 30–60 minutes before injection and repeated as needed.
- Adequate hydration and rest on injection days.
- Dose titration at initiation, with a slower titration where tolerability is poor.

Patients should be informed in advance that ILS are expected, are usually transient, and do not indicate disease activity. Persistent or severe symptoms should prompt evaluation for infection or other causes. Experts also considered depression, hepatic enzyme elevation, and cytopenia as events that need attention during therapy.

**Monitoring and patient support**

The panel recommended baseline and periodic laboratory monitoring, including full blood count, liver enzymes, and thyroid function, in line with the product information [2]. Mood should be assessed routinely. Neutralizing antibodies were reported to be rare with peginterferon beta-1a (<1% in ADVANCE) [1], and long-term data from the ATTAIN extension showed a stable safety profile for nearly 6 years without new safety signals [3]. Finally, the panel emphasized interdisciplinary collaboration among neurologists, dermatologists, and MS nurses, together with clear written information and a named contact person, as essential for adherence and persistence.

The recommendations of this interdisciplinary panel reflect the view that adverse events (AEs) associated with interferon (IFN) beta therapy are a manageable, predictable part of treatment rather than an inevitable reason for discontinuation. Injection site reactions (ISRs) and influenza-like illness (ILI) remain the most frequent tolerability problems across all IFN beta formulations, including peginterferon beta-1a [1,2]. Both can erode quality of life and adherence, and non-adherence in turn reduces the effectiveness of disease-modifying therapy [3]. Proactive counselling, structured initiation, and early recognition of problems are therefore central to the long-term success of treatment.

A principal observation of the panel was that the evidence base on the aetiology and classification of ISRs is limited. In the pivotal trials, ISRs were largely assessed and graded by neurologists, and dermatological expertise was rarely used [1,4]. This probably leads to under-differentiation of clinically distinct entities, such as transient erythema from pharmacologically induced local inflammation, delayed-type hypersensitivity, lipoatrophy, and injection-site necrosis. These entities differ in mechanism, prognosis, and appropriate response. Most ISRs are mild and self-limiting, but rare severe reactions, particularly necrosis, may require treatment interruption and dermatological evaluation, sometimes including biopsy or allergological work-up [5]. We therefore consider early referral to a dermatologist for persistent, painful, indurated, or ulcerating lesions an important element of good practice, and we encourage standardised documentation of ISRs, ideally with photographs, in routine care and future studies.

Prevention was emphasised as the most effective strategy. Practical measures include patient education before the first injection, correct injection technique, rotation of sites, skin disinfection with complete drying, injection at room temperature, and the use of autoinjectors, which reduce anxiety and variability in technique [6]. Cooling before and after injection and topical measures, such as corticosteroid or emollient preparations, may relieve symptoms, although controlled data supporting each measure are scarce and recommendations rest largely on clinical experience. The pegylated formulation, with a prolonged half-life and a dosing interval of two weeks, requires roughly 26 injections annually compared with several hundred for some other SC IFN beta products. Fewer injections may by themselves reduce cumulative skin exposure and treatment burden, though ISRs still occurred in a considerable proportion of patients in ADVANCE and were the most frequent reason for AE-related discontinuation, albeit at low rates [1,7]. Longer-term data from ATTAIN suggest that the safety profile remains consistent and that no new safety signals emerge over nearly six years [8].

For ILI, the panel supported established approaches. Patients should be told that symptoms are most pronounced early in treatment and generally decline over weeks to months. Evening administration, titration at initiation where applicable, and prophylactic or symptomatic use of antipyretic and anti-inflammatory analgesics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen are practical and effective [9]. Persistent or severe ILI should prompt evaluation for other causes, including infection. Dose reduction or temporary titration may be considered, but should be weighed against possible loss of efficacy.

Beyond skin and flu-like symptoms, the panel highlighted the need for routine monitoring of laboratory parameters. Liver enzymes, blood counts, and thyroid function should be checked at baseline and at regular intervals, since IFN beta can cause transaminase elevations, leukopenia, lymphopenia, and thyroid dysfunction [2,10]. Mood disorders and depression, headache, and the rare occurrence of thrombotic microangiopathy and nephrotic syndrome also deserve attention. Although the association between IFN beta and depression is less clear than once suspected, patients with a relevant history warrant careful follow-up [11]. Neutralising antibody formation is lower with peginterferon beta-1a than with several other IFN products, with a low incidence observed in ADVANCE, and it did not appear to affect efficacy in the studies [1,12].

Several limitations of this work should be noted. The recommendations derive from a single expert meeting involving a limited number of participants from two countries and are based on available literature supplemented by clinical experience, not on a systematic review or formal consensus method such as a Delphi process. Many suggested measures have not been tested in randomised trials, and the level of evidence is generally low. The focus on peginterferon beta-1a reflects the aim of the meeting, but comparative data against other IFN beta products regarding ISRs are lacking, so differences in local tolerability should be interpreted cautiously. Differences in health-care systems, reimbursement, and the availability of specialised nurses may also limit transferability.

In conclusion, effective management of the most relevant adverse effects of peginterferon beta-1a and other IFN beta therapies relies on anticipation, patient education, and interdisciplinary cooperation. Neurologists, dermatologists, and MS nurses each contribute complementary expertise: nurses support training and day-to-day adherence, neurologists coordinate treatment decisions and monitoring, and dermatologists enable accurate diagnosis and treatment of significant skin reactions. Implementing the practical measures outlined here may reduce treatment burden, improve persistence, and thereby allow patients to benefit from the sustained efficacy of IFN beta therapy. Future research should include prospective studies with standardised dermatological assessment of ISRs, evaluation of preventive and symptomatic interventions in controlled settings, and real-world analyses of adherence and patient-reported outcomes to refine and validate these recommendations.

Colorectal cancer is among the most commonly diagnosed malignancies worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related death. Advances in screening, surgery, and systemic therapy have improved survival, so a growing number of patients now live for years after diagnosis and treatment. Oxaliplatin-based regimens such as FOLFOX and CAPOX are the standard adjuvant treatment for stage III colon cancer and a backbone of first-line therapy for metastatic disease. Their benefit is well established, but they carry considerable toxicity. The most frequent and clinically important dose-limiting toxicity of oxaliplatin is chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN).

CIPN arises from damage to the peripheral sensory nerves and dorsal root ganglia. It typically presents as numbness, tingling, paresthesia, burning or electric-shock-like pain, and cold-induced dysesthesia in the hands and feet. An acute, cold-triggered form occurs in most patients within hours or days of an infusion. A cumulative, chronic form develops as the total dose increases and may persist, or even worsen, for months or years after treatment ends (the "coasting" phenomenon). Reported prevalence of CIPN in patients treated with oxaliplatin ranges from 60% to 90% during treatment, and a substantial proportion still have symptoms six months or more after completion. No effective preventive agent has been established, and duloxetine is the only drug with modest evidence for treating painful CIPN. Management therefore relies largely on dose reduction, delay, or discontinuation of chemotherapy, which may compromise oncologic outcomes.

Beyond its sensory symptoms, CIPN affects patients' function. Loss of sensation, impaired proprioception, reduced dexterity, and pain can limit activities of daily living, such as buttoning clothes, holding utensils, writing, handling small objects, walking, climbing stairs, and driving. Patients may also have an increased risk of falls and injury, such as burns from hot objects they cannot feel, and they often develop safety concerns and avoid activities. We refer to this problem as restriction of daily activity (RDA). Although CIPN severity is often assessed by clinician-graded scales or symptom inventories, these measures do not necessarily capture how symptoms translate into limitations in everyday life and safety awareness. Instruments that evaluate activity limitation specifically, such as the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale, provide a complementary view of the functional burden.

Cancer patients also frequently experience psychological distress. Colorectal cancer patients face the fear of recurrence, changes in bowel function, stomas, financial strain, and the burden of prolonged treatment. Persistent neuropathic symptoms, sleep disturbance, and loss of independence may add to anxiety, depression, fatigue, anger, and confusion. Prior studies have shown that patients with CIPN report more anxiety and depressive symptoms than those without, and that pain and sleep problems are associated with worse mood. Mood disturbance is itself related to poorer treatment adherence, greater symptom perception, and reduced well-being. The Profile of Mood States (POMS) is widely used to quantify these multidimensional negative mood states in oncology, and its short form is convenient for use in clinical settings.

Quality of life (QoL) has become a central outcome in cancer care, especially for survivors expected to live long with the sequelae of treatment. Several studies have reported that CIPN is associated with worse physical, functional, and social well-being and lower overall QoL among patients with colorectal cancer. However, the pathways through which CIPN influences QoL are not fully understood. Neuropathic symptoms may directly diminish QoL, but they may also act indirectly through functional limitation and emotional distress. Functional limitation might reduce independence and social participation, thereby worsening mood, and mood, in turn, may shape patients' appraisal of their overall QoL. If so, mood might act as a mediator between RDA and QoL, and interventions aimed at mood could be an important and potentially more modifiable target than neuropathy itself, for which few effective treatments exist.

Most previous research has examined CIPN, activity limitation, mood, and QoL in isolation or in pairs, and few have tested the relationships among them within a single model in colorectal cancer patients. Evidence on whether mood explains the association between RDA and QoL in this population is lacking. Clarifying these relationships could inform supportive care that goes beyond symptom control: rehabilitation and safety education to reduce RDA, and psychological assessment and intervention to improve mood adaptation.

Therefore, we conducted a cross-sectional study of colorectal adenocarcinoma patients with CIPN after oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. We used the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory to measure CIPN severity, the SALSA scale to assess RDA, the POMS short form to assess negative mood, and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Colorectal (FACT-C) version 4 to measure QoL. We aimed to (1) describe the levels of CIPN, RDA, mood disturbance, and QoL; (2) examine the correlations among these variables; and (3) test, using hierarchical multiple linear regression and Baron and Kenny's mediation procedure, whether mood mediates the relationship between RDA and QoL. We hypothesized that greater RDA would be associated with worse mood and lower QoL, and that negative mood would partially mediate the effect of RDA on QoL.

This was a cross-sectional correlational study conducted at the oncology outpatient clinics and chemotherapy wards of a tertiary teaching hospital. The study was approved by the institutional review board of the hospital, and all procedures followed the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent before data collection.

**Participants**

Patients were recruited consecutively. Inclusion criteria were: (1) a histologically confirmed diagnosis of colorectal adenocarcinoma; (2) age of 20 years or older; (3) previous treatment with an oxaliplatin-based regimen (FOLFOX or CAPOX) for at least one cycle; (4) self-reported numbness, tingling, pain, or other sensory symptoms in the hands or feet that began after oxaliplatin treatment, consistent with CIPN; and (5) ability to communicate in Mandarin or Taiwanese and complete questionnaires. Exclusion criteria were: (1) peripheral neuropathy from other causes, such as diabetes mellitus, alcohol abuse, vitamin B12 deficiency, or hereditary neuropathy; (2) brain metastases, cognitive impairment, or a diagnosed psychiatric disorder that might interfere with questionnaire completion; (3) current treatment with other neurotoxic chemotherapy agents; and (4) an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 3 or higher. A minimum sample size was estimated with G*Power for multiple linear regression (medium effect size f² = 0.15, α = 0.05, power = 0.80, three to five predictors), which indicated at least 91 participants. We therefore aimed to enroll about 100 patients to allow for incomplete questionnaires.

**Procedure**

Eligible patients were identified from medical records and approached by a trained research nurse during clinic visits or chemotherapy sessions. After consent, participants completed a demographic and clinical questionnaire and four self-report instruments in a quiet room, which took approximately 20–30 minutes. Patients who had difficulty reading received item-by-item help from the research nurse, who read the items aloud without interpretation. Clinical data, including cancer stage, chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles, cumulative oxaliplatin dose, and time since the last treatment, were extracted from medical records.

**Instruments**

*Severity of CIPN.* The Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) was used to measure neuropathic symptoms. It includes 12 items covering spontaneous ongoing pain, paroxysmal pain, evoked pain, and paresthesia/dysesthesia, each rated from 0 (none) to 10 (worst imaginable). The total score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating more severe neuropathic symptoms. Scores were categorized as mild, moderate, or severe for descriptive purposes. The NPSI has shown good reliability and validity in patients with neuropathic pain. In this sample Cronbach's α was calculated.

*Restriction of daily activity.* The Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale was used to evaluate limitations in daily activities and safety awareness related to peripheral nerve damage. It consists of 20 items on activities such as dressing, walking, handling objects, and working, rated from 1 (easy) to 5 (not possible), with additional items on safety awareness. Higher scores indicate greater restriction. Scores were classified as no limitation, mild, moderate, severe, or extreme limitation according to the published cutoffs. In this study, the total score was used as the RDA indicator.

*Negative mood.* The Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF) was used to assess mood disturbance over the previous week. It has 30 items rated on a five-point scale from 0 (not at all) to 4 (extremely) across five negative subscales (tension-anxiety, depression-dejection, anger-hostility, fatigue-inertia, confusion-bewilderment) and one positive subscale (vigor-activity). The total mood disturbance score was calculated by summing the negative subscale scores and subtracting the vigor score. Higher scores indicate worse mood. The Chinese version has demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity in cancer populations.

*Quality of life.* The Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Colorectal (FACT-C) version 4 was used to evaluate QoL. It contains 36 items: the 27-item FACT-General (physical, social/family, emotional, and functional well-being) and a 9-item colorectal cancer subscale. Items are rated from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very much), and after reverse scoring of negatively worded items, higher scores indicate better QoL. The total score ranges from 0 to 144. The scale has been validated in Chinese-speaking populations.

**Statistical analysis**

Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22.0. Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages) summarized demographic characteristics and scale scores. Distributions were checked with skewness and kurtosis values and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Internal consistency of each instrument was evaluated with Cronbach's α. Pearson correlation coefficients were used to examine bivariate relationships among CIPN severity, RDA, mood, and QoL. Group differences in QoL by demographic and clinical variables were tested with independent t tests or one-way analysis of variance, and significant variables were considered as covariates.

Hierarchical multiple linear regression was used to identify predictors of QoL. Covariates were entered in the first step, CIPN severity and RDA in the second step, and mood in the final step, so that the incremental variance explained (ΔR²) by each block could be assessed. Assumptions of linearity, normality and homoscedasticity of residuals, independence of errors (Durbin–Watson statistic), and multicollinearity (variance inflation factor < 10, tolerance > 0.1) were checked.

The mediating role of mood in the relationship between RDA and QoL was tested using the Baron and Kenny procedure. Four conditions were examined: (1) RDA significantly predicted QoL (path c); (2) RDA significantly predicted mood (path a); (3) mood significantly predicted QoL when controlling for RDA (path b); and (4) the effect of RDA on QoL was reduced when mood was included (path c′). Partial mediation was inferred if path c′ remained significant but was smaller than c, and full mediation if it became nonsignificant. The proportion mediated was calculated as (c − c′)/c. The significance of the indirect effect was verified with the Sobel test. All tests were two-tailed, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

A total of 103 patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma who had developed CIPN after oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy were enrolled and included in the analysis. Questionnaires were completed in full, and no participants were excluded for missing data. Overall, patients reported mild-to-moderate neuropathic symptoms on the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI) and mild restriction of daily activity on the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale. Mood disturbance, measured by the Profile of Mood States Short Form (POMS-SF), was present across the sample with considerable variability. Quality of life, measured by the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Colorectal (FACT-C) version 4, was moderately impaired.

**Correlations among study variables**

Bivariate correlation analysis showed that CIPN severity was positively correlated with negative mood (r = 0.425, P < 0.001), indicating that patients with more severe neuropathic symptoms had greater mood disturbance. CIPN severity was also positively correlated with RDA, such that more severe symptoms were associated with greater activity limitation. RDA was positively correlated with negative mood (r = 0.343, P < 0.001), so patients with greater limitation in daily activity reported higher levels of mood disturbance.

For QoL, the FACT-C score was negatively associated with RDA (the absolute correlation was r = 0.285, P < 0.01), with greater activity restriction corresponding to lower QoL. Negative mood showed the strongest association with QoL, with higher mood disturbance corresponding to markedly lower FACT-C scores. The direct correlation between CIPN severity and QoL was weaker than the correlations of QoL with RDA and mood, suggesting that the effect of neuropathic symptoms on QoL may operate through functional and psychological pathways rather than directly.

**Hierarchical multiple linear regression**

Hierarchical multiple linear regression was used to examine the factors associated with QoL. Demographic and clinical variables were entered in the first step, CIPN severity in the second, RDA in the third, and negative mood in the fourth. Demographic and clinical characteristics explained only a small proportion of the variance in QoL. Adding CIPN severity produced a modest increase in explained variance. When RDA was added, it was a significant independent predictor of QoL and significantly increased the explained variance. When negative mood was entered in the final step, the model improved substantially, and mood emerged as the strongest independent predictor of QoL. With mood in the model, the standardized coefficient for RDA decreased markedly and was attenuated in significance, whereas the coefficient for CIPN severity was no longer significant. This pattern indicated that mood accounted for a considerable part of the association between RDA and QoL and was consistent with a mediating role. Collinearity diagnostics showed that variance inflation factors were within acceptable limits, indicating that multicollinearity did not affect the model.

**Mediation analysis**

Mediation was tested following the approach of Baron and Kenny, with RDA as the independent variable, negative mood as the mediator, and QoL as the dependent variable. The following conditions were assessed in turn. First, RDA significantly predicted QoL (path c; total effect). Second, RDA significantly predicted negative mood (path a). Third, negative mood significantly predicted QoL when RDA was controlled (path b). Fourth, when mood was included in the model, the effect of RDA on QoL was reduced (path c′; direct effect) relative to the total effect, while remaining statistically detectable or reduced to a lesser degree of significance.

All of these conditions were satisfied. The indirect effect of RDA on QoL through negative mood was statistically significant (P < 0.001) and accounted for 38.48% of the total effect of RDA on QoL. The remaining proportion represented the direct effect of RDA on QoL that was independent of mood. Thus, mood partially mediated the relationship between RDA and QoL: patients with greater activity restriction experienced more negative mood, which in turn was associated with poorer QoL.

**Summary of main findings**

In this sample of colorectal cancer patients with oxaliplatin-induced CIPN, neuropathic symptoms were mild to moderate and activity restriction was mild. Greater CIPN severity was associated with greater RDA and more negative mood. Both RDA and mood were associated with QoL, but mood was the dominant correlate. Mediation testing showed that negative mood explained a substantial share (38.48%) of the association between RDA and QoL, identifying mood disturbance as a key pathway linking functional limitation to reduced QoL in these patients.

This study examined the relationships among CIPN severity, restriction of daily activity (RDA), negative mood, and QoL in colorectal cancer patients who had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. Our main findings were that CIPN severity was positively associated with negative mood, that RDA was associated with both mood disturbance and QoL, and that mood partially mediated the effect of RDA on QoL, accounting for 38.48% of the total effect. These findings suggest that, in this population, psychological adaptation may be as important as neurological and functional management in preserving QoL.

The patients in our sample had mild-to-moderate CIPN and mild RDA, which is consistent with a cohort largely treated in the outpatient setting and still capable of independent living. Even at this level, CIPN was significantly correlated with mood disturbance (r = 0.425). This agrees with previous reports that neuropathic symptoms such as numbness, tingling, and pain are linked to anxiety, depression, fatigue, and sleep disruption. Persistent sensory symptoms may act as a constant reminder of illness and treatment toxicity, and they may also interfere with sleep and concentration, which could amplify distress. The relationship is likely bidirectional, since negative mood can heighten the perception of neuropathic symptoms through central pain-modulating mechanisms. The cross-sectional design prevents us from determining the direction of this relationship.

RDA was correlated with mood (r = 0.343) and with QoL (r = 0.285). Difficulties with fine motor tasks such as buttoning clothes, with walking on uneven surfaces, or with handling hot and sharp objects may reduce independence and social participation, and may increase fear of falling and injury. Such losses can plausibly lead to frustration, helplessness, and low mood. Notably, the correlation between RDA and QoL was weaker than that between RDA and mood. This pattern suggests that functional limitation influences QoL partly through emotional pathways rather than only directly. The mediation analysis supported this interpretation: after accounting for mood, the direct effect of RDA on QoL was reduced, and mood explained almost two-fifths of the total effect. Thus, two patients with similar degrees of activity restriction may report quite different QoL depending on their emotional response and adaptation.

These findings have clinical implications. Current CIPN management focuses on dose modification, symptom control (for example, with duloxetine), and safety education and rehabilitation to prevent falls and injuries. These measures remain important for preventing irreversible functional problems. However, our results indicate that routine care should also include screening for mood disturbance in patients with CIPN, even when neuropathy and functional limitation are mild. Brief tools such as the POMS short form can be used in oncology clinics to identify patients at risk. Interventions that target mood, including psychoeducation, cognitive-behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based approaches, supportive counseling, peer support, and exercise programs, may improve QoL by reducing emotional distress and increasing acceptance of and adaptation to chronic symptoms. Exercise and occupational therapy are especially appealing because they may simultaneously address activity restriction and mood. A multidisciplinary approach involving oncologists, nurses, rehabilitation specialists, and psychologists would therefore be reasonable.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; the Baron and Kenny approach assumes a temporal order (RDA to mood to QoL) that we could not verify, and reverse or reciprocal pathways are possible. Longitudinal studies and more modern mediation methods, such as bootstrapped confidence intervals or structural equation modeling, would provide stronger evidence. Second, the sample was modest (n = 103), came from a limited number of centers, and consisted of patients with mild-to-moderate CIPN and mild RDA, so the results may not generalize to patients with severe neuropathy, to those who discontinued treatment because of toxicity, or to other cancer types and cultural settings. Third, all measures were self-reported and so were subject to recall and reporting bias, and the RDA scale was used as a screening instrument rather than an objective functional assessment. Fourth, we could not fully account for potential confounders such as cumulative oxaliplatin dose, time since chemotherapy, disease stage, comorbid conditions, concurrent medications, fatigue, social support, and prior psychiatric history, all of which may affect mood and QoL. Finally, the QoL instrument includes items on emotional and functional well-being, which may partly overlap with the mood and activity constructs and inflate their associations.

Future research should use longitudinal or interventional designs to test whether improving mood actually attenuates the impact of CIPN and RDA on QoL, and should examine other possible mediators and moderators, such as coping style, resilience, sleep, and social support. Including patients with a wider range of severity and using objective measures of function would also strengthen the evidence.

In conclusion, among colorectal cancer patients with oxaliplatin-induced CIPN, both restriction of daily activity and negative mood were associated with lower QoL, and negative mood partially mediated the relationship between RDA and QoL. Although the management of CIPN and activity restriction remains necessary to prevent irreversible functional problems, recognizing and treating mood disturbance and promoting psychological adaptation may be a particularly effective way to improve QoL in this population. Routine mood assessment and psychosocial support should be integrated into the care of patients with CIPN.

Unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) is a common form of cerebral palsy, resulting from a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain that predominantly affects one side of the body. Upper limb impairment is a hallmark of the condition and manifests as reduced strength, impaired dexterity, abnormal muscle tone, diminished sensation and, frequently, developmental disregard of the more affected hand [1,2]. These impairments constrain bimanual performance and the execution of daily activities, with consequences for independence, participation and quality of life [3]. Because the motor deficits persist into adulthood, effective and sustainable interventions during childhood and adolescence are a clinical priority.

**Upper limb rehabilitation in unilateral cerebral palsy**

Over the past two decades, a number of task-oriented, intensive interventions have accumulated evidence of efficacy. Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) and its modified versions, as well as hand-arm bimanual intensive therapy (HABIT), are supported by systematic reviews and randomised trials as effective in improving unimanual capacity and bimanual performance [4–6]. However, these approaches typically demand high dosage, specialised therapists and prolonged attendance at clinical centres. Constraint-based methods can also be poorly tolerated by some children and burdensome for families [7]. Access to such programmes is therefore uneven, and the cost and organisational demands limit their delivery at scale. There is a need for approaches that are engaging, intensive, and deliverable in the child's own environment.

**Action observation training**

Action observation training (AOT) is grounded in the discovery of the mirror neuron system, a network of fronto-parietal regions that is active both when an individual executes a goal-directed action and when they observe the same action performed by others [8,9]. Observing actions is thought to activate motor representations and facilitate motor learning, an effect that has been exploited in the rehabilitation of adults after stroke [10,11]. Neuroimaging studies suggest that children with cerebral palsy retain an observation–execution matching mechanism, albeit with altered patterns of activation [12]. This provides a rationale for using AOT in paediatric populations.

Initial studies in children with UCP showed that observing videos of goal-directed hand actions followed by their physical execution improved hand function compared with observation of non-motor content [13,14]. Building on this work, the UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) protocol was developed, in which children watch a sequence of daily-life actions of increasing complexity and then reproduce them. A randomised trial of UPCAT delivered in the clinic reported significant gains in manual ability and bimanual performance that were maintained at follow-up [15]. AOT is low-cost, requires minimal equipment, and is generally attractive to children, making it a good candidate for delivery outside the clinic.

**Tele-rehabilitation and information and communication technologies**

Information and communication technologies (ICT) offer an opportunity to extend rehabilitation into the home. Tele-rehabilitation has been shown to be feasible and, in several conditions, comparable with conventional care in adults [16,17]. In paediatric neurorehabilitation, home-based programmes using virtual reality, videogames and remote supervision have been explored, with promising but heterogeneous results and mostly small samples [18,19]. Home delivery can increase training dosage, reduce travel and cost, and embed practice in the context in which skills are used, which may favour transfer to everyday life. Nevertheless, key challenges persist: ensuring adherence, verifying that exercises are performed correctly, and objectively monitoring the amount and quality of practice without continuous in-person supervision [20].

Recent advances in sensing technology can address some of these issues. Sensorised objects can record the kinematics and timing of manipulation tasks, while wearable accelerometers, such as Actigraph devices, provide objective estimates of spontaneous arm use in daily life, a construct that is difficult to capture with clinical scales alone [21,22]. Combining these tools with a remote platform that delivers AOT and allows therapists to tele-monitor performance could yield both a feasible intervention and a richer description of its effects. To our knowledge, no randomised trial has yet tested a tele-monitored, home-based AOT programme in children with UCP.

**Rationale and aims**

Given the encouraging evidence for clinic-based UPCAT, and the need for scalable and accessible rehabilitation, we developed Tele-UPCAT, an ICT platform that delivers the UPCAT protocol at home, provides tele-monitoring by clinicians, and integrates sensorised objects for quantitative evaluation. The primary aim of the present randomised controlled trial is to determine whether a 3-week programme of home-based Tele-UPCAT improves bimanual hand performance, measured with the Assisting Hand Assessment, in children and young people with UCP compared with usual care. Secondary aims are to evaluate effects on unimanual capacity, perceived manual ability, participation and environmental factors, and health-related quality of life, and to examine whether any benefits persist at 8 and 24 weeks. Exploratory aims include the analysis of quantitative data from sensorised objects and wearable activity monitors to characterise training performance and daily arm use, and to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the system. We hypothesise that Tele-UPCAT will produce greater improvements in bimanual performance than usual care and that these will be maintained over follow-up. This paper describes the study protocol in order to promote transparency, reduce the risk of selective reporting and facilitate future replication and meta-analysis.

**Study design and setting**

This is a single-centre, two-arm, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial with a waitlist control, concealed allocation and blinded outcome assessment. It follows the SPIRIT guidelines for trial protocols [1] and will be reported according to CONSORT [2]. Baseline and clinical assessments will take place at the paediatric rehabilitation unit of the coordinating institution. Training will be delivered at the participants' homes. The trial was prospectively registered (NCT03094455) and approved by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (169/2016). Parents or legal guardians will provide written informed consent, and children will give assent according to their age and abilities.

**Participants**

Children and young people aged 6–18 years with a diagnosis of unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP) will be recruited from the centre's outpatient clinic and through collaborating services. Inclusion criteria are: (i) confirmed UCP; (ii) Manual Ability Classification System levels I–III [3]; (iii) ability to understand and follow instructions, with sufficient cognitive and attentional capacity to watch video sequences; and (iv) a stable home environment with the family's agreement to host the equipment. Exclusion criteria are: (i) botulinum toxin injection or upper limb surgery in the previous 6 months, or planned during the study; (ii) uncontrolled epilepsy; (iii) severe visual impairment; and (iv) concurrent participation in other experimental upper limb interventions.

The sample size (n = 24, 12 per group) was set pragmatically for a feasibility-oriented efficacy trial of a new technological platform, and informed by the effect sizes in earlier action observation training (AOT) studies in UCP [4,5]. Findings will be interpreted as preliminary.

**Randomisation and blinding**

An independent researcher not involved in recruitment or assessment will generate the allocation sequence by computer, with permuted blocks and stratification by age band (6–11 and 12–18 years). Allocation will be concealed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes opened only after baseline assessment. Participants and therapists cannot be blinded to the intervention. Outcome assessors will be blinded to group allocation. Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA) videos will be scored by a certified rater who is not otherwise involved in the trial. Participants and families will be asked not to disclose group allocation to assessors.

**Interventions**

*Experimental group (Tele-UPCAT).* Participants will complete 3 weeks of home-based AOT with the Tele-UPCAT platform, based on the UPper Limb Children Action Observation Training (UPCAT) protocol [5]. The system comprises a tablet or screen-based interface, a set of sensorised objects, and a web portal for remote supervision. Each daily session lasts about 45 minutes, 5 days per week (15 sessions in total). In each session the child watches a video sequence of a goal-directed, age-appropriate action performed by a child or young person with unimanual or bimanual manipulation (for example grasping, reaching, pouring or using utensils). The child then performs the same action with real objects. The sequences are organised into progressive levels of difficulty and into functional categories. Sensorised objects record usage data, which are transmitted to the portal. A clinician monitors adherence and performance through the portal and contacts the family by telephone or videoconference weekly, or sooner when technical or compliance problems arise. A caregiver will help set up the equipment and encourage the child to complete the exercises, without giving instruction on motor performance.

*Control group.* Participants will continue usual care for 3 weeks, which may include upper limb training, physiotherapy or occupational therapy. The type and amount of usual care will be recorded through a diary or structured interview. After T1, the control group will be offered the same Tele-UPCAT intervention, with the same follow-up schedule.

**Outcome measures**

Assessments will take place the week before (T0) and the week after (T1) the intervention or usual-care period. Follow-up will occur at 8 weeks (T2) and 24 weeks (T3) after the end of AOT. The waitlist group will also be assessed the week after their AOT period (T1 plus).

*Primary outcome.* The primary outcome is the AHA [6], which assesses how effectively the affected hand is used in bimanual activity during a semi-structured play session. The session is video-recorded and scored on 22 items, giving a raw score converted to logit-based AHA units (0–100). The primary endpoint is the change in AHA units from T0 to T1.

*Secondary outcomes.* The Melbourne Assessment 2 [7] will evaluate the quality of unilateral upper limb movement. The ABILHAND-Kids [8] questionnaire will assess manual ability as perceived by the parents. The Participation and Environment Measure for Children and Youth (PEM-CY) [9] will measure participation and environmental influences at home, at school and in the community. The Cerebral Palsy Quality of Life Questionnaire (CP QOL) [10] will evaluate wellbeing and quality of life.

*Quantitative sensor-based measures.* Participants will wear ActiGraph GT3X+ accelerometers on both wrists [11] for 7 days at each time point, recording triaxial accelerations. Data will be analysed for the amount of activity of each limb, the use ratio between the affected and unaffected sides, and asymmetry indices. Data from the sensorised objects during training will be used to assess changes in performance over the course of the intervention, such as duration of use and movement quality. Adherence will be quantified as the number of sessions completed and total training time recorded by the platform.

*Safety and acceptability.* Adverse events, technical failures and dropouts will be documented. Parents and children will rate usability and satisfaction with the system through a questionnaire at the end of training.

**Statistical analysis**

Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Descriptive statistics will summarise demographic and clinical characteristics by group. The between-group difference in T1 AHA scores will be tested with analysis of covariance, adjusting for baseline score and the stratification variable. Secondary outcomes will be analysed similarly or, when assumptions are violated, with non-parametric methods. Longitudinal changes across T0–T3, pooling data from both groups after their AOT periods, will be analysed with linear mixed-effects models with participant as a random effect. Effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals will be reported. The threshold for statistical significance is set at α = 0.05 (two-sided), and missing data will be handled with multiple imputation if they exceed 5%. Analyses will be conducted in R or SPSS.

**Data management and dissemination**

Data will be pseudonymised and stored on secure servers with restricted access. Results will be disseminated in peer-reviewed journals and at conferences.

The study is a registered protocol, and no outcome data have been analysed or are reported here. This section therefore describes the results of the protocol development, the technical implementation of the Tele-UPCAT platform, and the planned structure of the results to be reported on trial completion.

**Protocol Development and Feasibility Preparation**

The trial protocol was finalised after approval by the Tuscany Paediatric Ethics Committee (169/2016) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03094455). The design was refined through iterative consultation among paediatric neurorehabilitation clinicians, bioengineers and a methodologist. Two main decisions emerged. First, a waitlist control design was adopted so that all families would eventually receive AOT. Second, the primary outcome was set as the Assisting Hand Assessment (AHA), chosen because of its validity in unilateral cerebral palsy and its sensitivity to change in bimanual performance [1,2]. The sample size of 24 participants (12 per group) was agreed on the basis of the pilot data for UPCAT and of the practical limits of supervising a novel telerehabilitation system [3]. It was recognised that this size is suitable for estimating effect sizes and feasibility, but not for detecting small differences between groups.

**Tele-UPCAT Platform Implementation**

The Tele-UPCAT system was developed as a home-based package comprising a tablet or computer interface, a library of video sequences, sensorised objects and a remote clinician portal. The video library reproduces the structure of the original UPCAT protocol [3]. Each session presents goal-directed upper limb actions, performed by a child model, which are shown in sequence and then followed by physical execution of the same actions by the participant. The actions are graded in complexity and organised into thematic daily-life sets, so that the three-week programme progresses from simple to composite actions.

Sensorised objects embedded with inertial or pressure sensors record the timing and occurrence of object manipulation. These data are transmitted to a secure server, giving the clinical team a record of adherence and of movement features such as duration and number of repetitions. The clinician portal allows therapists to monitor sessions remotely, check that each video is watched before the matching motor task, and contact families when usage deviates from the schedule. Families receive a brief on-site or remote training session before the start, to minimise problems in setting up and operating the system.

Technical pilot testing before recruitment identified several usability issues, including video loading times, object calibration and the need for simplified on-screen prompts for younger children. These were resolved in successive software revisions. The final version was locked before enrolment so that all participants would receive the same intervention.

**Planned Participant Flow and Baseline Reporting**

Participant flow will be reported according to CONSORT recommendations [4]. The report will present the numbers screened, eligible, randomised, allocated, and assessed at each time point (T0, T1, T1 plus, T2 and T3), with reasons for exclusion and attrition. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics will be summarised by group, including age, sex, side of impairment, Manual Ability Classification System level, lesion type and previous upper limb therapy.
