Simple thresholding and region growing are fast but leak into neighboring structures and do not separate the body from the posterior elements [14]. Deformable models and active contours incorporate shape constraints and smoothness, but depend on initialization and may fail in pathologic cases [15,16]. Statistical shape and appearance models are robust and have been applied to the whole spine [17,18], yet their accuracy is limited by how well the training population represents the variability in shape, and they may bias the boundary toward the mean shape, which is undesirable when geometry itself is the outcome. Graph-cut and level-set formulations have also been described [19,20]. Many of these works emphasize anatomical identification or visualization and report overlap metrics, rather than the accuracy and precision of densitometric and geometric parameters, which determine clinical usefulness. Furthermore, few methods define VOIs relative to a reproducible, anatomically based local coordinate system, which is essential for longitudinal and multicenter comparison, because patient positioning and spinal curvature otherwise change the sampled region.

**Objectives and Contribution**

In this paper we present a multi-step segmentation methodology for lumbar vertebral bodies in spiral CT data that is designed explicitly for the measurement of BMD and geometry. The method first isolates the vertebral body from adjacent structures, then separates it from the posterior elements, and finally refines the boundary to capture the cortical shell. From the resulting surface a local anatomical coordinate system is derived, in which standardized VOIs are positioned independently of patient orientation. This yields densitometric and geometric measures that are comparable across examinations and subjects.

We evaluate the technique in terms of the criteria that matter for clinical application. Precision is assessed through intra- and inter-operator variability of the segmentation, the BMD values, and the coordinate system position in patient data. Accuracy is assessed using phantom data with known density and volume. By providing a validated, largely automated tool for three-dimensional vertebral analysis, we aim to establish the basis for studies that test whether volumetric density distribution and geometry improve the prediction of osteoporotic fractures.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first describe the image data and the segmentation algorithm, then the construction of the coordinate system and VOIs, followed by the validation protocol. Results for phantom and patient data are then presented and discussed with respect to limitations and future clinical application.

**Study Data**

Spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine were acquired from 20 postmenopausal women (age 55–80 years) as part of an ongoing osteoporosis study. Scans used a slice thickness of 1 mm, a reconstruction increment of 0.5 mm, 120 kVp, and a bone-density calibration phantom placed beneath the patient. Vertebrae L1–L3 were analyzed. For accuracy assessment, an anthropometric European Spine Phantom and six excised human vertebral specimens were scanned with identical protocols. The specimens' volumes were determined independently by water displacement (Archimedes' principle), and the phantom's nominal hydroxyapatite concentrations served as the BMD reference. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee.

**Segmentation Pipeline**

The segmentation consists of four consecutive steps: (1) preprocessing and seed definition, (2) coarse segmentation of the vertebral body by a region-based approach, (3) refinement by a deformable surface model, and (4) separation of the vertebral body from the posterior elements.

*Preprocessing and initialization.* Volumes were resampled to isotropic 0.5 mm voxels using trilinear interpolation and smoothed with a edge-preserving anisotropic diffusion filter [1] to reduce noise while retaining cortical boundaries. The operator placed one seed point at the center of each vertebral body and one point in the adjacent intervertebral disc above and below, which defined the approximate craniocaudal extent.

*Coarse segmentation.* A three-dimensional region-growing algorithm was started from the seed and constrained by an adaptive threshold. The threshold was computed from the local histogram of a spherical neighborhood as the midpoint between the trabecular and soft-tissue intensity modes, which makes the procedure robust against differences in bone density. Leakage into adjacent vertebrae or the ribs was prevented by morphological opening with a 3 mm structuring element and by restricting growth to the slab between the disc points. Holes inside the segmentation were closed by a slice-wise flood-fill followed by a 3D closing operation.

*Surface refinement.* The binary result was converted into a triangulated surface by marching cubes [2] and used as the initial state of a deformable simplex mesh [3]. Mesh vertices evolved under an internal smoothness force and an external force derived from the gradient magnitude of the image along the vertex normal, searching within ±2 mm for the strongest cortical edge. Iteration terminated when the mean vertex displacement fell below 0.01 mm. This step provided sub-voxel boundary localization, which is critical for volume and cortical-shell analysis.

*Removal of posterior elements.* The pedicles and posterior arch were excluded by fitting a plane through the narrowest region of each pedicle neck, identified from a distance-transform analysis of the segmented object. The vertebral body was defined as the part anterior to these planes. The operator could correct plane positions interactively, although this was rarely necessary.

**Local Anatomical Coordinate System**

A vertebra-specific coordinate system was derived from the segmented body surface. The origin was set at the centroid of the vertebral body. The craniocaudal axis (z) was defined as the normal of a least-squares plane fitted to the midpoints of the superior and inferior endplates, whose points were identified as surface vertices with normals within 30° of the preliminary axis. The sagittal direction (y) was obtained by projecting the vector from the centroid to the center of the pedicle-plane intersection onto the plane orthogonal to z, and the left–right axis (x) was the cross product of the two. The system was thereby independent of patient positioning and scanner orientation.

**Volumes of Interest and BMD Measurement**

Relative to this coordinate system, several volumes of interest (VOIs) were defined: (i) an elliptical trabecular VOI in the mid-vertebral region, inset from the cortical boundary by 2 mm and with a height of 50% of the vertebral body height; (ii) the whole vertebral body; (iii) a cortical shell VOI of 2 mm thickness inward from the surface; and (iv) a subcortical region beneath each endplate. VOI dimensions scaled with individual vertebral size so that comparable anatomical regions were assessed across subjects.

Hounsfield units were converted to equivalent hydroxyapatite density (mg/cm³) by linear regression against the calibration phantom rods, with correction for scan-specific offsets. Mean BMD was computed per VOI, with partial volume voxels at boundaries weighted by their fractional occupancy derived from the refined mesh.

**Geometric Analysis**

From the refined surface, vertebral body volume, anterior, middle, and posterior heights, endplate areas, and mean cross-sectional area at mid-height were calculated. Heights were measured parallel to the z-axis and cross-sections in planes orthogonal to it. Volume was computed using the divergence theorem applied to the closed triangular mesh.

**Accuracy Evaluation**

For BMD accuracy, phantom vertebrae with known hydroxyapatite concentrations were scanned and segmented, and relative differences between measured and nominal values were calculated. For volume accuracy, segmented volumes of the excised vertebrae were compared with water-displacement values. Accuracy error was expressed as the mean absolute percentage deviation.

**Precision Evaluation**

Intra-operator precision was assessed by having one operator repeat the entire procedure, including seed placement, on all patient vertebrae three times, separated by at least one week. Inter-operator precision was assessed with three trained operators working independently. Outcome variables were segmented volume, VOI BMD, and the position of the coordinate-system origin and axes. Precision was expressed as the root-mean-square coefficient of variation (RMS-CV%) [4] for volume and BMD, and as the root-mean-square standard deviation of origin position (mm) and axis orientation (degrees); the latter were additionally normalized to vertebral dimensions to allow percentage statements. Repeated scans were not acquired, so the reported precision reflects only the analysis rather than acquisition.

**Statistical Analysis**

Agreement between measured and reference values was examined by linear regression and Bland–Altman analysis [5]. Differences between operators were tested with repeated-measures ANOVA, with *p* < 0.05 considered significant. Analyses were performed in MATLAB (The MathWorks, Natick, MA), and the segmentation was implemented in C++ using the Insight Toolkit.

**Segmentation performance.** The multi-step segmentation was applied to all lumbar vertebral bodies (L1–L3) in the patient dataset. The algorithm converged without manual correction of the initial seed placement in 94% of cases. In the remaining cases, a single repositioning of the seed point in the vertebral body was sufficient to obtain a satisfactory result. Visual inspection of the axial, sagittal and coronal reformations showed that the segmented surface followed the cortical boundary closely, including in regions of low contrast between the vertebral body and the intervertebral disc. The most frequent deviations occurred at the posterior border where the vertebral body merges with the pedicles. These were corrected by the final separation step. Mean processing time was 4.2 ± 1.1 min per vertebra on a standard workstation, of which about 70% was spent on the initial region-growing and surface refinement stages.

**Local coordinate system.** The anatomical coordinate system was derived automatically from the segmented geometry. Its origin was placed at the centroid of the vertebral body, and its axes were aligned with the principal axes of the endplate-defined body. In all vertebrae the resulting axes agreed visually with the anatomical anterior–posterior, lateral and cranio-caudal directions. The volumes of interest (VOIs) defined relative to this system, namely the trabecular compartment, the cortical shell and the integral vertebral body, were reproducibly positioned. Because they were defined relative to the local system rather than the scanner geometry, they were independent of patient tilt and lordosis. Differences in patient positioning of up to 20° had no visible effect on the VOI placement.

**Precision.** Intra- and inter-operator precision were assessed on repeated segmentations by three trained operators. Precision is reported as the root-mean-square coefficient of variation (RMS CV%) (Table 1).

| Parameter | Intra-operator RMS CV (%) | Inter-operator RMS CV (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Vertebral body volume | 0.6 | 0.9 |
| Trabecular BMD | 0.8 | 1.2 |
| Integral BMD | 0.5 | 0.8 |
| Cortical BMD | 1.0 | 1.4 |
| Coordinate system origin | 0.4 | 0.7 |
| Coordinate system orientation | 0.5 | 0.9 |

All values were below 1.5%. As expected, precision was best for integral measures, which are less sensitive to local boundary variation, and lowest for cortical BMD, where the thin cortex makes partial-volume effects more influential. Inter-operator errors were consistently slightly larger than intra-operator errors. Bland–Altman analysis showed no systematic bias between operators, with mean differences in trabecular BMD of less than 1 mg/cm³ and limits of agreement within ±3 mg/cm³. Precision did not depend significantly on the vertebral level (p > 0.2) or on the BMD of the subject. The latter was also the case in osteoporotic patients with reduced trabecular density and mild deformities.

**Accuracy in phantom data.** Accuracy was evaluated using a European Spine Phantom and an anthropomorphic phantom with known geometry and calibrated hydroxyapatite inserts. For BMD, the mean deviation from the nominal values was 0.9% for the low-density insert, 0.7% for the medium-density insert and 0.6% for the high-density insert, with a maximum error of 1.4%. Linear regression of measured against nominal BMD gave a slope of 0.995 and r² > 0.99. For volume, the deviation of the segmented volume from the reference was 2.8 ± 0.9% for the anthropomorphic phantom vertebrae and 3.6% at maximum. The segmentation slightly overestimated the volume, a bias consistent with partial-volume voxels at the boundary being assigned to the object. Accuracy was not noticeably affected by the tube current setting, although a modest increase in the variability of BMD was seen at the lowest dose (CV change < 0.4 percentage points).

**Geometric analysis.** Beyond densitometry, the extracted surfaces provided geometric parameters of the vertebral bodies. In the patient cohort, the mean vertebral body volume increased from L1 to L3, as did endplate area and cross-sectional dimensions. Vertebral height measured at the anterior, middle and posterior positions allowed the quantification of wedging and biconcavity. Several vertebrae with mild deformities not classified as fractures by visual assessment showed an anterior-to-posterior height ratio below that of the remaining vertebrae. These results suggest that three-dimensional geometric indices could complement conventional morphometric grading. Male subjects had larger vertebral volumes and endplate areas than female subjects, whereas trabecular BMD showed the expected age-related decline in both sexes. Geometric parameters were measured with the same precision as BMD (RMS CV < 1.5%).

**Dependence of BMD on the VOI.** BMD values depended considerably on the VOI definition. Trabecular BMD in the central VOI was lower than that in a VOI adjacent to the endplates. The integral BMD, which includes the cortical shell, was higher than both by a clearly larger margin. Regional differences between the anterior and posterior parts of the trabecular compartment were also observed, with the posterior part showing slightly higher values on average. The ability to define such VOIs reproducibly relative to the local coordinate system was thus a prerequisite for comparing these regional values among subjects and in follow-up examinations.

**Comparison with a conventional method.** Trabecular BMD from our approach was compared with values obtained by the standard approach of placing an elliptical region of interest in three mid-vertebral slices. The two methods correlated strongly (r = 0.97), but the conventional method gave slightly lower values (mean difference −4.1 mg/cm³), reflecting the different sampling volumes. The conventional method had higher inter-operator variability (RMS CV 2.3%) than the new technique (1.2%).

**Methodological considerations**

The proposed multi-step segmentation extracts the vertebral body from spiral CT data and defines volumes of interest (VOIs) relative to a local anatomical coordinate system. Several design decisions explain why the results are precise and accurate. First, separating the vertebral body from the posterior elements and adjacent structures before any densitometric analysis removes the largest source of operator-dependent variability in conventional approaches, namely manual placement of regions of interest in single slices [1,2]. Second, anchoring the VOIs to a coordinate system derived from the vertebral geometry makes the BMD measurement largely independent of patient positioning and scanner orientation. This is essential for longitudinal studies, where small differences in repositioning would otherwise produce apparent density changes of the same order as the expected biological effect [3]. Third, the volumetric rather than slice-based analysis averages over many voxels, which reduces the influence of image noise and local heterogeneity of trabecular bone.

The low intra- and inter-operator variability suggests that the method could be applied in multicenter studies with limited operator training. Precision errors below 1.5% compare favorably with values reported for quantitative CT (QCT) of the spine, which typically range from 1% to 3% in vivo [3,4], and are clearly below the roughly 2–4% precision of DXA that limits its sensitivity to short-term change [5]. For clinical trials, this implies that smaller treatment effects or shorter intervals may be detectable with the same sample size.

**Accuracy and phantom validation**

Phantom measurements yielded BMD errors below 1.5% and volume errors below 4%. The larger volume error is expected, because volume depends directly on the boundary location. At the resolution of clinical spiral CT, partial volume effects blur the cortical surface by a fraction of a voxel. Because the cortex is thin, a sub-voxel boundary shift translates into a relatively large volume change, whereas BMD in the interior of the VOI is hardly affected. A systematic bias of this kind is generally stable and could be corrected by calibration, or at least it does not compromise comparisons within a study that uses a fixed protocol. Nevertheless, absolute geometric measures such as vertebral volume or cross-sectional area should be interpreted with this limitation in mind.

Phantom data cannot reproduce the full complexity of the in vivo situation. Osteophytes, severely osteoporotic vertebrae with very thin or porous cortices, endplate deformities, and vertebral fractures all challenge any boundary-detection scheme. Likewise, the patient cohort in which reproducibility was assessed was limited in size and was not selected to cover the full spectrum of pathology. The reported precision should therefore be regarded as representative of well-defined, non-fractured vertebrae. Further evaluation in larger cohorts, including prevalent fractures and advanced degenerative disease, is required to establish the robustness of the method and to quantify its failure rate.

**Relevance for fracture prediction**

Areal BMD from DXA remains the clinical standard, yet it explains only part of fracture risk, and a considerable proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients without osteoporosis by T-score criteria [6]. DXA projects a three-dimensional structure onto a plane and cannot separate cortical from trabecular bone, nor can it distinguish degenerative sclerosis from true bone mass. Our approach addresses these limitations in two ways. VOIs can be defined to isolate trabecular bone from the cortical shell and from the endplates, so that metabolically active trabecular bone, which responds early to disease and therapy, can be examined separately [7]. In addition, the simultaneous availability of geometric parameters allows biomechanically motivated descriptors, for example cross-sectional area, vertebral height, and their combination with density, to be derived from a single acquisition. Since vertebral strength depends on both bone mass distribution and structural dimensions [8], combining these descriptors in finite element models or simple composite indices may improve risk stratification beyond BMD alone. The present study did not test this hypothesis; it provides the measurement basis that makes such tests feasible.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The method relies on CT and therefore involves a higher radiation dose than DXA, although opportunistic use of scans acquired for other indications could mitigate this concern. Calibration with a reference phantom or a consistent scanner protocol is required for absolute BMD values, and the influence of different scanners, reconstruction kernels, and tube voltages was not examined exhaustively. The spatial resolution of clinical CT does not permit resolution of individual trabeculae, so the method yields density and macro-geometry rather than true microarchitecture. Finally, although the procedure is largely automatic, some interaction is still required, and processing time and the need for user intervention in difficult cases need to be documented for routine application.

**Conclusion and outlook**

We have presented a multi-step three-dimensional segmentation methodology for lumbar vertebral bodies that supports precise and accurate measurement of BMD in anatomically defined VOIs together with quantitative analysis of vertebral geometry. The low operator dependence and the reproducible positioning of the local coordinate system make it suitable for cross-sectional and longitudinal investigations. Future work will focus on validation in larger and more heterogeneous patient populations, on cross-scanner and cross-protocol harmonization, and on further automation to minimize user interaction. The central objective remains a prospective evaluation of whether the combined density and geometry parameters provided by this method improve the prediction of vertebral and other osteoporotic fractures relative to current clinical standards.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive and life-threatening disease characterized by sustained elevation of pulmonary arterial pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance, which ultimately leads to right ventricular hypertrophy, right heart failure, and death [1,2]. The pathological hallmarks of PAH include endothelial dysfunction, proliferation and apoptosis resistance of smooth muscle cells, medial hypertrophy, perivascular inflammation, and fibrosis of small pulmonary arteries [3]. Although current therapies targeting the prostacyclin, endothelin, and nitric oxide pathways improve symptoms and exercise capacity, they only modestly alter the underlying vascular remodeling, and long-term survival remains poor [4]. New therapeutic strategies that target additional pathogenic mechanisms are therefore needed.

The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) has been implicated in the pathogenesis of pulmonary hypertension. The classical axis, composed of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), angiotensin II (Ang II), and the Ang II type 1 receptor (AT1R), promotes vasoconstriction, cell proliferation, inflammation, and fibrosis [5]. Increased ACE activity and Ang II levels have been reported in patients with PAH and in experimental models, and AT1R blockade or ACE inhibition attenuates pulmonary vascular remodeling in some animal studies [6,7]. In contrast, the counter-regulatory axis, centered on ACE2, has attracted attention as a protective pathway. ACE2 converts Ang II to Ang-(1-7), which acts mainly through the Mas receptor to induce vasodilation and exert anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory effects [8]. Reduced pulmonary ACE2 expression has been observed in PAH, and ACE2 overexpression, ACE2 activators, or Ang-(1-7) administration ameliorate pulmonary hypertension in rodents [9–11].

ACE2 also converts Ang I to Ang-(1-9) by removing the C-terminal leucine residue [12]. Ang-(1-9) was long regarded as an inactive intermediate, serving mainly as a precursor of Ang-(1-7) through ACE-mediated cleavage. However, recent studies have shown that Ang-(1-9) has biological activity of its own. In rodent models of cardiovascular disease, Ang-(1-9) reduced cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis after myocardial infarction and in hypertensive rats, improved endothelial function, and attenuated vascular remodeling, independently of its conversion to Ang-(1-7) [13–15]. Ang-(1-9) has also been shown to reduce oxidative stress, to limit cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and to prevent neointimal formation and inflammation in injured vessels [16,17]. Notably, these effects were generally abolished by the Ang II type 2 receptor (AT2R) antagonist PD123319 rather than by the Mas receptor antagonist A779, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) acts as a functional ligand of AT2R [13,15]. AT2R signaling is typically associated with vasodilation, anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic actions, and modulation of apoptosis, and it has been proposed as a promising target in cardiovascular and lung diseases [18,19]. Activation of AT2R by selective agonists such as compound 21 has been reported to attenuate pulmonary hypertension and fibrosis in experimental models [20,21].

Despite this evidence, the effect of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension has not been examined. Because the pulmonary circulation expresses high levels of ACE and ACE2 and is exposed to substantial amounts of circulating angiotensin peptides, Ang-(1-9) may play a relevant role in regulating pulmonary vascular homeostasis. Furthermore, inflammation and apoptosis of endothelial cells are central to the initiation and progression of PAH. Endothelial injury and the release of inflammatory mediators, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), promote vascular remodeling and perivascular inflammatory cell infiltration [22,23]. Altered expression of apoptosis-related proteins, such as Bax, Bcl-2, and caspases, has been described in the lungs of animals with experimental pulmonary hypertension [24]. Whether Ang-(1-9) can modulate these processes in the pulmonary vasculature is unknown.

The monocrotaline (MCT) model is a widely used and well-characterized model of PAH. A single subcutaneous injection of MCT in rats is metabolized in the liver to the reactive pyrrole derivative, which causes pulmonary endothelial injury, followed by inflammation, medial hypertrophy of pulmonary arterioles, interstitial fibrosis, increased pulmonary arterial pressure, and right ventricular hypertrophy [25,26]. Because the model reproduces endothelial damage and inflammatory features that are important in human disease, it is suitable for evaluating candidate agents that target these mechanisms.

In the present study, we therefore hypothesized that Ang-(1-9) protects against the development of MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension through AT2R. We examined the effects of continuous Ang-(1-9) infusion on right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary arteriolar remodeling, endothelial damage, and pulmonary fibrosis in MCT-treated rats. To determine the receptor mechanism, we assessed whether the effects of Ang-(1-9) were blocked by an AT2R antagonist or a Mas receptor antagonist. In addition, we measured plasma lactate dehydrogenase and inflammatory cytokines, and evaluated the expression of apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue, to clarify the potential contributions of anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions to the effects of Ang-(1-9).

Animals and ethics

Male Sprague-Dawley rats (6 weeks old, 180–200 g) were housed under controlled conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 55 ± 5% humidity, 12-h light/dark cycle) with free access to standard chow and water. Animals were acclimated for one week before experimentation. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and conformed to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the US National Institutes of Health [1].

Experimental design

Rats were randomly assigned to groups (n = 8–10 per group): (1) control (saline pump plus vehicle injection); (2) Ang-(1-9) alone; (3) MCT plus saline; (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9); (5) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the AT2R antagonist PD123319; and (6) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the Mas receptor antagonist A779. Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) or saline was delivered via osmotic mini-pumps (Alzet model 2ML4) implanted subcutaneously in the dorsal region under isoflurane anesthesia and continued for 3 weeks. This dose was selected based on previous studies of cardiac and vascular remodeling [2,3]. Three days after pump implantation, rats received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT (50 mg/kg) dissolved in 1 N HCl, neutralized with NaOH to pH 7.4, or an equal volume of vehicle [4]. PD123319 (36 mg/kg/day) and A779 (100 µg/kg/day) were co-infused through separate mini-pumps beginning at the same time as Ang-(1-9) [5]. Body weight and general condition were monitored throughout. Experiments were terminated 3 weeks after pump implantation.

Hemodynamic measurements and right ventricular hypertrophy

Rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). A polyethylene catheter filled with heparinized saline was inserted via the right jugular vein into the right ventricle under pressure-waveform guidance, and right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was recorded using a pressure transducer and a data acquisition system (PowerLab, ADInstruments). After hemodynamic recording, blood was collected from the abdominal aorta into EDTA tubes and centrifuged (3,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C); plasma was stored at −80 °C. The heart was excised, and the right ventricle (RV) was dissected from the left ventricle plus septum (LV+S). Right ventricular hypertrophy was expressed as the Fulton index, RV/(LV+S), and as RV weight normalized to body weight.

Histology and morphometry

The left lung was perfused with saline, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin at constant pressure, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 4 µm. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Masson’s trichrome. For medial hypertrophy, pulmonary arterioles (external diameter 50–100 µm) were examined in at least 10 vessels per animal by an observer blinded to group allocation. Medial wall thickness was calculated as percentage: [(external diameter − internal diameter)/external diameter] × 100 [6]. Pulmonary fibrosis was assessed by the proportion of collagen-positive (blue) area in Masson-stained sections using ImageJ software (NIH), averaged across ten random fields per animal at 200× magnification.

Endothelial damage was evaluated by immunohistochemistry for von Willebrand factor (vWF) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). Deparaffinized sections underwent antigen retrieval in citrate buffer, blocked for endogenous peroxidase and nonspecific binding, and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and diaminobenzidine development. Positive staining in the vascular endothelium was quantified by densitometry.

Measurement of plasma LDH and cytokines

Plasma lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity was determined using a commercial colorimetric assay kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Plasma concentrations of TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β, and IL-6 were measured by rat-specific enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. All samples were assayed in duplicate, and concentrations were calculated from standard curves.

Western blot analysis

Right lung tissue was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and homogenized in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Lysates were centrifuged (12,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C), and protein concentrations in the supernatants were measured by the BCA method. Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE (10–12%) and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking in 5% nonfat milk for 1 h, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against Bax, Bcl-2, cleaved caspase-3, cleaved caspase-9, and β-actin (loading control). Membranes were then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry with ImageJ. Protein levels were normalized to β-actin and expressed relative to the control group.

TUNEL assay

Apoptotic cells in lung sections were detected using a terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) kit following the manufacturer’s protocol [7]. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. The apoptotic index was calculated as the percentage of TUNEL-positive nuclei among total nuclei in ten randomly selected fields per animal.

Drugs and reagents

Ang-(1-9), PD123319, A779, and MCT were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich or equivalent suppliers. Antibodies and ELISA kits were obtained from commercial vendors and used at the recommended dilutions. All other chemicals were of analytical grade.

Statistical analysis

Data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Normality of distribution was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test and homogeneity of variance with Levene’s test. Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test; Kruskal–Wallis testing with Dunn’s correction was used when assumptions were not met. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 8.0). A P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Investigators performing histological and biochemical analyses were blinded to group assignment.

Ang-(1-9) attenuates MCT-induced right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary hypertension

Three weeks after MCT injection, rats showed marked pulmonary hypertension. Right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was significantly higher in the MCT group than in the control group (p<0.01). The ratio of right ventricular weight to left ventricular plus septal weight (Fulton index, RV/[LV+S]) and the ratio of right ventricular weight to body weight were also increased. Co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced RVSP and both indices of right ventricular hypertrophy compared with MCT alone (p<0.05). Ang-(1-9) alone did not alter these parameters in control rats. Body weight gain was reduced in MCT-treated rats, and this was partly prevented by Ang-(1-9). Systemic arterial pressure and heart rate did not differ among groups, indicating that the hemodynamic benefit was not attributable to systemic blood pressure changes.

Ang-(1-9) improves pulmonary vascular remodeling and fibrosis

Histological examination of lung sections showed thickening of the pulmonary arteriolar wall and narrowing of the lumen in MCT rats. Quantitative analysis showed that the percentage of medial wall thickness was significantly increased by MCT (p<0.01) and was significantly lower in rats co-treated with Ang-(1-9) (p<0.05). The proportion of muscularized small pulmonary arterioles was similarly increased by MCT and reduced by Ang-(1-9). Immunostaining for von Willebrand factor showed loss of endothelial staining in the pulmonary arterioles of MCT rats, indicating endothelial damage. This loss was attenuated by Ang-(1-9). Masson's trichrome staining showed increased collagen deposition in perivascular and interstitial areas of the lungs of MCT rats, and the fibrotic area was significantly reduced by Ang-(1-9) treatment (p<0.05). Thus, Ang-(1-9) improved endothelial damage, medial hypertrophy and fibrosis in the lungs of MCT-treated rats.

Effects of AT2R and Mas receptor blockade

To identify the receptor responsible for the effects of Ang-(1-9), the AT2R antagonist PD123319 or the Mas receptor antagonist A779 was co-administered with Ang-(1-9) in MCT rats. PD123319 abolished the beneficial effects of Ang-(1-9) on RVSP and right ventricular hypertrophy, so that values were similar to those in the MCT group (p<0.05 vs. MCT+Ang-(1-9)). PD123319 likewise abrogated the improvement in medial wall thickness, endothelial staining and fibrosis. In contrast, A779 did not significantly modify the reductions in RVSP, right ventricular hypertrophy, vascular remodeling or fibrosis produced by Ang-(1-9). Neither antagonist alone, given with MCT, significantly changed the degree of pulmonary hypertension compared with MCT alone. These findings indicate that the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) are mediated by AT2R but not by the Mas receptor.

Ang-(1-9) reduces plasma LDH and inflammatory cytokines

Plasma LDH activity, a marker of tissue injury, was significantly elevated in MCT rats compared with controls (p<0.01), and this elevation was significantly attenuated by Ang-(1-9) (p<0.05). Plasma concentrations of TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β and IL-6 were all markedly higher in the MCT group than in the control group. Co-treatment with Ang-(1-9) significantly lowered the concentrations of each of these cytokines compared with MCT alone (p<0.05). The inhibitory effects of Ang-(1-9) on LDH and cytokine levels were reversed by PD123319 but not by A779, consistent with the AT2R-dependent mechanism observed for hemodynamic and histological outcomes.

Ang-(1-9) modulates apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue

Western blot analysis of lung homogenates showed that MCT altered the expression of apoptosis-related proteins. Expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax was increased, whereas expression of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 was decreased, resulting in a higher Bax/Bcl-2 ratio in the MCT group than in controls (p<0.01). Cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved caspase-9 were also significantly increased by MCT. Treatment with Ang-(1-9) significantly attenuated these changes: Bax expression and the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio were reduced, Bcl-2 expression was partly restored, and cleaved caspase-3 and -9 levels were lower than in the MCT group (p<0.05). Ang-(1-9) alone did not alter the expression of these proteins in control rats. As with the other outcomes, co-administration of PD123319 prevented the effects of Ang-(1-9) on Bax, Bcl-2 and caspase expression, whereas A779 had no significant effect. These data suggest that Ang-(1-9) reduces apoptosis in the lungs of MCT-treated rats through AT2R, which is in line with the preservation of endothelial integrity and the reduction in vascular remodeling.

Summary of findings

Together, the results show that continuous infusion of Ang-(1-9) prevented the development of MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension, as reflected by lower RVSP, reduced right ventricular hypertrophy, less pulmonary vascular remodeling and less fibrosis. These benefits were accompanied by decreased plasma LDH and proinflammatory cytokines and by normalization of apoptosis-related protein expression in the lung. All of these effects were blocked by an AT2R antagonist but not by a Mas receptor antagonist.

The present study demonstrates for the first time that continuous administration of Ang-(1-9) attenuates the development of monocrotaline (MCT)-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension in rats. Ang-(1-9) reduced right ventricular systolic pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy, limited endothelial damage, medial thickening of pulmonary arterioles and pulmonary fibrosis, and lowered plasma LDH and pro-inflammatory cytokines. It also normalized the expression of apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue. Notably, these beneficial effects were abolished by an AT2R antagonist but not by a Mas receptor antagonist, indicating that AT2R rather than Mas mediates the protective actions of Ang-(1-9) in this model.

The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) is increasingly recognized as a contributor to the pathogenesis of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The classical axis, comprising ACE, Ang II and the AT1 receptor, promotes vasoconstriction, proliferation, inflammation and fibrosis, whereas the counter-regulatory axis, comprising ACE2, Ang-(1-7) and Mas, opposes these actions [1,2]. Reduced pulmonary ACE2 expression and activity have been reported in experimental and human PAH, and ACE2 activation or Ang-(1-7) supplementation improves pulmonary hemodynamics in MCT and hypoxia models [3,4]. Ang-(1-9), formed from Ang I by ACE2, was long considered mainly a precursor of Ang-(1-7), but recent work has shown that it has intrinsic activity. In the heart, Ang-(1-9) prevents cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and adverse remodeling after myocardial infarction or in hypertension, and it reduces vascular remodeling and oxidative stress in hypertensive rats [5-7]. Our findings extend this protective profile to the pulmonary circulation.

The receptor mechanism is of particular interest. Earlier cardiac studies showed that the effects of Ang-(1-9) were blocked by the AT2R antagonist PD123319, with no involvement of Mas, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) acts through AT2R [5,6]. Our results agree with this. Although Ang-(1-9) has lower affinity for AT2R than Ang II, it may act as an endogenous ligand, particularly when AT1R-mediated Ang II effects are limited or when Ang II is cleared by ACE2. AT2R is generally associated with anti-proliferative, anti-fibrotic, anti-inflammatory and vasodilatory signaling, mediated by bradykinin, nitric oxide and cGMP, as well as activation of phosphatases [8,9]. Selective AT2R agonists such as compound 21 have been shown to attenuate pulmonary hypertension and fibrosis in rodents [10], which supports the concept that AT2R stimulation is beneficial in the pulmonary vasculature. The lack of effect of Mas blockade argues against conversion of Ang-(1-9) to Ang-(1-7) as a major mechanism, although we did not measure local peptide levels and cannot completely exclude a minor contribution.

Endothelial injury is considered an initiating event in MCT-induced PAH, as its active metabolite, monocrotaline pyrrole, damages pulmonary endothelial cells, causing inflammation, loss of barrier function and subsequent smooth muscle proliferation [11]. The lower plasma LDH and the preserved endothelial morphology in Ang-(1-9)-treated rats suggest that Ang-(1-9) protects against this early damage. Because LDH is a nonspecific marker of cell injury, this finding should be interpreted with caution, but it is consistent with the reduced apoptosis observed in lung tissue. MCT increased the pro-apoptotic proteins Bax, caspase-3 and caspase-9 and decreased anti-apoptotic Bcl-2; these changes were reversed by Ang-(1-9), indicating involvement of the mitochondrial pathway. Excessive endothelial apoptosis is thought to select apoptosis-resistant, hyperproliferative cells and thereby promote vascular obliteration [12]; thus, limiting early apoptosis may prevent the progression of vascular remodeling.

Inflammation is another key determinant of PAH. Elevated circulating TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and MCP-1 correlate with disease severity and outcome, and perivascular infiltration by macrophages and lymphocytes is a hallmark of both human and experimental disease [13,14]. Ang-(1-9) reduced these cytokines, which may reflect both a direct anti-inflammatory action through AT2R and an indirect effect resulting from less endothelial damage. AT2R activation has been shown to inhibit NF-κB signaling and cytokine production in several tissues [9], which provides a plausible mechanism. Reduced inflammation likely also contributed to the decreased pulmonary fibrosis, as inflammatory mediators drive fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, Ang-(1-9) was administered before and during MCT exposure, so our data demonstrate prevention rather than reversal of established PAH; the latter is more clinically relevant and should be tested in a treatment protocol. Second, the MCT model, although widely used, involves substantial systemic toxicity and inflammation and does not reproduce the plexiform lesions of human disease; confirmation in other models such as Sugen/hypoxia is desirable. Third, receptor involvement was inferred from pharmacological antagonists, and the specificity and dosing of these agents may influence interpretation; studies using AT2R-deficient animals or cell-specific knockdown would be more definitive. Fourth, we did not examine downstream signaling such as nitric oxide, cGMP, or NF-κB, nor did we assess effects on pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells directly. Finally, only one dose of Ang-(1-9) was used, and dose-response relationships and long-term safety remain unknown.

In conclusion, Ang-(1-9) ameliorates MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary vascular remodeling and fibrosis in rats by suppressing apoptosis and inflammation through AT2R, independently of Mas. These findings identify Ang-(1-9) as a protective component of the ACE2-centered counter-regulatory RAS in the pulmonary circulation and suggest that stimulation of AT2R, whether by Ang-(1-9) or related agonists, may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Further studies in established disease and additional models are needed to define its translational potential.

Masonry constructions of historical interest make up a large share of the built heritage in Italy and across Europe, and their preservation requires reliable tools for assessing structural safety under both ordinary and exceptional loads. Numerical modelling, and the finite element (FE) method in particular, is now routinely used for this purpose [1,2]. However, the predictive capability of an FE model depends heavily on the quality of its input data. Historical masonry is heterogeneous and anisotropic, its constituent materials vary from one structure to another, and its internal morphology is often unknown. Geometry may be altered by later interventions, damage, or settlements, and boundary conditions, such as the interaction with adjacent buildings and soil, are seldom well defined. As a consequence, mechanical parameters such as Young's modulus, density, and the stiffness of constraints are affected by considerable uncertainty, and direct in situ or laboratory testing is often limited by the need to minimise invasiveness on cultural heritage assets [3].

**Dynamic identification and model updating**

Ambient vibration testing is an attractive, non-destructive way of acquiring information on existing structures. Operational modal analysis techniques allow natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios to be extracted from output-only measurements [4,5]. These modal quantities depend on the global stiffness and mass distribution of the structure, and therefore they provide valuable information for calibrating numerical models. The process by which the uncertain parameters of an FE model are adjusted so that the computed modal response matches the experimental one is known as model updating [6,7]. Comparing calculated and measured modal data is only the first step. The discrepancy must then be reduced in a systematic and quantitative manner.

Two broad families of approaches can be distinguished. Direct methods modify the stiffness and mass matrices to reproduce the measured modal data exactly, but they often yield matrices lacking physical meaning and are poorly suited to complex models [6]. Iterative, parametric methods instead update physically meaningful parameters by minimising an objective function that measures the distance between numerical and experimental results. These include sensitivity-based approaches [8], Bayesian formulations [9], and global optimisation techniques such as genetic algorithms and surrogate-assisted strategies [10,11]. Model updating has been applied successfully to masonry towers, churches, arch bridges, and historic palaces [12–15], showing that dynamic data can substantially narrow the uncertainty on material properties and constraints.

**Challenges specific to masonry heritage structures**

Despite this progress, several difficulties remain. First, the inverse problem is generally ill-posed: different parameter sets may produce similar modal responses, and the solution may be non-unique or sensitive to measurement noise. Second, the pairing of numerical and experimental modes is not trivial, since mode shapes may swap order or change character during the iterations; criteria such as the Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) are commonly used, but their robustness depends on how the sensor layout samples the structure [16]. Third, the choice of the objective function, the number of free parameters, and the bounds imposed on them affect both convergence and the physical plausibility of the result. Finally, the computational cost of repeated modal analyses can be significant for detailed three-dimensional models. Procedures integrated directly within the FE environment, and capable of handling these issues automatically, are therefore of considerable practical value for professionals and researchers working on heritage conservation.

**The NOSA-ITACA code**

NOSA-ITACA is an FE software developed at the Institute of Information Science and Technologies of the National Research Council of Italy (ISTI-CNR) in Pisa [17]. It results from the integration of NOSA, a solver developed at ISTI-CNR, with the pre- and post-processor SALOME, and is distributed as open source. The code was conceived specifically for the structural analysis of masonry constructions and models masonry as a nonlinear material with zero or limited tensile strength, the so-called masonry-like or normal-rigid-no-tension material [18]. It has been used to study the static and dynamic behaviour of numerous historic buildings, including towers, churches, and bridges, in many cases in combination with experimental campaigns [19–21]. In those studies, model calibration was usually performed by manual trial and error, which is laborious, subjective, and hard to reproduce. An automatic updating tool within the code was thus a natural and needed development.

**Aims and contributions**

The present paper describes the model updating procedure implemented in NOSA-ITACA, whose purpose is to tune the free parameters of an FE model so as to match experimentally identified frequencies and mode shapes. The formulation, based on the minimisation of an objective function that combines frequency residuals and mode shape correlation, is presented together with the strategies adopted to preserve its robustness, namely mode pairing, parameter bounds, and the treatment of poorly conditioned problems. The main contributions are the availability of a systematic, reproducible updating tool in an open-source code dedicated to masonry structures, and a discussion of the numerical issues that affect its reliability.

The procedure is first verified on a simple benchmark case with known solution, which allows its accuracy and sensitivity to be assessed in a controlled setting. It is then applied to two real structures in Tuscany: the Clock Tower in Lucca, a slender medieval masonry tower, and the Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano, a historic multi-span arch bridge also known as the Devil's Bridge. These cases differ markedly in typology and in the nature of the uncertainties involved, and so they provide a meaningful test of the method.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 summarises the numerical method and the updating algorithm. Section 3 discusses robustness-related issues. Section 4 presents the benchmark case, and Sections 5 and 6 report the applications to the Clock Tower and the Maddalena bridge. Conclusions and future developments are given in Section 7.

**Numerical framework and model updating formulation**

The structural model is discretized with the finite-element method, and the undamped free vibrations are governed by the generalized eigenvalue problem

(K(p) − λ_i M(p)) φ_i = 0, i = 1,…,n,

where K and M are the global stiffness and mass matrices, λ_i = (2πf_i)² is the i-th eigenvalue, φ_i the corresponding mode shape, and p ∈ ℝ^m the vector of free parameters to be updated. In NOSA-ITACA, the masonry is modelled as a linear elastic isotropic material for modal analysis, so the parameters usually considered are Young's modulus and, when relevant, mass density of macro-regions with homogeneous properties. Stiffnesses of elastic restraints representing soil–structure interaction or connections to adjacent buildings may also be included. Poisson's ratio is kept fixed because modal quantities are only weakly sensitive to it [1].

The updating procedure searches for the parameter vector that minimizes the discrepancy between numerical and experimental modal data, obtained from operational modal analysis. The objective function is

J(p) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} w_{f,i} [(f_i^num(p) − f_i^exp)/f_i^exp]² + Σ_{i=1}^{n} w_{φ,i} [1 − MAC_i(p)],

with w_{f,i} and w_{φ,i} user-defined weights. The Modal Assurance Criterion is

MAC_i = |φ_i^{exp,T} φ_i^{num}|² / [(φ_i^{exp,T} φ_i^{exp})(φ_i^{num,T} φ_i^{num})],

where the numerical mode shape is reduced to the degrees of freedom instrumented during the tests. Bounds p_min ≤ p ≤ p_max, set from engineering judgement and literature values for historic masonry [2], constrain the minimization to physically admissible values.

**Mode pairing**

A principal source of ill-conditioning in modal updating is the incorrect association of numerical and experimental modes, since the order of the frequencies can change as parameters vary. At each iteration, each experimental mode is therefore paired with the numerical mode that maximizes the MAC, rather than with the mode having the same ordinal number. A pairing is accepted only if the MAC exceeds a threshold (typically 0.5–0.7); otherwise the iteration is flagged and the associated mode is excluded from the objective function. This strategy avoids discontinuities in J caused by mode switching.

**Optimization algorithm and sensitivities**

The minimization is carried out with an iterative gradient-based method of Gauss–Newton type with trust-region (Levenberg–Marquardt) regularization [3]. Sensitivities of eigenvalues to parameters are computed analytically from the eigenvalue derivative

∂λ_i/∂p_j = φ_i^T (∂K/∂p_j − λ_i ∂M/∂p_j) φ_i,

assuming mass-normalized modes. Because K and M depend linearly on Young's modulus and density of each region, the matrices ∂K/∂p_j and ∂M/∂p_j are obtained from the element contributions of the corresponding region without additional factorizations. Derivatives of the MAC are evaluated with eigenvector sensitivities according to Nelson's method [4], which requires the solution of one linear system per mode and parameter, reusing the factorization of the shifted stiffness matrix. When modes are closely spaced, Nelson's method becomes inaccurate; in those cases finite-difference approximations of the derivatives are used as a fallback.

The parameters are normalized by their initial values so that the Jacobian columns have comparable magnitudes. At each iteration the parameter increment Δp solves

(JᵀJ + μ I) Δp = −Jᵀ r,

where r is the residual vector and μ the damping factor, increased when J fails to decrease and reduced otherwise. Convergence is declared when the relative variation of J, the norm of Δp, or the gradient norm falls below prescribed tolerances, or when a maximum number of iterations is reached.

**Robustness issues**

Several measures address the robustness of the procedure.

*Parameter identifiability.* The singular values of the normalized Jacobian are inspected before the optimization to detect parameters to which the selected modes are insensitive or whose effects are nearly collinear. Such parameters are grouped, fixed, or regularized, since otherwise the problem is ill-posed and solutions depend on the starting point.

*Local minima.* Since J is non-convex, the algorithm is launched from several initial vectors sampled within the bounds (e.g., by Latin hypercube sampling), and the solution with the lowest J is retained. Dispersion of the converged parameters among runs provides a practical indication of uniqueness.

*Number of data versus unknowns.* The number of experimental quantities (frequencies and MAC values) should exceed the number of parameters. When this is not satisfied, a Tikhonov-type penalty term, α‖(p − p₀)/p₀‖², is added to J to keep the solution close to the initial estimate p₀.

*Mesh dependence.* Updated parameters are meaningful only for the mesh used, so a convergence check on the first modal frequencies is performed on successively refined meshes before updating.

**Validation on a simple case**

The procedure was first verified on a benchmark structure, a masonry-like portal frame discretized with solid elements and subdivided into regions with different Young's moduli. Synthetic "experimental" frequencies and mode shapes were generated from a reference parameter set, optionally corrupted with Gaussian noise (e.g., 1% on frequencies and 3% on mode components), and the algorithm was started from perturbed parameters. Accuracy was assessed by the error between recovered and reference parameters, and by the number of iterations needed for convergence.

**Application to historical structures**

The procedure was then applied to two structures in Tuscany. For the Clock Tower in Lucca, the three-dimensional model was built from geometric surveys and material investigations, and the unknowns were the Young's moduli of the main masonry portions together with the stiffness of the connection with adjacent buildings. The reference modal data came from ambient vibration tests [5]. For the Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano, the free parameters were the elastic moduli of the arches, piers, spandrel walls, and fill, with the experimental frequencies and mode shapes identified from dynamic monitoring. In both cases, initial parameters were assigned from the literature and in-situ tests, the weights were set to prioritize frequencies of well-identified modes, and the quality of the updated models was evaluated through the frequency errors and MAC values before and after updating.

**Simple case study: validation of the procedure**

The updating procedure was first tested on a cantilever masonry wall discretized with 8-node hexahedral elements. Reference "experimental" frequencies were generated numerically from a model with known Young's modulus values in two material zones (E₁ = 2.0 GPa, E₂ = 4.0 GPa). The updating was then started from deliberately perturbed values (E₁ = 3.5 GPa, E₂ = 1.5 GPa). The objective function combined the relative frequency residuals with a term based on the Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) between numerical and reference mode shapes [1,2]. Using the first five modes, the procedure converged in seven iterations and recovered both parameters to within 0.3% of the target values. The final frequency errors were below 0.1%, and the diagonal MAC values exceeded 0.999.

Robustness was examined by varying the starting point over a range of ±50% of the target values. Convergence to the correct minimum was obtained in all cases where the initial mode ordering matched the reference ordering. When the starting values caused two modes to swap order, the purely frequency-based pairing produced spurious residuals and convergence to a local minimum. Pairing modes through the MAC matrix rather than by ordinal number removed this problem and restored convergence from all starting points. When Gaussian noise (standard deviation 2%) was added to the reference frequencies, the identified moduli deviated by at most 4%. The parameters were therefore only mildly sensitive to measurement uncertainty. Including more modes than free parameters reduced this scatter, consistent with the better conditioning of an overdetermined problem [3].

**Clock Tower in Lucca**

The Clock Tower model comprised about 30,000 elements, with the masonry assumed to be a homogeneous, isotropic material. Ambient vibration tests had identified the first eight modes, in the range 1.0–6.5 Hz [4]. The free parameters were the Young's moduli of three macro-regions (the lower shaft, the upper shaft and the belfry) and an elastic stiffness for the connection with the adjacent buildings.

Before updating, the numerical frequencies were on average 14% higher than the experimental ones, with a maximum error of 22% for the second torsional mode. After updating, the mean error fell to 2.1% and the maximum to 4.3%. The MAC values for the first four modes (two bending modes per direction) increased from 0.82–0.93 to above 0.97. The torsional and higher-order modes improved less, with MAC values of about 0.90. This is attributable to the limited number of measured points and to the simplified geometry of the belfry.

The updated Young's moduli were 1.6 GPa for the lower shaft, 2.3 GPa for the upper shaft and 1.2 GPa for the belfry. These values lie within the ranges reported in the literature for historical brick masonry, and the ordering reflects the better state of preservation of the lower portions. The stiffness of the connection with neighbouring buildings had a marked effect on the second bending mode, and its inclusion reduced the frequency error of that mode from 9% to below 2%. A sensitivity analysis showed that the first two frequencies depended mainly on the moduli of the lower shaft, whereas the belfry modulus influenced only the higher modes. The belfry modulus was therefore identified with a larger uncertainty.

**Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano**

The Maddalena bridge is a multi-span masonry arch bridge with a markedly asymmetric profile. The finite-element model included the arches, piers, spandrel walls and infill. Experimental data consisted of the first six modes identified from ambient vibration measurements, between approximately 2 and 8 Hz [5]. The free parameters were the Young's moduli of the arches, the piers and the infill, grouped according to the three zones.

The initial model overestimated the frequencies by 8–19%. The updating converged in 12 iterations. The final errors were below 3% for all six modes, and the MAC values were above 0.93 for every mode, against a minimum of 0.71 before updating. The estimated moduli were 3.8 GPa for the arches, 5.1 GPa for the piers and 0.9 GPa for the infill. The low infill stiffness is consistent with its loose, heterogeneous nature, which contributes mass but little stiffness.

The problem proved more ill-conditioned than in the previous cases. The sensitivity matrix showed that the arch and infill moduli influenced the same modes in a similar way, giving a strong correlation between the two parameters. Different starting points therefore led to slightly different final sets, with the arch modulus varying by about ±8% and the infill modulus by about ±15% at practically equal objective values. Introducing bounds on the parameters, based on engineering judgement, and a regularization term penalizing deviations from the initial estimates reduced this non-uniqueness and led to consistent solutions from all starting points tested. The objective function value increased by less than 3% as a result of the regularization.

**Computational aspects and general remarks**

The computational cost was dominated by the repeated eigenvalue analyses. On a standard workstation, one updating iteration required about 40 s for the cantilever, 18 min for the tower and 25 min for the bridge. Evaluating the sensitivities by finite differences was acceptable for the small number of parameters used here, but the cost grows linearly with that number.

Across the three cases, the procedure reduced the mean frequency error from 8–14% to 2–3% and improved the mode shape correlation. The results also show that the quality of the updated model depends on the choice of parameters, on the number of identified modes and on reliable mode pairing, in addition to the optimization algorithm.

**Discussion**

The results show that the updating procedure implemented in NOSA-ITACA can reconcile numerical and experimental modal data for masonry structures of very different geometry and complexity. In the simple case study, where the target parameters were known a priori, the algorithm recovered the reference values with small residuals. This confirms that the formulation and its implementation are consistent. The two historical structures, which are more representative of real applications, tested the method under the uncertainties typical of heritage buildings: incomplete knowledge of material properties, internal morphology and boundary conditions, and a limited number of identified modes.

*Robustness and sensitivity.* The robustness analysis showed that the quality of the outcome depends on three factors: the choice of free parameters, the initial guess, and the pairing of numerical and experimental modes. Parameters to which the selected frequencies are weakly sensitive, such as the stiffness of poorly constrained portions of the structure, are only loosely identified. Updating them leads to ill-conditioning and to values that may compensate one another without any physical significance. This is a well-known limitation of sensitivity-based updating [1,2]. For this reason, we recommend restricting the parameter set to a small number of groups, each defined by structural or constructional criteria (e.g., distinct masonry typologies, different construction phases, or soil-structure interaction), rather than allowing unconstrained variation at element level. Imposing physically plausible bounds on the parameters improved convergence and prevented unrealistic solutions. Dependence on the starting point was mitigated by a preliminary manual calibration, which is common practice in the modelling of historic masonry [3].

Mode pairing is a further critical point. When modes are closely spaced or their order changes during the iterations, frequency-based residuals alone can drive the procedure toward the wrong local minimum. Including the Modal Assurance Criterion in the objective function reduced this risk, but it did not remove it, particularly when experimental mode shapes are identified from sparse sensor layouts. Careful design of the monitoring setup and judicious selection of the modes to be matched therefore remain essential preconditions.

*Interpretation of the case studies.* For the Clock Tower, the updated model improved the match of the first frequencies and mode shapes. The adjusted elastic moduli lie within ranges reported in the literature for comparable masonry [4], although they are best interpreted as effective, homogenised values. For the Maddalena bridge, the geometric and material complexity of the arches, spandrels, fill and piers makes a unique identification unlikely. Several parameter combinations produced comparable fits, so the updated values should be regarded as one admissible set rather than as a measurement of the true properties. This non-uniqueness is intrinsic to inverse problems based on a limited set of modal data. It also implies that the model, however well calibrated, should be used with awareness of the uncertainty that remains.

*Limitations.* Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the procedure operates in the linear elastic range, whereas masonry behaviour under strong actions is nonlinear and damage-sensitive. Modal data from ambient vibration involve very small strain amplitudes, so the updated stiffness may overestimate that available under seismic loading, because cracks are closed and the material is not damaged. Second, model-form errors, such as simplified geometry, assumed boundary conditions, or neglected non-structural masses, cannot be corrected by parameter tuning and may be absorbed by the updated parameters, distorting their meaning. Third, experimental frequencies and mode shapes carry identification uncertainty and are sensitive to environmental conditions, notably temperature and humidity [5]. These effects were not explicitly modelled, and the procedure is deterministic, providing point estimates without confidence intervals.

**Conclusions**

A model updating procedure for the finite-element code NOSA-ITACA has been presented and validated, with the aim of making the calibration of masonry models more systematic, objective and reproducible than purely manual tuning. The main conclusions are as follows.

1. The procedure is able to identify uncertain model parameters by minimising the discrepancy between numerical and experimental modal quantities, and it recovers known parameters in a controlled test.
2. Its reliability depends on parameterisation, bounds, initial values and correct mode pairing. A parsimonious, physically motivated set of parameters together with a combined frequency and mode-shape objective is recommended.
3. On real structures, the procedure yields models that reproduce the measured dynamic behaviour more closely, but the identified parameters should be seen as effective values, not unique ones, owing to non-uniqueness and model-form uncertainty.
4. Integration within NOSA-ITACA lets practitioners proceed directly from modal identification to a calibrated model that can then be used for static, dynamic and seismic assessments of heritage structures.

Future work will pursue several directions. A probabilistic or Bayesian extension would quantify parameter uncertainty and support risk-informed decisions [6]. Including additional data, such as static measurements, would reduce non-uniqueness. Accounting for environmental effects on the identified frequencies would improve the reliability of the target data. Finally, extending the approach to nonlinear models and to damage detection through repeated updating over time would enable the procedure to support long-term structural health monitoring of historical constructions.

The anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) has long been implicated in human memory. Damage to the thalamus, including the ATN and the mammillothalamic tract that connects it to the mammillary bodies, produces profound anterograde amnesia, as seen in Korsakoff's syndrome and in focal thalamic infarcts. The ATN is embedded in an extended hippocampal-diencephalic-cingulate network, the circuit of Papez, receiving input from the hippocampal formation via the fornix and the mammillary bodies, and projecting to the cingulate and prefrontal cortices and back to the hippocampal formation. Anatomically, it is therefore well placed to participate in the interactions between medial temporal and neocortical regions that underlie the formation of episodic memories. Nevertheless, the ATN has traditionally been regarded as a relay, passing information between structures, and direct electrophysiological evidence of what it does during human memory formation has been scarce.

We recently addressed this gap by recording local field potentials from the ATN in patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who had electrodes implanted for deep brain stimulation, while they performed a visual memory encoding task (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014). Theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the ATN was stronger during successful than unsuccessful encoding, as determined by subsequent recall. The presence of gamma oscillations suggested that the ATN carries out local processing relevant to memory, rather than merely relaying signals from elsewhere. That finding raised a further question: what mechanism organizes this activity within the ATN so that memory formation succeeds?

Oscillations in the theta frequency range are central to current accounts of memory. In rodents, hippocampal theta is prominent during exploration and learning, and the phase of theta at which stimulation is delivered determines whether long-term potentiation or depression is induced. Stimulation at the peak of theta tends to produce potentiation, whereas stimulation at the trough does not. In humans, theta power and theta synchrony between medial temporal and neocortical regions increase during successful encoding, and the timing of spiking relative to theta phase predicts memory performance. These observations are consistent with the view that theta provides temporal windows within which neuronal populations can be coordinated, allowing spike-timing-dependent plasticity to strengthen the appropriate connections.

Phase alignment is a key concept here. For oscillations to coordinate neural activity, their phase must be consistent across events. Following a stimulus, an ongoing rhythm may be reset or an evoked response may be generated, so that phases across trials become aligned at particular latencies. Such alignment, measured as intertrial phase coherence, means that incoming information arrives at a consistent point in the cycle, and that the excitability of the receiving neurons is consistently matched to the input. It has been proposed that synchronization of neuronal firing in the theta rhythm is a prerequisite for synaptic plasticity, since coincident presynaptic and postsynaptic activity is required to induce long-term changes. Phase alignment across trials upon presentation of to-be-remembered items could therefore be a necessary condition for encoding. Evidence for this has come from scalp EEG and from cortical and hippocampal recordings, where greater theta phase alignment after stimulus presentation predicts later recall or recognition. Whether the same applies in the thalamus, and the ATN in particular, has not been tested.

CFC is also thought to support memory, with the phase of a slower rhythm organizing the amplitude of faster oscillations. Theta-gamma coupling is proposed to allow multiple items, each represented in a gamma cycle, to be sequenced within a theta cycle, and it has been reported in the hippocampus and neocortex during memory tasks. The relation between theta phase alignment and CFC is plausible but untested. If theta phase is consistent across trials, then the gamma amplitude modulated by it will also be consistently timed. Phase alignment may thus be a precondition for CFC, which in turn could reflect the local processing that supports encoding. Alternatively, the two measures may be independent, reflecting distinct mechanisms. Distinguishing between these possibilities would clarify how the ATN contributes to memory formation.

Here we analyzed further the ATN recordings from our previous study to test two hypotheses. First, we hypothesized that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be greater during successful than unsuccessful memory encoding, as would be expected if it were necessary for synaptic plasticity. We assessed this using intertrial phase coherence following stimulus presentation, comparing items that were subsequently remembered with those that were forgotten, and examining the frequency range and the time course in which any difference arose. Second, we hypothesized that the degree of theta phase alignment would be related to the strength of theta-gamma CFC, such that the two phenomena would be linked in the same encoding process. We therefore tested for a correlation between phase alignment and coupling across participants and conditions.

Confirmation of these hypotheses would support an active role for the ATN in memory formation, in which the nucleus does not simply relay hippocampal output but engages in oscillatory processing, with theta phase alignment and its coupling to gamma activity contributing to successful encoding. This would also be of clinical relevance, since the ATN is a target for deep brain stimulation in epilepsy and has been proposed as a target for modulating memory.

Participants and recordings

Data were reanalyzed from the patients included in our previous report (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014). Participants were patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy or other neurological indications who had been implanted with deep brain stimulation electrodes in the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN), with simultaneous scalp EEG recorded during the experimental session. All participants gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Electrode positions were verified with postoperative imaging co-registered to preoperative MRI. Local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded from the contacts of the externalized electrodes in the days after implantation, before the implantable pulse generator was connected. Signals were recorded with a bipolar montage between adjacent contacts, amplified, and digitized at a sampling rate sufficient to resolve gamma activity. Scalp EEG was recorded concurrently from standard 10–20 positions, referenced to linked mastoids.

Task

Participants performed a verbal-visual paired-associate style encoding task followed by a recognition test. During encoding, participants viewed a series of stimuli (words presented with a fixation period preceding each item) and were instructed to memorize them for later testing. After a retention interval, they were presented with studied and new items and indicated whether each was old or new, with confidence rating where applicable. Encoding trials were classified retrospectively according to subsequent performance: trials in which the item was later correctly recognized were labeled successful encoding (remembered), and trials in which the item was later missed were labeled unsuccessful encoding (forgotten). Only participants with sufficient numbers of trials in both categories were included. Trial numbers were equated between conditions by random subsampling in each participant for all analyses sensitive to trial count, including phase-based measures, because such measures are biased by the number of trials.

Preprocessing

Data were high-pass filtered, notch filtered at line frequency, and segmented into epochs around stimulus onset including a baseline period. Epochs containing artifacts, identified by visual inspection and amplitude thresholds, were excluded. Epochs were extracted with sufficient padding to avoid edge effects in time-frequency decomposition.

Time-frequency decomposition and phase alignment

Time-frequency representations were computed for each epoch using complex Morlet wavelets, with the number of cycles chosen to balance temporal and spectral resolution (for example, three cycles at low frequencies, increasing with frequency). Instantaneous phase was extracted from the complex wavelet coefficients at each time and frequency point. Phase alignment across trials was quantified using the inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), the length of the mean resultant vector of unit phase vectors across trials:

ITPC(f,t) = |N⁻¹ Σ exp(iφ_n(f,t))|,

where N is the number of trials and φ_n the phase on trial n. ITPC was calculated separately for subsequently remembered and forgotten trials in each participant and ATN contact. Because ITPC depends on trial number, trial counts were equalized and subsampling was repeated many times, with the results averaged. The theta range (approximately 3–8 Hz) and a post-stimulus window encompassing the period in which theta-gamma coupling was previously found were examined. Differences in ITPC between remembered and forgotten trials were assessed across participants.

Cross-frequency coupling

Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling had been identified previously in the ATN. Here, coupling was quantified with a modulation index: the phase of the low-frequency signal and the amplitude envelope of the high-frequency signal were obtained from band-pass filtered, Hilbert-transformed or wavelet-derived signals. Gamma amplitude was binned by theta phase, and the modulation index was computed as the Kullback–Leibler divergence of the resulting amplitude distribution from a uniform distribution, normalized by log of the number of bins. Coupling was calculated for the same time windows and conditions as the ITPC analysis, with equalized trial counts. Coupling strength was normalized against surrogate data generated by shifting the amplitude time series relative to the phase series, yielding z-scored values.

Relationship between phase alignment and coupling

To test whether theta phase alignment related to cross-frequency coupling, we correlated ITPC in the theta band with the coupling measure across participants and conditions.
