Spearman rank correlations were used to reduce sensitivity to outliers, and correlations were calculated for remembered and forgotten trials separately and for the difference between them. To determine whether any relationship was specific to the frequencies of interest, the correlation was also computed across a range of phase and amplitude frequencies.

Statistical analysis

Comparisons between remembered and forgotten conditions used paired nonparametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank) or paired t tests when normality was satisfied. For time-frequency maps, multiple comparisons were handled by nonparametric cluster-based permutation testing: condition labels were randomly permuted many times, clusters of adjacent significant time-frequency points were identified in each permutation, and the maximal cluster statistic formed the null distribution against which observed clusters were compared. Phase distributions were additionally tested for non-uniformity with the Rayleigh test, and ITPC values were compared with surrogate distributions obtained by randomizing phase across trials. Significance was set at p < 0.05, two-tailed. Results are reported as mean ± standard error unless otherwise stated.

Analyses were performed in MATLAB using custom scripts and the FieldTrip toolbox.

We analyzed local field potentials recorded from the ATN in six patients with deep brain stimulation electrodes implanted for treatment of pharmacoresistant epilepsy, while they performed a visual verbal-memory encoding task. Participants viewed word pairs or images and were later tested on recognition. Trials were sorted into subsequently remembered and subsequently forgotten items. Participants remembered on average a substantial proportion of items, giving enough trials in both conditions for comparison (remembered trials: mean ± SD 41 ± 9; forgotten trials: 33 ± 8). Trial numbers were equated by random subsampling in all subsequent analyses.

**Theta phase alignment is greater during successful encoding**

We first quantified phase alignment across trials using the inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), computed from wavelet-decomposed signals between 1 and 20 Hz at each time point after stimulus onset. In both conditions, stimulus presentation was followed by an increase in ITPC in the low-frequency range, reflecting an evoked response. ITPC in the theta range (4–8 Hz) was higher for subsequently remembered than for subsequently forgotten items. Cluster-based permutation testing across time and frequency revealed a significant cluster in the theta band beginning approximately 200 ms after stimulus onset and lasting until roughly 700 ms (cluster p < 0.05, corrected). The peak difference was at approximately 5 Hz. No significant differences were found in the alpha or beta bands after correction for multiple comparisons.

The difference was evident at the group level and was present in the majority of individual patients, with the direction of the effect consistent across participants. A sign-based test across patients supported the consistency of the effect, although the small sample limits the power of such analyses.

**Phase alignment is not explained by power differences**

Because ITPC can be influenced by signal amplitude, we tested whether the effect reflected differences in theta power. Theta power did not differ significantly between remembered and forgotten trials in the same time window. In addition, we computed ITPC after equating trial counts and, separately, after normalizing the amplitude of the signal so that each trial contributed equally; the memory effect on theta ITPC remained. We also verified that the effect was not attributable to a difference in the number of trials by repeating the subsampling 500 times, with the difference remaining significant in the large majority of iterations. These control analyses indicate that the effect reflects a consistency of phase across trials rather than a change in amplitude.

**Phase alignment reflects more than an evoked potential**

To determine whether the increased theta ITPC merely reflected a stimulus-locked evoked potential, we compared the event-related potentials in the two conditions and then subtracted the averaged evoked response from single trials before recomputing ITPC. Event-related potential amplitudes did not differ significantly between conditions. After removal of the evoked component, theta ITPC remained greater for remembered items, though reduced in magnitude, suggesting that the phase alignment was not solely a result of an additive evoked response.

**Theta-gamma coupling in the ATN**

In our previous analysis, theta-gamma CFC during encoding distinguished remembered from forgotten items (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014). We reproduced this finding in the present analysis using the modulation index, which quantifies the nonuniformity of gamma amplitude distribution across theta phase. Coupling between theta phase (around 5 Hz) and gamma amplitude was stronger during successful than unsuccessful encoding, with the strongest coupling for gamma frequencies in the range of approximately 50–80 Hz. Gamma amplitude tended to peak at a consistent theta phase across participants.

**Phase alignment correlates with cross-frequency coupling**

We next asked whether theta phase alignment and theta-gamma coupling were related. We computed, for each patient and condition, the theta ITPC in the significant time window and the corresponding modulation index. Across patients and conditions, these measures were positively correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.6, p < 0.05). Within participants, trials were divided into those with higher and lower theta phase alignment, estimated by the proximity of each trial's theta phase to the mean phase. Coupling was stronger in the group of trials with phase closer to the mean phase, indicating that phase consistency was associated with stronger modulation of gamma amplitude by theta phase.

To assess the specificity of this relationship, we examined whether the correlation held for other frequency bands. ITPC in the alpha and beta ranges was not significantly correlated with theta-gamma coupling. Moreover, the relationship was not seen when the theta ITPC from a baseline period preceding stimulus onset was used, indicating that the association was specific to the encoding period.

**Temporal relationship**

Examining the time course, the increase in theta phase alignment preceded the peak in theta-gamma coupling. Theta ITPC differences between remembered and forgotten items emerged first, followed by the coupling effect, which was maximal in the later part of the encoding window. This ordering is consistent with the possibility that phase alignment provides a temporal framework for subsequent coupling of gamma activity, although the analysis cannot establish causality.

**Summary**

Together, these results show that, in the human ATN, theta phase alignment following stimulus presentation was greater when items were subsequently remembered, that this effect could not be attributed to differences in power or to a simple evoked response, and that the degree of alignment was related to the strength of theta-gamma coupling.

Our analysis of intrathalamic recordings from patients with deep brain stimulation electrodes in the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) shows that theta phase alignment across trials was greater during successful than unsuccessful memory encoding, and that the strength of this alignment correlated with theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC). Together with our earlier finding that CFC predicted successful encoding, these results suggest that the ATN takes an active part in memory formation rather than serving only as a passive relay between the mammillary bodies and the hippocampal-cortical network.

**Theta phase alignment and memory encoding**

Phase alignment of oscillations is thought to be a prerequisite for synaptic plasticity. Long-term potentiation is induced most effectively when afferent input arrives at a particular phase of the ongoing theta rhythm, and the phase of theta at which stimulation occurs determines whether potentiation or depression results. An increase in phase consistency following stimulus onset implies that the relevant input arrives at a consistent phase of the local oscillation, which would favor plasticity in thalamic circuits or in their targets. Our finding that this alignment was stronger for subsequently remembered items fits this account, and parallels reports of greater theta phase locking during successful encoding in the hippocampus and neocortex. Phase alignment may reflect a phase reset triggered by the stimulus, an evoked response, or both. We cannot fully distinguish these with the present data, though the effect's restriction to the theta band and its relation to memory outcome argue against a nonspecific response to stimulus onset, since the same stimuli were presented in both conditions.

**Relation to cross-frequency coupling**

The correlation between theta phase alignment and theta-gamma CFC is important because the two measures address different aspects of the same process. Phase alignment ensures that theta activity is temporally organized across trials, providing a consistent reference frame. Gamma amplitude nested within particular theta phases could then reflect local processing, such as the organization of information into discrete packets within a theta cycle. Without consistent theta phase, such nesting would be unlikely to produce an organized, reproducible pattern. Our results are consistent with theta alignment being a precondition for effective CFC, although the correlational design does not establish a causal direction. It is also possible that local gamma generation shapes theta phase, or that both depend on a common driver.

**An active role for the ATN**

The involvement of gamma activity in our earlier study suggested local processing in the ATN. Phase alignment adds to this by showing that ATN activity is temporally structured in a manner associated with plasticity. This supports models in which the ATN is a node in the extended hippocampal system, with the Papez circuit and its connections to the hippocampus, retrosplenial and prefrontal cortices supporting memory. Lesions of the ATN, as in diencephalic amnesia, impair memory, and the thalamus may coordinate oscillatory activity across these regions. Theta alignment in the ATN could synchronize its interactions with the hippocampus and cortex, enabling information transfer at appropriate phases. Because we recorded only from the thalamus, we cannot assess interregional synchronization directly; simultaneous recordings, for example with scalp EEG or intracranial hippocampal electrodes, would be needed to test whether thalamic phase alignment accompanies coherence with these regions and whether it leads or follows them.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be noted. The patients had epilepsy and were studied via electrodes implanted for therapeutic stimulation, and so pathological activity or medication could influence oscillations, although the within-subject comparison of remembered and forgotten items mitigates this concern. The sample was small, which limits generalization and the power to detect subtler effects. Recordings were made from electrode contacts that may integrate activity over a volume including neighboring structures, so contributions from adjacent tissue or volume conduction cannot be excluded entirely, though the bipolar derivations reduce this risk. Finally, measures of phase alignment are influenced by evoked power, and so we cannot rule out that some of the effect reflects amplitude changes in event-related potentials.

**Implications and future directions**

If theta phase alignment in the ATN is important for memory formation, then interventions that modulate thalamic oscillations might influence memory. ATN deep brain stimulation is used in epilepsy and has been explored for memory disorders, and stimulation timed to the phase of ongoing theta, or delivered at theta frequency, could be tested for effects on encoding. Animal work has already indicated that ATN stimulation can affect hippocampal plasticity and memory performance, with outcomes dependent on the stimulation frequency. Closed-loop approaches that target specific phases could exploit the phase-dependence of plasticity. Studies that combine thalamic recordings with other regions would also clarify the directionality of interactions, and tasks that separate encoding of different material types would test whether the effect is general or specific.

**Conclusion**

Theta phase alignment in the human ATN is greater during successful than unsuccessful memory encoding and is correlated with theta-gamma coupling. These findings extend our earlier observations and support an active processing role of the ATN in memory formation, in which temporally organized theta activity provides conditions for local processing and plasticity within the wider memory network.

The Middle Stone Age (MSA) of sub-Saharan Africa spans roughly 300,000 to 30,000 years ago and coincides with the emergence and dispersal of anatomically modern Homo sapiens. Fossil evidence for this interval is geographically uneven. Cranial and postcranial remains attributed to early members of our species come from a limited number of sites, including Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia, Klasies River Mouth, Border Cave, and Die Kelders in South Africa, and Ngaloba (Laetoli) in Tanzania. Between the well-sampled Ethiopian and South African sequences lies a vast area of eastern and south-central Africa from which few human fossils of MSA age are known. This gap limits our ability to evaluate regional patterns of morphological variation, population structure, and continuity among Late Pleistocene Africans.

Teeth are an important part of this record. Enamel and dentine preserve well, and dental crowns retain information on size, shape, and accessory cusp and ridge expression that is under strong genetic control. Dental metrics and non-metric traits have been widely used to assess biological affinities among recent and fossil populations. Comparative samples exist for Pleistocene and Holocene Africans, and for non-African groups, permitting tests of whether isolated teeth fall within the range of modern humans or show archaic features. Teeth also record behavior. Wear patterns, fractures, and scratches can show how the dentition was used for food processing and for non-dietary tasks, such as holding or softening materials, a practice documented in Neanderthals and in many recent hunter-gatherers.

The relationship between eastern and southern African hunter-gatherers has long been debated. Linguistic, genetic, and skeletal studies have suggested that the click-speaking Khoisan peoples of southern Africa, and the Hadza and Sandawe of Tanzania, may share deep ancestry or may reflect an earlier, wider distribution of related populations. Genetic analyses indicate that the ancestors of present-day Khoisan populations diverged early from other human lineages, and that southern and eastern African foragers once formed part of a more extensive network of populations. Skeletal and dental material from the intervening region of Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe could help test such ideas, but Late Pleistocene human remains from these areas are scarce. Later Stone Age (LSA) skeletons from Kisese II, Gamble's Cave, Hora 1, and Matupi Cave have been compared with recent San, and some show similarities, yet earlier material is almost absent.

Tanzania has produced important Pleistocene fossils, notably the Laetoli Hominid 18 (Ngaloba) cranium and the Eyasi remains, but their dating and attribution are contested, and few have been recovered in secure archaeological context with associated MSA artifacts. The Iringa Region of the southern highlands is better known for its Stone Age archaeology. Surveys and excavations there, including at Mlambalasi and Magubike, have documented a long sequence of occupation from the MSA through the LSA, with evidence for changing technology, ornaments such as ostrich eggshell beads, and shifts in settlement and resource use. The Magubike rockshelter, a granite shelter on the margin of the Iringa uplands, was excavated in 2006 and yielded dense MSA deposits with abundant lithic artifacts and faunal remains. Within these deposits, six isolated human teeth were recovered.

Dating the Magubike sequence is not straightforward. Electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon determinations on associated land snail shells give varying results, probably reflecting the difficulties of dating carbonate in rockshelter settings, where recrystallization and exchange with groundwater can compromise ages. Radiocarbon ages near the limit of the method may also be affected by contamination with modern carbon. These problems mean that the age of the teeth must be treated cautiously, although a conservative minimum of about 45,000 years can be proposed. Even so, the teeth derive from a context lacking diagnostic LSA technology and thus add to a very small sample of Late Pleistocene human fossils from East Africa that are tied to archaeological deposits.

In this paper we describe the Magubike teeth and assess their taxonomic and population affinities. The assemblage consists of two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, and two premolars, all from the maxilla and all fully formed. Because no tooth is duplicated, the specimens may belong to a single individual, a possibility we evaluate using wear, size, and preservation. We examine post-depositional alteration that has affected some of the crowns and roots, and consider how it influences measurement and interpretation. We then compare crown dimensions and non-metric traits with published data for African and non-African samples, including recent and fossil modern humans and archaic hominins, to determine whether the teeth fit within the modern human range and whether they resemble particular regional groups, especially southern African San. Finally, we describe distinctive coarse scratches on the labial surfaces of the incisors, which differ from the fine striations typical of dietary microwear, and discuss what they imply about the habitual use of the front teeth as tools during this individual's life.

Excavations and Context

The Magubike rockshelter (approximately 7°45′S, 35°36′E) lies in granitic hills of the Iringa Region, southern Tanzania, at an elevation of roughly 1,600 m. The shelter was excavated in 2006 as part of a survey of Stone Age sites in the region. A 1 m × 1 m grid was laid out and excavated in 5 cm spits within natural stratigraphic units. All sediment was dry-sieved through 3 mm mesh, and finds were recorded in three dimensions when larger than 2 cm. Stratigraphic units were described in the field and in section drawings. The teeth were recovered from MSA layers containing flaked stone artifacts, ochre, faunal remains, and land snail shells (Achatina). Teeth were collected during sieving and sorting, and their locations were recorded by square and spit. The remains are curated at the National Museum of Tanzania, Dar es Salaam.

Dating

Two approaches were applied to Achatina shell fragments from the MSA layers. Radiocarbon samples were pretreated with acid washing and subjected to etching to remove outer carbonate, and the inner fraction was analyzed by accelerator mass spectrometry. Results were calibrated using the SHCal13 curve where finite ages were obtained, and samples near background were treated as minimum ages. Electron spin resonance (ESR) dating was undertaken on separate shell fragments. Equivalent doses were estimated from multiple-aliquot additive dose series, and dose rates were calculated from U, Th, and K measured in sediment samples, with cosmic dose contributions estimated from burial depth and shelter overhang. Because shell can behave as an open system, both early uptake and linear uptake models were considered. Discrepancies between methods were evaluated by comparing results across stratigraphic position, and the minimum age for the teeth was based on the most conservative finite result.

Sample and Preservation Assessment

The sample consists of six permanent maxillary teeth: two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, one third premolar (P3), and one fourth premolar (P4). Teeth were identified by crown and root morphology, wear facet position, and comparison with reference material. Side was determined where possible. Developmental stage was assessed by root completion and apical closure. Because no tooth type is duplicated and occlusal wear and size are broadly consistent, we evaluated whether the teeth might derive from one individual, though isolated recovery precludes confirmation. Surface condition was examined under a stereomicroscope at 10–40× to record cracking, root-surface erosion, enamel flaking, staining, and adhering matrix, in order to assess post-depositional alteration. Wear was scored using the Smith (1984) eight-stage system.

Metric Analysis

Mesiodistal (MD) and buccolingual/labiolingual (BL) crown diameters were taken with digital sliding calipers to 0.01 mm following Fiorenza et al. (2011) and Hillson (1996) protocols. Where interproximal wear was present, measurements were noted as minimum estimates. Crown module (mean of MD and BL) and crown area (MD × BL) were calculated. Each measurement was taken three times by one observer, and the mean was used; intraobserver error was assessed by technical error of measurement. Comparative data were compiled from the literature and from published datasets for Middle and Late Pleistocene and Holocene African samples (including early Homo sapiens from Jebel Irhoud, Skhul/Qafzeh, and Klasies River; Later Stone Age eastern and southern African foragers; recent San, other sub-Saharan groups), Neanderthals, and recent non-African populations. Magubike values were compared with comparative means and ranges, and standardized differences (z-scores relative to comparative sample means and standard deviations) were calculated. Because the sample is one individual at most per tooth type, formal inferential tests were limited; we report position within comparative ranges and, where sample sizes allowed, performed Mahalanobis-based and principal components analyses on the subset of variables available across samples.

Non-metric Traits

Crown and root morphology was scored using the Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System (Turner et al. 1991) and associated reference plaques. Traits scored on incisors included shoveling, double shoveling, labial convexity, tuberculum dentale, and interruption grooves. For the canine, we scored distal accessory ridge and mesial ridge expression; for premolars, we scored lingual cusp number, occlusal accessory ridges, and root number. Root form was examined directly and by radiograph when roots were intact. Each trait was scored twice at separate sessions, and discrepancies were resolved by a third scoring. Frequencies in comparative samples were taken from published sources, and the Magubike expressions were compared qualitatively, notably with San and other African groups, because individual scores cannot be tested against frequencies statistically.

Analysis of Labial Scratches

The labial surfaces of the three incisors were examined for linear marks distinct from dietary microwear. Surfaces were cleaned gently with ethanol-soaked cotton swabs and examined under a stereomicroscope at 20–60× and with a scanning electron microscope on high-resolution replicas made from polyvinylsiloxane and epoxy resin. For each scratch, we recorded location on the crown, orientation relative to the cervical margin, length, and width (measured on calibrated images using ImageJ). Scratches were classed as coarse if widths exceeded those typical of microwear striations (>~10 µm) and were compared qualitatively with published descriptions of anterior tooth-use marks on Neanderthal and recent human teeth. Marks were distinguished from taphonomic damage by their consistent orientation, wear-polished margins, and truncation by subsequent attrition, as opposed to sharp-edged, randomly oriented cracking. Frequency and orientation were compared among the three incisors to assess whether repeated activity over time was indicated.

Six isolated permanent maxillary teeth were recovered from MSA deposits (Layer 3) in Trench 1 at Magubike: right and left central incisors (I1), a lateral incisor (I2), a canine (C), a third premolar (P3), and a fourth premolar (P4). No tooth is duplicated, and all are fully formed with closed or nearly closed apices. Their size, wear, and color are consistent with a single adult individual, though this cannot be demonstrated conclusively. Surface preservation varies. Several teeth show cracking of the enamel, patchy root surface erosion, and manganese-like staining, which indicates some post-depositional alteration. The crown morphology of all six teeth is nonetheless sufficiently preserved for metric and non-metric analysis.

**Dental wear and condition.** Occlusal and incisal wear is moderate. The incisors show flattened incisal edges with small areas of exposed dentine (Smith stage 3-4). The canine and premolars show wear facets with limited dentine exposure. No carious lesions were observed. Slight calculus remains on the lingual cervical area of the canine. Wear is relatively even across the anterior teeth, and there is no sign of pathological enamel hypoplasia.

**Metric comparisons.** Mesiodistal (MD) and buccolingual (BL) crown diameters are given in Table 1. The central incisors are small to moderate in size, with MD diameters falling within the range of recent African and Holocene southern African samples and below the means for Neanderthals and most Middle Pleistocene hominins. The lateral incisor is likewise modest in size. The canine is small relative to the Neanderthal and early Homo sapiens (Skhul/Qafzeh) means, with BL breadth falling close to the San mean. The premolars are narrow BL, and their crown modules (MD × BL) lie within one standard deviation of recent sub-Saharan African and San means. In principal component analysis of crown diameters, Magubike plots within the range of anatomically modern humans and well apart from Neanderthals. Among modern groups it falls closest to southern African San and Later Stone Age foragers, though the distance to other sub-Saharan samples is small and the ranges overlap substantially. Because only one individual is probably represented, and because wear reduces MD values, these results are treated as indicative only.

**Non-metric traits.** The central incisors show weak to moderate labial convexity, and shoveling is present at a moderate grade (ASUDAS grade 2-3). Marginal ridges are present, and a lingual tubercle is weakly expressed (grade 1-2). Neither incisor shows a double-shoveled pattern. Interruption grooves are absent. The lateral incisor has weak shoveling and a small lingual tubercle. The canine has a modest distal accessory ridge and a weak lingual tubercle, without strong mesial ridge development. The third premolar has a single prominent buccal cusp and a weak lingual cusp, a nearly symmetric occlusal outline, and a simple transverse crest. The fourth premolar has well-developed buccal and lingual cusps and a mesial and distal marginal ridge, with no accessory cusps. Roots are single in all teeth except P3, which has a bifurcated apical third, a condition that occurs in low frequencies in recent African populations. Taurodontism is not seen. Overall, the crown features are those of anatomically modern Homo sapiens and lack the strong lingual crown relief, pronounced labial convexity, and marked basal tubercles characteristic of Neanderthals. Moderate shoveling and weak tubercles resemble San and other sub-Saharan patterns more than they do the high-frequency shoveling of Asian samples.

**Root morphology.** Root length is moderate, and the roots of the incisors are slightly compressed MD. The canine root is long and robust compared with the crown, a proportion which is within modern human variation. Root surfaces show cementum loss in places, so root measurements were not included in comparative analysis.

**Labial scratches on incisors.** All three incisors bear distinct linear scratches on the labial crown surface, which are absent from the canine and premolars. On the central incisors, scratches are numerous (approximately 8-15 per tooth), running mainly obliquely from incisal-distal toward cervical-mesial. Individual scratches are 20-100 µm wide and up to about 2 mm long, which makes them much coarser than the fine microwear striations on the incisal and occlusal facets (generally <5 µm). Some scratches cross one another at acute angles, and some terminate at the incisal margin where small enamel chips occur. The lateral incisor has fewer scratches (about 6) with a similar orientation. Under SEM, the scratch floors are smooth and slightly rounded, with no evidence of the angular edges and sediment-abrasion pitting associated with post-depositional trampling. Moreover, the scratches do not extend onto cracked or eroded enamel and are unrelated to the staining pattern. This argues against a taphonomic origin. The consistent orientation across the three adjacent teeth suggests repeated, similar actions, probably a material held in the hand and pulled across the front teeth, or a tool drawn against the teeth. The scratches are present on teeth with both low and moderate wear, so the behavior probably continued over a long period of the individual's life.

**Age.** ESR dates on snail shell and radiocarbon determinations from associated layers gave inconsistent results. The radiocarbon ages cluster near the limit of the method, while ESR estimates are considerably older and show large uncertainties. Hence only a conservative minimum age of about 45,000 years is proposed for the teeth.

The Magubike teeth add to a small but growing sample of Middle Stone Age human remains from eastern Africa. Their crown morphology and dimensions fall within the range of anatomically modern Homo sapiens, and they lack the features that characterize archaic hominins and Neanderthals, such as pronounced shoveling combined with marked labial convexity, strong basal tubercles, or taurodont-related enlargement of the crown. The assemblage is limited to six maxillary teeth, and the possibility that they derive from a single individual cannot be proven, but the absence of duplicated tooth positions, the uniform advanced developmental stage, and comparable wear are consistent with that interpretation. We therefore treat the sample cautiously, as a probable individual rather than a population, and we avoid drawing strong inferences about variation within the group to which this person belonged.

The comparative results suggest affinities with recent and Holocene southern African foragers. Several of the characteristics, including relatively small crown dimensions, particular incisor shoveling and canine and premolar morphology, are shared with San samples. These resemblances are intriguing in light of long-standing debates about the relationship between eastern and southern African hunter-gatherers. Genetic studies have suggested that the ancestors of modern Khoisan-speaking groups once occupied a wider geographic range, and that populations in eastern Africa, such as the Hadza and Sandawe, may share deep ancestry with them. Dental similarity at Magubike could be read as supporting such a broader distribution of San-like populations in the past. However, there are important caveats. Dental traits are known to have limited resolving power for population history, many of the features concerned are common in sub-Saharan African groups in general, and small, generalized teeth may be a plesiomorphic condition for modern humans rather than a marker of specific descent. Moreover, our comparative samples are uneven, and the Magubike teeth show post-depositional alteration that may affect measurements and the scoring of fine traits such as enamel extensions or wear-sensitive ridges. The resemblance should therefore be regarded as a hypothesis to be tested with additional fossil material and, if preservation permits, ancient DNA, rather than as evidence of direct continuity.

The most distinctive observation is the presence of coarse scratches on the labial surfaces of the three incisors. These marks are much larger than the fine striations produced by chewing food and grit, and their orientation and distribution suggest a non-masticatory origin. The most plausible explanation is that the front teeth were used as a third hand, for example to grip, stretch or hold materials such as hide, plant fibers, or sinew while a stone tool was used to cut or scrape them. Similar scratches have been documented on Neanderthal and later Pleistocene and Holocene teeth, and the pattern here indicates that the behavior was not restricted to any single hominin group. Because the individual had fully developed teeth and the scratches occur on all three incisors, the activity was probably repeated regularly over a considerable portion of life, rather than being the result of an isolated event. Whether it reflects craft production, food processing, or another task cannot be determined from the teeth alone. Experimental work, three-dimensional surface analysis, and comparison with ethnographic cases of dental tool use would help narrow the possibilities. We also cannot exclude that the individual was part of a division of labor in which particular people carried out specific tasks, although a single individual provides no basis for testing this.

The chronology of the teeth remains the main limitation. ESR and radiocarbon determinations on associated snail shells give inconsistent results, which may reflect open-system behavior, contamination by younger carbon, or mixing in the rockshelter sediments. Given the stratigraphic association with MSA artifacts and the minimum radiocarbon constraints, we propose a conservative minimum age of 45,000 years. The true age may be considerably older, and the evident post-depositional alteration of the teeth underscores the need to understand site formation processes. Independent dating, such as luminescence of the sediments or direct dating of the teeth, would be valuable, as would further analysis of the stratigraphy and of potential bioturbation.

In conclusion, the Magubike teeth are a useful addition to the sparse hominin record of the Tanzanian MSA, a period and region where fossils are rare. They are morphologically modern, display some resemblance to the San of southern Africa, and provide behavioral evidence of repeated use of the incisors as tools. Each of these findings is constrained by the small sample size, taphonomic alteration, and uncertain age. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that the Iringa region preserves human remains in MSA contexts and that continued excavation, improved dating, and molecular approaches may clarify the biological and cultural connections among Stone Age foragers of eastern and southern Africa.

Central neurocytoma (CN) is a rare neuroepithelial tumor of the central nervous system that arises predominantly in the supratentorial ventricular system, most often at the septum pellucidum or the lateral ventricular wall near the foramen of Monro. It was first described by Hassoun and colleagues in 1982, who recognized a tumor of young adults that resembled oligodendroglioma on light microscopy but showed neuronal differentiation on immunohistochemical and ultrastructural study [1]. Before that report, such lesions were commonly misclassified as intraventricular oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas, or other glial neoplasms. The World Health Organization (WHO) now classifies CN as a grade II tumor within the group of neuronal and mixed neuronal-glial tumors, reflecting its generally indolent behavior and favorable outcome relative to other intraventricular neoplasms [2].

CN accounts for approximately 0.25% to 0.5% of all intracranial tumors, and for a larger share, up to about 10%, of intraventricular tumors [3,4]. The tumor shows a peak incidence in the second to fourth decades of life, with a mean age at diagnosis of about 30 years, and there is no clear sex predilection [3]. Because of its intraventricular location, CN commonly obstructs cerebrospinal fluid pathways at the foramen of Monro. Patients therefore usually present with obstructive hydrocephalus and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, such as headache, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance, and altered mental status [4]. The clinical course is typically short, with symptoms present for weeks to months before diagnosis. Intratumoral hemorrhage, though uncommon, can produce acute deterioration and has been reported in a minority of cases [5]. Extraventricular neurocytomas, which occur in the brain parenchyma, spinal cord, and other sites, are recognized as a related but distinct entity and are not the focus of this review [6].

Neuroimaging findings in CN are characteristic in appearance but not specific. On computed tomography, the tumor generally appears as a heterogeneous, iso- to hyperdense intraventricular mass with frequent calcifications and variable enhancement. On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), it is typically iso- to slightly hypointense on T1-weighted sequences and iso- to hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, often with a "bubbly" appearance produced by multiple cystic spaces, and with mild to moderate heterogeneous contrast enhancement [7]. Attachment to the septum pellucidum or ventricular wall is a useful clue. Nevertheless, these features overlap considerably with those of other intraventricular lesions, including subependymoma, ependymoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, choroid plexus papilloma, oligodendroglioma, and metastasis. Advanced techniques such as magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which may show a prominent glycine peak and elevated choline with reduced N-acetylaspartate, offer additional information, but definitive diagnosis still depends on histopathology [8].

Histologically, CN is composed of uniform round cells with central round nuclei, finely speckled chromatin, and clear perinuclear halos, set in a fibrillary neuropil-rich matrix. This "honeycomb" pattern closely mimics oligodendroglioma, and the resemblance explains many historical misdiagnoses. Immunohistochemistry is therefore essential. Synaptophysin shows strong, diffuse positivity and is considered the most reliable marker, whereas glial fibrillary acidic protein is generally negative in the tumor cells themselves. Other neuronal markers, including NeuN and neuron-specific enolase, further support the diagnosis [9]. Electron microscopy, which demonstrates neuronal differentiation with dense-core vesicles, microtubules, and synapse-like structures, was historically important but is now rarely required.

Management of CN centers on surgery. Maximal safe resection, ideally gross total resection (GTR), is the treatment of choice and is associated with excellent local control and long-term survival, with reported 5-year survival rates exceeding 90% [10]. Surgical approaches include transcortical-transventricular and transcallosal routes, and endoscopic techniques have been increasingly used in selected cases. However, the tumor's proximity to deep venous structures, the fornix, and the hypothalamus, together with its frequent vascularity and broad attachment to ventricular walls, can make GTR difficult or unsafe. For residual or recurrent disease, adjuvant conventional radiotherapy and stereotactic radiosurgery have been employed to improve tumor control, though the indications, optimal doses, and timing remain debated [11,12]. Chemotherapy has no established primary role but has been used as salvage treatment in recurrent or aggressive cases, with regimens that include platinum-based and alkylating agents [13].

Although CN is considered benign, a subset of tumors behave more aggressively, with early recurrence, cerebrospinal fluid dissemination, or malignant progression. Such tumors have been termed "atypical" neurocytomas, a designation associated with an elevated proliferative index, endothelial proliferation, and necrosis. The MIB-1 (Ki-67) labeling index has emerged as the most widely studied prognostic indicator, with values of 2% or higher being linked to higher recurrence rates and poorer outcomes in several series [14,15]. Beyond proliferative indices, molecular investigations have sought to characterize genetic alterations in CN, including chromosomal gains and losses and the roles of oncogenes such as MYCN, to clarify tumor biology and distinguish CN from morphologically similar entities [16].

Because of the rarity of CN, the literature consists largely of case reports and small retrospective series, and consensus on optimal management remains incomplete. This review therefore summarizes current knowledge on the clinical presentation, imaging, histopathology, and treatment of CN, with particular attention to the role of adjuvant therapies, prognostic histologic markers, and associated oncogenes, in order to support more accurate diagnosis and individualized treatment.

A narrative literature review was conducted to synthesize current evidence on the clinical management, histopathologic features, and molecular characteristics of central neurocytoma (CN). The review was designed in accordance with the general principles of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement for transparency in reporting [1], although a formal systematic review protocol was not registered, and no quantitative meta-analysis was planned because of the heterogeneity and rarity of the available data.

**Search Strategy**

A comprehensive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was performed for articles published from the first description of CN by Hassoun and colleagues in 1982 [2] through the date of the final search. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH) and free-text keywords, including "central neurocytoma," "intraventricular neurocytoma," "neurocytoma," "lateral ventricle tumor," "neuronal tumor," "synaptophysin," "MIB-1," "Ki-67," "gross total resection," "radiosurgery," "radiotherapy," and "chemotherapy." Boolean operators were used to combine concepts (e.g., "central neurocytoma" AND [“surgery” OR “radiotherapy” OR “radiosurgery” OR “chemotherapy”]; "central neurocytoma" AND [“immunohistochemistry” OR “MIB-1” OR “oncogene” OR “genetic”]). Reference lists of included articles and of previous reviews were manually screened to identify additional relevant publications not captured by the electronic search. Searches were restricted to English-language publications.

**Eligibility Criteria**

Articles were included if they (i) reported on patients with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of CN according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria [3]; (ii) described clinical presentation, imaging, surgical or adjuvant treatment, outcomes, histopathologic or immunohistochemical features, proliferative indices, or molecular and cytogenetic findings; and (iii) were original studies (retrospective or prospective cohorts, case series), systematic reviews, meta-analyses, or case reports contributing unique information. Because CN is rare, case reports and small series were retained when they described unusual presentations, atypical histology, recurrence, malignant progression, or novel therapeutic approaches. Exclusion criteria were: (i) studies focusing exclusively on extraventricular neurocytoma, unless they provided comparative histologic or molecular data; (ii) articles in which CN could not be distinguished from other intraventricular tumors; (iii) conference abstracts without full text, editorials, and non-peer-reviewed material; and (iv) duplicate reports of the same patient cohort, in which case the most complete or most recent publication was used.

**Study Selection**

Titles and abstracts of all retrieved records were screened independently by two reviewers for relevance. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were then assessed against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, if necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. Where overlapping patient populations were suspected, for example in multicenter or institutional series that were updated over time, the authors compared enrollment periods and institutions to avoid double counting.

**Data Extraction**

A standardized form was used to extract data from each included study. Extracted variables comprised study design, sample size, patient age and sex, presenting symptoms (e.g., headache, visual disturbance, signs of raised intracranial pressure), tumor location and size, presence of obstructive hydrocephalus, and neuroimaging characteristics on computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Treatment variables included the surgical approach (transcallosal, transcortical, or endoscopic), extent of resection (gross total resection [GTR] versus subtotal resection [STR]), use and modality of adjuvant therapy (conventional fractionated radiotherapy, stereotactic radiosurgery, or chemotherapy), and radiation dose. Outcome variables included local control, progression-free survival, overall survival, recurrence, perioperative morbidity and mortality, and neurocognitive or endocrine sequelae. Pathologic variables included light and electron microscopic findings, immunohistochemical markers (synaptophysin, neuron-specific enolase, NeuN, chromogranin, and glial fibrillary acidic protein), the MIB-1 (Ki-67) labeling index, and the presence of atypical features such as necrosis, vascular proliferation, and increased mitotic activity [3,4]. Molecular data included chromosomal alterations and oncogene or gene-expression findings, such as MYCN amplification and other genomic changes reported in CN [5].

**Classification of Atypical Neurocytoma**

Because the prognostic significance of proliferative activity is a central focus of this review, studies were examined for the cutoff values used to define atypical CN, most commonly an MIB-1 labeling index of 2% or 3% or greater [4,6]. Differences in cutoffs, staining protocols, and counting methods were recorded to allow qualitative comparison of their associations with recurrence and survival.

**Assessment of Quality and Risk of Bias**

The methodological quality of cohort studies and case series was appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists [7]. Key considerations included clarity of diagnostic criteria, consecutive inclusion of patients, completeness of follow-up, standardized outcome measurement, and appropriate reporting of extent of resection. Given the predominance of retrospective, single-institution studies, the potential for selection bias, publication bias, and heterogeneity in follow-up duration was acknowledged. Quality assessment was used to guide interpretation and weighting of evidence in the narrative synthesis rather than to exclude studies.

**Data Synthesis**

Owing to heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, treatment protocols, and outcome reporting, data were synthesized narratively and organized thematically into clinical presentation and diagnosis, surgical management, adjuvant radiotherapy and radiosurgery, chemotherapy, histopathologic and immunohistochemical features, proliferative indices and prognosis, and molecular and oncogenic characteristics. Where available, descriptive statistics such as ranges, medians, and reported percentages for local control and survival were summarized. Comparisons between treatment strategies, particularly GTR alone versus STR with adjuvant therapy, were presented qualitatively, with attention to the consistency of findings across studies and to the level of evidence. Areas of uncertainty and gaps in the literature were noted to inform recommendations for future research.

A total of 1,247 records were identified through database searching, of which 312 duplicates were removed. After screening of titles and abstracts, 186 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 74 studies comprising case series, retrospective cohorts, and institutional reports were included in the qualitative synthesis. Together these studies described approximately 1,100 patients with histologically confirmed central neurocytoma (CN). Because the included literature was heterogeneous and predominantly retrospective, findings are presented descriptively, and pooled estimates should be interpreted as approximate.

**Clinical presentation and demographics**

CN predominantly affected young adults, with a mean age at diagnosis of 28 to 36 years and a peak incidence in the third and fourth decades [1,2]. No significant sex predilection was reported in most series, although a slight male predominance was noted in some cohorts [2,3]. The most frequent presenting features were related to obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure, including headache (reported in 60–90% of patients), nausea and vomiting, visual disturbance, and papilledema [1,3]. Less common manifestations included memory impairment, gait disturbance, seizures, and focal deficits [4]. Symptom duration before diagnosis was typically short, ranging from several weeks to a few months. Intratumoral hemorrhage was uncommon but was described in a minority of cases, occasionally producing acute deterioration [5].

**Tumor location and imaging features**

The tumor was located in the lateral ventricles in the large majority of cases, usually attached to the septum pellucidum or the ventricular wall near the foramen of Monro, with frequent extension into the third ventricle [1,6]. Extraventricular neurocytomas were reported separately and accounted for a small proportion of cases [7]. On computed tomography, CN appeared as an iso- to slightly hyperdense mass, with calcifications in roughly half of cases [6]. Magnetic resonance imaging typically demonstrated a heterogeneous, isointense to hyperintense lesion on T2-weighted sequences with a characteristic "soap-bubble" appearance owing to multiple cystic spaces, and variable contrast enhancement [6,8]. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy occasionally showed a prominent glycine peak and decreased N-acetylaspartate, but these findings were not consistently reproducible [8]. Overall, imaging features overlapped substantially with those of ependymoma, subependymoma, oligodendroglioma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, and choroid plexus tumors, and radiological diagnosis alone was not reliable [6,8].

**Histopathologic and immunohistochemical findings**

Histologically, CN consisted of uniform round cells with round to oval nuclei, finely speckled chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli, set in a fibrillary neuropil-like matrix. Perinuclear halos produced an oligodendroglioma-like appearance, and delicate capillary networks and calcifications were common [9]. Synaptophysin was diffusely and strongly positive in virtually all reported cases and was the most useful diagnostic marker, particularly in the neuropil-rich areas [9,10]. Neuronal nuclear antigen (NeuN) and neuron-specific enolase were also frequently positive [10]. Glial fibrillary acidic protein was generally negative in tumor cells, although reactive astrocytes could be positive, and chromogranin expression was variable and usually weak or absent [9,10]. Ultrastructural studies, where performed, revealed neuronal differentiation with microtubules, dense-core granules, and synapse-like structures [9]. Atypical CN, defined by increased proliferative activity, necrosis, microvascular proliferation, or elevated mitoses, was identified in a minority of cases [11].

**Proliferative index and prognosis**

The MIB-1 labeling index (LI) was reported in a subset of studies. Most typical tumors had values below 2–3%, whereas atypical tumors exhibited higher indices [11,12]. Several series found that an MIB-1 LI of 2–3% or greater was associated with higher recurrence rates and shorter progression-free survival, independent of the extent of resection in some analyses [12,13]. Not all studies confirmed this association, and the threshold varied between reports, which limits its use as a standalone prognostic parameter [13].

**Molecular findings**

Molecular investigations were limited by small sample sizes. Genomic studies showed that CN lacked the IDH mutations and 1p/19q codeletion typical of oligodendroglioma, which assisted in differential diagnosis [14]. Gains on chromosome 2p, including amplification involving MYCN, were described in a subset of tumors, and MYCN overexpression was suggested to correlate with more aggressive behavior [15]. Other reported alterations included variable expression of genes involved in neuronal differentiation and growth factor signaling, such as VEGF and PDGF-related pathways, although none had yet been validated as clinically actionable [14,15].

**Surgical outcomes**

Surgery was the primary treatment in nearly all patients, using transcortical, transcallosal, or endoscopic approaches [16]. Gross total resection (GTR) was achieved in approximately 40–70% of cases, with the remainder undergoing subtotal resection because of tumor adherence to ventricular structures or vascularity [1,16]. Local control after GTR was excellent, with 5-year local control rates exceeding 85–95% and overall survival rates of 95–99% [1,16,17]. After subtotal resection without adjuvant therapy, recurrence or progression was considerably more frequent, with 5-year local control of approximately 45–65% [17]. Surgical morbidity included transient memory deficits, hemiparesis, intraventricular hemorrhage, and need for permanent cerebrospinal fluid diversion, and perioperative mortality was low [16]. Endoscopic resection was reported to relieve hydrocephalus effectively in selected small tumors, though GTR rates were lower in some series [18].

**Adjuvant radiotherapy, radiosurgery, and chemotherapy**

Conventional external beam radiotherapy (typically 50–54 Gy) after subtotal resection improved 5-year local control to approximately 85–95% [17,19]. Stereotactic radiosurgery, most often gamma knife, provided local control rates of 85–100% with median marginal doses of about 13–16 Gy, with a low incidence of complications in small residual tumors [19,20]. Chemotherapy was reported in few patients, mostly as salvage therapy for recurrent or atypical disease, using platinum-, etoposide-, cyclophosphamide-, or temozolomide-based regimens, with responses being variable and generally modest [21].

Central neurocytoma (CN) remains a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge despite its generally benign course. Since its original description by Hassoun and colleagues in 1982, the tumor has been recognized as a neuronal neoplasm of the supratentorial ventricular system, typically arising near the septum pellucidum and foramen of Monro in young adults [1,2]. The clinical presentation is dominated by obstructive hydrocephalus and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, including headache, nausea, and visual disturbance, reflecting the location of the tumor rather than any specific biological behavior [2,3]. Because these features are nonspecific, diagnosis depends heavily on the integration of imaging with histopathology.

The radiological appearance of CN is variable and overlaps considerably with that of other intraventricular tumors, including subependymoma, ependymoma, oligodendroglioma, choroid plexus papilloma, and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma [3,4]. The classic "bubbly" appearance, with cystic spaces, calcification, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement, is suggestive but not specific. Advanced techniques such as magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which may show a prominent glycine peak, have been proposed as adjuncts, yet their reliability is limited by small series [4]. Consequently, tissue diagnosis remains essential. Histologically, CN consists of uniform round cells with perinuclear clearing, which resemble oligodendroglioma on routine staining. Immunohistochemical demonstration of strong, diffuse synaptophysin expression, together with NeuN positivity and absence of GFAP in tumor cells, establishes neuronal differentiation and distinguishes CN from its mimics [5,6]. Awareness of this requirement is important, as historical misclassification as intraventricular oligodendroglioma likely distorted early outcome data.

Surgical resection is the cornerstone of treatment. Gross total resection (GTR) is associated with local control rates exceeding 90% and excellent long-term survival, and it also relieves hydrocephalus by restoring cerebrospinal fluid pathways [2,7]. However, the deep location, proximity to the fornices, thalamus, and basal ganglia, and the vascularity of some tumors can make complete removal difficult. Reported morbidity includes memory impairment, hemiparesis, and intraventricular hemorrhage, so the surgeon must weigh the extent of resection against functional risk [7,8]. Endoscopic and transcallosal or transcortical microsurgical approaches each have advantages; endoscopic techniques may be suitable for smaller tumors with hydrocephalus but have been associated with lower rates of GTR in larger lesions [8]. Direct comparisons are lacking, and selection of approach is currently guided by tumor size, ventricular size, and surgeon experience.

When GTR cannot be achieved, adjuvant therapy is frequently considered. Conventional radiotherapy at doses of approximately 50–54 Gy improves local control after subtotal resection, but concerns regarding neurocognitive effects and secondary malignancy, particularly in young patients, have encouraged the use of stereotactic radiosurgery [9,10]. Gamma Knife radiosurgery has produced high tumor control rates with marginal doses of roughly 13–16 Gy and a favorable toxicity profile, making it an attractive option for residual or recurrent disease of limited volume [10]. Whether radiation should be administered immediately after subtotal resection or reserved for progression is unresolved. Observation of asymptomatic residual tumor with serial imaging is reasonable given the indolent growth of many CNs, whereas early adjuvant treatment may be preferable for tumors with proliferative features. Chemotherapy, including platinum-based and alkylating regimens, has been used mainly in recurrent or aggressive cases after surgery and radiation have failed, with only anecdotal responses reported [11]. It should therefore be regarded as salvage therapy rather than a primary modality.

Prognostication has been refined by proliferative indices. A MIB-1 labeling index of 2% or less is generally associated with favorable outcome, whereas higher values correlate with increased recurrence and shorter progression-free survival, even after GTR [12,13]. Such tumors are often termed atypical CN, although the definition of atypia (mitotic activity, necrosis, microvascular proliferation) is not uniform across studies [12]. The MIB-1 index therefore offers practical guidance for intensity of follow-up and for decisions regarding adjuvant therapy, though cutoff values vary and interobserver variability in assessment is a recognized limitation. Prospective validation is needed before it can be used as a sole determinant of management.

Molecular understanding of CN is still evolving. Studies have examined genes such as MYCN, which has been amplified in a subset of tumors, along with alterations involving PDGFRA, VEGF, and other pathways relevant to neuronal differentiation and angiogenesis [14,15]. More recent genomic work indicates that CN lacks the IDH mutations and 1p/19q codeletion typical of oligodendroglioma and has a distinct profile, with FGFR1–TACC1 fusions reported in some cases [15]. These findings support its classification as a separate entity and may eventually identify therapeutic targets for refractory disease. However, the rarity of CN has restricted sample sizes, and many data derive from single-institution, retrospective series with inherent selection bias.

This review is subject to these same limitations. The evidence base consists largely of case reports and small retrospective cohorts, heterogeneous in surgical technique, radiation dosing, and follow-up duration, which prevents firm conclusions about the optimal adjuvant strategy. Late recurrences have been described after more than a decade, highlighting the need for long-term surveillance.

In conclusion, CN is a rare neuronal tumor with an excellent prognosis when treated appropriately. Accurate diagnosis requires immunohistochemical confirmation, with synaptophysin as the key marker, because imaging alone is insufficient. Maximal safe resection should be the primary goal, with radiosurgery or radiotherapy reserved for residual or recurrent disease, and chemotherapy for salvage. The MIB-1 labeling index is a useful prognostic indicator that can inform follow-up and adjuvant decisions. Multicenter collaboration and prospective registries, combined with molecular profiling, are needed to clarify tumor biology and to establish evidence-based, individualized treatment regimens for patients with CN.

Brain-controlled robots are a promising class of assistive devices for people with severe motor impairments, such as those resulting from spinal cord injury, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or brainstem stroke. Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) translate neural activity, most commonly recorded non-invasively with electroencephalography (EEG), into commands that drive external devices such as robotic arms, wheelchairs, or telepresence systems. Despite considerable progress, the practical use of such systems outside the laboratory remains limited. Decoding of user intentions from EEG is noisy and often unreliable, and performance varies strongly between users and sessions. Improving the interaction between humans and brain-controlled robots therefore remains a central challenge for the field.

One strategy to improve control is to give the system access to the user's own evaluation of its behavior. When humans observe an action that deviates from their expectation, characteristic neural responses arise. These include error-related potentials (ErrPs) in the EEG, which have been described for self-made errors, for errors made by others, and for errors made by machines or interfaces. Such responses have typically been reported over fronto-central regions and include components such as the error-related negativity and a subsequent positivity. If these signals can be detected reliably in single trials, they could provide an implicit, continuously available teaching signal. A brain-controlled robot could use this signal to adapt its decoding or control policy, for instance within a reinforcement learning framework, without requiring explicit feedback from the user. Previous work has shown the feasibility of this idea in simple settings, such as cursor movements, discrete gridworld navigation, or abstract robot movements, but it remains unclear how well it extends to more naturalistic and complex actions with real robots.

A second open question concerns the appearance of the robot. Humans readily attribute intentions and mental states to artificial agents, and the extent to which they do so seems to depend on how human-like these agents look and move. Research on action observation has suggested that the human mirror-neuron or action-observation network may respond differently to human and robotic agents, although results are mixed. Related ideas, such as the uncanny valley hypothesis, propose that strongly human-like but imperfect artificial agents may elicit aversive reactions. If brain responses during observation of robots depend on how humanlike the robot is, this would matter for designing assistive robots, since it would affect both acceptance by users and the nature of the signals available for decoding. Conversely, if the robot's appearance modulates the neural response, then an error-detection system may need to account for robot type.

In the present study we address these two issues with EEG recordings during robot observation. We ask first whether watching a robot perform an erroneous action versus a correct action elicits differential brain responses that can be decoded from single trials. We ask second whether brain activity during human-robot interaction is modulated by the robot's visual similarity to a human, and whether this modulation is also decodable. To this end, we designed two experiments with realistic, goal-directed robot actions. In experiment I, participants watched a robot arm pour liquid into a cup. In half of the trials the robot performed the action correctly, and in the other half it made an error and spilled some of the liquid. This task involves an everyday action with clear, easily recognized success and failure outcomes, and is relevant to the kinds of manipulation tasks that assistive robots are expected to perform. In experiment II, participants observed two different robots, one humanoid and one non-humanoid, attempting to grab a ball. In each case the robot either succeeded or failed. This design allowed us to test both the effect of action correctness and the effect of robot type, as well as their potential interaction.

For analysis, we relied on high-resolution EEG and on a decoding approach rather than on conventional averaged event-related potentials alone. Decoding from single trials is the relevant criterion for practical applications, in which responses must be identified on the fly. We used the Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) algorithm, which was originally developed for decoding oscillatory activity in motor imagery BMIs. FBCSP filters the signal into multiple frequency bands, learns spatial filters that maximize the variance difference between two classes in each band, selects informative features, and classifies them. This approach allows information distributed across frequencies and electrodes to be exploited without strong prior assumptions about the precise time course or topography of the effect. We applied the same pipeline to decode the correctness of the observed action in both experiments and the type of robot in experiment II.

We hypothesized that erroneous robot actions would evoke brain responses distinguishable from those evoked by correct actions, and that the visual appearance of the robot would additionally leave a decodable trace in the EEG. Our results show that both correctness and robot type could be decoded significantly above chance level for the majority of participants, although accuracies were often only slightly above chance. These findings suggest that non-invasive recordings of brain responses during robot observation contain information about both the correctness of the robot's action and the type of robot observed, and they point to both the potential and the current limits of using such signals to improve brain-controlled robots.

Participants

Experiment I included 12 healthy volunteers (age range 21–35 years) and Experiment II included 12 healthy volunteers, some of whom took part in both. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders. Participants gave written informed consent before the experiments, and the procedures were approved by the local ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Stimuli and Experimental Design

Stimuli were presented as videos on a monitor placed approximately 80 cm from the participant. Participants were seated comfortably and instructed to watch the videos attentively, avoid eye movements and blinks during the action, and refrain from moving.

Experiment I. Videos showed a robot arm pouring liquid from a bottle into a cup. In correct trials, the liquid was poured into the cup without incident. In erroneous trials, the robot misaligned the bottle and spilled part of the liquid next to the cup. Videos lasted about 6 s, and the two conditions were identical until the moment when the pouring trajectory diverged, which was marked in each video for later epoch alignment. Each participant completed 8 blocks of 40 trials, with correct and erroneous trials presented in pseudorandom order. Erroneous trials made up 50% of the trials to avoid unequal class sizes. Trials were separated by a fixation cross of 1.5–2.5 s with random jitter. Short breaks were given between blocks.

Experiment II. Participants watched videos of two robots attempting to grab a ball from a table: a humanoid robot with a head, torso, two arms and a human-like hand, and a non-humanoid industrial robot arm with a gripper. In each video the robot either successfully grasped the ball or failed (the ball slipped or was missed). The design was therefore 2 (robot type) × 2 (outcome). Each combination was shown 80 times in randomized order, split into 8 blocks. Videos lasted about 4 s and were separated by a jittered fixation interval. To keep attention on the task, participants occasionally (about 5% of trials) answered a question on whether the previous grasp was successful; these trials were excluded from analysis.

EEG Recording

EEG was recorded with a high-density cap of 128 active electrodes positioned according to an extended 10-5 system, with a sampling rate of 500 Hz. Signals were referenced to a midline electrode (Fz) and the ground was placed at AFz. Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ. Stimulus onset and event markers were sent via a parallel port, and a photodiode attached to the screen was used to verify video timing. Electrooculogram was derived from frontal channels near the eyes.

Preprocessing

Data were processed offline using EEGLAB and custom MATLAB and Python scripts. Signals were high-pass filtered at 0.5 Hz and low-pass filtered at 40 Hz, and re-referenced to the common average. Channels with persistent artifacts were identified by visual inspection and variance criteria, and interpolated. Independent component analysis was applied, and components related to eye movements, muscle, and cardiac activity were removed based on topography, spectrum and time course, assisted by automated classification. Data were then segmented into epochs from 0 to 1.5 s relative to the error-relevant event (the moment when the outcome of the action became visible). Epochs with amplitudes exceeding ±100 µV were rejected. Trial numbers were balanced across classes by random subsampling.

Decoding Analysis

Decoding used a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline. The epoched signals were band-pass filtered with a bank of nine non-overlapping 4-Hz-wide filters (Chebyshev type II) covering 4–40 Hz. In each band, common spatial pattern (CSP) filters were computed to maximize variance differences between two classes by solving a generalized eigenvalue problem on the class-wise covariance matrices. The three filter pairs with most extreme eigenvalues were kept per band, and the log-variance of the filtered signals was used as features. This gave 54 features per band-limited trial set and 54 in total after concatenation across bands in the final feature vector. Feature selection used mutual information to select the most discriminative features, followed by classification with regularized linear discriminant analysis.

Decoding tasks were: (1) correct vs. erroneous action in Experiment I; (2) correct vs. failed grasp in Experiment II, for each robot separately and pooled; and (3) humanoid vs. non-humanoid robot, irrespective of outcome. All models were trained within participants.

Performance was assessed by 10-fold cross-validation, repeated five times with different random partitions. CSP filters, feature selection and classifier were estimated only on training folds to avoid information leakage. Accuracy was the main metric, supplemented by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. For the robot type analysis, we ensured equal numbers of correct and erroneous trials per robot so the outcome could not drive classification.

Statistical Analysis

Significance of single-participant accuracy was determined with permutation tests: class labels were randomly shuffled 1000 times, the complete pipeline was rerun, and the p value was the proportion of permuted accuracies at least as high as the observed one. Significance was set at α = 0.05. At group level, accuracies were compared to chance (50%) with one-sample t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, depending on normality (Shapiro–Wilk test), and corrected for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni–Holm method. Differences in decoding accuracy between robot types were tested with paired tests. To assess which frequency bands contributed most, we examined the mutual information scores of the features by band and visualized CSP patterns for selected participants.

Experiment I: Decoding the correctness of robot action

Behavioral data. Participants reliably identified the outcome of the observed pouring action. Mean accuracy in the control question, asked in a subset of trials, was above 95%, indicating that participants attended to the videos and recognized whether liquid had been spilled.

Event-related responses. Grand-average EEG time-locked to the moment at which the outcome of the action became visible showed differences between erroneous and correct trials. Erroneous trials elicited a more pronounced negative deflection over fronto-central electrodes, followed by a positive deflection over centro-parietal sites. The differences emerged roughly 250–400 ms after the onset of the spill and continued for several hundred milliseconds. Their latency and topography were broadly consistent with error-related potentials previously reported during observation of erroneous actions. Amplitude and latency varied considerably between participants, and several participants showed only weak differences.

Single-trial decoding. The FBCSP pipeline decoded correct versus erroneous observation significantly above chance in the majority of participants. Mean accuracy across participants was modest, at approximately 60–65%, with a range from chance level in a few participants to about 75–80% in the best participants. Permutation testing showed that 11 of 15 participants exceeded the 95% chance-level confidence bound. Decoding accuracy was thus often only slightly above chance, but it was consistent across cross-validation folds in most participants who reached significance. Accuracies were also higher than those obtained with shuffled labels, whose distribution was centered at 50%.

Frequency and spatial features. Inspection of the filter-bank features showed that the most discriminative information was concentrated in low frequencies (roughly 4–13 Hz), with additional contributions from the beta band in some participants. The spatial patterns corresponding to the most discriminative CSP filters had maxima over frontal and central midline regions, with weaker contributions from parietal and temporal sites. This is consistent with the topographies of the averaged evoked responses. Because high-resolution EEG was recorded, the patterns were spatially fine-grained, but we did not observe consistent lateralization across participants.

Temporal characteristics. Decoding on sliding time windows showed that accuracy rose from chance level shortly after the onset of the erroneous event, peaked between approximately 400 and 800 ms, and then declined. Windows before the outcome became visible did not yield above-chance decoding, suggesting that the classifier did not exploit anticipatory activity or differences in the preceding video content.

Experiment II: Decoding action correctness and robot type

Behavioral data. Participants correctly reported whether the robot had grasped the ball in nearly all queried trials. Ratings of the two robots confirmed that the humanoid robot was perceived as more human-like than the non-humanoid robot.

Event-related responses. As in experiment I, failed grasps elicited differences from successful grasps over fronto-central and centro-parietal electrodes in a time window of approximately 300–700 ms after the outcome became evident. Differences between humanoid and non-humanoid robots were present as well, but were less spatially focal. They appeared mainly over occipito-parietal electrodes, and in some participants over frontal sites, starting early after video onset. Such early differences might partly reflect low-level visual differences between the robots, which we address below.

Decoding correctness. Decoding of grasp success versus failure was significantly above chance in most participants (11 of 14 for the humanoid robot and 10 of 14 for the non-humanoid robot). Mean accuracies were again modest, around 60–65%. A paired comparison of decoding accuracy between the humanoid and non-humanoid robot did not show a reliable difference, so we found no evidence that the robot's visual similarity to a human modulated how well error observation could be decoded. A classifier trained on one robot type and tested on the other performed above chance in several participants, though with reduced accuracy relative to within-robot training. This suggests partly shared error-related information across robot types.

Decoding robot type. Decoding of humanoid versus non-humanoid observation was significant in the majority of participants (12 of 14), with mean accuracies of approximately 60–70%. Accuracies were on average slightly higher than for correctness decoding, but they varied strongly between participants. The most discriminative filters had spatial patterns focused over posterior regions, with contributions from frontal channels, and the relevant spectral information was spread over theta, alpha, and beta bands.

Control analyses. Because the two robots differed in visual appearance and motion, the decodability of robot type could reflect low-level visual features rather than higher-level representations of human similarity. Our design cannot fully dissociate these factors. Decoding of robot type was nonetheless also possible in time windows in which both robots were stationary, though with lower accuracy, and the spatial patterns in these windows overlapped with those of the dynamic windows. Correctness decoding, in contrast, did not rely on these visual differences, since successful and failed grasps were balanced across robots.

Across participants, accuracy in experiment I did not correlate significantly with accuracy in experiment II for the participants who took part in both, which indicates that individual differences in decoding performance were not stable across tasks. The number of available trials per class correlated positively with accuracy, suggesting that more trials might improve decoding.

Summary. In both experiments, correct and erroneous robot actions could be decoded from single-trial EEG significantly above chance for most participants, and robot type could be decoded as well. Effects were often small, and there was marked inter-individual variability.

Our results show that EEG recorded while participants watched robots act contains information that can be decoded from single trials about whether the observed action was correct or erroneous, and about whether the robot was humanoid or non-humanoid.
