Cases were not all confirmed by culture, so some misclassification is possible, and controls may include asymptomatic or recently infected individuals, which would bias estimates toward the null. Exposure data were self-reported and collected retrospectively, creating the potential for recall bias, particularly because cases may have recalled risky behaviours more readily. Social desirability may have led participants to overreport hygiene practices. Because the study was restricted to Aden, generalisability to rural areas or to regions under different administrative and infrastructural conditions is uncertain. Finally, the study was conducted during a particular phase of the epidemic, and risk factors may change over time.

**Conclusions**

In this case-control study, not washing khat and using common-source water were independently associated with cholera in Aden. These findings indicate that both behavioural and infrastructural determinants sustain transmission. Interventions should combine safe water provision, household water treatment, hygiene promotion tailored to local practices such as khat consumption, and, where feasible, vaccination. Larger studies with laboratory-confirmed cases and environmental sampling are needed to confirm the role of khat and to guide targeted control in Yemen and comparable humanitarian emergencies.

The analysis of high-dimensional data is a central task in machine learning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD). It is also notoriously difficult. Many algorithms degrade as the number of features grows: nearest-neighbor search loses its discriminative power, distance-based clustering becomes unstable, and the sample size needed for reliable estimation increases dramatically. These phenomena are collectively known as the curse of dimensionality. Their practical importance has led to a large body of literature that investigates their origins and consequences, using tools from statistics, computer science, and mathematics.

A recurring observation is that the nominal dimension of a data set, meaning the number of coordinates used to represent each point, is often a poor predictor of how hard the data are to analyze. Data may lie close to a low-dimensional manifold, may be strongly clustered, or may have rapidly decaying variance along most directions. Conversely, data in a low-dimensional ambient space can exhibit behavior typical of high dimension. This motivates the notion of intrinsic dimension: a quantity meant to capture the effective complexity of the data, independent of the particular representation. Numerous estimators have been proposed, among them PCA-based approaches, fractal and correlation dimensions, and nearest-neighbor-based maximum likelihood estimators. They are often useful in practice, but they rest on different assumptions and are usually justified heuristically. They may give inconsistent answers on the same data, and it is rarely clear which properties a reasonable notion of dimension should satisfy.

From a mathematical perspective, a particularly illuminating explanation of the dimension curse is the concentration of measure phenomenon. In high-dimensional spaces such as spheres, cubes, or Gaussian spaces, every sufficiently regular function is almost constant on a set of nearly full measure. As a consequence, distances between random points concentrate around a typical value, and the contrast on which many ML algorithms rely vanishes. This link was recognized in the ML/KD literature, and it suggests that intrinsic dimension should be tied to concentration properties. Pestov developed this idea into an axiomatic approach: a dimension function for metric spaces with measure should, among other requirements, assign the expected dimension to standard objects, behave monotonically under suitable maps, and reflect the concentration phenomenon through a suitable observable diameter. Gromov's metric measure geometry supplies the framework for this, providing the notions of observable diameter, concentration function, and the distance between metric measure spaces.

Pestov's approach was developed for idealized objects, namely metric spaces with probability measures, whereas data sets are finite, may carry additional structure, and are analyzed by algorithms that use only certain features of that structure. The present work aims to bridge this gap. We introduce a model of a *geometric data set* that combines a metric measure space, which describes the geometry and distribution of the data, with a family of functions, or features, which describes what a given ML/KD algorithm can observe. This second ingredient makes the model adaptable: different algorithms, for instance those using only linear functionals, Lipschitz functions, or the outputs of a given class of classifiers, correspond to different feature classes and therefore to different notions of intrinsic dimension. We define isomorphism of geometric data sets and study the set of isomorphism classes.

Our first main contribution is structural. We introduce a metric on the set of isomorphism classes, inspired by the Gromov–Wasserstein and box distances, which makes it possible to quantify how close two data sets are, including a finite sample and the underlying distribution from which it is drawn. We also define a partial order, a form of domination, which expresses that one data set is a simplification of another, obtained through feature-preserving maps. We investigate the topological and order-theoretic properties of these objects, including compatibility between the order and the metric.

Our second main contribution is an axiomatic treatment of intrinsic dimension for geometric data sets. Building on Pestov's axioms, we formulate requirements for a dimension function: monotonicity with respect to the partial order, continuity or stability with respect to the metric, normalization on reference examples, and consistency with measure concentration. We show that these requirements are mutually compatible by constructing a concrete dimension function that satisfies them. The function is defined through the concentration behavior of the feature class, via a notion of separation or observable diameter, and we prove its basic properties, including its behavior under products and its relation to the classical notion of dimension on model spaces.

Third, we address computational feasibility. A definition that cannot be evaluated on real data would be of limited value to the ML/KD community. We show that our dimension function can be estimated from finite samples and we describe algorithms for doing so. Experiments on synthetic and real data sets illustrate that the resulting values reflect known intrinsic structure, that they respond sensibly to the choice of feature class, and that they correlate with the performance of specific algorithms, such as nearest-neighbor classification, on the data.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background from metric measure geometry and Pestov's axioms. Section 3 defines geometric data sets, their isomorphism classes, and the metric and partial order. Section 4 presents the axioms and the dimension function and proves its properties. Section 5 discusses estimation and computation, and Section 6 reports experiments. We conclude with a discussion of limitations and directions for future work.

We work in the framework of metric measure geometry and adapt it to finite data sets equipped with a family of functions that model the "observables" of a learning algorithm.

**Geometric data sets.** A geometric data set is a triple X = (X, d_X, μ_X), where (X, d_X) is a finite (or more generally compact) metric space and μ_X is a Borel probability measure on X, together with a class F_X of real-valued functions on X, typically the 1-Lipschitz functions or a subclass determined by the ML/KD task, for example the functions realizable by a given hypothesis class. Two geometric data sets are isomorphic if there is a measure-preserving isometry between the supports of their measures that maps F_X onto F_Y. We denote by 𝒢 the set of isomorphism classes. For a finite sample x_1,…,x_n, we take μ to be the empirical measure, optionally weighted, and d to be the Euclidean metric or another task-appropriate metric.

**Metric on 𝒢.** To compare data sets of different size and ambient space, we use a Gromov-type approach based on the Prokhorov and box distances. Let X and Y be geometric data sets. A parametrization of X is a Borel map φ: [0,1] → X with φ_*λ = μ_X, where λ is Lebesgue measure. We define the observable distance

d_conc(X,Y) = inf over parametrizations φ, ψ of d_H(φ^*F_X, ψ^*F_Y),

where d_H is the Hausdorff distance between the pulled-back function classes, measured in the Ky Fan metric on measurable functions on [0,1]. This is a concentration-type distance: it vanishes in the limit for Lévy families, and it is sensitive to the concentration behavior of the functions in F. We show that d_conc is a metric on 𝒢 and that sequences of finite samples of a fixed compact geometric data set converge to it in this metric when the empirical measures converge weakly. The proof uses the standard compactness of parametrizations and the stability of the Ky Fan metric under weak convergence.

**Partial order.** We say X dominates Y, written Y ≺ X, if there is a 1-Lipschitz, measure-preserving map π: X → Y with F_Y ∘ π ⊆ F_X. This relation is reflexive and transitive, and antisymmetric on 𝒢 by an argument based on the rigidity of measure-preserving isometric embeddings of compact spaces. We prove that ≺ is closed with respect to d_conc, which is needed for the compatibility of the dimension function with limits. Intuitively, Y ≺ X means that Y is a "compression" of X that loses no more concentration than the data itself carries.

**Axioms for intrinsic dimension.** Following Pestov, an intrinsic dimension function is a map dim: 𝒢 → [0,∞) satisfying:

1. *Monotonicity:* Y ≺ X implies dim(Y) ≤ dim(X).
2. *Continuity:* dim is continuous with respect to d_conc, or at least lower semicontinuous.
3. *Normalization:* dim of the standard Euclidean sphere or cube of dimension k, with the uniform measure and Lipschitz functions, equals k, up to a universal constant.
4. *Concentration (curse of dimensionality):* for any Lévy family (X_n), dim(X_n) → ∞.
5. *Product behavior:* dim(X × Y) ≤ dim(X) + dim(Y) for the ℓ₂-product, with equality up to constants for products of identical factors.

We establish which subsets of these axioms are consistent and show they are jointly satisfiable by the function constructed below.

**Dimension function.** Our construction is based on the observable diameter. For κ > 0, the κ-observable diameter of X is

ObsDiam_κ(X) = sup over f ∈ F_X of diam(f_*μ_X; 1−κ),

where diam(ν; 1−κ) is the smallest length of an interval carrying ν-mass at least 1−κ. For high-dimensional spheres or cubes this quantity decays as the dimension grows, reflecting measure concentration. We define the dimension via the inverse relationship with the observable diameter normalized by a reference scale:

dim(X) = sup over κ in a fixed range (0, κ₀] of c(κ) · (D_X / ObsDiam_κ(X))²,

where D_X is the metric (or L²-) diameter scale of X and c(κ) is a normalization constant chosen so that the unit sphere S^k receives value k. Using Lévy's isoperimetric inequality we show that ObsDiam_κ(S^k) ≍ √(log(1/κ)/k), which yields the normalization and the concentration axiom. Monotonicity follows because 1-Lipschitz measure-preserving maps cannot increase observable diameter. Continuity follows from Lipschitz-type estimates of ObsDiam_κ in d_conc, with a shift in κ.

**Computation.** For a finite sample of size n, we approximate F_X by a finite family of functions, in practice (a) distance functions to randomly chosen anchor points, (b) coordinate projections and random linear projections, and (c) functions derived from the algorithm under study, such as the classifier score of a k-nearest-neighbor model or the output of a trained network. For each f, we compute the empirical push-forward measure and its shortest (1−κ)-interval in O(n log n) time by sorting. The overall cost is O(mn log n) for m functions, plus the cost of evaluating them. We estimate D_X by the empirical standard deviation of pairwise distances computed on a subsample. We average over repeated subsamples and report standard deviations to quantify the sampling variability. By the convergence result above, the estimates are consistent as n and m increase.

**Experimental protocol.** We evaluate the dimension function on synthetic data (spheres, cubes, Gaussian mixtures, and linear and nonlinear manifolds embedded in higher-dimensional spaces) to check agreement with known dimension, and on real image and tabular data sets. For algorithm adaptation, we vary F_X to the function class of a given method and compare the resulting dimension with the observed performance degradation of that method as dimension increases. We also compare against standard estimators (PCA-based, maximum likelihood, correlation dimension) using the same samples.

We first summarize the structural results on geometric data sets, then the axiomatic dimension theory, and finally the experimental findings.

**Geometric data sets and their comparison.** We define a geometric data set as a triple (X, d, μ) consisting of a finite set X, a metric d, and a probability measure μ, together with a finite family of real-valued feature functions F that encode the geometry relevant to a given learning task. Two such data sets are isomorphic if there is a measure-preserving isometry that also carries the feature families onto one another. On the set of isomorphism classes we introduced a metric, denoted d_G, which combines a Gromov–Prokhorov-type (box) distance on the underlying metric measure spaces with a term comparing the feature families. We proved that d_G is a genuine metric, that it is complete on the class of data sets with bounded diameter, and that finite data sets sampled with increasing size from a fixed distribution converge to the underlying space in d_G with high probability. Convergence rates depend on the covering properties of the support but not on the ambient dimension.

We also introduced a partial order ≺ on isomorphism classes, based on 1-Lipschitz, measure-preserving maps (a Lipschitz-domination order in the spirit of Gromov). We showed that ≺ is closed with respect to d_G, so that limits of dominated sequences remain dominated. The order is compatible with observable diameter: if X ≺ Y, then the observable diameter of X is at most that of Y at every confidence level. Thus measure concentration in Y is inherited by X, matching the intuition that a data set which is a Lipschitz image of a highly concentrated one cannot be less concentrated.

**Axiomatic intrinsic dimension.** Following Pestov, we required a dimension function dim to satisfy four axioms: (i) it is monotone with respect to ≺ (if X ≺ Y then dim X ≤ dim Y); (ii) it is normalized, with dim equal to n on the standard n-dimensional Euclidean-type reference data sets (Hamming cubes and spheres with suitable scaling); (iii) it exhibits the concentration phenomenon, meaning that dim of a sequence of data sets diverges whenever the sequence is a Lévy family (concentrates); and (iv) it is stable under d_G-small perturbations in the sense of being continuous in a quantitative sense with respect to d_G.

Our first main result is that these axioms are consistent. We constructed a function dim, defined through the observable diameter of the data set at a prescribed confidence level and calibrated on the reference family, and proved that it satisfies (i)–(iii) exactly and (iv) in a Lipschitz-type form away from degenerate, nearly constant data. Specifically, the dimension is obtained as the inverse of the calibrated observable diameter function evaluated on the reference family, so that a data set receives the dimension n of the reference space with the same observable diameter. We further showed that dim is bounded above by a quantity depending only on the feature-induced covering numbers, which gives a computable upper estimate, and that on product data sets dim is subadditive up to a constant.

Our second main result is a separation theorem: dim cannot be replaced by a function that is both monotone for ≺ and strictly additive on products while also satisfying the concentration axiom. We derived this from the sublinear growth of observable diameters under ℓ₂-products, which clarifies why the subadditive form is the natural one.

**Computation.** The dimension function can be estimated from a sample in polynomial time. The estimator draws feature-function evaluations, computes empirical quantiles of the distribution of each feature (or of a Lipschitz combination), and evaluates the resulting empirical observable diameter. We proved a uniform deviation bound showing that, with N samples, the estimation error decays at rate O(N^{-1/2}) up to logarithmic factors in the size of the feature family.

**Experiments.** We evaluated the estimator on synthetic and real data. On synthetic data (uniform samples from cubes, spheres, and linear and curved manifolds embedded in higher-dimensional space), the estimated dimension tracked the true intrinsic dimension and was insensitive to the embedding dimension. For uniform samples from [0,1]^n, the estimate grew monotonically with n, and for low-dimensional manifolds embedded in R^100 it remained close to the manifold dimension, while it increased as isotropic noise of growing magnitude was added.

On image benchmarks (MNIST and CIFAR-10) and several tabular data sets, the estimated dimension was far below the ambient dimension, in the range of tens, and agreed in ordering with established estimators such as maximum-likelihood and correlation-dimension methods, though with smaller variance across subsamples. Class-restricted subsets typically had lower dimension than the full data set, consistent with monotonicity under restriction.

Finally, we tested adaptability by choosing the feature family F according to the algorithm in use: outputs of k-nearest-neighbor classifiers, linear classifiers, and a small neural network. The resulting dimension values differed between algorithms on the same data and correlated with the observed generalization difficulty: data sets and feature classes with higher estimated dimension showed larger gaps between training and test accuracy and a stronger degradation of nearest-neighbor accuracy as sample size shrank. These findings support the view that the geometric intrinsic dimension captures algorithm-relevant aspects of the curse of dimensionality.

The present work developed a framework for the intrinsic dimension of data sets rooted in Gromov's metric measure geometry and Pestov's axiomatic approach. We introduced geometric data sets as isomorphism classes of finite metric measure spaces equipped with a family of feature functions, endowed them with a metric and a partial order, and formulated axioms that a dimension function should satisfy. We then constructed a concrete dimension function, based on the concentration function and its relation to the observable diameter, that satisfies these axioms and can be computed from finite samples. In this final section we discuss the meaning and limitations of our results and outline directions for further research.

**Interpretation of the results.** The central conceptual point is that intrinsic dimension, in the sense relevant to the curse of dimensionality, is not purely a property of the support of a distribution, such as a manifold dimension or a covering number, but a joint property of the metric, the measure, and the class of functions through which the data are observed. This is the content of measure concentration: in high-dimensional spaces, Lipschitz functions are nearly constant on sets of almost full measure, which in turn explains the failure of distance-based algorithms such as nearest-neighbor search. By building the feature functions into the definition of a geometric data set, our model allows the dimension to depend on the algorithm or task under consideration. The experiments illustrate this: the same underlying point cloud can exhibit different dimension values depending on which class of features is admitted, and these values track the observed behavior of the corresponding learning methods better than purely geometric estimators do in several cases.

The partial order on geometric data sets, a variant of the Lipschitz order of Gromov, formalizes the idea that one data set is "less spread out" than another, as it is obtained from it by a measure-preserving, distance-nonincreasing map. The axioms require the dimension to be monotone with respect to this order, to behave in a prescribed way under products and under the passage to a limit, and to be normalized on standard examples. These requirements ensure that the dimension function is stable under small perturbations in our metric and that it behaves sensibly on Lévy families, where dimension should diverge. The fact that a concrete function satisfying all these properties exists, and is computable, supports the usefulness of the axiomatic approach beyond its original setting of topological groups and metric spaces with measure.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the dimension function is defined through concentration quantities, whose estimation from finite samples introduces statistical error. We provided consistency and stability statements with respect to our metric, but explicit sample-complexity bounds are currently coarse, and in very high ambient dimension the empirical estimates may require sample sizes that are impractical. Second, the computation involves optimization over the feature class, or at least over a sufficiently rich finite subfamily. For classes such as all 1-Lipschitz functions this is expensive, and we relied on approximations whose quality depends on the choice of the subfamily. Third, our axioms determine the dimension function only partially. Different functions satisfy them, and we have not identified a canonical one. The function we chose is natural from the viewpoint of concentration, but alternatives based on, for instance, entropy or spectral quantities may be preferable for particular applications. Fourth, our model treats data as a fixed finite metric measure space; it does not directly address the dependence of dimension on the data-generating process, such as noise models, or on dynamic settings where the distribution changes over time.

Moreover, the relation between our dimension and the performance of specific algorithms was demonstrated empirically rather than proved. We observed that low values of the dimension correlate with good behavior of, for example, nearest-neighbor classification and clustering, but a theoretical link in the form of performance guarantees remains to be established.

**Relation to existing approaches.** Classical estimators of intrinsic dimension, including those based on correlation dimension, local PCA, or nearest-neighbor distance statistics, aim to recover a local geometric dimension of an underlying manifold. Our notion is complementary: a data set lying on a low-dimensional manifold may still have a large concentration-based dimension if its measure is spread over a large and highly curved region, and conversely. We regard the two as measuring different aspects of data complexity, one local and structural, the other global and probabilistic. A combined view could be fruitful, for example by using local estimates to select feature classes adapted to the data.

**Future work.** Several directions appear promising. A theoretical analysis connecting the dimension function to generalization or runtime bounds of specific algorithms would turn the empirical correlations into guarantees. Developing faster estimators, possibly exploiting sampling, sketching, or learned feature classes such as those defined by neural networks, would extend applicability to large data sets. It would also be interesting to study the topology of the space of geometric data sets under our metric, including completeness, compactness criteria, and the structure of its Lévy-type sequences. Finally, extending the framework to supervised settings, where labels define a natural feature function, and to data with several modalities, could yield dimension notions tailored to learning tasks and provide diagnostics for feature selection and representation learning.

**Conclusion.** We have provided a mathematically grounded and computationally feasible model of the intrinsic dimension of data sets, combining metric measure geometry with an axiomatic characterization. The resulting dimension function respects the phenomenon of measure concentration, is adaptable to the choice of algorithm through the feature class, and is supported by experiments. We hope that this framework contributes to a more unified understanding of the dimension curse in machine learning and knowledge discovery.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for nearly one third of all deaths each year [1]. Epidemiological studies have consistently shown that premenopausal women have a lower incidence of coronary heart disease, hypertension, and heart failure than age-matched men, and that this relative protection diminishes after menopause [2,3]. The incidence of cardiovascular events in women rises sharply in the decade following the cessation of ovarian function, eventually approaching that of men [4]. These observations have led to the long-standing hypothesis that endogenous ovarian hormones, particularly 17β-estradiol (E2), confer protection against cardiac injury and adverse remodeling.

E2 is the most abundant and biologically potent estrogen in premenopausal women. Beyond its classical roles in reproductive physiology, E2 exerts pleiotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, including vasodilation, modulation of lipid metabolism, attenuation of inflammation, and inhibition of vascular smooth muscle proliferation [5,6]. In the myocardium, experimental studies indicate that E2 reduces cardiomyocyte apoptosis, limits infarct size after ischemia-reperfusion injury, attenuates pathological hypertrophy, and preserves mitochondrial function [7-9]. Ovariectomy in animal models aggravates cardiac dysfunction after pressure overload or myocardial infarction, and these deleterious effects are largely reversed by E2 supplementation [10,11]. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of E2 in maintaining cardiac homeostasis in women of reproductive age.

The biological actions of E2 are mediated primarily through estrogen receptors (ERs). Three ER subtypes have been identified in cardiomyocytes: the classical nuclear receptors ERα and ERβ, and the membrane-associated G protein-coupled estrogen receptor GPR30 (also known as GPER) [12,13]. ERα and ERβ are ligand-activated transcription factors encoded by separate genes, and they share a conserved structure comprising a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain. Upon E2 binding, they dimerize and translocate to the nucleus, where they regulate the transcription of target genes by binding to estrogen response elements or by interacting with other transcription factors such as AP-1 and Sp1 (the genomic pathway) [14]. In addition, a subpopulation of ERα and ERβ localizes at the plasma membrane and in caveolae, where it rapidly activates kinase cascades, including PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase signaling, within seconds to minutes (the nongenomic pathway) [15,16]. GPR30 further contributes to rapid estrogen signaling through the activation of adenylyl cyclase, transactivation of the epidermal growth factor receptor, and mobilization of intracellular calcium [17]. The relative contribution of each receptor subtype to cardioprotection is context dependent, and accumulating evidence suggests that the receptors may act cooperatively or in a compensatory manner depending on the type of cardiac insult [18,19].

Given the apparent cardioprotective effects of E2, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was initially promoted as a strategy for preventing CVD in postmenopausal women. Early observational studies supported this notion, reporting significant reductions in coronary events among HRT users [20]. However, large randomized controlled trials, notably the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study and the Women's Health Initiative, failed to demonstrate cardiovascular benefit and instead reported increased risks of thromboembolism, stroke, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer [21,22]. Subsequent analyses have proposed the "timing hypothesis," which suggests that the cardiovascular effects of estrogen depend on the age of the patient and the time elapsed since menopause, with benefit observed when therapy is initiated early [23]. Nevertheless, safety concerns, particularly regarding hormone-dependent malignancies, have substantially limited the clinical use of conventional estrogen therapy and stimulated the search for safer alternatives.

Phytoestrogens are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds whose structures resemble that of E2 and which can bind to ERs, with a generally higher affinity for ERβ than for ERα [24]. The major classes include isoflavones (genistein, daidzein), lignans, coumestans, and stilbenes such as resveratrol, which are abundant in soybeans, flaxseed, legumes, and grapes [25]. Populations consuming diets rich in these compounds, such as those in East Asia, display a lower incidence of CVD and fewer menopausal symptoms than Western populations [26]. Experimental studies have shown that phytoestrogens can reduce oxidative stress, improve endothelial function, inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis, and attenuate cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, in part through ER-dependent activation of PI3K/Akt and related survival pathways [27-29]. Because of their selective receptor binding and weaker estrogenic activity, phytoestrogens may behave as natural selective estrogen receptor modulators, potentially providing cardiovascular benefit with a reduced risk of adverse effects on the breast and uterus [30]. Clinical findings, however, remain inconsistent, reflecting variability in compounds, doses, study populations, and individual metabolism, such as the gut microbial conversion of daidzein to equol [31].

A better understanding of ER-mediated signaling in cardiomyocytes is therefore essential for the rational development of phytoestrogen-based therapies. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of estrogen and ER-mediated genomic and nongenomic pathways that underlie cardioprotection against diverse stresses. We further discuss the clinical implications of ERs and phytoestrogens and provide insights into the potential of phytoestrogens as alternatives in estrogen replacement therapy.

This review was conducted as a narrative literature review following the general principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to promote transparency in literature identification, selection, and synthesis [1]. Because the topic spans basic molecular biology, preclinical models, and clinical studies, a narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis, as heterogeneity in experimental designs, phytoestrogen preparations, doses, and outcome measures precluded quantitative pooling [2].

**Literature search strategy**

Relevant publications were identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase from database inception to the most recent search date. Searches combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords using Boolean operators. Terms were grouped into four conceptual domains: (i) estrogen and receptors ("17β-estradiol", "estrogen receptor alpha", "estrogen receptor beta", "ERα", "ERβ", "GPR30", "GPER"); (ii) cardiac tissue and cell types ("cardiomyocyte", "heart", "myocardium", "cardiac"); (iii) cardiovascular conditions and stresses ("cardioprotection", "ischemia/reperfusion", "myocardial infarction", "hypertrophy", "heart failure", "apoptosis", "oxidative stress", "doxorubicin"); and (iv) phytoestrogens and therapy ("phytoestrogen", "isoflavone", "genistein", "daidzein", "equol", "resveratrol", "coumestrol", "lignan", "flavonoid", "hormone replacement therapy", "estrogen replacement"). Reference lists of key articles and previous reviews were hand-searched to identify additional studies not captured electronically [3]. Clinical trial registries were consulted to identify relevant completed trials on phytoestrogen supplementation and cardiovascular endpoints.

**Eligibility criteria**

Studies were included if they: (1) investigated the role of E2 or its receptors (ERα, ERβ, GPR30) in cardiomyocytes or cardiac tissue, including genomic and nongenomic signaling; (2) examined cardioprotective effects of phytoestrogens or related compounds with demonstrated ER binding or ER-dependent activity; (3) reported clinical or epidemiological data on estrogen replacement therapy, ER polymorphisms, or phytoestrogen intake in relation to cardiovascular outcomes; or (4) were original research articles, clinical trials, meta-analyses, or high-quality reviews published in English. Priority was given to studies using ER-selective agonists or antagonists, receptor knockout or knockdown models, or ovariectomized animals, as these provide mechanistic evidence for receptor involvement [4].

Exclusion criteria were: studies focusing solely on non-cardiac tissues (e.g., breast, bone, or uterus) without relevance to cardiac signaling; reports on phytoestrogens lacking evidence of ER-related mechanisms; conference abstracts, editorials, and non-peer-reviewed material; and articles lacking sufficient methodological detail to interpret findings. Studies of vascular endothelium and smooth muscle were included selectively when they offered mechanistic insight applicable to cardiomyocyte signaling or helped contextualize clinical outcomes.

**Study selection and data extraction**

Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were then evaluated against the criteria above. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved through discussion among the authors. For each included study, information was extracted on the experimental model (cell line, primary cardiomyocytes, isolated heart, animal species, or human population), the estrogenic compound and dose, the receptor subtype implicated, the cardiac insult applied, the signaling pathways assessed, and the principal outcomes. For clinical studies, details on population characteristics (age, menopausal status), intervention duration, and cardiovascular endpoints were recorded [5].

**Thematic organization and synthesis**

Extracted evidence was organized into thematic categories reflecting the structure of the review. The first category addressed the biosynthesis, physiology, and cardiac actions of E2, including receptor expression patterns in cardiomyocytes. The second covered receptor-specific signaling: genomic pathways involving ligand-dependent nuclear translocation of ERα and ERβ and transcriptional regulation via estrogen response elements, and nongenomic pathways involving membrane-associated ERs and GPR30, with activation of PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, nitric oxide synthase, and calcium-handling cascades [6,7]. The third examined protective effects against specific insults, including ischemia/reperfusion injury, pressure-overload hypertrophy, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity. The fourth critically appraised clinical evidence on estrogen replacement therapy, including the divergent findings of large randomized trials and observational studies and the "timing hypothesis" [8]. The fifth evaluated phytoestrogens, grouped by chemical class (isoflavones, stilbenes, lignans, coumestans), with attention to relative ER affinity, receptor subtype selectivity, metabolism (e.g., equol production by gut microbiota), and bioavailability [9].

Findings were synthesized qualitatively. Concordant and discordant results across models were compared, and differences were considered in light of species, sex, hormonal status, dose, and treatment timing. Where available, evidence from receptor-selective pharmacological tools and genetic models was weighted more heavily than correlative observations when inferring receptor-specific mechanisms.

**Quality considerations and limitations**

Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied given the narrative design; nevertheless, methodological strengths and weaknesses, such as sample size, presence of appropriate controls, use of physiological versus supraphysiological concentrations, and confounding in observational research, were considered when interpreting findings [10]. Limitations of this approach include potential selection bias, restriction to English-language publications, and possible underrepresentation of negative or null results due to publication bias. Mechanistic insights derived from in vitro or rodent models may not fully translate to humans, and this caveat is explicitly noted where relevant. Chemical structures and receptor nomenclature follow current IUPHAR recommendations.

Estrogen receptor subtypes and their cardiomyocyte distribution

Literature analysis showed that the three ER subtypes, ERα, ERβ and GPR30 (GPER), are all expressed in cardiomyocytes, although their relative abundance varies with species, sex, developmental stage and disease state [1,2]. ERα and ERβ localize to the nucleus, plasma membrane caveolae and mitochondria, whereas GPR30 resides mainly at the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane [3,4]. Expression of ERβ was reported to increase in hypertrophied and failing myocardium, while ERα expression was frequently reduced after ischemic injury, suggesting that subtype balance shifts under stress [5,6].

Genomic signaling mediated by ERα and ERβ

Across the reviewed studies, E2 binding to ERα or ERβ induced receptor dimerization and binding to estrogen response elements in target gene promoters. In cardiomyocytes, this regulated genes involved in antioxidant defense (superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase), anti-apoptotic control (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL), calcium handling (SERCA2a) and energy metabolism (PGC-1α, NRF-1) [7–9]. Estrogen treatment also suppressed pro-hypertrophic transcriptional programs, including calcineurin/NFAT and GATA4 activity, and attenuated expression of fibrotic mediators such as TGF-β1 and collagen I [10,11]. ERα was most consistently linked to reduced infarct size and preserved contractile function after ischemia-reperfusion, whereas ERβ was more strongly associated with anti-hypertrophic and anti-fibrotic effects under pressure overload [6,12]. Ovariectomized animals displayed greater hypertrophy, mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis, and these changes were largely reversed by E2 replacement [13].

Nongenomic signaling pathways

Rapid E2 actions, occurring within seconds to minutes, were attributed to membrane-associated ERα, ERβ and GPR30. The most frequently reported cascade was activation of PI3K/Akt, which phosphorylated eNOS, GSK-3β and Bad, thereby promoting nitric oxide production, inhibiting mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and limiting apoptosis [14,15]. MAPK/ERK1/2 activation was also observed and was linked to survival signaling in cardiomyocytes exposed to hypoxia/reoxygenation [16]. Activation of GPR30 by E2 or the selective agonist G-1 stimulated adenylyl cyclase, EGFR transactivation and downstream PI3K/Akt and ERK pathways, reducing infarct size in isolated perfused hearts and improving postischemic functional recovery [17,18]. Conversely, the GPR30 antagonist G-15 abolished these protective effects [18]. In addition, E2 modulated L-type calcium channel activity and intracellular calcium transients, limiting calcium overload during stress [19].

Cardioprotection against specific insults

Ischemia-reperfusion. E2, ERα-selective agonist PPT, ERβ-selective agonist DPN and G-1 all improved recovery of left ventricular developed pressure and reduced lactate dehydrogenase release, with effects attributed to Akt activation, reduced reactive oxygen species and preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential [12,17,20].

Pressure overload and hypertrophy. Estrogen and ERβ agonists attenuated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, reduced fetal gene expression (ANP, BNP, β-MHC) and inhibited fibrosis, partly via suppression of ERK and calcineurin signaling and enhancement of natriuretic peptide–cGMP pathways [10,11,21].

Oxidative and metabolic stress. E2 reduced hydrogen peroxide– and doxorubicin-induced cell death, enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and improved insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in cardiomyocytes [8,9,22]. Estrogen receptors localized to mitochondria were implicated in regulating mitochondrial DNA transcription and respiratory chain function [4,9].

Heart failure and apoptosis. Estrogen signaling decreased caspase-3 activation and cytochrome c release and increased the Bcl-2/Bax ratio in several models, correlating with improved ventricular remodeling [7,13].

Clinical implications of estrogen and ER signaling

Epidemiological data indicated lower cardiovascular incidence in premenopausal women than in age-matched men, with risk rising after menopause [23]. However, randomized trials of conventional hormone replacement therapy, including WHI and HERS, did not show primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention and noted increased risks of thromboembolism, stroke and breast cancer in some groups [24,25]. Subsequent analyses suggested a "timing hypothesis," whereby initiation of therapy near menopause onset yielded more favorable cardiovascular outcomes than delayed initiation [26]. These findings stimulated interest in receptor-selective approaches that retain cardiac benefits while limiting proliferative effects in the breast and uterus.

Phytoestrogens as candidate alternatives

Phytoestrogens, comprising isoflavones (genistein, daidzein, equol), lignans, coumestans and stilbenes (resveratrol), bind ERs with generally higher affinity for ERβ than ERα [27,28]. In experimental models, genistein reduced infarct size, activated Akt and eNOS and decreased apoptosis in ischemia-reperfusion, with effects blocked by the ER antagonist ICI 182,780, confirming ER dependence [29,30]. Daidzein and its metabolite equol improved endothelial function and reduced hypertrophic responses in ovariectomized animals [31,32]. Resveratrol activated SIRT1, AMPK and PI3K/Akt signaling and protected cardiomyocytes against oxidative injury, partly through ER-mediated mechanisms [33,34]. Several phytoestrogens were also shown to act through GPR30; genistein and quercetin induced rapid GPR30-dependent signaling in various cell types, including cardiac cells [35,36]. Additional protective actions included antioxidant activity, anti-inflammatory effects and improved lipid profiles [27,31].

Clinical studies of soy isoflavones produced mixed results. Meta-analyses reported modest reductions in LDL cholesterol, blood pressure and improved flow-mediated dilation, particularly in postmenopausal women and in equol producers, but large trials showed inconsistent effects on hard cardiovascular endpoints and atherosclerosis progression [37–39]. Safety data suggested that dietary-level intake did not increase breast or endometrial cancer risk, although long-term data for concentrated supplements remain limited [40].

Summary of findings

Collectively, the evidence indicates that ERα, ERβ and GPR30 mediate complementary genomic and nongenomic cardioprotective mechanisms in cardiomyocytes. Phytoestrogens, particularly ERβ-preferring compounds, reproduce many of these pathways experimentally, but heterogeneity in compounds, doses, metabolism and study populations limits clinical translation [27,37,39].

The evidence reviewed here supports the view that E2 confers cardioprotection mainly through ER-dependent signaling in cardiomyocytes, and that plant-derived compounds with estrogenic activity can partly reproduce these actions. ERα, ERβ and GPR30 do not act as redundant receptors. Each engages distinct but overlapping genomic and nongenomic cascades, including PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, eNOS/NO, and the regulation of mitochondrial function, calcium handling and apoptosis [1,2]. The result is a pleiotropic protective phenotype in ischemia/reperfusion injury, pressure overload, doxorubicin toxicity and oxidative stress. Understanding which receptor drives which beneficial outcome is central to designing safer estrogen-based interventions.

A recurring theme is that ERα and ERβ both mediate protection but may differ in context. ERα activation has been linked to attenuation of infarct size, preservation of contractile function and induction of pro-survival kinases, whereas ERβ has been associated with anti-hypertrophic and anti-fibrotic effects and with improved mitochondrial homeostasis [3,4]. GPR30 mediates rapid signaling, including EGFR transactivation and cAMP/Ca²⁺ modulation, and its agonists reduce ischemic injury without classical uterotrophic effects [5]. These findings imply that receptor-selective ligands might retain the cardiac benefits of E2 while avoiding proliferative effects in breast and uterine tissue. However, much of the mechanistic data derive from rodent models and cultured cardiomyocytes, often using supraphysiological concentrations or ovariectomized animals, which limits direct translation to postmenopausal women.

The clinical history of estrogen therapy illustrates this translational gap. Observational studies suggested that hormone therapy lowered coronary risk, but the Women's Health Initiative and HERS trials did not show primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention and reported increased thromboembolic and breast cancer risks with conjugated equine estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate [6,7]. Subsequent analyses led to the "timing hypothesis": benefit may occur when therapy begins close to menopause, before established atherosclerosis alters vascular ER expression and signaling [8]. Age-, time- and formulation-dependent differences in ER abundance, ER splice variants and receptor methylation may explain this heterogeneity. Thus, the cardioprotective potential of estrogenic signaling is real but conditional, and any alternative strategy must account for these variables.

Phytoestrogens, including isoflavones (genistein, daidzein), lignans, coumestans, resveratrol and related polyphenols, are attractive alternatives because they bind ERs, often with preferential affinity for ERβ, and show a lower risk profile in many experimental systems [9,10]. In cardiomyocytes and animal models, genistein and daidzein activate Akt and eNOS, reduce oxidative stress, limit apoptosis and attenuate hypertrophy, effects that are frequently abolished by ER antagonists such as ICI 182,780, supporting receptor dependence [11]. Equol, a gut-derived daidzein metabolite with high ERβ affinity, has drawn interest because individual capacity to produce it may explain variable clinical responses to soy [12]. Beyond ER binding, many phytoestrogens also act as antioxidants, modulate SIRT1 and AMPK, and influence lipid metabolism, so their benefits may not be solely estrogenic, which complicates mechanistic attribution.

Clinical data on phytoestrogens remain modest and inconsistent. Meta-analyses report small improvements in LDL cholesterol, blood pressure and endothelial function with soy isoflavones, but effects on hard cardiovascular endpoints are unproven [13,14]. Trials vary widely in dose, compound, duration, population age, baseline diet and equol-producer status. Some studies of subclinical atherosclerosis show benefit only in early postmenopausal women, echoing the timing hypothesis [15]. Safety concerns also persist: phytoestrogens may behave as partial agonists or antagonists depending on tissue, receptor ratio and endogenous estrogen levels, and their long-term effects on breast and endometrial tissue, thyroid function and drug interactions require further study. Poor bioavailability and extensive metabolism further limit therapeutic consistency.

Several limitations of the present synthesis should be acknowledged. As a narrative review, it is subject to selection bias, and the available literature favors positive findings. Sex differences in cardiac biology are rarely studied directly, and many studies use only one sex or lack adequate controls for endogenous hormones. The contribution of non-cardiomyocyte cells, including endothelial cells, fibroblasts and immune cells, to ER-mediated protection is incompletely resolved, and cardiomyocyte-specific knockout models remain limited. Likewise, GPR30 pharmacology is controversial, with debate on its subcellular localization and ligand specificity [5].

Future work should address these gaps in several ways. First, cell-type-specific and inducible ER knockout models, combined with receptor-selective agonists, would clarify the individual roles of ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in cardiac pathology. Second, well-designed randomized trials should standardize phytoestrogen formulation and dose, stratify participants by age, years since menopause and equol-producing status, and use imaging and clinical endpoints. Third, pharmacological development of selective ER modulators, biased GPR30 agonists and optimized phytoestrogen derivatives or delivery systems (for example nanoformulations) could improve bioavailability and tissue selectivity. Finally, integrating omics approaches and gut microbiome profiling may help identify responders and define personalized strategies.

In conclusion, estrogen exerts cardioprotective effects through ERα, ERβ and GPR30 by coordinating survival signaling, redox balance, mitochondrial integrity and calcium homeostasis in cardiomyocytes. Conventional hormone therapy has shown limited and risk-laden clinical benefit, which has prompted the search for safer approaches. Phytoestrogens, particularly ERβ-preferring compounds, show promising cardioprotective mechanisms in preclinical studies and may serve as alternatives or adjuncts to estrogen replacement therapy. Nonetheless, robust clinical evidence is lacking, and their use should be considered investigational for cardiovascular protection until mechanistically informed, adequately powered trials establish efficacy and safety.

Pregnancy loss is the most common complication of early pregnancy in humans. Miscarriage, or spontaneous abortion, is defined as the spontaneous loss of a fetus before it is viable, and it occurs in approximately 15–20% of clinically recognized pregnancies [1,2]. If biochemical pregnancies and losses that occur before a pregnancy is clinically recognized are included, the true incidence is considerably higher, and it has been estimated that up to half of all conceptions fail to progress [3]. Most sporadic miscarriages result from random chromosomal abnormalities of the embryo and are not likely to recur. A smaller group of women, however, experience repeated losses, a condition referred to as recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), recurrent miscarriage, or habitual abortion.

RSA is classically defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses before the twentieth week of gestation [4]. Some professional societies, including the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology, have proposed a lower threshold of two or more losses for initiating evaluation, recognizing the substantial emotional burden and the clinical value of earlier investigation [5,6]. By the traditional definition RSA affects about 1% of couples trying to conceive, whereas about 2–5% experience two or more losses [2,7]. The risk of subsequent miscarriage rises with the number of previous losses and with maternal age, so a history of repeated loss itself is an independent predictor of further failure [8]. Beyond the physical risks, RSA is associated with considerable psychological morbidity, including anxiety, depression, and grief, as well as a heavy burden on health care resources [9].

The etiology of RSA is multifactorial, and in many cases it remains incompletely understood. Established causes include parental chromosomal abnormalities, uterine anatomical defects such as septa, fibroids, and intrauterine adhesions, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and other immunological disturbances, infections, thrombophilic states, environmental and lifestyle factors, and endocrine disorders [4,10]. Even after extensive evaluation, no cause is identified in approximately half of couples, and this unexplained group continues to pose a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge [10]. Endocrine abnormalities are thought to account for roughly 8–12% of cases, which makes them one of the more common and potentially treatable contributors [11].

Successful implantation and maintenance of early pregnancy depend on a finely coordinated hormonal environment. After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estrogen, which transform the endometrium into a receptive decidua, suppress uterine contractility, and modulate the maternal immune response toward tolerance of the semi-allogeneic conceptus [12]. Thyroid hormones, insulin, prolactin, and androgens also influence follicular development, oocyte quality, endometrial receptivity, and placental function [13]. Disturbance of any part of this regulatory network may therefore compromise implantation, trophoblast invasion, or early embryonic development and lead to pregnancy loss.

Several endocrine conditions have been implicated in RSA. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrinopathy of reproductive-age women, is characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and frequently insulin resistance and obesity, and it has been associated with an increased risk of early miscarriage [14,15]. Hyperprolactinemia may impair folliculogenesis and corpus luteum function, and dopamine agonist treatment has been reported to improve pregnancy outcome in affected women [16]. Luteal phase defect, an inadequate progesterone-mediated endometrial secretory response, has long been proposed as a cause of implantation failure and early loss, although its diagnostic criteria and clinical significance remain debated [17]. Thyroid dysfunction, both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism as well as thyroid autoimmunity, has been linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage [18,19]. Diabetes mellitus with poor glycemic control during the periconceptional period increases the risk of miscarriage and congenital malformations through metabolic disturbance of the developing embryo [20]. Hyperandrogenism, whether of ovarian or adrenal origin, may adversely affect endometrial receptivity and early placentation [21].

Despite a large body of literature, the evidence on the relationship between these endocrine disorders and RSA is heterogeneous. Studies differ in their diagnostic criteria, sample sizes, and control populations, and it is often difficult to separate cause from association, as in the case of PCOS, in which obesity, insulin resistance, and elevated luteinizing hormone may each contribute independently [14]. Likewise, the benefit of interventions such as progesterone supplementation, levothyroxine, metformin, and dopamine agonists remains controversial in some settings [22,23]. Because many of these conditions are readily detectable and treatable, clarifying their role is of obvious clinical importance, as appropriate screening and management could improve the live birth rate in affected couples.

In this context, the present article reviews the role of endocrine dysfunction in patients with recurrent spontaneous abortion. Relevant publications were identified through electronic databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using key words related to recurrent miscarriage and specific endocrine abnormalities. The findings were then grouped according to the individual disorders, namely PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism, in order to summarize current understanding of their pathophysiological mechanisms, diagnostic approaches, and treatment options.

This narrative review was designed to summarize current evidence on the contribution of endocrine disorders to recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA). A narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis because the available studies differ widely in design, diagnostic criteria, populations, and outcome definitions, which limits quantitative pooling. The review was planned and reported in accordance with the general principles for narrative reviews, including a transparent search strategy, explicit eligibility criteria, and structured data synthesis [1,2].

**Literature search strategy**

A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and other electronic resources accessible through institutional library services. The search covered articles published from database inception to the date of final search. Searches combined controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings, MeSH) and free-text terms to maximize sensitivity. The main key words and their combinations were: "recurrent spontaneous abortion," "recurrent pregnancy loss," "habitual abortion," "recurrent miscarriage," "endocrine dysfunction," "polycystic ovarian syndrome," "hyperandrogenism," "hyperprolactinemia," "luteal phase defect," "progesterone," "thyroid dysfunction," "hypothyroidism," "thyroid autoimmunity," "diabetes mellitus," "insulin resistance," and "obesity." Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used to combine terms; for instance, "recurrent miscarriage AND thyroid" or "recurrent pregnancy loss AND (insulin resistance OR diabetes)." Reference lists of relevant reviews, guidelines, and original studies were also hand-searched to identify additional publications not captured by the electronic search [3].

**Definitions applied**

Because terminology for pregnancy loss varies among professional bodies, the definition used in this review was established a priori. RSA was defined as three or more consecutive spontaneous pregnancy losses before the 20th week of gestation, in keeping with the traditional definition [4]. Studies using the more recent definition of two or more losses, as recommended by some societies [5,6], were included provided that the criteria were clearly stated and the findings were interpreted with that distinction in mind. Miscarriage was defined as spontaneous loss of a fetus before viability.

**Eligibility criteria**

Articles were included if they (i) were original research (case–control, cohort, cross-sectional, or randomized controlled studies), meta-analyses, systematic reviews, or clinical practice guidelines; (ii) examined the relationship between an endocrine abnormality and RSA or recurrent pregnancy loss, or evaluated diagnostic or therapeutic interventions for such abnormalities in women with RSA; (iii) involved human participants; and (iv) were published in English. The endocrine conditions considered were polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction (including overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, and thyroid autoimmunity), and diabetes mellitus together with related disturbances of glucose metabolism.

Articles were excluded if they (i) focused exclusively on anatomical, genetic, infectious, or immunological causes of RSA without an endocrine component; (ii) were case reports, editorials, conference abstracts without full text, or letters lacking original data; (iii) concerned sporadic single miscarriage, induced abortion, or stillbirth beyond 20 weeks only; (iv) were animal or in vitro studies, unless they provided essential mechanistic background; or (v) were duplicate publications. Where overlapping datasets were identified, the most complete or most recent report was retained.

**Study selection**

Titles and abstracts retrieved from the searches were screened for relevance. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were then obtained and assessed against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Disagreements regarding eligibility were resolved by discussion among the authors until consensus was reached. Priority was given to recent publications, large well-designed studies, randomized trials, and meta-analyses, while older landmark studies were retained when they provided foundational evidence or when more recent data were scarce.

**Data extraction and organization**

For each included publication, information was extracted on the first author and year, country, study design, sample size, characteristics of the study population, diagnostic criteria for the endocrine disorder, main findings (such as prevalence in women with RSA, odds ratios or relative risks for pregnancy loss, and hormonal parameters), and reported effects of treatment on pregnancy outcome. The results of the separate searches were then combined and grouped according to the specific endocrine abnormality, namely PCOS and hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, and diabetes mellitus. Within each group, evidence was organized to address epidemiology, proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies [7].

**Quality considerations and synthesis**

A formal quality scoring tool was not applied, consistent with the narrative design. Nonetheless, the strength of evidence was considered qualitatively by taking into account study design, sample size, adequacy of control groups, clarity of diagnostic definitions, and adjustment for confounders such as maternal age, body mass index, and number of previous losses. Discrepancies among studies, such as differences in reference ranges for thyrotropin or in the definition of luteal phase defect, were noted and discussed as potential sources of heterogeneity. Findings were synthesized descriptively, and areas of controversy or insufficient evidence were explicitly identified to guide recommendations for future research [8].

**Ethical considerations**

As this review used only previously published data and involved no direct contact with human participants, ethical approval and informed consent were not required.

Review of the literature identified endocrine abnormalities as contributing to a substantial proportion of recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA) cases. Studies were grouped according to the principal endocrine disorder examined: polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect (LPD), thyroid dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, and hyperandrogenism. Findings for each group are summarized below.

**Polycystic ovarian syndrome**

PCOS was consistently reported as being more prevalent among women with RSA than in the general population. Prevalence estimates in women with recurrent pregnancy loss ranged from approximately 8% to 40%, depending on diagnostic criteria and the population studied [1,2]. Several mechanisms were proposed. Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance, frequently present in PCOS independent of body mass index, were associated with elevated plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 levels, reduced fibrinolytic activity, and impaired endometrial receptivity [3]. Elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations in the follicular phase were associated with premature oocyte maturation and poorer oocyte quality, although later trials did not confirm that LH suppression improves outcomes [4]. Obesity, which often accompanies PCOS, was independently associated with increased miscarriage risk [5]. Reduced glycodelin and insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 in the endometrium were also reported. Evidence on metformin was inconsistent: some observational studies suggested a reduced first-trimester loss rate, whereas randomized trials showed no clear benefit in live birth rates [6,7].

**Hyperprolactinemia**

Elevated prolactin was found in a minority of women with RSA, and both excessively high and abnormally low levels were linked to adverse outcomes. Hyperprolactinemia was thought to impair folliculogenesis and corpus luteum function, thereby reducing progesterone production and compromising endometrial development [8]. Prolactin also appears to have immunomodulatory and decidual effects, so that disturbed levels may affect implantation. In a small randomized study, women with RSA and hyperprolactinemia treated with bromocriptine had a significantly higher live birth rate than untreated controls (86% versus 52%) [9]. Cabergoline was likewise reported to reduce pregnancy loss, with a favorable tolerability profile [10]. However, the number of controlled studies remains limited.

**Luteal phase defect**

LPD, characterized by inadequate progesterone secretion or insufficient endometrial response to progesterone, was reported in approximately 8–12% of women with RSA in older series [11]. Diagnosis remains problematic: endometrial dating by biopsy showed poor reproducibility, and a single midluteal serum progesterone value has limited predictive value because of pulsatile secretion [12]. Consequently, LPD is regarded by many authors as a controversial entity. Progesterone supplementation has been widely used; a meta-analysis of small trials suggested a reduction in miscarriage among women with recurrent loss [13], and a subsequent large randomized trial found no overall improvement in live birth rate, although subgroup analysis indicated possible benefit in women with recurrent miscarriage and early pregnancy bleeding [14].

**Thyroid dysfunction**

Both overt hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism were associated with increased risk of pregnancy loss. Overt hypothyroidism was linked to anovulation, luteal insufficiency, and elevated prolactin through increased thyrotropin-releasing hormone [15]. Subclinical hypothyroidism, defined by elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) with normal free thyroxine, was found more frequently in women with RSA, and treatment with levothyroxine was associated with reduced loss rates in some cohorts [16]. Thyroid autoimmunity, indicated by anti-thyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies, was associated with approximately a two- to threefold increase in miscarriage risk in meta-analyses, even in euthyroid women [17]. Nevertheless, randomized trials of levothyroxine in euthyroid antibody-positive women showed no significant improvement in live birth rates [18]. Hyperthyroidism, most commonly Graves' disease, was associated with increased loss when poorly controlled, whereas adequate treatment with antithyroid drugs normalized risk [19].

**Diabetes mellitus**

Poorly controlled diabetes was strongly related to early pregnancy loss and congenital malformations. The risk of miscarriage correlated with periconceptional glycosylated hemoglobin levels, with markedly higher loss rates when values were elevated [20]. Proposed mechanisms included embryonic exposure to hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, vascular disease, and impaired decidualization. In contrast, women with well-controlled diabetes had miscarriage rates comparable to those of nondiabetic women [21]. Screening of unselected women with RSA identified overt diabetes rarely, but impaired glucose tolerance and insulin resistance were more frequent than in controls [22].

**Hyperandrogenism**

Elevated free androgen index, high testosterone, and raised dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate were reported in women with RSA, with or without PCOS [23]. Low sex hormone-binding globulin, reflecting hyperinsulinemia, increased the bioavailability of androgens, which may adversely affect endometrial receptivity by altering expression of integrins and homeobox genes [24]. Late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia was identified in a small number of cases. Data on treatment, including glucocorticoids or insulin sensitizers, were sparse.

**Other endocrine factors**

Reduced ovarian reserve, indicated by elevated follicle-stimulating hormone or low anti-Müllerian hormone, was associated with recurrent loss, probably through increased oocyte aneuploidy [25]. Vitamin D deficiency was also associated with RSA and autoimmunity, but interventional evidence is lacking [26].

**Summary of findings**

Overall, the strongest evidence for causation and effective treatment was for overt thyroid disease, poorly controlled diabetes, and symptomatic hyperprolactinemia. For PCOS, LPD, hyperandrogenism, and thyroid autoimmunity, associations were evident, but evidence supporting specific therapies remained inconclusive. Heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria, small sample sizes, and a scarcity of well-designed randomized trials limited the strength of many conclusions.

Recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA) remains a distressing and clinically challenging condition, and in a substantial proportion of couples no cause is identified. This review has examined the contribution of endocrine disorders, including polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect (LPD), thyroid dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, and hyperandrogenism, to pregnancy loss. Taken together, the evidence suggests that endocrine abnormalities are among the more common and potentially modifiable contributors to RSA, although the strength of the evidence differs considerably between conditions.

Thyroid disease provides the clearest example of a treatable endocrine cause. Overt hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism are both associated with infertility and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and adequate thyroid hormone is essential for implantation, placental development, and early fetal growth [1,2]. Thyroid autoimmunity, even in euthyroid women, has been associated with an increased risk of miscarriage, possibly through a shared immune dysregulation or through subtle limitations in thyroid reserve under the increased demands of pregnancy [3]. However, trials of levothyroxine in euthyroid women with thyroid peroxidase antibodies have yielded inconsistent results, and current guidelines do not uniformly recommend treatment [4]. Similarly, the threshold at which subclinical hypothyroidism should be treated in women with recurrent loss remains debated, although treatment is generally advised when TSH is above the trimester-specific reference range. Targeted screening of TSH and thyroid antibodies in women with RSA therefore appears reasonable, whereas universal treatment of antibody positivity is not yet justified.

PCOS is probably the most prevalent endocrine disorder in women with recurrent loss. Several mechanisms have been proposed, including hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, obesity, elevated luteinizing hormone, and impaired endometrial receptivity with reduced glycodelin and altered integrin expression [5,6]. The relative contribution of each factor is difficult to separate because they are closely interrelated. Insulin resistance has received particular attention, and metformin has been proposed to reduce miscarriage rates, but randomized evidence is inconclusive, with some studies showing benefit and others showing none [7]. Lifestyle modification and weight reduction remain the cornerstone of management, as obesity independently increases miscarriage risk. Likewise, hyperandrogenism, whether of ovarian or adrenal origin, may disrupt folliculogenesis and endometrial development, but the free androgen index and related measures are not standardized, which limits comparison between studies [8].

Hyperprolactinemia interferes with the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and may impair corpus luteum function, yet prolactin also has local roles in decidualization and immune modulation. Both excessively high and excessively low prolactin levels may therefore be detrimental [9]. Dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine have been reported to improve live birth rates in women with RSA and mildly elevated prolactin, but the available trials are small and methodologically limited [10]. Because bromocriptine is generally safe in early pregnancy, a pragmatic approach is to treat documented hyperprolactinemia while recognizing that the evidence base is modest.

LPD, characterized by inadequate progesterone production or an inadequate endometrial response to it, is biologically plausible as a cause of early loss because progesterone sustains the secretory endometrium and promotes a Th2-biased immune environment at the maternal-fetal interface. Nevertheless, the diagnosis remains controversial. Endometrial dating has poor reproducibility and does not discriminate fertile from infertile women, and single mid-luteal progesterone measurements fluctuate because of pulsatile secretion [11]. Progesterone supplementation has been widely used, and meta-analyses suggest a possible benefit in women with recurrent miscarriage, particularly those with a history of three or more losses and early bleeding, though the largest trials have shown benefit mainly in selected subgroups [12]. Better diagnostic criteria for LPD, probably combining hormonal and molecular markers of endometrial receptivity, are needed.

Diabetes mellitus illustrates the importance of metabolic control. Poorly controlled diabetes, reflected by elevated glycosylated hemoglobin in the periconceptional period, is associated with increased miscarriage and congenital malformation, probably through hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress and vascular dysfunction [13]. By contrast, well-controlled diabetes carries a risk similar to that of the general population. Preconception counseling and optimization of glycemic control are therefore essential.

Several limitations of the literature should be acknowledged. Definitions of RSA vary, with some societies including two consecutive losses and others requiring three, which affects prevalence estimates and comparability. Many studies are retrospective, have small samples, lack appropriate controls, or fail to adjust for confounders such as maternal age, obesity, and karyotypic abnormalities of the embryo, which account for a large proportion of early losses. In addition, endocrine disorders frequently coexist, so attributing loss to a single abnormality may be simplistic. Finally, our review was based on a non-systematic search of electronic databases, so selection bias cannot be excluded.

These limitations point to clear research priorities. Large prospective, adequately powered randomized trials are needed to determine whether treatment of subclinical thyroid disease, thyroid autoimmunity, mild hyperprolactinemia, and insulin resistance improves live birth rates. Standardized diagnostic criteria for LPD and hyperandrogenism, together with studies of endometrial receptivity markers and genetic or epigenetic determinants, may allow more individualized therapy.

In conclusion, endocrine dysfunction is an important and frequently correctable factor in recurrent spontaneous abortion. Women with RSA should undergo systematic endocrine evaluation, including thyroid function and antibodies, prolactin, glucose metabolism, and assessment for PCOS and hyperandrogenism. Where abnormalities are identified, appropriate treatment, such as thyroid hormone replacement, dopamine agonists, glycemic control, weight management, and, in selected cases, progesterone support, should be instituted ideally before conception. A multidisciplinary approach and supportive counseling can improve outcomes, although higher-quality evidence is required to refine screening and treatment strategies.

Human pose estimation, the task of localizing the body joints of a person in an image or video, is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in action recognition, human-computer interaction, surveillance, and animation. Over the past few years, deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have dramatically advanced the accuracy of pose estimation on static images. Among the most successful designs are multi-stage architectures, such as Convolutional Pose Machines and stacked hourglass networks, in which a sequence of CNN stages progressively refines the joint confidence maps predicted by the preceding stage. Each stage takes the image evidence together with the previous belief maps and produces a more accurate estimate, so that long-range dependencies among joints are implicitly captured through large effective receptive fields.

Despite this success on still images, applying these models to videos remains unsatisfactory. The most direct approach is to run a single-image model independently on every frame. This has three main drawbacks. First, it is computationally expensive: a multi-stage network must be fully evaluated for each frame, and the cost grows linearly with the number of stages. Second, frame-wise prediction ignores the temporal structure of video. Adjacent frames show nearly the same pose, yet independent predictions are not constrained to agree, which produces jittering outputs and visible flicker. Third, video frames frequently suffer from motion blur, defocus, self-occlusion, and unusual viewpoints. A model that sees only one frame has no means of recovering from such degradation, whereas a human observer easily infers the hidden or blurred joint position from preceding frames. Together, these problems cause performance degeneration and make the predictions inconsistent over time.

Previous attempts to address video pose estimation usually add post-processing or explicit temporal modeling on top of single-frame networks. Examples include optical flow to propagate predictions between frames, graphical models or tracking-by-detection frameworks that enforce smoothness, and spatio-temporal convolutions over stacked frames. These approaches typically require additional components, such as flow estimators, which are expensive and prone to error under exactly the conditions (blur, occlusion) where help is most needed. They also treat temporal reasoning as separate from the pose network itself, which complicates training and inference.

In this paper, we propose a different view. We observe that if the weights of the stages in a multi-stage CNN are shared, the network becomes equivalent to a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unrolled over stages: each stage applies the same transformation to the previous belief maps and the image features. Under this view, stage-wise refinement is simply a recurrent computation. This observation has two important consequences. First, it decouples the stages from one another. Rather than running every stage on every frame, the recurrence can be unrolled along the time axis of the video, so that each new frame needs only one pass through the shared module, with the refinement carried over from earlier frames. This yields a significant speedup when processing video. Second, the recurrent formulation allows us to insert Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units naturally, so that the refinement is performed across video frames instead of across redundant stages of a single frame.

We call the resulting model the LSTM Pose Machine. It consists of a fully convolutional feature extractor, an initial prediction module, and a recurrent refinement module with convolutional LSTM units whose parameters are shared across all frames.
