For each locus, we defined credible sets of variants with posterior probability of causality, assuming a single causal variant, and then tested overlap with ChIP-Seq data for histone modifications (H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K27ac) and transcription factors (including ER, FOXA1 and GATA3) from mammary cell lines, as well as DNase hypersensitivity sites. Credible variants were significantly enriched in regulatory elements active in breast cells, supporting a regulatory mechanism for most associations.

At 18q12.3, the credible risk variants overlapped enhancer elements marked in breast epithelial cell lines. ChIA-PET data for RNA polymerase II and ER in MCF-7 cells indicated that these elements physically interact with the promoter of SETBP1, located some distance from the association signal. Expression analyses were consistent with this, and SETBP1 emerged as the most likely target gene in this region. SETBP1 has been implicated in leukaemia and in regulation of PP2A phosphatase activity, providing a possible link with tumorigenesis.

At 1q21.1, the association signal spanned a region containing several genes. Credible variants fell in elements marked by ER and FOXA1 binding and active enhancer histone marks. ChIA-PET interactions connected these elements to the promoters of RNF115 and PDZK1, whereas other nearby genes showed no such interaction. RNF115 encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase previously reported to be overexpressed in breast cancer, and PDZK1 is an estrogen-responsive scaffolding protein. These data nominate both genes as likely targets, although the possibility that the two are regulated jointly by the same element cannot be excluded.

**A coding variant in EXO1**

At 1q43, the association signal was best explained by a missense variant in EXO1, encoding the exonuclease 1 protein involved in DNA mismatch repair and homologous recombination (p.Glu670Gly). This variant was the top-ranked SNP in the region and accounted for most of the posterior probability in the credible set. The substitution lies in a region of the protein predicted to be functionally important, and was predicted to be deleterious by several in silico tools. Conditional analysis on this variant removed the association signal in the region, indicating that no additional independent signals were present. Although other noncoding variants in strong linkage disequilibrium cannot be excluded, the combination of statistical evidence and the known function of EXO1 in maintaining genome stability makes the amino-acid change a strong candidate for the causal variant.

**Contribution to familial risk**

Including the 15 new loci, the total number of known common susceptibility loci reaches approximately 94. Under a multiplicative model, the new variants explain an additional ~1.5% of the two-fold familial relative risk of breast cancer, increasing the proportion explained by all known common variants from about 14% to about 16%. Women in the top percentile of a polygenic risk score based on all variants had substantially higher risk than those in the middle of the distribution, and the new loci modestly improved risk stratification. These results indicate that many additional common variants with small effects remain to be discovered, and that larger studies and functional follow-up will be needed to identify the underlying causal variants and genes.

This meta-analysis of 11 GWAS and the iCOGS experiment, comprising more than 120,000 women of European ancestry, identified 15 previously unreported breast cancer susceptibility loci at genome-wide significance. Together with the 79 loci reported previously, these findings bring the number of known common susceptibility regions to about 94. The new associations have modest effect sizes, with per-allele odds ratios mostly between 1.02 and 1.10. Many of the variants are relatively common, and the loci were detectable only because of the sample size and the denser imputed coverage provided by the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel. This is consistent with a polygenic architecture in which many common variants of small effect contribute to risk. Each additional locus adds only a small increment to the explained familial risk, so the gains from further discovery are likely to diminish unless sample sizes grow substantially or other classes of variation are targeted.

A central challenge after GWAS discovery is moving from association signals to causal variants and target genes. Most signals lie in non-coding regions, where they are likely to affect regulatory elements. We therefore integrated the association results with ChIP-Seq data for histone marks and transcription factors in mammary cell lines, and with ChIA-PET chromatin interaction data from ENCODE. At 18q12.3, the credible risk variants overlapped regulatory elements that appeared to interact with the SETBP1 promoter, suggesting that SETBP1 is a likely target. SETBP1 has been implicated in myeloid malignancies, where it is mutated or overexpressed, and it may inhibit the tumor suppressor PP2A, which makes it a biologically plausible candidate for breast cancer. At 1q21.1, the regulatory annotation and the chromatin interaction data pointed to RNF115 and PDZK1. RNF115 encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that has been linked to estrogen receptor and growth factor receptor trafficking and degradation, and PDZK1 is an estrogen-responsive scaffold protein. These candidates are supported by in silico evidence and need functional validation. Experiments such as allele-specific expression, reporter assays, and genome editing of the risk variants in mammary cells would be needed to confirm the regulatory mechanisms and the direction of effect.

In contrast to most signals, one association appears to be driven by a missense variant in EXO1. EXO1 encodes exonuclease 1, which participates in DNA mismatch repair, homologous recombination, and telomere maintenance. The association with a coding substitution fits with the well-established role of DNA repair genes in breast cancer predisposition, as exemplified by BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, and CHEK2. Rare, high- and moderate-penetrance variants in these genes are known to confer risk, and our finding suggests that common variation affecting DNA repair function also contributes. Whether the amino-acid change alters EXO1 activity, stability, or protein interactions remains to be established. Variation in EXO1 has also been implicated in other cancers, and further study of its effect on tumor subtypes and on treatment response may be informative.

Several limitations should be noted. First, analyses were restricted to women of European ancestry, so the generalizability of these loci to other populations is unknown. Differences in linkage disequilibrium and allele frequencies may help fine-mapping in multi-ethnic studies, and replication in Asian, African, and Hispanic populations is a priority. Second, imputation based on the 1000 Genomes Project, although it greatly improves coverage, is less accurate for low-frequency variants, so some rarer variants of larger effect may have been missed or imperfectly tagged. Third, the combination of GWAS and custom-array data with different designs and coverage creates heterogeneity in imputation quality, which we addressed through quality filters and meta-analysis but which may still reduce power at some loci. Fourth, our functional annotations rely on cell line data, which may not capture regulatory activity in primary mammary epithelial cell types or in the tumor microenvironment. Chromatin interaction data are available for a limited number of cell types and conditions, so target genes may be missed or misassigned. Finally, we have not fully examined heterogeneity by tumor subtype, such as estrogen receptor status, grade, or HER2 status. Subtype-specific analyses are likely to reveal that some of these loci are specific to particular disease subtypes, which would aid in understanding etiology and in risk prediction.

The clinical implications of these findings relate mainly to risk stratification. Individually, the variants have little predictive value, but combined into a polygenic risk score they can identify women at differing levels of risk. Each new locus modestly improves the score, and when combined with family history, mammographic density, and lifestyle factors, such scores might support tailored screening strategies, for example by starting mammography earlier in women at higher risk or reducing screening intensity in those at lower risk. Prospective evaluation in population settings is needed before implementation.

In conclusion, we identified 15 new breast cancer susceptibility loci, increasing the proportion of familial risk explained by common variants. Integrating genetic association data with regulatory annotation highlighted SETBP1, RNF115, and PDZK1 as likely target genes, and identified a probable causal missense variant in EXO1. These results extend our understanding of the biological pathways involved in breast cancer development, including DNA repair, ubiquitin-mediated protein regulation, and estrogen signaling. They also demonstrate that increasing sample sizes and improved imputation continue to yield new discoveries. Future work should combine larger and more diverse samples, deeper fine-mapping, and systematic functional studies to translate these associations into mechanistic insight and, ultimately, into improved prevention and early detection.

Epilepsy affects roughly 1% of the world population, and approximately one third of patients continue to experience seizures despite adequate pharmacological treatment [1,2]. For selected patients with medically refractory focal epilepsy, surgical resection or ablation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ) is the most effective therapeutic option, and its success depends on accurate delineation of the brain regions responsible for seizure generation [3]. When non-invasive investigations (scalp EEG, video monitoring, MRI, PET, MEG) fail to provide concordant localization, invasive recordings are required.

**Invasive monitoring with SEEG**

Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG), introduced by Talairach and Bancaud in the 1950s, consists of the stereotactic implantation of multiple depth electrodes, each carrying several contacts, to sample cortical and subcortical structures in three dimensions [4]. Compared with subdural grids, SEEG gives access to deep and sulcal structures, allows bilateral exploration without craniotomy, and has a favorable complication profile [5,6]. SEEG is also increasingly used in cognitive and systems neuroscience, where intracranial recordings offer unique spatial and temporal resolution in humans [7].

The clinical value of SEEG depends on knowing which anatomical structure each contact records from. Electrophysiological traces can be interpreted, and a resection planned, only if contact positions are expressed in the patient's anatomical space and, for group studies, in a common reference space [8]. Typically, electrode trajectories are planned on pre-implant MRI, implantation is performed with a stereotactic frame or robotic assistance, and a post-implant CT or Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) is acquired to verify the final positions. Because of bending of the shaft, brain shift, and inaccuracies in the entry point or in the insertion depth, the final position generally differs from the plan [9,10]. Planned coordinates therefore cannot replace the true contact locations, which must be recovered from the post-implant image.

**Limitations of current localization approaches**

In most centers, contact localization is performed by manual or semi-manual procedures. The post-implant CT is co-registered with the pre-implant MRI, and contacts, visible as hyperdense artifacts, are identified one by one with 3D visualization tools. A single implant can comprise 10–20 electrodes and 100–200 contacts, so this task takes hours per patient, requires trained personnel, and is vulnerable to inter- and intra-rater variability. Several tools have eased this process. Some offer graphical interfaces for contact marking and for visualization on the patient's anatomy [11,12], others use semi-automatic procedures that require the user to specify the extremities of each electrode and then interpolate the contacts along the axis assuming a known inter-contact spacing [13,14]. Related approaches have been developed for deep brain stimulation (DBS) lead reconstruction [15,16] and for subdural grids [17]. However, DBS leads are few (typically one or two), have a different geometry, and are usually isolated in space, whereas SEEG implants involve many closely spaced electrodes, often crossing or running in proximity, and with variable numbers of contacts. To our knowledge, no fully automatic method has been proposed that exploits the characteristics of SEEG implants to segment contacts without manual intervention.

**Rationale and approach**

Automatic segmentation of SEEG contacts poses several challenges. Metal contacts produce streaking and blooming artifacts in CT that blur contact boundaries, particularly in the anisotropic voxels typical of CBCT. Adjacent electrodes may be close enough that their intensity profiles merge after thresholding. Moreover, simple thresholding and connected-component analysis cannot discriminate between electrodes and other high-density structures such as the skull, bolts, or cables. A reliable algorithm must therefore incorporate prior knowledge of the implant.

Such prior knowledge is available in the clinical workflow: the surgical plan defines, for each electrode, a target point and an entry point, which together provide an initial estimate of the electrode axis. Given that actual trajectories remain close to the planned ones, although deviations occur, the plan can be used to initialize and constrain the search for the real electrode axis and the contacts along it. The electrode manufacturer's specification supplies the number of contacts, their length and their spacing, which can further regularize the identification of individual contacts.

In this paper we present an automatic algorithm for segmenting SEEG contacts from a thresholded post-implant CBCT volume with a resolution of 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm. The method uses the planned entry and target points as an initial estimate of each electrode axis and refines it using the image data. We implemented it in DEETO (DEep Electrode Trajectory Orientation), an open-source C++ prototype based on the Insight Toolkit (ITK) [18], to facilitate reuse and extension by the community.

We evaluate the approach along three dimensions. First, we assess the computational time relative to manual segmentation. Second, we quantify accuracy against contact positions manually segmented by experts on a subset of patients. Third, we assess whether the resulting positions correctly map contacts to anatomical regions, which is the quantity ultimately relevant for interpreting the recordings. Because the algorithm relies on the plan, we additionally study its robustness to deviations of the implanted electrodes from the planned trajectories, using a larger cohort.

The remainder of the paper describes the data and the algorithm, reports the experimental results, and discusses the implications and limitations of the method for clinical and research applications of SEEG.

### Study population and data acquisition

Twenty-eight patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy who underwent SEEG implantation were retrospectively included. Electrodes (Dixi Medical, 5–18 contacts each; contact length 2 mm, inter-contact spacing 1.5 mm, diameter 0.8 mm) were implanted under stereotactic guidance following an individually planned trajectory defined by a target point (deep) and an entry point (cortical surface) for each electrode. Planning was performed on pre-operative T1-weighted MRI with gadolinium enhancement. After implantation, a Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) volume was acquired with the stereotactic frame removed (voxel size 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm). All patients provided informed consent, and data were anonymized before processing.

A subset of 12 patients (35 multilead electrodes, 200 contacts) was manually segmented by two trained experts using a 3D visualization tool; the contact centers they identified served as the ground truth. The remaining 16 patients were used only for the robustness analysis.

### Preprocessing and registration

The CBCT volume was rigidly registered to the pre-operative MRI using a mutual-information-based registration, so that planned entry and target points could be expressed in CBCT coordinates. Registration was visually checked. The CBCT was then thresholded to retain only voxels with intensities consistent with metal (a fixed high-intensity threshold chosen to exclude bone), producing a binary volume containing the electrode contacts and, occasionally, residual artefacts or bolts. Because the contacts are separated by non-metallic insulation, each electrode appears as a sequence of disconnected or weakly connected high-intensity segments.

### Segmentation algorithm

The algorithm was designed around the prior knowledge that each electrode is a nearly straight, rigid cylinder whose approximate axis is given by the line joining the planned entry point **e** and target point **t**. It proceeds independently for each electrode in four steps.

**1. Region of interest extraction.** For each electrode, the thresholded voxels lying within a cylindrical region of radius *r* around the planned axis segment **et** were selected. The radius was chosen larger than the expected deviation between planned and actual trajectories but smaller than half the minimum distance between neighboring electrodes, thereby limiting contamination from adjacent electrodes. The selected voxels were converted to physical coordinates, yielding a point set *P*.

**2. Axis refinement.** The planned axis was used as the initial estimate of the true electrode axis. The principal axis of *P* was computed by principal component analysis (PCA), giving a centroid **c** and a direction **d** (first eigenvector, oriented from entry to target). To reduce the influence of outliers, such as bolt voxels or artefact fragments, voxels whose orthogonal distance from the current axis exceeded a tolerance proportional to the electrode radius were discarded, and the fit was repeated until convergence of the direction (angular change below 10⁻³ rad) or a maximum number of iterations was reached.

**3. Contact detection along the axis.** The remaining voxels were projected onto the refined axis, and a one-dimensional intensity profile along the axis coordinate *s* was built by accumulating voxel counts in bins smaller than the voxel size. This profile is approximately periodic, with maxima at contacts and minima at insulating spacers. The profile was smoothed with a Gaussian kernel, and the contacts were localized from the profile’s local maxima. The known electrode geometry (number of contacts, contact length, and spacing, i.e., a 3.5 mm center-to-center pitch) was used to constrain the search: the position of the deepest contact was identified from the tip of the profile, and the remaining contact centers were placed at successive known offsets along the axis. Local adjustments of each center were obtained as the centroid of the voxels assigned to that contact, after which the centers were re-projected onto the axis.

**4. Output.** For each electrode, the algorithm returns the contact centers in CBCT/MRI space, the electrode axis, and the labelled voxels of each contact. Contacts were assigned to anatomical regions by transforming their coordinates into the MRI-derived parcellation (cortical and subcortical labels from automatic segmentation of the T1 image) and recording the label at each contact center; contacts located in white matter or outside the brain were identified accordingly.

### Implementation

The method was implemented in C++ as DEETO (Deep Electrode Tracking and Orientation), an open-source prototype based on the Insight Toolkit (ITK) for image I/O, thresholding, connected-component handling, and spatial transformations. The input consists of the thresholded volume and a text file containing planned entry and target points and the electrode model. Execution time was measured on a standard workstation.

### Performance evaluation

Accuracy was quantified in the 12 manually segmented subjects as the Euclidean distance between each automatically detected contact center and the corresponding manual one. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation across contacts and subjects. Computation time per subject was compared with the time reported by the experts for manual segmentation. To assess the effect on clinical interpretation, the anatomical label assigned to each contact by the automatic and manual segmentations was compared, and the proportion of concordant labels was computed.

### Robustness to deviations from the planned trajectory

To test the sensitivity of the algorithm to differences between planned and actual electrode positions, all 28 subjects were used. For each electrode, the planned target point was artificially displaced from its original position by a controlled distance (0–12 mm) in randomly chosen directions perpendicular to and along the planned axis, while the entry point was kept fixed, simulating deep-brain displacement of the implanted shaft. The segmentation was repeated for each displacement, and the robustness error was defined as the distance between contact positions obtained with the displaced plan and those obtained with the original plan. Displacement tests were repeated over multiple random draws, and the error was summarized as a function of the displacement magnitude.

**Dataset and experimental setting**

The algorithm was evaluated on 28 patients who underwent SEEG implantation, for a total of 28 post-implant thresholded Cone-Beam CT volumes (voxel size 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm). Planned entry and target points were available for every electrode. A subset of 12 subjects (35 multilead electrodes, 200 contacts) was manually segmented by two experts, and these segmentations served as ground truth for accuracy assessment. The remaining 16 subjects, together with the 12 annotated ones, were used in the robustness analysis. All results below were obtained with a single parameter configuration, fixed a priori and not tuned on the annotated subset.

**Computational performance**

On a standard workstation, DEETO segmented all electrodes of a subject in less than 1 s, excluding image loading and file input/output. Runtime scaled approximately linearly with the number of electrodes, and the number of contacts per electrode had a negligible effect. Manual segmentation by experts required a few hours per subject, so the automated procedure reduces processing time by several orders of magnitude. No interactive 3D visualization or user supervision was required during execution.

**Segmentation accuracy**

Accuracy was quantified as the Euclidean distance between the contact centroids estimated by the algorithm and the corresponding manually identified centroids. Across the 200 contacts of the 12 annotated subjects, the mean localization error was 0.5 mm with a standard deviation across subjects of 0.06 mm. This error is below the in-plane voxel size (0.4 mm) multiplied by roughly 1.25 and smaller than the slice thickness (0.8 mm), so it lies within the resolution of the data. The error was distributed homogeneously along the electrode axis: contacts close to the entry point and those near the target showed comparable deviations, and no systematic bias in any direction was observed. Errors were similar across subjects, indicating no dependence on individual implantation geometry. All 35 electrodes were detected, and every contact was assigned to the correct position in the sequence along its electrode. The residual discrepancies were of the same order as the variability expected between two manual raters, which suggests that the automatic output is a plausible substitute for expert segmentation.

**Anatomical mapping**

To assess the practical value of the segmentation, contact coordinates were transferred to each subject's anatomical space and labeled according to a cortical and subcortical parcellation of the co-registered MRI. For the annotated subset, the anatomical label assigned to each contact from the automatic centroids was compared with that obtained from the manual centroids. The labels agreed for the large majority of contacts. Disagreements occurred only for contacts lying within about one voxel of a boundary between adjacent structures, notably at the gray–white matter interface, where a sub-millimetric displacement can change the assigned label. Contacts were thus mapped to gray matter, white matter, and deep nuclei in a manner consistent with expert localization. This enabled each electrophysiological channel to be associated with a defined anatomical region without manual intervention, so the interpretability of the recordings was preserved.

**Robustness to deviations from the planned trajectory**

The algorithm uses the planned entry and target points as the initial estimate of the electrode axis, so its sensitivity to differences between planned and actual positions was examined. Using the full 28-subject cohort, we simulated deep-brain displacements by shifting the planned target point away from its original position by increasing distances, up to 12 mm, while keeping the entry point fixed. For each displacement we compared the resulting contact positions with those obtained from the unperturbed plan. The differences remained below 0.005 mm for all displacements tested (< 12 mm), a value far below the voxel size and therefore negligible in practice. Segmentation of all electrodes was successful in every perturbed configuration, and no electrode was lost or swapped with a neighboring one. This indicates that the axis refinement step converges to the same solution across a wide basin of initial conditions, so the accuracy of the final result is essentially independent of the quality of the initial estimate within the range investigated. The clinical relevance of this finding is that actual implantation errors, which usually amount to a few millimeters at the target, are well within the range handled by the method.

**Summary of findings**

In summary, the proposed method (i) completed segmentation in less than one second per subject, (ii) reproduced expert segmentation with a mean error of 0.5 mm ± 0.06 mm, (iii) yielded anatomical labels consistent with those derived from manual localization, and (iv) was stable against displacements of the electrode shaft of up to 12 mm from the planned trajectory. These results were consistent across all subjects and electrodes analyzed.

**Principal findings and interpretation**

The present work introduces DEETO, to our knowledge the first automatic algorithm dedicated to segmenting SEEG contacts in post-implant CBCT volumes. The algorithm's main design choice is to use the planned entry and target points as a prior for the electrode axis, rather than to search the whole volume for candidate structures. This turns a difficult, unconstrained detection problem into a local, well-posed one: contacts are searched along a known trajectory, and the data only need to refine this initial estimate. Such a prior is always available in clinical practice, since trajectories are planned before surgery for safety and targeting reasons [1,2]. The method therefore adds no acquisition or planning burden.

The sub-millimetric error (0.5 mm ± 0.06 mm) is below the in-plane voxel size of the CBCT (0.4 mm) by only a small margin, and it is comparable to the contact length and to the variability that is expected between human raters. This suggests that the residual discrepancy from manual segmentation is dominated by the resolution of the image and the intrinsic ambiguity in defining a contact centroid, rather than by a systematic failure of the algorithm. The processing time of less than one second per subject, against several hours for manual labelling, is the most evident practical gain. It makes it feasible to process every implant routinely and to repeat the analysis after parameter changes, which is unrealistic with manual workflows.

**Robustness to deviations from the plan**

A recognized limitation of any plan-driven method is that the implanted electrode seldom follows the planned trajectory exactly. Bending of the shaft, skull-entry deflection and anchor-bolt tolerances all lead to deep-brain deviations that increase with trajectory length [3]. Our experiments on the 28-subject cohort show that, for displacements up to 12 mm, the segmentation error stays below 0.005 mm. This indicates that the plan is used only to initialize the search and that the final localization is driven by the image data. Because reported targeting errors in SEEG are typically a few millimetres [3,4], the tested range covers the clinically relevant situation with a considerable safety margin. We note, however, that the displacements were evaluated within the cohort and that the figure applies to the electrode geometries and thresholds used here; extreme deformations, such as markedly curved shafts, were not explicitly studied.

**Clinical and research implications**

Accurate contact localization is a prerequisite for interpreting SEEG traces, because the same electrophysiological pattern has different meaning in grey matter, white matter or a different anatomical structure. Mapping contacts to anatomical atlases or patient-specific parcellations was achieved reliably in our data, which should help clinicians relate electrical activity to anatomy, and should help researchers perform group analyses and connectivity studies using intracranial recordings [5]. Importantly, the procedure can be run by a non-expert, which lowers the barrier for centres that lack dedicated image-analysis staff and reduces dependency on specialist supervision. By replacing a subjective, operator-dependent task with a deterministic one, the method also improves reproducibility across patients, operators and centres.

Releasing DEETO as open-source C++ software based on ITK allows independent verification, integration into existing pipelines, and extension by other groups. We regard this as important for a tool intended to support clinical decision-making.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the quantitative validation relied on 12 subjects (35 electrodes, 200 contacts) manually segmented by experts. This is a modest sample, and the manual reference is itself imperfect, so the reported error combines algorithmic and reference uncertainty. Second, the algorithm operates on a thresholded CBCT volume, so its behaviour depends on image quality and threshold selection. Metal artefacts, closely spaced or crossing electrodes, and other hardware could lead to merged or missing contacts. Third, the approach assumes that the planned entry and target points are available and that each electrode has been correctly associated with its plan; a wrongly labelled trajectory would propagate to the result. Fourth, the evaluation used a single imaging protocol and a limited number of electrode models. Generalization to conventional CT, to different voxel sizes, and to other manufacturers' designs remains to be shown. Finally, co-registration between the post-implant image and the pre-operative MRI used for anatomical labelling introduces its own error [6], which is not included in the segmentation error and will affect the final anatomical assignment, particularly near tissue boundaries.

**Future directions**

Future work should extend validation to larger, multicentre datasets with multiple independent raters, so that inter-rater variability can be compared directly with the algorithm's error. Automatic estimation of the number and spacing of contacts, handling of electrodes with different geometries, and automatic detection of mismatched plans would increase autonomy. Incorporating shaft curvature into the trajectory model could improve performance in cases of strong deformation. Integration with automatic registration and atlas-labelling steps would give an end-to-end pipeline from post-implant imaging to anatomically referenced recordings. Finally, the effect of improved localization on clinical outcomes, such as seizure-onset zone delineation and surgical planning, should be assessed prospectively.

**Conclusions**

We have presented a fast, accurate and open-source algorithm for automatic segmentation of SEEG electrode contacts in CBCT, guided by the planned trajectories. It achieved sub-millimetric agreement with expert manual segmentation, processed a subject in under a second, and tolerated deep-brain deviations from the plan. These properties allow non-experts to identify the anatomical location of SEEG contacts reliably and quickly, which should facilitate both clinical interpretation of recordings and research use of intracranial data. Validation on larger and more heterogeneous datasets will be the next step towards routine clinical adoption.

Video captioning is the task of automatically generating a natural language description of a short video clip. It sits at the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing, and it supports applications such as video retrieval, assistive technology for visually impaired users, and human-robot interaction. Compared with image captioning, the task is harder because a model must capture temporal dynamics, recognize actions and events, and compose them into a fluent sentence. Recent progress has been driven largely by sequence-to-sequence architectures, which encode a sequence of frame-level or clip-level visual features with a recurrent network and decode a caption word by word [Venugopalan et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2016]. Attention mechanisms and richer multimodal features have further improved such systems.

Despite this progress, standard training procedures have a notable limitation. Nearly all captioning models are trained to minimize word-level cross-entropy loss, in which the decoder is conditioned on the ground-truth previous word at each step. This creates two well-documented problems. The first is exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]: at test time the model must condition on its own, possibly erroneous, predictions, a distribution it never encountered during training. The second is a mismatch between the training objective and the evaluation criteria. Captioning systems are judged using sentence-level metrics such as BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002], METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005], ROUGE-L [Lin, 2004], and CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], none of which is directly optimized by word-level likelihood. Because these metrics are non-differentiable, they cannot be used as losses in ordinary gradient-based training.

**Reinforcement learning for sentence-level metrics.** A natural remedy is to cast caption generation as a sequential decision problem and apply reinforcement learning, treating the decoder as a stochastic policy and the evaluation metric as a reward. Policy gradient methods such as REINFORCE [Williams, 1992] have been used for this purpose in image captioning, machine translation, and summarization [Ranzato et al., 2016; Rennie et al., 2017; Paulus et al., 2018]. In the first part of this work, we apply policy gradient training to video captioning and directly optimize task-based metrics. We also study a mixed-loss formulation that combines the reinforcement objective with the cross-entropy loss, which stabilizes training and keeps the generated sentences fluent. We evaluate several metric rewards across multiple video captioning datasets, and show significant improvements over a strong cross-entropy baseline on both automatic metrics and human evaluation.

**Limitations of phrase-matching rewards.** Optimizing a metric also exposes its weaknesses. Metrics such as CIDEr reward n-gram overlap with reference captions, but n-gram overlap is only a rough proxy for semantic correctness. A generated caption may share many phrases with a reference and yet contradict it, for example by describing the wrong object or the opposite action. Conversely, a caption may be a valid description of the video while sharing few phrases with the references. Moreover, a policy trained to maximize such a metric will exploit it, and may produce sentences that obtain high scores through repeated or ungrammatical phrases, or that include a high-scoring but logically inconsistent fragment. For example, a caption that ends with a plausible common phrase can score highly even though it contradicts the content of the video. Such behaviors are especially problematic in video captioning, where each video is typically annotated with only a small number of reference sentences that cover a limited set of possible descriptions.

**Entailment-enhanced rewards.** To address this, we propose a novel reward, CIDEnt, that augments phrase-matching metrics with a measure of logical agreement between the generated caption and the references. Our approach draws on textual entailment, the task of deciding whether one sentence logically follows from another, contradicts it, or is neutral with respect to it [Dagan et al., 2006; Bowman et al., 2015]. We train an entailment classifier and use it to score each generated caption against the ground-truth captions. The CIDEr score is then adjusted according to the entailment probability: partial matches are credited only when they are logically implied by the references, and a penalty is applied when the caption is judged to contradict them. In this way the reward preserves the benefit of consensus-based n-gram matching while filtering out matches that are semantically wrong. To our knowledge, this is the first use of entailment as a component of a reward for captioning.

**Contributions.** Our contributions are summarized as follows:

1. We present a reinforcement learning framework for video captioning that uses policy gradient and mixed-loss training to optimize sentence-level metrics directly, and we show significant gains over a cross-entropy baseline on multiple datasets, confirmed by human evaluation.

2. We introduce CIDEnt, an entailment-corrected variant of CIDEr that allows only logically implied partial matches and penalizes contradictions, providing a reward that is better aligned with semantic correctness than phrase matching alone.

3. We provide extensive experiments and analysis, including comparisons among different metric rewards and qualitative examples, showing that the CIDEnt reward yields further significant improvements over the CIDEr reward and achieves a new state-of-the-art result on the MSR-VTT dataset [Xu et al., 2016].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on video captioning, reinforcement learning for sequence generation, and entailment. We then describe our baseline model, the reinforcement learning formulations, and the CIDEnt reward. Finally, we present experimental results, human evaluation, and analysis.

**3.1 Baseline Attention-Based Sequence-to-Sequence Model**

Our baseline follows the encoder–decoder framework with soft attention [Bahdanau et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015]. Given a video, we uniformly sample frames and extract a feature vector for each frame using a pretrained convolutional network (ResNet-152 [He et al., 2016]), yielding a sequence x = (x_1, ..., x_n). A bidirectional LSTM encoder [Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997] maps this sequence to hidden states h_1, ..., h_n. A unidirectional LSTM decoder generates the caption w = (w_1, ..., w_T) one word at a time. At step t, the decoder computes a context vector c_t = Σ_i α_{ti} h_i, where the attention weights α_{ti} are a softmax over scores produced by a small feed-forward network that takes the previous decoder state and h_i as input. The distribution over the next word is p(w_t | w_{<t}, x) = softmax(W_o [s_t; c_t] + b_o), where s_t is the decoder state.

The baseline is trained by minimizing the word-level cross-entropy loss (XE):

L_XE(θ) = −Σ_t log p_θ(w*_t | w*_{<t}, x),

where w* is the ground-truth caption. This objective has two well-known weaknesses. First, training uses teacher forcing, whereas at test time the model conditions on its own predictions (exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]). Second, it optimizes per-word likelihood rather than the sentence-level metrics used for evaluation, such as BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr and ROUGE-L.

**3.2 Reinforcement Learning with Sentence-Level Rewards**

To address these issues, we treat the decoder as a stochastic policy p_θ whose actions are the words generated and whose state is defined by the video and the words so far. After a full caption w^s is sampled, a sentence-level reward r(w^s) is computed against the reference captions. The training objective is to minimize the negative expected reward:

L_RL(θ) = −E_{w^s∼p_θ}[r(w^s)].

Using the REINFORCE algorithm [Williams, 1992], the gradient is approximated with a single sample:

∇_θ L_RL ≈ −(r(w^s) − b) ∇_θ log p_θ(w^s),

where b is a baseline that reduces variance without introducing bias. Following the self-critical approach [Rennie et al., 2017], we use the reward of the caption obtained by greedy (test-time) decoding, r(ŵ), as b. This encourages sampled captions that outperform the current inference-time output and requires no additional estimator of expected reward.

Purely RL-based training can be unstable and may produce fluent-looking but ungrammatical sequences, because the reward is sparse and the action space is large. Following [Paulus et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016], we therefore use a mixed loss that combines both objectives:

L_MIXED = λ L_RL + (1 − λ) L_XE,

where λ ∈ [0, 1] is a tunable hyperparameter. The XE term acts as a language-model regularizer that keeps the policy close to fluent text. Training proceeds in two stages: the model is first pretrained with XE until convergence, then fine-tuned with the mixed loss.

We consider several rewards, including CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002] and METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005]. Among these, CIDEr is the most natural choice, as it was designed for captioning and weights n-grams by TF-IDF to emphasize informative content. Because the reward is not differentiable, the policy gradient is the means by which the metric is optimized directly.

**3.3 Entailment-Enhanced Reward (CIDEnt)**

Phrase-matching metrics such as CIDEr reward n-gram overlap with the references and cannot judge whether a candidate is semantically consistent with them. A generated caption may therefore receive a high score despite containing a contradictory phrase. For example, "a man is playing a guitar" and "a man is playing a piano" share most n-grams, yet they describe incompatible events. Conversely, a valid paraphrase with little lexical overlap is penalized. Optimizing such a reward with RL can exacerbate these errors, since the policy learns to exploit the weaknesses of the metric.

To mitigate this, we introduce a reward based on textual entailment. We use an entailment classifier that, given a premise and a hypothesis, outputs probabilities for three classes: entailment, contradiction and neutral. We employ the decomposable attention model [Parikh et al., 2016] trained on SNLI [Bowman et al., 2015], which is lightweight enough to be called at every training step. For a sampled caption w^s, the ground-truth caption serves as the premise and the sampled caption as the hypothesis. We take the entailment score Ent(w^s) as the probability of the entailment class, maximized over the available reference captions, since any reference may logically imply the generated content.

The CIDEnt reward then uses this score to filter the CIDEr reward:

CIDEnt(w^s) = CIDEr(w^s) − λ_p, if Ent(w^s) < β,
CIDEnt(w^s) = CIDEr(w^s), otherwise,

where β is an entailment-probability threshold and λ_p is a constant penalty. Thus a caption keeps its CIDEr reward only when it is logically implied by a reference; otherwise its reward is reduced, discouraging contradictory or unsupported partial matches. Because the penalty is applied only when entailment is low, correct captions with high n-gram overlap are unaffected, and the training signal retains the fine-grained gradation provided by CIDEr. We use the CIDEnt reward in place of r in the policy-gradient and mixed-loss formulations above, together with the self-critical baseline, so that the baseline is computed with the same reward on the greedy output.

**3.4 Implementation Details**

Videos are represented by a fixed number of uniformly sampled frames, and captions are tokenized and truncated to a maximum length, with infrequent words mapped to an unknown token. All models are optimized with Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2015] with dropout regularization. Hyperparameters, including λ, β, λ_p, and learning rates, are selected on the validation set. At test time, captions are generated with beam search. For the RL stage, sampling is performed from the model's output distribution, and the reward is computed online for each sample in the minibatch.

**Experimental Setup Summary.** We evaluate on MSR-VTT [1], the primary benchmark, and on YouTube2Text/MSVD [2] and the Flickr30k image-captioning dataset [3] to test generalization. Performance is reported with BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr, computed using the Microsoft COCO evaluation server [4]. All reinforcement-learning (RL) models are initialized from a cross-entropy (XE) pretrained baseline. Reported numbers are on the test split unless otherwise stated. Hyperparameters were tuned on the validation set.

**Baseline and Metric-Reward Results**

Table 1 compares the XE baseline with models fine-tuned using policy gradient (REINFORCE with a baseline estimator) and the mixed-loss objective, which interpolates XE and RL losses to preserve fluency. Optimizing CIDEr as the reward yields the largest gains on CIDEr and generally improves the other metrics. On MSR-VTT, the CIDEr-reward model improves CIDEr by several points over the XE baseline and also improves BLEU-4 and METEOR. Using BLEU as the reward raises BLEU-4 most strongly, but gains transfer less consistently to other metrics, indicating partial overfitting to the optimized metric. This pattern is consistent with prior work on image captioning [5, 6]. The mixed-loss variants are more stable than pure policy gradient and typically give modestly higher scores. Their outputs show fewer ungrammatical or truncated sentences.

Results on MSVD follow the same trend: CIDEr-based RL consistently outperforms the XE baseline on all four metrics, and the improvements exceed the variance observed across random seeds. Gains on Flickr30k are smaller but in the same direction, suggesting that sentence-level reward optimization is not specific to video.

**Analysis of CIDEr-Reward Failure Modes**

Although CIDEr-reward models improve automatic scores, qualitative inspection reveals that high-reward captions can contain phrase matches that are logically inconsistent with the video. Examples include captions ending in fragments such as "a man is playing a guitar in a" or captions that match many n-grams of the reference while changing a key entity or action (e.g., "a man is playing a piano" against "a man is playing a guitar"). Because CIDEr scores n-gram overlap with TF-IDF weighting, such captions receive substantial partial credit. This motivates the entailment-corrected reward.

**Entailment-Enhanced Reward (CIDEnt)**

CIDEnt uses an entailment classifier, trained on SNLI [7], to estimate whether the generated caption is entailed by the ground-truth reference. The CIDEr score is retained only when the entailment probability exceeds a threshold; otherwise a penalty is applied, scaling the reward downward. Table 2 shows that CIDEnt gives additional gains over the CIDEr-reward model on MSR-VTT, improving CIDEr, METEOR, and BLEU-4. It is particularly effective at increasing the CIDEr score, and the improvement is statistically significant under a bootstrap test (p < 0.05). With these gains, CIDEnt-RL achieves the new best published results on MSR-VTT, surpassing previously reported systems, including those that use additional modalities such as audio, category information, or ensembles [8, 9]. We note that our model is a single model that uses only visual features.

On MSVD, CIDEnt also improves over the CIDEr-reward model, although the margins are smaller, which we attribute to the dataset's more homogeneous captions and limited size. Ablations on the entailment threshold and penalty value show that results are fairly robust across a moderate range, whereas overly high penalties reduce the learning signal and slow convergence.

**Human Evaluation**

Automatic metrics correlate imperfectly with human judgment, so we conducted pairwise human evaluation on 1,000 randomly selected MSR-VTT test videos using crowd workers. Annotators saw the video and two anonymized captions, and selected the better one on relevance (agreement with video content) and coherence (fluency and logical consistency), with a tie option. Each pair was judged by multiple annotators, and the order was randomized.

The CIDEr-RL model was preferred over the XE baseline on both relevance and coherence by a clear margin. CIDEnt-RL was in turn preferred over CIDEr-RL, with the larger improvement on relevance, consistent with the claim that entailment correction penalizes contradictory partial matches. Inter-annotator agreement was moderate, and the preference differences remained after majority-vote aggregation.

**Qualitative Examples**

Qualitative comparisons illustrate the differences. The XE baseline often produces generic captions, while the CIDEr-RL model produces more specific but occasionally contradictory ones, such as wrong objects or repeated words. CIDEnt-RL captions more often preserve the correct subject-action-object structure and avoid dangling endings. Failure cases remain for rare actions and fine-grained objects, and in cases where the entailment classifier is itself wrong, such as when paraphrases with differing vocabulary are judged non-entailed.

**Discussion**

Three findings emerge. First, sentence-level optimization with policy gradient or mixed loss addresses the train-test mismatch of XE training and yields consistent gains on several datasets. Second, the reward choice strongly influences which metrics improve, and optimizing a single metric can exploit its weaknesses. Third, adding logical-entailment verification to a phrase-matching reward gives further measurable improvements in both automatic and human evaluations. The additional cost of CIDEnt is small, since the entailment classifier is applied only to sampled captions during fine-tuning and is not needed at inference time.

**Discussion**

*Impact of sentence-level optimization.* Our experiments indicate that much of the gap between cross-entropy-trained captioners and human references stems from the mismatch between the training objective and the evaluation criteria. Cross-entropy training with teacher forcing penalizes each token independently and exposes the decoder only to ground-truth prefixes, which leads to exposure bias at inference time [Ranzato et al., 2016]. Policy-gradient and mixed-loss training reduce this discrepancy by letting the model sample its own sequences and receive a sequence-level signal. The mixed-loss variant was consistently the more stable of the two, which agrees with the observation that pure REINFORCE suffers from high-variance gradient estimates and benefits from a cross-entropy term that anchors the policy to fluent outputs [Paulus et al., 2018]. The gains held across datasets and were corroborated by human judgments, which suggests the improvements are not merely an artifact of metric overfitting. Nevertheless, optimizing a single metric can inflate that metric disproportionately, and we observed that improvements in the optimized score were not always matched by equal improvements in the others.

*Why entailment helps.* The CIDEnt reward was motivated by a specific weakness of n-gram consensus metrics: they credit lexical overlap regardless of whether a generated phrase is logically compatible with the reference. A caption such as "a man is playing a guitar" and a reference stating "a man is playing a piano" share most of their n-grams, yet the caption is factually wrong. By using an entailment classifier to estimate whether the generated sentence is implied by the reference, and by discounting the CIDEr score when a contradiction or neutral relation is detected, the reward better separates partially correct phrase matches from logically consistent ones. Qualitative inspection showed that the resulting model more often avoids contradictory object, action, or count substitutions, and more reliably preserves the relational structure of the reference. This is consistent with the broader view that reward design, rather than architecture alone, determines which errors a reinforcement-learned generator learns to avoid.

*Limitations.* Several caveats should be noted. First, the entailment reward depends on the quality of the underlying classifier, which was trained on image-caption and general text inference data and may transfer imperfectly to video descriptions. Errors in the classifier can introduce noisy or biased reward signals, and a sufficiently adaptive policy could learn to exploit systematic weaknesses in it, a form of reward hacking. Second, entailment is computed against reference captions rather than the video itself, so the reward inherits the incompleteness of the human annotations: a correct but unreferenced detail may be treated as neutral or even contradictory. Third, the threshold-style or score-adjusting mechanism we employ is a heuristic; the penalty magnitude and the handling of neutral cases were selected empirically and may not be optimal for other datasets. Fourth, sampling-based training increases computational cost relative to cross-entropy training, and the entailment computation adds further overhead per sampled caption. Finally, our visual representation is limited to pretrained frame- and clip-level features, so some errors likely arise from perception rather than language generation, and no reward can fully compensate for that.

*Broader implications.* The approach illustrates a general strategy: augment a surface-level similarity metric with a semantic-consistency model that captures a property the metric ignores. The same principle could be applied to other conditional generation tasks, such as image captioning, summarization, and dialogue, where faithfulness to the source or reference is crucial [Pasunuru and Bansal, 2017]. It also complements work on learned evaluation metrics and adversarial rewards, suggesting that combinations of complementary reward components may be more robust than any single score.

**Conclusion**

We studied the training of video captioning models with objectives that more closely match how captions are evaluated. Moving from word-level cross-entropy to sequence-level reinforcement learning, particularly with mixed-loss training, yielded substantial and consistent improvements under both automatic and human evaluation across multiple datasets. Building on this, we introduced CIDEnt, an entailment-corrected variant of the CIDEr reward that credits only logically consistent partial matches and penalizes contradictions. This reward produced further significant gains over CIDEr-based optimization and established a new state of the art on MSR-VTT at the time of evaluation. Together, these results show that both the optimization procedure and the semantic content of the reward are decisive for caption quality.

Several directions follow naturally. Entailment models grounded directly in video, rather than in reference text alone, would remove dependence on annotation coverage. Jointly training or adapting the entailment component with the captioner could reduce domain mismatch and guard against reward exploitation. Variance-reduction techniques, such as self-critical baselines, and multi-metric or multi-task reward combinations could further improve stability and balance across evaluation criteria. Finally, applying entailment-style rewards to other sequence generation problems would test the generality of the idea. We hope this work encourages more careful reward design that targets the semantic properties we ultimately want generated language to satisfy.

Online retailers, airlines, hotels, and advertising platforms share a common operational challenge: a finite stock of items must be allocated to a sequence of heterogeneous customers whose identities and preferences are revealed only upon arrival. Each allocation decision is irrevocable, and selling an item to one customer forecloses the opportunity to sell it to a later, possibly more valuable, customer. In e-commerce settings, the decision is richer still. The seller chooses not only which items to offer (the assortment) but also the prices at which they are offered, and customers choose among the offered options according to individual preferences. This paper studies a general model that captures these decisions jointly, and develops simple algorithms with provably best-possible performance guarantees.

We adopt the framework of competitive analysis, in which an online algorithm is compared against a clairvoyant optimal solution that knows the entire arrival sequence in advance. The sequence is chosen adversarially and need not follow any stochastic pattern. This worst-case perspective is attractive when demand is difficult to forecast, is non-stationary, or is subject to sudden shifts, as is common during promotions, demand shocks, or when forecasting models are misspecified. The guarantee obtained is robust: it holds for every possible sequence of customers.

The foundational result in this area is the online bipartite matching problem of Karp, Vazirani, and Vazirani [1], whose RANKING algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 1-1/e, which is optimal among randomized algorithms. Subsequent work extended this guarantee to vertex-weighted matching [2], and to the AdWords and budgeted allocation problems through the "balancing" or "water-filling" approach of Mehta et al. [3] and Buchbinder, Jain, and Naor [4]. A unifying primal-dual perspective was developed by Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg [5]. In the revenue management literature, related guarantees were established for assortment problems in which customers choose according to a choice model: Golrezaei, Nazerzadeh, and Rusmevichientong [6] gave a 1-1/e competitive algorithm for online assortment with inventory constraints, and later work extended these ideas to richer choice structures and to personalized settings [7,8]. A common feature of this literature is that each item has a single, fixed price or weight. The competitive ratio 1-1/e is then achieved by discounting each item's price by an increasing function of the fraction of its inventory already consumed.

Fixed prices are a significant restriction in practice. Hotels sell the same room at several fare classes; airlines offer a ladder of fares for each cabin; online retailers adjust prices over time and across customer segments. When an item may be sold at multiple prices, the problem changes qualitatively. A low price sells units that might later have sold at a higher price, so the algorithm must trade off the immediate revenue, the opportunity cost of inventory, and the possibility that high-priced customers never arrive. Classical single-leg revenue management results with multiple fare classes [9,10] show that the best achievable competitive ratio depends on the range of prices, and this dependence cannot be avoided under adversarial arrivals. Ball and Queyranne [11] characterized the optimal ratio for a single resource with fare classes, and related results exist for one-way trading and online knapsack problems [12,13], where ratios depend on the ratio between the largest and smallest values. These results suggest that the right notion of performance in our setting is a weight-dependent competitive ratio, determined by the sets of feasible prices supplied in advance.

**Our contributions.** We study a general online allocation problem in which each item has finite inventory and a set of feasible prices, and customers arrive sequentially with choice behavior over item-price pairs. This formulation subsumes online matching, AdWords-type problems, and online assortment as special cases in which every item has a single price. Our main contributions are as follows.

First, we construct a class of universal value functions that assign to each item an opportunity cost as a function of its remaining inventory. These functions are designed so that the selection of items and the selection of prices are integrated into a single decision: upon each arrival, the algorithm offers the item-price combinations maximizing the customer's contribution net of the value-function opportunity cost. The resulting algorithms are simple and intuitive, require no forecasts, and extend the water-filling logic of earlier work to multiple prices.

Second, we prove that these algorithms achieve weight-dependent competitive ratios that depend only on the sets of feasible prices, and we show matching upper bounds establishing that no online algorithm can do better. The ratio recovers 1-1/e when each item has a single price and degrades gracefully as the price sets become more spread out. Our analysis proceeds through a primal-dual argument in which the value function is derived from a differential-equation characterization of the tightest feasible dual update.

Third, we evaluate the algorithms empirically on the publicly available hotel data set of Bodea et al. [14], in which multiple room types are each sold at multiple fares. Worst-case algorithms are by design conservative, and as expected they can be outperformed on typical instances by methods that forecast and learn future demand. We therefore also study "hybrid" approaches that combine our value functions with forecast-based or learning-based policies. We find that the hybrids deliver the best performance, retaining robustness while exploiting predictable structure in demand.

**Organization.** Section 2 formalizes the model and reviews preliminaries. Section 3 presents the value functions and algorithms. Section 4 proves the competitive guarantees, and Section 5 establishes matching impossibility results. Section 6 reports the numerical study on the hotel data, and Section 7 concludes.

We study an online allocation problem in which a set of items I, each with a finite initial inventory, is sold to customers arriving sequentially. Item i has a finite set of feasible prices P_i = {p_{i,1} < ... < p_{i,m_i}}. When customer t arrives, the algorithm observes her choice model, offers an assortment of item-price pairs, and the customer selects at most one pair (or leaves) according to this model. The decision is irrevocable, and each sale reduces the inventory of the item by one. The objective is to maximize total revenue. We evaluate algorithms by competitive analysis against a clairvoyant optimum that knows the entire arrival sequence in advance, and we do not assume any stochastic structure on the arrivals [Mehta et al., 2007; Buchbinder et al., 2007].

**Model and benchmark.** For the matching special case, customer t has a value v_{t,i,p} for each item-price pair and purchases the offered pair maximizing nonnegative utility. For the assortment case, we use a general choice model in which the purchase probabilities for an offered set S are given by a function φ_t(·|S). To obtain a tractable benchmark, we upper bound the clairvoyant optimum by a linear program (LP) whose variables x_{t,i,p} represent the (fractional) amount of item i sold to customer t at price p. Constraints require that, for each item, total sales do not exceed inventory, and that, for each customer, the allocation be consistent with a feasible assortment, expressed through the standard choice-based LP relaxation [Golrezaei et al., 2014]. The algorithm's revenue is compared with the optimal LP value, which yields a guarantee against the true offline optimum as well.

**Weight-dependent competitive ratio.** Because multiple prices per item change the achievable guarantee, the competitive ratio depends on the price sets. For item i, let the ratio of its extreme prices be p_{i,m_i}/p_{i,1}. We define a ratio α(P) determined by the collection of price sets, obtained as the solution of a small system of equations over the price levels (described below). When every item has a single price, α reduces to 1−1/e. As the prices become more dispersed, α decreases. We show matching upper bounds by constructing adversarial instances, so the ratio is tight for each price set.

**Value-function algorithm.** The algorithm is a primal-dual style procedure built on a universal value function. For each item i, let y_i ∈ [0,1] denote the fraction of its inventory sold so far. We define a nondecreasing function Ψ_i(y) that represents the opportunity cost, or "marginal value", of selling a unit of item i at inventory level y. Ψ_i is piecewise defined across the price levels of item i: on the segment of inventory in which price p_{i,k} is "active", Ψ_i grows exponentially, and thresholds between segments are chosen so that Ψ_i crosses each price level p_{i,k} at a prescribed fill level. These thresholds are the parameters determined by the system of equations defining α. Intuitively, low prices are accepted only while inventory is plentiful, and as inventory depletes, only higher prices become competitive.

When customer t arrives, the algorithm computes the adjusted revenue of each item-price pair, p − Ψ_i(y_i), and offers the assortment (or makes the match) maximizing the customer's expected adjusted revenue. In the matching setting this is a simple argmax; in the assortment setting it is a choice-based optimization problem, which is solvable in polynomial time for the standard models we consider (multinomial logit, and more generally models with efficiently solvable assortment optimization) [Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004]. Because the value function integrates item and price selection, no separate pricing step is needed: pairs with negative adjusted revenue are never offered.

**Analysis.** We use a dual-fitting argument [Devanur et al., 2013]. We maintain a dual solution in which the dual variable for item i's inventory constraint equals Ψ_i(y_i) averaged appropriately, and the dual variable for customer t equals her expected adjusted revenue under the chosen assortment. By construction of the offered set, the dual constraints are satisfied approximately, up to a factor of α. A per-step inequality shows that the increase in primal revenue is at least α times the increase in dual objective. Summing over customers and applying weak duality gives revenue ≥ α · LP ≥ α · OPT. The principal technical step is choosing Ψ_i to make the per-step inequality hold with equality simultaneously on all price segments, which leads to the equation system defining α. For the upper bound, we construct instances in which customers arrive in phases, each phase targeting a distinct price level, and use Yao's principle to extend the bound to randomized algorithms [Yao, 1977].

**Extensions.** The same value functions apply to (i) online matching with vertex weights and multiple prices, (ii) the AdWords-type setting with budgets [Mehta et al., 2007], and (iii) assortment problems with general choice models, using the same dual-fitting template with the choice-based LP.

**Computational experiments.** We evaluate our algorithms on the publicly available hotel dataset of Bodea et al. [2009], which records booking transactions for multiple hotel properties, including room types, fares, arrival dates, and lengths of stay. We construct items as room types with inventories scaled to induce varying demand-to-capacity ratios, and feasible prices as the observed fare classes. Customers are generated from the transaction sequence, with choice models estimated from the data by maximum likelihood under a multinomial logit specification.

We compare the following methods: (a) our value-function algorithm; (b) a greedy policy that offers the revenue-maximizing assortment ignoring inventory; (c) a forecast-based policy that estimates future demand and solves a LP-based booking-limit or bid-price control, periodically re-solved [Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004]; and (d) a hybrid combining (a) and (c), in which the value function is blended with LP-derived bid prices, using a convex combination whose weight is tuned on a held-out period. Performance is measured as the ratio of realized revenue to the hindsight-optimal LP revenue, averaged over multiple sampled arrival orders, including adversarially permuted sequences to test robustness. We report means and standard errors across replications and vary inventory levels and forecast error to assess sensitivity.

We first present the theoretical guarantees of our algorithms, followed by the numerical results on the hotel data set.

**Competitive ratio guarantees.** Let each item i have a set of feasible prices with minimum price m_i and maximum price M_i, and let the weight-dependent parameter be determined by the ratio M_i/m_i. Our first main result concerns the single-item-type benchmark, in which the value function is constructed from a threshold structure over prices. For a single item with feasible prices r_1 < ... < r_k, the algorithm ties the price offered to the fraction of inventory already sold. Prices are "unlocked" progressively as inventory depletes, and the unlock points are chosen so that the marginal revenue from selling at each price equals the marginal decrease in the value function. We show that this construction yields a competitive ratio c(r_1,...,r_k) that is the unique solution of a system of equalities over the price levels. When k=1 the ratio reduces to 1-1/e, matching the known results for online matching and Adwords [1,2]. As the price set becomes dense on [m, M], the ratio converges to a limit that depends only on M/m, and it is strictly below 1-1/e whenever M>m.

Our second result is a matching upper bound. For any price set, no online algorithm, deterministic or randomized, can achieve a ratio better than c(r_1,...,r_k). The proof constructs an adversarial arrival sequence in which customers arrive in phases, each phase willing to pay only the next higher price. Within each phase the adversary exploits upper-triangular structure, as in the classical hard instances for online bipartite matching [1,3]. The algorithm's revenue is bounded by a factor that is exactly equal to that of our algorithm, so the bound is tight for every price set, not only in the limit.

Our third result extends the guarantee to the general setting with multiple items and heterogeneous customers. We show that the same universal value functions, applied through a primal-dual argument, give a ratio of min_i c_i, where c_i is the ratio for the price set of item i. This holds for (a) online matching with vertex weights, (b) the Adwords-type problem with budgets, and (c) assortment planning under a general choice model, where each arriving customer is offered a set of item-price pairs and purchases according to a known random utility model. In the assortment case, the algorithm selects at each arrival the assortment maximizing expected revenue net of the value-function opportunity cost. The analysis shows that this assortment optimization problem preserves the structure necessary for the dual-fitting argument. Because the value functions are universal and do not depend on the arrival sequence, they can be computed offline from the price sets alone.

We also characterize how the ratio scales. For prices spanning a range with M/m = 2, the ratio is approximately 0.54 in the continuous limit, and it decays as roughly 1/(1+ln(M/m)) for large ratios. Hence the loss from price heterogeneity is modest for narrow price ranges but substantial when prices differ by an order of magnitude or more.

**Numerical results on hotel data.** We evaluated the algorithms on the data set of Bodea et al. [4], which contains booking transactions for five hotels, with several room types and multiple fares per room type over arrival horizons of many days. We converted each transaction sequence into an online instance with room types as items, fares as feasible prices, and capacities set to a fraction of observed demand to induce scarcity. Customer choice was modeled by a multinomial logit model fit to the training portion of the data.

We compared four methods: (i) a myopic greedy policy that offers the highest-revenue assortment without regard to inventory; (ii) our value-function algorithm, which is robust but uses no forecasts; (iii) a forecast-based policy that solves a deterministic linear program using estimated arrival rates and re-solves periodically [5]; and (iv) a hybrid in which the re-solved LP is combined with our value-function opportunity costs, using a convex combination of the two sets of item valuations.

Performance was measured as realized revenue relative to the offline optimum computed with hindsight. Across instances, greedy attained on average about 80% of the optimum, with poor results at tight capacities. Our value-function algorithm improved on greedy at tight capacities, but was somewhat conservative when capacity was ample, because its worst-case design leads to reserving inventory for high-price customers who may not arrive. The forecast-based policy performed well when the test period resembled the training period, but its revenue degraded markedly when demand was perturbed, for example when arrival rates were scaled or the mix of customer types was shifted. The value-function algorithm was far less sensitive to such perturbations, consistent with its worst-case guarantee.

The hybrid policy achieved the best performance in nearly all settings. Under unperturbed demand it matched or slightly exceeded the forecast-based policy, and under perturbed demand it recovered most of the loss suffered by the forecast-based policy, outperforming each component on average. These results suggest that the value functions act as a protective regularizer against forecast error, while the forecasts supply the instance-specific information the robust algorithm lacks. The observed ratios of all of our methods were well above their theoretical worst-case guarantees, as expected, since the hotel sequences are not adversarial.

This paper studied a general online allocation problem in which finite inventories of items must be assigned to sequentially arriving, heterogeneous customers, and in which each item may be sold at one of several feasible prices. Earlier work on online matching, AdWords, and assortment planning has largely assumed a single price per item, which yields the well-known 1-1/e competitive ratio [Karp et al. 1990; Mehta et al. 2007; Golrezaei et al. 2014]. We extended these results to the multi-price setting. We designed a class of universal value functions that jointly govern which items and which prices are offered, and we showed that the resulting algorithms attain weight-dependent competitive ratios that match corresponding upper bounds. The ratios depend only on the sets of feasible prices supplied in advance, and they reduce to 1-1/e when each item has a single price.

**Discussion of theoretical findings.** Three observations stand out. First, the price set acts as a structural parameter of the problem. When feasible prices are widely spread, an algorithm faces a sharper tension between selling an item early at a low price and reserving it for a later, higher-paying customer. The resulting competitive ratio is therefore worse than 1-1/e, and our tight bounds quantify the loss precisely. Second, the value-function approach shows that the usual primal-dual and inventory-balancing intuition carries over to this setting. An item's value should decrease as its inventory is depleted, and this discount can be calibrated to the price structure so that the choice of item and the choice of price are made in one step. This avoids separate heuristics for pricing and for assortment. Third, the same construction extends across matching, advertising, and assortment settings, which suggests that these problems share a common structure once prices are treated as part of the decision.

The tightness of the results has a practical interpretation. No online algorithm that ignores distributional information can guarantee more than our ratio in the worst case, so any improvement in practice must come from assumptions about the arrival sequence. Our guarantees are best seen as a floor on performance. They hold even if the arrival process is adversarial, nonstationary, or misspecified. This property is valuable in e-commerce settings, where demand shifts because of promotions, events, or competitor actions, and where forecasting models may fail without warning.

**Empirical findings.** The experiments on the hotel data set of Bodea et al. (2009) show how this robustness interacts with learning. Forecast-based methods exploit historical regularities and can perform very well when the future resembles the past. They can also degrade when it does not. Our worst-case algorithms are stable but conservative on typical instances. The hybrid algorithms, which combine a forecast-driven or learning-based component with our value functions, achieved the best performance in our tests. A plausible explanation is that the value functions supply a principled protection against over-commitment of scarce inventory, while the learning component supplies information about likely demand that a purely adversarial algorithm discards. We view this as evidence that worst-case and data-driven approaches are complements, not competitors. The hybrid retains a degree of the worst-case guarantee while achieving a better average outcome.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be noted. The competitive ratios are worst-case and may be pessimistic for realistic demand. Our model assumes that customer behavior, whether a choice model or a valuation threshold, is known to the seller or can be queried at decision time. In practice, such models must be estimated, and estimation error could weaken the guarantees. Inventory in our setting is consumed one unit at a time and is not replenished, so we do not address cancellations, overbooking, or multi-night stays, all of which matter in the hotel domain. The empirical evaluation uses a single data set from one industry, and the hybrid construction was tested in a limited number of configurations. We therefore regard the empirical results as an indication of promise and not as definitive evidence of general superiority.

**Directions for future research.** Several extensions follow naturally. One is to handle bundled or multi-unit requests, such as multi-night hotel stays, where the consumption of several inventory units must be coordinated across time. Another is to study the intermediate regimes between adversarial and stochastic arrivals, such as random-order, bounded-drift, or corrupted-stochastic models.
