In these regimes the weight-dependent ratios might be improved while some robustness is retained. A third direction is to provide formal guarantees for the hybrid algorithms, for example by characterizing how much weight a learning component can receive without the competitive ratio falling below a chosen fraction of the optimal worst-case ratio. A fourth is to treat endogenous price sets, in which the seller chooses the feasible prices subject to business rules, and to examine how the ratio guides that design. Finally, fairness and customer-experience considerations, such as price consistency across customers, may constrain the use of dynamic prices and deserve analysis.

**Conclusion.** We have shown that multiple prices can be incorporated into online matching, assortment, and advertising problems through a single family of value functions, and that the resulting algorithms achieve the best possible competitive ratios as a function of the price sets. The algorithms are simple enough to implement in real systems. Our computational study further suggests that embedding them in hybrid methods with forecasting and learning produces strong practical performance. Together, these results provide both a theoretical foundation and a practical tool for joint item and price selection under limited inventory and uncertain demand.

Graphs are a natural way to represent relational data, and they appear in social networks, web graphs, citation networks, biological networks, and recommender systems. Many of these graphs are now very large. Social and web graphs routinely contain billions of edges, which is more than a single machine can store or process efficiently. A standard solution is distributed computation on a cluster [1, 2]. Systems such as Pregel [3], GraphLab [4], PowerGraph [5], and GraphX [6] distribute a graph across machines and run iterative algorithms in parallel. Examples include PageRank, connected components, shortest paths, and collaborative filtering.

The efficiency of these systems depends heavily on how the graph is partitioned. Graph partitioning (GP) assigns the vertices or edges of a graph to different machines. A good partition has two properties. First, the workload is balanced, so that no machine becomes a bottleneck. Second, the communication between machines is small, because network cost often dominates the running time of distributed graph algorithms. Finding an optimal balanced partition is NP-hard [7], so practical methods rely on heuristics.

Existing GP methods fall into two groups. Offline methods, such as METIS [8] and spectral approaches [9], require the whole graph to be available and loaded into memory before partitioning. They can produce high-quality partitions, but their time and memory costs are high. For graphs with billions of edges, partitioning may take longer than the downstream computation. Streaming graph partitioning (SGP) was proposed to address this problem [10, 11]. An SGP method reads the graph as a stream of vertices or edges and assigns each item to a machine on arrival, using only limited information about the items already seen. SGP therefore needs little memory, runs in a single pass, and can be parallelized. It also suits graphs that arrive continuously or are too large to load.

There are two basic strategies for partitioning a graph. Edge-cut assigns each vertex to a machine, and edges whose endpoints lie on different machines are cut. Vertex-cut assigns each edge to a machine, and a vertex whose edges lie on several machines is replicated on all of them. Edge-cut quality is measured by the number of cut edges, and vertex-cut quality by the replication factor, which is the average number of machines holding a copy of each vertex. Most existing SGP methods, including linear deterministic greedy and Fennel [10, 11, 12], use edge-cut. Few SGP methods use vertex-cut. Representative examples are the hashing and greedy heuristics in PowerGraph [5] and the high-degree-replicated-first strategy in HDRF [13].

Vertex-cut is the more suitable strategy for natural graphs. The degrees of vertices in such graphs usually follow a highly skewed power-law distribution [14, 15]. A small number of hub vertices have very large degrees, while most vertices have few neighbors. Under edge-cut, a hub vertex placed on one machine has many cut edges, which causes heavy communication and an unbalanced load. Balancing the number of vertices per machine does not balance the number of edges, which determines the actual workload. Vertex-cut avoids this problem. It spreads the edges of a hub across many machines at the price of replicating that vertex. Because most vertices have low degree, few vertices need to be replicated, and the total replication remains modest. Both theoretical analysis and experiments [5, 16] have shown that vertex-cut outperforms edge-cut on power-law graphs.

Despite this advantage, current vertex-cut SGP methods have limitations. Hash-based methods are fast and balanced, but they ignore graph structure and produce a high replication factor. Greedy methods that use the placement of previously seen edges reduce replication, but they can behave poorly early in the stream, when little information is available, and they may degrade balance. Methods that use vertex degrees need either the full degree information, which a one-pass stream does not provide, or partial degrees estimated during the stream. These considerations show that a simple and effective vertex-cut method for streaming natural graphs is still needed.

In this paper, we propose a novel SGP method for natural graphs called S-PowerGraph. S-PowerGraph uses vertex-cut and builds on the power-law structure of natural graphs. It makes each placement decision from the current state of the partitions, without storing the graph or making multiple passes. The method is simple to implement, has low time and memory overhead, and achieves a lower replication factor than existing methods while keeping the load balanced.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

- We propose S-PowerGraph, a new streaming vertex-cut partitioning method designed for graphs with skewed power-law degree distributions.
- We show that the method is efficient in time and space, and that it needs only a single pass over the edge stream.
- We conduct experiments on several large natural graphs and synthetic graphs. The results show that S-PowerGraph outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in replication factor and load balance, and that these improvements carry over to the running time of distributed graph algorithms.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and introduces the notation. Section 3 describes S-PowerGraph. Section 4 reports experimental results, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

We consider an undirected graph G = (V, E) with |V| = n vertices and |E| = m edges, to be distributed over p machines. Under vertex-cut, each edge is assigned to exactly one machine, and a vertex is replicated on every machine that holds at least one of its incident edges [1]. Let A(v) ⊆ {1,…,p} denote the set of machines on which vertex v is replicated, and let E_i be the set of edges on machine i. The quality of a partition is measured by two quantities. The first is the replication factor, RF = (1/n) Σ_v |A(v)|, which reflects communication cost because replicas of a vertex must synchronize their state. The second is the load imbalance, λ = max_i |E_i| / (m/p), which reflects computational balance. The objective is to minimize RF subject to λ ≤ 1 + ε for a small tolerance ε.

**Streaming Setting**

Edges arrive one at a time as a stream, and each must be irrevocably assigned to a machine upon arrival. The partitioner keeps only compact state: the current load of each machine, a table of the replica sets A(v), and a partial degree counter d(v) for each vertex, equal to the number of edges of v observed so far. No edge is stored after assignment, so memory is O(np) bits for the replica table plus O(n) for the counters, and the time per edge is O(p).

**Motivation**

In natural graphs the degree distribution follows a power law, P(d) ∝ d^(−α), with 2 < α < 3 typically [2]. A few high-degree vertices are incident to a large share of edges. Edge-cut methods place such hubs on one machine and cut many edges to their neighbors, which causes both communication and load skew [1]. Under vertex-cut, replicating a hub is cheap relative to the number of edges it saves from being cut, while low-degree vertices are rarely replicated if their edges are co-located. Existing streaming vertex-cut heuristics include hashing, the greedy heuristic of PowerGraph [1], and the degree-based hashing (DBH) [3] and HDRF [4] methods. Greedy considers only replica locality and load, while DBH and HDRF use degree information to decide which endpoint to replicate. S-PowerGraph builds on these ideas, combining replica locality, degree awareness, and load balancing in a single scoring rule.

**The S-PowerGraph Algorithm**

For an arriving edge e = (u, v), the partial degrees are first incremented, d(u) ← d(u)+1 and d(v) ← d(v)+1. We define the normalized degrees

θ(u) = d(u) / (d(u) + d(v)), θ(v) = 1 − θ(u).

A vertex with small θ is relatively low-degree and should be kept intact, whereas the higher-degree endpoint is the better one to replicate. For each machine i we compute a score

C(e, i) = C_rep(e, i) + C_bal(i).

The replication term is

C_rep(e, i) = g(u, i) + g(v, i),

where g(x, i) = 1 + (1 − θ(x)) if i ∈ A(x) and g(x, i) = 0 otherwise, with θ(x) the normalized degree of x. A machine already holding the lower-degree endpoint therefore receives a larger reward than one holding only the higher-degree endpoint. Consequently, when the replica sets of u and v are disjoint, the edge is placed with the lower-degree vertex, and the hub is replicated. This matches the power-law motivation: the hub is likely to be replicated anyway, whereas replicating a low-degree vertex yields little benefit.

The balance term is

C_bal(i) = λ_b · (maxsize − |E_i|) / (ζ + maxsize − minsize),

where maxsize and minsize are the largest and smallest current machine loads, ζ > 0 is a small constant to avoid division by zero, and λ_b ≥ 0 controls the weight of balance. This term lies in [0, λ_b) and favors lightly loaded machines. When λ_b is small, locality dominates; when it is large, the method approaches round-robin assignment. We use λ_b as a tunable parameter and examine its sensitivity experimentally.

The edge is assigned to i* = argmax_i C(e, i), with ties broken uniformly at random. Afterwards, |E_{i*}| is incremented and i* is added to A(u) and A(v) if not already present.

**Complexity and Properties**

Each edge requires O(p) work to evaluate scores, giving total time O(mp), and the method is single-pass. Because the algorithm depends only on local state, it can be parallelized by letting several loaders process disjoint portions of the stream with periodically synchronized or locally approximated replica tables and load counters, as is done in prior systems [1], [4]. Using partial rather than true degrees makes the method fully online. For random-order streams, partial degrees are unbiased estimates of the final degree ratios up to scaling, so θ approximates the true relative degree increasingly well as the stream progresses. The reward in C_rep ensures that when both endpoints are already co-located on a machine, that machine receives the highest replication score, and no new replica is created. The balance term guarantees that no machine can remain permanently overloaded, since a machine with maximal load receives zero balance reward while less-loaded machines receive positive reward.

**Experimental Protocol**

We evaluate on large natural graphs, including social and web graphs from public repositories [5], and on synthetic power-law graphs with varying exponent α generated by standard preferential-attachment or configuration-model procedures [2]. Stream orders include random, breadth-first, and depth-first orderings to assess robustness to locality in the stream. The number of machines p varies from 4 to 128. Baselines are hashing, Greedy [1], DBH [3], HDRF [4], and the edge-cut streaming method LDG [6] and Fennel [7] (with edge-cut results converted to equivalent replication measures where applicable). We report RF, λ, and partitioning time. To measure downstream effects, we run PageRank and connected components on the partitions in a PowerGraph-style framework [1] and record runtime and network traffic. All results are averaged over repeated runs with different random seeds for tie-breaking and ordering.

We evaluate S-PowerGraph on real and synthetic graphs, comparing partition quality, load balance, partitioning time, and downstream distributed computation performance.

**Experimental Setup.** The real datasets are four large natural graphs: a Twitter follower graph, a LiveJournal social network, a web graph crawled from the UK domain, and an Orkut community network. Their edge counts range from roughly 69 million to 1.5 billion, and all show heavy-tailed degree distributions. The synthetic graphs were generated with power-law exponents α ∈ {1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4} at a fixed size of 10 million vertices, so we could study how skewness affects each method. Edges arrive in a random order by default; we also test BFS and DFS orderings.

We compare against the following baselines: Random (hash) edge placement [1], Grid [2], DBH [3], Greedy vertex-cut as in PowerGraph [4], HDRF [5], and the edge-cut streaming methods LDG [6] and Fennel [7]. For the edge-cut methods, we convert the resulting vertex assignments to replication factors by the standard procedure so that all methods can be compared on the same metric. Each experiment uses 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 partitions, and the balance tolerance is set to 1.05 for all methods. Reported values are averages over five runs with different stream orderings. The main metrics are the replication factor (RF, the mean number of machine copies per vertex), the relative load imbalance (maximum partition size divided by the mean), and the partitioning time. Downstream experiments run PageRank (30 iterations) and connected components on a 32-machine cluster.

**Replication Factor.** Table 1 gives the RF at 32 partitions. S-PowerGraph achieves the lowest RF on all real graphs. On Twitter it obtains an RF of 4.7, compared with 5.6 for HDRF, 6.9 for Greedy, 7.8 for DBH, and 11.9 for Grid. On the UK web graph, where locality is strong, S-PowerGraph reaches 1.9 against 2.4 for HDRF and 2.9 for Greedy. The improvement over the strongest baseline ranges from 9% (LiveJournal) to 21% (Twitter). Random placement yields the worst RF in every case, often more than twice that of S-PowerGraph. The edge-cut methods LDG and Fennel, after conversion, have much higher RF than all vertex-cut methods other than Random, which is consistent with the known difficulty of cutting edges around high-degree hubs [4]. As the number of partitions increases from 8 to 128, RF grows for all methods, but it grows more slowly for S-PowerGraph; at 128 partitions its advantage over HDRF on Twitter widens to 24%.

**Effect of Skewness.** On synthetic graphs, the gain of S-PowerGraph grows as the degree distribution becomes more skewed. At α = 2.4 (mildly skewed), it is about 6% better than HDRF in RF, while at α = 1.8 the gap is about 17%. DBH performs well for highly skewed graphs but degrades as skewness decreases, whereas Greedy shows the opposite trend. S-PowerGraph is stable across the whole range, indicating that its handling of high-degree vertices does not rely on extreme skew. These results support the premise that vertex-cut is particularly suited to natural graphs, and that explicitly exploiting the degree distribution brings additional benefit.

**Load Balance.** All vertex-cut methods other than Random satisfy the imposed tolerance. S-PowerGraph's measured imbalance is between 1.01 and 1.04 across settings, similar to HDRF (1.01–1.05) and lower than Greedy, which reaches 1.05 on some orderings. Grid and DBH, which have no explicit balance control, show imbalance up to 1.12 on Twitter, caused by hubs concentrating edges. Edge-cut methods balance vertices but not edges, yielding edge imbalance above 1.3 on skewed graphs.

**Sensitivity to Stream Order.** Greedy-style heuristics are known to be sensitive to ordering [4,5]. With BFS and DFS orders, Greedy's RF on LiveJournal rises by 18% and 22% relative to random order, respectively, since consecutive edges concentrate on few partitions. S-PowerGraph changes by less than 5% under either order and keeps the best RF in all cases. In contrast, DBH and Random are order-independent by construction but yield a consistently higher RF. Under BFS order, the advantage of S-PowerGraph over HDRF is somewhat reduced (about 6% on Twitter), though still consistent.

**Partitioning Time and Memory.** Because S-PowerGraph makes a single pass and keeps only per-vertex partial degrees and replica sets, its cost per edge is O(k) for k partitions. On Twitter with 32 partitions it processes the stream in 412 s, comparable to HDRF (398 s) and Greedy (365 s), and far faster than the offline method METIS [8], which ran out of memory on the two largest graphs. Hash-based methods are fastest (about 90–120 s) but yield poor quality. The memory footprint of S-PowerGraph is within 3% of HDRF.

**Downstream Performance.** Lower RF translates into reduced communication. For PageRank on Twitter, the total runtime with S-PowerGraph partitions is 23% lower than with HDRF, 37% lower than with Greedy, and 58% lower than with Random, with network traffic reduced by similar proportions. When partitioning time is included, S-PowerGraph still gives the shortest end-to-end time for jobs of 10 or more iterations; for fewer iterations hash-based methods can be preferable. Connected components shows the same ranking, though with smaller gains (14% over HDRF), as the algorithm converges in few iterations. Runtime correlates strongly with RF across methods (Pearson r = 0.96), confirming RF as a reliable proxy for communication cost.

**Ablation.** Removing the degree-aware term from the scoring function raises RF by 8–13%, and removing the balance term leads to imbalance above 1.2 on Twitter. Both components are therefore necessary, and the former is chiefly responsible for the gains on skewed graphs.

In this paper, we have proposed S-PowerGraph, a streaming graph partitioning method for natural graphs based on the vertex-cut strategy. Natural graphs typically exhibit highly skewed power-law degree distributions, under which edge-cut methods tend to produce either severe load imbalance or a large number of cut edges, because a small number of high-degree vertices are incident to a large fraction of all edges [1, 2]. By assigning edges rather than vertices to machines and allowing vertices to be replicated, vertex-cut partitioning spreads the load of high-degree vertices across the cluster. S-PowerGraph adapts this idea to the streaming setting, in which each edge is placed upon arrival using only limited information about the already-assigned part of the graph. Our experiments on several large natural graphs and synthetic graphs show that the method achieves lower replication and better balance than state-of-the-art baselines, while retaining the low computational cost that motivates streaming approaches in the first place.

**Discussion of the results.** The empirical findings are consistent with the design rationale of the method. The main quality measure for vertex-cut partitioning is the replication factor, which determines both the memory footprint and the communication volume of synchronization between replicas in gather-apply-scatter style computation [1]. Our results indicate that S-PowerGraph reduces this factor relative to hash-based and greedy streaming heuristics, and that the advantage is most visible on graphs with the heaviest skew. This is expected: when edges incident to a high-degree vertex are allowed to be cut, the replication cost is concentrated on a few vertices, whereas low-degree vertices, which constitute the vast majority, remain mostly unreplicated. The synthetic graphs, whose skew can be controlled, support this interpretation, since the gap between S-PowerGraph and edge-cut-oriented or degree-oblivious baselines widens as the power-law exponent decreases. We also observed that the load balance obtained by S-PowerGraph is competitive with or better than that of the baselines, which indicates that improvements in replication are not obtained at the expense of balanced workloads.

Another noteworthy observation concerns efficiency. Because each edge is processed once and the per-edge decision requires only a small amount of state, the running time and memory overhead of S-PowerGraph are close to those of simple streaming heuristics and far below those of offline partitioners, which need the whole graph in memory and multiple passes [3]. The simplicity of the method is therefore not merely an aesthetic property but a practical one: it makes the approach easy to implement within existing graph processing systems and to run in parallel over multiple input streams.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, as with other streaming methods, the quality of the partition depends on the order in which edges arrive. Adversarial or highly structured orderings, such as edges sorted by source vertex, may degrade the information available to the heuristic, and although we evaluated different orderings to a limited extent, a more systematic study of order sensitivity is needed. Second, our evaluation focuses on partition-quality metrics and partitioning cost; while these are widely accepted proxies for downstream performance, they do not fully capture the behavior of specific algorithms such as PageRank, connected components, or triangle counting under real network conditions and heterogeneous clusters. Third, S-PowerGraph exploits the power-law property of natural graphs. On graphs with near-uniform degree distributions, such as road networks or meshes, edge-cut methods may be as good or better, and the benefit of vertex-cut would be smaller [4]. Finally, the method maintains partial degree and placement information for vertices, whose memory cost grows with the number of vertices; for graphs with billions of vertices, this state may itself become a bottleneck unless compact or approximate data structures are used.

**Implications and future work.** The results suggest that, for natural graphs, practitioners should consider vertex-cut streaming partitioning as a default choice when ingestion speed and memory are limiting factors. The approach is also complementary to restreaming and refinement techniques, which repeat the pass over the data using information from earlier passes and have been shown to improve edge-cut quality [5]. Extending S-PowerGraph with such multi-pass refinement is a natural direction, and would offer a controllable trade-off between partitioning time and quality. Other directions include handling dynamic graphs in which edges are inserted and deleted over time, so that partitions can be maintained incrementally rather than recomputed; incorporating heterogeneous machine capacities and communication costs into the placement objective; and providing theoretical guarantees on the expected replication factor under power-law degree models, as has been done for random and greedy vertex-cut placement [1]. It would also be valuable to integrate the method into a full distributed system and to measure end-to-end job completion time across a broad range of graph algorithms.

**Conclusion.** We have presented S-PowerGraph, a simple and effective streaming vertex-cut partitioning method designed for the skewed degree distributions of natural graphs. By placing edges online with a rule that deliberately favors replicating high-degree vertices, the method lowers replication and maintains balanced loads at a computational cost comparable to that of lightweight streaming heuristics. Experiments on large real and synthetic graphs show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Despite the limitations discussed above, we believe that S-PowerGraph provides a practical foundation for scalable distributed graph analytics and a useful starting point for further work on streaming vertex-cut partitioning.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic inflammatory disease that primarily affects the joints and, if inadequately controlled, leads to progressive structural damage, functional disability, reduced quality of life and increased mortality. The prevalence of RA in Germany is estimated at roughly 0.5–1% of the adult population, and the disease causes substantial direct and indirect costs for the health care system and society. Over the past two decades, the treatment of RA has changed considerably. Early and aggressive treatment with conventional synthetic disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs), most notably methotrexate, is the cornerstone of therapy. Patients who do not reach the treatment target with csDMARDs, or who do not tolerate them, are candidates for biological DMARDs (bDMARDs). Current European guidelines recommend a treat-to-target strategy aiming at remission or at least low disease activity.

Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors were the first class of bDMARDs introduced and are still the most frequently used first-line biologicals in clinical practice. Since then, bDMARDs with other modes of action have become available, including the T-cell co-stimulation modulator abatacept, the interleukin-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab and the B-cell depleting antibody rituximab. These agents have demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials and have markedly improved outcomes for many patients with RA.

Despite these advances, a considerable proportion of patients do not achieve or maintain an adequate response to their first bDMARD. Primary non-response, secondary loss of efficacy, for example through development of anti-drug antibodies, and adverse events or patient preference lead to treatment discontinuation. Observational studies and registry data consistently show that persistence with a first anti-TNF therapy is far from ideal, with a substantial share of patients stopping treatment within the first year. As a consequence, many patients receive a second and, in some cases, a third bDMARD during the course of their disease.

The question of how to proceed after failure of a first anti-TNF is clinically important. Guidelines recommend that patients with an inadequate response to a first bDMARD should receive another bDMARD, but they do not clearly prefer one strategy over another. Treatment options include cycling to a second anti-TNF or switching to a biological with a different mode of action. Evidence from randomised trials, registries and some observational studies suggests that switching to a non-anti-TNF agent such as rituximab may be associated with better clinical outcomes than cycling to another anti-TNF, whereas other studies have found comparable effectiveness. Overall, the evidence base is heterogeneous, and the comparison is complicated by differences in patient populations, reasons for discontinuing the first agent, outcome definitions and follow-up.

Drug survival, or treatment persistence, is a widely used measure in observational research. It reflects the time a patient remains on a given therapy and integrates aspects of effectiveness, safety, tolerability and patient and physician satisfaction. It is therefore considered a pragmatic proxy for overall treatment success in real-world settings. While drug survival of first-line bDMARDs has been described in numerous studies, considerably less is known about the persistence of second-line bDMARD therapy. In particular, it is not well established whether the mode of action of the second bDMARD is associated with different persistence rates. Moreover, many existing studies are based on selected registry populations or specialist centres, and they often do not distinguish between permanent discontinuation, temporary interruption followed by re-initiation, and switching to a further bDMARD. This distinction matters, because a treatment gap followed by re-start has different clinical implications than definitive cessation or a switch to a third agent.

Claims data from statutory health insurance funds offer an opportunity to study treatment patterns in an unselected, real-world population over time. They capture all reimbursed prescriptions regardless of the prescriber, include a broad range of patients treated in routine care, and allow assessment of comorbidity and co-medication before and during treatment. Their limitations, notably the lack of clinical information such as disease activity and reasons for discontinuation, must be considered in interpretation, but they allow robust analyses of persistence and treatment sequences.

Against this background, we aimed to assess, in a large German claims database, the proportions of RA patients who discontinued, re-initiated or continued a second bDMARD, as well as the proportion who switched to a third bDMARD within 12 months after starting the second agent. We focused on patients whose first bDMARD was an anti-TNF and compared those who received a second anti-TNF with those who received a bDMARD with a different mode of action. In addition, we estimated drug survival of the second bDMARD and explored patient characteristics, including age, sex, comorbidity and prior medication, that were associated with earlier discontinuation or switching. We hypothesised that persistence would be higher in patients who changed to a non-anti-TNF mode of action than in those who cycled to another anti-TNF.

Study design and data source

We conducted a retrospective, non-interventional cohort study using German claims data from a statutory health insurance fund. The database covers inpatient and outpatient diagnoses (ICD-10-GM codes), outpatient prescriptions dispensed in pharmacies (coded by Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical [ATC] classification and Central Pharmaceutical Number), inpatient procedures, and demographic information (age, sex, date of death). The observation period ran from January 2010 to December 2013. The data were anonymized before analysis in accordance with German data protection regulations, so informed consent and ethics approval were not required for this secondary data analysis.

Study population

Patients were eligible if they had at least one inpatient or confirmed outpatient diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (ICD-10-GM M05.– or M06.–, excluding M06.1 and M06.3) and continuous insurance coverage during the observation period. Biological DMARDs (bDMARDs) were identified by ATC code. Anti-TNF agents comprised adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab and infliximab. Non-anti-TNF bDMARDs comprised abatacept, rituximab and tocilizumab.

Patients were included in the analysis if they had at least one prescription of an anti-TNF agent (first bDMARD) and at least one subsequent prescription of a second bDMARD that differed from the first anti-TNF agent. The second bDMARD could therefore be another anti-TNF (anti-TNF cycling) or a bDMARD with a different mode of action (non-anti-TNF). To ensure that the second bDMARD was a true second-line therapy, patients with bDMARD prescriptions before the first anti-TNF in a pre-observation period were excluded. Patients with a follow-up shorter than the required period, other than due to death, were excluded.

Index date and follow-up

The index date was the date of the first prescription of the second bDMARD. Follow-up started at the index date and lasted 12 months or until death, whichever came first. The pre-index period of up to 12 months before the index date was used to describe baseline characteristics.

Treatment episodes and outcome definitions

Treatment episodes were constructed from prescription dates and the defined daily dose or the labelled dosing interval of each substance. A grace period (permissible gap) of 60 days between the theoretical end of supply of one prescription and the next prescription was allowed to account for stockpiling and irregular dispensing; longer gaps were regarded as discontinuation. The following mutually exclusive outcomes were defined for the 12-month follow-up:

1. Continuation: continued prescriptions of the second bDMARD without a gap exceeding the grace period and without prescription of another bDMARD.
2. Switch: prescription of a third bDMARD different from the second bDMARD during follow-up. Switching was assigned to the date of the first prescription of the third agent.
3. Discontinuation without re-start: no further prescription of the second bDMARD after a gap exceeding the grace period, and no other bDMARD prescribed until the end of follow-up.
4. Discontinuation with re-start: a gap exceeding the grace period followed by a new prescription of the same second bDMARD within follow-up.

Drug survival was defined as time from the index date to discontinuation (gap exceeding the grace period, with or without re-start) or switch to a third bDMARD, whichever came first. Patients who were still on treatment at the end of follow-up or who died were censored.

Covariates

Covariates were assessed in the 12 months before the index date. They comprised age, sex, and comorbidity measured by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adapted for claims data. We also assessed concomitant and previous medication: conventional synthetic DMARDs (e.g., methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine), glucocorticoids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and painkillers (non-opioid and opioid analgesics). Further variables were the specific first anti-TNF agent, the specific second bDMARD, the time between the first anti-TNF and the second bDMARD, and selected comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes and depression.

Statistical analysis

Patient characteristics were described with means and standard deviations for continuous variables and absolute and relative frequencies for categorical variables. Patients receiving an anti-TNF as second bDMARD were compared with those receiving a non-anti-TNF bDMARD. Differences were tested using t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables, depending on distribution, and chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables. Proportions of patients continuing, discontinuing, re-starting or switching were compared between groups with chi-square tests.

Drug survival was estimated with the Kaplan–Meier method and groups were compared with the log-rank test. Mean drug survival time within the 12-month window was reported in days. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify factors independently associated with discontinuation (including re-start) or switch. The model included the mode of action of the second bDMARD (anti-TNF vs. non-anti-TNF), age, sex, CCI, and the medication variables listed above. Results are reported as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals. The proportional hazards assumption was checked using log-minus-log plots and Schoenfeld residuals. A two-sided p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. No adjustment for multiple testing was made because the analyses were exploratory. All analyses were performed with SAS or SPSS statistical software.

Because claims data record dispensed prescriptions rather than actual intake, and contain no clinical measures of disease activity, the reasons for discontinuation or switching could not be determined; these limitations were considered in interpreting the results.

A total of 2667 patients with RA and at least one anti-TNF prescription were identified in the claims database between 2010 and 2013. Of these, 451 patients (16.9%) received a second bDMARD that differed from the first anti-TNF and had at least one follow-up prescription of that drug, and they formed the study population. Of these, 340 patients (75.4%) received a second anti-TNF and 111 patients (24.6%) received a non-anti-TNF bDMARD as second-line therapy.

**Patient characteristics**

Patients in the anti-TNF group were younger than those in the non-anti-TNF group (mean age 52.6 vs. 55.9 years). The groups were otherwise broadly comparable with respect to sex distribution and the use of concomitant conventional synthetic DMARDs and glucocorticoids. Comorbidity, measured by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), was similar between groups, although a higher CCI was associated with poorer persistence in the multivariable analysis (see below). Previous painkiller medication was common in both groups. Baseline characteristics of both groups are shown in Table 1.

**Treatment outcomes during 12 months of follow-up**

Treatment pathways during the 12-month follow-up are summarized in Table 2. Overall, 56.8% of patients continued their second bDMARD for the full follow-up period, and 60% were on treatment if patients who re-started therapy after a gap were included.

Switching to a third bDMARD was significantly more frequent in the second anti-TNF group than in the non-anti-TNF group (28.8% vs. 11.7%, p < 0.001). Discontinuation without re-start occurred in 14.1% of patients in the anti-TNF group and 19.8% in the non-anti-TNF group, a difference that was not statistically significant (p = 0.179). Re-start after a treatment interruption was observed in 3.8% of anti-TNF patients and 1.8% of non-anti-TNF patients (p = 0.387). Continuation of the second bDMARD without discontinuation or switch was more common among non-anti-TNF patients than among anti-TNF patients (66.7% vs. 53.5%, p < 0.050).

Thus, the higher rate of switching in the anti-TNF group was the main driver of the difference in persistence, while simple discontinuation without further bDMARD therapy was numerically, but not significantly, more common in the non-anti-TNF group.

**Drug survival**

Drug survival differed between the two groups. The mean drug survival time of the second bDMARD was longer in patients receiving a non-anti-TNF (295 days) than in patients receiving a second anti-TNF (264 days; log-rank p = 0.016). Kaplan–Meier curves (Figure 1) showed that the curves separated early during follow-up, with a higher proportion of anti-TNF patients stopping or switching therapy within the first six months, and that the difference persisted until the end of the 12-month observation period.

**Factors associated with discontinuation or switch**

A Cox proportional hazards regression was performed to identify independent variables associated with the combined endpoint of discontinuation (including re-start) or switch to a third bDMARD (Table 3). The prescription of an anti-TNF as second bDMARD was associated with a significantly higher hazard of discontinuation or switch compared with a non-anti-TNF bDMARD (HR = 1.512). A higher comorbidity level, as measured by the CCI, was also independently associated with earlier discontinuation or switch (HR = 1.112 per point increase). In contrast, previous painkiller medication was associated with later discontinuation or switch (HR = 0.629), indicating a lower hazard of treatment failure in patients who had received analgesic therapy before the start of the second bDMARD.

Other covariates entered into the model, including age, sex, and concomitant medication with conventional DMARDs or glucocorticoids, were not significantly associated with the risk of discontinuation or switch after adjustment for the other variables.

**Summary of main findings**

In summary, only about 57% of patients with RA continued their second bDMARD therapy throughout 12 months of follow-up, and about 60% did so when re-starters were counted. Patients who received a non-anti-TNF bDMARD after a first anti-TNF were less likely to switch to a third bDMARD, had a higher probability of continuing therapy, and had longer drug survival than those who cycled to a second anti-TNF. After adjustment for patient characteristics, the use of an anti-TNF as second bDMARD and a higher comorbidity burden remained independently associated with earlier treatment failure, whereas prior painkiller use was associated with longer persistence.

In this analysis of German claims data, we examined the persistence of a second bDMARD in RA patients who had previously received an anti-TNF. About 57% of patients continued the second bDMARD for 12 months, and about 60% when re-starters were included. Patients who received a non-anti-TNF agent as second-line therapy were less likely to switch to a third bDMARD and had longer drug survival than patients who received a second anti-TNF. Receiving an anti-TNF as the second bDMARD and a higher comorbidity burden were associated with earlier discontinuation or switching, whereas prior painkiller use was associated with later discontinuation or switching.

Our findings agree with a number of registry and cohort studies suggesting that, after failure of a first anti-TNF, changing the mode of action may be at least as good as, and often better than, cycling to another anti-TNF. Several observational studies, including data from Swedish and Swiss registries, reported better retention or better clinical response with rituximab or abatacept than with a second anti-TNF. The randomized trial by Gomez-Reino and colleagues, and later work such as the ROC trial, produced somewhat mixed results. The latter found non-anti-TNF therapy to be superior in achieving good clinical response in patients who had discontinued a first anti-TNF because of inefficacy. The higher switching rate to a third bDMARD in our second anti-TNF group (28.8% vs. 11.7%) suggests that, in routine care, anti-TNF cycling often does not provide sustained benefit, whether because of lack of efficacy or adverse events. Our data cannot distinguish between these reasons, since claims data contain no information on the reasons for discontinuation.

The difference in discontinuation without re-start (14.1% vs. 19.8%) was not statistically significant, so the advantage of non-anti-TNF agents seems to arise mainly from fewer switches to a further bDMARD. This may partly reflect prescribing behaviour. Physicians may be more willing to move on quickly from a second anti-TNF, particularly if the first anti-TNF failed, whereas they may allow non-anti-TNF drugs, notably rituximab with its intermittent dosing and slower onset, more time. Differences in administration schedules also complicate persistence measurement for agents given in cycles. We addressed this using permissible gap definitions, but misclassification cannot be fully excluded.

The multivariable analysis showed that a second anti-TNF carried a roughly 50% higher hazard of discontinuation or switching (HR 1.512) than a non-anti-TNF. A higher Charlson Comorbidity Index was also associated with earlier discontinuation or switching (HR 1.112 per point). Comorbidity may increase the risk of adverse events, the reluctance of patients or physicians to continue therapy, or the occurrence of contraindications, and this is consistent with other reports of poorer persistence in multimorbid patients. The finding that previous painkiller use was associated with later discontinuation or switching (HR 0.629) is less obvious. One explanation is that patients with greater symptom burden and pain may have fewer alternatives and remain on therapy, or that concomitant analgesics help control residual symptoms and thereby reduce the need to change biologic therapy. Alternatively, painkiller use may be a marker of closer physician contact or different patient behaviour. This association should be interpreted cautiously and needs confirmation.

Patients in the non-anti-TNF group were somewhat older than those in the anti-TNF group (55.9 vs. 52.6 years). Age and sex did not appear to be the dominant determinants of persistence in our models, but residual confounding by disease activity, seropositivity, disease duration and previous treatment history is likely. Channeling bias is a particular concern: rituximab, for example, is often preferred in patients with a history of malignancy, lymphoma, or severe infection, and these patients may differ in persistence for reasons unrelated to the drug.

Several limitations should be noted. First, claims data lack clinical information such as disease activity scores, laboratory values, and patient-reported outcomes, so we could not assess effectiveness or the reasons for stopping. Persistence is a surrogate that integrates efficacy, tolerability, patient preference, and physician decisions. Second, the sample was small, particularly in the non-anti-TNF group (n = 111), which limited statistical power and precluded reliable comparisons between individual agents or between specific modes of action, such as rituximab, abatacept, and tocilizumab. Third, the follow-up of 12 months is short and does not permit conclusions about long-term survival. Fourth, the data come from a single German claims database covering 2010–2013, which may limit generalisability to other populations and to the current treatment landscape, in which JAK inhibitors, additional biologics, and biosimilars are available. Fifth, our inclusion criteria required a follow-up prescription of the second bDMARD, which may have excluded very early discontinuers and led to overestimation of persistence. Finally, we could not account for concomitant csDMARD or glucocorticoid dosing in detail.

Despite these limitations, the study has strengths. It reflects real-world prescribing in an unselected insured population, includes a considerable number of patients who would typically be excluded from clinical trials, and uses a clear definition of discontinuation, re-start, and switching, allowing a differentiated view of treatment trajectories beyond simple persistence.

In conclusion, only about 57% of RA patients continued their second bDMARD for 12 months, or around 60% if re-starts were counted, showing that treatment failure or intolerance remains common even beyond first-line biologic therapy. Patients who received a non-anti-TNF agent after an anti-TNF had a higher probability of continuing therapy, longer drug survival, and fewer switches to a third bDMARD than those who received a second anti-TNF. Comorbidity was a negative predictor of persistence. These findings support considering a change in mode of action when a first anti-TNF fails, although they do not establish causality. Prospective studies with clinical outcome data and larger samples are needed to confirm these results and to identify patients who benefit most from each strategy.

The Antarctic ice sheet holds enough ice to raise global mean sea level by about 58 m, most of it in the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS). Although the EAIS has long been considered stable relative to the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, parts of it rest on bedrock well below sea level and drain through outlet glaciers that are sensitive to ocean forcing. The Wilkes Subglacial Basin and the Aurora Subglacial Basin together hold a marine-based ice volume equivalent to several metres of sea level. Whether these basins are vulnerable to atmospheric and oceanic warming is a central question for projections of future sea-level rise, and it can be addressed only by examining how the ice sheet responded in past warm climates.

The Pliocene epoch (5.3–2.6 Myr ago) is a particularly useful target. Atmospheric CO2 concentrations during the mid-Pliocene warm period (about 3.3–3.0 Myr ago) were approximately 350–450 ppm, comparable to present-day and near-future values, and global mean temperatures were roughly 2–3 °C above pre-industrial levels. Continental configurations and topography were similar to today, although the details of subglacial topography remain uncertain. Reconstructions of Pliocene sea level nevertheless vary widely, from a few metres to more than 25 m above present, depending on the proxy, the correction for glacial isostatic adjustment and dynamic topography, and the assumptions made about ice sheet sources. Such high estimates imply substantial loss of Greenland, West Antarctic and possibly East Antarctic ice. In contrast, the most recent assessment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (AR5) concluded that Pliocene sea level on Milankovitch timescales likely did not exceed +20 m, and that the Antarctic contribution was constrained mainly by indirect evidence.

Geological evidence from the East Antarctic margin and interior gives a seemingly contradictory picture. Marine sediment cores from Wilkes Land and Prydz Bay, and from the Ross Sea, record episodes of reduced sea ice, elevated productivity and ice-margin retreat during the Pliocene, and have been interpreted as showing that marine-based sectors of the EAIS retreated inland. Isotopic and provenance data from offshore sediments point in the same direction. Terrestrial records, on the other hand, such as high-elevation geomorphology of the Transantarctic Mountains, the persistence of ancient surfaces and buried ice in the Dry Valleys, and the survival of sparse tundra-like deposits at elevation, have been used to argue either for a persistently cold, stable interior or for substantial thinning and warm episodes. The two lines of evidence need not conflict if marginal retreat occurred together with interior thickening, a pattern predicted by some models because a warmer atmosphere and reduced sea ice carry more moisture to the continent, increasing snowfall over the high plateau. Testing this prediction requires direct constraints on past ice surface elevations.

Cosmogenic nuclide exposure dating of bedrock and glacial erratics provides such constraints. Nuclides such as 10Be, 26Al and 21Ne accumulate in rock surfaces exposed above the ice, and so record when mountain summits and nunataks were last uncovered. In Antarctica, where erosion rates are among the lowest on Earth, nuclide concentrations can preserve information over millions of years, and paired nuclides allow burial and complex exposure histories to be identified. Elevation transects of exposure ages along outlet glaciers can document ice thickness changes through time. A considerable dataset has now been assembled for the Transantarctic Mountains, Dronning Maud Land and the Lambert–Amery system. However, the interpretation of exposure ages is not straightforward. Cold-based ice can cover surfaces without eroding them, producing inherited nuclides. Ages are therefore minimum or ambiguous constraints, and individual sites are strongly influenced by local glaciological conditions. Synthesis across regions, together with a physical framework to interpret regional trends, is therefore needed.

Ice sheet models offer such a framework but are themselves sensitive to uncertain boundary conditions, including bedrock topography, climate forcing, basal sliding and ocean melt. Simulations of Pliocene Antarctica have produced a wide range of ice volumes, and some show a major retreat in the Wilkes and Aurora basins while others retain a nearly modern ice sheet. Comparing model output with geological data at specific sites narrows these uncertainties and clarifies whether the geological records are mutually consistent.

In this study we combine new cosmogenic nuclide exposure ages from East Antarctica with previously published data to reconstruct Plio-Pleistocene changes in ice thickness along the EAIS margin and interior. We then use a three-dimensional thermomechanical ice sheet model driven with mid-Pliocene boundary conditions to test whether the exposure record can be explained by interior thickening accompanied by retreat in the major subglacial basins. We evaluate the implied net EAIS contribution to sea level in the context of West Antarctic and Greenland contributions and the AR5 estimate. Finally, we consider the role of the climatic transition around 3 Myr ago, when cooling, expanded sea ice and reduced moisture transport are expected to have reduced snow accumulation and thinned the ice sheet, at least in coastal areas.

Cosmogenic nuclide exposure ages were compiled from nunataks and moraine sequences in the Transantarctic Mountains, Dronning Maud Land and the Prince Charles Mountains, and combined with new measurements from the Aurora Basin sector. Ice sheet simulations were then used to place the exposure data in the context of continental-scale ice volume.

**Field sampling.** Samples of bedrock and glacial erratics were collected from elevation transects at sites bordering the present ice margin. Sampling targeted flat, stable surfaces showing no evidence of recent toppling, burial by till or snow, or significant surface erosion. We recorded sample location by handheld GPS and elevation by barometric altimetry calibrated against differential GPS benchmarks. Topographic shielding was measured with a clinometer and compass. Sample thickness was measured directly. Only the uppermost few centimetres of each rock were taken, using a hammer and chisel or a rock saw.

**Laboratory procedures.** Samples were crushed and sieved to 250–500 µm. Quartz was isolated by magnetic separation, froth flotation and repeated leaching in dilute HF/HNO₃, until purity was verified by ICP-OES measurement of aluminium (<150 ppm). Beryllium and aluminium were extracted following standard ion-exchange chromatography after dissolution in concentrated HF, with a ⁹Be carrier added. For samples with low concentrations, a few grains were additionally processed for ²¹Ne by stepwise heating and noble-gas mass spectrometry. Be and Al were precipitated as hydroxides, oxidised to BeO and Al₂O₃, and mixed with niobium or silver powder before pressing into cathodes. ¹⁰Be/⁹Be and ²⁶Al/²⁷Al ratios were measured by accelerator mass spectrometry, normalised to the standards KN-5-2 and ICN01-5-1 (¹⁰Be) and ZAL94 (²⁶Al). Procedural blanks were processed with each batch of samples, and their ratios were subtracted with uncertainties propagated in quadrature.

**Exposure age calculation.** Ages were calculated using the CRONUS-Earth online calculator framework with an Antarctic sea-level high-latitude production rate and time-dependent Lal/Stone scaling. Atmospheric pressure was derived from the ERA reanalysis pressure–elevation relationship appropriate for Antarctica instead of the standard atmosphere, which overestimates pressure. Sample density was set to 2.65 g cm⁻³. We report minimum exposure ages assuming zero erosion and also ages for erosion rates of 0.1–1 m Myr⁻¹, constrained where nuclides were close to saturation. Samples with ²⁶Al/¹⁰Be ratios falling below the constant-exposure field were interpreted as having complex histories involving burial by ice, and were treated as indicating at least one episode of cover. In these cases, the ages are minimum estimates of total history rather than the timing of final deglaciation. Previously published ages were recalculated with the same production-rate scheme to ensure internal consistency.

**Reconstructing ice thickness change.** Exposure age–elevation relationships were used to infer the timing and rate of ice surface lowering. Where a transect exhibited an age increase with elevation, we fitted linear regressions with uncertainty weighting. Sites with older ages at the highest elevations were used to infer when the ice surface last stood above the sample. Inheritance from earlier exposure was evaluated through nuclide pair relationships and by comparing neighbouring samples. Outliers were identified using reduced chi-squared and removed only when statistically justified and geomorphologically explainable. To compare sites, ice-surface elevation changes were corrected for glacio-isostatic adjustment using a simple Earth model, and for changes in the geoid where relevant.

**Ice sheet model.** We used the thermomechanical ice sheet model PISM (Parallel Ice Sheet Model) run on a 10 km grid across the Antarctic continent, using a hybrid of the shallow-ice and shallow-shelf approximations. Present-day bed topography was taken from Bedmap2, and geothermal heat flux from a published geophysical estimate. Basal sliding followed a pseudo-plastic power law with till friction angle dependent on bed elevation. Surface mass balance was calculated with a positive-degree-day scheme (melt factors for snow and ice of 3 and 8 mm w.e. K⁻¹ d⁻¹). Ice shelf calving was handled with a combination of eigencalving and a thickness threshold, and sub-shelf melt was parameterised as a function of ocean temperature. Bedrock response used an elastic lithosphere–relaxing asthenosphere model.

**Mid-Pliocene boundary conditions.** Mid-Pliocene atmospheric and oceanic forcing was derived from PlioMIP climate model output, expressed as anomalies relative to the pre-industrial simulation and added to present-day observational climatologies (precipitation scaled exponentially with temperature change, ~5% per K). Atmospheric CO₂ was set at 400 ppm. Initial topography used the PRISM4 reconstruction, with reduced ice volume and the Wilkes and Aurora subglacial basins assumed to be isostatically adjusted. Ocean warming was applied to sub-shelf melt rates, and we tested sensitivity to the magnitude by varying ocean temperature anomalies between 0 and +3 °C.

**Experiment design.** Simulations were spun up for 100 kyr from present-day ice and then run for 500 kyr under constant mid-Pliocene forcing, allowing equilibrium to be approached. Orbital variability was explored by modulating the forcing between cold and warm orbital extremes with a glacial index. We carried out an ensemble varying key uncertain parameters: positive-degree-day factors, basal sliding exponent, calving threshold, ocean melt coefficient, and precipitation scaling. Ensemble members were scored against the present-day ice thickness and extent, and against the exposure age constraints. Model outputs for ice-thickness change at the sample locations were interpolated and compared directly with the exposure data.

**Sea-level contribution.** Ice volume changes were converted to sea-level equivalent above floatation, taking into account the density contrast and the area of the ocean. Contributions from West Antarctica and Greenland were taken from published simulations and combined with the East Antarctic results, and compared against the IPCC AR5 assessment.

Exposure ages from the Transantarctic Mountains and the East Antarctic coast and margin nunataks record a coherent pattern of surface lowering since the Pliocene. We compiled 214 new and previously published 10Be, 26Al and 21Ne exposure ages from 17 sites, and report here both the compiled data and the ice sheet model experiments.

**Exposure ages and elevation transects.** Samples from the highest elevations at interior sites (more than 150 m above the present ice surface) yield minimum exposure ages of 2.5 to 5.1 Myr, with the oldest ages in the Dry Valleys region and the Sør Rondane and Prince Charles Mountains. Cosmogenic nuclide concentrations in these samples approach the values expected for steady-state erosion, and erosion rates calculated from 10Be alone are 0.1 to 0.6 m Myr⁻¹. Paired 26Al/10Be ratios in 38 samples fall below the constant-exposure line, indicating burial or intermittent cover by ice. For these samples, simple burial histories imply that the high-elevation surfaces were covered by ice for cumulative periods of 0.4 to 1.9 Myr after initial exposure.

At interior sites, the pattern is of older exposure ages at higher elevations. Ages at 50 to 150 m above the modern ice decrease systematically to 0.1 to 1.2 Myr, consistent with progressive thinning. In contrast, the coastal and outlet glacier sites show a different pattern. Near the coast, exposure ages above 100 m rarely exceed 1 Myr, and the oldest surfaces at these locations have been shaped by repeated Pleistocene glaciations. Cosmogenic inheritance is common in the youngest coastal samples (about 20% of samples show ages inconsistent with deglaciation chronologies), but it does not change the regional pattern.

Taken together, the data imply that interior ice surfaces were higher than at present at times in the Pliocene by tens to about 150 m, depending on the site, and that thinning occurred in several steps rather than a single event. The most robust thinning signal in the dataset is between 3.3 and 2.5 Myr, when ages from mid-elevation surfaces cluster. A second cluster occurs at 1.2 to 0.8 Myr, coinciding with the mid-Pleistocene transition in glacial cycles.

**Model simulations of the mid-Pliocene.** We ran the ice sheet model with mid-Pliocene boundary conditions: temperatures and precipitation from a climate model simulation with 400 ppm CO2, reduced ice sheet topography, and isostatically adjusted bedrock. The simulation was initialized from modern ice and run for 100 kyr to equilibrium. The resulting East Antarctic ice sheet shows a distinct pattern: ice thickens by 50 to 250 m in the interior domes, where increased snowfall from warmer, moister air outweighs enhanced melting. Along the coast at lower elevations, margins retreat inland and thin by 100 to 400 m.

The largest changes occur in the marine-based basins. In the Wilkes Subglacial Basin, grounding lines retreat by up to 600 km inland, and the basin is largely deglaciated. The Aurora Subglacial Basin loses about 70% of its modern ice area. Together these two basins contribute 3.8 to 6.9 m of sea level equivalent. The remainder of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet gains volume in the interior, offsetting about 1.5 to 2.4 m of the loss. The net East Antarctic contribution to Pliocene sea level is therefore +2.1 to +4.8 m relative to present, depending on the choice of climate forcing and basal sliding parameters.

**Model–data comparison.** Modeled ice thickness changes were compared with the exposure age sites by extracting the simulated surface elevation change at each location. At 12 of 17 sites the simulated sign of the thickness change matches that inferred from the ages. The model reproduces interior thickening at the Dry Valleys, Sør Rondane and Prince Charles Mountains sites, with a mean absolute difference of 62 m between simulated and inferred maximum elevations. It overestimates thinning at the Wilkes and Dronning Maud Land coastal sites, where modeled retreat exceeds that suggested by the data. Sensitivity experiments in which Pliocene precipitation was reduced by 20% eliminate interior thickening at 8 sites, and produce a poorer fit to the ages, indicating that enhanced moisture delivery is necessary to explain the interior record.

**Sensitivity to forcing.** Varying atmospheric CO2 between 350 and 450 ppm changes the East Antarctic contribution from +1.2 to +6.0 m. Ocean temperatures have a strong control on grounding line retreat in the Wilkes and Aurora basins: a 1°C increase in subsurface ocean temperature adds 0.9 m of sea level equivalent. Including West Antarctic and Greenland contributions of +3 to +8 m and +0.5 to +2 m, respectively, from published simulations, the combined Pliocene sea level highstand is +7 to +15 m in most experiments, with a maximum of 19 m, below +20 m.

**Late Pliocene cooling.** In experiments imposing cooler conditions representative of the period after 3 Myr, with lower temperatures and greater winter sea ice extent, precipitation along the coast declines by 15 to 30% and the interior accumulation falls by 10 to 20%. The ice surface thins by 40 to 120 m near the coast, and the thinning is driven by reduced snowfall rather than increased melt. This is consistent with the exposure ages showing coastal thinning after about 3 Myr.

Our exposure age compilation and model experiments together point to a Pliocene EAIS that differed from the present in its spatial pattern of thickness change more than in its total volume. Exposure ages from nunataks and mountain ranges across the interior, including the Transantarctic Mountains and Dronning Maud Land, record surfaces that were last covered by thicker ice during the Pliocene and have been progressively exposed since. This interior thickening is counterintuitive if warmth is assumed to cause uniform ice loss, but it is consistent with a warmer atmosphere carrying more moisture to a cold, high-elevation interior where temperatures remain well below freezing and the surface mass balance is accumulation-dominated. Our simulations with mid-Pliocene boundary conditions reproduce this behaviour, which strengthens the case that the exposure age signal reflects a large-scale response to climate and not local glaciological effects.

The model also indicates that the marine-based Wilkes Subglacial and Aurora Basins largely melted under Pliocene forcing. These basins are grounded well below sea level on retrograde slopes and are therefore vulnerable to ocean-driven retreat. The retreat there offsets much of the volume gained in the interior, so the net EAIS contribution to sea level is modest. This partitioning matters for interpreting far-field sea-level reconstructions. A Pliocene highstand does not require a uniformly smaller East Antarctic ice sheet, and a combination of interior growth and marginal or basin loss can yield a small net change. Exposure ages from the interior alone might suggest ice volume stability or growth, while the offsetting retreat in the basins is largely invisible to such data because few outcrops constrain it. Only the model, or sedimentary and geochemical records from the margins, can address that part of the system.

Adding plausible contributions from West Antarctica and Greenland, our results are consistent with the AR5 assessment that Pliocene global mean sea level likely did not exceed about +20 m on Milankovitch timescales. Higher estimates have often assumed substantial East Antarctic retreat and typically do not account for compensating interior growth. We do not exclude short-lived excursions beyond this bound during exceptionally warm orbital configurations, since both the exposure ages and the equilibrium-style simulations integrate over long periods. However, our results argue against a persistent large-scale collapse of the EAIS during the Late Pliocene.

The exposure ages further suggest that the decline in interior and coastal thickness since about 3 Myr is linked to the onset of colder climate. Cooling expanded sea ice, which would have increased the distance between open-ocean moisture sources and the ice sheet and reduced the efficiency of atmospheric moisture transport. Lower precipitation then reduced accumulation, and the ice sheet thinned, at least in coastal areas where the effect on snowfall is greatest. This is an indirect mechanism in which cooling thins ice by starving it of snow, in contrast to the usual association of cooling with ice growth. It implies that the sensitivity of the EAIS to temperature is not monotonic and depends on the coupling between sea ice, moisture supply and accumulation. The same coupling may operate in the future, but in the opposite direction: reduced sea ice and a warmer, moister atmosphere could promote accumulation gains in the interior even as the margins and marine basins respond to oceanic warming.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. Exposure ages are sparse and spatially biased towards ice-free mountain areas, and they record minimum exposure durations affected by inheritance, erosion and complex burial histories. Interpreting them as thickness changes assumes that ice cover was sufficient to shield the surfaces, and cold-based ice may preserve nuclide inventories, so some ages may reflect prior exposure. The ice sheet model depends on the prescribed climate forcing, which is derived from a limited set of Pliocene reconstructions and simulations with uncertain sea-ice extent, precipitation and ocean temperature. Basal conditions, bedrock topography, isostatic adjustment and sub-shelf melt parameterisations are also uncertain, and these directly affect the simulated retreat in the Wilkes and Aurora Basins. Steady-state simulations cannot capture hysteresis or the timing of retreat and regrowth within Milankovitch cycles. Finally, the Pliocene was not a perfect analogue for the future: atmospheric CO2 was similar to present, but the ice sheet was adjusting to different bed topography and to slow, long-lasting forcing instead of rapid anthropogenic change.

In conclusion, a combined exposure age and modelling approach indicates that the Pliocene EAIS thickened in its interior while the Wilkes Subglacial and Aurora Basins largely melted, producing a limited net sea-level contribution consistent with AR5 bounds. The subsequent cooling and sea-ice expansion since about 3 Myr reduced moisture delivery and thinned the ice sheet, particularly near the coast. Future work should extend exposure age coverage, especially in sectors adjacent to the marine basins, and combine ice sheet models with coupled climate simulations that represent sea-ice and moisture transport interactions. Such efforts will better constrain how East Antarctica will respond to continued warming.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary malignancy of the liver and a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Its incidence continues to rise, particularly in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hepatitis B infection is endemic, and in Western countries, where hepatitis C, alcohol-related liver disease, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease are major contributors. Because HCC usually arises in the setting of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis, treatment decisions must balance tumor burden against underlying hepatic function. Curative options, including resection, liver transplantation, and local ablation, are available only to patients diagnosed at an early stage. Unfortunately, a large proportion of patients are diagnosed at an intermediate or advanced stage, when curative treatment is no longer feasible.

For patients with intermediate-stage disease, namely those with multinodular, unresectable HCC, preserved liver function, and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread, transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE) is the recommended first-line therapy in major clinical guidelines, including the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer staging system. TACE exploits the fact that HCC receives its blood supply predominantly from the hepatic artery, whereas normal hepatic parenchyma is supplied mainly by the portal vein. Selective delivery of a chemotherapeutic agent, followed by embolization of the tumor-feeding arteries, produces both a high local drug concentration and ischemic necrosis. Randomized trials and meta-analyses have shown that TACE improves survival in carefully selected patients compared with conservative management. Nevertheless, TACE has important limitations. Complete tumor necrosis is achieved in a minority of patients, and recurrence and progression are common. Moreover, embolization induces hypoxia in residual viable tumor, which upregulates hypoxia-inducible factor-1α and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other pro-angiogenic factors. This response may promote neovascularization, tumor revascularization, and metastasis, thereby undermining the benefit of the procedure. Repeated TACE sessions may also worsen liver function.

These observations provided the rationale for combining TACE with systemic antiangiogenic therapy. Sorafenib, an oral multikinase inhibitor, targets Raf kinase, VEGF receptors, and platelet-derived growth factor receptor-β, thereby exerting both antiproliferative and antiangiogenic effects. In the SHARP and Asia-Pacific trials, sorafenib significantly prolonged overall survival and time to progression in patients with advanced HCC compared with placebo, establishing it as the first effective systemic agent for this disease. It was therefore hypothesized that sorafenib could counteract the surge in angiogenic signaling following TACE, delay tumor progression, and ultimately improve survival. Preclinical data and early-phase studies supported the feasibility and apparent safety of the combination, and several retrospective and non-randomized studies, particularly from Asia, reported encouraging outcomes.

However, results from prospective randomized trials have been less consistent. The SPACE trial, a phase II study of drug-eluting bead TACE with sorafenib or placebo, showed a trend toward improved time to progression but no significant survival benefit. The post-TACE trial conducted in Japan and Korea found no improvement in time to progression with sorafenib after TACE. The TACE 2 trial in the United Kingdom, as well as a trial from China, also investigated the combination in double-blind, placebo-controlled designs, with variable findings. Differences among these studies in patient populations, etiologies of liver disease, TACE techniques (conventional versus drug-eluting beads), timing of sorafenib initiation, treatment duration, and dose intensity may have contributed to heterogeneous results. In addition, the small sample sizes of some trials limited their statistical power to detect differences in survival. Open-label studies and retrospective analyses are further susceptible to bias, which complicates interpretation of the overall evidence.

Safety is another important consideration. Sorafenib is associated with characteristic adverse events, including hand and foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, diarrhea, fatigue, hypertension, and anorexia, which frequently necessitate dose reduction or interruption. When sorafenib is added to TACE, which itself causes post-embolization syndrome and may transiently impair liver function, the tolerability of combined treatment may be reduced, and reduced adherence may in turn diminish efficacy. Quantitative assessment of the incremental toxicity of the combination relative to TACE alone is therefore essential for balanced clinical decision-making.

Several previous meta-analyses have evaluated TACE plus sorafenib, but many pooled randomized and non-randomized studies, including retrospective cohorts and open-label trials, which introduces substantial heterogeneity and risk of bias. To provide a more reliable estimate of the effect of the combination, it is preferable to restrict the analysis to double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials, in which performance and detection biases are minimized, particularly for subjective outcomes such as radiological progression and adverse event reporting.

Therefore, we conducted a meta-analysis of double-blind randomized controlled trials comparing TACE combined with sorafenib with TACE plus placebo in patients with HCC. We aimed to evaluate the effects of the combination on time to progression and overall survival, and to quantify the risks of sorafenib-related adverse events, including HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. We also sought to explore sources of heterogeneity through subgroup analysis, so as to clarify the benefit–risk profile of this combination strategy.

This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The protocol defined the research question, eligibility criteria, outcomes, and analytic approach before data extraction.

**Search strategy**

We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception to the date of the final search. The search combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to the intervention and disease: "hepatocellular carcinoma," "liver cancer," "HCC," "transcatheter arterial chemoembolization," "transarterial chemoembolization," "TACE," "sorafenib," "Nexavar," "randomized," "double-blind," and "placebo." No language restrictions were applied initially. We also manually screened the reference lists of included trials, previous meta-analyses, and relevant reviews, as well as abstracts from major oncology and hepatology meetings, to identify additional eligible studies.

**Eligibility criteria**

Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) randomized controlled trial with a double-blind, placebo-controlled design; (2) participants were adults with HCC diagnosed by histology or by accepted noninvasive imaging criteria; (3) the experimental arm received TACE (conventional or drug-eluting bead) combined with sorafenib, and the control arm received TACE combined with placebo; and (4) the study reported at least one outcome of interest, namely time to progression (TTP), overall survival (OS), or sorafenib-related adverse events. Exclusion criteria were non-randomized or open-label designs, studies comparing sorafenib with other systemic agents, studies in which sorafenib was given after TACE failure as a salvage therapy without a placebo control, duplicate publications, conference abstracts without sufficient data, and animal or in vitro studies. When multiple reports described the same trial, the most complete or most recent dataset was used.

**Study selection and data extraction**

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed the full texts of potentially eligible records. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consultation with a third reviewer. Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardized form. Extracted items included first author, year of publication, trial name, countries of enrollment, sample size per arm, patient characteristics (age, sex, etiology of liver disease, Child-Pugh class, ECOG performance status, tumor stage), TACE regimen and schedule, sorafenib dose and timing relative to TACE, duration of follow-up, hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for TTP and OS, and the number of patients experiencing each adverse event. Adverse events of interest were hand and foot skin reaction (HFSR), rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea; where available, we extracted any-grade events, and otherwise used the grading reported by the trial. When HRs were not reported directly, they were estimated from Kaplan-Meier curves or other published statistics using established methods.

**Risk of bias assessment**

Methodological quality was assessed independently by two reviewers with the Cochrane Collaboration risk of bias tool, which evaluates random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other sources of bias. Each domain was rated as low, unclear, or high risk. We additionally recorded whether analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. Disagreements were resolved by consensus.

**Outcomes**

The primary efficacy outcomes were TTP, defined as the interval from randomization to radiologic tumor progression, and OS, defined as the interval from randomization to death from any cause. The safety outcomes were the incidence of sorafenib-related adverse events, namely HFSR, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea.

**Statistical analysis**

For time-to-event outcomes, log HRs and their standard errors were pooled using the inverse-variance method, and results are presented as HRs with 95% CIs. An HR below 1 favored the experimental (TACE plus sorafenib) group. For adverse events, risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs were calculated and pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel method.
