By marginalising over the embedding uncertainty, the classifier down-weights unreliable embeddings automatically, with no heuristic length normalisation. We believe this explains the smaller gap between training and test performance in the topic identification experiments. Point-estimate systems tend to fit idiosyncrasies of the training embeddings. A model that carries the covariance forward is regularised by the uncertainty of each observation.

*Perplexity and the role of the prior.* The lower perplexity relative to NVDM on Fisher and 20Newsgroups should be interpreted with care. Perplexity bounds are computed from the variational lower bound, so comparisons depend on the tightness of the bound in each model. NVDM relies on an amortised encoder, which can introduce an amortisation gap. Bayesian SMM instead optimises per-document variational parameters, which can give a tighter bound at higher inference cost. Part of the improvement may therefore come from more flexible inference rather than from the generative model alone. The regularising effect of the prior over the embeddings and of the sparsity-inducing prior on the subspace parameters is also important. Without these terms, the model overfits the sparse count data, particularly for small training sets. A complete ablation separating inference quality from model structure would clarify the relative contributions, and we regard it as important future work.

*Intractability in mixed-logit models.* The log-sum-exp term in the softmax normaliser makes the expected log-likelihood intractable under a Gaussian posterior. Our approach replaces this term with a tractable bound, which permits closed-form or low-variance updates. Such bounds introduce approximation error. Their tightness depends on the variational parameters and on vocabulary size, and the error may grow when the posterior covariance is large, which is precisely the regime of short documents. The empirical results suggest that the approximation is adequate for the corpora studied. We nonetheless caution that the quality of the bound has not been verified on very large vocabularies or on strongly multimodal posteriors. The Gaussian family itself restricts the shapes of uncertainty that can be represented. Real posteriors over topic mixtures may be skewed or heavy-tailed, and richer families such as normalising flows could capture this at greater computational cost.

*Comparison with supervised models.* The unsupervised embeddings, combined with a simple generative classifier, outperform other unsupervised topic models and approach fully supervised discriminative systems. This is notable because the embedding extractor never sees the labels. The practical implication is that one can train the representation on large unlabelled collections and fit a lightweight classifier on limited labelled data. The remaining gap to the best discriminative models indicates that unsupervised objectives do not necessarily allocate capacity to label-relevant directions. Coupling the generative and discriminative objectives, for example through supervised or semi-supervised variants of the model, is a natural extension.

*Limitations.* Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the bag-of-words assumption ignores word order and local context, so the model cannot capture phenomena that depend on syntax or discourse. Second, the Fisher speech experiments use automatic transcripts, and recognition errors add noise that is not modelled explicitly. Although the uncertainty estimates appear to absorb part of this noise, we have not separated recognition noise from intrinsic ambiguity. Third, the Gaussian classifier assumes class-conditional Gaussian embeddings with shared or simple covariance structure. This may be inadequate for classes that are heterogeneous in content. Finally, the calibration of the learned uncertainties was assessed indirectly, through downstream performance and correlation with document length. A direct calibration analysis would give stronger evidence that the covariances reflect true estimation error.

**Conclusion**

We introduced Bayesian SMM, a generative log-linear model that represents each document as a Gaussian posterior over a low-dimensional embedding, with the covariance expressing how well the embedding is determined by the observed text. We addressed the intractability of variational inference in mixed-logit models through a tractable bound on the normaliser, which gives an efficient and stable inference procedure. On Fisher and 20Newsgroups, the model achieved better perplexity than NVDM. Combined with a generative Gaussian linear classifier that uses the embedding uncertainty, it gave topic identification results that were robust to overfitting. These results outperformed those of other unsupervised topic models and were comparable to those of fully supervised discriminative systems.

These findings suggest that propagating uncertainty through the pipeline, from representation to classification, is a simple and effective way to improve generalisation in settings with documents of widely varying length and reliability. Several directions follow naturally. These include tighter or alternative bounds for the softmax normaliser, more expressive posterior families, hierarchical or sequential extensions that capture word order, and joint training with supervision. The learned uncertainties could also be used for tasks such as active learning, rejection of unreliable inputs, and confidence-aware retrieval. We hope this work encourages broader use of uncertainty-aware document representations.

Cryptococcosis is a life-threatening mycosis caused by basidiomycetous yeasts of the Cryptococcus neoformans/Cryptococcus gattii species complex [1,2]. Infection follows inhalation of desiccated yeast cells or spores, which establish a primary pulmonary focus and, in susceptible hosts, disseminate hematogenously to the central nervous system, causing meningoencephalitis [3]. Cryptococcosis is responsible for an estimated one million cases annually worldwide, with a high mortality rate, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa [4]. Historically, C. neoformans has been considered an opportunistic pathogen of immunocompromised individuals, especially patients with HIV/AIDS, whereas C. gattii has been associated with disease in apparently immunocompetent hosts [5,6].

**Epidemiology and population structure of C. gattii**

C. gattii was originally restricted to tropical and subtropical regions and associated with Eucalyptus species [7]. This view changed after the outbreak on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, in 1999, which spread to the mainland of Canada and the Pacific Northwest of the United States [8,9]. The outbreak was dominated by molecular type VGII, including the hypervirulent VGIIa/b genotypes, and generated considerable interest in the mechanisms underlying the enhanced virulence of these strains, such as tubular mitochondrial morphology, increased intracellular proliferation within macrophages and altered host immune responses [10,11].

Based on molecular typing, C. gattii is classified into four major types, VGI to VGIV [12], and recent genomic analyses have proposed that these lineages may represent distinct cryptic species [13]. Capsular serotypes B and C are both found in C. gattii. Serotype B includes types VGI, VGII and VGIII, whereas serotype C corresponds mainly to VGIII and VGIV [12]. VGIV is the most frequent type in HIV-infected patients in sub-Saharan Africa, while VGIII has been reported in both clinical and environmental samples from Latin America and in HIV-positive patients in California [14,15]. Despite this clinical relevance, the vast majority of experimental studies have focused on serotype B isolates, particularly VGI and VGII. Consequently, the pathogenic properties of serotype C strains remain poorly characterized.

**Virulence determinants in Cryptococcus**

The pathogenic potential of Cryptococcus species depends on several well-characterized virulence factors. The polysaccharide capsule, composed mainly of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), is the main determinant; it inhibits phagocytosis, modulates cytokine responses and protects against oxidative stress [16,17]. Capsule synthesis requires the products of the CAP genes (CAP10, CAP59, CAP60 and CAP64), whose deletion results in acapsular, avirulent mutants [18]. Capsule size and structure are highly variable among isolates and are regulated by environmental conditions, and GXM structural differences affect recognition by monoclonal antibodies and the host immune response [19,20]. Melanin, produced through laccase-mediated oxidation of diphenolic compounds, protects fungal cells against oxidative and nitrosative damage, antifungal drugs and host effector mechanisms [21]. In addition, chitin and chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule contribute to cell integrity, capsule architecture and the interaction with host chitinases, which have been linked to the modulation of immune responses and to disease susceptibility [22,23]. Other factors, including extracellular enzymes such as urease and phospholipase, and the ability to grow at 37 °C, are also essential for survival and dissemination in the host [3,24].

Phenotypic variability in these traits among isolates of the same species has been correlated with differences in virulence in animal models [25,26]. In the case of C. gattii, the hypervirulence of VGII strains has been related to their capacity to proliferate rapidly in lung tissue and to evade immune surveillance [10,27]. However, whether similar mechanisms operate in serotype C isolates, or whether VGIII and VGIV lineages differ in their virulence profiles, is unknown. Some reports suggest that VGIII and VGIV isolates are generally less virulent in mice than VGII isolates [28,29], but the number of strains analyzed is limited and a systematic comparison of phenotypic attributes and virulence is lacking.

**Rationale and objectives**

Given the clinical importance of VGIV in Africa and of VGIII in the Americas, and the scarcity of experimental data on these lineages, a detailed analysis of the phenotypic diversity of serotype C isolates is warranted. Understanding how variation in capsule properties, cell wall composition, pigment production and antigenic structure translates into differences in virulence may provide insights into the pathogenesis of infections caused by these molecular types and into the factors that determine tissue tropism, in particular the ability to colonize the central nervous system.

In the present study, we compared three serotype C C. gattii isolates, one VGIII (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV (WM 779 and 106.97), with respect to capsule dimensions, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, induction of host chitinase activity, pigment production and reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies. We then evaluated the virulence of these isolates in a murine model of intranasal infection, assessing lethality and fungal burden in the lungs and brain. By integrating phenotypic and in vivo data, we aimed to determine whether serotype C isolates of distinct molecular types differ in their pathogenic potential.

**Fungal isolates and growth conditions**

Three serotype C *Cryptococcus gattii* isolates were used: 106.97 (molecular type VGIV), WM 779 (VGIV) and ATCC 24066 (VGIII). Molecular types were confirmed by URA5-RFLP analysis [1]. Stocks were stored at −80 °C in 20% glycerol and recovered on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 30 °C. For most assays, yeast cells were cultured in Sabouraud broth for 24 h at 30 °C with shaking (200 rpm), washed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and counted in a Neubauer chamber. Capsule induction was performed in a minimal medium (15 mM glucose, 10 mM MgSO₄, 29.4 mM KH₂PO₄, 13 mM glycine, 3 µM thiamine, pH 5.5) for 48 h at 37 °C [2].

**Capsule measurements**

Cells grown under capsule-inducing conditions were counterstained with India ink and examined with an optical microscope. Capsule thickness was defined as the distance between the cell wall and the outer edge of the India ink exclusion zone. Cell body diameter and capsule thickness were measured in at least 50 cells per isolate using ImageJ software. The capsule-to-cell ratio was calculated as capsule thickness divided by cell body radius.

**Expression of capsule-associated genes**

Total RNA was extracted from yeast cells grown in minimal medium using a mechanical disruption/TRIzol protocol and treated with DNase I. cDNA was synthesized with oligo(dT) primers and reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green for *CAP10*, *CAP59*, *CAP60* and *CAP64*. Transcript levels were normalized to the housekeeping gene *ACT1* and expressed relative to isolate ATCC 24066 using the 2^−ΔΔCt method [3]. Three independent biological replicates were analyzed in technical duplicate.

**Chitooligomer distribution and chitin staining**

Chitooligomers were detected by incubating fixed cells with wheat germ agglutinin conjugated to fluorescein isothiocyanate (WGA-FITC; 10 µg/mL, 1 h, 37 °C) [4]. Cells were washed, mounted and imaged by fluorescence microscopy. Fluorescence patterns (e.g., budding sites, cell body and capsule-associated signals) were scored qualitatively in at least 100 cells per isolate, and fluorescence intensity was quantified with ImageJ.

**Pigment production**

Melanin production was assessed by spotting 10⁶ cells onto minimal medium agar containing 1 mM L-DOPA and incubating at 30 °C and 37 °C in the dark for up to 7 days. Pigmentation was documented photographically daily. For quantification, cells were grown in liquid L-DOPA medium for 5 days, collected, and the absorbance of culture supernatants was read at 475 nm. In addition, cell-associated pigment was extracted by treatment with 1 M sodium hydroxide at 100 °C and quantified spectrophotometrically against a standard curve of synthetic melanin.

**Reactivity with anti-glucuronoxylomannan antibodies**

Reactivity of the isolates with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) to glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) was evaluated by immunofluorescence and ELISA. For immunofluorescence, encapsulated cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin and incubated with mAbs 18B7 (IgG1), 12A1 (IgM) and 13F1 (IgM) [5] (10 µg/mL), followed by fluorescein-conjugated anti-mouse IgG or IgM. Samples were examined by fluorescence microscopy using identical exposure settings. For ELISA, GXM was isolated from culture supernatants by hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide precipitation [6], used to coat polystyrene plates (1 µg/mL), and probed with serial dilutions of each mAb. Binding was detected with alkaline phosphatase-conjugated secondary antibodies and p-nitrophenyl phosphate, reading absorbance at 405 nm.

**Animals and ethics**

Female C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) were housed under specific pathogen-free conditions with free access to food and water. All procedures followed national guidelines for animal care and were approved by the institutional animal ethics committee.

**Murine infection and survival**

Mice were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine and infected intranasally with 10⁴ yeast cells in 50 µL PBS (25 µL per nostril). Groups of 10 animals per isolate were monitored daily for survival, and animals showing signs of terminal disease were euthanized. Survival curves were compared using the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test.

**Fungal burden**

In parallel experiments, groups of five mice per isolate were euthanized at 7 and 14 days post-infection. Lungs and brains were aseptically removed, weighed and homogenized in sterile PBS. Serial dilutions were plated on Sabouraud agar and colony-forming units (CFU) were counted after 48–72 h at 30 °C. Results are expressed as log₁₀ CFU per gram of tissue.

**Host chitinase activity**

Chitinase activity was measured in lung homogenates supernatants from infected and uninfected mice using the fluorogenic substrates 4-methylumbelliferyl β-D-N,N′-diacetylchitobioside and 4-methylumbelliferyl β-D-N,N′,N″-triacetylchitotrioside [7]. Reactions were carried out in citrate-phosphate buffer (pH 5.2) at 37 °C and stopped with glycine-NaOH (pH 10.6). Fluorescence (excitation 360 nm, emission 450 nm) was measured, and activity was normalized to total protein determined by the Bradford method.

**Statistical analysis**

Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation from at least three independent experiments unless otherwise stated. Normality was verified using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons among three isolates were performed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, or by Kruskal–Wallis with Dunn’s test for non-parametric data. Fungal burden between time points was analyzed by two-way ANOVA. Differences were considered significant at *P* < 0.05. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism.

**Capsule dimensions and expression of CAP genes differ among serotype C isolates**

Microscopic analysis of cells grown under capsule-inducing conditions showed that the three serotype C isolates differed in capsule size. Isolate ATCC 24066 (VGIII) produced a significantly smaller capsule than WM 779 and 106.97 (both VGIV), as measured by India ink counterstaining and by the ratio of capsule thickness to cell body diameter (p < 0.05). Cell body dimensions were similar among isolates, so the differences were attributable to the capsule. WM 779 and 106.97 did not differ significantly from each other in this analysis.

We then quantified transcripts of the capsule-associated genes *CAP59*, *CAP60*, *CAP64* and *CAP10* by RT-qPCR, normalized to *ACT1*. Expression patterns differed by isolate. ATCC 24066 showed lower relative expression of *CAP59* and *CAP64* than both VGIV isolates, whereas *CAP10* and *CAP60* showed isolate-specific profiles that did not follow molecular type. Capsule size therefore tracked, at least partly, with expression of a subset of CAP genes, consistent with their role in capsule assembly [1,2].

**Chitooligomer distribution and host chitinase induction**

Chitin-derived structures were detected with wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), which binds chitooligomers. All isolates were labeled, but the distribution differed. In ATCC 24066, fluorescence was distributed throughout the cell and was often concentrated at the cell periphery. In WM 779 and 106.97, labeling was more punctate and unevenly distributed, with intense signals at buds and septa. Fluorescence intensity differed significantly among isolates, with WM 779 showing the lowest signal.

Because fungal chitin-like molecules can modulate host chitinase responses [3], we measured chitinase activity in lung homogenates of mice 7 days after infection. ATCC 24066 induced markedly higher chitinase activity than both VGIV isolates, which did not differ significantly from uninfected controls or from each other. Chitinase induction thus segregated by molecular type and correlated inversely with capsule size.

**Pigment production and antibody reactivity**

Melanization was assessed on L-DOPA medium. WM 779 produced pigment faster and more intensely than the other isolates, with visible pigmentation after 24 h and the highest absorbance in quantitative assays of extracted pigment. Isolates 106.97 and ATCC 24066 pigmented more slowly and to a lesser extent. Laccase activity measured in cell suspensions followed the same ranking.

Glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) epitope expression was analyzed by immunofluorescence with a panel of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) of different specificities. Each isolate produced a distinct reactivity pattern. Some mAbs labeled the capsule of all isolates with different intensities and spatial patterns (annular or punctate), whereas others reacted with only one or two isolates. ELISA of culture supernatants gave concordant results, indicating that the three isolates differ in GXM antigenic structure and not only in capsule size. Reactivity did not segregate strictly by molecular type, since the two VGIV isolates also differed from each other in their antibody profiles.

**Virulence in a murine model of cryptococcosis**

Mice were infected intranasally to compare virulence. Survival differed markedly among groups. Animals infected with WM 779 or 106.97 succumbed to infection with similar kinetics, and survival curves did not differ significantly (log-rank test, p > 0.05). In contrast, mice infected with ATCC 24066 showed significantly prolonged survival, and a substantial proportion of animals were alive at the end of the observation period.

Fungal burden was determined by CFU counts in lungs and brains at defined times after infection. Lung colonization by WM 779 and 106.97 was significantly higher than that by ATCC 24066 at the time points analyzed. Isolate ATCC 24066 persisted in the lungs at lower levels, but no CFUs were recovered from the brain at any time point, whereas both VGIV isolates were recovered from brain tissue. Thus, the reduced lethality of ATCC 24066 was associated with an inability to disseminate to or colonize the central nervous system.

**Association between phenotypes and pathogenic outcome**

Considered together, the phenotypes distinguished ATCC 24066 from the VGIV isolates in several respects: a smaller capsule, lower expression of selected CAP genes, a different chitooligomer distribution, and stronger induction of host chitinase activity. These features were associated with low pulmonary burden, absence of brain colonization and reduced lethality. The two VGIV isolates were similar in virulence despite differences in melanin production and GXM antigenic profile. In particular, the highly pigmented WM 779 was not more lethal than 106.97, indicating that in this model enhanced pigment production did not by itself confer greater virulence. These results show that serotype C isolates vary widely in virulence-associated traits and that the diversity extends both between and within the VGIII and VGIV molecular types.

**Phenotypic and pathogenic heterogeneity within serotype C C. gattii**

Most studies of C. gattii pathogenesis have centered on the serotype B VGII isolates responsible for the Vancouver Island and Pacific Northwest outbreaks [1,2]. Our results show that serotype C isolates, which are less studied, are also heterogeneous in virulence-associated traits and in their behavior in vivo. Two VGIV isolates (WM 779 and 106.97) and one VGIII isolate (ATCC 24066) differed in capsule size, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, pigment production, reactivity with anti-glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) antibodies, and the ability to disseminate to the brain. This diversity is consistent with the genetic divergence among C. gattii molecular types, which are now proposed to represent distinct cryptic species [3]. It also cautions against extrapolating from one lineage or isolate to the whole serotype.

**Capsule, GXM and cell wall architecture**

The capsule is the main virulence determinant of Cryptococcus, and its size and composition affect phagocytosis, complement activation, and immune modulation [4]. The smaller capsule dimensions and different CAP expression profile of ATCC 24066 relative to the VGIV isolates suggest differences in capsule regulation. CAP59, CAP60, CAP64 and CAP10 are required for capsule synthesis and for GXM xylosylation and O-acetylation [5]. The differences in expression we observed are therefore likely to be reflected in GXM structure. The distinct reactivity patterns of the three isolates with monoclonal antibodies to GXM support this interpretation, since epitope recognition depends on the pattern of xylose and O-acetyl substitution [6]. Antigenic variation in GXM can alter antibody-mediated protection and may influence diagnostic performance, which is relevant because serological tests are known to vary in sensitivity across C. gattii types [7]. We did not determine GXM structure directly, so the link between CAP expression and GXM structure remains inferential. Structural analysis by NMR or mass spectrometry would be an obvious next step.

Chitin and chitooligomers contribute to cell wall integrity, to capsule anchoring, and to the modulation of host responses [8,9]. The different distribution of chitooligomers in ATCC 24066 and the induction of host chitinase activity by this isolate suggest differences in cell wall organization and in how the fungus is sensed by the host. Mammalian chitinases and chitinase-like proteins shape type 2 immune responses in cryptococcosis [10]. Differential induction of chitinolytic activity could therefore contribute to the distinct outcomes observed, although causality cannot be established from our data.

**Melanin and other determinants**

The greater pigment production of WM 779 is notable, since melanin protects against oxidative and nitrosative stress, as well as antifungal agents, and has been associated with dissemination to the central nervous system [11]. However, pigment production alone did not predict virulence. WM 779 and 106.97 behaved similarly in lethality and pulmonary burden despite their differences in pigmentation, and the weaker pigment producer was not simply the least virulent. This indicates that virulence in these isolates is multifactorial, and that individual traits are not good predictors of outcome. Different combinations of traits can produce similar pathogenic results, which has also been seen in comparisons of C. neoformans and C. gattii strains [12].

**Pathogenic outcomes in vivo**

In the intranasal model, both VGIV isolates caused lethality and reached high pulmonary fungal burdens, while ATCC 24066 caused reduced lethality and failed to reach the brain. This is of interest because the VGIII and VGIV types are both associated with infections in immunocompromised patients, including HIV-infected individuals [13,14]. Our data show that, at least in an immunocompetent murine host, VGIV isolates can be markedly pathogenic. The inability of ATCC 24066 to disseminate to the brain may reflect reduced capacity to survive within macrophages, to cross the blood–brain barrier, or to escape the lung, all of which are processes linked to capsule properties, melanin, and cell wall remodeling [15]. The induction of host chitinase activity by this isolate may also favor containment in the lung. These possibilities were not tested directly. It is also possible that the long history of laboratory passage of ATCC 24066, an old reference strain, contributed to attenuation, as repeated subculture is known to reduce virulence in some Cryptococcus strains [16].

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be considered. We examined only three isolates, so differences attributed to molecular type may in part reflect strain-level variation. The VGIII isolate in particular may not be representative of its group. Only one mouse strain and one infection route were used, and host genetic background influences the outcome of cryptococcosis [17]. The experiments also did not address immune responses in detail, so the mechanisms linking phenotype to pathogenicity remain to be defined.

**Conclusions**

Serotype C C. gattii isolates of the VGIII and VGIV molecular types differ substantially in capsule properties, cell wall organization, pigment production, GXM antigenicity, and pathogenic behavior. VGIV isolates WM 779 and 106.97 were highly pathogenic in mice, whereas the VGIII isolate ATCC 24066 was attenuated and failed to disseminate to the brain. These findings show that serotype C isolates are phenotypically diverse and that pathogenic potential cannot be inferred from serotype or a single phenotypic trait. Future work should include larger panels of clinical and environmental VGIII and VGIV isolates, structural characterization of GXM, and analysis of host immune responses, including chitinase-mediated pathways, to identify the determinants of virulence in these understudied lineages.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common life-limiting genetic disease among African Americans, affecting more than 100,000 people in the United States and millions worldwide [1,2]. It results from a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene that produces hemoglobin S. Under deoxygenated conditions, hemoglobin S polymerizes, causing red blood cell rigidity, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion. Beyond these primary events, chronic hemolysis, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent inflammation contribute to progressive multi-organ injury [3,4]. Although advances in newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccination, and hydroxyurea therapy have substantially improved survival in childhood, pulmonary complications remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality across the lifespan [5,6].

Pulmonary disease in SCD encompasses a broad spectrum of acute and chronic conditions, including acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoxemia, thromboembolic disease, and obstructive airway disease [7,8]. ACS, defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxemia, is the second most common cause of hospitalization and a leading cause of death among patients with SCD [9]. Recurrent ACS is itself associated with the development of chronic lung disease, creating a cycle of progressive pulmonary injury [10]. Understanding modifiable risk factors for ACS and other pulmonary complications is therefore a priority.

Asthma has long been recognized as one of these potential risk factors. Early observational studies described an association between asthma and ACS, painful vaso-occlusive episodes, and early mortality in SCD [11–13]. In the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease, children with a physician diagnosis of asthma experienced a higher incidence of ACS and pain episodes than those without, and asthma was associated with an increased risk of early death in adults [11,12]. Subsequent studies have supported these findings, although results have not been uniform, and the strength of associations varies with how asthma is defined [14,15]. The mechanisms linking asthma to SCD complications are not fully elucidated but may include airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction-induced hypoxia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and systemic inflammatory amplification that promotes sickling and vascular adhesion [16,17].

More recently, attention has turned to wheezing, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, as a possible marker of disease severity in SCD. Longitudinal data from infant and childhood cohorts demonstrate that wheezing is common in young children with SCD and is associated with higher rates of ACS, pain, and hospitalization [18,19]. These observations suggest that wheezing may reflect a distinct SCD-related phenotype, rather than simply representing coexisting atopic asthma. Indeed, wheeze in SCD may arise from multiple processes, including pulmonary vascular congestion, fat or thromboembolism, prior pulmonary infarction, infection, and airway hyperresponsiveness, in addition to classic allergic airway inflammation [20].

Establishing a diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is therefore challenging. According to national and international guidelines, asthma is diagnosed on the basis of a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, together with objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction that is typically reversible with bronchodilators [21,22]. In SCD, however, several of these features are highly prevalent and frequently occur in isolation. Wheezing has been reported in up to approximately 30–50% of children with SCD, exceeding the prevalence in the general African American population [18,23]. Obstructive patterns on spirometry are common, yet many patients also display restrictive physiology or mixed defects, complicating interpretation [24,25]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, measured by methacholine or exercise challenge, has been described in a substantial proportion of children with SCD, including many without clinical asthma [26,27]. Bronchodilator responsiveness is likewise frequent, even among patients with no history of wheeze [28]. Consequently, the relationships among symptoms, physiologic abnormalities, and clinical asthma remain poorly defined, and the true prevalence of asthma in SCD is uncertain, with estimates ranging from approximately 10% to more than 40% depending on the definition and population studied [29,30].

This diagnostic ambiguity has practical consequences. Underdiagnosis may deprive patients of effective controller therapy, whereas overdiagnosis may expose them to unnecessary medications and divert attention from other treatable causes of respiratory symptoms. Management is further complicated by limited evidence: patients with SCD have been largely excluded from asthma clinical trials, and recommendations rely heavily on extrapolation from the general population [31]. Particular concerns include the potential risks of systemic corticosteroids, which have been associated with rebound pain crises and readmission in SCD, and the uncertain role of β-agonists and other asthma therapies in this population [32,33]. Whether biologic therapies or disease-modifying treatments such as hydroxyurea alter airway outcomes also remains unknown.

Given these gaps, a critical appraisal of current knowledge is warranted. In this review, we summarize: (1) the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness among patients with SCD; (2) the evidence supporting associations of these features with SCD morbidity; (3) current understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD; (4) existing approaches to the diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD; and (5) future research directions needed to improve respiratory outcomes in this vulnerable population.

We conducted a narrative review of the literature on asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) in patients with sickle cell disease (SCD). A narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis because the available studies differ substantially in design, population, case definitions, and outcome measures, which limits quantitative synthesis [1,2]. The review was structured around five predefined themes: (1) epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness; (2) associations with SCD-related morbidity and mortality; (3) pathophysiology of airway inflammation; (4) current approaches to the diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD; and (5) future research directions.

**Search strategy**

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for articles published from database inception through the date of the final search. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords for the condition and the respiratory outcomes: "sickle cell disease," "sickle cell anemia," "hemoglobin SS," "hemoglobin SC," "asthma," "wheeze," "wheezing," "airway obstruction," "airway hyperresponsiveness," "bronchial hyperreactivity," "bronchodilator response," "pulmonary function," "spirometry," "acute chest syndrome," "vaso-occlusive pain," and "inhaled corticosteroids." Boolean operators were used to combine the concepts. Additional searches addressed inflammatory mechanisms, including "eosinophil," "IgE," "atopy," "cytokine," "hemolysis," "nitric oxide," and "leukotriene." Reference lists of key articles, prior reviews, and consensus guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications [3,4]. ClinicalTrials.gov was queried to identify ongoing or recently completed trials relevant to future directions.

**Eligibility criteria**

We included original research articles (prospective and retrospective cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, and clinical trials), registry analyses, and clinical practice guidelines that reported on respiratory outcomes in children or adults with SCD. Studies were eligible if they reported at least one of the following: prevalence or incidence of physician-diagnosed asthma or wheezing; spirometric or plethysmographic measures of airflow obstruction; bronchodilator responsiveness or bronchial provocation testing; associations between these respiratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes (pain episodes, acute chest syndrome [ACS], hospitalization, or mortality); biomarkers of airway or systemic inflammation; or therapeutic interventions for asthma or wheezing in SCD. Basic science and translational studies, including murine models, were included when they informed mechanisms of airway inflammation in SCD. We excluded articles not published in English, conference abstracts without full-text data, case reports, and studies focusing exclusively on pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, or sleep-disordered breathing without relevant airway outcomes. General population asthma guidelines were reviewed to provide diagnostic and therapeutic context [5,6].

**Study selection and data extraction**

Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were reviewed. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved by discussion among the authors. For each included study, we extracted the following information where available: study design, setting, sample size, age group, SCD genotype, definitions used for asthma, wheeze, airway obstruction, and AHR, methods of pulmonary function testing, comparison groups, principal findings, and adjustment for confounders. Because definitions of asthma vary across studies (e.g., parental report, physician diagnosis, medication use, or administrative codes), we recorded the definition used in each study and considered this when interpreting prevalence estimates [7]. Similarly, we noted whether airway obstruction was defined by the forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity ratio relative to the lower limit of normal or by fixed thresholds, and which reference equations were used, given the known impact of race-specific equations on interpretation [8].

**Synthesis and appraisal**

Findings were synthesized qualitatively within each thematic domain. For epidemiologic data, we compared prevalence estimates across studies and with those of the general African American population, taking into account age, geography, and case definition. For studies of morbidity, we emphasized those that used longitudinal designs and adjusted for relevant covariates such as age, genotype, hydroxyurea use, and hemoglobin level, and we highlighted where evidence derived from single-center or retrospective studies might be subject to selection and ascertainment bias. For mechanistic evidence, we distinguished human studies from animal and in vitro studies. We did not perform a formal risk-of-bias assessment or pooled quantitative analysis; instead, we considered study size, design, and consistency of findings across cohorts when weighing the strength of evidence [2].

For the diagnosis and management section, we compared recommendations from national asthma guidelines and SCD-specific expert panel recommendations, and we identified areas in which evidence specific to SCD was lacking and recommendations were extrapolated from the general population [5,6,9]. Particular attention was given to the role of spirometry, bronchodilator reversibility testing, and methacholine challenge in distinguishing asthma from isolated wheeze or AHR in SCD, as well as to the safety and efficacy of corticosteroids, given reports of rebound pain and ACS after systemic steroid exposure [10]. Gaps in knowledge identified across the preceding sections were used to generate the proposed future directions, including prospective phenotyping, biomarker development, and clinical trials of asthma therapies in SCD.

Because this review synthesizes published literature, the findings are organized by the five themes outlined above. Citations refer to the studies identified in the literature search.

**Epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness**

Reported asthma prevalence in children with SCD ranges from approximately 10% to 48%, depending on case definition and study design [1–3]. Studies relying on physician diagnosis typically report prevalence of 20–30%, which exceeds the 8–13% observed in African American children without SCD [2,4]. Prospective cohorts using standardized criteria, such as the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease and the Sleep and Asthma Cohort, found that fewer children met full diagnostic criteria than were initially labeled as asthmatic [3,5]. Parent-reported wheezing was considerably more common than asthma, occurring in up to 50–70% of children in some cohorts, and frequently occurred without a physician diagnosis, atopy, or family history of asthma [5,6].

Airway obstruction on spirometry was observed in a minority of patients, with reductions in the FEV1/FVC ratio in 10–25% of children [7,8]. By contrast, restrictive patterns became more prevalent with advancing age and were reported in up to 20–74% of adults [8,9]. Bronchodilator responsiveness was seen in 25–50% of children with SCD, including many without a clinical asthma diagnosis or baseline obstruction [7,10]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, assessed by methacholine challenge, was documented in roughly 50–70% of children with SCD, a proportion that did not differ consistently between those with and without wheeze or asthma [10,11]. These physiologic features frequently appeared in isolation: in several cohorts, fewer than half of children with bronchodilator responsiveness or airway hyperresponsiveness had a clinical asthma diagnosis [10,11].

**Associations with SCD morbidity**

Asthma has been repeatedly associated with higher rates of acute chest syndrome (ACS). In a Cooperative Study analysis, children with asthma had approximately 2.4 times the incidence of ACS and more frequent pain episodes than those without asthma [1]. Subsequent single-center and registry studies confirmed increased ACS recurrence and hospitalization among children with asthma, and asthma-associated ACS episodes were more often accompanied by wheezing and respiratory failure [12,13]. Asthma was also linked to earlier mortality; in the Cooperative Study, adults with asthma had increased risk of death compared with those without [14].

Wheezing independent of asthma diagnosis was likewise associated with morbidity. Children with SCD and recurrent wheezing had higher rates of ACS and vaso-occlusive pain than non-wheezing peers, and these associations persisted after adjustment for asthma diagnosis in some analyses [6,15]. Lower baseline hemoglobin, higher white blood cell counts, and elevated markers of hemolysis were associated with wheeze, suggesting that disease severity may contribute to respiratory symptoms [5,15]. Airway obstruction and airway hyperresponsiveness showed less consistent relationships with outcomes; some studies reported higher pain and ACS rates with airway hyperresponsiveness, whereas others found no association [10,11,16]. Declines in FEV1 over time were reported more often in patients with SCD and a history of asthma or ACS, though longitudinal data remain limited [8,16].

**Pathophysiology of airway inflammation**

Evidence supports several overlapping mechanisms. Atopic features, such as elevated IgE, allergic sensitization, and eosinophilia, were present in a subset of patients but were not universally increased relative to controls, and sensitization rates were generally comparable to those in African American children without SCD [17,18]. Markers of type 2 inflammation therefore appear relevant only in a proportion of patients with SCD and asthma.

Alternative, non-atopic mechanisms were also described. Chronic hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, which depletes nitric oxide and may promote airway smooth muscle constriction; reduced exhaled nitric oxide and elevated arginase activity have been reported in SCD [19,20]. Systemic inflammation, with increased circulating IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, leukotrienes, and secretory phospholipase A2, was observed in patients with wheeze and during ACS [20,21]. Elevated urinary leukotriene E4 and neutrophil activation were noted in children with SCD, particularly those with wheeze [21]. Recurrent microvascular occlusion, pulmonary fat embolism, and subclinical infection or aspiration may further injure the airway and contribute to remodeling [9,22]. Together these findings suggest that airway disease in SCD is heterogeneous, with both asthma-like and SCD-specific inflammatory phenotypes.

**Diagnosis and management**

Current guidelines from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute recommend that asthma in SCD be diagnosed using the same criteria as in the general population: a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms plus demonstrable reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry [23]. Because wheezing, bronchodilator responsiveness, and airway hyperresponsiveness are common and nonspecific in SCD, reliance on any one feature risks overdiagnosis [5,10]. Consequently, the guidelines encourage objective testing, ideally by a pulmonary or asthma specialist, particularly when symptoms are atypical [23].

Management evidence is sparse. No randomized trials have evaluated asthma controller therapy for preventing SCD complications. Observational data suggest that inhaled corticosteroids are commonly prescribed, but adherence is variable [24]. Systemic corticosteroids effectively treat asthma exacerbations and ACS but have been associated with rebound pain and readmission in SCD, warranting caution [25]. Beta-agonists appear generally safe, and bronchodilator use during ACS was associated with improved outcomes in some retrospective reports [12,26]. Hydroxyurea was associated with fewer ACS episodes and lower asthma-related symptoms in small studies, though its specific effect on airway disease is uncertain [26].

**Future directions**

Identified gaps included standardized phenotyping, prospective longitudinal cohorts that link airway physiology with clinical outcomes, biomarkers distinguishing atopic from hemolysis-related airway disease, and randomized trials of controller therapies and biologics in SCD-associated wheeze and asthma [5,20,24].

The question posed by the title, whether wheeze in sickle cell disease (SCD) represents asthma or something else, does not yield a single answer. The evidence reviewed here indicates that wheezing, airflow obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) are each common in SCD, frequently occur independently of one another, and are associated with greater morbidity regardless of whether criteria for asthma are met [1,2]. This overlap complicates diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment, and it suggests that SCD itself may generate airway phenotypes that only partly resemble atopic asthma in the general population.

Prevalence estimates of physician-diagnosed asthma in children with SCD, generally 20–30%, exceed those in African American children without SCD, although the difference is smaller than once thought [3,4]. Wheezing is reported even more often and is not always accompanied by a diagnosis of asthma [5]. Spirometric obstruction and AHR are also frequent, yet they are not specific. Obstruction in SCD may reflect small airway disease from repeated microvascular occlusion, prior acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary vascular disease, or intravascular volume shifts, and not only reversible bronchoconstriction [6,7]. AHR to methacholine may occur in patients without symptoms or atopy, and its meaning in this population remains uncertain [8]. Consequently, applying standard asthma definitions can both over- and under-diagnose the condition. Some patients labeled as having asthma may have wheeze from other causes, while others with true asthma may be missed because their symptoms are attributed to SCD.

Regardless of terminology, the clinical associations are consistent. Asthma and wheeze have been linked to more frequent vaso-occlusive pain episodes, higher rates of ACS, and increased mortality in some cohorts [1,9,10]. Wheezing in the absence of an asthma diagnosis appears to identify a subgroup at similar or greater risk, supporting its use as a clinical marker of severity [2]. Causality is unresolved. Airway inflammation and hypoxia could precipitate sickling and pain, ACS could injure the airways and produce later obstruction, or a shared process such as systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction could drive both. Most studies are observational, and many are cross-sectional or retrospective, which limits inference about the direction of effect. Variable definitions of asthma, wheeze, and ACS, along with differences in age and in the use of hydroxyurea, add heterogeneity to the literature.

Pathophysiologic data suggest that airway inflammation in SCD differs from classic type 2 asthma. Chronic hemolysis, release of free heme and arginase, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, oxidative stress, and elevated cytokines may promote airway smooth muscle dysfunction and inflammation [11,12]. Atopy and eosinophilic inflammation are present in some patients, and genetic or environmental factors, such as air pollution and tobacco smoke exposure, likely contribute [13]. However, biomarkers such as IgE, eosinophil counts, and exhaled nitric oxide have not been well validated for distinguishing phenotypes in SCD, and exhaled nitric oxide may be affected by SCD-specific changes in nitric oxide metabolism. Delineating endotypes, perhaps combining clinical features, inflammatory markers, and lung function trajectories, is a priority.

These uncertainties affect management. Current guidance largely extrapolates from general asthma guidelines, recommending a diagnosis based on recurrent symptoms, reversible obstruction, and exclusion of alternatives, with stepwise therapy using inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators [14]. Several cautions apply. Systemic corticosteroids have been associated with rebound pain and readmission in patients with SCD, so they should be used judiciously during exacerbations and ACS [15]. Beta-agonists are generally safe and effective but need to be balanced against limited evidence for their use in non-reversible obstruction. Whether inhaled corticosteroids reduce pain or ACS in wheezing patients without asthma has not been tested in adequately powered trials. Likewise, the effects of hydroxyurea, transfusion, and newer disease-modifying agents on airway outcomes are poorly characterized, although hydroxyurea may reduce ACS and wheeze-related events [16]. Clinicians should therefore assess respiratory symptoms at each visit, obtain spirometry when feasible, and consider referral to pulmonology for persistent or severe symptoms.

Several limitations of the current evidence should be acknowledged. Studies are often small and single-center, and few include longitudinal pulmonary function data from early childhood into adulthood. Racial differences in spirometric reference equations may affect the interpretation of obstruction. Few studies have separated patients with isolated wheeze, isolated AHR, and asthma by established criteria. These gaps constrain conclusions about prognosis and optimal therapy.

Future work should move in four directions. First, prospective birth or early childhood cohorts with standardized phenotyping could clarify the natural history of wheeze and its relationship to ACS and lung function decline. Second, mechanistic studies integrating inflammatory profiling, hemolysis markers, and genetics could define whether distinct endotypes exist and identify therapeutic targets. Third, randomized trials are needed to test asthma-directed therapies, such as inhaled corticosteroids and biologics, in well-characterized SCD populations, with outcomes including pain, ACS, and quality of life. Fourth, consensus definitions and diagnostic algorithms specific to SCD would improve comparability across studies and guide clinical practice.

In conclusion, wheeze in SCD should not be dismissed as a benign symptom or automatically equated with asthma. It marks a population at increased risk of serious complications, and it arises from heterogeneous mechanisms that include, but are not limited to, asthma. Until better evidence is available, clinicians should evaluate wheezing systematically, treat confirmed asthma according to guidelines while avoiding systemic corticosteroids where possible, and optimize SCD-directed therapy. Collaborative, longitudinal, and interventional research is essential to determine whether treating airway disease can alter the course of SCD.

Large-scale data collection from individuals underpins personalized services, public-health surveillance, and the training of modern machine learning models. At the same time, the data that users contribute are frequently sensitive, and centralized collection exposes them to breaches, misuse, and untrusted curators. Differential privacy (DP) [1] offers a rigorous guarantee that the output of an analysis is insensitive to any single individual's record, but its standard formulation presumes a trusted aggregator. Local differential privacy (LDP) [2], [3] removes this assumption: each user perturbs her data on her own device before transmission, so the aggregator never observes raw values. Because of this strong threat model, LDP has been deployed in industrial systems such as Google's RAPPOR [4], Apple's iOS and macOS telemetry [5], and Microsoft's telemetry collection [6].

Most of the LDP literature considers simple data types. Substantial progress has been made on categorical frequency estimation [4], [7], [8], heavy-hitter identification [9], and mean estimation for numerical attributes [10], [11]. Real-world data, however, are often richer. In particular, key-value data, the basic data model of NoSQL stores, appear in user-profile databases, e-commerce logs, and smart-device records. A key-value pair couples a categorical key (e.g., a product or an app) with a numerical value (e.g., a rating or usage time). Such data arise naturally in applications such as estimating how many users own a certain item and what average rating they give it.

## Challenges of Key-Value Data under LDP

Key-value data cannot be handled by applying existing mechanisms independently to keys and values. First, the key and value are correlated: a value is meaningful only if its key is present, and perturbing them separately wastes the privacy budget and yields biased estimates. Second, a user typically holds many keys, so the data are high-dimensional and sparse, and the privacy budget must be split across potentially many coordinates, degrading utility. Third, the value domain is continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation that preserves unbiased aggregates. PrivKV [12] was the first work to formalize LDP for key-value data, perturbing each pair by a sequence of value and key randomization steps and supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, such as interactive variants, reduce estimation error [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is small or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited.

A further limitation is that current methods deliver only marginal statistics: the frequency of each key and the mean of the values of each key. Many downstream tasks require conditional information. Naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems all depend on conditional probabilities or conditional means, such as the probability that a user holds key B given that she holds key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15]. Estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic.

## Our Contributions

In this paper, we address these gaps by designing new perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and by building conditional analysis on top of them. Our main contributions are as follows.

1. **New key-value perturbation mechanisms.** We propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. The mechanisms are designed so that unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean can be derived in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, showing improved accuracy over existing approaches.

2. **Conditional frequency estimation.** We introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error.

3. **Conditional mean estimation.** We develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means.

4. **Support for learning tasks.** We show how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream learning tasks, and illustrate this with classification based on conditional probabilities.

5. **Extensive evaluation.** We conduct experiments on synthetic datasets with varied distributions and on real-world rating datasets. The results show that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful.

## Organization

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on LDP and key-value data. Section III presents preliminaries, including the formal definition of LDP and the problem statement. Section IV describes the proposed perturbation mechanisms and their theoretical analysis. Section V develops conditional frequency and conditional mean estimation. Section VI reports experimental results, and Section VII concludes the paper.

**Problem Setting and Preliminaries**

Consider a population of n users, each holding a key-value pair ⟨k, v⟩, where k ∈ K = {1,…,d} is a discrete key and v ∈ [−1,1] is a numerical value. (Users holding multiple pairs are handled by sampling one pair uniformly, which is standard in prior work [1].) An untrusted aggregator wishes to estimate (i) the key frequency f_k, (ii) the mean value m_k of each key, (iii) the conditional frequency f_{k|c} = Pr[key k | condition c], and (iv) the conditional mean m_{k|c} = E[v | key k, condition c], where c is a predicate on a second key or attribute held by the same user. Each user perturbs the pair locally with a randomized mechanism M satisfying ε-LDP [2]: for all inputs x, x′ and outputs y, Pr[M(x)=y] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(x′)=y]. By sequential composition [3], when a user's report is split into components with budgets ε₁ and ε₂, the overall guarantee is (ε₁+ε₂)-LDP.

We build on randomized response (RR) [4] for categorical data and on stochastic rounding for numerical data [5]. A value v is discretized to v* ∈ {−1,1} with Pr[v*=1] = (1+v)/2, which is unbiased, and v* is then flipped by RR with keep probability e^{ε₂}/(e^{ε₂}+1). The prior key-value mechanism PrivKV [1] perturbs the value first and then the key-presence bit, which couples the two estimates and induces bias in the mean when the key is absent. Our design aims to remove this coupling.

**Key-Value Perturbation Mechanism**

Each user encodes its input as a d-dimensional vector in which a held key k carries the discretized value v* ∈ {−1,1} and every other entry is 0. A report is generated by sampling one coordinate j and perturbing only that coordinate, so the output domain is {−1,0,1}. The sampling step is analogous to the one in [6], and the estimator is rescaled by d to correct for it.

For the sampled coordinate with true entry x ∈ {−1,0,1}, the mechanism outputs y with probability

Pr[y | x] = p if y = x, and q = (1−p)/2 otherwise,

with p = e^ε/(e^ε+2). The ratio p/q = 2e^ε/(1−p)… more precisely, p/q = 2e^ε/2 = e^ε after normalization, so the mechanism satisfies ε-LDP, since any two inputs differ only by the ratio p/q. Using a three-way mechanism over the joint key-value domain spends the whole budget once rather than splitting it between key and value, which gives lower variance than sequential perturbation at equal ε.

**Unbiased Estimators**

Let n_y(j) be the number of reports that sample coordinate j and output y ∈ {−1,0,1}, and let N_j be the number of reports sampling j. Defining the debiased counts

ĉ₊ = (n₊ − qN_j)/(p−q), ĉ₋ = (n₋ − qN_j)/(p−q),

where n₊ and n₋ denote the counts of outputs +1 and −1 on coordinate j, we have E[ĉ₊] = c₊ and E[ĉ₋] = c₋, the true counts of users holding key j with discretized value +1 and −1 respectively. The key frequency estimator is

f̂_j = (ĉ₊ + ĉ₋)/N_j,

and the mean estimator is

m̂_j = (ĉ₊ − ĉ₋)/(ĉ₊ + ĉ₋).

The frequency estimator is unbiased because the sampling is uniform and the debiasing is linear. The mean estimator is a ratio of unbiased quantities and is therefore asymptotically unbiased; a second-order Taylor expansion shows the bias is O(1/(n f_j)). Because estimates may fall outside [−1,1] or be negative, we apply a post-processing projection (clipping and normalization), which preserves LDP by the post-processing property [3] and does not increase the expected error. The variance of ĉ₊ is of order d·q(1−q)/(p−q)² per user, so the mean squared error scales as O(d e^ε/(n(e^ε−1)²)).

**Iterative Refinement**

To reduce error on sparse keys, we optionally run a two-round protocol. In round one, a fraction of users reports under the mechanism above, producing preliminary estimates m̂_j. These estimates are broadcast, and in round two the remaining users apply the same mechanism but the aggregator calibrates the estimate by replacing the uninformative prior used in debiasing with m̂_j. This is analogous to the iterative scheme in [1] but is applied to the aggregated statistics, so no user is queried twice and the privacy guarantee remains ε.

**Conditional Frequency and Conditional Mean Estimation**

Let a user additionally hold a categorical attribute a ∈ A (or a predicate c(·) thereof). Conditional statistics require joint information on (a, k, v). We consider two strategies.

*Joint encoding.* The user forms the composite key (a, k), so the domain has size |A|·d, and applies the mechanism above. The aggregator obtains f̂_{(a,k)} and m̂_{(a,k)} directly and computes

f̂_{k|a} = f̂_{(a,k)} / Σ_{k′} f̂_{(a,k′)}, m̂_{k|a} = m̂_{(a,k)}.

This is simple and asymptotically unbiased, but the variance grows with |A|d.

*Split-budget encoding.* The user spends ε_a on a (using generalized RR [7]) and ε_k = ε − ε_a on the key-value pair. For a pair of reports (ã, ỹ), the joint distribution is related to the true one through the Kronecker product of the two perturbation matrices, P = P_a ⊗ P_kv. The aggregator estimates the joint distribution by inverting this matrix:

π̂ = (P_a⁻¹ ⊗ P_kv⁻¹) r,

where r is the empirical distribution of reports. Because the inverse of a Kronecker product factorizes, the computation costs O(|A|² + d²) rather than O(|A|²d²). Conditional frequency is then f̂_{k|a} = π̂(a,k)/Σ_{k′} π̂(a,k′), and the conditional mean follows by applying the mean estimator to the signed components of π̂. The budget split ε_a is chosen by minimizing the approximate variance expression derived above, which we do by one-dimensional numerical search.

For a general condition c defined on a subset A_c ⊆ A, we aggregate π̂(a,k) over a ∈ A_c before normalization. As with the marginal estimators, we project π̂ onto the probability simplex [8] before forming ratios, which stabilizes the conditional estimates when the denominators are small.

**Privacy and Utility Analysis**

Each user's report is produced by a single invocation of an ε-LDP mechanism (joint encoding) or by composition of two mechanisms whose budgets sum to ε (split encoding), so both protocols satisfy ε-LDP. Utility guarantees follow by applying Hoeffding-type concentration to the debiased counts, giving, with probability at least 1−δ, a maximum error of O(√(d log(d/δ)·e^ε/n)/(e^ε−1)) over all keys for frequency, with corresponding bounds for conditional estimates that scale with the inverse of the conditioning mass.

**Experimental Setup.** We evaluate the proposed mechanisms on synthetic and real-world key-value datasets. The synthetic data contain 10⁵ users and 100 keys. Key frequencies follow either a uniform or a Zipf distribution, and values are drawn from a truncated Gaussian on [−1, 1]. The real-world datasets are a movie-rating dataset (MovieLens [1]) and an e-commerce rating dataset, with ratings rescaled to [−1, 1]. We compare our mechanisms with PrivKV [2] and its iterative variants PrivKVM and PrivKVM+, as well as with the naive baseline that applies randomized response to keys and a Duchi-style mechanism [3] to values with the budget split evenly. The privacy budget ε ranges from 0.5 to 5 and is split between key and value perturbation. Accuracy is measured by mean squared error (MSE) for frequency estimation and mean estimation, and by mean absolute error for conditional queries. All results are averaged over 100 independent runs. We report standard deviations where they are non-negligible.

**Frequency Estimation.** Figure 1 shows the MSE of key frequency estimation as ε varies. Our mechanism achieves the lowest error at every privacy level on all datasets. At ε = 1 on the Zipf synthetic data, it reduces MSE by roughly 38% relative to PrivKV and by about 61% relative to the naive baseline. The gap narrows as ε grows, since all mechanisms approach the sampling-error floor, but remains visible even at ε = 5. The advantage is largest for low-frequency keys. Such keys are most affected by the noise injected through fake key-value pairs for unsampled keys, which the new perturbation design reduces. Varying the number of users confirms that MSE decreases approximately as 1/n for all methods, in line with the variance analysis. Our curve has the smallest constant. Varying the key-domain size shows that the baselines degrade as the domain grows, because the sampling probability for each key shrinks. Our mechanism degrades more gracefully.

**Mean Estimation.** Figure 2 reports MSE of value mean estimation. PrivKV without iteration shows a systematic bias for keys with small frequency, since the estimator is conditioned on a noisy subset of users. PrivKVM reduces this bias only after several iterations, and each iteration consumes part of the privacy budget [2]. With a fixed total budget, increasing the number of iterations first helps and then hurts, as the per-round budget shrinks. Our mechanism needs a single round and is unbiased by construction. At ε = 2 it lowers MSE by 25–45% relative to the best configuration of PrivKVM across the datasets. On the real datasets the improvement is more modest for popular keys (about 10–15%) but remains consistent. Allocating the budget unevenly between keys and values also matters. The best split gives a larger share to the value component when values have high variance. A near-even split is robust and loses less than 8% in MSE relative to the best split found by grid search.

**Conditional Frequency Estimation.** We evaluate conditional frequency estimation by querying P(key k | key j present) for randomly selected key pairs. Ground truth is computed from the unperturbed data. We compare our estimator with a baseline that estimates joint and marginal frequencies separately and takes their ratio. Our method reduces mean absolute error by a factor of 1.8 to 3.2 across ε ∈ [1, 4]. The ratio baseline is unstable when the conditioning key is rare, since the noisy denominator can be near zero or negative. Our estimator avoids this instability through a constrained, normalized post-processing step. Error increases as the conditioning key becomes rarer for all methods, consistent with the effective sample size being proportional to the conditioning frequency. The growth is markedly slower for our approach. Accuracy for pairs among the top-10 keys approaches that of the unconditional case.

**Conditional Mean Estimation.** For value analysis, we estimate the mean value of key k among users who also hold key j. Figure 4 shows that the error is higher than for unconditional means, as expected, because the conditioning reduces the effective population. Nevertheless, the proposed conditional mean estimator attains errors within a factor of about 1.5 of the unconditional estimator at ε = 3, whereas the naive combination of independently perturbed estimates yields errors 3–5 times larger. The estimates also preserve the ranking of keys by conditional mean with high fidelity. Kendall's τ between estimated and true rankings exceeds 0.9 at ε ≥ 3 on MovieLens.

**Downstream Learning Tasks.** To verify that the released conditional statistics are useful, we use them to fit a naive Bayes–style classifier that predicts whether a user's rating of a target item is positive, given the presence of other keys and their values. Using statistics from our mechanism, accuracy at ε = 4 is within 2–3 percentage points of the non-private classifier. Statistics obtained from PrivKV-based ratio estimates lose 7–10 points. At ε = 1 all private variants degrade, but ours retains a clear margin over the majority-class baseline, whereas the competing statistics often fall to it. This indicates that the reduction in estimation error carries over to downstream performance.

**Sensitivity and Efficiency.** We examine the effect of the value domain discretization granularity. Accuracy improves up to a moderate number of bins and then plateaus, so the method is not sensitive to this parameter. Communication cost per user is constant and comparable to PrivKV, since each user sends one key-value pair. Server-side computation for the conditional queries is linear in the number of reports for each query and completes in under a second for 10⁵ users on a single core. Because our mechanism does not require multiple interaction rounds, it also avoids the latency and budget-splitting overhead of iterative methods.

**Summary.** Across datasets and privacy levels, the proposed mechanisms yield consistently lower error for frequency, mean, and conditional estimation than existing approaches. The gains are greatest in the regimes that matter in practice: small ε, rare keys, and conditioned queries.

**Discussion**

*Interpretation of the results.* The experiments indicate that the main source of error in existing key-value LDP protocols such as PrivKV [1] is the coupling between key and value perturbation. When a user's key is flipped or absent, the value reported is either discarded or replaced with a random surrogate. This introduces bias into the value estimate, which iterative calibration only partly corrects. Our mechanisms reduce this error by allocating the privacy budget more carefully across the key and value components. They also use estimators that account explicitly for the distortion caused by perturbation. The gains are largest in the regime of small ε and large key domains. This is the regime in which sequential composition and domain-size effects hurt randomized-response-based schemes most [2], [3]. As ε grows, the difference between mechanisms shrinks, as expected, because all of them approach the non-private estimator.

The conditional estimators add a further observation. Conditional frequency and conditional mean are ratios of quantities that are each noisy under LDP, so their variance can be much larger than that of the marginal estimates, especially when the conditioning event is rare. Our results show that the estimation error depends on the support of the condition as well as on ε and the population size n. Conditional statistics are therefore reliable only when the conditioning event has enough mass, roughly when the expected number of contributing users is well above the noise standard deviation, which scales as O(1/(ε√n)). This matches the general lower bounds for locally private estimation [4]. It also gives a practical rule for analysts: conditions should be chosen with this sensitivity in mind, and estimates for low-support conditions should be accompanied by confidence intervals.

*Implications for downstream learning.* Many learning procedures, including naive Bayes classifiers, decision-tree split criteria, and recommendation models based on conditional preferences, need only conditional probabilities and conditional means. Releasing these statistics under LDP therefore lets such models be trained without access to raw records. Because the released statistics are post-processing outputs of ε-LDP reports, any model built from them inherits the same guarantee [5]. The utility of such models is limited by the weakest conditional estimate used. For this reason we recommend that practitioners prune or merge sparse keys before training, using public information or a small privacy-budgeted preliminary round.

*Limitations.* Several limitations should be noted.

1. Our mechanisms assume that each user holds a single key-value pair, or a sampled one, from a known and finite key domain. Real NoSQL records often contain many pairs per user. Extending to this setting requires sampling or padding strategies, which trade privacy budget against truncation bias [6]. We have not yet analyzed this trade-off fully.
2. Values are assumed to be bounded and normalized to [−1, 1]. When the true distribution is heavy-tailed, clipping introduces bias that is unrelated to the privacy noise and that our analysis does not capture.
3. We consider conditions on a single key. Conjunctive or hierarchical conditions across several keys would multiply the number of queries. This forces either budget splitting or a reduction in effective sample size, and the variance would grow accordingly.
4. Our guarantees are for the non-interactive, single-round setting with an honest-but-curious aggregator. We do not consider poisoning or manipulation by malicious clients. LDP protocols are known to be vulnerable to such attacks, because a small group of adversarial users can distort frequency and mean estimates by crafting outputs [7]. Key-value protocols are likely to be especially exposed, since an attacker can influence the key and value channels at the same time.
5. The experiments, although covering synthetic and real-world data, use a limited range of key-domain sizes and skewness. The relative ranking of mechanisms may change on workloads with very different characteristics.

*Future directions.* Four directions follow from these limitations. The first is adaptive budget allocation, in which the split between key and value perturbation is tuned to the estimated data distribution, possibly using a short exploratory phase. The second is multi-key and multi-attribute conditional analysis, where techniques such as marginal release with consistency post-processing [8] could reduce the cost of answering many conditional queries. The third is robust aggregation, covering detection of anomalous reports and estimators that bound the influence of any small group of users. The fourth is a shuffle-model variant, which could amplify privacy and permit a smaller local noise level at the same central guarantee [9]. Finally, a direct study of end-to-end learning accuracy, rather than estimation error alone, would clarify how perturbation error propagates into model quality.

**Conclusion**

This paper studied the collection and analysis of key-value data under local differential privacy. We designed new perturbation mechanisms for key-value pairs. We then built on them conditional frequency estimation for keys and conditional mean estimation for values, which are the primitives needed by many learning tasks. The estimators are unbiased or bias-corrected, and their error characteristics are analyzed explicitly. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed mechanisms achieve consistently lower estimation error than state-of-the-art competitors, particularly under strict privacy budgets and large key domains.

Two broader points follow. First, the accuracy of conditional statistics under LDP is governed by the support of the condition as well as by the privacy parameter, and this should guide how such statistics are requested and used. Second, careful joint design of key and value perturbation, rather than treating them as independent problems, is the main source of utility improvement over earlier approaches. We believe these findings, together with the extensions outlined above, help make privacy-preserving analysis of NoSQL-style data practical for distributed settings in which users do not trust the collector.

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is an extracorporeal blood purification technique that removes large molecular weight substances from the circulation, such as autoantibodies, immune complexes, paraproteins, and toxins, and replaces the removed plasma with albumin solutions or fresh frozen plasma. It is established as first-line or adjunctive therapy in a wide range of neurological, hematological, renal, and immune-mediated diseases, including thrombotic microangiopathies, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic crises, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and humoral rejection after transplantation. Plasma can be separated either by centrifugation or by membrane filtration. In membrane-based TPE, blood is pumped through a highly permeable plasmafilter, and the separated plasma is discarded and replaced.

Any extracorporeal circuit exposes blood to artificial surfaces and thereby activates the coagulation cascade and platelets, with a risk of clotting of the filter and lines. Clotting reduces the efficacy of the procedure, causes blood loss, and increases costs and workload. Anticoagulation is therefore needed. Unfractionated heparin is the most widely used agent in membrane-based TPE, but its use is limited by the risk of bleeding, which is particularly relevant in patients with thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, recent surgery or biopsy, uremic platelet dysfunction, or active vasculitis with hemorrhagic lesions. Heparin may also induce heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and its effect is variable and difficult to predict. Moreover, TPE itself removes coagulation factors and may alter the response to heparin. Low molecular weight heparins and other agents such as argatroban or nafamostat have been used, but they share a systemic effect and are costly or not universally available.

Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) was developed to confine the anticoagulant effect to the extracorporeal circuit. Citrate chelates ionized calcium, a cofactor essential for several steps of the coagulation cascade, so that infusing citrate at the beginning of the circuit decreases ionized calcium and prevents clotting. Part of the citrate-calcium complex is removed in the effluent, and the remainder returns to the patient, where it is rapidly metabolized by the liver, skeletal muscle, and kidney cortex to bicarbonate, releasing calcium.
