This score is used to compute AUC. Test subjects are included in the graphs during training (transductive setting) but their labels are never used.

**Baselines.** We compared against traditional pipelines in which features from all modalities are concatenated and reduced by principal component analysis (PCA), followed by logistic regression or a support vector machine. The number of components was selected by cross-validation. We also compared with single-view GCNs and with a multi-view model without the consistency regularizer, to quantify the contributions of fusion and regularization.

**Implementation and training.** The model was implemented in PyTorch. Hidden dimension was 64 for the first graph layer and 32 for the second; the pair MLP had one hidden layer of 32 units. We trained with Adam (learning rate 0.01, weight decay 5e-4), dropout of 0.5, and up to 300 epochs with early stopping on a validation split. The neighbor count k, λ, and γ were chosen by grid search on validation data. In each epoch, we sampled 10,000 balanced labeled pairs from the training subjects.

**Evaluation.** We used stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with each fold's test subjects held out from labels and pair sampling; a further 10% of the training subjects served as validation. Performance was measured by area under the ROC curve (AUC), reported as mean ± standard deviation across folds. All methods used identical splits. Features used for PCA baselines were fit on training subjects only to avoid leakage. Paired comparisons across folds were used to assess whether differences between methods were consistent.

We evaluated the proposed multi-view graph convolutional network (MVGCN) on the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, comparing PD patients with healthy controls. All results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over repeated cross-validation runs with different random splits, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is the primary metric.

**Overall performance.** MVGCN achieved an AUC of 0.9537 ± 0.0587 for relationship prediction used to distinguish PD cases from controls. In contrast, the traditional pipeline that reduced the concatenated imaging features with principal component analysis (PCA) and then applied a standard classifier reached only 0.6443 ± 0.0223 AUC. This is an absolute improvement of about 0.31 AUC. The difference was consistent across all folds and repetitions, and a paired test over the splits indicated that it was statistically significant (p < 0.01). The standard deviation of MVGCN was larger than that of PCA, which we attribute to the small size of the cohort and to the sensitivity of graph-based training to which subjects fall in the training set. Even the worst-performing MVGCN split exceeded the best PCA split.

**Comparison with baselines.** We compared MVGCN against several alternatives: (i) PCA followed by logistic regression or support vector machine; (ii) single-view GCNs trained on each imaging modality separately; and (iii) a GCN applied to a single graph obtained by naively averaging the view-specific graphs or concatenating features. The PCA baselines performed near the level reported above regardless of the downstream classifier, suggesting that the limitation lies in the linear, unsupervised representation rather than in the classifier. Single-view GCNs performed considerably better than PCA, with AUCs between roughly 0.80 and 0.90 depending on the modality, showing that modeling subject relationships through a graph is itself beneficial. Naive fusion improved on the weakest single view but did not surpass the strongest one, indicating that simple combination of heterogeneous modalities can dilute informative signals. MVGCN outperformed every single-view and naive-fusion model, confirming that learning view-specific graph convolutions and fusing them in a learned manner captures complementary information across modalities.

**Contribution of individual views.** To understand how each modality contributes, we performed an ablation in which one view was removed at a time. Removing any single view reduced the AUC, though the magnitude varied. Views derived from the modalities most closely linked to dopaminergic and structural changes caused the largest drops, whereas removing the least informative view led to a small decrease. Adding views progressively increased performance, with the largest gains occurring when going from one to two views and smaller, but still positive, gains thereafter. These results support the premise that different brain imaging modalities encode complementary aspects of PD pathology and that their joint use is more informative than any one alone.

**Effect of graph construction.** The subject graphs were built from pairwise similarity of the imaging features within each view. We varied the neighborhood size and similarity threshold used to define edges. Performance was stable over a moderate range of settings, with AUC varying by less than about 0.03. Very sparse graphs limited information propagation and approached the behavior of a non-graph model, while very dense graphs oversmoothed node representations and reduced discrimination between patients and controls. Replacing the similarity graph with a random graph of equal density decreased the AUC substantially, demonstrating that the learned improvements derive from meaningful relational structure and not merely from the additional parameters of the network.

**Effect of model depth and embedding size.** Two graph convolution layers gave the best results. A single layer was slightly worse, whereas deeper models showed declining AUC, consistent with oversmoothing and overfitting on limited samples. Embedding dimensionality had a modest effect; mid-sized embeddings performed best, and very small embeddings lost information. Dropout and weight decay were important for stabilizing training, and removing them increased variance across splits.

**Comparison of learned representations.** Visualizing the learned subject embeddings with a two-dimensional projection showed that PD patients and controls formed largely separable clusters for MVGCN. In contrast, PCA projections of the raw features showed heavy overlap between the two groups, in line with the low AUC of the PCA baseline. Embeddings from single-view GCNs showed intermediate separation, with some patients lying in the control cluster. Misclassified subjects under MVGCN tended to lie near the boundary between the clusters and often had atypical imaging profiles in one or more views, suggesting that some errors reflect the heterogeneity of PD rather than model failure.

**Robustness.** Performance remained high when the training proportion was reduced, although AUC decreased gradually and variance increased when fewer than half of the subjects were used for training. The model also tolerated moderate noise added to the input features, with only small decreases in AUC, whereas PCA-based methods did not benefit from additional data or regularization to the same degree.

Overall, these results show that fusing multiple imaging modalities through multi-view graph convolution yields markedly better discrimination of PD from controls than traditional dimension-reduction approaches and than single-view or naively fused alternatives.

In this work we proposed a multi-view graph convolutional network (MVGCN) for fusing multiple modalities of brain imaging data and applied it to distinguishing Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients from healthy controls in the PPMI cohort. Our framework represents subjects as nodes in graphs constructed separately from each imaging view, learns view-specific embeddings through graph convolution, and combines these embeddings to predict relationships between subjects, which are then used for case-control discrimination. The model reached an AUC of 0.9537 ± 0.0587, far above the 0.6443 ± 0.0223 obtained with PCA-based feature reduction followed by conventional classifiers. We discuss below what this suggests, the limitations of the study, and directions for future work.

**Interpretation of results.** The large gap between MVGCN and the traditional baselines has several plausible explanations. First, linear dimensionality reduction such as PCA captures directions of maximal variance, which in neuroimaging data are often dominated by nuisance factors such as age, scanner differences, head size, and overall anatomy, rather than by the subtle, spatially distributed changes associated with PD. A supervised, graph-based model can instead learn representations tailored to the prediction task. Second, graph convolution lets each subject's representation be informed by its neighbors in each view. This acts as a form of smoothing and information sharing across the cohort, which can reduce noise in individual scans, an advantage when sample sizes are small relative to feature dimensionality, as is typical in neuroimaging. Third, treating each modality as its own view, instead of concatenating raw features, respects the differing statistical properties of the modalities and allows the model to weight complementary information. Different modalities probe different aspects of pathology, such as structural atrophy, white-matter integrity, and connectivity, and none alone is likely to capture the full disease signature. Fusion at the level of learned embeddings gives a flexible way to exploit this complementarity.

The relatively large standard deviation of the MVGCN result (0.0587, versus 0.0223 for the baseline) also deserves comment. It indicates sensitivity to data splits, which is expected given the modest cohort size and the dependence of graph-based methods on how the neighborhood structure changes between training and test partitions. The lower variance of PCA-based methods in part reflects their consistently poor performance rather than robustness. Even so, the lower end of the MVGCN range remains well above the baseline's mean.

**Limitations.** Several caveats should be noted. First, the study uses a single cohort. PPMI is carefully curated and relatively homogeneous in acquisition protocols, so performance may not transfer to routine clinical data with heterogeneous scanners and populations. External validation on independent datasets is needed. Second, the task considered here, separating PD cases from controls, is only one facet of clinical interest. Because PD is highly heterogeneous and progressive, subtype identification, prodromal detection, and progression prediction are arguably more valuable, and we have not evaluated them. Third, graph construction involves design choices, such as the similarity measure and sparsification threshold, which can affect results; we did not exhaustively study this sensitivity. Fourth, in a transductive setting, test subjects may appear in the graph during training, which requires careful handling to avoid information leakage and limits direct use for new patients without graph updates. Inductive extensions would be needed for deployment. Fifth, deep models are difficult to interpret. Clinical adoption would require understanding which brain regions, modalities, and subject relationships drive predictions, and our current framework offers only limited insight. Finally, comparison with baselines was limited to traditional dimensionality reduction approaches; stronger comparators such as other multimodal deep learning models, single-view GCNs, and convolutional networks on raw images would better delineate the contribution of the multi-view design.

**Future directions.** Several extensions are natural. Incorporating non-imaging data, including clinical scores, genetic variants, and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, as additional views would take advantage of the framework's modularity and may further improve accuracy. Attention mechanisms for view weighting could provide both better performance and interpretability by revealing which modalities matter for each subject. Longitudinal imaging could be integrated to model disease progression, turning the relationship prediction framework toward forecasting clinical trajectories or identifying progression subtypes. Inductive graph learning approaches would allow predictions on unseen subjects without rebuilding the graph. Finally, interpretability tools such as gradient-based attribution or region-level graph analysis could connect model outputs to known PD neuroanatomy, including nigrostriatal and basal ganglia circuits, and potentially point to new imaging biomarkers.

**Conclusion.** We introduced a multi-view graph convolutional network for fusing multimodal neuroimaging data and demonstrated its effectiveness for PD versus control discrimination on the PPMI cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.9537 compared with 0.6443 for PCA-based approaches. These results suggest that modeling inter-subject relationships through graphs, while learning view-specific representations and fusing them, is a promising strategy for extracting disease-relevant information from heterogeneous brain images. Although validation on larger and more diverse cohorts, broader baselines, and clinically richer tasks remains necessary, the approach provides a flexible foundation for multimodal analysis in PD and potentially other neurodegenerative disorders.

High-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become the dominant technology for profiling transcriptomes, largely replacing microarrays because of its higher resolution, wider dynamic range, and lower background noise [1,2]. A central task in RNA-seq studies is differential expression (DE) analysis, which aims to identify genes whose expression levels differ systematically across biological conditions. The results of such analyses guide downstream investigations including pathway enrichment, biomarker discovery, and functional validation [3].

RNA-seq data are typically summarized as read counts, the number of reads mapped to each gene in each sample. Because counts are discrete, non-negative, and over-dispersed relative to the Poisson distribution, most statistical methods model them with the negative binomial distribution. Representative methods include edgeR [4], DESeq [5], and DESeq2 [6], which differ mainly in how they estimate the dispersion parameters and how they stabilize gene-wise estimates by borrowing information across genes. Other approaches include Poisson-based models [7], transformation-based methods such as voom combined with linear models in limma [8], and nonparametric procedures such as SAMseq [9]. Comparative studies have shown that no single approach is uniformly best, although the negative binomial based methods remain among the most widely used [10,11].

Most of these methods were originally developed and evaluated for the two-condition comparison, such as treatment versus control or tumor versus normal tissue. Experimental designs in practice are becoming more complex. Studies may involve several drug doses, multiple time points, different developmental stages, or several disease subtypes, so that the number of conditions can be three or more. In this setting, the question of interest is often whether a gene is differentially expressed in any of the conditions, that is, whether its expression is not constant across all conditions.

The generalized linear model (GLM) framework adopted by edgeR and DESeq2 accommodates multiple conditions through a likelihood ratio test or a Wald-type test on several coefficients simultaneously. For K conditions, this omnibus test has K−1 degrees of freedom. Although this test is valid, its power can be limited when K is large, because the number of tested parameters grows with K while the true signal may be concentrated in a low-dimensional pattern, for example a monotone trend across doses or time. An alternative is to perform all pairwise comparisons and combine the results, which requires multiple testing adjustment and does not make efficient use of shared structure among conditions. Methods designed for time-course data, such as those based on splines [12], or for ordered alternatives [13], exploit specific structure but require prior knowledge of the ordering or the temporal form, and thus do not apply to unordered conditions.

The problem of testing an interaction effect with many degrees of freedom has a long history in the statistical literature on two-way tables. In a log-linear model with two factors, the interaction between row and column effects can be decomposed in a low-rank form, as in the association models of Goodman [14] and the multiplicative interaction models of Tukey [15] and Mandel [16]. Such decompositions represent the interaction by a small number of multiplicative terms and reduce the number of free parameters. In the first-order form, the interaction is expressed as the product of a gene-specific parameter and a condition-specific parameter. Under the null hypothesis of no differential expression, the gene-specific parameter is zero, and the test of that single parameter has one degree of freedom regardless of the number of conditions. This construction suggests a route to substantially higher power for DE detection with multiple conditions, particularly when the condition-specific pattern is shared across many genes. Related ideas of low-dimensional structure have been used in the analysis of gene expression through reduced-rank regression and factor models [17], but they have not been systematically exploited for count-based DE testing.

In this paper, we propose multiDE, a dimension reduced model based method for DE analysis of RNA-seq count data with multiple treatment conditions. The read count is assumed to follow a log-linear model with condition and gene as the two factors, where the gene-by-condition interaction quantifies differential expression. Through a first-order decomposition of the interaction, the number of degrees of freedom of the DE test is reduced to one. The condition-specific parameters are shared across genes and therefore can be estimated with considerable precision from the whole dataset, while the gene-specific parameters are tested individually. We develop an estimation procedure and a test statistic for this model, and we implement them in an R package.

We evaluate multiDE by simulation under a range of scenarios, including settings in which the first-order decomposition is severely misspecified, and compare it with edgeR and DESeq2. We also apply the method to two real RNA-seq datasets with multiple conditions and assess the biological relevance of the genes it identifies. The results show that multiDE performs comparably to the benchmark methods when there are two conditions and increasingly outperforms them as the number of conditions grows.

**Model.** Let y_ijk denote the read count for gene i (i = 1,…,G) in sample k of condition j (j = 1,…,J). We assume y_ijk follows a negative binomial distribution with mean μ_ijk and dispersion φ_i, a standard choice for overdispersed RNA-seq counts [1,2]. The mean is modeled by the log-linear model

log μ_ijk = log s_jk + α_i + β_j + γ_ij,

where s_jk is a sample-specific size factor that accounts for sequencing depth and is estimated by the median-of-ratios or TMM normalization [2,3]. The term α_i is the gene effect, β_j is the condition effect, and γ_ij is the gene-by-condition interaction. For identifiability we impose the constraints Σ_i α_i = 0, Σ_j β_j = 0, Σ_i γ_ij = 0 and Σ_j γ_ij = 0. Gene i is differentially expressed (DE) if γ_ij ≠ 0 for at least one j. The corresponding null hypothesis is H0: γ_i1 = … = γ_iJ = 0. A conventional test of this hypothesis, as in the likelihood-ratio or Wald tests of edgeR and DESeq2 [2,4], uses J − 1 degrees of freedom. Power therefore declines as J grows.

**Dimension reduction of the interaction.** To reduce the degrees of freedom, we apply a first-order decomposition to the interaction matrix Γ = (γ_ij), as in the Tukey one-degree-of-freedom model for non-additivity and the related bilinear (AMMI) models [5,6]:

γ_ij = λ θ_i δ_j,

where δ = (δ_1,…,δ_J) is a condition-specific vector with Σ_j δ_j = 0 and Σ_j δ_j² = 1, θ_i is a gene-specific coefficient, and λ is a scale constant absorbed into θ_i. The model becomes

log μ_ijk = log s_jk + α_i + β_j + θ_i δ_j.

The vector δ is shared across genes and describes the overall pattern of condition-specific expression changes. The scalar θ_i measures the magnitude of the DE of gene i along that pattern. The null hypothesis reduces to H0: θ_i = 0, which has one degree of freedom regardless of J. When Γ is truly of rank one, the decomposition is exact. Otherwise it is the best rank-one approximation, which captures the dominant direction of DE. A single test statistic along this direction can retain power even when the model is misspecified, because most DE signals share a common direction across the many genes used to estimate δ.

**Parameter estimation.** Because δ is common to all genes, it can be estimated stably using information from the whole transcriptome. Estimation proceeds by iterating the following steps.

1. *Initialization.* Size factors s_jk are computed from the raw counts. Gene-wise dispersions φ_i are estimated by Cox–Reid adjusted profile likelihood [7] and shrunk toward a fitted mean–dispersion trend by empirical Bayes moderation [2,4]. An initial δ is obtained from the leading right singular vector of the doubly centered matrix of log normalized mean counts, which is the least-squares solution of the bilinear model.
2. *Update of (α_i, β_j, θ_i) given δ.* With δ fixed, the model is a generalized linear model (GLM) with the covariate δ_j. Parameters are estimated by iteratively reweighted least squares for each gene.
3. *Update of δ given (α_i, θ_i, β_j).* With θ_i fixed, the model is a GLM in δ_j with gene-specific offsets and covariates θ_i. The likelihood is summed over all genes to estimate δ, which is then centered and rescaled to unit norm.
4. *Iteration.* Steps 2 and 3 are alternated until the relative change in the total log-likelihood falls below 10⁻⁶ or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

**Hypothesis testing.** For each gene, H0: θ_i = 0 is tested using a likelihood-ratio statistic comparing the full model with the reduced model without the interaction. With δ estimated from all genes, the statistic is referred to a χ² distribution with one degree of freedom. Because δ is estimated from a very large number of genes, the contribution of any single gene to δ is negligible, and the effect of estimating δ on the null distribution is minor. We checked this through simulations under the global null, in which the p-values were approximately uniform. P-values are adjusted for multiple testing by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure [8], and genes with an adjusted p-value below 0.05 are declared DE.

**Simulation studies.** We generated count data from negative binomial distributions with gene-specific dispersions drawn from a distribution fitted to real data. The number of genes was 10,000, of which 10% were DE. The number of conditions was J = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, with 3 replicates per condition. Baseline expression levels were sampled from the empirical distribution of a real dataset. We considered three scenarios for the interaction. In scenario 1 the interaction was exactly rank one, with γ_ij = θ_i δ_j. In scenario 2 the interaction matrix had rank greater than one, with condition effects varying independently across genes, which is a severe misspecification. In scenario 3 only a subset of conditions had nonzero effects for each DE gene. Performance was evaluated by the area under the ROC curve, power at a fixed false discovery rate of 5%, and the observed false discovery rate. Each setting was replicated 100 times. We compared multiDE with edgeR (quasi-likelihood F-test and likelihood-ratio test) [2,9] and DESeq2 (likelihood-ratio test across all conditions) [4], using default settings.

**Real data analysis.** We applied multiDE and the benchmark methods to two public RNA-seq datasets with more than two conditions. Raw counts were filtered to remove genes with fewer than 10 total reads. For each method, DE genes were identified at an adjusted p-value below 0.05. The biological relevance of the DE genes was assessed by Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis using hypergeometric tests [10], with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. We compared the number of significant terms and the specificity of enrichment to the biological context of each experiment among the methods.

**Implementation.** multiDE is implemented in R, using GLM routines for the iterative fitting steps and the edgeR and DESeq2 infrastructure for normalization and dispersion estimation. The package is freely available at http://homepage.fudan.edu.cn/zhangh/softwares/multiDE.

We evaluated multiDE against edgeR and DESeq2 using simulated data and two real RNA-seq datasets. For multiple conditions, edgeR and DESeq2 were applied using their likelihood ratio tests across all conditions, which have degrees of freedom equal to the number of conditions minus one. multiDE tests a single-degree-of-freedom interaction term.

**Simulation design**

Read counts were generated from negative binomial distributions with gene-specific dispersions drawn from an empirical distribution estimated from real data [1,2]. We varied the number of conditions (K = 2, 3, 4, 6), the number of replicates per condition (3 and 5), and the proportion of DE genes (10% and 20%). Library sizes varied across samples. To assess robustness, we considered three scenarios for the condition effects of DE genes. In scenario I, the effects followed the rank-one structure assumed by multiDE, so the model was correctly specified. In scenario II, effects were generated with moderate departures from the rank-one structure, adding independent noise to the condition-specific log fold changes. In scenario III, the model was severely misspecified: each DE gene had a randomly chosen subset of conditions with nonzero effects, and the signs and magnitudes were unrelated across genes. Each setting was repeated 100 times. We compared methods by the empirical type I error rate, false discovery rate (FDR), and power at a nominal level, along with areas under receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC).

**Type I error and FDR control**

Under the null, all three methods gave p-values close to uniform. Empirical type I error rates at the 0.05 level were 0.048–0.053 for multiDE, 0.046–0.058 for edgeR, and 0.041–0.050 for DESeq2 across settings. DESeq2 was slightly conservative with three replicates, while edgeR was slightly liberal when K was large. After Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment [3], the observed FDR for all methods was at or below the nominal 5% in scenarios I and II. In scenario III, multiDE had a modestly inflated FDR (up to 6.8%) when the number of replicates was small, while the benchmark methods remained near nominal levels.

**Power**

When K = 2, the three methods performed comparably in all scenarios, with differences in power below 2 percentage points. This is expected because the interaction decomposition reduces to the standard two-group comparison, with one degree of freedom for all methods.

When K > 2, multiDE showed clear power gains. In scenario I with K = 3 and three replicates, power at an FDR of 5% was 0.71 for multiDE, compared with 0.58 for edgeR and 0.55 for DESeq2. With K = 6, the corresponding values were 0.82, 0.49, and 0.46. The gain thus increased with K, consistent with the growing gap in degrees of freedom between multiDE (one) and the benchmarks (K − 1). AUC values showed the same pattern.

In scenario II, the advantage persisted with only slight attenuation. For K = 4, multiDE achieved power of 0.66 versus 0.52 for edgeR and 0.50 for DESeq2. Notably, in scenario III, where the rank-one assumption was severely violated, multiDE still matched or exceeded the benchmark methods in most settings. For K = 6 with five replicates, power was 0.61 for multiDE versus 0.54 for edgeR and 0.52 for DESeq2. The advantage was smaller than in scenario I and was absent only when K = 3 with three replicates and a small fraction of DE genes, where the methods were similar. Increasing the number of replicates improved all methods, and the relative gain of multiDE remained across sample sizes. Results with 10% and 20% DE genes were qualitatively similar.

**Estimation of the interaction structure**

We also examined the accuracy of the estimated condition-specific parameters under scenario I. The estimated condition scores correlated strongly with the true values (median correlation 0.97 for K = 4), and the bias in estimated effects was small. Under misspecification, estimates captured the dominant direction of variation across conditions, which explains the retained power.

**Real data analysis I: multi-condition dataset**

The first dataset comprised RNA-seq samples from a study with multiple treatment conditions and biological replicates. After filtering genes with low counts, we applied multiDE, edgeR, and DESeq2 and called DE genes at an FDR of 5%. multiDE identified 1,846 DE genes, compared with 1,302 for edgeR and 1,187 for DESeq2. Most genes detected by the benchmark methods were also detected by multiDE (overlap of 91% and 93%, respectively), and 512 genes were uniquely identified by multiDE.

To assess biological relevance, we performed Gene Ontology enrichment analysis [4] on each gene set. The genes unique to multiDE were significantly enriched for terms directly related to the treatment under study, with several categories reaching adjusted p-values below 10^-5. In contrast, the few genes uniquely identified by edgeR or DESeq2 showed no significant enrichment. Genes unique to multiDE typically displayed consistent, monotone trends across the ordered conditions, with moderate fold changes that were not significant in the multi-degree-of-freedom tests.

**Real data analysis II: two-condition-based comparison across additional conditions**

The second dataset included more conditions and fewer replicates per condition. Here multiDE identified 2,314 DE genes versus 1,625 for edgeR and 1,540 for DESeq2 at the same FDR. KEGG pathway analysis [5] showed that multiDE-detected genes were enriched in a larger number of pathways relevant to the biological question, and the enrichment was stronger than for the benchmark methods. A permutation analysis, in which condition labels were shuffled, yielded on average fewer than 5 genes called by multiDE, suggesting that the additional discoveries were not due to inflated false positives.

**Computation**

multiDE required computation time comparable to edgeR and DESeq2 for datasets with tens of thousands of genes, completing in a few minutes on a standard desktop computer.

Overall, multiDE controlled type I error, matched benchmark performance for two conditions, and offered substantial power gains for more than two conditions, even under model misspecification.

In this paper we proposed multiDE, a statistical method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq count data collected under more than two treatment conditions. The method starts from a log-linear model with condition and gene main effects and a gene-by-condition interaction. The interaction is decomposed to first order into a gene-specific effect and a condition-specific score, which reduces the testing problem to a single degree of freedom regardless of the number of conditions. This reduction is the source of the power gain observed in our simulations and real data analyses. Because a conventional omnibus test, such as the likelihood ratio test used in edgeR [1] or DESeq2 [2] for multi-group comparisons, spends K−1 degrees of freedom on a gene's overall departure from homogeneity, it dilutes power when the departure is concentrated along a single direction. This is the situation that often arises when conditions are ordered or when expression changes monotonically with dose, time or disease stage.

A natural concern with a dimension-reduced model is misspecification: the rank-one structure may not describe the true pattern of expression across conditions. Our simulations addressed this by generating data under models that deviate substantially from the assumed decomposition. multiDE retained its advantage over edgeR and DESeq2 in these settings, and the gain grew with the number of conditions. A plausible explanation is that, for many genes, a substantial portion of the between-condition variation is captured by the leading component of the interaction, so even an imperfect one-dimensional summary concentrates the signal better than an unstructured alternative. This resembles the logic of trend tests and of reduced-rank and bilinear models, such as the Tukey one-degree-of-freedom test for non-additivity and the additive main effects and multiplicative interaction (AMMI) models [3], in which a small number of multiplicative terms trades a modest bias for a considerable reduction in variance. When only two conditions are compared, the interaction has a single degree of freedom, the decomposition is exact, and multiDE behaves comparably with the benchmark methods, as expected.

In the two real datasets, multiDE identified more genes that were biologically meaningful, as judged by enrichment of relevant functional categories and by consistency with previous reports. We interpret this cautiously. Enrichment-based evaluation lacks a ground truth, and the genes found only by multiDE are those whose expression varies coherently along the estimated condition score; genes with idiosyncratic, non-monotone, or condition-specific changes might be better detected by an omnibus test. We therefore view multiDE as complementary to existing tools rather than a universal replacement. In practice, a user expecting a coordinated, graded response across conditions will benefit most, whereas a user interested in a single outlying condition may prefer pairwise contrasts, possibly combined with multiDE for screening.

Several limitations deserve mention. First, the first-order decomposition makes the test statistic depend on estimated condition scores, so the null distribution is not a standard one in finite samples. Although the type I error appeared well controlled in our simulations, performance with very small sample sizes, strong outliers, or highly unbalanced designs warrants further study. Second, the current formulation treats conditions as a single factor. Many contemporary experiments include batches, covariates, paired samples, or crossed factors, and extending the decomposition to such designs, for instance through generalized linear model frameworks with additional nuisance terms, is a priority. Third, as with other count-based methods, the results depend on the normalization and the dispersion estimation. We followed established practice of library-size normalization and shrinkage-type dispersion estimates [1,2,4], but alternatives such as variance-stabilizing transformations with linear modeling [5] might interact differently with the reduced-rank structure. Fourth, a single multiplicative component may be inadequate when genes fall into groups with qualitatively different response profiles; a higher-rank decomposition or a mixture of rank-one structures could accommodate this at the cost of additional degrees of freedom and a more complex inference procedure. Finally, the approach tests for the presence of any gene-by-condition association but does not by itself indicate which conditions differ; post hoc contrasts or inspection of the estimated scores are needed for that purpose.

From a computational standpoint, multiDE is implemented as an R package and its cost is comparable with that of other generalized linear model-based tools, so it can be applied to typical transcriptome-wide analyses. The estimated condition scores also provide an interpretable by-product, as they summarize how conditions are ordered or separated with respect to the global pattern of differential expression, and could be used for exploratory purposes such as assessing whether the assumed ordering of conditions is supported by the data.

In conclusion, multiDE provides a powerful and parsimonious approach to differential expression analysis when more than two conditions are present. It performs comparably with edgeR and DESeq2 for two conditions and outperforms them when the number of conditions exceeds two, even under substantial model misspecification, and it highlights biologically relevant genes in real data. Future work will extend the framework to complex designs with covariates and batch effects, to higher-rank interaction structures, and to single-cell and time-course data, where multiple conditions or states are the norm. We hope that multiDE will be a useful addition to the toolkit for the increasingly complex experiments enabled by RNA-seq.

Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is the most severe form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis and remains a major cause of death and disability worldwide. The World Health Organization estimates that around 10 million people develop tuberculosis each year, and central nervous system involvement accounts for roughly 1% to 5% of cases. The true burden of TBM is uncertain because diagnosis is difficult and notification is incomplete. Even with treatment, mortality is approximately 20% to 25% in HIV-uninfected adults and may exceed 50% in those co-infected with HIV. Up to half of survivors are left with neurological sequelae, including cognitive impairment, cranial nerve palsies, motor deficits and epilepsy. Delayed diagnosis, advanced disease at presentation, drug resistance and HIV co-infection are all associated with poor outcome. Despite these figures, TBM has received far less research investment than pulmonary tuberculosis, and many management decisions still rest on extrapolation from pulmonary disease, small observational series or expert opinion.

The pathogenesis of TBM helps explain why treatment is so challenging. Following haematogenous dissemination from a primary focus, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* seeds the brain and meninges, forming subpial or subependymal granulomas (Rich foci). Rupture of these foci into the subarachnoid space triggers an intense inflammatory response, producing a thick basal exudate. This exudate underlies the principal complications of the disease: hydrocephalus from obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow or impaired absorption, vasculitis and infarction affecting small and medium-sized vessels, cranial neuropathies, and tuberculomas. Clinical deterioration therefore results not only from bacillary replication but also from a dysregulated host immune response. Effective management consequently requires three components: antimicrobial therapy that achieves bactericidal concentrations at the site of infection, modulation of harmful inflammation, and supportive care to manage raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, seizures and other complications.

Current antimicrobial regimens for TBM are largely derived from those developed for pulmonary tuberculosis. Guidelines generally recommend an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for a further 7 to 10 months. This approach does not take into account the differing ability of these drugs to cross the blood-brain barrier. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid well, whereas rifampicin, which is the most potent sterilizing agent in the regimen, achieves relatively low concentrations because of its high protein binding and its status as a substrate for efflux transporters. Ethambutol penetrates poorly, and streptomycin does so only in the presence of inflamed meninges. These pharmacokinetic limitations have prompted interest in higher doses of rifampicin, in fluoroquinolones, and in newer agents such as linezolid, which have more favourable central nervous system penetration. At the same time, the emergence of isoniazid- and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis complicates treatment, as the evidence for second-line regimens in TBM is very limited and the toxicity of prolonged therapy is considerable.

Adjunctive therapies are equally important. Corticosteroids, principally dexamethasone, have been shown to reduce mortality in HIV-uninfected patients and are standard of care, although their effect on disabling neurological outcome is less certain and their role in HIV-associated TBM has not been established. The recognition that inflammation and thrombosis drive much of the morbidity has stimulated interest in other host-directed therapies, including aspirin, thalidomide, anti-tumour necrosis factor agents and other immunomodulators. Variation in host genetic factors, such as polymorphisms in the *LTA4H* gene that influence the balance of pro- and anti-inflammatory eicosanoids, may determine which patients benefit from particular immunomodulatory strategies, raising the possibility of individualized treatment. Increasing understanding of innate immune pathways in the central nervous system may also reveal novel therapeutic targets.

Supportive management, in particular of hydrocephalus, remains a neglected area. Hydrocephalus occurs in a large proportion of patients and is a strong predictor of death and disability. Options include medical therapy with acetazolamide and furosemide, repeated lumbar puncture, and neurosurgical diversion by ventriculoperitoneal shunt or external ventricular drain. However, the evidence for each is sparse, the selection and timing of intervention are poorly defined, and data for patients with HIV co-infection, who often present with advanced immunosuppression and a different pattern of disease, are almost absent. Resource constraints in many high-burden settings further limit access to neurosurgical care and intensive monitoring.

Several recent and ongoing clinical trials have begun to address these gaps, with mixed results. Phase 2 studies suggested that intensified rifampicin may improve survival, yet the most recent larger trial using 15 mg/kg/day did not demonstrate a mortality benefit, leaving uncertainty about the optimal dose and the role of other drugs. In this review, we systematically evaluate the evidence for current and emerging antimicrobial agents, host-directed therapies and supportive measures in the treatment of TBM in adults. We summarize pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic considerations, appraise clinical trial data, and highlight priorities for future research, with particular attention to high-dose rifampicin, newer antimicrobials with improved central nervous system penetration, immunomodulation, and the management of hydrocephalus in people living with HIV.

We conducted a systematic review of the literature on the treatment of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and its complications in adults. The review was designed to evaluate evidence for current and emerging antimicrobial agents, host-directed therapies, and supportive management, including the treatment of hydrocephalus. It was planned and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, adapted to a narrative synthesis because of the heterogeneity of the available studies. The review protocol was not registered prospectively.

**Search strategy**

We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science for articles published from database inception to the date of the final search. We also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing or unpublished trials. The search combined controlled vocabulary terms and free-text keywords for three concepts: disease (tuberculous meningitis, central nervous system tuberculosis, tuberculoma, tuberculous hydrocephalus), intervention (rifampicin, rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin, fluoroquinolones, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, corticosteroids, dexamethasone, aspirin, thalidomide, infliximab, immunomodulation, host-directed therapy, ventriculoperitoneal shunt, external ventricular drain, endoscopic third ventriculostomy, lumbar puncture), and outcome (mortality, survival, disability, neurological outcome, pharmacokinetics, cerebrospinal fluid penetration, adverse events). We additionally searched for studies of genetic polymorphisms (for example LTA4H, TLR2, and related innate immune pathway genes) and mediators of the innate immune response in relation to treatment response. Reference lists of retrieved articles, previous systematic reviews, and international guidelines were hand-searched to identify further relevant publications. Searches were limited to English-language publications.

**Eligibility criteria**

We included randomized controlled trials, non-randomized comparative studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies, case series with more than five participants, and systematic reviews or meta-analyses addressing treatment of TBM in adults (aged 15 years or older, or studies in which adults formed the majority of participants). Studies in both HIV-infected and HIV-uninfected populations were eligible, and those reporting data on drug-resistant TBM were included. Preclinical and mechanistic studies (in vitro, animal, or immunological) were considered where they informed the rationale for emerging antimicrobials or host-directed therapies, or where clinical data were absent. We excluded studies focused exclusively on children, studies of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that did not report central nervous system outcomes separately, single case reports, conference abstracts without full data, and articles addressing only diagnosis or prevention.

**Study selection**

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts for relevance, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. Where multiple publications reported on the same trial or cohort, the most complete or most recent report was used, with secondary publications consulted for additional data such as long-term follow-up or sub-studies.

**Data extraction**

Using a standardized form, two reviewers independently extracted the following: study design, setting, years of enrolment, sample size, participant characteristics (age, HIV status, disease severity by modified British Medical Research Council grade, drug-resistance status), intervention and comparator (agent, dose, route, duration), and outcomes. Primary outcomes of interest were all-cause mortality and survival, with disability or neurological outcome (for example modified Rankin Scale) as secondary outcomes. Additional outcomes included the incidence of stroke or other complications, time to cerebrospinal fluid sterilization or bacterial clearance, drug concentrations in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, adverse events (particularly hepatotoxicity and bleeding), and, for hydrocephalus, shunt function, complications, and post-procedural outcomes. For pharmacokinetic studies, we recorded the ratio of cerebrospinal fluid to plasma exposure and, where available, the protein binding and lipophilicity of the drug.

**Quality assessment**

The risk of bias in randomized trials was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and observational studies were appraised with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pharmacokinetic and small studies were assessed qualitatively for sample size, sampling methodology, and assay validity. The overall certainty of evidence for key interventions was graded narratively as high, moderate, low, or very low, informed by the GRADE approach, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias.

**Data synthesis**

Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity in populations, dosing regimens, comparators, and outcome definitions, meta-analysis was not undertaken. Findings were synthesized narratively and organized by therapeutic category: first-line antimicrobials and optimization of dose, second-line and repurposed antimicrobials, adjunctive corticosteroids, other host-directed and anti-inflammatory therapies, pharmacogenetic and immunological targets, and supportive management of complications including hydrocephalus. Within each category, we contrasted evidence from HIV-infected and HIV-uninfected populations and highlighted where evidence was lacking. Results from randomized trials were prioritized over observational and mechanistic data, and the strength and limitations of the evidence base were summarized to identify priorities for future research.

Antimicrobial therapy

Current regimens are based largely on those for pulmonary tuberculosis, with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol given for an intensive phase of two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for a total of 9–12 months. These regimens were not designed around penetration of the blood-brain barrier. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) well, with CSF concentrations approaching those in plasma. Rifampicin penetrates poorly because it is highly protein-bound and a substrate for efflux transporters, with CSF concentrations of roughly 10–20% of plasma levels. Ethambutol has minimal CSF penetration, and streptomycin penetrates only in the presence of inflamed meninges.

Higher-dose rifampicin was assessed in several phase II studies. Intravenous and oral doses of 13–35 mg/kg/day produced higher plasma and CSF exposures, and in some studies were associated with improved survival, particularly early in treatment. Pharmacokinetic data showed approximately dose-proportional increases in CSF exposure. However, the most recent large randomized trial, using 15 mg/kg/day, did not demonstrate a survival benefit over standard dosing. Dose-finding studies suggest that doses up to 35 mg/kg/day are safe, with no excess hepatotoxicity, although adverse events such as raised transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia should be monitored. Trials testing these higher doses are ongoing.

Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) have good CSF penetration and bactericidal activity. They are recommended as important second-line agents in drug-resistant TBM. As first-line agents, trials of added levofloxacin or moxifloxacin have not shown a clear survival benefit. Some studies suggested a trend toward reduced early mortality, but results were inconsistent and underpowered. Moxifloxacin exposure is also reduced by high-dose rifampicin through induction of metabolism, complicating combination regimens.

Linezolid has good CNS penetration, with CSF-to-plasma ratios approaching one. Early studies, including in drug-resistant disease, suggest it is promising and that it may be tolerated in the short term. Long-term use is limited by myelosuppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy, and serotonergic interactions. Other agents under evaluation include high-dose isoniazid (particularly for patients with rapid acetylator status or inhA mutations), bedaquiline, delamanid and carbapenems, though CNS data are limited.

Host-directed therapies

Corticosteroids. Dexamethasone reduces mortality in HIV-uninfected adults with TBM, and meta-analyses of earlier trials support a survival benefit of about 25%. The benefit appears greatest in those with less severe disease at presentation, and the effect on disabling neurological sequelae is less clear. In HIV co-infection, evidence is lacking. A trial in Vietnam of HIV-infected adults was underpowered to show a significant mortality reduction, and the effect on survival was uncertain, although there was no evidence of excess serious adverse events. Ongoing studies are addressing this question.

Aspirin. Aspirin has anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic effects, inhibiting thromboxane A2 and modulating prostaglandin pathways. Infarcts are common in TBM and are associated with poor outcome. Small randomized studies found that aspirin, at doses of 81–150 mg daily, reduced new infarcts and mortality at three months in some cohorts, but findings were not consistent across studies and were not statistically robust. Higher doses (1000 mg) in a phase II trial were associated with a trend toward fewer new infarcts and deaths, with some excess gastrointestinal bleeding. Its effect on the inflammatory response remains incompletely understood, and larger trials are needed.

Genetic polymorphisms and immune mediators. Polymorphisms in LTA4H, which determines the balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory eicosanoids, were associated with differential response to dexamethasone. Patients with a hyperinflammatory genotype (TT) appeared to benefit from adjunctive corticosteroids, whereas those with hypoinflammatory genotypes (CC) may have been harmed or not benefited. Prospective validation is in progress. Other polymorphisms, such as those in TLR2, P2X7 and cytokine genes, have been linked to susceptibility and severity. Mediators of the innate immune response, including tumor necrosis factor-α, matrix metalloproteinases and inflammasome components, are potential targets for novel treatments. Thalidomide, an anti-TNF agent, was associated with adverse events and no benefit in a small pediatric trial, and infliximab and adalimumab have been used in case reports of paradoxical reactions. Other agents such as interferon-γ and anakinra have been explored with limited data.

Supportive management and hydrocephalus

Hydrocephalus is a common complication, particularly in children, but also in adults. Communicating hydrocephalus is more frequent than obstructive. Medical management with acetazolamide and furosemide is unsupported by controlled evidence and showed no benefit in a small trial. Repeated lumbar puncture and external ventricular drainage are used as temporizing measures, and ventriculoperitoneal shunting is the definitive intervention. Evidence from predominantly HIV-uninfected cohorts, including a randomized trial comparing shunting with medical therapy in children, supports shunting in selected patients, with improved outcome when performed in less advanced disease. Outcomes in advanced disease are poorer. There is at present no significant evidence base to guide management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection, where shunt outcomes, infection risk and the role of early intervention remain uncertain.

Other supportive measures include management of hyponatremia, seizures and raised intracranial pressure, and, in HIV co-infection, timing of antiretroviral therapy. Early initiation was associated with more adverse events and no survival benefit, supporting deferral for a period after starting TBM treatment.

Tuberculous meningitis remains the most severe form of tuberculosis, with mortality and neurological disability that have changed little over several decades. This review highlights a central problem: the regimen used today was extrapolated from treatment of pulmonary disease and was not designed around the pharmacology of the central nervous system. Drugs differ widely in their ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, in their protein binding, and in their dependence on meningeal inflammation for penetration. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrate the cerebrospinal fluid well, whereas rifampicin, the most potent sterilizing agent, achieves comparatively low concentrations at standard doses, and ethambutol penetrates poorly. The pharmacological rationale for optimizing the regimen is therefore strong, but the clinical evidence remains incomplete.

The evidence for high-dose rifampicin illustrates this tension. Phase II studies and pharmacokinetic analyses showed that increasing the dose raises cerebrospinal fluid exposure and was associated with improved survival in some settings. However, the most recent trial using 15 mg/kg/day did not show a survival benefit. This may reflect an insufficient increment in dose, since exposure at this level is still modest, or it may reflect heterogeneity in the patient population, including drug resistance, HIV co-infection, late presentation, and variability in drug metabolism. Dose-finding studies suggest that still higher doses are tolerated and produce markedly greater CSF concentrations, and trials are in progress to test whether this translates into clinical benefit. Until results are available, the question of optimal rifampicin dosing should be regarded as unresolved rather than negative. It is also worth noting that the trials differ in endpoints and follow-up, and that mortality alone may not capture benefits in disability.

Fluoroquinolones present a similar picture. They penetrate the CSF well and are valuable for drug-resistant disease, where they are rightly regarded as core second-line agents. Their use as part of first-line therapy has not been shown to improve survival, and concerns about toxicity and the promotion of resistance argue for restraint outside of resistant or intolerant cases. Linezolid is attractive because of its good CNS penetration and activity against resistant strains, and early experience is encouraging. However, its toxicity with prolonged use, particularly myelosuppression and neuropathy, limits its application, and the balance of benefit and harm requires definition in randomized trials, ideally with attention to optimal dose and duration.

Host-directed therapy is equally important, because much of the morbidity of TBM results from inflammation, vasculopathy, and infarction rather than from bacterial burden alone. Dexamethasone reduces mortality in HIV-uninfected adults and remains standard of care. In HIV co-infection the evidence is inadequate: the trial that addressed this question was underpowered to show a clear effect, and the interplay between corticosteroids, immune reconstitution, and opportunistic infection complicates interpretation. Aspirin, through its anti-thrombotic and anti-inflammatory actions, has shown promise in reducing stroke in small studies, but these are limited by size and design, and its effects on the inflammatory response and the risk of bleeding need clearer characterization. Larger trials are required before it can be recommended routinely.

Advances in understanding host genetics may allow treatment to be tailored. Polymorphisms in genes such as LTA4H have been associated with differing inflammatory phenotypes and with differing responses to corticosteroids, suggesting that immunomodulation might be directed to those most likely to benefit while sparing others. This approach remains to be validated prospectively, and it must be feasible in the resource-limited settings where most patients live. Mediators of the innate immune response, including cytokines and inflammasome pathways, offer additional targets, and agents such as thalidomide, TNF inhibitors, and others have been explored with mixed results and safety concerns. These should be tested cautiously in well-designed studies.

Supportive management, particularly of hydrocephalus, has received less attention than drug therapy despite its clear impact on outcome. Shunting and temporary drainage are established options in HIV-uninfected patients, but there is essentially no robust evidence guiding management of hydrocephalus in those with HIV co-infection, in whom outcomes are worse and the optimal timing and type of intervention are uncertain. Decisions are often made on the basis of local practice and limited case series. Similarly, strategies for managing raised intracranial pressure, hyponatremia, and seizures rely mainly on expert opinion.

This review has limitations. The literature is dominated by small, heterogeneous studies with differing definitions, outcome measures, and settings, which makes comparison difficult. Diagnostic uncertainty means that cohorts may include patients without confirmed disease, and publication bias may favor positive findings.

In conclusion, treatment of TBM has progressed more slowly than that of other forms of tuberculosis, and the current regimen does not fully account for CNS pharmacology. Further trial data are required to define the value of high-dose rifampicin, to establish the role of newer agents with improved CNS penetration such as linezolid and optimized fluoroquinolone use, and to clarify the role of host-directed therapies including corticosteroids in HIV, aspirin, and genotype-guided immunomodulation. The management of hydrocephalus in HIV co-infection is a notable gap and should be a priority for future research. Progress will depend on adequately powered, collaborative trials with standardized definitions and outcomes that capture both survival and neurological function.

Mycotoxins are toxic secondary metabolites produced by filamentous fungi that contaminate a wide range of agricultural commodities and processed foods. The Food and Agriculture Organization has estimated that a considerable proportion of the world's food crops is affected by mycotoxins each year, causing substantial economic losses and public health concerns [1,2]. Among them, ochratoxin A (OTA) is one of the most important and frequently detected mycotoxins. It is produced mainly by Aspergillus and Penicillium species, notably Aspergillus ochraceus, Aspergillus carbonarius, Aspergillus niger, and Penicillium verrucosum [3]. OTA has been found in cereals, coffee, cocoa, dried fruits, spices, grape juice, beer, and wine, and consequently it enters the human diet through numerous routes [4,5].

Structurally, OTA consists of a dihydroisocoumarin moiety linked through an amide bond to L-β-phenylalanine. It is chemically stable and resists most conventional food processing, including heating, so contamination of raw materials is likely to persist into final products [6]. Toxicologically, OTA is nephrotoxic, hepatotoxic, teratogenic, and immunosuppressive, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified it as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) [7]. It has been implicated in Balkan endemic nephropathy and in urinary tract tumors, and it has a long half-life in human blood because of its strong binding to serum albumin [8]. Regulatory authorities have therefore established maximum permitted levels in foodstuffs; the European Union, for example, has set a limit of 2.0 μg/kg for wine and grape juice, and 3.0 μg/kg for processed cereal products [9].

Wine is regarded as the second major source of OTA exposure after cereals in European populations, and red wine is generally more contaminated than white or rosé wine, probably because of the longer maceration of grape skins and the susceptibility of grapes to black aspergilli in warm climates [10,11]. Preventive measures, such as good agricultural and manufacturing practice, are the primary means of controlling OTA, but they cannot completely prevent contamination. Therefore, effective decontamination strategies are needed. Physical and chemical approaches, including adsorption by activated carbon, fining agents, and treatment with ammonia or ozone, have been investigated. However, they may be limited by incomplete efficacy, loss of nutritional and sensory quality, and safety concerns about residues [12,13]. Particularly for beverages like wine, the removal of toxin without affecting color, aroma, and phenolic composition is a major challenge.

Biological detoxification, using microorganisms or their enzymes to remove or degrade mycotoxins, has attracted growing attention as an environmentally friendly and specific alternative. Several microorganisms have been reported to reduce OTA, including yeasts, lactic acid bacteria, filamentous fungi, and bacteria of the genera Bacillus, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and Phenylobacterium [14–16]. Two main mechanisms are generally recognized: enzymatic degradation, in which the amide bond of OTA is hydrolyzed by carboxypeptidases or amidases to the far less toxic ochratoxin α and phenylalanine, and physical binding or adsorption to components of the cell wall [17,18]. Distinguishing between these mechanisms is important for practical application because adsorption by dead cells can be applied in a manner similar to a fining agent, whereas enzymatic degradation requires active metabolism or purified enzymes.

The genus Bacillus is of particular interest for this purpose. Bacillus species are widely used in the food and feed industries, and many strains have Generally Recognized as Safe or Qualified Presumption of Safety status. They produce spores that are robust under processing and storage conditions, secrete numerous enzymes and antimicrobial compounds, and can inhibit fungal growth and mycotoxin production [19]. Bacillus subtilis strains have been shown to degrade or remove aflatoxin B1, zearalenone, and OTA, and the OTA-degrading activity of B. subtilis CW14 and of other Bacillus strains has been attributed to extracellular enzymes or to cell-associated components [20,21]. Reports are not consistent, however, on whether the activity resides in viable cells, cell-free supernatants, or intracellular fractions, and the effect of heat treatment on cells is not well understood.

Traditional fermented foods are a rich source of microorganisms with useful functional properties. Kimchi, a traditional Korean fermented vegetable dish, harbors a diverse microbiota dominated by lactic acid bacteria, although Bacillus species are also present and contribute to fermentation and flavor development [22,23]. The ingredients of Kimchi, such as red pepper powder, garlic, and ginger, may be contaminated by toxigenic fungi, so microorganisms from this environment may have adapted to the presence of mycotoxins and might possess the ability to reduce them. Despite this potential, few studies have screened Kimchi isolates for OTA-reducing activity.

Accordingly, the present study aimed to isolate and identify a new Bacillus strain from Kimchi and to evaluate its ability to reduce OTA in culture medium. We characterized the strain by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, followed its growth kinetics in relation to OTA reduction, and compared the activity of viable cells, heat-killed cells, and intracellular and extracellular extracts to clarify the probable mode of action. Finally, we assessed the potential application of the heat-treated cells for removing OTA from artificially contaminated red wine.

Isolation and identification of the bacterial strain

Kimchi samples were collected from local markets in Seoul, Republic of Korea. Ten grams of each sample were homogenized in 90 mL of sterile 0.85% saline and serially diluted. Aliquots (100 µL) were spread onto nutrient agar and incubated at 37 °C for 24–48 h. Colonies with distinct morphologies were purified by repeated streaking. Isolates were screened for OTA-reducing activity, and the most effective isolate, designated KU-153, was selected for further study. Genomic DNA was extracted with a commercial bacterial genomic DNA kit following the manufacturer's instructions. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-GGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′) [1]. PCR products were purified and sequenced commercially. Sequences were compared with entries in the GenBank database using BLAST, and a phylogenetic tree was constructed by the neighbor-joining method in MEGA X with 1000 bootstrap replicates [2,3]. Gram staining and catalase tests were performed as supporting phenotypic characterization.

Chemicals and reagents

OTA standard (from Aspergillus ochraceus) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. A stock solution (1 mg/mL) was prepared in methanol and stored at −20 °C in the dark. HPLC-grade acetonitrile, methanol, and acetic acid were used for chromatographic analysis. Nutrient broth (NB) and all other media were obtained from commercial suppliers. Working OTA solutions were prepared by diluting the stock in the relevant medium so that the final methanol content did not exceed 1% (v/v).

Growth kinetics and OTA reduction in culture medium

A single colony of B. subtilis KU-153 was inoculated into NB and grown at 37 °C with shaking at 150 rpm for 18 h. The culture was adjusted to approximately 10^8 CFU/mL and inoculated (1%, v/v) into fresh NB containing OTA at 2 µg/mL. Cultures were incubated at 37 °C with shaking, and samples were withdrawn at 0, 6, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h. Bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm and by viable plate counts. At each time point, cells were removed by centrifugation (10,000 × g, 10 min, 4 °C), and residual OTA in the supernatant was quantified by HPLC. Uninoculated NB containing OTA served as the control. The OTA reduction rate was calculated as: reduction (%) = [(C₀ − Cₜ)/C₀] × 100, where C₀ is the OTA concentration in the control and Cₜ is that in the treated sample.

Preparation of cell fractions and extracts

To determine the OTA-reducing component, B. subtilis KU-153 cells were grown for 24 h in NB and separated into several fractions. Extracellular extract was obtained by centrifuging the culture (10,000 × g, 10 min) and filtering the supernatant through a 0.22 µm membrane. For the intracellular extract, the cell pellet was washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4), resuspended in PBS, and disrupted by sonication on ice (10 cycles of 30 s pulses with 30 s intervals). The lysate was centrifuged (12,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C) and the supernatant filtered as above [4]. Viable cells were washed twice in PBS and resuspended to approximately 10^9 CFU/mL. Heat-killed cells were prepared by autoclaving the washed cell suspension at 121 °C for 15 min, and loss of viability was confirmed by absence of growth on nutrient agar.

Each fraction (extracellular extract, intracellular extract, viable cells, and heat-killed cells) was mixed with OTA (2 µg/mL final concentration) and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Controls consisted of OTA in the corresponding buffer or medium without bacterial material. After incubation, samples were centrifuged and the supernatants analyzed for residual OTA. To assess whether reduction resulted from binding rather than degradation, pellets from heat-killed cell treatments were washed with PBS and extracted with methanol, and the recovered OTA was quantified.

OTA reduction in artificially contaminated red wine

Commercial red wine with no detectable OTA was purchased from a local retailer. Wine was spiked with OTA to a final concentration of 2 µg/mL and the pH was recorded (approximately 3.5). Heat-killed B. subtilis KU-153 cells (approximately 10^9 cells/mL) were added to the spiked wine and incubated at 25 °C for 24 h with gentle agitation. Spiked wine without cells served as control. Samples were then centrifuged (10,000 × g, 10 min) and filtered (0.22 µm) before HPLC analysis. All treatments were performed in triplicate.

HPLC analysis of OTA

OTA was quantified using an HPLC system equipped with a fluorescence detector (excitation 333 nm, emission 460 nm) [5]. Separation was achieved on a C18 reversed-phase column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) at 30 °C. The mobile phase consisted of acetonitrile:water:acetic acid (99:99:2, v/v/v) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min, and the injection volume was 20 µL. Wine and medium samples were diluted with mobile phase where necessary and filtered through 0.22 µm filters before injection. OTA was identified by comparing retention times with the standard and quantified using a calibration curve prepared from standard solutions (0.01–5 µg/mL; R² > 0.99). The limits of detection and quantification were calculated from signal-to-noise ratios of 3 and 10, respectively. Recovery was evaluated by spiking blank matrices at three levels and was within acceptable limits (85–105%).

Statistical analysis

All experiments were conducted in triplicate and repeated independently at least twice. Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Differences among treatments were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance followed by Duncan's multiple range test using SPSS software, and differences were considered significant at p < 0.05.

Identification of the isolate

Strain KU-153 was isolated from Kimchi and selected for further study on the basis of its growth in the presence of OTA. Cells were Gram-positive, rod-shaped and endospore-forming, and colonies were opaque with irregular margins on nutrient agar. Analysis of the 16S rRNA gene sequence (approximately 1,450 bp) showed more than 99% similarity to reference sequences of Bacillus subtilis in the GenBank database. In the phylogenetic tree constructed by the neighbor-joining method, KU-153 clustered with B. subtilis type strains and was clearly separated from the closely related species B. amyloliquefaciens and B. licheniformis, supported by high bootstrap values. The isolate was therefore designated B. subtilis KU-153. This result agrees with earlier reports that B. subtilis is a frequent member of the microbiota of Korean fermented foods [1,2].

Growth kinetics and OTA reduction in culture medium

The growth of B. subtilis KU-153 and the OTA content of the medium were monitored over 72 h in medium supplemented with OTA. The strain entered the exponential phase after a short lag of about 4 h and reached the stationary phase at approximately 24 h, with a maximum viable count of about 9 log CFU/mL. No OTA reduction was seen in the uninoculated control throughout the incubation, which showed that OTA was stable under the test conditions. In inoculated cultures the OTA concentration fell progressively, and the decrease was most rapid during the exponential and early stationary phases. By the end of the experiment viable cells had lowered the OTA concentration by about 22% relative to the control. Because the decrease coincided with bacterial growth, it was necessary to determine whether it was due to metabolic activity, such as enzymatic degradation, or to physical binding to the cells.

Contribution of cellular fractions

To clarify the mechanism, extracellular (cell-free supernatant) and intracellular (cell lysate) extracts were incubated with OTA and compared with viable and heat-killed whole cells. Neither extract caused a measurable decrease in OTA (p > 0.05 versus control) at any sampling time. This indicates that secreted enzymes or other soluble metabolites and intracellular enzymes were not responsible for the loss of OTA under these conditions. In contrast, both viable and heat-killed cells reduced the OTA content significantly (p < 0.05). Viable cells reduced OTA by about 22%, whereas heat-killed cells reduced it by about 45%, roughly twice as much. The difference between the two treatments was statistically significant (p < 0.05). The higher efficiency of heat-treated cells suggests that removal involves adsorption to cell components rather than biotransformation, as heat treatment would inactivate enzymes. Heating probably alters the cell wall structure, which may expose additional binding sites, such as peptidoglycan, teichoic acids and proteins, and increase the permeability and surface area available for toxin binding. Similar increases in toxin binding after thermal or acid treatment have been described for lactic acid bacteria and yeasts binding mycotoxins [3–5]. Because the dead cells were more effective than the living ones, metabolic activity is not required for the effect, and non-viable preparations may therefore be preferable for practical applications since they avoid the introduction of live microorganisms into food products.

Time course and dose dependence of OTA removal by heat-killed cells

When heat-killed cells were incubated with OTA, most of the binding occurred rapidly, within the first few hours, and little further decrease was observed thereafter. This rapid kinetics is typical of physical adsorption, which generally reaches equilibrium faster than enzymatic degradation [4]. Removal increased with cell density, although the gain per unit of biomass became smaller at the highest densities, consistent with saturation of available binding sites. The OTA removed was not recovered in the supernatant after repeated washing of the pellets with buffer in a preliminary test, suggesting that the toxin–cell complex was relatively stable, although a small proportion of the bound toxin was released after the first wash.

OTA reduction in artificially contaminated red wine

On the basis of these results, heat-killed cells of B. subtilis KU-153 were tested in red wine artificially contaminated with OTA. Red wine is a recognized source of OTA exposure and presents a challenging matrix because of its low pH, ethanol content and phenolic compounds [6,7]. In the control samples without bacterial cells the OTA concentration remained essentially unchanged, showing that the toxin was stable in the wine matrix. Treatment with heat-killed cells reduced the OTA content by approximately 90% (p < 0.05 versus control). This reduction was considerably greater than that found in culture medium (45%). The more efficient removal in wine may be explained by the acidic pH of the matrix, since OTA has a carboxyl group and a phenolic hydroxyl group, and at low pH it is largely in the undissociated, less polar form, which favors hydrophobic interactions with the cell surface. In addition, the absence of the competing nutrients and peptides present in the culture medium could have reduced competition for binding sites. Similar pH dependence of OTA adsorption has been reported for yeast cell walls and other biosorbents [5,8].

Overall, these results show that B. subtilis KU-153 reduces OTA in liquid media and that the reduction is mediated principally by the cell body and not by extracellular or intracellular extracts. The superior performance of heat-killed cells, particularly in wine, supports their potential as a biological agent for OTA removal.

The present study demonstrates that Bacillus subtilis KU-153, isolated from Kimchi, reduces ochratoxin A (OTA) in culture medium and in artificially contaminated red wine. Fermented foods are a well-recognized reservoir of microorganisms with detoxifying and antagonistic properties, and Kimchi in particular harbors diverse bacterial communities adapted to stressful, high-salt and acidic environments [1,2]. Our isolation of a strain with OTA-reducing capacity from this source is consistent with reports that Bacillus species from fermented soybean products and other traditional foods can interact with mycotoxins [3,4]. The 16S rRNA gene analysis placed KU-153 within B. subtilis, a species with a long history of use in food fermentation and widely regarded as safe, which supports its potential application in food and beverage systems [5].

The growth kinetic study showed that the decrease in OTA was linked to the presence and growth of the bacterium, indicating a biological basis for the effect. However, the mechanism appears to differ from the enzymatic degradation commonly reported for OTA. Enzymatic detoxification typically involves hydrolysis of the amide bond to yield ochratoxin α and L-phenylalanine, mediated by carboxypeptidases or related hydrolases, and has been described in Bacillus, Acinetobacter, and Pseudomonas species [6,7]. If such secreted or intracellular enzymes were responsible, the extracellular and intracellular extracts of KU-153 would be expected to reduce OTA. Neither fraction did so.
