This suggests that KU-153 does not rely on a readily extractable, active hydrolase under the conditions tested, although we cannot exclude enzyme instability during extraction, a requirement for cofactors, or low expression under the culture conditions used.

The most notable finding is that heat-killed cells removed more OTA (45%) than viable cells (22%). This pattern strongly points to physical adsorption or binding to cell components rather than metabolic degradation. Similar behavior has been described for lactic acid bacteria, yeasts, and Bacillus cells, where the cell wall, rich in peptidoglycan, teichoic acids, polysaccharides, and proteins, binds mycotoxins through hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic forces [8,9]. Heat treatment can alter cell wall architecture, denature surface proteins, and increase the accessibility or number of binding sites, thereby enhancing adsorption [10,11]. In viable cells, metabolic activity may modify the microenvironment, for instance through pH changes or release of competing metabolites, and active cells may also release bound toxin, resulting in lower net removal. The advantage of non-viable cells is also practical: they pose no risk of further microbial growth, do not alter the sensory properties of the product through metabolic activity, and are easier to standardize and store [12].

The approximately 90% reduction of OTA in artificially contaminated red wine is particularly relevant, since wine is an important dietary source of OTA and the toxin is frequently detected in red wines from Mediterranean regions [13,14]. The higher removal in wine than in culture medium may reflect the effect of wine conditions, such as low pH and the presence of ethanol, on the ionization state of OTA. At acidic pH the carboxyl group of OTA is less dissociated, making the molecule more hydrophobic and favoring its adsorption to cell surfaces [15]. The simpler composition of the model medium versus the competing phenolic compounds of wine would be expected to reduce, not increase, binding, so the strong effect observed in wine suggests that the physicochemical environment is highly favorable to adsorption. Nonetheless, binding in complex matrices can be reversible, and the stability of the OTA–cell complex under gastrointestinal conditions, or during further processing, should be confirmed. Treatment of wine with heat-killed cells followed by removal of the biomass by filtration or sedimentation resembles the use of fining agents, which suggests a feasible route for implementation [16].

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, OTA was quantified only as the residual toxin, and we did not analyze degradation products such as ochratoxin α, so the relative contributions of adsorption and degradation cannot be conclusively separated. Desorption experiments and analysis of the cell pellet and supernatant would clarify this. Second, the wine experiments used artificially contaminated samples; naturally contaminated wines may behave differently owing to matrix interactions, and the effects of the treatment on color, polyphenol content, aroma, and other quality attributes were not examined. Third, the optimal conditions for cell dose, contact time, temperature, and pH were not systematically optimized. Finally, the safety of the strain, including the absence of toxin genes and antibiotic resistance determinants, must be evaluated before application, as some B. subtilis isolates can carry undesirable traits [5].

In conclusion, B. subtilis KU-153, newly isolated from Kimchi, significantly reduced OTA in culture medium, and heat-killed cells were more effective (45%) than viable cells (22%), while cell-free intracellular and extracellular extracts had no effect. These results suggest that OTA reduction by this strain is mediated mainly by binding to the cell surface rather than by secreted or intracellular enzymes. Heat-treated cells decreased OTA by approximately 90% in artificially contaminated red wine, highlighting the strain’s potential as a biological agent for mitigating OTA in beverages. Further work should define the binding mechanism and its reversibility, identify any degradation products, evaluate performance in naturally contaminated products and effects on product quality, and assess the safety of the strain, so that its biocontrol potential can be translated into practical applications.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) encompasses a broad spectrum of anomalies, from mild acetabular dysplasia and subluxation to complete, high-riding dislocation of the femoral head. Its reported incidence varies widely with geographic region, ethnic background, and diagnostic criteria, ranging from about 1 per 1,000 live births for dislocation to more than 10 per 1,000 when milder instability and radiographic dysplasia are included [1,2]. When the condition is recognized early, in the neonatal period or the first months of life, conservative treatment with a harness or abduction splint is successful in most cases [3]. In many settings, however, screening is incomplete, and children present late, after walking age, with established dislocation or residual dysplasia. Residual acetabular dysplasia may also persist despite initially successful reduction [4,5].

Untreated or inadequately treated DDH has well-documented consequences. Persistent acetabular insufficiency leads to abnormal load distribution across the joint, labral damage, and early osteoarthritis, and dysplasia is considered one of the most important causes of secondary hip arthrosis in young adults [6,7]. The spontaneous remodeling potential of the acetabulum declines with age, and beyond roughly 18 to 24 months, it is generally considered unreliable [8]. In children older than 2 years, closed reduction becomes increasingly unlikely to succeed, and open reduction, often combined with femoral shortening and a pelvic osteotomy, is usually required to obtain a stable concentric joint [9,10].

Several pelvic osteotomies have been proposed to correct acetabular deficiency in children. They are broadly divided into redirectional procedures, such as the Salter, Steel, Tönnis, and Ganz osteotomies, which rotate the acetabulum as a unit, and reshaping procedures, such as the Pemberton and Dega osteotomies, which hinge the acetabular roof through the iliac cortices and alter its volume and configuration [11–13]. Salter's innominate osteotomy provides anterior and lateral cover but requires a stable, concentric reduction and may increase intra-articular pressure through medialization and lengthening of the limb [14]. The Pemberton osteotomy is a pericapsular procedure that reduces acetabular volume, and it depends on a flexible triradiate cartilage [12]. Each technique has specific indications and limitations, and no single procedure has been shown to be superior across all patterns of dysplasia.

The osteotomy described by Dega in 1953 is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy that runs from the outer cortex of the ilium toward the triradiate cartilage, leaving the inner cortex intact at the hinge [15]. The acetabular roof is then levered downward and held with a bone graft. Depending on the site of the deficiency, the osteotomy can be modified to increase anterior, lateral, or posterior coverage, which makes it attractive for the heterogeneous acetabular deformities seen in DDH, including those associated with neuromuscular disease [16,17]. Since its original description, the procedure has been refined by several authors, and it has gained renewed interest because of its versatility, relatively low morbidity, and the avoidance of internal fixation in many cases [18,19]. Nevertheless, most published reports on the Dega osteotomy are short or medium term, involve small or mixed series, or combine different etiologies, and the English-language literature on its long-term outcome in idiopathic DDH remains limited [20,21].

Long-term data are particularly important in DDH, since the ultimate goal of treatment is not only radiographic normalization in childhood but also preservation of a painless, functional hip into adulthood. Radiographic indices such as the acetabular index, center-edge angle, and Sharp angle may look satisfactory at skeletal maturity, yet degenerative changes may emerge decades later [22]. Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is the most feared complication of treatment, especially after open reduction, and it is a major determinant of poor outcome [23,24]. Other factors suggested to influence prognosis include age at surgery, degree of preoperative dislocation, the need for femoral osteotomy, residual acetabular dysplasia, and the quality of the reduction [9,25]. However, the relative weight of these predictors for the long-term survival of the hip after a Dega osteotomy has not been clearly established.

Assessment of acetabular morphology and femoral head coverage has also evolved. Plain radiographs may be difficult to interpret in the young child because of variable ossification and projection, and computed tomography has been used to define the three-dimensional pattern of acetabular deficiency and to verify reduction [26]. Whether such imaging adds prognostic or operative value in children undergoing Dega osteotomy is uncertain.

The purpose of this multicenter study was therefore to report the long-term clinical and radiographic results of the Dega osteotomy in children younger than 8 years with DDH, treated between 1988 and 2000 and followed for at least 13 years. We combined prospectively and retrospectively collected cases to analyze outcomes, complications, and the need for secondary surgery. We paid particular attention to the factors predictive of hip arthrosis and to the survival of the hip after the procedure, with the aim of clarifying the indications and expected long-term results of the Dega osteotomy in this population.

This multicenter study was conducted at three tertiary pediatric orthopedic centers. It was approved by the institutional review board at each center, and informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all prospectively enrolled patients. For retrospective cases, consent for the use of anonymized data was obtained in accordance with local regulations. The study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

**Patients**

All children younger than 8 years who underwent a Dega osteotomy for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) between January 1988 and October 2000 were considered eligible. Seventeen hips were identified retrospectively from hospital records and radiographic archives. Forty-one hips were enrolled prospectively after a standardized protocol was introduced. Inclusion criteria were: (1) a diagnosis of DDH, including acetabular dysplasia, subluxation, and complete dislocation; (2) age at surgery between 2 and 8 years; (3) a Dega osteotomy performed as part of the index procedure; and (4) a minimum follow-up of 13 years. Exclusion criteria were teratologic or neuromuscular dislocations, syndromic conditions (e.g., arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele), previous surgery on the affected hip, and incomplete clinical or radiographic records. Fifty-eight hips in 48 children (ten bilateral cases) met these criteria. Demographic data, laterality, age at diagnosis, previous treatment (such as Pavlik harness, closed reduction, or traction), and age at surgery were recorded. Dislocations were graded according to the Tönnis classification [1].

**Surgical technique**

All procedures were performed or supervised by experienced pediatric orthopedic surgeons using the technique originally described by Dega [2] and modified by later authors [3]. Under general anesthesia, the hip was approached through an anterior iliofemoral (Smith-Petersen) incision. The iliac apophysis was split and the lateral wall of the ilium subperiosteally exposed down to the capsule. A curved incomplete osteotomy was made through the lateral cortex from just above the anterior inferior iliac spine toward the posterior limb of the triradiate cartilage, preserving the medial cortex and the continuity of the sciatic buttress. The acetabular roof was then levered downward and outward with a curved osteotome to redirect the acetabulum, and the osteotomy was held open with a wedge-shaped bone graft. The graft was taken from the iliac wing or, in some cases, was a bank allograft. Kirschner wires were used for fixation at the surgeon's discretion.

Open reduction was performed through the same incision when the femoral head was dislocated, with capsulotomy, resection of the ligamentum teres and pulvinar, release of the transverse acetabular ligament, and capsulorrhaphy. Adductor tenotomy and psoas release were performed as needed. Femoral shortening, with or without derotation or varization, was added when the reduction was under tension or when excessive anteversion was present [4]. Postoperatively, the children were immobilized in a hip spica cast for 4–6 weeks in cases of open reduction or femoral osteotomy; others were mobilized according to surgeon preference. Weight bearing was progressively restored after radiographic evidence of union.

**Radiographic evaluation**

Standardized anteroposterior pelvic radiographs were obtained with the patient supine and the lower limbs in neutral rotation. Radiographs were taken preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, at 6 weeks or at cast removal, at 6-month intervals (and/or as clinically indicated) for 3 years, and then annually until the last follow-up. The following parameters were measured: acetabular index [5], center–edge angle of Wiberg [6], femoral head coverage, Sharp angle, and Shenton's line continuity. Hip congruency and joint space were assessed. Proximal femoral growth disturbance and avascular necrosis (AVN) were graded according to the Kalamchi and MacEwen classification [7]. Osteoarthritic changes at final follow-up were graded according to the Tönnis grading system [1], and the final radiographic result was classified using the criteria of Severin [8].

A single-cut computed tomographic (CT) scan through the acetabular roof was obtained in all prospectively enrolled patients to assess acetabular version, acetabular anteversion angle, and the position of the femoral head in relation to the acetabulum [9]. CT was used preoperatively and at the first postoperative follow-up to confirm concentric reduction and graft position. To reduce radiation exposure, a single low-dose axial slice at the level of the femoral heads was used.

All radiographic measurements were made independently by two observers not involved in the surgery. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Interobserver reliability was assessed with the intraclass correlation coefficient.

**Clinical evaluation**

Clinical examination was performed at each visit and at the final follow-up. Parameters included pain, gait (presence of limp and Trendelenburg sign), range of motion, limb length discrepancy, and activity level. Functional outcome was graded using the modified McKay criteria [10]. The final clinical outcome was dichotomized as favorable (excellent or good) or unfavorable (fair or poor). Hips were deemed to have failed if they had persistent pain, required a secondary surgical procedure (acetabuloplasty, arthroplasty, or other), or both. Complications, including redislocation, residual subluxation, infection, graft displacement, loss of correction, and AVN, were recorded.

**Outcome measures and predictive factors**

The primary outcome was hip survival, defined as the absence of a secondary operation (acetabuloplasty or arthroplasty) during follow-up, together with a favorable clinical result. Secondary outcomes included radiographic indices at final follow-up and the incidence of complications. Potential predictors of hip arthrosis and failure were analyzed: age at surgery, Tönnis grade, previous treatment, laterality, concomitant femoral osteotomy, preoperative and postoperative acetabular index, the correction achieved, postoperative center–edge angle, presence of AVN, and CT-derived acetabular version.

**Statistical analysis**

Continuous variables are presented as means with standard deviations and ranges, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups used Student's t test or the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate. Associations between potential predictors and hip arthrosis were evaluated with univariate analysis, and significant variables were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model. Hip survival was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with secondary surgery or pain as the endpoint, and groups were compared using the log-rank test [11]. Receiver operating characteristic curves were used to determine cut-off values for radiographic predictors. Because bilateral cases contribute correlated observations, sensitivity analyses were performed with one randomly selected hip per patient. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with SPSS software.

A total of 58 hips in 48 children (38 girls, 10 boys) were included; 41 hips were assessed prospectively and 17 retrospectively. Ten patients underwent bilateral surgery. The mean age at operation was 4.6 years (range 2.0–7.9 years), and the mean follow-up was 17.8 years (range 13–25 years). All patients had reached skeletal maturity at the final evaluation, and none were lost to follow-up. Twenty-three hips were classified as dislocated, 21 as subluxated, and 14 as dysplastic with a centered femoral head. Eighteen hips had undergone previous treatment (closed reduction, bracing, or both) before the index procedure. Concomitant femoral shortening and derotation osteotomy was performed in 27 hips, and open reduction was performed in 24 hips.

**Radiographic outcomes**

The mean acetabular index improved from 35.2° (range 24–52°) preoperatively to 19.4° (range 8–31°) immediately postoperatively, a mean correction of 15.8° (p < 0.001). At the last follow-up the mean acetabular index was 8.1° in skeletally mature hips, based on the sourcil angle, and the mean center-edge angle was 27.3° (range 4–42°). Preoperatively, the mean center-edge angle could be measured in only 31 hips and was 3.5°. The mean acetabular index at 3 years was not significantly different from the value at the last follow-up (p = 0.21), indicating that the correction obtained was maintained with growth. Single-cut computed tomography in the 41 prospectively followed hips showed deficiency of the acetabular roof in the anterior or lateral region in 29 hips, and global deficiency in 12. The osteotomy hinged at the triradiate cartilage without evidence of premature physeal closure in any patient.

According to Severin's classification, 38 hips (65.5%) were class I or II, 10 (17.2%) were class III, and 10 (17.2%) were class IV or higher at the last follow-up. Signs of osteoarthritis (Tönnis grade ≥1) were present in 19 hips (32.8%): grade 1 in 11, grade 2 in 5, and grade 3 in 3 hips. Age at surgery was a significant predictor of final Severin class; children operated on before 4 years of age had a higher proportion of class I–II hips (78%) than those older than 6 years (48%; p = 0.03). Preoperative severity was also related to outcome, as dislocated hips had poorer final results than dysplastic or subluxated hips (p = 0.02).

**Clinical outcomes**

The final clinical outcome, assessed with the modified Harris Hip Score and the presence of pain, was favorable in 44 hips (75.9%) and unfavorable in 14 hips (24.1%). The mean Harris Hip Score at the last follow-up was 91.4 points (range 48–100). Thirty-nine patients reported no pain, and 6 reported occasional mild pain after strenuous activity. Mean limb length discrepancy was 0.8 cm (range 0–2.5 cm), and a positive Trendelenburg sign was present in 7 hips. Range of motion was generally preserved, with a mean flexion of 118° and mean abduction of 38°; a reduction in internal rotation was the most common limitation.

**Reoperations and survival**

Eleven hips (19.0%) required a second surgery during the follow-up period. Five hips underwent repeat acetabuloplasty or a pelvic osteotomy for residual dysplasia, at a mean of 3.2 years after the index operation. Four hips underwent total hip arthroplasty at a mean of 17.5 years (range 12–23 years) after the Dega osteotomy, and two hips had both a further acetabular procedure and later arthroplasty. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed a hip survival rate, with any further surgery as the endpoint, of 92% at 5 years, 85% at 10 years, and 79% at 20 years. When the endpoint was conversion to arthroplasty, survival at 20 years was 93%.

Hips that required reoperation had a significantly higher preoperative acetabular index (mean 40.1° vs 33.9°; p = 0.01) and a larger residual acetabular index at 1 year (p = 0.02) than those that did not. Insufficient correction, defined as a postoperative acetabular index above 25°, was found in 9 hips, and 6 of them (66.7%) subsequently needed another procedure.

**Complications**

Complications were recorded in 15 hips (25.9%). Avascular necrosis of the femoral head occurred in 7 hips (12.1%), graded according to Kalamchi and MacEwen as type I in 1, type II in 3, and type III in 3 hips. All hips affected by avascular necrosis had an unfavorable final outcome, characterized by pain, another surgery, or both. Six of these hips had been dislocated before surgery and had undergone open reduction. Avascular necrosis was more frequent in hips treated previously by closed reduction or bracing (4 of 18) than in untreated hips (3 of 40), although the difference did not reach significance (p = 0.07). Redislocation or persistent subluxation was seen in 3 hips (5.2%), all of which had insufficient acetabular coverage. Transient femoral nerve neurapraxia occurred in 1 hip and resolved within 3 months. Superficial wound infection occurred in 2 hips and resolved with oral antibiotics. Loss of fixation or graft displacement was seen in 2 hips, without clinical consequences. No deep infection or injury to the triradiate cartilage was recorded.

**Prospective versus retrospective cases**

There were no significant differences between prospective and retrospective cohorts in age at surgery, preoperative acetabular index, final center-edge angle, or proportion of favorable outcomes (78.0% vs 70.6%; p = 0.54). Likewise, no significant differences in the outcome were found between hips treated in the different participating centers.

**Predictors of outcome**

In multivariate logistic regression, avascular necrosis (odds ratio 24.6; 95% CI 3.1–194), age at surgery older than 6 years (odds ratio 4.8; 95% CI 1.2–19.1), and a postoperative acetabular index above 25° (odds ratio 5.9; 95% CI 1.4–24.7) were independently associated with an unfavorable outcome. Sex, laterality, and concomitant femoral osteotomy were not significant predictors.

The Dega osteotomy, a partial transiliac osteotomy that hinges on the intact triradiate cartilage, was used in this series to reshape the dysplastic acetabulum in children aged 2–8 years. After a minimum follow-up of 13 years, 75.9% of hips had a favorable clinical outcome, and 11 hips required a second procedure. These results support the Dega osteotomy as a reliable option for this age group, but they also show where it falls short, chiefly in hips that develop avascular necrosis (AVN).

Reported results of acetabular osteotomies in DDH vary widely, mainly because of differences in patient age, in the definition of success, and in the length of follow-up [1,2]. Short and mid-term series of the Dega and Pemberton osteotomies often report satisfactory radiographic results in 80–90% of hips [3,4]. Our figure is somewhat lower, but it comes from a considerably longer observation period, and it relies on a composite clinical definition of success in which pain or reoperation counts as failure. Studies with comparable follow-up into adulthood show that hips that look satisfactory at skeletal maturity may still deteriorate later [5,6]. This supports the use of long-term endpoints, and our rate is probably a more realistic estimate of the lasting benefit of the procedure.

The most important finding was the effect of AVN. Every hip that developed AVN ended in failure, whether through pain, further surgery, or both. This agrees with earlier work identifying AVN as the main determinant of poor long-term outcome in DDH regardless of the method of treatment [7,8]. AVN may follow prior closed or open reduction, prolonged immobilization in extreme positions, or femoral shortening, and the acetabular osteotomy itself is unlikely to be its sole cause. Even so, an osteotomy cannot rescue a femoral head with growth disturbance. Surgeons should therefore make every effort to reduce the risk of AVN by avoiding forced abduction and excessive internal rotation, by using femoral shortening when reduction is under tension, and by taking care with the soft tissues during open reduction [9]. Counseling families that the presence of AVN largely determines the prognosis seems appropriate.

The Dega osteotomy has several theoretical and practical advantages. It redirects the weight-bearing surface of the acetabulum while preserving the posterior column, so the pelvic ring is not destabilized and the volume of the true pelvis is not changed, unlike with the Salter or Pemberton osteotomies [3,10]. The incomplete cut through the inner cortex permits correction of the posterior and lateral deficiencies typical of DDH rather than anterior coverage alone. The use of a single-cut computed tomographic scan in our prospective patients helped define the location of the deficiency and supported the choice of the type of Dega osteotomy, whether lateral or with posterior extension. Such three-dimensional assessment of acetabular morphology is increasingly recommended, because plain radiographs often underestimate posterior deficiency [11]. The relatively simple technique, lack of internal fixation in most cases, and good remodeling potential of the iliac graft are further benefits in young children.

Eleven hips needed secondary surgery, either acetabuloplasty or arthroplasty. Residual acetabular dysplasia is a known issue after osteotomy in children, particularly when surgery is performed after the age of 6 years, when remodeling potential is limited and the triradiate cartilage has less capacity to respond [12]. Older age at surgery, greater preoperative acetabular index, and higher initial dislocation grade have been linked with inferior results [5,13]. Our data are consistent with these observations. In this regard the radiographic parameters we studied, including the acetabular index, center-edge angle, and Severin classification, may be used as predictors of future arthrosis, and hips showing persistent abnormalities at skeletal maturity should be watched closely and treated early with a secondary procedure before degenerative change develops [6].

Some limitations must be acknowledged. The study is multicenter and includes both prospective and retrospective cases, which introduces heterogeneity in surgical technique, concomitant femoral procedures, and postoperative care. There was no control group treated with another osteotomy or nonoperatively, so we cannot make direct comparisons with alternative methods. The sample is modest, and bilateral cases contribute two hips per child, which may overstate statistical independence. Computed tomography was done only in the prospective group and with a single cut, which gives limited information on the three-dimensional morphology. Some patients may have been lost to follow-up, and the minimum of 13 years, although long for pediatric orthopedics, still falls short of the time at which most hips develop symptomatic osteoarthritis. Strengths include the long follow-up, the consecutive series, the standardized radiographic schedule, and the explicit analysis of hip survival.

In conclusion, in this pediatric population the Dega osteotomy proved to be an adequate measure for the management of DDH in children aged 2–8 years, with a favorable clinical outcome in three quarters of hips after 13–25 years. The procedure is technically reproducible, preserves pelvic anatomy, and allows individualized correction of acetabular deficiency. Avascular necrosis was the worst complication, and all affected hips failed, so prevention of AVN remains crucial for long-term success. Residual dysplasia can be managed with a secondary acetabuloplasty, and regular follow-up until skeletal maturity and beyond is advisable. Larger comparative studies with three-dimensional imaging and even longer follow-up are needed to define the ideal indications and to clarify how the Dega osteotomy compares with other acetabular procedures.

Infectious illnesses such as influenza, common cold and diarrhea are among the most frequent causes of illness-related absenteeism among school children. In Denmark, as in many other high-income countries, children spend a large part of their waking hours in school, where they are in close daily contact with many peers in shared classrooms, canteens and toilet facilities. These settings facilitate the transmission of pathogens through direct contact, contaminated surfaces and the fecal-oral route. Infections acquired at school are rarely confined to the child: they spread to families and the wider community, causing parental absence from work, health care use and, in some cases, serious complications. Illness-related absenteeism may also affect children's learning, social participation and well-being, and repeated absence has been associated with poorer academic achievement and school drop-out.

Hand hygiene is widely regarded as one of the most effective and least costly measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases. Systematic reviews have concluded that hand washing with soap reduces the incidence of diarrhea and respiratory infections, and that school-based hand hygiene programs can reduce infection-related absenteeism. However, the evidence base has important limitations. Many studies have been conducted in low-income settings, where sanitation conditions, baseline infection burden and the feasibility of interventions differ substantially from those in Northern Europe. Studies from high-income countries are fewer, often small, and frequently based on a few classes or schools. Most have not been randomized, and those that were have often had short follow-up, limited statistical power, or lacked adjustment for clustering. Outcome measurement has also been a challenge, as many studies rely on school registers of absenteeism, which seldom distinguish illness from other causes, or on retrospective questionnaires, which are vulnerable to recall bias.

Hand hygiene behavior in schools is shaped by more than knowledge. School toilets are frequently reported by children as unpleasant, dirty, lacking soap or paper, or offering little privacy, and many children avoid using them during the school day. Poor toilet conditions may lead to withholding of urine and stool, with possible consequences for children's comfort, concentration and health, and may reduce hand washing after toilet use. Moreover, hand washing before meals is typically not organized in Danish schools, and children seldom have routines for washing hands at times when it matters. Interventions that combine education with changes in the physical and organizational environment may therefore be more effective than education alone, because they address both motivation and opportunity. Despite this, to our knowledge no previous trials have included education about healthy and appropriate toilet behavior as part of the curriculum, and none have tested the effect of supplementary cleaning of school toilets during the school day.

Another gap concerns the scale and methods of data collection. Large trials of infectious illness require frequent, valid and low-burden measurement of symptoms and absence. Traditional diaries and repeated questionnaires are costly and often suffer from low response and incomplete data. Short message service (SMS, text message) is widely used in Denmark and offers a possible way to collect repeated information directly from parents at short intervals, reducing recall problems. Yet the feasibility, response patterns and validity of SMS data collection in large school populations have rarely been examined.

Against this background, the Hi Five study was designed to develop, implement and evaluate a multi-component school-based intervention aimed at improving hand hygiene and well-being and reducing infectious illness among Danish school children aged 6–15 years. The name reflects the five elements that guided the work: hygiene, infection, health, hand washing and well-being. The intervention consisted of three components: a curriculum component on hand hygiene, infection and toilet behavior; mandatory daily hand washing before lunch; and extra cleaning of school toilets during the school day. The intervention was developed in collaboration with teachers, school leaders, cleaning staff and children, and was informed by existing evidence and by principles for health promotion in school settings. The study was conducted as a cluster-randomized controlled trial in a national random sample of schools, with two intervention arms and a control arm, to allow assessment of the effect of the intervention package and of its components in a real-life school context. The primary aim was to reduce the prevalence of infections among children in intervention schools by 20% compared with control schools. Secondary aims were to assess effects on illness-related absenteeism, hand hygiene behavior, toilet behavior and well-being, and to evaluate the implementation process, including fidelity, dose and acceptability to pupils and staff.

The purpose of this paper is to describe the development of the Hi Five intervention and the design of its effect and process evaluations. Publishing the design in detail promotes transparency, allows readers to distinguish between pre-specified and post hoc analyses, and offers guidance for researchers planning similar trials. The paper also describes the use of SMS text messages to collect data on infectious illness and absenteeism in a large study population, thereby providing a basis for future evaluation of this method.

The Hi Five study was designed as a three-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial with schools as the unit of randomization. The study was conducted in Danish public schools and included pupils from preschool class to ninth grade (6–15 years). The intervention was developed in 2011–2012 and implemented from August 2012 to June 2013.

**Setting and recruitment**

A national random sample of schools was drawn from the Danish Ministry of Education register of public schools. Schools were eligible if they had at least two classes per grade level in the relevant grades, and special-needs schools were excluded. Selected schools were invited by letter and telephone to participate. Headmasters gave consent on behalf of the school, and parents or guardians received written information and could decline participation for their child. Forty-four schools agreed to participate. A total of 8,438 pupils were enrolled.

**Randomization**

After baseline data collection, schools were randomized by an independent statistician using computer-generated random numbers. Randomization was stratified by school size and geographical region. Schools were allocated to one of two intervention groups (n = 29 in total) or to a control group (n = 15). Because of the nature of the intervention, schools and teachers could not be blinded. Data analysts were blinded to allocation where possible.

**Intervention**

The intervention was developed through literature review, consultation with experts in hygiene, microbiology, health promotion and pedagogy, and pilot testing with teachers and pupils. It consisted of three components:

1. *Curriculum component.* Teaching materials covered hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, and healthy and appropriate toilet behavior. Materials were tailored to three age groups (preschool to 3rd grade, 4th–6th grade, and 7th–9th grade) and comprised lesson plans, practical exercises, experiments and discussions. Teachers received written instructions and an introductory seminar. The materials were intended to be taught during three to four lessons per semester and integrated into subjects such as science and health education.

2. *Mandatory hand washing.* Pupils washed their hands with soap and water under teacher supervision before lunch each school day. Schools were supplied with soap and paper towels as needed. Teachers were instructed in the hand-washing procedure and in how to organize the routine in their class.

3. *Extra toilet cleaning.* Schools were provided with additional cleaning of pupil toilets during the school day, in addition to the standard daily cleaning. Cleaning was performed by school cleaning staff or contracted cleaners according to a written procedure.

The two intervention arms differed in the components they received (curriculum plus hand washing, and curriculum plus hand washing plus extra toilet cleaning). Control schools continued usual practice and received no intervention materials during the study period, but were offered the materials after the trial ended.

**Data collection**

Baseline data were collected from December 2011 to April 2012, and follow-up data from December 2012 to April 2013.

*Questionnaires.* Pupils completed web-based questionnaires at baseline and follow-up, with younger children assisted by teachers or parents. Questionnaires covered hand-washing behavior, toilet habits, school toilet satisfaction, and well-being, using validated instruments where available. Parents of the youngest pupils answered proxy questionnaires. Teachers and school leaders provided information on school characteristics, hygiene facilities and routines.

*Infectious illness and absenteeism.* Data were collected through short message service (SMS, text message). Parents received a text message every other week during the data collection periods asking about their child’s illness and absence in the preceding period. Questions included whether the child had had diarrhea, vomiting, influenza-like illness or other infection, and the number of days absent due to illness. Non-responders received one reminder. Parents could also respond through a web-based form. Response rates were monitored to evaluate the usability of SMS for large-scale data collection.

*Hygiene facilities.* Trained staff recorded the condition of school toilets and hand-washing facilities (e.g., availability of soap, paper towels, toilet paper, and cleanliness) using a standardized checklist.

*Process evaluation.* Process data assessed reach, dose delivered, fidelity, and acceptability. Teachers completed logbooks and questionnaires on how many lessons were taught, how often hand washing was carried out, and barriers and facilitators. Selected schools were visited for observations and interviews with teachers, pupils, school leaders and cleaning staff. Soap and paper towel consumption was recorded.

**Outcomes**

The primary outcome was the proportion of pupils with infectious illness (diarrhea, vomiting or influenza-like illness) reported by SMS during follow-up. Secondary outcomes were illness-related absenteeism, self-reported hand-washing behavior, toilet behavior and satisfaction with school toilets, and well-being, including school satisfaction.

**Sample size**

The study aimed to detect a 20% relative reduction in the prevalence of infections in intervention schools compared with control schools. Sample size calculations accounted for clustering at school level, with an assumed intracluster correlation coefficient based on previous school studies, a significance level of 5% and a power of 80%. The number of schools and pupils enrolled was sufficient under these assumptions.

**Statistical analysis**

Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle, comparing each intervention arm and the combined intervention group with the control group. Multilevel regression models (logistic, Poisson or negative binomial, and linear, depending on the outcome) with random effects for school and class will be used to account for clustering, adjusting for baseline values, age, sex, and the stratification variables. Repeated SMS responses will be analyzed with generalized estimating equations or mixed models. Subgroup analyses will explore effects by age group, sex and baseline hygiene. Missing data will be handled using multiple imputation, with sensitivity analyses. Process data will be analyzed descriptively and used in dose–response analyses.

**Ethics**

According to Danish legislation, questionnaire-based studies do not require ethical committee approval. The study was approved by the Danish Data Protection Agency and registered in the ISRCTN registry (ISRCTN19287682).

This is a design paper, so the results presented here describe the outcomes of the development, recruitment, randomization and baseline data collection phases. Effect estimates are not reported.

**Recruitment and randomization**

A national random sample of Danish schools was drawn from the register of public schools. Schools were invited by letter and telephone, and 44 schools agreed to participate. After stratification by school size and geographic region, schools were randomized by an independent statistician. Twenty-nine schools were allocated to one of two intervention groups and 15 to the control group. Intervention group 1 (n = 14 schools) received the curriculum component and the mandatory hand washing component. Intervention group 2 (n = 15 schools) received these two components plus extra cleaning of the school toilets during the school day. No schools withdrew between randomization and the start of the intervention.

**Study population**

In total, 8,438 children in grades 0 to 9 (ages 6 to 15 years) were enrolled across the 44 schools. This corresponded to 4,000 to 4,500 children in the two intervention groups combined and about 2,000 in the control group. Class sizes were comparable across the three arms, as were the proportions of girls and boys. The median school size was approximately 500 pupils (range 120 to 900). The distribution of schools across regions reflected the national distribution of the school population, and both urban and rural schools were represented.

**Baseline data collection**

Baseline data were collected from December 2011 to April 2012. Pupils in grades 0 to 3 completed a short questionnaire with the help of teachers or parents, while pupils in grades 4 to 9 completed a web-based questionnaire in school. The questionnaire covered hand washing habits, toileting behavior, perceived school toilet standards, well-being, and general health. Parents of the youngest children provided background information, including household characteristics. The response rate at baseline was high, and most enrolled pupils contributed data. Missing data were mainly related to absence on the day of data collection.

Baseline observations of school facilities were completed in all schools. These included the number of toilets, the availability of soap and paper towels, and the condition and cleanliness of the toilets. Considerable variation was seen between schools, and many schools had toilets in poor condition or with limited supplies of soap. Hand washing facilities in classrooms were rare, so washing before lunch required pupils to use the toilet areas or designated sinks.

**Intervention development**

The intervention was developed through a process combining literature review, input from teachers, school leaders, cleaning staff and pupils, and pilot testing in schools not included in the trial. Several adjustments were made as a result of this process. The curriculum was designed as three teaching sessions per school year level, adapted to age groups (grades 0 to 3, 4 to 6, and 7 to 9). The material covered the spread of infection, hand washing technique, and healthy and appropriate toilet behavior. Teachers were provided with a manual and ready-to-use material, and they received a short introductory course.

The hand washing component required all pupils to wash their hands before lunch every school day. Schools were supplied with soap and paper towels, and teachers organized the routine in class. The extra cleaning component involved a cleaning of all pupil toilets at midday in addition to the normal cleaning routine, carried out by cleaning staff employed by the school or municipality. Cleaning staff received instruction on the content and timing of the extra cleaning, and a checklist was used to document each cleaning.

**Implementation**

The intervention ran from August 2012 to June 2013 in all 29 intervention schools. Schools received a start-up package and visits from project staff early in the school year. Process evaluation tools were developed to capture dose delivered and received, including teacher logs, cleaning checklists, pupil questionnaires, and interviews with a sample of teachers, school leaders and cleaning staff. Procedures for monitoring fidelity were in place in all intervention schools.

**Outcome data collection**

Infectious illness and absenteeism were collected by SMS text messages sent to parents. Parents received messages at regular intervals asking whether their child had been absent from school or had experienced symptoms of illness, such as diarrhea, vomiting, fever, cough or sore throat, in the preceding period. Parents replied with a short numeric code. Most parents had a mobile phone number registered, and the system was tested for reliability before launch. The SMS system generated a large dataset of repeated measurements for each child during the intervention period. Participation in the SMS data collection was high at the beginning and was maintained through reminders, though a proportion of parents did not reply to all messages.

Follow-up questionnaire data were collected from December 2012 to April 2013, using the same instruments as at baseline. Registry data on school-level absenteeism were also obtained to supplement the SMS data.

**Analysis plan**

The primary outcome is the number of infectious illness episodes per child during the intervention period, and secondary outcomes are illness-related absenteeism, hand hygiene behavior, and well-being. Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle and account for clustering at school and class level using multilevel models. The study was designed to detect a 20% reduction in infection prevalence in intervention schools compared with control schools, and the achieved sample size was sufficient for this given the assumed intra-cluster correlation.

**Trial registration**

The trial was registered in the ISRCTN registry (ISRCTN19287682) on 21 December 2012, after baseline data collection and the start of the intervention period.

The Hi Five study is, to our knowledge, one of the largest randomized trials of a school-based hand hygiene intervention to date. It fills a gap in international research in several respects. Previous studies have often been small, have used non-randomized designs, or have been conducted in settings with different hygiene conditions from those in Denmark. Hi Five is a three-armed cluster-randomized trial with a national random sample of schools and more than 8,000 children aged 6–15 years. It is also, as far as we know, the first multi-component hand hygiene intervention to include education on healthy and appropriate toilet behavior in the curriculum, and the first to evaluate supplementary cleaning of school toilets during the school day. Because the intervention targets hand washing, toilet behavior and toilet cleanliness together, the study addresses both individual behavior and the physical environment, which is in line with current recommendations for settings-based health promotion.

Several design choices strengthen the study. Randomization at school level limits contamination between children, who would otherwise share classrooms, toilets and break areas. Stratification and the use of a national sample improve generalizability to Danish public schools. The inclusion of two intervention arms makes it possible to explore whether the addition of extra toilet cleaning gives added benefit over the curriculum and hand washing components alone. The wide age range allows us to examine whether effects differ between younger and older children, who differ in hygiene habits, toilet behavior and capacity to engage with educational material. Finally, the combination of an effect evaluation with a process evaluation will allow us to interpret the findings in light of how the intervention was actually delivered, received and perceived by pupils, teachers and cleaning staff. Without such information, a null result could not be distinguished from poor implementation, and a positive result could not be linked to specific components.

A further contribution is the use of short message service (SMS, text message) to collect data on infectious illness and absenteeism. Collecting such data in large populations is difficult. Registry data on absenteeism are generally unavailable in Danish schools, and retrospective questionnaires are prone to recall bias. Repeated text messages to parents are a low-burden and timely alternative, and we expect them to yield more accurate information on symptoms and illness-related absence. The study will therefore provide new knowledge about the feasibility, response rates and validity of SMS data collection, which may be useful in future large-scale school-based studies.

The study also has limitations that should be considered. Blinding of participants and school staff is not possible in a behavioral intervention of this kind, and the control schools were aware of their participation. Outcomes such as parent-reported illness and absenteeism may therefore be influenced by expectations, and the reporting of symptoms may differ between intervention and control groups. We have tried to limit this by using standardized questions, by collecting the same data in all arms, and by including more objective measures where possible. Self-reported hygiene behavior and well-being are likewise susceptible to social desirability bias, particularly among children who have received hygiene education. Another limitation is the relatively short intervention and follow-up period of one school year, with follow-up data collected from December to April. This is the main season for influenza and gastrointestinal infections, which is an advantage for detecting effects, but it means that we cannot assess long-term sustainability of behavior change. Seasonal variation and local outbreaks may also affect infection rates unevenly across schools, although randomization should balance these influences across arms on average. The sample size was calculated to detect a 20% reduction in infections, and the study may be underpowered to detect smaller yet still relevant effects, or effects in subgroups. Finally, as with all cluster-randomized trials, loss to follow-up and variable response to the text messages may reduce the precision of the estimates, and we will address missing data in the analyses.

The intervention was designed to be feasible within the ordinary framework of Danish schools. Mandatory daily hand washing before lunch and the curriculum activities require limited resources, and extra toilet cleaning is a concrete measure that schools can implement through existing cleaning services. If the intervention proves effective, it could be scaled up with relatively modest costs. If effects are limited, the process evaluation may help identify barriers, such as insufficient time, poor hand washing facilities, or low motivation among pupils, which could inform improvements to the program or to school facilities. Since poor toilet standards are a well-known concern among Danish school children and may lead them to avoid using school toilets, the intervention may also have benefits beyond infection control, for example on well-being and comfort at school. The well-being outcomes in Hi Five are included to capture such effects.

In conclusion, the Hi Five study is a large, randomized, multi-component school-based trial designed to evaluate whether improved hand hygiene, healthy toilet behavior education and extra toilet cleaning can reduce infectious illness and improve hygiene and well-being among Danish school children. The study is strengthened by its randomized design, national sample, and combined effect and process evaluation, and it will also provide new insight into the use of text messages for data collection. The results will show whether a feasible and scalable intervention can reduce infections and illness-related absenteeism in schools, and they may inform future school health policy and research in Denmark and elsewhere.

The proliferation of multi-homed devices, such as smartphones equipped with both WiFi and cellular interfaces and servers connected to several networks, has created an opportunity to use multiple network paths simultaneously. Traditional TCP binds a connection to a single pair of IP addresses and therefore a single path, leaving additional connectivity idle and offering no resilience when the active path degrades. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) [1], standardized by the IETF in RFC 6824 and later revised in RFC 8684, addresses this limitation. It extends TCP so that a single transport connection can be split into several subflows, each traversing a different path, while remaining transparent to applications. By aggregating the capacity of the available paths, MPTCP can improve throughput, increase robustness against link failures, and support seamless handover between access networks [2], [3].

Despite these benefits, MPTCP must still provide the same service guarantee as TCP: a reliable, in-order byte stream delivered to the application. Data are assigned a connection-level sequence number at the sender, transmitted over different subflows, and reordered at the receiver in a connection-level buffer before delivery. When paths differ in delay and bandwidth, as is typical for heterogeneous combinations such as WiFi and LTE, packets sent later on a fast path may arrive before packets sent earlier on a slow path. The receiver must then hold the early arrivals until the missing data come in. This out-of-order (OFO) arrival problem inflates the receive buffer occupancy, increases application-level delay and jitter, and can cause head-of-line blocking [4]. When the receive window is exhausted by buffered out-of-order data, the sender is stalled and the aggregate throughput may fall below that of the best single path [5], [6]. The problem is therefore not only a latency concern but also a fundamental obstacle to realizing the potential gains of multipath transport.

The packet scheduler, which decides on which subflow each packet is transmitted, plays a central role in mitigating this problem. The default scheduler in the Linux MPTCP implementation, minRTT, selects the available subflow with the smallest smoothed round-trip time that has space in its congestion window [7]. Although simple, it ignores the bandwidth and delay differences that determine when a packet will actually arrive, and it performs poorly under path heterogeneity. Round-robin scheduling is even less informed, since it distributes packets evenly regardless of path quality. Numerous alternatives have been proposed. Some, such as DAPS [8], plan the allocation of packets to paths in advance, using delay and window information so that packets arrive in order. Others, such as BLEST [9], estimate whether using a slow subflow will block the connection-level send window and skip that subflow when blocking is likely. ECF [10] considers the completion time of the remaining data on fast and slow paths and may wait for the fast path rather than use a slow one. Other approaches reinject or retransmit packets on faster paths [11], or use learning-based techniques to adapt scheduling decisions [12]. While these schemes yield improvements in particular scenarios, many rely on round-trip time as a proxy for path delay.

The use of RTT is problematic for in-order delivery. What determines the order of arrival at the receiver is the one-way, forward delay of each path, not the round-trip delay. RTT includes the reverse path delay, which may differ substantially from the forward delay owing to asymmetric routing, asymmetric link capacities, and different queueing on acknowledgments' return path. In cellular and WiFi networks, uplink and downlink characteristics are often markedly different, and ACK compression or delay can further distort RTT samples. A scheduler guided by RTT may thus mispredict arrival times and dispatch packets in an order that causes reordering. Moreover, delay alone is insufficient: the time a packet spends in the network also depends on the transmission time governed by path throughput and on queueing behind packets already sent on the same path. An effective scheduler must account jointly for forward delay and throughput differences.

Motivated by these observations, we propose the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP. FDPS estimates the forward delay of each subflow and combines it with an estimate of subflow throughput to predict the arrival time of a packet if it were sent on each path. The sender then dispatches packets so that those with earlier sequence numbers are expected to arrive earlier, and so that the arrival sequence at the receiver closely follows the transmission sequence. By making scheduling decisions on the basis of the forward path characteristics, FDPS reduces the dependence on potentially misleading round-trip measurements and limits the buffering needed for reordering.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we analyze why RTT-based and delay-agnostic scheduling lead to out-of-order arrivals in heterogeneous multipath environments. Second, we design FDPS, which uses estimated forward delay and throughput differences among paths to schedule packets. Third, we evaluate FDPS through simulations under a variety of network conditions, varying bandwidth, delay, and asymmetry, and compare it with several existing schedulers. The results show that FDPS substantially improves in-order arrival at the receiver, reducing the reordering burden relative to the baselines.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on MPTCP scheduling. Section III describes the design of FDPS. Section IV presents the simulation setup and results. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future work.

FDPS operates at the sender of an MPTCP connection. It estimates the forward delay and throughput of each subflow and uses these estimates to decide which subflow carries each packet, so that packets reach the receiver in the order of their data sequence numbers. The subsections below cover the system model, forward delay estimation, the scheduling rule, and the simulation setup.

**System Model**

We consider an MPTCP connection with N subflows, indexed i = 1,…,N, between a sender and a receiver, following the architecture in RFC 6824 [1]. Each subflow i has its own congestion window cwnd_i, smoothed round-trip time srtt_i, and subflow-level sequence space. A connection-level data sequence number (DSN) orders the byte stream across subflows. The scheduler assigns each DSN-mapped segment to a subflow that has available congestion window space. The receiver reorders segments in a shared receive buffer before delivering them to the application. A segment arriving with a DSN greater than the next expected one is out of order and must wait in the buffer. This causes head-of-line blocking and, when the buffer is limited, throttles throughput [2], [3].

For subflow i, the one-way forward delay D_i is the time from transmission at the sender to arrival at the receiver. It consists of propagation delay p_i, transmission delay s/B_i for a segment of size s on a path of bandwidth B_i, and queueing delay q_i:

D_i = p_i + s/B_i + q_i.

Using srtt_i/2 as a proxy for D_i is common [4], but it fails on asymmetric paths and when reverse-path congestion inflates ACK delays. FDPS therefore estimates the forward component directly.

**Forward Delay Estimation**

The receiver stamps each arriving segment with its local clock and returns the stamp in a TCP option carried on the ACK, in the manner of the TCP timestamp option [5]. The sender records the send time T_s of each segment. Clocks are not assumed to be synchronized. Instead, the sender computes a relative forward delay,

d_i(k) = T_r(k) − T_s(k),

which equals D_i(k) plus an unknown constant clock offset δ. For subflow i, the sender keeps the minimum observed value d_i^min, which approximates p_i + s/B_i + δ when queues are empty. The offset δ is the same for all subflows because it is a property of the host pair. Differences between subflows are therefore unaffected by δ. The queueing-inclusive delay of the k-th sample is then

D̂_i(k) = d_i(k) − d_min,

where d_min = min_j d_j^min. The result is a delay estimate of each path relative to the fastest one. The estimate is smoothed with an exponentially weighted moving average,

D̄_i ← (1 − α) D̄_i + α D̂_i(k),

with α = 1/8, following the srtt convention [6]. Samples from retransmitted segments are discarded to avoid ambiguity.

Throughput is estimated per subflow as the ratio cwnd_i/srtt_i, which gives the sending rate R_i the congestion controller currently permits. This is smoothed over a window of the most recent ACKs to dampen short-term oscillation.

**Scheduling Rule**

Suppose the scheduler is about to send a segment of size s on subflow i at time t. Its expected arrival time is

A_i = t + D̄_i + Q_i/R_i,

where Q_i is the amount of data already queued or in flight on subflow i beyond what has been acknowledged, and Q_i/R_i is the expected additional wait. The scheduler seeks to give consecutive DSNs arrival times that are monotonically non-decreasing.

FDPS maintains A_last, the largest expected arrival time among segments already scheduled. For the next segment, it builds the candidate set

C = { i : cwnd_i − inflight_i ≥ s }.

It then selects the subflow whose expected arrival time is closest to, but not earlier than, A_last:

i* = argmin_{i∈C, A_i ≥ A_last} (A_i − A_last).

This choice keeps the segment from overtaking earlier ones. If no subflow satisfies the constraint, because all candidates would deliver earlier than A_last, the scheduler selects the subflow with the largest A_i, which minimizes the reordering. If C is empty, transmission waits until an ACK opens a window. After the assignment, A_last is updated to A_{i*} and Q_{i*} is increased by s.

Because a fast subflow may often be blocked by its window while a slow subflow is idle, FDPS also uses the throughput estimates. A slow subflow is assigned a segment only if its expected arrival is no later than that of a faster subflow after it becomes available. This means that, when delay differences are large, the slow path is used only for segments whose DSNs are far enough ahead of those on the fast path. In practice, the slow subflow receives earlier DSNs than the fast subflow in proportion to the delay gap D̄_slow − D̄_fast multiplied by R_fast. This is the same principle used by delay-aware schedulers such as DAPS [7], but here it is driven by measured forward delays instead of RTT ratios.

Retransmissions are sent on the subflow with the smallest A_i, and opportunistic retransmission and penalization [3] are retained when the receive window blocks progress.

**Simulation Setup**

We implemented FDPS in the ns-3 simulator using the MPTCP module [8]. The topology contains one sender and one receiver connected by two to four disjoint paths. Each path has its own bottleneck link. Bandwidth is varied from 1 to 50 Mbps and one-way propagation delay from 10 to 200 ms, to create both homogeneous and heterogeneous conditions. Bottleneck queue sizes equal the bandwidth-delay product, and random loss rates range from 0 to 2%. Background TCP cross traffic is added in selected scenarios to create dynamic queueing delay. Each subflow uses the coupled congestion control algorithm LIA [9]. The application is a bulk transfer lasting 100 s, and the receive buffer is set to 64 KB–2 MB.

We compare FDPS with the default minimum-RTT scheduler [10], round-robin, and DAPS [7]. The performance metrics are:

1. the number of out-of-order packets at the receiver, measured as the fraction of segments arriving with DSN greater than expected;
2. the reordering delay, i.e. the time a segment waits in the receive buffer before delivery;
3. the maximum receive buffer occupancy;
4. the aggregate goodput.

Each scenario is repeated 20 times with different random seeds, and we report means with 95% confidence intervals.

We evaluated FDPS through simulations in the ns-2 network simulator with the MPTCP module. The topology consisted of one multihomed sender and one multihomed receiver connected by two disjoint paths, with a shared 1 Mbps bottleneck for each path where background traffic was introduced. We compared FDPS with three schedulers: the default round-robin (RR) scheduler, the lowest-RTT-first (minRTT) scheduler used in the Linux MPTCP implementation [1], and a delay-aware scheduler based on round-trip estimates (DAPS) [2]. Coupled congestion control [3] was used for all schedulers. Each scenario was run 20 times with different random seeds, and we report means with 95% confidence intervals. The metrics were (i) the number of out-of-order (OFO) packets observed at the receiver, (ii) the receive-buffer occupancy, (iii) the out-of-order delay, defined as the time a packet waits in the reordering queue, and (iv) the aggregate goodput.

**Effect of path delay heterogeneity.** We first fixed the bandwidth of both paths at 10 Mbps and increased the one-way delay of path 2 from 20 ms to 200 ms while keeping path 1 at 20 ms. When the delays were equal, all schedulers produced few out-of-order packets. As the delay difference grew, the OFO count of RR increased almost linearly, since RR ignores path characteristics. MinRTT performed better than RR but still degraded markedly beyond a 80 ms difference, because RTT includes reverse-path queueing and therefore misestimates the forward delay. DAPS reduced reordering relative to minRTT but was sensitive to RTT fluctuation. FDPS yielded the lowest OFO count in every case; at a 200 ms difference it reduced the number of OFO packets by approximately 62% relative to RR, 41% relative to minRTT, and 27% relative to DAPS. The mean out-of-order delay followed the same trend, with FDPS remaining within a small multiple of the forward delay difference, whereas the other schedulers exhibited substantially longer tails.

**Effect of bandwidth heterogeneity.** Next, we fixed the delays at 50 ms and varied the bandwidth ratio between the two paths from 1:1 to 1:10. RR performed poorly at high ratios because it assigned equal numbers of packets to a slow path and a fast path, causing packets on the slow path to arrive long after later packets sent on the fast path. MinRTT tended to fill the fast path first and used the slow path only when the fast window was full, which produced bursts of late packets. FDPS assigned packets in proportion to estimated throughput and compensated for the forward delay differences, so that the arrival sequence was close to the sending sequence. At a 1:10 ratio, FDPS decreased the receive-buffer occupancy by about 35% compared with minRTT and 50% compared with RR. Goodput of FDPS was comparable to or slightly higher than that of the others (within 3%), indicating that the improved ordering did not come at the expense of bandwidth utilization.

**Effect of asymmetric reverse paths.** Because FDPS relies on forward delay rather than RTT, we examined scenarios in which the reverse path was congested by additional traffic, raising ACK delay on one path without changing its forward delay. In this setting, RTT-based schedulers (minRTT and DAPS) wrongly identified the congested-ACK path as slow and shifted traffic away from it, resulting in underutilization and increased reordering. FDPS was largely unaffected: its OFO count increased by less than 8% as the reverse load rose from 0 to 80% of capacity, whereas minRTT and DAPS rose by 45% and 31%, respectively. This confirms the benefit of estimating one-way delay for scheduling decisions.

**Effect of loss and dynamic conditions.** We then introduced random packet loss on one path, varying the loss rate from 0% to 3%. All schedulers experienced more reordering owing to retransmissions and window reductions. Nevertheless, FDPS retained the lowest OFO count, and its advantage over minRTT widened from 25% at 0.5% loss to 38% at 3% loss. In a dynamic scenario in which the bandwidth of one path alternated between 10 Mbps and 2 Mbps every 20 s, FDPS adapted within about two to three RTTs, as its delay and throughput estimates were updated from acknowledgments. The receive-buffer occupancy of FDPS showed smaller oscillations than the others, and its peak occupancy was about 30% lower than that of DAPS.

**Impact of receive-buffer size.** Finally, we limited the receive buffer from 64 KB to 1 MB under moderately heterogeneous paths (10 Mbps/40 ms and 5 Mbps/120 ms). With small buffers, reordering caused head-of-line blocking that throttled the sender through window advertisement. Goodput of RR and minRTT dropped by roughly 40% and 28% at 64 KB relative to the 1 MB case, while FDPS dropped by only 12%. Thus, FDPS is particularly beneficial for memory-constrained devices such as mobile terminals, which are a main target of MPTCP [4].

**Overhead and sensitivity.** The computational overhead of FDPS was negligible in simulation, requiring only per-path updates of delay and throughput estimates at each acknowledgment. We also varied the smoothing factor of the delay estimator between 0.1 and 0.9; OFO counts changed by less than 6% across this range, suggesting the algorithm is robust to parameter selection.

Overall, the results consistently show that FDPS maintains in-order arrival more effectively than RR, minRTT, and DAPS across delay, bandwidth, loss, and reverse-path variations, while preserving aggregate throughput.

The results of this study show that scheduling decisions based on estimated forward delay and path throughput can substantially reduce out-of-order (OFO) arrivals at the MPTCP receiver. Compared with the default minimum-RTT scheduler and other earlier approaches, FDPS maintained a higher proportion of in-order packets, and it kept the receive-buffer occupancy and resequencing delay lower across the heterogeneous scenarios we simulated. This section interprets these findings, discusses their implications and limitations, and outlines directions for future work.

**Interpretation of results**

The improvement obtained by FDPS follows from the way it models the problem. Round-trip-time-based schedulers, such as the default lowest-RTT-first policy in the Linux MPTCP implementation [1], implicitly assume that the RTT represents the time a data packet needs to reach the receiver. In practice, the RTT combines forward and reverse delays, and the reverse path carrying acknowledgments may be congested or asymmetric in ways unrelated to the data direction [2]. When the forward and reverse delays diverge, an RTT-based scheduler misjudges the arrival time of packets on each path and assigns packets to paths in an order that causes reordering. By estimating the forward delay directly, FDPS gets closer to the quantity that actually determines arrival order at the receiver. Combining this estimate with the throughput difference between paths allows the sender to decide how many packets to place on each path so that packets sent later on a fast path do not overtake earlier packets on a slow path, and vice versa.

The gains were most pronounced when the paths differed strongly in delay and bandwidth, which is the condition under which reordering is the most harmful. This agrees with earlier observations that path heterogeneity, such as combining WiFi and cellular links, is the main cause of receive-buffer blocking and throughput degradation in MPTCP [3], [4]. When the paths were similar, all schedulers performed comparably, and FDPS offered little additional benefit but also no penalty. This indicates that the algorithm degrades gracefully and does not introduce overhead in favorable conditions.

Reducing OFO packets has practical consequences beyond the metric itself. Smaller reordering queues lower the buffer requirements at the receiver, which matters for memory-constrained mobile devices. They also reduce the delay jitter perceived by the application, which benefits delay-sensitive services such as video streaming and interactive applications. Furthermore, fewer reordering events reduce the chance that the sender's congestion window and the connection-level send window are stalled by a slow subflow, so the aggregate throughput approaches the sum of the path capacities more closely [5].

**Comparison with related work**

Several earlier schedulers attempt to mitigate reordering. Some use opportunistic retransmission and penalization to unblock the connection-level window [3], while others schedule according to estimated arrival times or block a slow path when it would delay delivery [6], [7]. These techniques mostly react to reordering after it begins to occur or rely on RTT-derived estimates. FDPS, in contrast, tries to prevent reordering proactively at the time of dispatch. The approach is therefore complementary to reactive mechanisms, and combining them may produce additional gains.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the accuracy of FDPS depends on the quality of the forward-delay estimates. Measuring one-way delay without synchronized clocks requires approximations, for example using timestamp differences and tracking their relative variation. Such estimates may be noisy under rapidly changing wireless conditions, and estimation errors may cause incorrect dispatch decisions. Second, our evaluation was performed in simulation. Although we varied bandwidth, delay, and loss rate, simulations cannot capture all the effects of real networks, such as middlebox interference, cross-traffic dynamics, and operating-system behavior. Third, we considered a limited number of subflows, mostly two, and long-lived bulk transfers. The behavior with many subflows, short flows, or highly bursty application traffic remains to be examined. Fourth, the interaction between FDPS and different coupled congestion control algorithms [8] was only partly explored, and congestion window fluctuations may affect the throughput estimates on which the scheduler relies.

**Future work**

Several directions follow from these limitations. Implementing FDPS in a real MPTCP kernel and testing it on actual WiFi and LTE or 5G testbeds would validate the simulation results and expose practical issues in delay estimation. More robust estimators, possibly based on filtering or lightweight learning, could improve performance when path characteristics change quickly. It would also be valuable to extend the algorithm to account for application requirements, such as deadlines or energy consumption, and to evaluate it with modern congestion control schemes and with multiple concurrent flows competing at shared bottlenecks.

**Conclusion**

This paper presented FDPS, a forward-delay-based packet scheduling algorithm for MPTCP that addresses the out-of-order delivery problem arising from heterogeneous paths. By dispatching packets according to the estimated forward delay and throughput differences among the available paths, the scheduler arranges for packets to arrive at the receiver in a sequence close to their transmission order. Simulation results under a variety of network conditions showed that FDPS significantly increases in-order arrivals relative to several existing schedulers, particularly when path heterogeneity is large, while remaining competitive when paths are similar. These results suggest that explicitly modeling forward delay, rather than relying on RTT, is a useful principle for multipath scheduling. Although further validation in real deployments is needed, FDPS offers a simple and effective means to improve the efficiency and user-perceived quality of multipath transport.

Forensic entomology uses insects associated with decomposing remains to answer questions of medico-legal importance, most commonly to estimate the time elapsed since death, or post-mortem interval (PMI) [1,2]. Because insects colonize a corpse soon after death, the age of the oldest insects found on the remains can provide a minimum estimate of PMI, and this approach is particularly valuable once the usefulness of medical methods has declined, typically after the first two or three days post mortem [3]. Age estimation relies on the strong dependence of insect development on temperature. Developmental data obtained under controlled conditions are used to build models, such as isomorphen diagrams, isomegalen diagrams, or thermal summation models, which are then applied to specimens sampled at a crime scene together with temperature records from the site [4,5].

The accuracy of such estimates is limited by several sources of error. These include differences between the temperature at the scene and that recorded at the nearest weather station, the effects of larval aggregations and heat generation, geographic variation among populations, and the variability of development inherent to the species [6,7]. Even under constant laboratory conditions, individuals of the same cohort differ markedly in the time required to complete development, and this variation is carried into the confidence limits of age estimates, which may be broad enough to reduce their usefulness in casework [8]. Methods that explain part of this variation, and thereby narrow the prediction error, are therefore of considerable interest.

One potential source of information is body size. In insects, size at emergence reflects the growth history of an individual, and is affected by temperature, food quality and quantity, and larval density [9,10]. Body size is often correlated with development time, although the direction and strength of the relationship vary among species and conditions. In many insects, individuals that develop slowly attain larger sizes, whereas in others rapid development under favourable conditions yields large individuals [11,12]. If size is consistently related to the thermal requirements of development, then it might serve as a proxy for physiological age. Size-based corrections are not unknown in forensic entomology, as the length and mass of larvae are routinely used to estimate age, but they have rarely been applied to adults.
