Adult size is a stable and easily measured trait, remains constant after sclerotization, and can be recorded from specimens preserved in the field, which suggests that it could improve age predictions for insects that colonize remains late in decomposition.

Beetles are a major component of the fauna of decomposing remains and are especially useful when remains are at advanced stages of decay and fly evidence is absent or ambiguous [13,14]. However, the development of forensically relevant beetles has received much less attention than that of blow flies, and models for beetle age estimation are comparatively few [15]. Among them, the rove beetle Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Staphylinidae) is a large, widely distributed predatory species, occurring across the Holarctic and introduced to other regions [16]. Adults and larvae are frequently recorded on carcasses and human cadavers, where they feed mainly on fly eggs and larvae and on other small invertebrates, and they arrive during the bloated and decay stages [17,18]. Its regular occurrence in forensic cases, and its record of use in PMI estimation, make it a good candidate for improving developmental models [19]. Previous studies have described its development at constant temperatures and provided thermal requirements, but they did not evaluate how variation among individuals could be reduced [20,21].

The thermal summation approach expresses development as a constant amount of accumulated degree-days (K) above a lower developmental threshold (t0) required to complete a stage [22]. Under this model, K is assumed to be the same for all individuals, and age is estimated by dividing the accumulated thermal units by the temperature excess over the threshold. If K in fact varies with body size, using a single mean value will introduce error that could be removed by using size-specific values. Because sexual size dimorphism and sex-specific growth patterns are common in beetles, it is also possible that the relationship between size and K differs between males and females, and that sex-specific models might further increase accuracy [23]. Sex can be determined easily in adult C. maxillosus, so such models would be feasible in practice.

Here we test the concept that size at emergence can be used to predict the physiological age of adult C. maxillosus and thereby improve the accuracy of age estimates. We first determined, using a laboratory rearing experiment, the relationship between thermal summation value needed for emergence and beetle size, expressed as body length. We then built general, sex-specific, and size-based models and compared their predictive performance in an independent validation study, by testing whether K estimated from beetle size was closer to the true value than K from the general thermal summation model. We hypothesized that larger beetles would have lower K values and that the best predictions would be obtained from sex-specific models using body length as the predictor.

Beetles used in the experiments originated from a laboratory colony established from adults of C. maxillosus collected with baited pitfall traps in a mixed forest near Poznań, western Poland. Adults were kept in plastic containers (20 × 15 × 10 cm) filled with moist peat, at 22 °C and a 16:8 h light:dark photoperiod. They were fed minced pork and live blowfly larvae (Lucilia sericata), which also served as oviposition and larval food substrates [1,2]. Eggs were collected daily and transferred to separate containers to obtain cohorts of known age. Individuals from the second laboratory generation were used in all experiments to reduce the influence of field-derived maternal effects.

**Development study (model building)**

Newly hatched larvae were randomly assigned to one of four constant temperatures (15, 18, 21 and 24 °C ± 0.5 °C) in incubators with a 16:8 h light:dark photoperiod. At each temperature, larvae were reared individually in 250 ml containers with a 5 cm layer of moist peat and fed ad libitum with minced pork and fly larvae, replaced every two days to avoid decay and mold. Sample size at each temperature was 60 individuals at the start of the experiment. Containers were inspected twice daily (08:00 and 20:00), and the dates of moulting, wandering, pupation and adult emergence were recorded. Development time to emergence was calculated from egg hatching to the first appearance of the adult beetle, expressed in hours and converted to days.

Newly emerged adults were left for 24 h to allow cuticle hardening and were then killed by freezing at −20 °C. Body length was measured as the distance from the anterior margin of the head to the tip of the abdomen, with the abdomen in a natural, non-extended position, using a stereomicroscope equipped with a calibrated digital camera and image analysis software (accuracy 0.01 mm). Pronotum width was also measured as a secondary size index. Each beetle was measured twice and the mean was used; measurement repeatability, assessed with the intraclass correlation coefficient, exceeded 0.95. Sex was determined by examining the terminal abdominal sternites [3]. Dry body mass was not used because it requires destructive drying that would be unsuitable for a forensic protocol.

**Thermal summation**

The thermal summation value (K, in degree-days, °D) required for emergence was calculated for each individual using the linear degree-day model [4]:

K = D(T − T₀),

where D is development time in days, T is rearing temperature and T₀ is the lower developmental threshold. T₀ was estimated by linear regression of development rate (1/D) against temperature, as the x-intercept, using mean development rates of all individuals at each temperature [4,5]. Individual K values were then computed using this T₀. Effects of temperature on development time and survival were tested with ANOVA and chi-square tests, respectively.

**Relationship between K and beetle size**

The relationship between K and beetle length was analysed with linear regression. Models were fitted for (i) all individuals pooled, (ii) males and (iii) females separately. Sex, length and their interaction were tested with analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) to determine whether slopes and intercepts differed between sexes. Temperature was included as a covariate to verify that the K–size relationship was not an artefact of rearing temperature. Residuals were inspected for normality (Shapiro–Wilk test) and homoscedasticity, and the Box–Cox transformation was applied when assumptions were violated. Alternative models using pronotum width as a predictor were compared with length-based models using Akaike's information criterion (AIC).

**Validation study**

An independent group of beetles was reared to test the accuracy of age estimates. Larvae from different parental pairs than those used for model building were reared at three constant temperatures (16, 19 and 23 °C) and at one fluctuating regime (mean 19 °C, range 14–24 °C, changing in a sinusoidal pattern), with 40 individuals per treatment and the same rearing protocol. Development time, sex and body length at emergence were recorded as before. For each validation individual, the true K was calculated from its known development time and temperature history; under fluctuating temperatures, K was obtained by summing hourly degree-hours above T₀ and dividing by 24.

Age at emergence was then estimated in a forensic-like manner using four approaches: (1) the general model, in which the mean K of the model-building dataset was used for all beetles; (2) a model regressing K on length for pooled sexes; (3) a sex-specific model regressing K on length; and (4) a model using pronotum width. Estimated K was converted to estimated development time by dividing by the mean temperature above T₀. Accuracy was expressed as the absolute error between estimated and true K (|K_est − K_true|) and as the relative error (percentage of true K).

**Statistical analysis**

Absolute errors of the different approaches were compared with the Friedman test followed by Wilcoxon signed-rank post hoc tests with Bonferroni correction, because errors were not normally distributed and observations were paired within individuals. Differences among temperature treatments were assessed using Kruskal–Wallis tests. Mean error and the proportion of estimates within 10% of the true value were also reported. All tests were two-tailed with α = 0.05. Analyses were performed in R version 4.2 [6], with the packages car, MASS and ggplot2. Values are given as mean ± SD unless otherwise stated.

Development time and thermal requirements

Beetles completed development from egg to adult emergence at all tested temperatures, although survival varied among treatments. Total development time decreased markedly with rising temperature, from a mean of approximately 60 days at the lowest temperature to roughly 21 days at the highest. The relationship between development rate and temperature was linear within the intermediate range, and the general thermal summation model, fitted to pooled data for both sexes, yielded a lower developmental threshold (t0) of 9.4 ± 0.8 °C and a mean thermal constant (K) of 262 ± 11 degree-days (DD) [see Ikemoto and Takai, 2000, for the fitting method]. Despite this clear temperature dependence, individual variation in development time within each temperature was considerable. The coefficient of variation in K ranged from 8% to 17%, and the range of individual K values within a single temperature often exceeded 60 DD. Applying the general model to estimate age of emerging adults would therefore produce relatively large errors, especially for individuals at the extremes of the distribution.

Body size at emergence

Beetle length at emergence varied from 11.2 to 19.6 mm (mean 15.4 ± 1.8 mm). Females were on average slightly larger than males (15.8 vs. 15.0 mm; t-test, P < 0.01), although the size ranges overlapped almost completely. Temperature had a significant effect on size: beetles reared at intermediate temperatures tended to be larger than those from the extremes (ANOVA, P < 0.001), though temperature explained only a small part of the total variance in length. Sex and temperature did not significantly interact in their effect on body length (P > 0.05).

Relationship between thermal summation value and size

Thermal summation value required for emergence was negatively correlated with beetle length (Pearson r = −0.62, P < 0.001, n = 214). Larger beetles thus emerged at lower K, meaning that they had completed development with a smaller accumulated thermal sum than smaller individuals. This relationship was evident in both sexes, but the slope differed between them. In females K decreased by 11.3 DD per mm of body length (R² = 0.43), while in males the decrease was 9.1 DD per mm (R² = 0.36). Analysis of covariance indicated significant effects of both length (P < 0.001) and sex (P = 0.02) on K, with no significant interaction, though the intercepts differed between sexes. Residuals of all regressions were approximately normally distributed and homoscedastic, and inclusion of a quadratic term in length did not significantly improve model fit (P > 0.1).

The relationship remained significant when the effect of temperature was accounted for. In a model including both rearing temperature and length, length retained a strong and significant effect on K (P < 0.001), whereas temperature had a smaller effect, suggesting that the size–K relationship reflects individual variation rather than being a by-product of temperature effects on both traits.

Candidate models for age prediction

Four types of model were compared for predicting K: (i) the general thermal summation model using mean K for all individuals; (ii) a sex-specific model using mean K for males and females separately; (iii) a general regression of K against beetle length; and (iv) sex-specific regressions of K against beetle length. According to Akaike's information criterion, the sex-specific length-based regressions were best supported (ΔAIC > 12 relative to all other models), followed by the general length-based regression. The mean-K models showed the poorest fit, and including sex alone offered only marginal improvement over the general model.

Validation of predictions

The models were tested using an independent validation dataset of 96 beetles reared under conditions not used in model construction. For each individual, K was estimated from each model and compared with the true K calculated from observed development time and temperature. The mean absolute error of K estimated using the general thermal summation model was 21.4 DD, corresponding to an error in age estimate of approximately 3.2 days at 20 °C. Estimates based on beetle length were significantly closer to the true K (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P < 0.001). The general length-based model reduced the mean absolute error to 15.1 DD, and the sex-specific length models gave the lowest error of 12.8 DD, equivalent to an age error of about 1.9 days. Thus, the use of size reduced the error by approximately 40% relative to the general model.

The improvement was consistent across temperature treatments. Size-based estimates were more accurate than those from the general model in 78% of individuals when length alone was used and in 84% of individuals when sex-specific regressions were used. The advantage was most pronounced for beetles at the extremes of the size distribution. For very small individuals, the general model underestimated true K by an average of 28 DD, while for very large beetles it overestimated K by a similar amount; the length-based models largely eliminated this systematic bias. The 95% prediction intervals of the sex-specific length models were narrower than those of the general model (mean width 49 vs. 62 DD), and the proportion of validation individuals falling within the predicted interval was close to the nominal level (93% vs. 95%, respectively), indicating that the narrower intervals did not compromise reliability.

Comparison between sexes

When validation results were analysed separately for each sex, the sex-specific length models performed particularly well for females (mean absolute error 11.6 DD) and slightly less well for males (14.0 DD). Applying a model from the wrong sex increased the error by an average of 3.5 DD, showing that sex determination is beneficial when estimating age from size, although even sex-mismatched length models outperformed the general thermal summation model.

The present study demonstrates that body size at emergence carries information on the physiological age of Creophilus maxillosus, expressed as the thermal summation value (K) required to complete development. Larger beetles emerged at lower K than smaller ones, and models that incorporated beetle length predicted K significantly more accurately than the general thermal summation model. Sex-specific regressions of K against body length performed best. These findings support the concept that size at emergence can be used to refine age estimates in forensic entomology, where large intraspecific variation in development time is a major source of error [1,2].

The negative relationship between K and size is somewhat counterintuitive, since in many insects larger adults result from prolonged development and therefore higher thermal requirements [3]. However, the pattern observed here is consistent with a growing body of evidence that, in species developing on ephemeral and deteriorating resources, individuals with access to high-quality food or favourable conditions grow faster and attain both larger size and earlier emergence [4,5]. Variation in larval nutrition, competition, and the condition of the carrion substrate can all generate positive covariance between growth rate and final size, producing a negative correlation between size and development time. Such a pattern may also reflect genetic variation in growth efficiency or maternal effects, which are known to influence offspring performance in beetles [6]. Because the mechanism was not tested directly here, these explanations remain hypotheses, and experiments manipulating food quantity, larval density, and temperature independently would clarify their relative importance.

The improved accuracy of sex-specific models is expected given sexual size dimorphism and sex-specific differences in development reported for Staphylinidae and other Coleoptera [7]. Females and males may follow different trade-offs between size and development time, so that a single regression blurs the relationship. In forensic practice, sex of adult beetles is easily determined, so the use of sex-specific models adds little practical burden while reducing error. Beetle length was also a better predictor than the alternative size measures, probably because it is simple to measure, reproducible, and strongly correlated with overall body mass. This simplicity is important if the method is to be adopted by practitioners, as it requires no specialised equipment beyond standard microscopy and calipers or image analysis.

The practical significance of these results lies in the way adult beetles are used in casework. C. maxillosus is a common and frequently reported predator on decomposing remains, and the presence of newly emerged teneral adults may provide information on the minimum time since colonization, which in this species can extend over several weeks [8]. Conventional estimates based on the mean K ignore variation among individuals, so that the resulting PMI estimate is applied equally to small and large beetles. Incorporating size narrows the discrepancy between estimated and true K, and thus should reduce both bias and the width of the uncertainty interval around the PMI. The improvement was confirmed in an independent validation data set, which suggests that the models are not merely artefacts of overfitting.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the models were calibrated under controlled laboratory conditions, usually at constant temperatures, whereas development on a real corpse takes place under fluctuating temperatures and variable resource availability. Constant and fluctuating temperatures can yield different development rates and different body sizes [9], and the size–K relationship may therefore differ in the field. Second, the beetles in this study came from a limited number of laboratory lines or populations, and geographic variation in size and development, which is well documented in forensically important insects [10], could affect transferability. Third, the lower developmental threshold used in the thermal summation approach is a simplification, and nonlinearity near thermal extremes may introduce additional error. Finally, adult size can change little after emergence, but the age of an adult found at the scene is not necessarily its time since emergence, so the approach is most useful for freshly emerged individuals or when combined with other age indicators of adults.

Future research should therefore validate size-based models under natural and fluctuating thermal regimes, include beetles from different populations and substrates, and test whether similar relationships occur in other forensically relevant Coleoptera and Diptera. Studies on larvae and pupae, where size is routinely used to estimate age, might also explore whether final adult size, or size at earlier stages, can be combined to better constrain development time. Integrating size with other covariates such as rearing density or food type, perhaps within a Bayesian framework, may further improve precision and permit explicit quantification of uncertainty [11].

In conclusion, the size of C. maxillosus at emergence is a significant predictor of the thermal requirements of development, with larger individuals completing development at lower K. Models using beetle length as a predictor, especially those fitted separately for males and females, yielded more accurate estimates of physiological age than the general thermal summation model. Incorporating adult size into age estimation can therefore reduce error caused by intraspecific variation and improve the reliability of PMI estimates, provided that models are adequately validated for local conditions before use in casework.

Crowdsourcing has become a standard tool for tasks that are difficult to automate, such as labeling images, transcribing audio, and judging relevance [1, 2]. Its success rests largely on decomposing work into short, well-defined microtasks that anonymous workers can complete quickly and independently. Many problems of interest, however, are complex and open-ended, and they do not decompose naturally. Asking a worker to "build a map of what causes what" or "describe the structure of a domain" typically yields low-quality, redundant, or abandoned contributions, because workers favor brief, repetitive tasks over sustained, creative effort [3, 4]. Designing mechanisms that elicit high-quality structured knowledge from many independent workers, while keeping each contribution small, remains a central challenge.

We study one important instance of this challenge: using the crowd to explore large networks whose topology is not known in advance and can only be revealed through human judgment. Networks of this type arise in many settings, including social ties, hyperlinked information, concept hierarchies, and knowledge graphs [5, 6]. Exhaustive querying is infeasible, since the number of candidate node pairs grows quadratically with the number of nodes, and the underlying networks are typically sparse. Efficient exploration therefore requires directing limited worker effort toward the parts of the network most likely to contain meaningful edges, without relying on workers coordinating with each other or sustaining long sessions.

We focus on the network of causal attributions, in which a directed edge from one concept to another indicates that the first is perceived as a cause of the second. Causal knowledge underlies explanation, prediction, planning, and decision making [7, 8], and a large-scale map of causal beliefs would be valuable for several reasons. It could support automated reasoning and question answering, supply background knowledge for causal inference from observational data [9], and allow study of how people perceive and organize causes and effects. Existing resources are limited. Curated knowledge bases cover few causal relations, and automatic extraction from text suffers from the implicit, ambiguous, and context-dependent ways causality is expressed in language [10, 11]. Causal relationships are also more subjective than taxonomic ones: people disagree about strength, directness, and even direction, which makes the crowd both an appealing and a demanding source of data.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we run experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) examining how workers propose and validate individual causal relationships. We compare alternative question formats and assess how reliably workers generate plausible causes and effects of a given concept and how consistently other workers confirm them. These experiments establish which microtasks yield trustworthy edges and inform the design of the larger system.

Second, we introduce a method that allows independent crowd workers to explore large networks. The core of the method, which we call Iterative Pathway Refinement, builds on a simple idea: each worker receives a pathway, a chain of concepts linked by previously collected causal edges, and performs a small modification such as inserting, replacing, or extending a step. The refined pathway is then passed to subsequent workers. Because every worker sees the accumulated work of predecessors, the process concentrates effort on promising regions of the network and gradually discovers longer and more intricate causal chains, yet each task remains a short microtask requiring no direct communication. This design is related to iterative and sequential crowd workflows [12, 13] but is tailored to graph exploration, and we provide a theoretical analysis showing that it explores the network efficiently under a natural model of worker behavior. We also evaluate the method on synthetic networks with known structure, where discovered edges can be compared against ground truth and against baselines such as random and breadth-first querying.

Third, we deploy the method on AMT to extract a large-scale causal attribution network and analyze it from several perspectives. We examine its structural properties, including degree distributions, connectivity, hubs, and the prevalence of cycles and feedback, and compare them with those of other real-world networks [14]. We also study the workers who built it, characterizing their activity patterns, the distribution of effort across participants, the quality and novelty of their contributions, and the efficiency of the process in terms of edges discovered per unit of cost. These analyses show how workers navigate the space of concepts and reveal characteristics of causal perception, such as which kinds of concepts act as common causes or common effects and how causal chains tend to be organized around abstract versus concrete events.

The resulting data bear on both crowdsourcing and the study of causality. For crowdsourcing, our results show that a carefully structured sequence of independent microtasks can accomplish exploration that would otherwise require sustained, coordinated effort. For research on causality, the network offers an empirical window on lay causal beliefs, which may complement formal causal discovery methods and help prioritize hypotheses for testing [9, 15].

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on crowdsourcing complex tasks, network exploration, and causal knowledge acquisition. We then describe the worker experiments, present Iterative Pathway Refinement with its theoretical analysis and synthetic evaluation, and report the deployment on AMT together with the analysis of the resulting network and worker behavior. We conclude with limitations and directions for future work.

We conducted all experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Workers were restricted to those with an approval rate above 95% and at least 500 completed tasks, and were paid at rates calibrated to approximately the U.S. federal minimum wage. Workers could complete any number of tasks, but each task was independent and no worker saw the global network.

**Microtask Design**

We studied two elementary microtasks. In the *proposal* task, a worker is shown a focal event or phenomenon (e.g., "obesity") and asked to type, in free text, a direct cause (backward direction) or a direct effect (forward direction). In the *validation* task, a worker is shown a candidate pair (A, B) and asked whether A directly causes B, with response options of yes, no, or unsure. Each pair was presented in random order and direction to control for position effects. Instructions defined "direct" causation as the absence of an intermediate step the worker would consider necessary to mention, and included worked examples and a brief qualification quiz.

To test how proposal and validation behave, we ran a pilot with 50 seed concepts drawn from news headlines and encyclopedic health, economic, and environmental topics. Each seed received 10 proposals per direction. Free-text responses were normalized by lowercasing, removing stop words, and lemmatizing, then merged when their embedding cosine similarity exceeded 0.85 [1] and a manual audit confirmed equivalence. Each proposed relationship was validated by five independent workers, and we measured agreement using Fleiss' kappa [2]. We compared proposal framing (open-ended versus suggestion-assisted) and validation framing (binary versus three-option) in between-subject conditions, assigning workers randomly.

**Iterative Pathway Refinement**

Exploring a large network by asking workers to enumerate it is infeasible, as no worker can hold the whole structure and effort concentrates on popular nodes. Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR) instead builds the network through independent microtasks that each extend or refine a pathway. The procedure maintains a pool of pathways, each a sequence of nodes v₀ → v₁ → … → v_k linked by validated causal edges. At each step:

1. **Selection.** A pathway is sampled from the pool with probability proportional to a priority score that favors short pathways and nodes with few observed neighbors, balancing exploration and exploitation.
2. **Extension.** A worker is shown the terminal node and asked to propose a direct effect (or, for backward exploration, a cause). The proposal is appended to the pathway.
3. **Refinement.** A different worker is shown the pathway endpoints and asked whether intermediate steps are missing; if so, they insert a node between two adjacent nodes, which splits one edge into two.
4. **Validation.** Each new edge is validated by independent workers, and is added to the network only if a majority endorses it. Rejected edges are recorded and not re-queried.

Because each task depends only on the current pathway state, workers need not coordinate. Refinement permits discovery of mediating structure that single-step proposals would miss, and the pool grows adaptively toward under-explored regions.

We analyzed IPR as an exploration process on a hidden graph G with an edge oracle subject to noise. Under the assumptions that worker proposals sample neighbors of the queried node with probabilities bounded below by p_min and validation errors are independent with rate ε < 0.5, we derived bounds on the expected number of queries needed to recover all nodes within distance d of a seed, and showed that majority voting over m validators drives the false-edge probability down exponentially in m [3]. The priority rule ensures that each node's neighborhood is sampled at a rate bounded away from zero, which yields coverage guarantees comparable to coupon-collector arguments [4].

**Synthetic Evaluation**

We evaluated IPR on synthetic networks of 1,000 to 100,000 nodes generated from Erdős–Rényi, Barabási–Albert [5], and stochastic block models, with directed edges. Simulated workers proposed a neighbor drawn from the true neighborhood with a probability of success s (0.6–0.95) and otherwise proposed a random node, and validated edges with accuracy 1−ε (ε ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}). We compared IPR with (a) random-edge querying, (b) breadth-first expansion, and (c) a single-step proposal baseline without refinement. Metrics were edge recall, precision, and the number of queries needed to reach 80% recall. Each configuration was repeated 50 times, and we report means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

**Large-Scale Deployment**

We deployed IPR on AMT starting from 100 seed concepts spanning health, environment, economics, politics, and technology. The deployment ran for several weeks and collected proposals, refinements, and validations. Each candidate edge received at least three validations, with a fourth and fifth added when the first three disagreed. We retained edges with majority endorsement. Attention checks, consisting of known true and known false causal pairs, were interleaved at a rate of 5%, and workers failing more than 30% were excluded and their responses discarded.

**Network and Worker Analyses**

We characterized the resulting network using degree distributions (fit with maximum-likelihood power-law estimation [6]), weakly and strongly connected components, clustering, path lengths, and cycle frequency. Community structure was identified with the Louvain algorithm [7]. To study causal perception, we examined reciprocal edges, transitivity of causal judgments (whether A→B and B→C implies endorsement of A→C), and the relationship between node abstraction and degree.

For worker behavior, we computed tasks per worker, session length, time per task, agreement with the majority, and the yield of new nodes and edges per unit of payment. We used Mann–Whitney U tests and Spearman correlations, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. Efficiency was defined as validated edges per dollar and compared across task types and exploration depths.

**Ethics**

The study involved no personally identifiable information beyond anonymized AMT worker IDs, which were hashed before analysis. Participation was voluntary and workers could abandon tasks at any time.

We first report results from the experiments on individual causal relationships, then evaluate Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR) on synthetic networks, and finally describe the causal attribution network obtained from AMT and the behavior of the workers who built it.

**Proposing and validating individual causal relations.** In the proposal experiment, 300 workers each provided causes or effects for a set of seed concepts. Workers produced valid, interpretable responses in 91% of cases, and responses were highly skewed toward a small set of common concepts: the ten most frequent responses accounted for 18% of all proposals. Proposals of effects were generated more quickly than proposals of causes (median 14 s versus 19 s; Mann-Whitney U, p < 0.01), suggesting that forward reasoning is cognitively easier than backward reasoning, consistent with prior work on causal perception [1,2]. In the validation experiment, each proposed relation was rated by five independent workers. Agreement among raters was moderate (Fleiss' κ = 0.52), and majority-vote validation retained 74% of proposed edges. Rejected relations were disproportionately those that reversed the direction of causation or expressed mere correlation (e.g., "umbrella" and "rain"), which together comprised 58% of rejections. Validation was approximately three times faster than proposal, and its accuracy against an expert-labeled subset of 200 edges was 0.86, supporting a pipeline in which cheap validation filters open-ended proposals.

**Evaluation of Iterative Pathway Refinement on synthetic networks.** We simulated workers exploring synthetic networks of 10,000 nodes with Erdős–Rényi, scale-free, and community-structured topologies. Simulated workers returned a true neighbor with probability p = 0.9 and otherwise returned noise. In IPR, each worker receives a pathway of concepts built by earlier workers and refines or extends it by modifying one step, so that pathways accumulate improvements without any worker needing global knowledge. We compared IPR with two baselines: independent random exploration, in which each worker starts from a random seed, and a breadth-first crowd strategy that assigns every node once.

IPR discovered a larger fraction of the nodes and edges per unit of worker effort than both baselines across all topologies. With a budget of 5,000 microtasks, IPR recovered 62% of edges in the scale-free network, compared with 34% for random exploration and 41% for breadth-first assignment. The advantage was largest in heavy-tailed networks, where pathway refinement concentrated effort around hubs and then propagated outward to peripheral nodes. In Erdős–Rényi graphs the improvement was smaller (51% versus 39% and 42%), as expected given the lack of structural heterogeneity. The coverage curve of IPR grew approximately as predicted by our theoretical analysis, with the number of discovered nodes scaling near-linearly in the number of tasks until saturation, and deviations from the predicted curve under 6% across 50 simulation runs. Performance degraded gracefully with noise: reducing p from 0.9 to 0.7 lowered final edge recovery by 11% for IPR but by 19% for the breadth-first strategy, because refinement steps allowed later workers to correct earlier errors.

**The crowd-constructed causal attribution network.** We deployed IPR on AMT with 1,850 workers over three weeks, yielding 21,400 validated causal edges among 9,100 unique concepts. Mean worker contribution was 11.6 edges, but the distribution was heavy-tailed: the most active 5% of workers produced 31% of the edges. The resulting network was sparse (mean degree 4.7) and had a giant weakly connected component containing 96% of nodes. In-degree and out-degree distributions were both well described by power laws with exponents of 2.4 and 2.9, respectively, indicating that a small number of concepts act as frequent causes or frequent effects. High in-degree nodes were typically outcomes such as "stress," "obesity," and "death," whereas high out-degree nodes included "poverty," "smoking," and "lack of sleep." The correlation between in-degree and out-degree was weak (Spearman ρ = 0.21), meaning that concepts tended to specialize as either causes or effects.

The network exhibited a clustering coefficient of 0.07, about 20 times that of a degree-matched random graph, and an average shortest path length of 7.3 along directed paths. Cycles were present but rare: 3.2% of nodes participated in a directed cycle, most commonly feedback loops such as those between "anxiety" and "insomnia." Community detection (modularity Q = 0.61) revealed thematic clusters corresponding to health, economics, environment, and interpersonal relations, with relatively few edges between them. Edges crossing clusters were more often rejected in validation (31% versus 22%), indicating that distant causal claims are judged less plausible. We also observed that approximately 27% of two-step chains were judged transitive when tested directly, showing that perceived causality does not propagate freely along paths, in line with findings on causal chain attenuation [3].

**Worker activity and efficiency.** Worker response times decreased with experience: median time per task fell from 24 s in a worker's first five tasks to 15 s after fifty tasks, while validation acceptance rates were unchanged (p = 0.4), implying learning without loss of quality. Over the deployment, the cost per validated edge was $0.043 under IPR. In a matched pilot with random exploration this cost was $0.081, and the proportion of duplicate edges was 38% compared with 14% under IPR. Refinement steps accounted for 43% of IPR tasks, and edges produced through refinement were more likely to be validated than those from initial proposals (82% versus 71%, p < 0.001). Finally, pathway length increased steadily as refinements accumulated, plateauing at approximately six steps, after which workers tended to substitute rather than extend concepts. These results indicate that IPR efficiently directs independent workers toward unexplored and plausible regions of the causal network.

This work set out to address a central difficulty in crowdsourcing: how to harness independent workers, who prefer short and repetitive microtasks, to explore a large network whose topology is unknown and whose structure cannot be specified in advance. Using causal attribution as a testbed, we showed that workers can reliably propose and validate individual causal relationships, and that these microtasks can be composed into a principled exploration procedure, Iterative Pathway Refinement (IPR), which yields a large-scale causal network without requiring any worker to understand or hold the global structure.

**Summary of findings.** Our initial experiments indicated that workers produce plausible causes and effects when prompted with a single concept, and that a second round of independent validation effectively filters low-quality proposals. This mirrors prior findings that redundancy and verification stages can improve the quality of open-ended crowd output [1,2]. Building on this, IPR directs worker effort toward pathways that are most informative for expanding the network, rather than expanding all nodes uniformly. On synthetic networks, this focus produced more efficient coverage of the relevant structure per unit of worker effort than naive breadth-first or random exploration, consistent with the theoretical analysis of the mechanism. Deployed on AMT, the method produced a large causal attribution network whose structure and the associated worker activity patterns offered insight into both the network itself and the people who built it.

**Implications for crowd exploration.** The method contributes a general pattern: decompose exploration into local, independent, verifiable steps and use aggregated outputs to decide what to ask next. Because the approach relies only on local queries (“what does X cause?” or “what causes Y?”), it is applicable to other networks that crowds can plausibly navigate, such as social, conceptual, or information networks. This adds to work on workflow design and algorithmic management of crowds, where complex tasks are decomposed into microtasks [3,4], and extends it to settings in which the object being constructed is a graph of unknown size. A key practical lesson is that efficiency gains arise less from improving individual worker performance than from allocating queries intelligently, which is attractive since it is compatible with the incentive and attention constraints of microtask markets.

**Implications for the study of causality.** The resulting network represents causal perception rather than ground-truth causation. Workers’ proposals reflect commonsense beliefs, salience, and linguistic framing, and the structure of the network reveals them. Such data complement experimental and observational approaches to causal inference [5,6] and the psychological literature on how people reason about causes [7]. For example, regularities in which concepts act as hubs, how long causal chains tend to be, and where workers disagree on direction may indicate systematic biases such as preference for proximal, familiar, or negatively valenced causes. Such a network can also serve as a source of priors for causal discovery algorithms, helping to constrain candidate structures or to suggest variables worth measuring, though its use for this purpose requires care because perceived and actual causal relations may diverge.

**Limitations.** Several limitations qualify our conclusions. First, the AMT workforce is not representative of the general population, so the network reflects the perceptions of a particular demographic, largely English-speaking and Western, and cultural differences in causal attribution [8] are likely under-represented. Second, free-text concepts must be normalized to nodes, and any normalization (manual or automatic) introduces errors, such as merging distinct concepts or splitting synonymous ones. Third, validation by independent workers establishes plausibility, not correctness; widely held misconceptions may pass validation. Fourth, we treated edges mostly as binary and did not fully capture strength, mechanism, conditionality, or the possibility of cycles and feedback, all of which matter for causal reasoning. Finally, the theoretical guarantees for IPR rely on assumptions about worker reliability and network structure that real data satisfy only approximately; our synthetic evaluations probe robustness but cannot cover all deviations.

**Future work.** Several directions follow naturally. Richer microtasks could elicit edge strength, sign, temporal delay, or mediating mechanisms, enabling weighted or signed causal graphs. Adaptive worker assignment that models individual reliability could further reduce cost, drawing on work on truth inference and task routing in crowdsourcing [9]. Comparing networks across populations would test hypotheses about cultural and demographic differences in causal beliefs. Integrating crowd-derived networks with machine-extracted causal statements from text [10] might combine the breadth of automated methods with the judgment of human validators. Finally, evaluating the network against curated causal knowledge and against intervention data would clarify when perceived causal structure aligns with real mechanisms, and would show whether such networks improve downstream causal inference.

**Conclusion.** We have presented and evaluated a method for exploring large networks through independent crowd microtasks, instantiated for causal attribution. Iterative Pathway Refinement offers a theoretically motivated and empirically efficient means of building a large causal network from the contributions of many workers who each see only a small piece of it. The resulting network and the behavior of its contributors provide a new window into causal perception, and the underlying approach offers a template for crowdsourcing other large, open-ended structures that no single worker could construct alone.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation of the synovial joints, progressive destruction of articular cartilage and bone, and substantial disability if inadequately treated [1]. The autoimmune nature of RA is reflected in the production of a broad spectrum of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor directed against the Fc portion of IgG and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) [2,3]. ACPA are detectable in sera and synovial fluids of approximately 60–70% of RA patients, may appear years before clinical onset, and are associated with a more severe, erosive disease course. ACPA seropositivity is therefore incorporated into the current classification criteria for RA [4,5].

**Citrullination and ACPA in RA**

Citrullination is a post-translational modification in which peptidylarginine residues are converted to peptidylcitrulline by calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs). This conversion removes a positive charge, alters the hydrogen-bonding capacity and isoelectric point of the protein, and can promote unfolding, enhanced proteolytic susceptibility, and the generation of neoepitopes that escape immunological tolerance [6,7]. Citrullination occurs physiologically during apoptosis, differentiation, and inflammation, and is therefore not unique to RA. However, in the genetically susceptible host, particularly carriers of HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, citrullinated peptides are presented with higher affinity to CD4+ T cells, which supports B cell activation and ACPA production [8,9]. Smoking and other mucosal insults, as well as periodontal infection, have been proposed as triggers of citrullination that precede joint involvement [10].

A growing number of citrullinated autoantigens have been identified in the rheumatoid joint, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, α-enolase, and type II collagen [11–14]. Citrullinated proteins and PAD enzymes are abundant in the inflamed synovium, and ACPA can form immune complexes with these antigens, activating complement and Fc receptor-bearing cells and thereby amplifying inflammation [15]. ACPA reactive with cartilage-derived citrullinated epitopes have also been reported to induce or enhance arthritis in experimental models, suggesting that antigens within the cartilage itself may be pathogenically relevant targets [16].

**Aggrecan as an autoantigen in arthritis**

The large aggregating proteoglycan (PG) aggrecan is one of the most abundant macromolecules of articular cartilage, where it provides compressive resistance through its highly charged glycosaminoglycan chains. Aggrecan comprises three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular and glycosaminoglycan-attachment region. The N-terminal G1 domain binds hyaluronan and link protein, anchoring the molecule within the extracellular matrix [17]. Aggrecan has long been recognized as an arthritogenic autoantigen. Immunization of BALB/c mice with human cartilage PG induces a progressive, erosive polyarthritis (proteoglycan-induced arthritis, PGIA) that resembles human RA, with autoantibody production and T cell-dependent disease [18,19]. In addition, T cell responses to human PG, and in particular to peptides from the G1 domain, have been detected in RA patients [20,21].

Importantly, more recent studies demonstrated that T cells from RA patients respond to citrullinated aggrecan peptides, and that citrullinated epitopes within the G1 domain bind with high affinity to shared-epitope-containing HLA-DR molecules [22,23]. Citrullinated PG epitopes can also be recognized by T cells in the SKG and PGIA mouse models [24]. These findings suggest that citrullinated aggrecan may serve as a joint-specific target of both T and B cell responses. This could help explain the localization of the autoimmune attack to the joints, despite the systemic distribution of ACPA and of citrullinating enzymes.

**Knowledge gap and aims**

Despite this evidence, a fundamental question remains unanswered: whether the aggrecan molecule is actually citrullinated in vivo in human cartilage. Most studies have employed synthetic citrullinated peptides or in vitro modified proteins, which establish the immunological potential of citrullinated aggrecan but do not demonstrate the presence of the modified protein in the tissue. Cartilage is avascular and has low cellular density, and its matrix proteins turn over slowly, which could favor the accumulation of post-translational modifications. Moreover, it is unknown whether citrullinated PG (CitPG) occurs in normal cartilage or only in diseased tissue, which fragments of the molecule carry the modification, and whether its distribution differs between osteoarthritis (OA) and RA. Clarifying these points is essential for judging whether CitPG can serve as a target for ACPA, form local immune complexes, and contribute to the initiation or perpetuation of joint inflammation.

In the present study, we therefore sought to determine whether citrullinated aggrecan is present in human articular cartilage and to characterize its molecular features. We used sera from ACPA-positive RA patients to probe PG purified from normal cartilage and cartilage extracts from OA and RA patients, and we identified the PG fragments, particularly those containing the G1 and G3 domains, that carry citrulline-containing epitopes. We confirmed the citrullination status of an in vitro citrullinated recombinant human G1 domain (rhG1) using both antibody-based and chemical detection, and used molecular modeling to explore the potential sites of citrullination within this domain. Finally, we quantified CitPG-specific serum autoantibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and compared the immunohistochemical localization of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage. Together, these approaches aim to establish CitPG as a bona fide in vivo cartilage autoantigen and to define its potential relevance to ACPA-mediated autoimmunity in RA.

**Human cartilage specimens and sera**

Human articular cartilage was obtained with institutional review board approval and written informed consent. Normal cartilage came from tissue donors with no history of joint disease. OA cartilage came from patients undergoing total knee replacement, and RA cartilage came from patients undergoing joint replacement surgery. Specimens were kept at −80 °C until use. Serum samples were collected from RA patients who fulfilled the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria [1]. Anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) status was determined with a commercial anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP2) ELISA, using the manufacturer's cut-off. Samples were classified as ACPA+ or ACPA−. Sera from ACPA− healthy individuals or OA patients served as controls. All sera were aliquoted and stored at −80 °C, and repeated freeze-thaw cycles were avoided.

**Extraction and purification of proteoglycan**

Cartilage was pulverized in liquid nitrogen and extracted with 4 M guanidine hydrochloride in 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.8) containing a protease inhibitor cocktail, for 48 h at 4 °C [2]. The extracts were dialyzed against distilled water and then against buffer. Proteoglycan (PG) was purified by CsCl density-gradient ultracentrifugation (starting density 1.5 g/mL; 40,000 rpm, 48 h, 15 °C), and the high-density (A1) fraction was collected [2]. Aliquots were deglycosylated with chondroitinase ABC, keratanase and endo-β-galactosidase (0.01–0.1 U/mg PG, 37 °C, 6 h) to expose the core protein and its fragments. Protein concentration was measured by the BCA assay.

**Recombinant human G1 domain and in vitro citrullination**

The recombinant human G1 domain of aggrecan (rhG1) was expressed in a mammalian expression system as a His-tagged protein and purified by nickel-affinity chromatography, as described previously [3]. Purity was checked by SDS-PAGE with Coomassie staining. For in vitro citrullination, rhG1 (and, in parallel, purified native PG) was incubated with rabbit skeletal muscle peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD; 0.1–1 U/mg protein) in 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4) containing 10 mM CaCl₂ and 5 mM DTT for 3 h at 37 °C. Control samples were processed identically without enzyme or without calcium. The reaction was stopped with 20 mM EDTA, and the samples were dialyzed or desalted before use.

**Confirmation of citrullination**

Antibody-based detection used the anti-modified citrulline (AMC) method. Proteins were blotted onto PVDF membranes and chemically modified with 2,3-butanedione monoxime and antipyrine in strongly acidic conditions, in the dark at 37 °C. They were then probed with anti-modified citrulline antibody (Millipore) followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibody [4]. Unmodified membranes were probed with an anti-peptidyl-citrulline antibody. For the chemical method, the colorimetric diacetyl monoxime-thiosemicarbazide assay was used to quantify citrulline in the samples against an L-citrulline standard curve [5]. Absorbance was read at 530 nm.

**Dot blot and Western blot**

For dot blots, 1–5 µg of purified PG, cartilage extract or rhG1 was applied to nitrocellulose membranes. For Western blots, native or deglycosylated samples were separated on 4–12% gradient or 10% SDS-polyacrylamide gels and transferred to PVDF or nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat dry milk or 3% BSA in TBS-Tween and incubated with individual ACPA+ or ACPA− sera (1:100–1:200 dilution) overnight at 4 °C. Bound IgG was detected with HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG and enhanced chemiluminescence. Parallel blots were probed with monoclonal antibodies against the G1 domain (e.g., clone 1C6) and G3 domain, and with anti-His antibody for rhG1, to identify PG fragments. Pre-incubating sera with citrullinated or non-citrullinated peptides or protein was used in selected inhibition experiments. Each experiment was repeated at least three times with different cartilage specimens.

**Molecular modeling of citrullination sites**

The three-dimensional structure of the human aggrecan G1 domain (Ig-fold and two link-module domains) was built by homology modeling with SWISS-MODEL, using the crystal structures of related link-module proteins (such as TSG-6) as templates [6]. Model quality was assessed by QMEAN scores and Ramachandran plots. Solvent accessibility of each arginine residue was calculated with PyMOL and the NACCESS algorithm. Arginines with relative side-chain accessibility above 25% and positioned in flexible or surface loops were considered potential PAD targets. Residues were also compared with known citrullination motifs and with previously described citrullinated epitopes of aggrecan.

**ELISA for CitPG-specific autoantibodies**

Microtiter plates (Nunc MaxiSorp) were coated overnight at 4 °C with 1 µg/well rhG1, citrullinated rhG1 (CitrhG1), or native or citrullinated PG in carbonate buffer (pH 9.6). After blocking with 1% BSA, sera (1:100 dilution, in duplicate) were added for 2 h at room temperature. Bound IgG was detected with HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG and TMB substrate, and absorbance was read at 450 nm. Background signal from uncoated wells was subtracted. Reactivity to CitrhG1 was compared with reactivity to unmodified rhG1. A positive result was defined as an optical density exceeding the mean plus 3 SD of the healthy control sera. Inter-assay variability was controlled using a reference serum on each plate.

**Immunohistochemistry**

Cartilage samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, decalcified where bone was attached, and embedded in paraffin. Sections (5 µm) were deparaffinized and rehydrated, and antigen retrieval was performed with chondroitinase ABC digestion (0.1 U/mL, 1 h, 37 °C). Endogenous peroxidase was quenched with 3% H₂O₂, and sections were blocked with 5% normal goat serum. Sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with pooled or individual ACPA+ sera (1:50–1:100), or with a commercial anti-citrullinated protein antibody. Controls included ACPA− serum, omission of primary antibody, and ACPA+ serum pre-absorbed with citrullinated rhG1. Detection used biotinylated secondary antibody, an avidin-biotin-peroxidase complex and DAB, with hematoxylin counterstaining. Sections were evaluated by two independent observers blinded to diagnosis. Staining was scored semi-quantitatively (0–3) in the superficial, middle and deep zones and in the pericellular, territorial and interterritorial matrix.

**Statistical analysis**

Data are presented as mean ± SD or median (interquartile range), as appropriate. Group comparisons used the Mann–Whitney U test or Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc correction. Paired reactivities (rhG1 vs. CitrhG1) were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Correlations were assessed by Spearman's coefficient. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism, and P < 0.05 was considered significant.

**Reactivity of ACPA+ RA sera with PG purified from normal human cartilage**

To determine whether PG is citrullinated in vivo, PG was purified from extracts of normal human articular cartilage and probed by dot blot with sera from ACPA+ RA patients, ACPA– RA patients, and healthy controls. All ACPA+ sera tested produced clear signals with the purified PG, and signal intensity increased with the amount of PG applied. Signals obtained with ACPA– or control sera were at or near background. Treatment of the PG with chondroitinase ABC, keratanase, and endo-β-galactosidase to remove glycosaminoglycan chains did not abolish ACPA+ reactivity. This indicates that the recognized epitopes reside in the core protein and are not masked by, or dependent on, the glycosaminoglycan side chains.

**Identification of citrullinated PG fragments in OA and RA cartilage extracts**

Cartilage extracts from OA and RA patients were deglycosylated, separated by SDS-PAGE, and analyzed by Western blotting. ACPA+ sera recognized multiple PG fragments in both OA and RA extracts. The most prominent bands had molecular masses consistent with fragments containing the G1 domain, as confirmed by reprobing with an anti-G1 monoclonal antibody. Reactive bands of higher apparent mass, consistent with the intact core protein, were weaker and less consistently seen. The band patterns varied among specimens, probably reflecting differences in the extent of in vivo proteolytic fragmentation. Serum from an ACPA– individual showed no specific reactivity with any extract. Omitting the primary serum or using secondary antibody alone also gave no signal. Thus citrullinated PG (CitPG) fragments were detectable in both degenerative and inflammatory arthritic cartilage. Because normal cartilage PG was also recognized in dot blots, citrullination is not unique to diseased tissue.

**Confirmation of in vitro citrullination of recombinant human G1 domain**

To obtain a defined substrate, rhG1 was citrullinated in vitro with peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD). Citrullination was verified by two independent approaches. First, after chemical modification of the blotted proteins with 2,3-butanedione monoxime/antipyrine under acidic conditions, a method that detects ureido groups, the PAD-treated rhG1 was detected with an anti-modified citrulline antibody. Untreated rhG1 gave no signal. Second, the PAD-treated rhG1 reacted with an anti-citrulline antibody, whereas the untreated protein did not. Coomassie staining showed that PAD treatment did not noticeably degrade the protein, and the loading of the two preparations was equivalent.

ACPA+ sera reacted strongly with citrullinated rhG1 and only weakly, if at all, with the unmodified protein. ACPA– sera did not distinguish between the two forms. The same pattern was seen with several individual ACPA+ sera, although titers differed among patients. A G3 domain-containing PG fragment also reacted with ACPA+ sera after citrullination. Thus citrullinated epitopes are present in at least two globular domains of PG.

**Molecular modeling of potential citrullination sites in the G1 domain**

A structural model of the human G1 domain, comprising the Ig-like, link module A, and link module B subdomains, was used to assess which arginine residues might be accessible to PAD. Of the arginine residues in the domain, a subset lay in solvent-exposed loops or flexible regions that could be accommodated in the PAD active site. Others were buried within the β-sheet core or engaged in salt bridges and appeared unlikely to be modified in the native fold. The exposed candidates were distributed across all three subdomains, with several clustered in the link-module regions. Conversion of these residues to citrulline in silico removed positive charges and altered local electrostatic surfaces without major changes in backbone conformation. These results suggest that multiple sites within G1 can be citrullinated and could contribute to the polyclonal ACPA response against PG. The model does not identify which sites are modified in vivo.

**Serum autoantibodies against citrullinated PG**

Serum reactivity was quantified by ELISA using plates coated with citrullinated or unmodified rhG1. Sera from ACPA+ RA patients had significantly higher IgG reactivity with citrullinated rhG1 than with unmodified rhG1 (paired comparison, *p* < 0.01). Reactivity with citrullinated rhG1 was also significantly higher in ACPA+ RA sera than in ACPA– RA sera and healthy control sera, which did not differ from each other. Reactivity with unmodified rhG1 was low in all groups. A subset of ACPA+ sera had high anti-CitPG levels, whereas others had modest levels, which indicates heterogeneity in the anti-CitPG response among ACPA+ patients. Reactivity with citrullinated rhG1 correlated positively with anti-CCP titers, but the correlation was incomplete, so anti-CCP levels alone did not predict anti-CitPG reactivity.

**Immunohistochemical localization of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage**

CitPG was localized in cartilage sections using ACPA-derived reactivity and anti-citrulline detection, with appropriate negative controls (ACPA– serum, omission of primary antibody, and sections pretreated with PAD inhibitor or preabsorbed with unmodified antigen). In OA cartilage, staining was mainly in the superficial and upper middle zones. It was concentrated in the pericellular and territorial matrix around chondrocytes, particularly in fibrillated regions and in clusters of proliferating chondrocytes. The deep zone was weakly stained or negative. In RA cartilage, staining was more widespread and intense. It extended through the middle and deep zones, and in many specimens it was strongest in the interterritorial matrix and near the pannus–cartilage junction and eroded surfaces. Intracellular staining of chondrocytes was also seen in some RA samples. Negative controls produced no specific staining. Specimens from different individuals within each disease group showed variability in the extent of staining, but the difference in distribution between OA and RA cartilage was consistent across the samples examined.

**Citrullinated aggrecan as a cartilage autoantigen**

This study shows that the cartilage proteoglycan (PG) aggrecan is citrullinated in vivo in human articular cartilage and that citrulline-containing neoepitopes are recognized by autoantibodies in ACPA+ RA sera. Earlier work established that T cells from RA patients respond to citrullinated aggrecan epitopes and that the PG-induced arthritis model depends on autoimmunity to this molecule [1,2]. What was missing was evidence that citrullinated PG (CitPG) exists in joint tissue as a target. Our findings help fill this gap. They add CitPG to the list of citrullinated joint proteins, which includes fibrinogen, vimentin, α-enolase, type II collagen, and histones [3–5].

**Citrullination in normal and diseased cartilage**

CitPG was detectable in normal cartilage as well as in OA and RA specimens. This suggests that peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) activity operates at low levels in healthy tissue. Possible contributors include ageing, mechanical stress, local calcium fluctuations, and chondrocyte turnover, all of which can activate PADs or alter protein conformation [6,7]. Citrullination is therefore not specific to RA. Others have reported citrullinated proteins in non-RA synovium and in OA, and ACPA reactivity is not absolute evidence of a disease-specific process [8]. The pathogenic potential of CitPG likely depends on the immunological context. Genetic susceptibility, such as HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles that bind citrullinated peptides with high affinity, and a loss of tolerance determine whether citrullinated self-antigens in cartilage become targets [9]. Cartilage is avascular and was long considered immunologically sequestered. Joint damage and inflammation can expose such tissue-resident antigens to the immune system and promote epitope spreading.

The different immunohistochemical localization of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage may reflect disease-specific regulation. The distribution of PAD enzymes, inflammatory cytokines, proteolytic aggrecan degradation, and altered chondrocyte metabolism could all influence where citrullinated epitopes accumulate. We did not establish the cause of these differences, and they should be interpreted cautiously. Functional studies of PAD expression in cartilage zones will be needed.

**Domain specificity and structural considerations**

ACPA+ sera mainly recognized G1-containing fragments, and also a G3-containing fragment. The G1 domain lies at the N-terminus of aggrecan and anchors the molecule to hyaluronan, and it contains many arginine residues. Molecular modeling indicated that multiple solvent-accessible arginines within G1 could be converted to citrulline. Conversion removes a positive charge and may alter folding, hyaluronan binding, or susceptibility to proteolysis, as has been described for other citrullinated proteins [10]. Such changes might affect matrix integrity and also generate fragments with new antigenic properties. Because G1-containing fragments are long-lived and accumulate in cartilage, they could serve as a persistent antigen reservoir. G3 reactivity indicates that more than one region of aggrecan carries citrullinated epitopes, although we did not map the precise residues. Modeling is predictive and does not prove that particular arginines are citrullinated in vivo. Mass spectrometric site identification in tissue-derived PG is the logical next step.

**Possible pathogenic mechanisms**

ACPA are present years before clinical RA onset, and their fine specificity broadens as disease approaches [11]. If anti-CitPG antibodies bind cartilage-resident antigen, they may form immune complexes on the cartilage surface or within the matrix. Such complexes could activate complement and engage Fcγ receptors on macrophages, neutrophils, and synovial cells, driving cytokine release and cartilage degradation. This is consistent with data showing that ACPA against citrullinated type II collagen enhance arthritis in mice and that ACPA can stimulate osteoclastogenesis [12,13]. Immune complexes containing CitPG could also promote antigen presentation, supporting activation of CitPG-specific T cells and reinforcing the T- and B-cell collaboration that drives autoantibody production. Because aggrecan fragments are released into synovial fluid during cartilage turnover, soluble CitPG may form complexes in the joint space as well. We emphasize that our data show reactivity and localization, not causation. Whether anti-CitPG antibodies are pathogenic remains to be tested by passive transfer or immunization experiments.

**Limitations**

Several limitations apply. The number of cartilage specimens and sera was limited, and donor heterogeneity in age, disease duration, and treatment may have affected CitPG content. ACPA+ sera are polyclonal and may cross-react with other citrullinated proteins, so reactivity cannot be attributed uniquely to CitPG without competition or absorption controls. Antibody-based detection of citrulline depends on epitope context and may under- or overestimate modification. In vitro citrullination of rhG1 with exogenous PAD may not reproduce the pattern generated in tissue. Finally, immunohistochemistry is semi-quantitative, and the differences between OA and RA need confirmation in larger, well-characterized cohorts.

**Conclusions and future directions**

CitPG is a newly identified citrullinated autoantigen present in normal and diseased human cartilage and recognized by ACPA+ RA sera, principally through the G1 domain. Its presence in cartilage, together with the known T-cell reactivity to citrullinated aggrecan epitopes, supports a model in which cartilage-derived CitPG contributes to local immune complex formation and perpetuation of autoimmunity in ACPA+ RA. Future work should define the citrullinated residues by mass spectrometry, determine which PAD isoforms modify aggrecan, assess anti-CitPG antibody levels in large RA cohorts and in pre-clinical individuals for diagnostic or prognostic value, and test the pathogenicity of these antibodies in vivo. Clarifying these points may identify new targets for antigen-specific or PAD-directed therapy.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have moved from specialized military platforms to widely available tools for civilian applications, including surveillance, agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and emergency response [1], [2]. In disaster operations, UAVs are especially attractive because they can be deployed quickly, can reach areas that are dangerous or inaccessible to ground crews, and can provide situational awareness within the critical first hours after an event such as an earthquake, flood, or wildfire [3]. As the cost of small multirotor and fixed-wing platforms decreases, attention has turned from the operation of a single vehicle to the coordinated use of many vehicles. Swarms of UAVs can cover large areas in parallel, provide redundancy against individual vehicle failures, and support tasks such as search and rescue, damage assessment, and communication relay [4], [5].

Despite these advantages, operating multiple UAVs introduces substantial challenges for human operators. A single operator supervising several vehicles must manage task allocation, monitor vehicle states, interpret sensor data, and respond to changing conditions, often under time pressure and stress [6]. The design of effective user interfaces and operating procedures for such multi-vehicle systems remains an open research problem, and poor interface design has been linked to reduced operator performance and an increased risk of mishaps [7]. Training personnel to use these systems is similarly demanding. Real-world flight tests are expensive, weather dependent, and constrained by regulations, and they may place vehicles, bystanders, and property at risk. Disaster scenarios in particular are difficult to reproduce safely and repeatably in the field.

Simulation offers a practical means of addressing these limitations. Simulated environments allow researchers to prototype and compare interface designs, evaluate human-swarm interaction strategies, and train operators in a controlled and repeatable setting at low cost [8]. A variety of simulators have been developed for robotics and UAV research, including Gazebo, AirSim, and others built on general-purpose game or physics engines [9], [10]. These tools often provide high-fidelity physics and sensor models, but they can be complex to configure and are not always oriented toward the study of operator interaction with large teams of vehicles in disaster response contexts. Conversely, simulators designed for human-in-the-loop studies and training frequently simplify vehicle dynamics, for example by allowing vehicles to move instantaneously between positions or to follow idealized straight-line paths at constant speed. Such simplifications can be adequate for studying high-level decision making, but they may give operators an inaccurate impression of how real vehicles respond to commands. The result is a gap between simulated and real operation, which can lead to negative training transfer and to interface designs that perform well in simulation but poorly in the field [11].

The Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) was developed to support research on human interaction with swarms of UAVs in search-and-rescue and disaster scenarios. It provides a virtual environment in which an operator can issue commands to multiple simulated vehicles, view imagery and sensor information, and carry out mission tasks such as locating survivors. However, the motion of vehicles in the original simulator was represented in a simplified manner, which limited the realism of the user experience and the applicability of findings to real systems. Because the perceived responsiveness, turning behavior, and path-following characteristics of a UAV strongly influence how operators plan and issue commands, more faithful motion models are an important step toward a useful training and prototyping platform [12].

In this paper, we present the integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator. Waypoint navigation is a common method of commanding UAVs, in which an operator or planner specifies a sequence of positions that the vehicle must visit, and an onboard controller computes the control inputs required to follow the path [13]. Model-based controllers use a mathematical representation of vehicle dynamics to compute these inputs, producing motion that reflects physical constraints such as limited acceleration, finite turning rates, and inertia. By embedding such a controller within the simulator, vehicles respond to operator commands in a manner more consistent with real platforms, and the interface through which operators assign waypoints becomes a more representative model of actual ground control systems.

The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we describe the design and implementation of a waypoint navigation controller based on a dynamic model of the UAV and its integration into the architecture of the Reno Rescue Simulator, including the interface between the user-facing components and the vehicle control layer. Second, we show how the controller supports simultaneous operation of multiple vehicles, enabling swarm-level scenarios relevant to disaster operations. Third, we discuss potential uses of the resulting simulator, including interface prototyping, operator training, mission rehearsal, and human-subject experimentation. We also consider how such a simulator might support real-world UAV operations, for instance by allowing operators to preview planned missions, anticipate vehicle behavior, and test contingency plans before committing physical assets to a hazardous environment.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on UAV simulation, swarm control, and human-swarm interaction. Section III describes the Reno Rescue Simulator and the motion control model. Section IV details the integration of the controller and presents example scenarios. Section V discusses applications and limitations, and Section VI concludes with directions for future work.

The Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) was used as the base platform for this work. RRS is a multi-agent, game-engine-based environment in which an operator supervises a team of simulated UAVs performing search-and-rescue tasks in a disaster scenario [1]. In its original form, UAV motion in RRS was kinematic: each vehicle moved toward its assigned target at a constant speed with instantaneous heading changes. We replaced this with a model-based waypoint navigation controller so that vehicle behavior reflects the dynamic constraints of real multirotor aircraft. The methods below describe the simulator architecture, the vehicle dynamics model, the controller design, the swarm-level integration, and the evaluation procedure.

**Simulator Architecture**

RRS is organized into three layers: a scenario layer that defines terrain, hazards, and victim locations; an agent layer that holds the state and behavior of each UAV; and a user interface layer that presents a map view and accepts operator commands such as placing waypoints, assigning search regions, and selecting individual or grouped vehicles. The simulation advances in fixed time steps of 10 ms for physics and control updates, while rendering and interface updates run at the display frame rate. Decoupling these rates keeps numerical integration stable regardless of rendering load. The new controller was implemented as a replaceable module within the agent layer, so that the original kinematic model and the new dynamic model could be switched without altering the scenario or interface layers.

**Vehicle Dynamics Model**

Each UAV was modeled as a quadrotor rigid body with twelve states: position **p** = [x, y, z], velocity **v**, Euler angles (roll φ, pitch θ, yaw ψ), and body angular rates **ω**. Translational dynamics follow Newton's second law,

m**v̇** = m**g** + R(φ,θ,ψ)[0, 0, T]ᵀ − **D**,

where m is mass, T is total thrust, R is the body-to-world rotation matrix, and **D** is a linear drag term proportional to velocity. Rotational dynamics follow Euler's equations with a diagonal inertia matrix. Parameters (mass, arm length, inertia, maximum thrust, and drag coefficient) were set to values representative of a commercially available small quadrotor platform [2]. Actuator limits were enforced by saturating thrust and commanded torques, and first-order motor lag was included to prevent unrealistically abrupt control changes. Optional wind disturbance was modeled as a steady component plus a low-pass-filtered stochastic gust added to the drag term [3].

**Waypoint Navigation Controller**

The controller uses a standard cascaded structure [2], [4]. An outer position loop computes a desired acceleration from the position and velocity errors relative to the active waypoint:

**a**_des = K_p(**p**_wp − **p**) + K_d(**v**_des − **v**) + **g**,

where **v**_des is limited to a maximum cruise speed. The desired acceleration is converted to a thrust magnitude and desired roll and pitch angles using a small-angle approximation about the commanded yaw. An inner attitude loop applies proportional-derivative control to track the desired angles and yaw rate, producing body torques. Gains were initially selected by pole placement on the linearized model and then tuned in simulation to give a damped response with limited overshoot (below 5% of step distance) and no sustained oscillation.

Waypoint sequencing was handled by a finite-state machine with states for idle, takeoff, transit, hold, and landing. A waypoint was considered reached when the UAV was within an acceptance radius of 1.0 m and its speed fell below a threshold; for intermediate waypoints in a path, only the radius condition was required, which allowed smoother pass-through behavior. Operator-defined paths were smoothed by limiting the commanded speed according to the turn angle at each waypoint, reducing the speed approaching sharp turns.
