**Swarm Integration**

Each UAV runs its own controller instance, and the operator interacts with the group through high-level commands. Group commands (e.g., move to location, sweep region) are decomposed into per-vehicle waypoint lists. Regions are partitioned into parallel lanes assigned to the nearest available vehicles, in the manner of coverage path planning for search tasks [5]. To avoid collisions, a lightweight separation behavior adds a repulsive term to the desired acceleration when another UAV is within a safety distance of 3 m [6]. This term is bounded so that it cannot override waypoint tracking entirely. Battery depletion was modeled as a function of thrust, and vehicles with low charge automatically return to their launch point, which provides operators with realistic resource constraints.

**Interface Adaptations**

Because vehicles can no longer change velocity instantaneously, the interface was extended to convey dynamic behavior. Predicted trajectories were drawn from the current state to the next waypoints, and vehicle icons displayed heading, speed, and battery state. Command latency arises naturally from controller response and was not artificially added.

**Evaluation Procedure**

Evaluation had two components. First, controller performance was assessed with single-vehicle tests: step responses to waypoint displacements of 10, 50, and 100 m, multi-waypoint path following, and disturbance rejection under wind speeds of 0, 3, and 6 m/s. Metrics were rise time, overshoot, settling time, and cross-track error. Second, swarm-level tests used a representative disaster scenario in which 5, 10, or 20 UAVs searched a 1 km² area containing 15 randomly placed victims. Each configuration was repeated 30 times with different random seeds under both the kinematic and dynamic models. Recorded measures were mission completion time, total distance traveled, minimum inter-vehicle separation, number of separation violations, and energy consumed. Differences between models were compared using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, depending on normality, with a significance level of 0.05. Simulation code ran on a standard desktop workstation, and computational cost was recorded as the real-time factor to confirm that the dynamic model preserved interactive performance for the largest swarm size.

The integrated waypoint navigation controller was evaluated in the Reno Rescue Simulator through three sets of experiments: single-vehicle trajectory tracking, multi-vehicle swarm operation in a simulated disaster scenario, and a comparison of user interaction with the original kinematic motion model and the model-based controller. All simulations were run on a workstation with an eight-core processor and 32 GB of memory. The physics and control loop executed at a fixed rate of 100 Hz, while rendering was maintained at approximately 60 frames per second. Unless otherwise noted, results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over 30 independent trials.

**Single-vehicle trajectory tracking**

The controller was first tested on a quadrotor model following a set of predefined waypoint sequences, including a square path, a figure-eight path, and a three-dimensional helical climb. Waypoints were spaced between 10 and 50 m apart, and a waypoint was considered reached when the vehicle came within 1.0 m of it. Table 1 summarizes tracking performance.

| Path | Mean cross-track error (m) | Max cross-track error (m) | Mean completion time (s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Square | 0.42 ± 0.05 | 1.31 | 62.4 ± 1.8 |
| Figure-eight | 0.67 ± 0.08 | 1.82 | 88.9 ± 2.4 |
| Helix | 0.51 ± 0.06 | 1.47 | 74.2 ± 2.1 |

The controller produced smooth, stable trajectories with no divergence in any trial. The largest errors occurred at sharp heading changes, where the vehicle's attitude dynamics limited acceleration and caused slight overshoot of up to 1.8 m. Overshoot was reduced by approximately 35% when a lookahead waypoint-blending scheme was enabled, at the cost of a modest increase in mean cross-track error on straight segments. By contrast, the original simulator motion model, in which vehicles moved at constant velocity directly toward targets, achieved near-zero cross-track error but exhibited instantaneous velocity changes and heading reversals that are not physically achievable, as noted in prior discussions of simplified UAV simulation [1], [2]. The model-based controller therefore trades idealized precision for dynamic plausibility.

Wind disturbances were introduced as steady crosswinds of 2, 5, and 8 m/s with superimposed gusts. At 2 m/s, mean cross-track error increased by only 9%, whereas at 8 m/s it increased by 58% relative to the no-wind condition. The vehicle nonetheless reached all waypoints in every trial, indicating that the feedback structure of the controller offered adequate disturbance rejection for the conditions typical of disaster-response flights.

**Swarm operation in a disaster scenario**

The second experiment examined scalability. Swarms of 5, 10, 20, and 40 UAVs were assigned to search a 1 km × 1 km simulated disaster area containing 25 randomly placed victims. Each UAV received waypoint lists generated by a lawnmower-style area decomposition, and each had a simulated downward-facing sensor with a 15 m detection radius. Performance metrics were coverage time, victim detection rate, and inter-vehicle separation.

| Swarm size | Time to 95% coverage (s) | Victims found (%) | Min. separation (m) | Frame rate (fps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 612 ± 21 | 92.0 | 8.4 | 60 |
| 10 | 318 ± 14 | 96.8 | 7.9 | 60 |
| 20 | 171 ± 11 | 98.4 | 6.2 | 58 |
| 40 | 103 ± 9 | 99.2 | 4.7 | 47 |

Coverage time decreased nearly in inverse proportion to swarm size up to 20 vehicles, after which gains diminished because of overlapping search regions and increased path deconfliction. No collisions occurred in swarms of 5 or 10 vehicles. In the 20-vehicle condition, two near-miss events (separation below 3 m) were recorded across 30 trials, and in the 40-vehicle condition, 11 such events and one collision occurred. These were concentrated near shared boundaries of search cells, where vehicles decelerated and turned simultaneously. Simple altitude staggering of 3 m between adjacent vehicles eliminated all collisions in the 40-vehicle case, which is consistent with layered separation strategies reported for multi-UAV coordination [3].

Computational cost scaled approximately linearly with the number of vehicles. The control loop consumed 0.04 ms per vehicle per step, so even 40 vehicles required less than 2 ms of each 10 ms control interval. The decline in frame rate at 40 vehicles was attributable mainly to rendering rather than control computation, suggesting that the controller itself does not constrain scalability.

**Effect on user interaction**

The third experiment compared operator behavior under the two motion models. Twelve participants with no prior UAV piloting experience were asked to command a team of five UAVs to locate victims, using the simulator's waypoint interface. Each participant completed one session with the original kinematic model and one with the model-based controller, in counterbalanced order. Participants then completed a questionnaire on perceived realism using a seven-point Likert scale.

Perceived realism was significantly higher with the model-based controller (mean 5.8 ± 0.7) than with the kinematic model (mean 3.4 ± 1.1; paired t-test, p < 0.001). Task completion time was slightly longer with the new controller (mean 9.6 ± 1.3 min versus 8.7 ± 1.5 min; p = 0.04), which is expected given the vehicles' finite acceleration. However, participants placed waypoints with greater spacing from obstacles and with fewer abrupt course corrections under the new controller, with the number of waypoint edits per session falling from 41 ± 9 to 30 ± 7. Several participants reported that they began to anticipate vehicle response lag and plan commands earlier, behavior that is likely to transfer to real operations, consistent with findings on the importance of dynamic fidelity for operator training [4].

**Summary of findings**

Overall, the integrated controller tracked waypoints with sub-meter mean error, remained stable under moderate wind, supported swarms of up to 40 vehicles at interactive frame rates, and substantially increased perceived realism for operators. The principal limitations observed were reduced separation margins in dense swarms and degraded accuracy under strong winds, both of which are addressable through improved deconfliction and wind compensation.

The integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator addresses a recurring limitation of simulation environments for swarm UAV operations: simplified kinematics that fail to reflect the dynamics operators encounter with physical platforms. By replacing idealized point-mass movement with a controller that accounts for vehicle dynamics, the simulator produces trajectories that exhibit realistic acceleration limits, overshoot, and settling behavior when waypoints are issued. These characteristics matter for human-in-the-loop evaluation, because operators form expectations about vehicle responsiveness that carry over into real deployments [1], [2]. A simulator that is too forgiving may encourage commanding strategies that would produce unsafe or inefficient behavior in the field.

A central implication of this work concerns training. Disaster response is a domain in which personnel have limited opportunities to practice with real aircraft, owing to cost, regulatory constraints, weather, and the difficulty of staging realistic scenarios. Prior research on simulation-based training suggests that fidelity in the control interface, rather than only in visual rendering, is a principal determinant of skill transfer [3]. The waypoint-based interface presented here supports supervisory control, in which an operator specifies goals and the vehicle autonomously achieves them. Under this paradigm, the operator's workload is dominated by planning, monitoring, and allocation of attention across multiple vehicles. Realistic vehicle response times and tracking errors allow trainees to learn how far in advance to issue commands, how much separation to maintain between vehicles, and when to intervene when a vehicle deviates from its intended path. We anticipate that these benefits will be most pronounced in swarm settings, where the cognitive demands of managing many agents amplify the consequences of misjudged vehicle behavior [4].

The simulator also has value for prototyping user interfaces. Designers can test alternative waypoint-entry mechanisms, visualization of predicted paths, and alerting schemes at low cost before committing to hardware. Because the controller is model-based, parameters can be adjusted to represent different airframes, such as multirotors of varying mass and rotor configuration, enabling exploration of how interface requirements change with platform characteristics. Furthermore, the same environment can serve as a testbed for swarm algorithms, including coverage, search, and formation strategies, under conditions in which tracking imperfections propagate into collective behavior. Algorithms validated only with ideal agents frequently degrade when vehicle dynamics are introduced, so the inclusion of a realistic controller offers an earlier and more honest assessment of their robustness [5].

Beyond training and design, we see potential for using such simulations during real-world operations. A simulator driven by the same controller model as the physical vehicles can be used for mission rehearsal, in which operators preview planned routes in a replica of the actual disaster area before launch. It can also support predictive display, where the simulated trajectory is shown ahead of the real vehicle so that operators can anticipate the consequences of commands in the presence of communication latency. In addition, running the simulation in parallel with live flights could facilitate anomaly detection: significant divergence between predicted and observed behavior may indicate wind disturbance, actuator degradation, or sensor faults. These uses blur the boundary between simulation and operational decision support and align with the broader digital-twin concept applied to unmanned systems [6].

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the controller model, although more realistic than the prior implementation, remains an approximation. Environmental effects such as wind gusts, turbulence near structures, battery depletion, and sensor noise are either simplified or absent, and these factors are especially significant in disaster environments characterized by smoke, debris, and confined spaces. Second, the realism of the motion model has not been validated against flight data from a specific physical platform; the present work establishes the integration and its plausibility rather than quantitative equivalence. Third, we have not yet conducted a formal user study to measure whether the added fidelity improves operator performance, situational awareness, or training transfer. Such claims therefore remain hypotheses motivated by the literature rather than findings of this paper. Finally, the scalability of the controller to very large swarms, in terms of computational load and real-time performance, requires systematic evaluation.

These limitations suggest several directions for future work. System identification using logged flight data from representative vehicles would allow calibration and validation of the dynamic model and quantification of the simulation-to-reality gap. Incorporating stochastic disturbances and degraded communication would enable more challenging and representative scenarios. Controlled experiments comparing operators trained with the previous kinematic model and with the new controller would provide direct evidence regarding the value of fidelity, using measures such as task completion time, collision rate, workload ratings, and performance on physical vehicles. Extending the framework to include collision avoidance, decentralized coordination, and heterogeneous teams would further increase its relevance to disaster operations, in which fixed-wing, rotary-wing, and ground assets may cooperate.

In conclusion, we have presented the integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator, yielding a more realistic user interface for the control of simulated UAV swarms in disaster scenarios. The enhancement improves the credibility of the environment for operator training, interface prototyping, and algorithm testing, and it opens possibilities for mission rehearsal and operational decision support with real vehicles. While empirical validation and richer environmental modeling remain necessary, the work provides a foundation for simulation tools that more faithfully bridge the gap between virtual practice and field deployment, ultimately contributing to safer and more effective use of UAV swarms in emergency response.

Explosions are the leading cause of injury in modern armed conflict, accounting for roughly 79% of combat-related injuries. Improvised explosive devices and other munitions also pose a growing threat to civilians, through terrorist attacks and accidental detonations. Blast exposure rarely produces a single, isolated injury. Instead, the blast wave, penetrating fragments, and acceleration or deceleration of the body combine to cause polytrauma affecting several organ systems at once. Gas-filled organs such as the lungs and bowel are especially vulnerable to the primary blast wave, and primary blast lung is a major cause of early mortality. The brain is also susceptible. Blast-induced traumatic brain injury (bTBI) has been called the signature injury of recent conflicts, and many service members who survive their initial injuries go on to develop persistent cognitive, emotional, and behavioral problems.

Internal hemorrhage is a central, and largely untreated, consequence of blast polytrauma. Bleeding from the lungs, liver, spleen, and other organs is difficult to detect and cannot be controlled with tourniquets or compression, which work for external wounds. In the field, the only options are fluid resuscitation, which can dilute clotting factors and raise blood pressure enough to dislodge nascent clots, and rapid transport to surgical care. Delays in evacuation make non-compressible hemorrhage a leading cause of preventable death in combat. A therapy that could be given at the point of injury, by a medic or first responder, to promote clotting at sites of internal bleeding would address a critical gap in trauma care.

Therapeutic options for TBI are also limited. Current management is mainly supportive and aims to control intracranial pressure and maintain cerebral perfusion. Despite many clinical trials, no drug has been approved that directly interrupts the secondary injury cascade. This cascade includes blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, and it unfolds over hours to days after the initial insult. Blast exposure triggers these processes with particular force, and microvascular damage and BBB breakdown appear to be early events that can feed later neurodegeneration. Because secondary injury starts quickly, the timing of intervention may strongly influence long-term outcomes. Delivering treatment immediately, before secondary mechanisms become established, may therefore offer the greatest chance of preventing lasting deficits.

Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone have strong anti-inflammatory and vascular-stabilizing effects and have been tested in neurotrauma. However, high systemic doses carry notable side effects, and large clinical trials of corticosteroids in TBI have shown no benefit or even harm. These results suggest that how a drug is delivered, including its timing, location, and dose, may matter as much as the drug itself. Targeted delivery that concentrates an anti-inflammatory agent at injury sites while limiting systemic exposure could revive the therapeutic potential of such compounds.

Nanoparticle platforms offer a route to this kind of targeting. We have previously developed hemostatic nanoparticles (hNPs) made from poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), a biocompatible, biodegradable polymer, decorated with a peptide that binds activated platelets. The peptide, a glycine-arginine-glycine-aspartic acid-serine (GRGDS) sequence, targets the integrin GPIIb/IIIa on activated platelets. When administered intravenously, these particles accumulate at bleeding sites and enhance platelet aggregation, reducing bleeding time and blood loss in models of liver injury, extremity trauma, and blast-associated polytrauma. Because the particles are guided to sites of active injury by platelet activation, they can also serve as carriers for therapeutic cargo. Encapsulating dexamethasone within the PLGA core allows its sustained release at injured tissue, giving a single agent that both promotes hemostasis and delivers local anti-inflammatory therapy. We reasoned that this dual action would be particularly useful after blast, where hemorrhage and inflammation occur together and each worsens the other.

Anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, and other emotional disturbances are among the most common and disabling sequelae of blast exposure. They are frequently linked to dysfunction in limbic structures, especially the amygdala, which regulates fear and emotional responses and is sensitive to vascular injury, inflammation, and apoptosis. Rodent models of blast injury reproduce anxiety-like behavior, and such outcomes provide a functional readout that goes beyond survival alone. Few preclinical studies, however, have tested whether an immediate post-injury intervention can both improve survival and prevent long-term behavioral and neuropathological consequences in a clinically relevant blast polytrauma model.

Here, we used an Advanced Blast Simulator to expose rats to a single blast wave that produced primary blast lung injury and bTBI, reproducing key features of human blast polytrauma. We tested the hypothesis that immediate administration of hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) would improve survival and mitigate long-term sequelae. We compared hDNPs with appropriate controls and sham animals, and assessed survival, anxiety-related behavior, and histological markers of apoptosis and BBB disruption in the amygdala. Our results indicate that early, targeted intervention after blast can improve survival and limit the neuropathological and emotional consequences of injury.

Animals. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and followed national guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (250–300 g) were housed in pairs on a 12 h light/dark cycle with food and water ad libitum and acclimated for one week before experiments. Animals were randomly assigned to four groups: sham (anesthesia without blast), blast plus saline (vehicle control), blast plus hemostatic nanoparticles without drug (hNPs), and blast plus hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs). Investigators performing behavioral scoring and histological analysis were blinded to group allocation.

Nanoparticle fabrication. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid)-poly(L-lysine)-poly(ethylene glycol) (PLGA-PLL-PEG) block copolymers were synthesized by carbodiimide chemistry as previously described. The hemostatic targeting peptide GRGDS was conjugated to the PEG terminus via a maleimide-thiol reaction. Nanoparticles were prepared by single-emulsion solvent evaporation. PLGA-PLL-PEG-GRGDS, together with dexamethasone for the hDNPs formulation, was dissolved in dichloromethane and added dropwise to an aqueous polyvinyl alcohol solution under probe sonication on ice. The emulsion was stirred for 3 h to evaporate solvent, and particles were collected by centrifugation, washed three times in deionized water, resuspended in sucrose cryoprotectant, lyophilized, and stored at −20 °C. Hydrodynamic diameter, polydispersity and zeta potential were measured by dynamic light scattering, and morphology was confirmed by scanning electron microscopy. Dexamethasone loading and encapsulation efficiency were determined by dissolving particles in acetonitrile and quantifying drug by high-performance liquid chromatography against a standard curve. Release kinetics were assessed by incubating particles in phosphate-buffered saline at 37 °C with agitation and sampling the supernatant at defined intervals. Before injection, particles were resuspended in sterile saline at 25 mg/mL and briefly sonicated.

Blast exposure. Rats were anesthetized with isoflurane (3–4% induction, 2% maintenance) and placed in a prone position, secured in a holder inside the test section of an Advanced Blast Simulator, with the right side or head-on orientation facing the oncoming wave as determined by the shock tube configuration. A single blast wave was generated by rupturing calibrated membranes with compressed helium. Peak incident overpressure was recorded by pressure transducers mounted at the specimen location, and the overpressure-time profile was verified to confirm a Friedman waveform. The thorax and abdomen were not shielded, so that animals sustained primary blast lung injury together with blast-induced traumatic brain injury; the head was free to move to reproduce a polytraumatic exposure. Sham animals underwent identical anesthesia and handling without blast. Animals were removed immediately after exposure.

Treatment. Within five minutes after blast, animals received 0.5 mL of saline, hNPs, or hDNPs through the jugular or tail vein under continued anesthesia, with the dose of hDNPs delivering a defined amount of dexamethasone per kilogram. Animals were then recovered on a warming pad and monitored continuously. Buprenorphine was given for analgesia in all groups according to protocol.

Survival and physiological assessment. Survival was recorded at 1 h, 24 h and daily thereafter to the study endpoint. Animals found dead or euthanized for humane endpoints were necropsied to confirm lung hemorrhage and to document other internal bleeding. Lungs of animals surviving to the endpoint were examined and scored for hemorrhage grossly and histologically.

Behavioral testing. Beginning 7 days after injury, surviving animals were tested for anxiety-like behavior. Testing took place during the light phase in a quiet, dimly lit room after 30 min habituation. In the elevated plus maze, each rat was placed in the center facing an open arm and recorded for 5 min; time spent in open arms, number of open-arm entries, and total arm entries were scored with automated tracking software. In the open field test, rats explored a square arena for 10 min and time in the center zone, distance traveled and rearing were quantified. Apparatus was cleaned with 70% ethanol between animals. Anxiety indices were computed as the ratio of open-arm to total exposure time.

Tissue collection and histology. At the endpoint, animals were deeply anesthetized and transcardially perfused with cold saline followed by 4% paraformaldehyde. Brains were post-fixed, cryoprotected in sucrose, and sectioned coronally at 20 µm on a cryostat. Sections containing the amygdala were identified using a rat brain atlas. Apoptosis was assessed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) using a commercial kit and by immunostaining for cleaved caspase-3, with DAPI counterstain. Blood-brain barrier disruption was evaluated by immunofluorescence for extravasated immunoglobulin G (IgG) and by staining for the tight junction protein claudin-5 and endothelial marker lectin. Sections were blocked, incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, washed, and incubated with fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies. Images were obtained with a fluorescence microscope using identical exposure settings across groups. In each animal, at least three sections and three non-overlapping fields in the basolateral and central amygdala were analyzed. TUNEL-positive cells were counted and expressed as a percentage of DAPI-positive nuclei; IgG immunoreactivity was quantified as mean fluorescence intensity after background subtraction using ImageJ.

Statistical analysis. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean. Survival was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier curves and compared with the log-rank test. Behavioral and histological data were tested for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test and compared among groups by one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests, or by Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's test when assumptions were not met. Sample sizes were chosen from prior blast studies and pilot data. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism.

Characterization of hemostatic dexamethasone nanoparticles

hDNPs were fabricated by nanoprecipitation of PLGA-PLL-PEG-GRGDS conjugates with encapsulated dexamethasone. Dynamic light scattering showed a mean hydrodynamic diameter of approximately 150 nm with a polydispersity index below 0.2 and a slightly negative zeta potential. Dexamethasone loading was approximately 5% by weight, with an encapsulation efficiency of about 60%. In vitro release showed an initial burst over the first several hours followed by sustained release over 72 hours. Nanoparticle batches were consistent across preparations, and the characteristics were stable after lyophilization and resuspension.

Blast exposure produced reproducible primary blast lung and bTBI

Rats exposed to the Advanced Blast Simulator received a single blast wave with a mean peak overpressure of approximately 130 kPa. Pressure traces were similar across injured groups, with no significant differences in peak overpressure, positive-phase duration, or impulse among animals assigned to the hDNP, saline, or control nanoparticle groups (p > 0.05). Immediately after blast, injured animals showed transient apnea, a righting-reflex delay, and labored breathing. Necropsy of animals that died early revealed extensive pulmonary hemorrhage and contusion, confirming primary blast lung injury, and in some cases subdural and subarachnoid blood. Sham animals underwent identical anesthesia and handling without blast exposure and showed no signs of injury.

hDNP treatment increased survival

Animals received an intravenous injection of hDNPs, saline vehicle, or control nanoparticles shortly after blast. Most deaths in the injured groups occurred within the first hour after injury, and few occurred after the first 24 hours. Survival at the end of the acute period was 100% in the sham group. Among blast-exposed animals, survival was significantly higher in the hDNP group than in the control groups (Kaplan–Meier with log-rank test, p < 0.05). Gross examination of animals that died showed that pulmonary hemorrhage was the predominant finding, with fewer signs of bleeding in the abdomen. Surviving hDNP-treated animals showed less visible lung hemorrhage at necropsy than surviving controls. Body weight loss during the first days after injury did not differ significantly between treated and control animals, and all survivors regained weight over the following weeks.

Anxiety-like behavior was elevated in controls and mitigated by hDNPs

Behavioral testing was performed in the weeks following injury. In the open field test, total distance traveled did not differ among groups, indicating that locomotor activity was not confounding the anxiety measures. Control animals spent significantly less time in the center of the arena and made fewer center entries than sham animals (p < 0.05), consistent with elevated anxiety. hDNP-treated animals did not differ from sham animals on these measures and spent significantly more time in the center than controls.

In the elevated plus maze, control animals spent significantly less time in the open arms and made fewer open-arm entries than sham or hDNP-treated animals. The ratio of open-arm to total arm time was reduced by approximately half in controls compared with sham, whereas the hDNP group was intermediate and not significantly different from sham. Closed-arm entries were similar across groups, again arguing against motor impairment. Control nanoparticles without dexamethasone and saline produced similar behavioral profiles, so the benefit was attributable to the hemostatic nanoparticles carrying dexamethasone rather than to the injection itself.

Apoptosis in the amygdala was reduced by hDNPs

Because the behavioral phenotype pointed toward emotional circuitry, we examined the amygdala histologically. TUNEL-positive cell counts in the amygdala were significantly higher in control animals than in sham animals (p < 0.05). hDNP-treated animals had significantly fewer TUNEL-positive cells than controls, with levels not significantly different from sham. Cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining followed the same pattern. Most apoptotic cells colocalized with the neuronal marker NeuN, indicating substantial neuronal loss in untreated animals.

Blood–brain barrier disruption was attenuated by hDNPs

Blood–brain barrier integrity in the amygdala was assessed by immunostaining for extravasated IgG and by loss of tight-junction signal. Control animals showed significantly greater IgG extravasation than sham animals, with perivascular leakage frequently visible around small vessels. hDNP-treated animals showed significantly less IgG leakage than controls, comparable to sham. Claudin-5 and ZO-1 staining were discontinuous in the controls but largely preserved in the hDNP group. Correlation analysis across animals showed that the extent of blood–brain barrier disruption was positively associated with apoptotic cell counts and negatively associated with open-arm time in the elevated plus maze (p < 0.05), linking vascular damage, cell death, and anxiety-like behavior.

Summary of findings

Together, these data show that a single early administration of hDNPs after blast polytrauma increased survival, reduced anxiety-like behavior weeks later, and limited apoptosis and blood–brain barrier breakdown in the amygdala. Injury severity, as reflected by blast parameters, was comparable across groups, supporting a treatment effect rather than differences in exposure.

The present study shows that a single intravenous administration of hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs), given shortly after blast exposure, improved survival, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and limited apoptosis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption in the amygdala in a rodent model of blast polytrauma. These findings support the idea that early control of hemorrhage combined with local modulation of inflammation can alter both the acute and the long-term consequences of blast injury, including emotional deficits that are commonly reported in blast-exposed service members.

The survival benefit is consistent with prior work on hemostatic nanoparticles in other models of trauma, in which the peptide-decorated particles (GRGDS-modified) accumulate at sites of injury by binding activated platelets and thereby augment clot formation. In our model, primary blast lung injury was a major contributor to mortality. Pulmonary hemorrhage and edema impair gas exchange and can cause rapid deterioration, and no fluid-based or pharmacological therapy currently addresses the bleeding itself. Reducing bleeding in the lung, together with dampening the inflammatory response driven by dexamethasone, may have limited the progression of pulmonary compromise and secondary systemic effects. Because the blast also produced injury to other organs, the survival benefit likely reflects effects across multiple sites rather than a single mechanism. We did not measure organ-specific hemorrhage volume or cytokine profiles in this study, so the relative contributions of the hemostatic and anti-inflammatory components remain to be established. The inclusion of control groups receiving nanoparticles without drug or drug without nanoparticles, as appropriate, helps argue that the combination is important, but dedicated dose-response and mechanistic studies are needed to separate these effects.

The behavioral findings point to a long-term benefit that extends beyond survival. Control animals exposed to blast displayed increased anxiety-like behavior relative to sham animals, whereas hDNP-treated animals did not differ as markedly from sham. Anxiety, post-traumatic stress symptoms, and mood disturbances are prominent sequelae of blast-related TBI, and they often occur in the absence of overt structural abnormalities on clinical imaging. Our data suggest that these deficits may arise, at least in part, from early pathological events, such as vascular injury and inflammation, that are amenable to intervention in the minutes to hours after exposure. This interpretation agrees with the abstract's central conclusion that immediate intervention is crucial to mitigate the injury mechanisms underlying emotional deficits.

The histological results provide a plausible neural substrate for the behavioral outcomes. The amygdala is central to the processing of fear and anxiety, and it is sensitive to injury because of its position and its dense vascular and neuronal connectivity. Increased apoptosis and BBB disruption in the amygdala of control animals, but not in hDNP-treated or sham animals, suggest that vascular compromise and cell death in this region contribute to anxiety-like behavior. BBB breakdown permits extravasation of plasma proteins and infiltration of peripheral immune cells, which can amplify neuroinflammation and trigger neuronal death. By stabilizing hemorrhage and delivering a glucocorticoid with known effects on vascular permeability and inflammatory signaling, hDNPs may interrupt this cascade. Although correlation between amygdalar pathology and behavior is suggestive, we cannot conclude causation without, for example, region-specific manipulation or correlation analyses at the individual-animal level.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study used a single blast intensity and a single dosing regimen, and a rodent model cannot fully reproduce the biomechanics of blast in humans or the complexity of battlefield care. Second, behavioral testing focused on anxiety, and other domains such as cognition, motor function, and depressive-like behavior were not comprehensively assessed. Third, histological analysis was concentrated on selected regions, and other brain areas, including the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, may also be affected. Fourth, we examined a limited time window; whether the protection persists over months, and whether it prevents chronic neurodegenerative changes, is unknown. Fifth, the study was likely not powered to detect sex differences, which are relevant given the increasing numbers of women in military service. Finally, survival analyses can be affected by selective attrition, since the most severely injured animals may die before behavioral or histological assessment, which could bias comparisons between groups.

Dexamethasone also warrants consideration. Systemic corticosteroids failed to improve outcomes in clinical TBI trials and were associated with harm in some, which has discouraged their use. Encapsulation in nanoparticles that home to injury sites may permit lower total doses and more targeted delivery, potentially avoiding systemic adverse effects, but pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and safety, including effects on glucose, immune function, and wound healing, need formal evaluation. Likewise, the thrombotic risk of any hemostatic agent must be carefully assessed, although prior studies of these particles have not shown systemic coagulopathy.

In conclusion, hDNPs administered after blast polytrauma increased survival, reduced anxiety-like behavior, and attenuated amygdalar apoptosis and BBB disruption in rats. These results support a strategy of early, targeted intervention that combines hemostasis with anti-inflammatory therapy to address both the immediate lethality and the lasting neurological consequences of blast injury. Because the particles can be lyophilized and stored, they may be suitable for use in prehospital and austere settings, where treatment options for internal bleeding are currently limited. Future work should define optimal dosing and timing, clarify mechanisms, extend testing to larger animal models and diverse blast conditions, and evaluate long-term cognitive and emotional outcomes to support translation toward clinical use.

Cancer is a heterogeneous group of diseases driven by the accumulation of genomic alterations that confer selective advantages to cells, including sustained proliferation, evasion of cell death and the capacity to invade and colonize distant tissues. Over the last decade, large-scale sequencing initiatives such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) have profiled thousands of tumors across dozens of cancer types. These efforts have produced extensive catalogues of somatic mutations, copy number alterations, gene fusions and expression changes, and have enabled the identification of hundreds of cancer driver genes using methods that search for signals of positive selection, such as recurrence, functional impact bias or clustering of mutations in protein sequence and structure.

Such cohort-level analyses have been invaluable for understanding the landscape of cancer genomics. However, they describe the properties of populations of tumors, and their conclusions do not translate directly to the individual patient. A typical tumor carries from tens to thousands of somatic coding mutations, and only a handful of them, sometimes just one or none, affect known driver genes. The remaining alterations are usually considered passengers, although some may be rare drivers, may modulate the effect of the main drivers, or may represent unexplored therapeutic opportunities. Moreover, tumors of the same histological type frequently differ in their molecular makeup, and the same gene can play different roles, as oncogene or tumor suppressor, depending on the tissue. Interpreting the alterations found in a single patient therefore requires placing them in the context of the tumor type, the available knowledge on driver genes, and the functional and structural consequences of each variant.

Precision oncology aims precisely at this goal: matching each patient with the therapy most likely to be effective on the basis of the molecular characteristics of the tumor. Clinical sequencing, from targeted gene panels to whole exomes and genomes, is becoming increasingly common, and molecular tumor boards are being established in many hospitals. Nevertheless, translating a list of variants into clinically meaningful information remains a major bottleneck. Several resources address parts of this problem. Databases such as COSMIC, cBioPortal and the ICGC Data Portal provide access to mutation data and cohort-level exploration; OncoKB, CIViC, the Cancer Genome Interpreter and My Cancer Genome curate evidence on the oncogenic effect and clinical actionability of variants and on drug responses; and tools such as IntOGen compile cancer driver genes derived from large cohorts. Yet these resources typically differ in scope, in the nomenclature and annotations they use, and in whether they emphasize the cohort or the individual. Clinicians and researchers must often consult several of them and integrate the results manually, which is time-consuming and prone to inconsistency.

A further limitation is that most interpretation strategies treat genes as isolated entities. Proteins function within complex networks of physical interactions, and the consequences of a mutation depend on its cellular environment. A mutation may disrupt a protein-protein interface and rewire specific interactions, affect a catalytic or ligand-binding site, or destabilize the fold. Network-based approaches have shown that cancer genes tend to occupy particular positions in the interactome and that mutations in different genes can converge on the same pathways or complexes. Likewise, three-dimensional structural information, whether experimental or derived from homology modelling, allows mutations to be mapped onto functional regions, pockets and interfaces, providing mechanistic hypotheses about their impact and, potentially, about druggability. Incorporating these layers into the interpretation of personal cancer genomes remains uncommon in accessible tools.

Another challenge is the need for a coherent view that combines complementary perspectives. A cohort-centric view answers questions such as how frequently a gene is mutated in a tumor type, whether it is a recognized driver, and what the typical patterns of co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity are. A patient-centric view asks which of the mutations in a given tumor are likely to be functionally relevant, how they relate to each other in terms of pathways and interactions, and whether there is evidence of clinical actionability. Bridging both views allows an individual profile to be compared with relevant cohorts, helping to distinguish expected from unusual alterations and to prioritize variants for follow-up.

Here we present Cancer PanorOmics, a web-based resource designed to provide a comprehensive, multi-layered view of personal cancer genomes. The platform integrates data and annotations for 26 tumor types, including cancer driver predictions, mutation frequencies and patterns, and clinical and scientific evidence on variants, genes and therapies. Users can explore cohort-level information for each tumor type and, in parallel, submit or select the variants of an individual tumor to obtain a patient-centric report. In addition, the resource maps mutations onto the human interactome to reveal their cellular context, and onto protein structures, with quasi-atomic detail whenever available, to highlight potential functional consequences. By combining these perspectives in a single, accessible interface, Cancer PanorOmics aims to facilitate the interpretation of individual tumors and, together with appropriate genetic counselling and medical advice, to contribute to the identification of actionable alterations that can guide clinical decision-making.

Data sources and cohort definition

Somatic mutation, copy number and clinical data for 26 tumor types were collected from public cohorts, mainly The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), and were retrieved through cBioPortal and the corresponding data portals. Tumor types were defined by the cohort's primary site and histology. Variants were mapped to the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome, and coordinates were lifted over where necessary. Only point mutations and short insertions/deletions in coding regions were considered for the cohort-level analyses. Synonymous variants were retained for background mutation rate estimation but excluded from driver identification.

Identification of cancer driver genes

Tumor type specific driver genes were identified by combining the outputs of complementary methods that detect signals of positive selection. These included methods based on mutational clustering within the protein sequence (OncodriveCLUST), functional impact bias (OncodriveFM), and recurrence relative to a gene-specific background mutation rate (MutSigCV and dNdScv-like approaches). Each method was run separately for every tumor type. P values were corrected for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, and genes with q < 0.05 were considered significant. Results from individual methods were integrated by a rank-based combination, and genes were assigned a confidence tier according to the number of methods supporting them. Genes were also cross-referenced with the Cancer Gene Census and with curated lists of known drivers to flag previously described cancer genes. Drivers were further classified as oncogenes or tumor suppressors on the basis of the distribution of missense and truncating mutations.

Annotation of variants

Variants from a personal genome, supplied as VCF or MAF files or as a list of gene/protein changes, were annotated with the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor. Annotations included the consequence type, affected transcript and protein position. Functional impact was estimated with SIFT, PolyPhen-2 and the Mutation Assessor score, and the scores were combined into a consensus categorization (high, medium, low or neutral impact). Population frequencies from the 1000 Genomes Project and gnomAD were used to filter likely germline polymorphisms. Variants with allele frequency above 1% were labeled as common polymorphisms. For each variant, we also queried its recurrence in the tumor cohorts and in COSMIC.

Patient-centric and cohort-centric views

In the cohort-centric view, users select a tumor type and explore its driver genes, mutation frequencies, mutual exclusivity and co-occurrence patterns, and the distribution of mutations along protein domains. Mutual exclusivity and co-occurrence between gene pairs were assessed with a one-sided Fisher's exact test, with multiple testing correction. In the patient-centric view, each mutated gene in the submitted genome is placed in the context of the selected tumor type. The system reports whether the gene is a driver in that tumor type, whether the exact variant or the same residue is recurrently mutated, and the predicted impact. Genes and variants are ranked by a score combining driver status, recurrence, functional impact and presence in clinical evidence databases, so that putative drivers are prioritized over passenger events.

Clinical and scientific evidence

Information on the clinical relevance of alterations was obtained from the Cancer Genome Interpreter catalog of validated oncogenic mutations, CIViC, OncoKB-compatible public resources, and DGIdb. Evidence was classified by level (approved therapies, clinical trials, case reports and preclinical data) and by the nature of the association (sensitivity, resistance or prognosis). Alterations were matched to evidence at the level of the exact variant, the gene or the mutation type, and matches were annotated by tumor type, distinguishing evidence from the same tumor type from evidence extrapolated from other tumors. Relevant literature was linked through PubMed identifiers. Drug-target relationships were retrieved from ChEMBL and DrugBank.

Interactome mapping

To explore the cellular environment of mutations, we built a human protein-protein interaction network by integrating curated experimental interactions from BioGRID, IntAct, HPRD and Reactome. Only interactions supported by direct experimental evidence were retained. Mutated genes from a patient were mapped onto this network, and their first-order neighbors, shared interactors and connected components were computed using NetworkX. The network was annotated with driver status, mutation frequency in the tumor type and drug targets. Over-represented pathways among the mutated genes and their neighbors were identified with a hypergeometric test using KEGG and Reactome annotations, with FDR correction.

Structural annotation

Protein structural information was obtained from the Protein Data Bank and from homology models in ModBase and SWISS-MODEL. Protein residues were mapped to structures with SIFTS and, for models, to UniProt positions. Mutated residues were classified as being located in the protein core, on the surface or at an interface, according to relative solvent accessibility computed with DSSP. Interface residues were identified from structures of complexes, defined as residues whose accessible surface area changes upon complex formation. Residues within 4 Å of a bound ligand, small molecule or nucleic acid were labeled as binding site positions. Structures were displayed with an embedded NGL viewer, highlighting the mutated residues and their neighbors.

Implementation

The back end was implemented in Python with a relational database storing cohort data, annotations and evidence. Precomputed results for each tumor type are served through a RESTful API. The front end uses HTML5, JavaScript and D3.js for interactive visualizations, including lollipop plots, oncoprints and network diagrams. Uploaded patient data are processed in memory, are not shared, and are deleted after the session. The resource is freely available without registration.

Limitations and intended use

The results are intended for research and to support interpretation by clinical experts. They do not replace genetic counselling or medical advice, and all findings require validation with appropriate clinical-grade assays.

Cancer PanorOmics is organized around two complementary entry points: a cohort-centric view, in which the user explores the alterations and driver genes of a given tumor type, and a patient-centric view, in which the user uploads the variants of an individual tumor and obtains a contextualized report. Both views rely on the same underlying integrated database, which covers 26 tumor types and combines somatic mutation data from large sequencing consortia, curated catalogues of driver genes, clinical annotations of variant actionability, protein interaction networks and structural information.

**Cohort-centric view: the landscape of each tumor type**

For each of the 26 tumor types, the resource reports the set of genes identified as cancer drivers by complementary computational methods, together with their mutation frequencies and the type of alterations observed (missense, truncating, in-frame indels, copy number changes). Users can query a gene and immediately see in which tumor types it is recurrently altered, whether it acts predominantly as an oncogene or a tumor suppressor based on its mutational pattern, and how its alterations are distributed along the protein sequence. Mutation hotspots and domain-level enrichment are displayed in lollipop-style plots, allowing the user to assess whether a mutation falls in a recurrently mutated position or in a functionally annotated region.

We also provide a summary of co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity between driver alterations within each cohort. These patterns help place a gene in a pathway context: mutually exclusive alterations frequently affect the same pathway, whereas co-occurring alterations may point to cooperating events. The cohort view therefore serves as a reference frame against which individual tumors can be compared.

**Patient-centric view: interpreting a single tumor**

The patient-centric view accepts a list of variants from a single tumor and a selected tumor type. Each variant is first mapped to genes and protein positions and classified by consequence. The resource then assigns to each alteration a level of evidence for its relevance to cancer. A variant may be (i) a known driver mutation, because it falls in a recurrent hotspot or is documented in curated databases; (ii) a mutation in a known driver gene whose individual effect is uncertain; or (iii) a passenger-like alteration in a gene with no evidence of involvement in the tumor type. This stratification typically reduces the set of candidates from the tens to hundreds of coding variants found in a tumor to a handful of alterations that deserve attention.

For the variants of interest, the report links to clinical evidence on therapeutic response, resistance and prognosis, indicating the tumor type in which each association was established and the level of supporting evidence. When an alteration has known relevance only in a different tumor type, this is flagged explicitly, so users can distinguish on-label from off-label considerations. Variants that may be of germline origin or are located in genes associated with hereditary cancer predisposition are highlighted, as these call for genetic counselling.

An important feature is the comparison of the patient’s profile with the cohort of the same tumor type. The report indicates how frequent each altered driver is, which other drivers are typically co-altered, and how many driver alterations the patient carries relative to the cohort distribution. Tumors with unusual combinations, such as alterations that are normally mutually exclusive or absence of any known driver, are thus easily recognized and may suggest further inspection of the data or the involvement of less characterized genes.

**Placing mutations in the cellular environment**

To go beyond the gene level, Cancer PanorOmics maps the mutated proteins onto the human interactome. For every patient, the resource builds a network containing the altered proteins and their direct interaction partners, with known drivers and drug targets highlighted. This representation shows whether several alterations converge on the same complex or pathway, and which neighbors of a mutated protein are themselves targetable. In this way, a mutation in a gene without a direct therapeutic agent may nevertheless be connected to an actionable node of the network.

Where interaction interfaces are known, mutations are further mapped onto them, enabling the identification of variants that may specifically perturb a given interaction rather than abolish the whole protein function. Such interface-specific effects can explain why some mutations in the same gene have distinct phenotypic consequences.

**Structural details of mutations**

When experimental structures or reliable homology models are available, mutations are visualized in three dimensions through an embedded molecular viewer. The structural view reports the location of the residue relative to ligand-binding sites, active sites, protein–protein interfaces and buried or exposed regions, as well as the local environment of the substituted amino acid. For drug targets, the mapping of mutations relative to the drug-binding pocket helps rationalize known resistance mutations and may suggest potential effects of uncharacterized variants in the same region. Structural coverage is limited to proteins and regions with suitable templates, and the resource indicates the source and quality of each model so users can judge its reliability.

**Use cases and accessibility**

We illustrate the resource with example tumors from different cancer types, in which the pipeline reduces the list of somatic variants to a small set of candidate drivers, retrieves associated clinical evidence, and identifies network or structural context for additional alterations. The web interface requires no registration, accepts standard variant file formats, and produces interactive reports that can be downloaded. All results are intended as decision support to be discussed with clinicians and genetic counsellors rather than as prescriptions for treatment.

Cancer PanorOmics was designed to address a practical gap between the large cohort-level catalogues of cancer drivers and the interpretation needed for a single patient. Whereas resources such as cBioPortal, IntOGen, COSMIC or OncoKB each provide valuable pieces of information, the clinician or researcher who holds a personal cancer genome must still move among several tools, formats and conceptual frameworks. By integrating cohort-based evidence for 26 tumor types with patient-centric annotation, interactome context and structural information, our resource offers a single entry point that situates each alteration within its tumor type, its cellular neighborhood and, when possible, its three-dimensional protein environment. We refer to this combination as a "PanorOmic" view, since it is intended to broaden the perspective from isolated variants to the functional landscape in which they act.

A central premise of the resource is that the same alteration can have very different significance depending on tumor type and on the other alterations present in the tumor. The cohort-centric view allows users to ask whether a gene is a recognized driver in the tumor type of interest, how frequently it is altered, and with which other genes it is co-mutated or mutually exclusive. The patient-centric view reverses the question: given the set of variants in one tumor, which are likely drivers, which are likely passengers, and which have therapeutic or prognostic annotations? Because most individual tumors harbor only a few known driver events among many private mutations, this ability to prioritize is essential. Mapping variants onto the interactome further helps to interpret alterations in genes that are not recurrently mutated at the cohort level but that interact with, or converge on, established cancer pathways. Such "long-tail" events are numerous and are precisely those for which conventional frequency-based evidence is weakest.

The structural layer adds a complementary dimension. Locating a mutation in a protein structure or model can suggest whether it affects a catalytic site, a protein-protein interface, a ligand-binding pocket or the protein core, thus generating mechanistic hypotheses that can be tested experimentally. Combined with interactome mapping, it can suggest which interactions are likely to be perturbed. We emphasize, however, that the structural coverage of the human proteome remains incomplete, and that homology models vary in reliability. The structural annotations should therefore be read as hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the resource depends on the quality and representativeness of the underlying data. Public cohorts are biased toward tumor types, populations and clinical settings that have been extensively sequenced, and rarer tumors or under-represented ancestries may have less reliable driver and frequency estimates. Second, the current focus is largely on somatic single-nucleotide variants and small indels; copy-number changes, structural rearrangements, non-coding mutations, epigenetic alterations and transcriptional state are only partly captured, even though they often determine tumor behavior and treatment response. Third, driver prediction methods have inherent error rates, and the classification of a variant as a driver or passenger is probabilistic. Fourth, clinical annotations of actionability evolve rapidly and differ across knowledge bases and regulatory jurisdictions; any resource that aggregates them requires continuous curation to avoid becoming outdated. Finally, interactome data are incomplete and context-independent, so an interaction recorded in a database may not occur in the specific tissue or cell state of the tumor under study.

For these reasons, Cancer PanorOmics is intended as a research and decision-support tool and not as a stand-alone diagnostic system. Its output cannot replace expert molecular tumor board review, validated clinical-grade assays or the judgment of the treating physician. The abstract's reference to appropriate genetic counselling and medical advice is deliberate: some alterations detected in tumor sequencing may reflect germline variants with implications for the patient and relatives, and the interpretation of any actionable finding must take into account comorbidities, prior therapies, availability of drugs and clinical trials, and patient preferences. We also note that data privacy is an important consideration when personal genomic data are analyzed through web services, and users should ensure that their use complies with applicable ethical and legal requirements.

Looking forward, there are several clear directions for development. Incorporating additional data types, such as expression, copy number, fusion and methylation profiles, would enable a more comprehensive characterization of each tumor. Expanding the number of tumor types and cohorts, especially those from diverse populations and from metastatic and treated disease, would improve the generalizability of the cohort-based statistics. Integrating emerging structural predictions across the proteome should extend the fraction of variants that can be placed in a structural context, and coupling these with pathway-level and network-based models might allow the prediction of combined effects of multiple mutations and of potential vulnerabilities such as synthetic lethality. Finally, systematic benchmarking against clinical outcomes and the feedback of users in translational and clinical settings will be necessary to establish which components of the PanorOmic view are most useful in practice.

In conclusion, Cancer PanorOmics provides an accessible, integrative framework for interpreting individual cancer genomes in light of population-scale evidence, molecular networks and protein structure. By combining cohort- and patient-centric perspectives, it facilitates the identification of potential drivers and actionable alterations and the generation of mechanistic hypotheses. Used together with expert clinical and genetic evaluation, we expect it to support the broader goal of precision oncology: guiding treatment decisions on the basis of the specific molecular features of each patient's tumor.

Knitting is among the oldest and most widely practiced methods of producing textiles, and knitted fabric is ubiquitous in apparel, sportswear, medical products, and technical textiles. Industrial knitting machines can produce entire garments automatically with little or no sewing, which makes them attractive for on-demand and customized manufacturing [McCann et al. 2016; Narayanan et al. 2018]. Yet the potential for personalization remains largely untapped. Programming a knitting machine requires low-level control over individual stitches, needle movements, and yarn carriers, and the proprietary software that ships with commercial machines is aimed at trained technicians rather than casual designers. As a result, the people who wear knitted garments are rarely able to shape them.

Recent research has begun to close this gap. Several systems let users generate knitting instructions from three-dimensional surface meshes, either by converting a mesh into a stitch mesh [Yuksel et al. 2012; Wu et al. 2019] or by tracing a surface with courses of stitches that are then scheduled for machine execution [Narayanan et al. 2018; Popescu et al. 2018]. Other work provides domain-specific languages and compilers that expose machine capabilities to expert programmers [Ikeda et al. 2020; Lin et al. 2018]. Interactive tools for hand knitting and for pattern design have also been proposed [Kaspar et al. 2019; Igarashi et al. 2008]. While powerful, these approaches generally sit at one of two extremes. Mesh-based methods give broad geometric freedom but offer little intuitive control over the garment's structure, such as the placement of sleeves, hems, and necklines, and they can yield instructions that are hard to edit once generated. Low-level languages and stitch-level editors, in contrast, give precise control but demand substantial knitting expertise and effort for even modest garments.

Garment design in practice rarely starts from an arbitrary surface or from individual stitches. Designers typically begin from familiar components such as bodies, sleeves, and collars, and adapt them by changing measurements, then add surface decoration such as colorwork, textures, and lace. Computer-aided design (CAD) software for sewn clothing reflects this workflow through parametric panels and templates, and image editing software provides layers that can be composited and reused. Knitting, however, has distinctive constraints that complicate the direct application of these ideas. Fabric is constructed row by row, so shape changes are expressed as increases and decreases that must follow valid machine operations. Stitch patterns interact with shaping, because cables, ribs, and lace alter the local width and height of the fabric, and a pattern designed for one size must be adapted when the garment is resized. Finally, the connectivity between pieces determines how the garment can be scheduled and knitted.

In this paper we present Knitting Skeletons, an interactive design system that combines concepts from CAD and image editing for the composition of machine-knitted garments. Our central idea is to represent a garment as an assembly of parametric knitted primitives, each of which is a simple, regular shape with a well-defined stitch layout, such as a tube, a cone, or a flat panel. These primitives are connected through a skeletal structure that specifies how they join and how their parameters, including length, circumference, and taper, may vary. Because every primitive has a regular structure, the system can automatically lay out stitches, determine the shaping operations needed to join and transition between pieces, and produce a valid knitting program without user intervention at the level of individual needles.

On top of this geometric representation, we introduce stitch pattern layers inspired by raster image editors. Users paint or place patterns, such as colorwork motifs and textured stitches, on layers that are mapped onto the surface of the garment. Each layer is assigned a resampling behavior that defines how it responds when the underlying shape changes. For instance, a motif may be preserved at constant scale and tiled, stretched to fit new dimensions, or cropped, while a texture may be repeated to fill additional area. Since the primitives are regular, this resampling can be evaluated quickly, which allows the system to give real-time visual feedback as the user manipulates both shape and pattern.

The system serves two groups of users. Casual users can select from existing templates, adjust a few high-level parameters, and apply patterns to obtain a customized garment without knowing how the machine operates. More advanced users can author new templates by composing primitives and defining parameters and constraints, then share them with others. Because shape and pattern are described parametrically and separately, customizations can be transferred between users and between bodies: a pattern designed for one person's garment can be reapplied to another's garment of different dimensions, and a tailored fit can be reused with new surface designs.

Our contributions are as follows:

- A parametric representation of knitted garments built from composable primitives with automated stitch layout and shaping.
- A layered stitch pattern model with distinct resampling behaviors that adapt patterns to changes in garment shape.
- An interactive interface that offers real-time feedback and supports both casual customization and template authoring for advanced users.
- A demonstration of the system on a variety of garments and patterns, including the transfer of shape and pattern customizations between users, with several designs fabricated on an industrial knitting machine.

By raising the level of abstraction from stitches and meshes to primitives and layers, our approach aims to make the customization of machine-knitted garments accessible, while retaining the structure needed to generate reliable machine instructions.

Our system represents a garment as a composition of parametric knitted primitives, called skeletons, onto which stitch pattern layers are applied. We first describe the primitive representation, then composition and automated layout, then the patterning layers and their resampling behaviours, and finally the compilation to machine instructions.

**Knitting Skeletons as Parametric Primitives**

A skeleton is a low-dimensional description of a knitted piece that captures its topology and the way its stitch grid deforms. Each skeleton is a tube or sheet defined by a small set of parameters (e.g., width, length, and taper angles) and a set of boundary edges, called ports, where it can connect to other skeletons. The stitch grid is generated procedurally from these parameters. Following prior work on stitch meshes [1] and on knit-aware shaping [2], we model the fabric as a quad-dominant grid of stitches in which each row corresponds to a knitting pass. Shaping is expressed through increases and decreases, whose positions are determined by the skeleton's parameters so that the target width profile is achieved at every row.

Because each primitive is regular, row and column counts are closed-form functions of its parameters and of the user's gauge, measured as stitches and rows per unit length from a swatch of the target yarn and machine [3]. Changing a parameter therefore requires only re-evaluating these functions, not re-meshing or re-optimizing. We provide primitives for common garment components, including rectangular panels, tapered tubes for sleeves and torsos, and shaped caps for shoulders and necklines. Advanced users may define new templates by specifying a parameterization, a set of ports, and a shaping function that maps row index to stitch count. Templates are stored in a serializable format so they can be shared.

**Composition and Automated Layout**

Garments are built by connecting ports of different skeletons in a graph. Each edge of the graph specifies a join, either a seam, a continuous knit-through transfer, or a held-stitch connection, in the manner of machine-knitting scheduling frameworks [4]. When two ports are joined, their stitch counts must be compatible. Rather than demanding exact matches from the user, the system resolves mismatches automatically. We treat the constraint as a small linear system over the parameters of the connected skeletons: each join contributes an equation equating port widths measured in stitches, while user-pinned parameters are held fixed. Unpinned parameters are solved in the least-squares sense and rounded to integers, with a local adjustment of shaping rows to absorb rounding error. If the system is over-constrained, the interface highlights the conflicting joins.

After parameters are resolved, the layout stage positions each skeleton in a common two-dimensional knitting coordinate frame and determines the knitting order. Pieces joined by continuous transfer are placed on the same needle bed segment, whereas seamed pieces are scheduled independently. Because primitives are regular, layout reduces to a traversal of the composition graph and does not require a global search, which keeps it fast enough to run on every edit.

**Stitch Pattern Layers**

Surface patterning follows an image-editing metaphor. A pattern layer is a two-dimensional array of stitch operations (knit, purl, tuck, miss, and cable or lace operations) defined in a layer-local coordinate system. Layers are stacked and combined by blend modes, with a mask controlling where each layer is visible. Each layer is mapped onto a skeleton through that skeleton's parameterization, so that pattern coordinates follow the garment's shaping instead of the raw needle grid.

Since the garment's stitch count changes with the user's measurements and gauge, a layer must be resampled to fit. We offer three behaviours, each suited to different pattern types. (1) *Tiling* repeats the pattern unit and truncates at borders, preserving stitch-level appearance for textures such as ribs and seed stitch. (2) *Stretching* resamples the layer by nearest-neighbour lookup in the pattern's coordinate frame, preserving the global motif, such as a colorwork image, at the expense of stitch-level fidelity [5]. (3) *Anchored* placement fixes the pattern to a chosen reference, such as a seam or the center line, at its native size, and fills the remainder with a background layer, which suits motifs like cables or logos that should not be distorted. Because operations such as cables change stitch counts locally, we validate each resampled layer and replace operations that would violate local constraints with the nearest valid operation, for instance by substituting plain knit for a cable crossing that straddles a boundary.

Layers are evaluated at the stitch level, with cost proportional to the number of stitches, so the preview can update in real time. The preview renders the stitch grid with a yarn-like shading model, offering immediate feedback on both shape and pattern.

**Compilation to Machine Instructions**

Once layout and patterning are complete, the stitch grid is converted to a sequence of machine operations. We target a V-bed knitting machine, and use an intermediate representation of stitch operations with loop dependencies [6]. Increases and decreases are realized by racking and transfers, and each pass is assigned to a bed and direction to respect carriage constraints. The resulting program is verified with a simulator for needle conflicts and loop-ordering errors before being exported.

**Transferring Customizations**

Since shape and pattern are stored as parameters and layers rather than as fixed stitch grids, a customization can be transferred between users. A shared garment records its composition graph, pinned and free parameters, and layers with their resampling behaviours. When applied to a new user, the system substitutes that user's measurements and gauge, re-solves the free parameters, and re-resamples the layers, so the original design intent is preserved at a new size.

**Implementation**

The system is implemented as an interactive desktop application. We evaluate its output by knitting garments on an industrial flat-bed machine and by assessing the responsiveness of layout and preview across a range of garment sizes.

We evaluated Knitting Skeletons along four axes: the range of garments and patterns the system can express, the fidelity of the interactive preview to the knitted result, system performance, and the usability of the tool for casual and advanced users. All garments were fabricated on a industrial V-bed knitting machine (Shima Seiki SWG091N2, 15 gauge) using a mid-weight acrylic yarn, and compiled to machine instructions through our back end, which follows the scheduling approach of prior knitting compilers [1, 2].

**Garment Gallery.** Figure 1 shows a set of garments composed entirely within our tool: a raglan sweater, a drop-shoulder pullover, a hooded vest, a pair of mittens, a tube scarf with a pocket, and a child's hat. Each was assembled from between three and nine primitives (e.g., tube, cone, sleeve, and hem segments) joined along skeleton edges. Composition required no manual stitch-level editing. Every garment was knit successfully on the first attempt, with no dropped stitches or transfer failures. Garments involving branching topology, such as the sweater and the mittens, relied on the automated layout to place short-row shaping and split regions consistently. Compared with hand-authored programs for similar garments in existing knitting DSLs [3], which required several hundred lines of code, equivalent designs in our tool were produced through direct manipulation of fewer than ten parameters per primitive.

**Pattern Layers.** We demonstrate surface patterning with layers that use three resampling behaviours: stretch, which rescales a pattern to fit the primitive; tile, which repeats it; and crop, which preserves its native scale. Figure 2 shows a single colorwork motif applied under each behaviour to a sleeve whose length was varied by 40%. Stretch preserved the global composition but distorted stitch aspect ratio, tiling preserved local appearance but introduced seams at non-integer repeats, and cropping maintained scale but truncated motifs. Layering enabled combinations that would be tedious to produce by hand, such as a tiled cable panel over a stretched gradient of textured stitches (Figure 3). When layers overlapped, the compositing order produced the expected results in all 24 test combinations, including those mixing knit-purl textures with colorwork, where we resolve conflicts by giving priority to the upper layer.

**Preview Fidelity.** To assess whether the real-time preview predicts the fabricated result, we compared rendered previews against photographs of 12 swatches and garments. Stitch counts of the generated programs matched the preview exactly, since both derive from the same parametric representation. Measured dimensions of the finished pieces deviated from the nominal dimensions by 3.8% on average (maximum 7.1%), primarily along the course direction in textured regions where rib and purl-heavy patterns contract the fabric. This is consistent with known gauge variation across stitch types [4]. We did not model this effect in the preview; however, users can compensate with per-layer gauge scaling, which reduced the mean error to 2.1% in a follow-up trial on four garments.

**Performance.** We measured update latency on a laptop with a 3.0 GHz quad-core CPU and no dedicated GPU. For garments with up to 40,000 stitches, parameter edits (e.g., dragging a sleeve length handle) triggered layout and pattern resampling in a median of 18 ms (95th percentile 41 ms), supporting interactive rates. The largest garment, an adult sweater of roughly 95,000 stitches, updated in a median of 52 ms. Full compilation to machine code took between 1.4 and 6.8 seconds. Because primitives are regular, layout is computed per primitive and only affected primitives and their neighbors are recomputed on edit; disabling this caching increased median latency for the sweater to 310 ms.

**Transferring Customizations.** A central claim of our approach is that shape and pattern customizations are portable.
