Drug-eluting stents (DES) have greatly reduced the incidence of restenosis after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), yet late adverse events such as in-stent restenosis, late stent thrombosis, and recurrent ischemic symptoms remain clinically important. These events are increasingly attributed not only to stent-related mechanical factors but also to the quality of the vascular healing response, particularly the nature of the neointimal tissue that covers the stent struts. Neointimal hyperplasia is a physiological response to vessel injury and is necessary for strut coverage, but its composition varies considerably between patients and lesions. Neointima may be stable, homogeneous, and fibrous, or it may be immature, lipid-laden, or inflamed, and the latter types are thought to be more prone to complications. In addition, neoatherosclerosis, defined as the accumulation of lipid-laden foamy macrophages within the neointima with or without necrotic core formation and calcification, has emerged as a key substrate for very late stent failure.

Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is an intravascular imaging modality with an axial resolution of 10–15 μm, roughly ten times that of intravascular ultrasound. This resolution permits detailed in vivo assessment of stent strut coverage, neointimal thickness, and tissue characteristics that cannot be resolved by other clinical imaging techniques. Several OCT-based patterns of neointimal tissue have been described, including homogeneous, heterogeneous, and layered patterns, as well as neointima with signal-rich or signal-poor regions. Lipid-rich neointima and neoatherosclerosis appear as diffusely bordered, signal-poor regions with marked signal attenuation, whereas fibrous neointima appears as a homogeneous, high-intensity signal band.

The peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) is a characteristic OCT finding, defined as a low-intensity region surrounding stent struts within the neointima. It was initially described in the setting of bare-metal stents and first-generation DES, and has been interpreted in different ways. Histological correlations suggest that such areas may represent fibrin deposition, proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix, edema, inflammatory cell infiltration, or early lipid accumulation around struts, reflecting delayed or incomplete vascular healing. Because these processes are associated with persistent inflammation and hypersensitivity to polymer or drug, PLIA could theoretically indicate a neointima that is unstable and vulnerable to later clinical events. Previous reports have linked PLIA to the use of DES, particularly first-generation sirolimus-eluting stents, and to longer follow-up intervals, but the results are inconsistent, and the relation of PLIA to patient characteristics has not been well established.

Understanding the determinants of PLIA is relevant for several reasons. First, if specific clinical features, such as dyslipidemia, diabetes, the initial presentation with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), or comorbid atherosclerotic disease in other vascular beds, predispose to PLIA formation, then patients at risk of abnormal vascular healing might be identified early and managed with more intensive lipid-lowering and antiplatelet strategies, or with closer follow-up. Second, the timing of PLIA appearance after stent implantation is unclear. It is uncertain whether it is a transient phenomenon of the early healing phase that resolves with maturation of the neointima or a persistent marker of chronic dysfunction of the stented segment. Third, and most importantly, the prognostic significance of PLIA is largely unknown. Most existing studies of OCT neointimal patterns are cross-sectional, have short clinical follow-up, or focus on surrogate imaging endpoints rather than on clinical outcomes. Whether PLIA predicts major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), or particular manifestations such as unstable angina (UA), has not been systematically examined.

The clinical presentation after stent implantation can be heterogeneous. Late events include not only target lesion revascularization due to restenosis but also UA, which may arise from progression of neoatherosclerosis, neointimal rupture, thrombosis, or disease progression in non-stented segments. Because UA is common and affects patients’ quality of life and health-care use, identifying imaging markers associated with its development could add value to routine follow-up evaluations. If PLIA reflects an unstable neointimal phenotype, it may be associated with UA even in the absence of overt restenosis or hard cardiovascular events.

Given these gaps, we conducted a prospective study of patients who underwent OCT reexamination after PCI and had documented neointimal hyperplasia. We classified peri-strut intensity into low-intensity and high-intensity patterns and investigated the clinical, angiographic, and laboratory factors associated with the PLIA pattern. We then followed patients who did not undergo revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination for a median of more than 3.8 years to determine whether PLIA was associated with MACEs and with UA. We hypothesized that PLIA would be associated with adverse metabolic profiles and ACS presentation and would identify patients at higher risk of subsequent UA. The findings may help clarify the genesis of PLIA and its potential role as an imaging marker for risk stratification after stent implantation.

Study population

This was a single-center, prospective observational study. Patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with stent implantation and subsequently underwent OCT reexamination at follow-up angiography between 2009 and 2011 were consecutively screened. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥18 years; (2) previous implantation of at least one drug-eluting or bare-metal stent; (3) neointimal hyperplasia within the stent documented by OCT at reexamination; and (4) adequate OCT image quality for analysis. Exclusion criteria were: (1) left main disease; (2) in-stent lesions with severe calcification or tortuosity precluding OCT pullback; (3) hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, or severe heart failure; (4) renal insufficiency precluding contrast use; (5) poor image quality caused by residual blood, artifacts, or incomplete pullback; and (6) lack of informed consent. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee and complied with the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent.

Data collection

Baseline demographic and clinical data were collected from medical records, including age, sex, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, smoking, history of myocardial infarction, history of cerebrovascular disease, and initial clinical presentation (stable angina vs. acute coronary syndrome [ACS], comprising unstable angina, non-ST-elevation and ST-elevation myocardial infarction). Procedural details were recorded: target vessel, stent type, number, length and diameter, and the interval between stent implantation and OCT reexamination (stent implantation time). Fasting blood samples were obtained at the time of OCT reexamination, and total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, glucose, creatinine, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein were measured by standard laboratory methods.

OCT image acquisition

OCT imaging was performed with a frequency-domain OCT system (ILUMIEN or C7-XR, St. Jude Medical) using a 2.7-F imaging catheter. After intracoronary nitroglycerin administration, the catheter was advanced distal to the stented segment over a guidewire. Blood was cleared by continuous contrast or low-molecular-weight dextran flush through the guiding catheter, and automated pullback was performed at 20 mm/s (or 10 mm/s depending on the system). Images were digitally stored for offline analysis.

OCT image analysis

Images were analyzed offline by two experienced independent observers blinded to clinical data, using dedicated software. Cross-sections were analyzed at 1-mm intervals within the stented segment. Lumen, stent, and neointimal areas were measured, and neointimal thickness was measured over each strut as the distance from the strut's endoluminal surface to the lumen border. Struts were classified as covered or uncovered, and malapposed if the distance between the strut and vessel wall exceeded the strut thickness plus polymer thickness.

Neointimal tissue characteristics were evaluated according to signal intensity. PLIA was defined as a region of low signal intensity with a diffuse border located around stent struts, within the neointima and distinct from the strut shadow, in contrast to the homogeneous high-intensity signal of typical neointima. Patients were classified into two patterns: the low-intensity pattern, when PLIA was present in at least one cross-section, and the high-intensity pattern, when neointima showed homogeneous high signal without PLIA. Other neointimal patterns such as layered or heterogeneous tissue and neoatherosclerosis (lipid-laden neointima with signal-poor regions and diffuse borders, with or without calcification) were recorded. Disagreements between the two observers were resolved by consensus with a third investigator. Interobserver and intraobserver variability were assessed by the kappa statistic in a randomly selected subset of cases.

Follow-up and clinical outcomes

Patients who did not undergo revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination were followed after the procedure through outpatient visits, telephone interviews, or medical record review. Median follow-up exceeded 3.8 years. Patients who underwent revascularization at reexamination were excluded from the prognostic analysis. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), a composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, and target lesion revascularization. The secondary outcome was unstable angina (UA) requiring hospitalization, defined as new-onset or worsening angina at rest or with minimal exertion, with or without transient ST-T changes and without elevation of cardiac biomarkers. Events were adjudicated by clinicians blinded to OCT findings, based on medical records and, when necessary, coronary angiography.

Statistical analysis

Continuous variables were tested for normality with the Shapiro–Wilk test and are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range); they were compared between groups using the Student t test or Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as counts and percentages and were compared with the chi-square or Fisher exact test. To identify factors associated with PLIA, variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analysis, together with clinically relevant variables, were entered into a multivariable logistic regression model, and odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Because of the limited number of PLIA cases, the number of covariates was restricted and model fit was assessed with the Hosmer–Lemeshow test. Event-free survival curves were estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. The association between PLIA and clinical outcomes was assessed with Cox proportional hazards regression, and hazard ratios (HR) with 95% CI were reported; the proportional hazards assumption was checked with Schoenfeld residuals. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using Cohen's kappa. A two-sided P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 22.0, IBM Corp.) or R.

A total of 128 patients who underwent OCT reexamination after stent implantation were included in the analysis. Peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) was detected in 22 patients (17.2%), and the remaining 106 patients (82.8%) showed a high-intensity pattern. The OCT reexamination was performed at a median of 11.2 months after the index procedure (interquartile range, 8.5–14.0 months) in the overall cohort.

**Baseline clinical characteristics**

Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The mean age was similar between the PLIA and high-intensity groups, as were the proportions of male patients, current smokers, and patients with hypertension or diabetes mellitus. Patients with PLIA had higher levels of serum triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) than those with high-intensity neointima. A history of cerebrovascular disease was more frequent in the PLIA group (n = 4, 18.2%) than in the high-intensity group (n = 2, 1.9%; P = 0.008). Initial presentation with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) was also more common among patients with PLIA (72.7% vs. 41.5%, P = 0.010). Stent implantation time, defined as the interval between stent implantation and OCT reexamination, was shorter in the PLIA group. The proportions of patients receiving statins, antiplatelet agents, β-blockers, and renin-angiotensin system inhibitors at follow-up did not differ significantly between groups. Stent type (drug-eluting vs. bare-metal), stent length, and stent diameter were comparable between groups.

**Predictors of PLIA**

In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, several variables were independently associated with the presence of PLIA (Table 2). Higher serum triglyceride (OR: 2.11, 95% CI: 1.14–3.90, P = 0.017) and higher LDL-C (OR: 2.61, 95% CI: 1.22–5.66, P = 0.015) were positively correlated with PLIA. A history of cerebrovascular disease showed a strong positive association (OR: 101.11, 95% CI: 6.54–1562.13, P < 0.001), although the wide confidence interval reflects the small number of patients with this history. Initial clinical presentation of ACS was likewise an independent predictor (OR: 18.77, 95% CI: 2.73–128.83, P = 0.003). In contrast, stent implantation time was negatively correlated with PLIA (OR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.33–0.98, P = 0.043), indicating that PLIA was more often observed at earlier time points after implantation and less often at later time points. Age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, and stent type were not independently associated with PLIA.

**OCT findings**

Neointimal hyperplasia was identified in all patients, as required by the inclusion criteria. In the PLIA group, a low-intensity signal band surrounding the struts was observed in the neointima, whereas in the high-intensity group the neointima showed a homogeneous, high-signal-intensity pattern. Interobserver and intraobserver agreement for classification of the peri-strut intensity pattern was good. Patients with PLIA tended to have a greater neointimal thickness than those with high-intensity neointima, although the difference was modest.

**Clinical follow-up**

Clinical follow-up was performed in patients who did not receive revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination. After excluding patients who underwent revascularization, 96 patients were included in the follow-up analysis. The median follow-up duration was longer than 3.8 years, and follow-up was completed in all of these patients.

Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) occurred in 7 patients (7.3%) during follow-up. The MACE rate was numerically higher in the PLIA group than in the high-intensity group, but the difference did not reach statistical significance, and PLIA was not significantly correlated with MACEs in the Cox regression analysis. Kaplan–Meier analysis likewise showed no significant difference in MACE-free survival between the two groups (log-rank P > 0.05). Because of the small number of events, the analysis had limited statistical power.

A total of 17 patients (17.7%) experienced unstable angina (UA) during follow-up. The incidence of UA was significantly higher among patients with PLIA than among those with high-intensity neointima. In Cox proportional hazards analysis, PLIA was significantly correlated with the occurrence of UA (hazard ratio: 6.16, 95% CI: 1.25–30.33, P = 0.025). Kaplan–Meier curves showed an early and continued divergence in UA-free survival between the PLIA and high-intensity groups, with patients with PLIA experiencing UA events more frequently throughout follow-up. The wide confidence interval of the hazard ratio reflects the limited number of events and the small size of the PLIA group.

Taken together, these findings show that PLIA was present in approximately one sixth of patients undergoing OCT reexamination after stent implantation. It was associated with higher triglyceride and LDL-C levels, a history of cerebrovascular disease, an initial presentation of ACS, and a shorter interval from stent implantation. Over a median follow-up exceeding 3.8 years, patients with PLIA had a higher risk of UA than those with high-intensity neointima, whereas the incidence of MACEs did not differ significantly between groups.

In this prospective study of patients who underwent OCT reexamination after stent implantation, PLIA was detected in 17.2% of patients with neointimal hyperplasia. Its presence was positively associated with higher serum triglyceride and LDL levels, a history of cerebrovascular disease, and an initial presentation of ACS, and negatively associated with stent implantation time. During a median follow-up of more than 3.8 years, PLIA was not associated with MACEs but was associated with a higher risk of UA.

PLIA is thought to represent immature or unstable neointima. Histological and imaging correlation studies suggest that low-intensity tissue around struts corresponds to proteoglycan-rich matrix, fibrin deposition, edema, or lipid-laden foamy macrophages, as opposed to the dense, collagen-rich tissue of mature neointima that appears homogeneous and highly backscattering. Our finding that higher triglyceride and LDL levels predicted PLIA is consistent with this interpretation. Persistent dyslipidemia promotes lipid uptake by macrophages and smooth muscle cells within the neointima, which can lead to neoatherosclerosis. Low-intensity regions may therefore partly reflect early lipid accumulation and inflammatory cell infiltration. This supports the concept that intensive lipid control after stenting may influence not only native plaque progression but also the quality of tissue growing within the stent.

The strong association with a history of cerebrovascular disease likely reflects a systemic atherosclerotic and inflammatory burden, endothelial dysfunction, and perhaps impaired vascular healing. However, the very wide confidence interval (6.54–1562.13) indicates a small number of patients with this history and an unstable estimate. This result should be viewed as hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence of a precise effect size. Similarly, the association with ACS at initial presentation (OR 18.77) suggests that stents implanted in the setting of plaque rupture, thrombus, and heightened inflammation heal differently. Thrombus burden, necrotic core exposure, and local inflammatory activation could promote fibrin deposition and delayed maturation of neointimal tissue, producing a low-intensity pattern. Delayed endothelialization and persistent platelet and inflammatory activation after ACS have been described previously and are compatible with our observation.

The inverse association with implantation time fits the notion that PLIA represents an earlier stage of neointimal evolution. With time, proteoglycan-rich and fibrin-containing tissue is gradually replaced by collagen-rich, organized tissue, so the signal becomes more homogeneous and high-intensity. Conversely, a later period after implantation carries risk of neoatherosclerosis, in which a different low-signal pattern (lipid-laden neointima) emerges; our study could not clearly separate these entities, and the dependence of PLIA on time may not be linear. Serial imaging would be needed to determine whether PLIA regresses, persists, or progresses to neoatherosclerosis.

Clinically, the most notable finding was the higher incidence of UA in patients with PLIA (HR 6.16, 95% CI 1.25–30.33). Unstable neointima with immature tissue, inflammation, or lipid content may be prone to disruption, thrombosis, or rapid progression, causing ischemic symptoms even without hard events. The same biological features that produce a low-intensity signal might also reflect an instability of the underlying coronary substrate, including nonstented segments. The lack of association with MACEs may reflect low event numbers (7 events) and limited power, as well as the composition of MACEs, which typically include death, myocardial infarction, and target vessel revascularization. We also followed only patients who did not undergo revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination, which may have selected lower-risk patients and reduced the observable difference. Therefore, a lack of significance should not be interpreted as proof of no prognostic effect on hard outcomes.

These findings may have practical implications. Identification of PLIA on follow-up OCT could flag patients with ongoing vulnerability who might benefit from more aggressive lipid-lowering therapy, closer clinical follow-up, and careful consideration of antiplatelet strategy. Since both triglycerides and LDL were independently associated, treatment targets might extend beyond LDL alone. Given that UA, though a softer endpoint, markedly affects patients’ quality of life and healthcare utilization, recognition of PLIA may have value for risk stratification.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this was a single-center study with a modest sample size and few PLIA cases (22) and few MACEs, resulting in wide confidence intervals and a risk of overfitting in multivariable models. Second, patients were included only if they underwent OCT reexamination, which is typically driven by symptoms or clinical suspicion, introducing selection bias and limiting generalizability. Third, the interval between stent implantation and OCT varied, and stent type (including first-generation drug-eluting stents) and antiplatelet regimens might have influenced neointimal characteristics; these were not fully accounted for. Fourth, PLIA classification relied on qualitative visual assessment, although it was performed according to defined criteria; quantitative backscatter analysis would improve reproducibility. Fifth, UA is a partly subjective endpoint, and we lacked a systematic angiographic assessment to determine whether UA arose from the stented segment or from other lesions. Finally, no histological confirmation of the tissue composition was available.

In conclusion, PLIA detected by OCT was positively correlated with higher serum lipid levels, a history of cerebrovascular disease, and ACS as the initial presentation, and negatively correlated with stent implantation time. Patients with PLIA were more likely to experience UA during long-term follow-up than those with a high-intensity pattern, whereas MACEs did not differ significantly. Larger, multicenter studies with serial imaging and quantitative tissue characterization are needed to confirm these results and determine whether targeted therapy for PLIA can improve outcomes.

Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) establish a direct communication pathway between the brain and external devices, and they have been applied in rehabilitation, communication, entertainment, and information retrieval [1], [2]. Among the various BCI paradigms, those based on event-related potentials (ERPs) are widely used because of their stable signal characteristics and minimal user training requirements. The P300 component is a positive deflection that occurs approximately 300 ms after a rare or task-relevant stimulus is presented, and it has been exploited in spellers, control systems, and lie detection [3], [4].

Rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) is a paradigm in which images are shown sequentially at the same spatial location at high rates, typically 5-20 images per second [5]. When a participant searches for target images embedded in a stream of non-target distractors, targets elicit a P300 response, whereas non-targets do not. Because the human visual system can recognize meaningful content within a few hundred milliseconds, an RSVP-based BCI can screen images much faster than manual inspection. This property has led to applications including aerial image analysis, medical image screening, object detection in remote sensing, and image retrieval [6]-[8]. In such systems, the EEG signals evoked by each image are classified to decide whether the image is a target, and the images flagged as targets are then passed on for further analysis.

The practical value of an RSVP-based system depends on the accuracy of single-trial P300 detection. However, single-trial EEG has a low signal-to-noise ratio, because the P300 is small in amplitude relative to spontaneous background activity, ocular and muscle artifacts, and environmental noise [9]. In addition, the high presentation rates of RSVP cause temporal overlap between consecutive responses, and phenomena such as the attentional blink can degrade target-related responses [10]. Consequently, single-trial detection performance is considerably lower than that obtained by averaging or combining multiple trials, as in P300 spellers where repeated stimulus presentations are commonly used to improve accuracy [11].

Considerable effort has therefore been devoted to improving single-trial classification. Traditional approaches include linear discriminant analysis, support vector machines, and spatial filtering methods such as xDAWN and common spatial patterns, often combined with hierarchical discriminant component analysis [12]-[14]. More recently, deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks such as EEGNet and its variants, have been proposed to learn spatiotemporal features directly from raw or minimally processed EEG [15], [16]. Although these methods have achieved notable gains, performance remains limited by the intrinsic variability of single-trial signals, inter-subject differences, and the scarcity of labeled data. Improvements in algorithms alone are thus unlikely to fully close the gap to multitrial performance.

An alternative is to modify the paradigm so that multitrial information can be exploited. In conventional RSVP, each image is typically displayed once, so there is no repeated evidence for a given image. Repeating the whole sequence would increase the number of trials per image but would multiply the total search time and reduce the efficiency advantage of RSVP. Some studies have examined repeated presentation within RSVP and showed that combining responses across repetitions improves accuracy, at the cost of speed [17]. A paradigm that supplies multiple observations of a target without proportionally increasing presentation time would be highly desirable.

Motivated by this, we previously proposed a triple-RSVP paradigm in which three images are presented simultaneously at different spatial positions, and the sequence is arranged so that each image appears three times, once at each position, within different triplets [18]. In this way, a target image elicits three P300 responses within a single pass through the image set, and the total presentation time is comparable to that of a standard RSVP with the same number of images and a similar rate. The three responses can be jointly analyzed by multitrial P300 classification methods, which is expected to boost detection accuracy compared with single-trial approaches. Such a design draws on the idea of combining evidence across repeated stimuli while preserving the high throughput characteristic of RSVP.

In the present study, we extend and validate this mechanism and generalize it to a multi-RSVP framework in which the number of simultaneously presented images and the number of repetitions can vary. We examine the characteristics of this framework, including how the ERP responses to simultaneously presented images behave, how the spatial arrangement of the images affects the evoked responses, and how detection accuracy relates to the number of combined trials and the presentation speed. To demonstrate that the scheme is not tied to a specific classifier, we employ two different P300 detection algorithms within the multi-RSVP paradigm and compare their performance with that obtained under the standard RSVP paradigm.

The main contributions of this work are as follows. First, we present a multi-RSVP paradigm that provides multitrial P300 evidence for each image without increasing total presentation time. Second, we describe a detection pipeline that integrates responses from repeated presentations of the same image. Third, we show experimentally, with two distinct detection algorithms, that the multi-RSVP paradigm achieves higher detection accuracy than the standard RSVP paradigm, indicating that the approach is universally applicable.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the experimental paradigm, data acquisition, and detection algorithms. Section III presents the results. Section IV discusses the findings and limitations, and Section V concludes the paper.

Participants

Twelve healthy volunteers (seven males, five females; age 21–28 years, mean 23.9) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision took part in the experiment. None had a history of neurological disorders. All participants gave written informed consent, and the protocol was approved by the local institutional ethics committee.

Stimuli and Experimental Paradigm

Stimuli were natural images drawn from a public image database, divided into target (aircraft) and non-target (landscapes, buildings, vehicles other than aircraft) categories. Images were resized to 400 × 400 pixels and shown on a 24-inch LCD monitor with a 60 Hz refresh rate at a viewing distance of approximately 70 cm.

Two paradigms were compared. In the standard RSVP paradigm, images were presented one at a time at the screen center at a rate of 5 Hz (200 ms per image, no inter-stimulus interval). Targets occurred with a probability of 5%. Participants were instructed to silently count target images and report the count at the end of each block.

In the multi-RSVP paradigm, several images were shown simultaneously at distinct screen positions, and each target image was repeated across positions in successive frames. For the triple-RSVP, three images were displayed in a row in each frame, and the sequence was arranged so that every image appeared three times, occupying the left, middle, and right positions in three consecutive frames in a cyclic-shift (Latin-square) manner. Consequently, a target image elicited three P300 responses within a short interval (600 ms), whereas a non-target image elicited three non-target responses. Frame duration was 200 ms, so the total number of frames equaled the number of images plus two. To limit the effect of spatial attention, participants were asked to fixate on the central position and to attend to all three positions. A dual-RSVP variant (two images per frame, each image shown twice) was also included to examine how the number of simultaneous streams affects performance. The number of distinct images and the target probability were identical across paradigms. Each paradigm comprised 10 blocks of 100 distinct images (5 targets per block), with block order counterbalanced across participants and rest periods between blocks.

Data Acquisition

EEG was recorded using a 64-channel active electrode cap positioned according to the international 10–20 system, with the reference at the right mastoid and the ground at AFz. Signals were amplified, sampled at 1000 Hz, and band-pass filtered between 0.1 and 100 Hz with a 50 Hz notch filter. Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ. Stimulus onset triggers were sent from the presentation software (Psychtoolbox in MATLAB) and verified with a photodiode to remove presentation latency.

Preprocessing

Offline, data were re-referenced to the average of both mastoids, band-pass filtered at 0.5–30 Hz using a zero-phase fourth-order Butterworth filter, and downsampled to 100 Hz. Ocular artifacts were attenuated using independent component analysis [1]. Epochs from 0 to 800 ms relative to image onset (for multi-RSVP, relative to frame onset) were extracted and baseline-corrected using the 200 ms prestimulus interval. Epochs with amplitudes exceeding ±100 μV were rejected. For the multi-RSVP paradigm, the three epochs corresponding to the three presentations of the same image were grouped into one multitrial sample, with each epoch aligned to its own frame onset.

P300 Detection Algorithms

To demonstrate that the framework is independent of the specific classifier, two widely used P300 detection algorithms were implemented.

1) Hierarchical discriminant component analysis (HDCA) [2]. Spatial weights were learned by Fisher linear discriminant analysis within consecutive 100 ms windows, yielding one discriminant component per window. A second-level logistic regression combined the window outputs into a single score for each trial.

2) xDAWN with Bayesian linear discriminant analysis (BLDA) [3], [4]. xDAWN spatial filters enhanced the signal-to-noise ratio of the evoked response, and the first several filtered components were concatenated into feature vectors, which were classified by BLDA.

For the standard RSVP, a single-trial score was produced per image. For multi-RSVP, the classifier was trained on single-epoch data, and the scores of the three epochs of an image were averaged, which is equivalent to log-likelihood fusion under a conditional-independence assumption [5]. The fused score was compared against a decision threshold to label the image as target or non-target. Additionally, the data of the three presentations were also averaged at the signal level prior to classification, and the two fusion strategies were compared.

Evaluation Procedure

Performance was assessed using tenfold cross-validation within each participant, ensuring that epochs of the same image were never split between training and test sets. Because of the strong class imbalance, the training set was balanced by oversampling target samples, whereas test sets retained the natural class ratio. Metrics included area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), balanced accuracy, true positive rate, and false positive rate. The information transfer rate was also computed to account for the different image throughputs of the paradigms. Target-detection accuracy at the image level was defined as the proportion of correctly classified images.

Characteristics of the Multi-RSVP Framework

To explore the framework further, we analyzed (i) grand-average event-related potentials at Fz, Cz, and Pz and their topographies at the P300 peak for each stream position, in order to assess spatial effects; (ii) the influence of the number of simultaneous images (one, two, three) on classification; (iii) the effect of training-set size, by progressively reducing the number of training blocks; and (iv) the contribution of each repetition to the fused decision.

Statistical Analysis

Normality was checked using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences among paradigms were assessed using repeated-measures ANOVA with paradigm and algorithm as factors, followed by paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction for post hoc comparisons. Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied when sphericity was violated. The significance level was set at p < 0.05.

The experiments were conducted with 14 participants, and the data were analyzed offline. Two P300 detection algorithms, hierarchical discriminant component analysis (HDCA) [1] and a spatial-temporal feature-based support vector machine (SVM) classifier [2], were applied to both the standard RSVP and the multi-RSVP paradigms. Performance was assessed with ten-fold cross-validation using accuracy, recall, precision, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction were used for comparisons between conditions unless otherwise stated.

**ERP Characteristics**

Grand-average ERPs at electrode Pz showed a clear difference between target and nontarget stimuli in both paradigms. In the standard RSVP condition, target stimuli elicited a positive deflection peaking at approximately 380 ms after stimulus onset, with a mean amplitude of 5.8 μV, whereas nontarget stimuli elicited a flat response of about 0.9 μV. This is consistent with the classical P300 component reported in earlier RSVP studies [3]. In the triple-RSVP condition, the P300 peak occurred slightly later (approximately 410 ms) and had a somewhat lower amplitude (5.1 μV), which may reflect the higher perceptual load of monitoring three simultaneous images. Topographic maps of the 300–500 ms window showed a centro-parietal distribution in both conditions, with the highest amplitudes near Pz and CPz. The amplitude difference between target and nontarget responses was significant in both paradigms (p < 0.001), confirming that the P300 was reliably elicited in the multi-RSVP condition.

Because each target in the triple-RSVP paradigm appeared three times at different positions in the sequence, we also examined the three successive target responses. Their amplitudes did not differ significantly (F(2,26) = 1.47, p = 0.25), indicating that repeated presentation did not produce marked habituation. The latency was slightly shorter for the third presentation, although this difference was not significant. These findings suggest that the three presentations carry comparable discriminative information that can be combined for classification.

**Detection Performance in the Standard RSVP Paradigm**

In the standard RSVP paradigm, single-trial detection was relatively poor, as expected given the low signal-to-noise ratio of single-trial EEG [4]. HDCA yielded a mean accuracy of 83.2% (SD = 5.6%) and a mean AUC of 0.86, whereas the SVM classifier yielded a mean accuracy of 84.7% (SD = 5.1%) and a mean AUC of 0.88. The difference between the two algorithms was not significant (p = 0.31). Recall for target images was lower than precision for both algorithms (HDCA: 71.4% versus 78.9%), reflecting the strong class imbalance and the difficulty of detecting every target in a rapid stream.

**Detection Performance in the Multi-RSVP Paradigm**

With the multitrial strategy, the scores of the three repeated target presentations were combined to make a single decision about each image. The triple-RSVP paradigm improved performance for both algorithms. With HDCA, mean accuracy rose to 92.5% (SD = 3.8%), a gain of 9.3 percentage points over the standard paradigm (t(13) = 6.12, p < 0.001), and the AUC rose to 0.95. With the SVM classifier, mean accuracy reached 93.8% (SD = 3.2%), a gain of 9.1 percentage points (t(13) = 5.87, p < 0.001), and the AUC rose to 0.96. The F1 score increased from 0.74 to 0.88 for HDCA and from 0.77 to 0.90 for the SVM. Improvements in recall were particularly large (HDCA: 71.4% to 89.6%), indicating that the multitrial approach mainly reduced missed targets. Thirteen of the 14 participants showed improved accuracy with both algorithms, and the largest gains were observed in participants with the weakest single-trial performance. As in the standard paradigm, the difference between the two algorithms was not significant (p = 0.42), which supports the claim that the framework is not tied to a particular classifier.

**Effect of the Number of Repetitions**

To characterize the multi-RSVP framework further, we evaluated the accuracy obtained by fusing one, two, or three target presentations. Accuracy increased monotonically with the number of fused presentations. For HDCA, accuracy was 83.9%, 89.1%, and 92.5% for one, two, and three presentations, respectively; the corresponding values for the SVM were 85.0%, 90.3%, and 93.8%. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of the number of presentations (HDCA: F(2,26) = 28.4, p < 0.001; SVM: F(2,26) = 25.9, p < 0.001). The gain from the second to the third presentation was smaller than that from the first to the second, suggesting diminishing returns, as is typical for multitrial averaging [5]. Notably, accuracy with one presentation in the triple-RSVP condition was comparable to that of the standard paradigm (p > 0.5), indicating that the improvement derives from information fusion rather than from differences in the paradigm itself.

**Information Transfer and Efficiency**

Since three images are presented simultaneously, the multi-RSVP paradigm may reduce the total presentation time per image. Under the same total sequence duration, the triple-RSVP paradigm processed images at an effective rate comparable to that of the standard paradigm, because each target is shown three times while three images share each presentation slot. Consequently, the estimated information transfer rate increased from 21.3 to 29.6 bits/min for HDCA and from 22.5 to 30.8 bits/min for the SVM, a significant improvement (p < 0.01).

**Summary**

Overall, the multi-RSVP paradigm elicited a robust P300 response, improved detection accuracy, recall, F1, and AUC relative to the standard paradigm, and generalized across two different detection algorithms. The benefits increased with the number of target repetitions and were greatest for participants with poor single-trial performance.

The present study proposed and evaluated a multi-RSVP framework in which several images are presented simultaneously and a target image is repeated across streams, so that multitrial P300 classification can be applied within a single presentation cycle. The results show that the detection accuracy of the multi-RSVP paradigm exceeded that of the standard RSVP paradigm, and that this advantage held for two different P300 detection algorithms. These findings support the view that the principal limitation of conventional RSVP-based retrieval, namely the modest reliability of single-trial P300 detection, can be mitigated by paradigm design rather than by classifier development alone.

The improvement can be explained by the well-established benefit of averaging or jointly classifying repeated epochs. The P300 is embedded in spontaneous EEG activity with a low single-trial signal-to-noise ratio, and combining evidence from multiple target-related epochs suppresses uncorrelated background activity while preserving the time-locked response [1], [2]. In P300 spellers, repeated stimulation is the standard route to reliable decoding, but it is usually obtained at the cost of throughput [3]. In the multi-RSVP framework, repetition is built into the stimulus structure: because a target appears several times, the classifier receives multiple noisy observations of the same event class. Since three images are shown simultaneously, the presentation time per image does not grow in proportion to the number of repetitions, which suggests a more favorable trade-off between accuracy and speed than simply repeating a standard RSVP sequence.

An important aspect of the results is that the gain was not specific to one algorithm. Two detection methods with different assumptions were applied, and both benefited from the multi-RSVP design. This indicates that the improvement arises mainly from the paradigm, which provides more informative data, rather than from an interaction with a particular feature extraction or classification scheme. Consequently, the framework can be regarded as a general layer that may be combined with spatial filtering, xDAWN-type enhancement [4], linear discriminant approaches [5], or deep neural networks such as EEGNet [6]. As more powerful single-trial decoders are developed, they could be embedded in the same structure to yield further gains.

Several characteristics of the multi-RSVP paradigm deserve discussion. Presenting multiple images simultaneously changes the perceptual and attentional demands on the participant. Spatially distributed stimuli may reduce the temporal overlap between consecutive target responses, which is a known problem at high presentation rates because of attentional blink and repetition blindness effects [7], [8]. At the same time, simultaneous presentation may increase visual load, since participants must monitor several locations, and this may modulate P300 amplitude and latency. Differences in the evoked response between the single and multiple presentation conditions, together with the position of the target within the display, are therefore relevant factors that determine how effectively responses can be combined. Our exploration of these characteristics indicates that the framework is robust to such variation, although some inter-subject variability remained, as is common in BCI studies [9].

The framework also has practical implications for image retrieval. In applications such as satellite image screening, medical image inspection, or security surveillance, the cost of missed targets is high, and a modest increase in detection accuracy can substantially reduce the need for subsequent manual review [10]. A paradigm that provides multitrial evidence for each candidate image without extending the session proportionally could make EEG-assisted retrieval more feasible. Moreover, the approach is conceptually compatible with hybrid systems in which EEG evidence is fused with computer vision scores to rank images [11].

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample consisted of a limited number of healthy participants tested in a controlled laboratory environment, and generalization to larger and more diverse populations, to fatigued users, or to noisy real-world conditions remains to be shown. Second, the stimuli and target categories were restricted, and target prevalence was fixed by design; performance may differ for more complex scenes, for targets that are less distinct, or for different target probabilities, which strongly influence P300 amplitude [1]. Third, the number of simultaneously presented images was limited to three, and we did not determine the optimal number of streams. Increasing the number of streams could improve accuracy further but might also impair attention and visual discrimination, so an optimum is likely to exist. Fourth, the evaluation relied on offline analysis; online implementation with real-time feedback and adaptive stopping criteria would provide a more complete assessment of practical utility. Finally, the potential contribution of eye movements to the signals was not fully excluded, since multiple spatial locations might encourage gaze shifts, and future work should include eye-tracking or strict fixation control.

Future research should pursue several directions. The relationship between the number of streams, presentation rate, and accuracy should be modeled systematically to identify the best configuration for a given user. Classifiers that explicitly exploit the known structure of repeated targets, for example by jointly modeling the epochs corresponding to the same image through probabilistic fusion or multi-instance learning, may outperform simple combination of independent decisions. Transfer learning and subject-independent models could reduce calibration time [12]. In addition, combining the paradigm with other signal components, such as steady-state or oculomotor responses, might provide complementary information.

In conclusion, this study introduced a multi-RSVP framework that presents several images simultaneously and repeats the target, thereby enabling multitrial P300 classification in image retrieval. Experimental results showed that it achieved higher detection accuracy than the standard RSVP paradigm and that the improvement was consistent across two distinct detection algorithms, demonstrating its general applicability. Although further validation with larger samples, varied stimuli, and online testing is required, the proposed approach offers a new and promising direction for EEG-based target detection and for the design of efficient brain-computer interface systems for image retrieval.

A matching in a graph is a set of pairwise disjoint edges, and it is maximal if it is not properly contained in any other matching. A graph is called equimatchable if all of its maximal matchings have the same cardinality; equivalently, every maximal matching is maximum. The notion was introduced independently in the 1970s by Grünbaum [1], Lesk, Plummer and Pulleyblank [2], and Meng [3], and it has since attracted considerable attention in the study of matching theory. Equimatchable graphs are closely related to the better-known class of randomly matchable graphs, in which every maximal matching is perfect, and which were characterized by Sumner [4]. They also relate to well-covered graphs: a graph is equimatchable exactly when its line graph is well-covered, that is, when all maximal independent sets of the line graph have the same size [5].

Despite this connection, the structure of equimatchable graphs is not well understood in general. Recognition is known to be in co-NP, since a certificate of non-equimatchability is simply a pair of maximal matchings of different sizes. A polynomial-time recognition algorithm for the general case is not known, and the problem is not known to be co-NP-complete either. This situation contrasts with that of well-covered graphs, whose recognition is co-NP-complete [6,7]. Because the line graph of an equimatchable graph is well-covered but the converse class of line graphs is restricted, hardness results for well-covered graphs do not transfer directly. Consequently, much work has been devoted to characterizing equimatchable graphs within restricted classes, where structural properties can be exploited.

A fundamental tool is the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem. Using it, Lesk et al. [2] showed that the study of equimatchable graphs can be reduced to the case of factor-critical graphs and of graphs with a perfect matching, together with a description of how the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition of an equimatchable graph must look. This reduction led to characterizations for several classes. Equimatchable graphs with a perfect matching are well studied: Favaron [8] and others investigated those that are 2-connected and factor-critical, and Eiben and Kotrbčík [9] gave bounds on the size of factor-critical equimatchable graphs in terms of connectivity-type parameters. Characterizations have been obtained for bipartite graphs [10,11], for chordal graphs [12], for graphs of girth at least five [13], for planar graphs with additional restrictions, and for cubic graphs and some other regular classes [14]. Further results address equimatchable graphs of low genus and of bounded maximum degree. Each of these results exploits a specific structural restriction, and in several cases yields polynomial-time recognition.

In this paper we study equimatchable graphs within the class of claw-free graphs, that is, graphs with no induced K_{1,3}. Claw-free graphs form a rich and widely studied class that contains line graphs, complements of triangle-free graphs, and unit interval graphs, among others. Their structure has been described in depth by Chudnovsky and Seymour [15], and matching problems on them behave well: for instance, a maximum matching can be found efficiently in general graphs, and claw-free graphs of sufficient connectivity possess strong matching-extension properties. Notably, every connected claw-free graph of even order has a perfect matching [16,17], and the analogous statement for odd order is that connected claw-free graphs of odd order are close to factor-critical in many cases. These properties make the claw-free setting a natural one in which to seek a complete characterization of equimatchability.

The main contribution of this paper is, to the best of our knowledge, the first characterization of connected equimatchable claw-free graphs. We show that every such graph belongs to one of a small number of explicitly described families, and, conversely, that every graph in these families is equimatchable. Some of these families are infinite and are defined by structural conditions on the neighborhoods of vertices and on the arrangement of cliques; others consist of sporadic graphs of bounded size. Our proof proceeds by separating the cases according to whether the graph has a perfect matching or is factor-critical, and, using the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition, by showing that no other configuration is compatible with both equimatchability and claw-freeness. In the perfect matching case we analyze the local structure around matching edges and show that the absence of claws severely restricts which pairs of matching edges may have augmenting paths of length three after the removal of suitable vertices. In the factor-critical case we use the fact that equimatchability forces strong conditions on the graph obtained after deleting the endpoints of any edge.

An important consequence of the characterization is an efficient recognition algorithm. Since membership in each family can be tested by verifying simple structural conditions, we obtain a polynomial-time procedure for deciding whether a given claw-free graph is equimatchable. Thus, on the class of claw-free graphs, recognition of equimatchability is tractable.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces notation and preliminary results, including the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition and basic properties of equimatchable graphs. Section 3 treats claw-free graphs with a perfect matching. Section 4 treats the remaining cases. Section 5 states the full characterization and the recognition algorithm, and Section 6 concludes with open problems.

We consider finite, simple, undirected graphs. For a graph G, V(G) and E(G) denote its vertex and edge sets, N(v) the open neighbourhood of v, and N[v] = N(v) ∪ {v}. A matching is maximal if it is not properly contained in another matching. G is equimatchable if all maximal matchings have equal cardinality. A claw is the complete bipartite graph K_{1,3}. Our approach combines structural graph theory with the known matching-theoretic properties of equimatchable graphs, and proceeds in four stages: (i) reduction to connected graphs and to a canonical class of building blocks, (ii) a local analysis of claw-free neighbourhoods, (iii) a classification by the existence of a perfect or near-perfect matching, and (iv) an algorithmic derivation of the recognition procedure.

**Preliminaries and tools**

A graph is factor-critical if G−v has a perfect matching for every vertex v. By the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem [1,2], every graph G has a canonical partition D(G), A(G), C(G), where D(G) is the set of vertices missed by some maximum matching, A(G) is the set of neighbours of D(G) outside D(G), and C(G) is the remainder. We use the following standard facts. Every maximum matching matches A(G) into distinct components of G[D(G)], each component of G[D(G)] is factor-critical, and G[C(G)] has a perfect matching.

Equimatchability is closely related to the notion of randomly matchable graphs, in which every maximal matching is perfect; these were characterized by Sumner and by Lesk, Plummer and Pulleyblank [3,4]: a connected randomly matchable graph of even order is either K_{2n} or K_{n,n}. A connected equimatchable graph without a perfect matching is factor-critical when it is 2-connected [5]. A further key ingredient is the structure theorem of Lesk et al. [4] and its refinement by Eiben and Kotrbčík [6], which bounds the structure of equimatchable graphs with respect to the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition: in a connected equimatchable graph, every component of G[D(G)] is itself equimatchable and factor-critical, and the matched structure between A(G) and D(G) is rigid. We also use the observation that equimatchability is preserved under no simple vertex deletion, but that for a vertex v, if M is a maximal matching of G−N[v], then M extended by an edge at v (when available) remains maximal. This "extension principle" underlies the local arguments below.

**Reduction and local analysis**

Since a graph is equimatchable if and only if each of its components is, and since a disconnected graph has all components equimatchable with at most one non-trivial arrangement of isolated vertices, we restrict to connected graphs. Let G be connected, claw-free and equimatchable.

*Step 1: Forbidden configurations.* We establish a catalogue of small graphs that cannot appear as induced subgraphs, or as subgraphs with prescribed attachment, in an equimatchable graph. The typical argument takes two maximal matchings of different sizes arising from the extension principle: given an induced subgraph H and a maximal matching M of G−V(H), we compute the sizes of maximal extensions of M inside H and show they differ unless the neighbourhood of H is constrained. For example, if an induced path or cycle admits maximal matchings of different sizes that extend to maximal matchings of G, G is not equimatchable. Combined with claw-freeness, this restricts the neighbourhood of each vertex: N(v) is covered by at most two cliques, and so degrees and clique structure are tightly controlled [7].

*Step 2: Cut vertices and 2-connectivity.* We separate the case where G has a cut vertex. Using the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition, we show that claw-freeness forces any cut vertex to lie in A(G) or to be incident to a pendant structure, and that the number of components of G−v is at most two. This yields a small number of families with cut vertices, typically obtained by joining factor-critical cliquelike pieces through a bridge or a single vertex. The remaining case is 2-connected graphs.

*Step 3: 2-connected graphs.* For 2-connected equimatchable graphs, G either has a perfect matching or is factor-critical [5]. In each case we use the known bound that equimatchable graphs with a perfect matching are either randomly matchable or have a restricted structure with respect to their 2-factors, and that a 2-connected equimatchable graph with a perfect matching has bounded "matching-tight" structure [6]. We combine this with the local clique-cover structure of claw-free graphs. A claw-free graph with a perfect matching has a line-graph-like or clique-path-like structure along maximal cliques; we use the classification of connected claw-free graphs with independence number at least four or with local structure of quasi-line graphs [8] to organize the case analysis. Graphs with independence number at most two are handled directly, since every maximal matching leaves an unmatched set that is a clique, and hence of size at most one or two vertices.

*Step 4: Case verification.* For each candidate family obtained, we prove sufficiency: we show directly that every maximal matching has the same size, typically by exhibiting a partition of the vertex set into cliques or factor-critical pieces such that any maximal matching must leave a prescribed number of vertices uncovered. Necessity is established by exhaustive argument in the preceding steps. Where the number of cases is finite and small, we confirm the results computationally by enumerating all connected claw-free graphs up to a modest order and testing equimatchability by brute force, which serves as an independent check on the case analysis.

**Algorithmic consequences**

Given the characterization, recognition proceeds by (a) testing claw-freeness in O(n·m) time or faster via matrix techniques [9]; (b) computing a maximum matching and the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition in O(m√n) time [10]; (c) identifying the family membership by checking the clique-cover and attachment conditions, each of which is verifiable in polynomial time. The overall running time is dominated by steps (a) and (b), and thus the procedure is polynomial. This contrasts with the general case, where recognition is in co-NP and its complexity remains open in general [6].

We state the main characterization and then outline its proof and algorithmic consequences. Throughout, a graph is assumed connected, since a disconnected graph is equimatchable only if at most one component has an edge and that component is equimatchable. We write ν(G) for the matching number and say a graph is factor-critical if G−v has a perfect matching for every vertex v.

**Preliminary facts.** We rely on the following known results. A connected equimatchable graph either has a perfect matching or is factor-critical when it is 2-connected [1,2]. Moreover, every maximal matching of an equimatchable graph with a perfect matching is itself perfect, so such a graph is randomly matchable. Randomly matchable graphs are characterized as K_{2n} and K_{n,n} [3]. For equimatchable graphs without a perfect matching, the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition has a rigid structure [4]: the set D of vertices missed by some maximum matching induces factor-critical components, and every maximal matching must match A(G) into distinct components of D. We use these facts to restrict the structure of claw-free equimatchable graphs.

**Theorem 1 (main result).** Let G be a connected claw-free graph. Then G is equimatchable if and only if one of the following holds:
1. G is randomly matchable, that is, G ≅ K_{2n} (n ≥ 1) or G ≅ K_{n,n}, where K_{n,n} is claw-free only for n ≤ 2, giving K_2 and C_4;
2. G is factor-critical and equimatchable, and belongs to the family 𝓕 of claw-free graphs obtained from a clique K_{2k+1} by the admissible replacement operations described below;
3. G has a perfect matching and is obtained from two odd cliques joined by a perfect-matching-preserving connection of the type described in Definition 3 (the family 𝓖);
4. G has a cut vertex and is formed from three odd cliques sharing a common structure as in Definition 4 (the family 𝓗);
5. G has at most a bounded number of vertices and belongs to a finite list of exceptional graphs, given in Table 1.

**Definition 2 (family 𝓕).** Let K be a clique of odd order and let S be a set of vertices of K. Attach to each vertex of S a pendant clique, with attachment such that each neighborhood outside K is a clique. G is in 𝓕 if every maximal matching of G leaves exactly one vertex uncovered. The claw-freeness condition forces each vertex of K to have a neighborhood outside K that is a clique, and the equimatchability condition forces the attached cliques to be of odd order, so that each can be matched internally leaving one vertex, which must be matched outward.

**Structural lemmas.**

**Lemma 1.** If G is connected, claw-free and equimatchable with ν(G) ≥ 3, then G has no induced path P_5 whose removal leaves a component of even order that is not a clique.

*Proof sketch.* Suppose such a path exists. Claw-freeness forces the neighborhood of each interior vertex to be covered by two cliques. Choose a maximal matching containing the two end edges of the path and a second maximal matching that replaces them with the middle edges. A counting argument on the remaining even component, which has a perfect matching by [1], shows that the sizes differ by one. This contradicts equimatchability. ∎

**Lemma 2.** Let G be connected, claw-free and equimatchable with a cut vertex v. Then G−v has exactly two or three components, each a clique of odd order when it has no neighbor-induced even part, and v is adjacent to all vertices of at least two components.

*Proof sketch.* Since v is not the center of an induced claw, G−v has at most two components in which v has a non-neighbor-complete attachment, and at most three components in total. If two components were even, a maximal matching could cover v from either side and the sizes would differ. The case analysis reduces to the structures in 𝓗. ∎

**Lemma 3.** Let G be 2-connected, claw-free and equimatchable. Then either G is factor-critical or G has a perfect matching, and in the latter case the vertex set partitions into two odd cliques A and B with the edges between them forming a matching or a complete bipartite subgraph on a bounded number of vertices.

*Proof sketch.* A 2-connected claw-free graph of even order has a perfect matching [5], and by [2] equimatchability then forces every maximal matching to be perfect. Take a maximal clique A with maximum number of vertices having neighbors outside A. Claw-freeness makes the neighborhood of each outside vertex a union of at most two cliques, and iterating gives the two-clique partition. A maximal matching that leaves an A-vertex and a B-vertex unmatched but adjacent would extend, so no such nonadjacent exposed pair may exist; this yields the connection pattern of 𝓖. ∎

**Proof of Theorem 1.** Sufficiency follows by direct verification: in each listed family, any maximal matching is shown to cover all but a prescribed number of vertices, using that a matching within each clique leaves at most one vertex uncovered and the connecting edges can only match the leftover vertices in the manner forced by parity. Necessity follows by cases. If G has a cut vertex, Lemma 2 gives 𝓗. Otherwise G is 2-connected; if |V(G)| is even, Lemma 3 gives 𝓖 or randomly matchable graphs, and if odd, G is factor-critical and the Gallai–Edmonds structure [4] together with Lemma 1 gives 𝓕. Small graphs not covered by the generic arguments, with ν(G) ≤ 2, were enumerated exhaustively and yield Table 1. ∎

**Algorithmic consequence.**

**Corollary 4.** Equimatchability of a claw-free graph can be decided in polynomial time.

*Proof.* Claw-freeness can be tested in O(n^{3.5}) time or better by standard methods [6]. Given a claw-free input, compute its blocks and a maximum matching in O(m√n) time [7]. Determine whether G is factor-critical or has a perfect matching, then test membership in 𝓕, 𝓖 and 𝓗 by computing a clique cover of each neighborhood, which is polynomial for claw-free graphs since neighborhoods are covered by two cliques. Exceptional graphs are checked by constant-size isomorphism tests. ∎

Thus equimatchability, which is co-NP-hard to test in general only through its definition but is polynomially recognizable in several restricted classes [2], is also efficiently recognizable here.

The characterization presented in this paper shows that equimatchable claw-free graphs, despite the apparent generality of the class, admit a rather rigid structure. Every connected equimatchable claw-free graph we have examined falls into one of a small number of families, and membership in these families can be tested using only local and degree-based information together with standard matching computations. We discuss here the implications of this result, its relation to earlier work on equimatchability, and several directions that remain open.

**Relation to previous work.** Equimatchable graphs were introduced in the 1970s in the context of randomly matchable graphs [Lesk, Plummer and Pulleyblank, 1984], and their structure has since been studied through the Gallai-Edmonds decomposition. A fundamental observation is that a connected equimatchable graph without a perfect matching is factor-critical, and that the bounded-size behavior of such graphs is tightly controlled by their 2-connected components [Favaron, 1986; Eiben and Kotrbčík, 2015]. Eiben and Kotrbčík showed that the number of vertices of a 2-connected equimatchable factor-critical graph is bounded in terms of its maximum matching size and its connectivity-related parameters, while for graphs with a perfect matching the situation is closer to that of randomly matchable graphs, which are known to be K_{2n} or K_{n,n} [Sumner, 1979]. Our results are consistent with these facts: the families we identify in the claw-free setting either have a perfect matching and are close to the complete or complete bipartite templates, or are factor-critical and exhibit the clique-like or chain-of-cliques structure forced by the absence of claws.

Previous characterizations of equimatchable graphs were obtained for restricted classes, such as graphs of girth at least five [Frendrup, Hartnell and Vestergaard, 2010], chordal graphs [Kawarabayashi, Plummer and Saito, 2006], planar graphs with high connectivity, and graphs of small genus or bounded degree. Claw-freeness is a different kind of restriction, since it does not bound degrees or forbid dense substructures, yet it still constrains neighborhoods strongly enough to make a complete description possible. To our knowledge the present work is the first to give such a description for this class.

**Why claw-freeness helps.** Equimatchability fails precisely when some maximal matching leaves an unmatched set whose size differs from that of another. The obstructions are therefore local: an augmenting-type configuration, such as a path of length three whose endpoints are exposed after removal of a suitable edge, forces a size difference. In a claw-free graph the neighborhood of each vertex is covered by two cliques, which limits the number of independent unmatched neighbors and allows these obstructions to be analyzed through a small number of cases. Our proofs exploit this by showing that any vertex whose removal leaves several nontrivial components, or any vertex lying in a sufficiently rich clique intersection, produces two maximal matchings of different sizes. What remains after excluding these configurations are the families listed in our main theorem.

**Algorithmic consequences.** Since the families are explicitly described, recognition reduces to verifying structural conditions: connectivity, the existence or absence of a perfect matching, the clique-cover structure of neighborhoods, and the sizes of certain components. Each step can be carried out in polynomial time using maximum matching algorithms [Edmonds, 1965; Micali and Vazirani, 1980] and standard claw-free recognition. This contrasts with the general case, where recognition of equimatchable graphs is in co-NP and, as far as we know, not known to be polynomial; deciding whether a graph has a maximal matching of size different from the maximum is closely related to the NP-hard minimum maximal matching problem [Yannakakis and Gavril, 1980]. Our result thus identifies a nontrivial class in which this obstacle disappears. Moreover, because the minimum maximal matching problem is NP-hard even for restricted classes, the fact that equimatchability collapses the problem to a single value in our families explains why the recognition problem becomes tractable here.

**Limitations.** Several caveats apply. First, our characterization is stated for connected graphs; disconnected graphs are equimatchable exactly when each component is, so this is not a real restriction, but it must be kept in mind when counting or enumerating. Second, the case analysis underlying the proofs is extensive, and while it yields a complete classification, it offers limited conceptual insight into why particular families arise. A more unified argument, perhaps via the Gallai-Edmonds decomposition combined with the known structure of claw-free graphs [Chudnovsky and Seymour, 2008], could shorten the proofs and illuminate the result. Third, the running time we obtain is polynomial but not optimized; we expect that a linear or near-linear algorithm is possible by exploiting the explicit structure.

**Open problems.** Several questions follow naturally. The first concerns neighboring classes: can similar characterizations be obtained for K_{1,3}-free graphs with additional relaxations, such as quasi-line graphs, or for graphs excluding other small induced subgraphs such as the paw, the diamond, or K_{1,4}? Since claw-free graphs generalize line graphs, an equimatchable claw-free graph that is a line graph corresponds to a graph in which all maximal sets of pairwise intersecting-free edge selections, that is, maximal matchings of the line graph, have equal size; this relates equimatchability to the equality of sizes of maximal induced matchings of the root graph and merits separate study. Second, one may ask for characterizations of edge-weighted or vertex-weighted analogues, where all maximal matchings must have equal weight. Third, the complexity of recognizing equimatchable graphs in general remains open, and we hope that the structural phenomena observed here can guide progress toward a polynomial algorithm or a hardness proof.

**Conclusion.** We have described the equimatchable claw-free graphs by identifying the families that comprise them, and we have shown that this description yields an efficient recognition algorithm. The result extends the short list of graph classes for which equimatchability is understood and suggests that forbidden induced subgraph conditions are a promising route to further structural results on this property.

Voltage-gated sodium channels (VGSCs) are essential for the initiation and propagation of action potentials in neurons, cardiac myocytes, and skeletal muscle. Their rapid activation and inactivation, occurring within milliseconds of membrane depolarization, underlie the electrical excitability of these tissues. The importance of precise sodium channel function is underscored by the large number of inherited and acquired diseases linked to channel dysfunction. Mutations in the genes encoding sodium channel α-subunits cause epilepsy, chronic pain syndromes, cardiac arrhythmias such as Brugada and long QT syndromes, myotonias, and periodic paralyses. Despite decades of study, many aspects of how these channels are assembled, regulated, and coordinated remain incompletely understood.

The pore-forming α-subunit of mammalian VGSCs is a single polypeptide of about 2,000 amino acids organized into four homologous domains (DI–DIV), each containing six transmembrane segments (S1–S6). Segments S1–S4 of each domain form the voltage-sensing module, whereas S5 and S6 from the four domains come together to form the central ion-conducting pore. This pseudotetrameric architecture is thought to have arisen through two rounds of gene duplication from an ancestral single-domain channel resembling bacterial sodium channels and modern potassium channels. Whereas potassium channels and bacterial sodium channels assemble as homo- or heterotetramers of individual subunits, eukaryotic sodium channels are widely believed to be functional as monomers, with a single α-subunit sufficing to form a complete pore. This view has been reinforced by recent cryo-electron microscopy structures of sodium channels, which typically show a single α-subunit associated with auxiliary β-subunits and regulatory proteins.

However, several lines of evidence are difficult to reconcile with a strictly monomeric model. Co-expression of wild-type and mutant sodium channels has in some cases produced dominant-negative effects or altered gating that are hard to explain if each channel acts independently. In the heart, mutations in SCN5A, which encodes Nav1.5, can exert dominant-negative effects on co-expressed wild-type channels, and this has been linked to Brugada syndrome. Biochemical studies have indicated that sodium channel α-subunits can be co-immunoprecipitated from native tissues and heterologous systems, and that β-subunits can promote or stabilize such associations. Additionally, functional studies have reported that the gating of neighboring channels can be coordinated, with cooperative openings producing unusual current kinetics and apparent non-independence of single-channel events. Together, these observations suggest that sodium channels may interact physically and functionally, yet no mechanistic framework has established whether such interactions reflect true assembly of higher-order complexes or incidental clustering.

Regulatory partner proteins are plausible candidates for mediating such interactions. Among them, the 14-3-3 family of proteins is notable. These small acidic proteins exist as obligate dimers, with each monomer able to bind phosphorylated motifs on target proteins. By virtue of their dimeric structure, 14-3-3 proteins can bridge two separate client proteins or two sites on the same protein, thereby acting as molecular scaffolds. They regulate numerous ion channels, including potassium and calcium channels, affecting trafficking, localization, and gating. For sodium channels, 14-3-3 has been reported to interact with the DIII–DIV linker region and the C-terminal domain of Nav1.5, and to modulate inactivation properties. The C-terminal region is also a hub for calmodulin and fibroblast growth factor homologous factors, which fine-tune channel gating. Whether 14-3-3 could serve as a physical and functional linker between two α-subunits has not been tested.

Understanding whether sodium channels function as dimers has substantial implications. If two α-subunits gate in a coupled manner, then the effect of a single mutation could be transmitted to a partner channel, offering a mechanistic explanation for dominant-negative behavior and for the variable phenotypes seen in heterozygous patients. Coupled gating would also complicate pharmacology, since drug binding to one subunit could allosterically influence the other. Furthermore, interfering with the dimerization interface or the 14-3-3-mediated coupling might provide a new route to modulate channel activity without directly blocking the pore, an approach that could improve selectivity compared with existing sodium channel blockers.

In this study, we sought to determine whether sodium channel α-subunits assemble and function as dimers. Using Nav1.5 as a primary model, we combined biochemical, biophysical, and electrophysiological approaches to test for direct physical interaction between α-subunits and to examine whether their gating is coupled. We mapped the region of the channel that mediates dimerization and tested the role of 14-3-3 in coordinating the behavior of the two subunits. By expressing channels with differing properties, including pharmacologically or mutationally altered subunits, we asked whether modifying one subunit influences the gating of its partner. Finally, because sodium channel isoforms share considerable sequence similarity in the relevant regions, we examined whether dimerization and coupled gating are conserved across other mammalian sodium channels.

Our results show that sodium channel α-subunits associate as dimers, that a defined cytoplasmic region mediates this interaction, and that 14-3-3 is required for coupled gating of the two pores. These findings challenge the prevailing monomeric paradigm and provide a framework for reinterpreting sodium channel structure, function, and disease mechanisms, while suggesting new therapeutic targets for sodium channelopathies.

Plasmids and constructs. Human Nav1.5 (SCN5A) cDNA, along with Nav1.2, Nav1.4 and Nav1.7 cDNAs, were used in mammalian expression vectors. For co-immunoprecipitation and FRET experiments, channels were tagged at the C-terminus with HA, FLAG, mCerulean (CFP) or mVenus (YFP). Truncations and point mutations in the proposed dimerization region and the 14-3-3 binding site were generated by site-directed mutagenesis (QuikChange) and verified by Sanger sequencing. The 14-3-3η isoform was cloned with or without a fluorescent tag. A dominant-negative 14-3-3 construct (difopein) was used to disrupt 14-3-3 binding. Concatenated constructs were not used unless stated.

Cell culture and transfection. HEK293 cells and tsA201 cells were maintained in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum and penicillin/streptomycin at 37°C and 5% CO2. Cells were transfected with Lipofectamine 2000 or polyethylenimine at 60–80% confluence.
