For electrophysiology, cells were co-transfected with a GFP marker (0.2 µg) and channel plasmids (1–2 µg total) and recorded 24–48 h later. For coupling experiments, wild-type and mutant channels were co-expressed at a 1:1 DNA ratio. Neonatal rat ventricular myocytes were isolated by enzymatic digestion and used for endogenous channel analysis.

Co-immunoprecipitation and western blotting. Cells were lysed in buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% deoxycholate and protease/phosphatase inhibitors. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation at 14,000 g for 15 min at 4°C, and 500 µg protein was incubated with anti-HA or anti-FLAG antibody-conjugated agarose beads overnight at 4°C. Beads were washed five times, and proteins eluted in Laemmli buffer at 37°C for 30 min (to avoid aggregation of the channels). Samples were separated on 4–12% gradient SDS-PAGE gels, transferred to PVDF membranes, and probed with antibodies against HA, FLAG, pan-Nav, and 14-3-3. Detection was by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and chemiluminescence. Endogenous co-immunoprecipitation from heart tissue lysates used an anti-Nav1.5 antibody, with IgG as a negative control.

Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET). Cells expressing CFP- and YFP-tagged channels were imaged on a confocal microscope using sensitized-emission FRET. Three images were acquired (CFP, YFP, and FRET channels), and background and bleed-through corrections were applied using cells expressing CFP or YFP alone. Apparent FRET efficiency was calculated from corrected images in membrane regions of interest. Cells co-expressing CFP and YFP as free proteins served as negative controls, and a CFP–YFP fusion as the positive control. FRET efficiency was plotted against the acceptor:donor ratio to assess binding specificity. Acceptor photobleaching was used to validate selected results.

Electrophysiology. Whole-cell sodium currents were recorded at room temperature with an Axopatch 200B amplifier and Digidata 1440A, controlled by pClamp software. Pipettes (1.5–3 MΩ) were filled with (in mM) 10 NaF, 110 CsF, 20 CsCl, 10 EGTA, 10 HEPES (pH 7.35 with CsOH). The bath contained 140 NaCl, 4 KCl, 1.8 CaCl2, 0.75 MgCl2, 5 glucose, 10 HEPES (pH 7.35 with NaOH). Series resistance was compensated by at least 80%, and currents were sampled at 20–50 kHz and filtered at 5 kHz. Activation was assessed using 50-ms depolarizations from –120 mV to +60 mV in 5-mV steps. Steady-state inactivation was measured using 500-ms prepulses followed by a test pulse. Conductance–voltage and inactivation curves were fit with Boltzmann functions to obtain V1/2 and slope factors. Recovery from inactivation was measured with a two-pulse protocol and fit with exponential functions. Late current was measured as the persistent current at the end of long depolarizations, normalized to peak.

Assessment of coupled gating. To test functional coupling, wild-type channels were co-expressed with mutants carrying altered voltage dependence, drug sensitivity, or loss of function. A dimer-based model predicts that the mutant shifts or alters the gating of the co-expressed wild-type channel; this was evaluated by comparing the gating parameters of the co-expressed population with those of each channel alone, and by testing for a single or double Boltzmann distribution. Dominant-negative effects of pore-dead or trafficking-defective mutants on wild-type current density were also quantified. Pharmacological coupling was tested using a use-dependent or high-affinity blocker applied to drug-sensitive wild-type channels co-expressed with drug-resistant mutants, and the fraction of current blocked was compared with that predicted for independent channels. The effect of 14-3-3 was tested by co-expression of difopein, mutation of its binding site, or overexpression of 14-3-3η.

Surface biotinylation. Surface proteins were labeled with sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin for 30 min at 4°C, quenched with glycine, and isolated with streptavidin beads. Surface and total fractions were analyzed by western blot to ensure that mutants did not alter trafficking.

Structural modeling. Cryo-EM structures of human Nav channels were used to model the dimer interface and the 14-3-3 binding region. Docking of 14-3-3 to the phosphorylated binding motif was performed with HADDOCK, and models were visualized in PyMOL.

Data analysis and statistics. Data were analyzed with Clampfit, Origin and GraphPad Prism and are presented as mean ± SEM. Comparisons between two groups used Student’s t-test (or Mann–Whitney test when normality was not satisfied), and multiple groups were compared with one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey or Bonferroni post hoc tests. P < 0.05 was considered significant. Each experiment was replicated in at least three independent transfections, and n denotes the number of cells.

Sodium channel α-subunits physically interact in heterologous cells and native tissue

To test whether Nav α-subunits associate with each other, we first co-expressed differentially tagged human Nav1.5 constructs (HA- and FLAG-tagged) in HEK293 cells. Immunoprecipitation with anti-FLAG antibody pulled down HA-Nav1.5, whereas no HA signal was recovered from cells expressing HA-Nav1.5 alone or from lysates mixed after separate expression, indicating that the interaction occurs in the cell and not during lysis. The interaction persisted in the presence of the β1 subunit and was also detected for endogenous channels immunoprecipitated from mouse and human cardiac tissue lysates, where antibodies against Nav1.5 co-precipitated Nav1.5 from a differently epitope-tagged pool or, in wild-type tissue, enriched species that were detected by a second, independent anti-Nav1.5 antibody. A proximity ligation assay in isolated cardiomyocytes yielded punctate signals along the sarcolemma and intercalated discs, consistent with Nav1.5–Nav1.5 proximity in situ. FRET between Nav1.5-CFP and Nav1.5-YFP at the plasma membrane gave efficiencies significantly higher than those of the negative control pair (Nav1.5-CFP with membrane-anchored YFP), supporting close association in living cells.

Identification of the dimerization region

To map the interacting region, we generated truncations and domain-level constructs of Nav1.5 and tested their ability to co-precipitate full-length channel. Full-length channels interacted with the N-terminal and cytoplasmic domain I–II linker fragments weakly or not at all, while fragments containing the intracellular C-terminus robustly co-precipitated the full-length channel. Progressive deletion within the C-terminal domain narrowed the interaction to a segment proximal to the EF-hand-like region and the IQ motif. Deleting this segment (ΔDI) in the full-length channel abolished co-immunoprecipitation with wild-type channel, yet ΔDI channels still trafficked to the membrane, as indicated by surface biotinylation and by robust sodium currents, though with reduced density. Thus the segment is dispensable for channel function but required for α–α association. A peptide corresponding to this region disrupted the interaction when added to lysates, further supporting direct involvement.

14-3-3 mediates the interaction

Because 14-3-3 proteins are dimeric adaptors known to bind the Nav1.5 C-terminus, we asked whether they bridge the two α-subunits. Co-immunoprecipitation showed 14-3-3 in complexes with Nav1.5, and the amount of Nav1.5–Nav1.5 interaction was reduced by the 14-3-3 antagonist difopein but not by a control construct (R18 mutant). Difopein also reduced FRET between Nav1.5-CFP and Nav1.5-YFP. Mutating the 14-3-3 binding site in the dimerization region abolished both 14-3-3 co-precipitation and α–α interaction, whereas knockdown of 14-3-3η decreased the interaction. Together these data indicate that the two α-subunits are linked through a 14-3-3 dimer bound to the C-terminal region of each channel.

Dimeric channels exhibit coupled gating

We next examined whether physical association has functional consequences. We co-expressed wild-type Nav1.5 with a mutant channel carrying a dominant-negative loss-of-function variant (the Brugada syndrome mutation, L325R) that produces no current on its own. If channels assembled independently, the current from the wild-type channel should scale with its expression and be unchanged by the mutant. Instead, co-expression reduced peak current beyond what was expected from the wild-type channel alone, and it shifted the voltage dependence of activation and inactivation of the remaining current, which was prevented by deleting the dimerization region from the mutant channel or by difopein treatment. Thus the mutant exerts a dominant-negative effect that depends on dimerization and 14-3-3.

To test coupling more directly, we co-expressed Nav1.5 channels with distinct gating properties, wild-type and a variant with a depolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation. Co-expressed channels showed activation and inactivation curves that were intermediate and single-Boltzmann in shape, not the sum of two independent populations. Disrupting dimerization with difopein or by ΔDI restored two distinguishable components. Single-channel recordings in cell-attached patches revealed concerted openings: the two channels frequently opened and closed together, with a coupling coefficient significantly higher than predicted for independent channels. Coupled events showed larger conductance levels than single events, in multiples of the unitary conductance. Difopein reduced the frequency of coupled openings and increased independent openings.

Conservation among mammalian sodium channels

Finally, we asked whether dimerization is specific to Nav1.5. Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated homomeric interactions of Nav1.1, Nav1.2, and Nav1.7, all of which share a conserved sequence in the C-terminal region identified above. Nav1.5 also interacted with other isoforms in co-expression experiments, suggesting that heteromeric dimers can form. Dominant-negative effects of a pathogenic Nav1.2 mutant on wild-type Nav1.2 currents were similarly relieved by difopein. Thus the mechanism of 14-3-3-dependent dimerization and coupled gating appears conserved across mammalian sodium channels.

Our results indicate that voltage-gated sodium channel α-subunits do not necessarily operate as isolated monomers. Biochemical, imaging and electrophysiological evidence supports the conclusion that two α-subunits physically associate, and that this association has functional consequences: the channels gate in a coupled manner. We further map the region that mediates dimerization and show that the adaptor protein 14-3-3 is required for coupled gating. Because the mechanism is conserved across mammalian sodium channel isoforms, it likely represents a general feature of this channel family rather than an idiosyncrasy of a single isoform.

**Reconciling dimerization with the monomer paradigm.** The idea that a sodium channel is a single pseudo-tetrameric polypeptide, with four homologous domains forming one pore, has been supported by decades of structural and functional work, and by the recent cryo-EM structures. We do not dispute that a single α-subunit contains all the elements needed to form a conducting, voltage-sensitive pore. Our findings instead suggest that this unit can be organized into a higher-order assembly in native membranes. This may explain why structures of purified, detergent-solubilized channels have not revealed dimers: the interaction may depend on 14-3-3 or other cellular factors that are lost during purification, or may be too dynamic to survive such preparations. It may also help explain several long-standing observations that were difficult to fit with a monomeric model, including non-ideal gating kinetics, dominant-negative effects of some disease-associated variants, and the unexpected effects of co-expressing wild-type and mutant channels. Coupled gating provides a simple framework for these observations, since a mutation in one subunit could alter the behavior of its partner.

**Role of 14-3-3.** 14-3-3 proteins are themselves dimers and are well known to bridge two target proteins, so they are a logical candidate for linking two α-subunits through their cytoplasmic regions. Our data show that disrupting the interaction removes the coupling of gating, which indicates that 14-3-3 is not simply a bystander modulator but is part of the mechanism that transmits conformational changes between subunits. An important question is whether 14-3-3 is the sole determinant of physical association or whether it stabilizes a contact that also involves direct α–α interactions. The identification of a dimerization region suggests that both may contribute. Because 14-3-3 binding typically depends on phosphorylation, the coupling could be regulated by signaling pathways, allowing cells to tune channel cooperativity in response to physiological state. Such regulation would add a new layer of control over excitability, and may differ among tissues with different kinase and 14-3-3 isoform profiles.

**Conservation and physiological implications.** The conservation of dimerization among mammalian sodium channels suggests strong selective pressure and a functional role. Coupled gating could synchronize the opening of neighboring channels, producing larger and more rapid sodium influx than independent channels would generate, which could sharpen action potential upstroke and enhance propagation reliability. Conversely, it could alter the effective voltage dependence and recovery from inactivation of the channel population. Heteromeric assemblies of different isoforms, if they occur, would greatly expand the functional diversity available to a cell, and might influence pharmacology, since drug binding to one subunit could affect its partner.

**Implications for channelopathies.** Hundreds of sodium channel mutations cause epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmias, pain disorders and myotonias. Many of these are heterozygous, so mutant and wild-type subunits are co-expressed. If channels dimerize, mutant subunits could exert effects on wild-type partners, and the phenotype would not be predicted from the properties of the mutant channel alone. This perspective may help explain variable penetrance and genotype–phenotype discrepancies. It also suggests new therapeutic strategies: rather than targeting the pore, one could disrupt or stabilize the dimer interface, or modulate 14-3-3 binding, to normalize gating. Existing drugs may also need to be reevaluated in light of possible cooperative effects.

**Limitations and future directions.** Several issues remain open. The stoichiometry is consistent with dimers, but we cannot exclude that larger oligomers form under some conditions. The precise structural arrangement of the two α-subunits and the pathway by which conformational change is communicated through 14-3-3 are unresolved; high-resolution structures of the complex in the presence of 14-3-3, together with cross-linking and mutational mapping, will be needed. Most of our experiments used heterologous expression systems, and it is important to establish the prevalence and functional impact of dimers in native neurons, cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, and how auxiliary β-subunits and other partners influence assembly. Finally, it will be important to test directly whether disease-associated mutations act through the dimer, and whether disrupting the interface can rescue pathological phenotypes.

**Conclusion.** We show that sodium channel α-subunits assemble as dimers whose gating is coupled through 14-3-3, and that this mechanism is conserved across mammalian isoforms. This finding revises the prevailing view of sodium channel organization, offers an explanation for several unexplained functional observations, and identifies the dimer interface and its regulation as potential new targets for treating sodium channelopathies.

Nursing is a profession grounded in ethical commitments, and the quality of nursing care depends largely on the values that guide nurses' judgments and actions. Professional values are defined as standards of action accepted by those in a profession, and they provide a framework for evaluating beliefs and attitudes that influence behavior [1, 2]. They serve as the foundation of nurses' practice, guide interactions with patients, colleagues and other members of the healthcare team, and shape the resolution of ethical dilemmas [3]. Professional codes of ethics, such as those of the American Nurses Association and the International Council of Nurses, articulate these values explicitly, including altruism, autonomy, human dignity, integrity and social justice [4, 5].

Healthcare systems worldwide are changing rapidly. Technological advances, rising patient expectations, resource constraints, increasing workloads and growing cultural diversity have created complex ethical challenges for nurses [6]. In this context, nurses are required to have knowledge and awareness of professional values as standards for providing safe, high-quality and ethical care. Evidence suggests that when nurses internalize professional values, they show greater job satisfaction, stronger professional commitment, and a lower tendency to leave the profession [7, 8]. Conversely, conflicts between personal and professional values, or a lack of clarity about the latter, may lead to moral distress, burnout and compromised patient care [9].

Nurses' perspectives on professional values affect their decision-making and the care they deliver. Values operate as a lens through which nurses interpret clinical situations, prioritize patient needs and decide on a course of action [10]. Accordingly, understanding how nurses rank the importance of different values can reveal the strengths and gaps in professional socialization and can inform strategies to reinforce ethical practice. Professional values are not innate; they are acquired through a process that begins in nursing education, continues through clinical experience and is shaped by organizational culture, role models and personal characteristics [11]. Therefore, demographic and professional variables such as age, work experience, education level and participation in ethics training may influence how nurses perceive these values [12, 13].

Several instruments have been developed to measure professional values in nursing. One of the most widely used is the Nursing Professional Values Scale, developed by Weis and Schank on the basis of the American Nurses Association Code for Nurses and later revised (NPVS-R) to reflect updated versions of the code [14, 15]. The scale has been used with students and practicing nurses in many countries, and studies using it have reported varying results. Some report high overall scores, with patient-centered values such as confidentiality, privacy and accountability ranked highest [16, 17]. Others have found that values related to professional development, participation in professional associations, research and health policy are rated lower [18, 19]. Such discrepancies imply that cultural, religious, organizational and educational contexts shape how professional values are perceived and prioritized [20].

In Iran, nursing has developed substantially over recent decades, with the expansion of university-based education, graduate programs and efforts to define professional standards. Nevertheless, Iranian nurses work in settings characterized by nursing shortages, heavy workloads, limited autonomy and sometimes inadequate institutional support, all of which may hinder the application of professional values in practice [21, 22]. Moreover, the Iranian cultural and Islamic context places strong emphasis on values such as respect for human dignity, confidentiality and compassion, which may influence nurses' value priorities differently from those in Western countries where most value research has been conducted [23]. Although some Iranian studies have examined professional values among nursing students and nurses, findings are inconsistent, and few have been conducted in the southeastern region of the country, including Kerman [24, 25]. Regional differences in educational resources, workforce composition and cultural characteristics make local evidence valuable for planning appropriate interventions.

Furthermore, the continuing emergence of ethical challenges in clinical settings, such as end-of-life decisions, patient rights, resource allocation and the protection of patient privacy in the era of electronic records, makes it essential for nursing managers and educators to know which values nurses regard as important and which are undervalued [6, 26]. If values such as participation in research, involvement in professional associations and contribution to health policy are given low priority, this may impede the advancement of the profession, evidence-based practice and nurses' influence on healthcare decision-making [18]. Identifying such gaps can guide the design of in-service training, ethics education and organizational policies that foster a supportive ethical climate.

Despite the recognized importance of professional values, there is limited information on how clinical nurses in hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences perceive them and which personal and professional characteristics are associated with their perceptions. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses working in educational hospitals of Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran, using the Persian version of the NPVS-R, and to examine the relationship between nurses' perceptions and their demographic and professional characteristics.

This cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted from April to September 2016 in four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, southeastern Iran. These hospitals are the main referral and teaching centers in the province and offer a wide range of medical and surgical services. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [1].

**Study population and sampling**

The target population was all clinical nurses working in the participating hospitals. Inclusion criteria were a bachelor's degree or higher in nursing, at least six months of clinical experience, direct involvement in patient care, and willingness to participate. Nurses in management positions without direct patient care responsibilities and those who did not complete the questionnaire were excluded.

The sample size was calculated from the standard deviation of professional values scores reported in a comparable study [2]. With a 95% confidence level, a precision of 1.5 points, and an anticipated standard deviation of approximately 12, the minimum sample was about 245 nurses. To allow for possible attrition, 280 questionnaires were distributed, and 250 were completed and entered into the analysis (response rate 89%).

Stratified random sampling was used. Each hospital was treated as a stratum, and the number of nurses selected from each was proportional to its total nursing workforce. Within each hospital, a list of eligible nurses was obtained from the nursing office, and participants were chosen by simple random sampling with a computer-generated random number table.

**Data collection instruments**

Data were collected with a two-part questionnaire. The first part gathered demographic and professional characteristics: age, gender, marital status, educational level, work experience, employment type, ward of employment, and participation in professional ethics training courses, including workshops and in-service programs.

The second part was the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), developed by Weis and Schank [3,4]. The instrument was derived from the American Nurses Association Code of Ethics for Nurses and measures the importance nurses assign to professional values. The revised version has 26 items rated on a five-point Likert scale from 1 (not important) to 5 (most important). Total scores range from 26 to 130, and higher scores indicate greater perceived importance of professional values. The items cluster into three factors: caring, activism, and professionalism [4]. For interpretation, scores were categorized into low, moderate, and high levels based on tertiles of the possible range.

The Persian version of the NPVS-R was used. It had been translated using the forward-backward procedure, and its validity and reliability had been established in Iranian samples [5]. In the present study, content validity was reviewed again by ten faculty members of the School of Nursing and Midwifery, who judged the items clear and appropriate for the clinical context. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha in a pilot of 20 nurses who were not included in the main sample, and the alpha coefficient was 0.92, indicating excellent reliability. Cronbach's alpha in the main sample was similar.

**Data collection procedure**

After approval was obtained and permission was granted by the hospital authorities, the researcher visited the wards on different shifts to reach nurses working in rotating schedules. Selected nurses received an explanation of the study aims and procedures and were assured that participation was voluntary. Written informed consent was then obtained. The questionnaires were self-administered, anonymous, and completed in about 10 to 15 minutes. They were collected the same day or within two days in sealed envelopes to preserve confidentiality and reduce social desirability bias. Completed questionnaires were checked for missing data, and those with more than 10% unanswered items were excluded.

**Statistical analysis**

Data were analyzed with SPSS version 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The normality of the distribution of the total score was assessed with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and by inspecting histograms and Q-Q plots. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations, were used to summarize demographic characteristics and the NPVS-R item and total scores. Items were ranked by mean score to identify the values considered most and least important.

Relationships between the total score and demographic variables were examined using inferential tests. Independent-samples t-tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc Tukey tests compared mean scores across categorical variables such as gender, marital status, educational level, ward, and participation in ethics training. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to examine associations between the total score and continuous variables such as age and work experience. Variables with a P value below 0.2 in the univariate analyses were entered into a multiple linear regression model to identify independent predictors, and the assumptions of linearity, independence of residuals, homoscedasticity, and absence of multicollinearity were checked. A P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

**Ethical considerations**

The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. Participants gave written informed consent after being told the objectives and the voluntary nature of participation, their right to withdraw at any time without any consequence for their employment, and the confidentiality of their information. No names or identifying details were recorded, and the data were used for research purposes only. Permission to use the Persian version of the NPVS-R was obtained from the authors of the translated instrument.

A total of 250 clinical nurses from four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences participated in the study, and all returned questionnaires were complete enough for analysis. The mean age of participants was 33.4 ± 6.8 years, and the mean work experience was 9.1 ± 6.3 years. Most participants were female (n = 187, 74.8%), married (n = 183, 73.2%), and held a bachelor's degree in nursing (n = 228, 91.2%). Approximately half of the nurses (n = 129, 51.6%) reported having participated in a professional ethics training course or workshop. The distribution of participants across hospitals was proportional to the number of nurses employed in each setting, in accordance with the stratified sampling design.

**Total score of professional values**

The total score on the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R) was 102.57 ± 11.94 (possible range 26–130), which indicates a high level of perceived importance of professional values. When expressed as an item mean, the score was approximately 3.95 of 5, and no participant obtained a total score in the lowest quartile of the possible range. The scores were approximately normally distributed (skewness = −0.62; kurtosis = 0.41), which supported the use of parametric tests. The internal consistency of the Persian version in the present sample was satisfactory (Cronbach's alpha = 0.93), a value comparable to those reported in earlier validation studies of the instrument [1,2].

**Importance of individual items**

The items rated as most important by the nurses were "Maintaining confidentiality of patients" (mean = 4.78 ± 0.52), "Safeguarding patients' right to privacy" (4.74 ± 0.55), "Accepting responsibility for own actions and judgments" (4.69 ± 0.58), "Protecting the safety of patients" (4.66 ± 0.60), and "Maintaining patient trust" (4.61 ± 0.63). In contrast, the lowest-rated items were "Recognizing role of professional nursing associations in shaping healthcare policy" (3.21 ± 1.02), "Participating in nursing research and/or implementing research findings appropriate to practice" (3.35 ± 0.99), "Participating in activities of professional nursing associations" (3.41 ± 1.01), "Promoting the profession's image to the public" (3.58 ± 0.97), and "Initiating actions to improve environments of practice" (3.62 ± 0.94). Thus, values directly related to patient-centered ethical care were consistently prioritized over those concerning professional development, research, and policy engagement. This pattern is similar to that reported among nurses in other national and international contexts [3,4].

**Relationship with demographic and occupational variables**

Bivariate analyses showed statistically significant relationships between the NPVS-R total score and three variables: age, work experience, and participation in professional ethics training (Table 1). Age was positively correlated with the total score (r = 0.19, P = 0.003), as was work experience (r = 0.22, P < 0.001). Nurses who had attended professional ethics training obtained higher mean scores (104.31 ± 11.20) than those who had not (100.72 ± 12.37), and the difference was statistically significant (t = 2.46, P = 0.015).

No statistically significant differences were found in mean scores by gender (men: 101.84 ± 12.51; women: 102.80 ± 11.78; P = 0.58), marital status (P = 0.34), educational level (P = 0.21), or employment type (permanent, contractual, or temporary; P = 0.47). Mean scores also did not differ significantly across the four hospitals (F = 1.12, P = 0.34), indicating that the perceived importance of professional values was relatively homogeneous across the study settings. Similarly, the clinical ward in which nurses worked (e.g., medical, surgical, intensive care, emergency) was not significantly associated with total scores (P = 0.29).

**Multivariable analysis**

To determine the independent contribution of the significant variables, a multiple linear regression model was fitted including age, work experience, and ethics training. Because age and work experience were strongly correlated (r = 0.86), the variance inflation factors were examined and were found to be above the conventional threshold for age (VIF = 4.9). Even so, the model was statistically significant (F = 8.97, P < 0.001) and explained 9.8% of the variance in the total score (adjusted R² = 0.087). In this model, work experience (β = 0.21, P = 0.012) and participation in ethics training (β = 0.14, P = 0.026) remained significant predictors, whereas age was no longer significant (β = 0.03, P = 0.74). Accordingly, longer clinical experience and exposure to ethics education were independently associated with higher perceived importance of professional values.

**Summary of findings**

In summary, nurses attached a high overall importance to professional values, particularly those concerning confidentiality, privacy, accountability, and patient safety. Values concerning participation in professional associations, research utilization, and involvement in health policy were rated as comparatively less important. Age, work experience, and attendance at ethics training were associated with higher scores, and work experience and ethics training retained their associations after adjustment for the other variables.

The present study examined the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses in educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences. The total mean score of professional values was high (102.57 ± 11.94), indicating that nurses regard professional values as important in their practice. This finding is consistent with studies conducted in Iran, Turkey, the United States, and other countries, in which nurses and nursing students also reported high levels of professional values [1-4]. Such agreement across diverse settings suggests that core nursing values are widely recognized, probably because they are embedded in nursing education, professional codes of ethics, and the moral expectations placed on the discipline [5]. However, a high overall score may mask variability among individual items, and the item-level results here warrant closer attention.

Nurses assigned the greatest importance to maintaining patient confidentiality and safeguarding patients' right to privacy. This is in line with findings from other studies using the NPVS-R and similar instruments, in which items on confidentiality, privacy, and patient protection were consistently ranked highest [2, 6, 7]. These values are concrete, directly observable in daily bedside care, and reinforced by legal requirements, institutional policies, and religious and cultural norms. In the Iranian context, respect for privacy and dignity is strongly tied to Islamic and cultural beliefs, which may further explain their prominence [8]. The emphasis on these values is encouraging, since trust between nurse and patient depends on them, and breaches of confidentiality can lead to harm and loss of trust in healthcare services.

In contrast, recognizing the role of professional nursing associations in shaping healthcare policy and participating in nursing research or implementing research findings were rated lowest. Similar patterns have been reported in earlier studies, where values concerning professional development, research, and policy involvement ranked below patient-centered values [3, 9]. Several explanations are plausible. Clinical nurses, burdened by heavy workloads, staff shortages, and shift work, may perceive research and association activity as peripheral to their immediate responsibilities. Limited access to resources, insufficient institutional support, and a lack of training in research utilization may further reduce their appreciation of these activities [10]. In addition, nursing associations in Iran have historically had limited influence on health policy, so nurses may not see a tangible link between associations and their practice [11]. Yet evidence-based practice and collective professional advocacy are essential for improving care quality and strengthening the profession's autonomy. The gap between valuing individual patient-focused ethics and valuing the broader professional and scientific dimensions of nursing therefore represents a notable weakness.

A statistically significant relationship was found between professional values scores and nurses' age, work experience, and participation in professional ethics training. The association with age and experience agrees with other reports that older and more experienced nurses hold stronger professional values [4, 12]. With time, nurses encounter more ethical dilemmas, develop greater moral sensitivity, and internalize the norms of their profession through socialization and reflective practice. Experience may also foster a stronger professional identity and commitment. However, some studies have reported no such relationship or even the opposite, perhaps reflecting differences in organizational culture, burnout, and the instruments used [13]. The positive influence of ethics training is particularly important because it is a modifiable factor. Nurses who had attended professional ethics courses assigned higher importance to values, supporting the view that education and continuing professional development can shape ethical awareness and attitudes [14, 15]. This underscores the need for structured, ongoing ethics education rather than reliance on informal learning alone.

These findings have practical implications. Nursing managers and educators should design in-service programs that strengthen understanding of all professional values, including those related to research, policy participation, and professional collaboration. Case-based discussion, ethics rounds, mentoring by experienced nurses, and reflective practice could be integrated into such programs. Hospital administrators might also encourage research utilization by providing time, access to databases, and recognition for evidence-based initiatives, and could facilitate nurses' engagement with professional associations. Younger and less experienced nurses may benefit especially from targeted support, since they scored lower. At the undergraduate level, curricula should emphasize the connection between professional values, evidence-based practice, and the social responsibilities of nursing.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inferences about the relationships between demographic variables and professional values. Data were self-reported, so social desirability bias may have inflated scores, particularly for socially valued items such as confidentiality. The study was conducted in educational hospitals of a single university, which limits generalizability to other regions and healthcare settings. In addition, the NPVS-R measures the perceived importance of values rather than their actual enactment in practice, so the results cannot show whether nurses' stated values are reflected in their behavior.

In conclusion, although clinical nurses' overall ratings of professional values were high, the importance attached to certain values, especially those related to nursing research and the role of professional associations in health policy, was lower. Age, work experience, and participation in professional ethics training were associated with higher scores. Given the growing ethical challenges in healthcare, educational programs are needed to enhance nurses' awareness and comprehensive understanding of the full range of professional values. Future research should use mixed methods designs, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches, to develop an instrument that evaluates how values are actually applied in nursing practice, and should include multicenter samples and longitudinal designs to clarify how values develop over time and how interventions influence them.

Colonization of freshwater habitats by marine organisms is among the most significant ecological transitions in vertebrate evolution. Freshwater and seawater impose opposite osmoregulatory challenges: fish in hyperosmotic environments lose water and gain ions, whereas fish in hypoosmotic environments gain water and lose ions [1,2]. Teleosts maintain internal osmolality at roughly one third of seawater through coordinated activity of the gills, intestine, kidney and skin, which regulate ion uptake and secretion [3]. Although only about 2.5% of teleost species are diadromous, these species must cope with both extremes within a single lifetime, and they provide valuable models for understanding the physiological flexibility that may precede, or facilitate, permanent habitat shifts [4,5].

The central molecular machinery of fish osmoregulation involves membrane transporters and the ATPases that energize them. Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) generates the electrochemical gradients that drive secondary ion transport, and its gill activity typically increases in seawater, where it supports salt secretion by ionocytes, and in some species also in freshwater [6,7]. Vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (HA) is implicated in freshwater ion uptake, where it hyperpolarizes the apical membrane and allows Na+ entry through channels [8,9]. The intestine also contributes substantially, by absorbing water and monovalent ions in seawater-acclimated fish and by participating in ion uptake in freshwater [10]. Changes in the activity or expression of these enzymes therefore are commonly used as indicators of osmoregulatory acclimation and adaptation [11].

Landlocking, the permanent isolation of diadromous populations in freshwater, offers natural experiments on the evolution of osmoregulation. In several lineages, such as alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus), threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) and sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka), freshwater-resident populations have differentiated from their migratory ancestors in salinity tolerance, ionocyte function and ATPase regulation, sometimes within a few hundred generations [12-15]. Such studies reveal that loss of the marine phase may relax selection on seawater performance and may drive evolution of traits favoring freshwater life, although the tempo and the physiological targets of this divergence vary among taxa [16]. Whether divergence also modifies tolerance to low salinity, and which physiological processes underlie it, remains poorly understood.

Galaxias maculatus (Jenyns, 1848), the common galaxias or puyen, is one of the most widely distributed freshwater fishes of the Southern Hemisphere, occurring in Australia, New Zealand, South America and various islands [17]. Most populations are amphidromous: adults spawn in the upper estuary or lower river during high tides, larvae are carried to the sea, where they develop for several months, and juveniles return to rivers to grow and mature [18]. However, numerous landlocked populations complete the full life cycle in freshwater lakes, in which larvae do not migrate to the sea [19]. In Patagonia, a number of such populations inhabit lakes formed or modified after the retreat of ice sheets at the end of the last glaciation, roughly 10,000 to 15,000 years ago [20,21]. Phylogeographic studies have shown that these populations are genetically structured and that landlocking has occurred repeatedly and independently across the species’ range [22,23].

Landlocked G. maculatus differ from their diadromous counterparts in life history and morphology, including body size, growth, reproductive timing and larval development [24,25]. Some work has also suggested differences in physiological responses to salinity, since juveniles and adults of this species show considerable euryhalinity [26,27]. Nevertheless, it is unclear whether the shift to a permanently freshwater life has been accompanied by a loss of salinity tolerance, as might be expected from relaxed selection, or by some other form of divergence. Moreover, the demographic context in which this divergence occurred is rarely documented, even though it is essential for interpreting adaptive change. Founder events and subsequent expansion may generate genetic differentiation through drift alone, and so physiological differences must be considered against a background of population history [28].

Mitochondrial DNA is well suited to reconstructing recent colonization scenarios, because of its high mutation rate, haploid inheritance and small effective population size, which allow fast detection of bottlenecks, founder effects and demographic expansions [29,30]. Combining analysis of haplotype genealogies and diversity indices with physiological experiments enables direct comparison of historical and functional divergence within the same pair of populations. Such an integrative approach is particularly informative when the time of isolation is short, as it allows evolutionary changes to be linked to specific ecological events [31].

In the present study, we examined an amphidromous population and a landlocked lake population of G. maculatus from the Andean region of Patagonia. First, we used mtDNA sequences to assess genetic diversity and differentiation and to infer the colonization history of the lake, testing the hypothesis of a recent founder event from the diadromous stock followed by population expansion. Second, we compared the osmoregulatory performance of both populations by measuring survival over eight days across salinities from 0 to 30 ppt, after progressive acclimation. Third, we quantified the activity of NKA, HA and other ATPases in gills and intestine to determine whether differences in tolerance are mirrored by differences in these enzymatic systems. We predicted that landlocked fish would show reduced tolerance to high salinity, as a consequence of relaxed selection in freshwater. Our results show instead that divergence has been unexpectedly pronounced at low salinities, indicating rapid adaptive modification of the osmoregulatory system within a few thousand years of isolation.

Sampling and study populations

Adult Galaxias maculatus were collected in the Valdivia River estuary (diadromous population; Chile, ~39°S) and in Lake Pirihueico (landlocked population; Andean region, ~39°S), a lake formed after the last deglaciation. Fish were captured with beach seine nets and minnow traps under permits issued by the national fisheries authority. For genetic analyses, a fin clip was taken from each fish and preserved in 95% ethanol at −20 °C. For physiological experiments, live fish were transported in aerated containers to the laboratory and held for four weeks in dechlorinated fresh water (0 ppt) at 12 ± 1 °C under a natural photoperiod, and fed daily with commercial pellets. Fish of similar size were used in both populations to reduce size-related variation in osmoregulatory capacity [1,2].

DNA extraction, amplification and sequencing

Total genomic DNA was extracted from fin tissue using a standard proteinase K digestion followed by phenol–chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation [3]. A fragment of the mitochondrial control region (D-loop) was amplified by PCR with primers previously used in galaxiids [4]. Reactions (25 µL) contained 50 ng DNA, 1× buffer, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM of each dNTP, 0.4 µM of each primer and 1 U Taq polymerase. Cycling consisted of an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 3 min; 35 cycles of 94 °C for 45 s, 55 °C for 45 s and 72 °C for 60 s; and a final extension at 72 °C for 7 min. Products were checked on 1.5% agarose gels, purified and sequenced in both directions on an automated sequencer. Sequences were edited and aligned using Clustal W [5] with manual verification, and deposited in GenBank.

Population genetic analyses

Haplotype diversity (H), the average number of nucleotide differences (Π), nucleotide diversity and the number of polymorphic sites were estimated for each population in Arlequin [6] and DnaSP [7]. Genetic differentiation was evaluated using pairwise GST (based on haplotype frequencies) and NST (which also incorporates sequence divergence), and the significance of NST > GST was assessed by permutation tests [8]. Significance was determined with 10,000 permutations. The genealogical relationships among haplotypes were reconstructed using a median-joining network [9]. To evaluate demographic history, Tajima's D [10] and Fu's Fs [11] were calculated, and mismatch distributions were compared with expectations under a sudden expansion model, with the sum of squared deviations and raggedness index used as goodness-of-fit statistics [12]. The time since expansion was estimated from the mismatch parameter τ using τ = 2μt, where μ is the mutation rate per sequence per generation, applying a range of mutation rates reported for teleost control regions [13] and a generation time of one year [14]. Colonization of the lake was interpreted by comparing the position and frequency of lake haplotypes relative to those of the diadromous stock in the network.

Salinity challenge

Fish from each population were randomly assigned to experimental salinities of 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 ppt (n = 10 fish per salinity per population, in duplicate tanks of 5 fish each). Experimental water was prepared by mixing dechlorinated fresh water with artificial sea salt, and salinity was verified with a calibrated refractometer. To avoid osmotic shock, fish were acclimated progressively by raising salinity by 5 ppt per day until the target value was reached, after which they were maintained for 8 days. Control fish remained at 0 ppt. Tanks (50 L) were aerated, kept at 12 ± 1 °C, and one third of the water was renewed every second day with water of the corresponding salinity. Fish were not fed during the final 24 h before sampling. Mortality was recorded daily, and survival at the end of the experiment was calculated for each salinity and population. Survivors were anaesthetized with benzocaine (50 mg L⁻¹) and euthanized by spinal transection, in accordance with institutional guidelines for animal care [15]. Gills and the whole intestine were dissected on ice, rinsed in cold saline, frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until analysis.

ATPase activity assays

Tissues were homogenized in ice-cold buffer (250 mM sucrose, 30 mM Tris, 10 mM EDTA, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 5,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C; the supernatant was used for assays. Protein concentration was determined by the Bradford method using bovine serum albumin as standard [16]. ATPase activity was measured as the release of inorganic phosphate from ATP [17]. Total ATPase activity was determined in the presence of Mg²⁺, Na⁺ and K⁺. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (NKA) activity was defined as the ouabain-sensitive fraction (1 mM ouabain), and H⁺-ATPase (HA) activity as the fraction sensitive to N-ethylmaleimide (NEM, 1 mM) or bafilomycin A1 [18]. The remaining activity, insensitive to both inhibitors, was recorded as other ATPases. Samples were assayed in triplicate at 30 °C for 30 min, and reactions were stopped with trichloroacetic acid. Activities were expressed as µmol Pi mg protein⁻¹ h⁻¹.

Statistical analysis

Survival between populations at each salinity was compared with Fisher's exact test, and survival curves over the 8-day period were compared with Kaplan–Meier analysis and log-rank tests [19]. Enzyme activities were checked for normality (Shapiro–Wilk) and homogeneity of variances (Levene), and log-transformed when necessary. The effects of population, salinity and their interaction on the activity of each ATPase type in each tissue were assessed using two-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey's post hoc tests for multiple comparisons. When assumptions were not met, non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied. Pairwise population differences within each salinity were evaluated with t-tests or Mann–Whitney tests, with Bonferroni correction. All analyses were conducted in R [20], and differences were considered significant at P < 0.05.

Mitochondrial DNA diversity and population structure

A total of 52 individuals (26 per population) were sequenced for the mtDNA control region, yielding an alignment of 640 bp with 29 variable sites. Twenty-one haplotypes were identified. The diadromous population from the estuary showed higher diversity (haplotype diversity H = 0.92 ± 0.03; average number of nucleotide differences Π = 4.8) than the landlocked lake population (H = 0.54 ± 0.09; Π = 1.3). Only two haplotypes were shared between populations, and both were the most frequent haplotypes in the diadromous sample. Most lake haplotypes were private and differed from one another by one or two mutations.

Differentiation between populations was significant for both haplotype frequency (GST = 0.21, P < 0.001) and phylogeographic structure (NST = 0.29, P < 0.001). NST was higher than GST, although the difference between the two statistics was not significant, indicating that the haplotypes within each population were related to one another to a degree consistent with recent shared ancestry [1,2].

The haplotype network had a star-like topology in the lake population. A central haplotype, shared with the diadromous population, was surrounded by numerous low-frequency derived haplotypes, each separated from the center by one or two substitutions. Diadromous haplotypes were instead distributed across several divergent lineages, with longer branches and no dominant central node. This pattern is consistent with a recent founder event from the diadromous stock followed by demographic expansion in the lake. Tajima's D and Fu's FS were significantly negative for the landlocked population (D = −1.92, P < 0.05; FS = −6.4, P < 0.01) but not for the diadromous population, which supports expansion. The mismatch distribution of the lake population was unimodal and did not differ from the sudden expansion model (SSD = 0.004, P = 0.38), with a peak at about one pairwise difference, which implies a recent expansion event.

Survival under salinity challenge

Survival following progressive acclimation and 8 days of exposure differed markedly between populations (Figure 1). Landlocked fish survived at 100% from 0 to 20 ppt. Survival declined to 85% at 25 ppt and to 40% at 30 ppt. By contrast, diadromous fish showed 100% survival only between 10 and 15 ppt. Their survival was reduced at 0 ppt (62%) and 5 ppt (80%), and at 20, 25 and 30 ppt it was 85%, 55% and 20%, respectively. Survival curves differed significantly between populations (log-rank test, P < 0.001). The difference was greatest in freshwater and low-salinity treatments (0 and 5 ppt; Fisher's exact test, P < 0.01 for each), and was also significant at 20 ppt (P < 0.05). Mortality in diadromous fish at low salinity occurred mainly during the first 3 days of exposure. Thus the landlocked population was unexpectedly more tolerant of the full range of salinities, including hyperosmotic conditions, despite a history of confinement to freshwater.

Gill ATPase activity

In gills, total ATPase activity, NKA activity, and HA activity were measured across salinities. NKA activity showed a significant effect of salinity (two-way ANOVA, P < 0.001) but no overall effect of population and no significant interaction. In both populations, NKA activity was lowest at 10–15 ppt and increased toward both extremes, producing a U-shaped response. HA activity was significantly higher at low salinities (0–5 ppt) than at higher salinities in both populations (P < 0.01), but there were no significant differences between populations at any salinity (Tukey post hoc, P > 0.05).

The residual ATPase activity, insensitive to the inhibitors ouabain and bafilomycin, differed between populations. At 0 and 5 ppt, landlocked fish showed about 1.6- to 2-fold higher residual activity in gills than diadromous fish (P < 0.01), while at salinities of 10 ppt and above the populations did not differ. This indicates the involvement of ATPases other than NKA and HA in the gill response of landlocked fish to hyposmotic conditions.

Intestinal ATPase activity

In the intestine, NKA activity increased with salinity in both populations (P < 0.001), consistent with enhanced water absorption in hyperosmotic media. Differences between populations were detected only at the lowest salinities: at 0 ppt, intestinal NKA activity was higher in landlocked than in diadromous fish (P < 0.05), and at 5 ppt the same trend was observed but was not significant. HA activity in the intestine was low and showed no significant variation with salinity or population. As in the gills, residual ATPase activity was significantly higher in the landlocked population at 0 and 5 ppt (P < 0.05), while the populations converged at intermediate and high salinities.

Relationship between enzyme activity and mortality

Differences in mortality between populations were not mirrored by differences in NKA or HA activity. At 20–30 ppt, where survival differed, enzyme activities in gills and intestine were statistically indistinguishable between populations. Conversely, the higher gill and intestinal activities observed in landlocked fish at low salinity coincided with differences in survival only at 0 and 5 ppt, and the magnitude of the enzymatic differences did not scale with the magnitude of mortality differences. Correlations between mean enzyme activity and survival at each salinity were weak and nonsignificant for NKA (r = −0.31, P = 0.27) and HA (r = 0.18, P = 0.53). Together, these results indicate that the population divergence in tolerance cannot be explained by the activity of NKA and HA alone.

The results presented here show that a landlocked population of Galaxias maculatus, established after the last deglaciation, has diverged from its amphidromous ancestor in both genetic composition and osmoregulatory physiology. The mtDNA data indicate a recent founder event from the diadromous stock followed by demographic expansion in the lake. This is consistent with the glacial history of Patagonia, where retreating ice opened new basins that were colonized by diadromous fishes [1,2]. The reduced haplotype and nucleotide diversity of the landlocked population, together with significant GST and NST values, match expectations for a small number of colonizers experiencing drift and subsequent isolation [3]. The star-like genealogy typical of expansion suggests that the lake provided abundant ecological opportunity, as reported for other landlocked galaxiids and osmerids [4,5].

The physiological results were less expected. Losing the marine phase of the life cycle might be predicted to relax selection on hypoosmoregulatory capacity, leading to reduced salinity tolerance, as described in some landlocked populations of other species [6,7]. Instead, landlocked G. maculatus survived at 100% from 0 to 20 ppt, while the diadromous fish did so only between 10 and 15 ppt. Several explanations are possible. First, the wider tolerance of the landlocked fish may reflect retention of the ancestral euryhaline phenotype together with improved performance at low salinity, so that the lake population has broadened rather than lost its tolerance. Second, the diadromous fish used here may have been near the limits of their tolerance because of their recent estuarine and freshwater history, handling, or the acclimation regime. Third, the lake environment may impose selection on ionic regulation, for instance through low ion concentrations in glacial waters, favoring efficient ion uptake [8]. Because we compared only one landlocked and one diadromous population, we cannot separate selection from drift or from plasticity and maternal effects. Replicated lake populations and common-garden rearing would be needed to distinguish these possibilities [9].

The enzymatic data add nuance. Differences in gill and intestinal ATPase activity between populations emerged mainly at the lowest salinities, which fits the interpretation that divergence concerns mostly hyposmotic regulation. Na+/K+-ATPase is the central driver of ion transport in teleost gills and intestine, and its activity commonly rises with salinity in euryhaline species [10,11]. H+-ATPase contributes to ion uptake in freshwater by establishing electrochemical gradients that facilitate Na+ entry [12]. Differences in activities other than NKA and HA, presumably other ATPases such as Ca2+-ATPase or Mg2+-ATPase, indicate that the divergence is not limited to the best-known pumps and may include broader remodeling of ion and cellular homeostasis [13]. However, population differences in mortality were not mirrored by differences in NKA or HA activity. Thus, enzyme activity measured as total tissue-level capacity is a poor predictor of survival under salinity challenge. Other processes likely contribute, including the abundance and distribution of ionocytes, isoform expression, paracellular permeability through claudins and other tight junction proteins, hormonal control by cortisol and prolactin, kidney function, and behavioral responses [14,15]. Differences in enzyme activity may also reflect different timing of acclimation, so that a single sampling point after eight days could miss transient peaks. Future work should combine transcriptomic and proteomic approaches with cellular histology to identify the molecular basis of the divergence.

An important implication is the timescale. Postglacial lakes of the Andes were formed roughly 10,000–15,000 years ago, and the genetic evidence suggests that colonization was even more recent. Rapid physiological divergence over such a short period is compatible with studies of sticklebacks, alewives, and salmonids, in which freshwater populations diverged in osmoregulatory traits within decades to thousands of years [16–18]. The speed of change in G. maculatus suggests either that standing variation in the ancestral amphidromous population was substantial, which is plausible for a species exposed to wide environmental variation during its migratory life cycle, or that plasticity facilitated initial persistence and was later refined by selection [19]. The low mitochondrial diversity of the lake population does not preclude abundant variation in nuclear loci underlying physiological traits. Mitochondrial markers reveal demographic history but not necessarily adaptive loci, so genome-scale data will be required to detect selection signatures in genes related to ion transport.

Our findings also bear on conservation and management. G. maculatus is widely distributed in the Southern Hemisphere, and landlocked populations may represent evolutionarily distinct units with specific physiological properties. Their broad salinity tolerance could influence their capacity to cope with environmental change, but also their potential to disperse through estuaries, which may affect gene flow and the risk of invasion or translocation. Recognizing such populations as distinct units is therefore important for management [20].

In conclusion, the landlocked population of G. maculatus in the Andean lake derives from a recent colonization by diadromous fish, shows reduced genetic diversity, and displays a markedly broader tolerance to low and intermediate salinities than its amphidromous relatives. Differences in gill and intestinal ATPase activity occur primarily at low salinities and involve enzymes beyond NKA and HA, yet they do not explain differences in mortality, implying that additional mechanisms underlie the divergence. These results demonstrate rapid adaptive modification of the osmoregulatory system associated with a drastic change in habitat and life cycle over a few thousand years. Future studies using replicated populations, common-garden experiments, and genomic and transcriptomic tools should clarify the roles of plasticity, standing variation, and selection in this process.

Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide, and its burden continues to grow with population aging and changing lifestyles [1]. Surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy are the principal treatment modalities, but the clinical utility of many chemotherapeutic agents is limited by dose-dependent toxicity to normal tissues, acquired multidrug resistance and tumor recurrence [2,3]. The search for new antitumor agents with novel structures, distinct mechanisms of action and improved selectivity therefore remains a priority in drug discovery.

**Natural products as a source of antitumor agents**

Natural products and their derivatives have historically contributed a substantial proportion of approved anticancer drugs, including paclitaxel, vincristine, doxorubicin and mitomycin C [4,5]. Microorganisms are especially valuable producers because they can be cultured and scaled up by fermentation, avoiding the supply problems associated with plant and animal sources. However, repeated screening of microorganisms from conventional terrestrial habitats has led to high rediscovery rates of known compounds [6]. Attention has consequently shifted to underexplored environments, notably the oceans, where microbial diversity is vast and where unusual physicochemical conditions drive distinctive secondary metabolism [7]. Several marine-derived compounds, such as cytarabine, trabectedin, eribulin and brentuximab vedotin, have reached clinical use, which underscores the potential of this resource [8].

**Antarctic microorganisms as a resource for bioactive substances**

The Antarctic is among the most extreme environments on Earth, characterized by persistently low temperatures, strong ultraviolet radiation, seasonal light variation, desiccation, high salinity in some habitats and scarce nutrients [9]. Microorganisms inhabiting these environments have evolved physiological and biochemical adaptations, including cold-active enzymes, cryoprotectants, membrane modifications and unique secondary metabolic pathways [10,11]. Such adaptations are thought to give rise to metabolites with novel scaffolds and bioactivities. Antarctic bacteria, actinomycetes and fungi have been reported to produce antibacterial, antifungal, antioxidant and cytotoxic compounds [12–14]. For example, new cytotoxic polyketides, alkaloids and peptides have been obtained from Antarctic sediment- and sponge-associated microorganisms [15,16]. Nevertheless, compared with other regions, Antarctic microbial resources remain poorly explored, largely because of the difficulty of sampling and the specialized conditions required for cultivation. Most studies have concentrated on sediments, soils and host-associated organisms, whereas microorganisms from surface seawater and meltwater have received considerably less attention, despite being exposed to strong environmental fluctuations that may stimulate the production of protective metabolites [17].

**Bacillus species and antitumor activity**

The genus *Bacillus* comprises a metabolically versatile group of spore-forming bacteria that are widely distributed in terrestrial and marine habitats, including polar regions [18]. Members of this genus produce a remarkable range of bioactive substances, such as lipopeptides (surfactin, iturin and fengycin), polyketides, bacteriocins, enzymes such as L-asparaginase, and exopolysaccharides [19,20]. Several of these have been shown to inhibit tumor cell proliferation and to induce apoptosis, cell cycle arrest or membrane disruption in cancer cell lines, often with limited toxicity to normal cells [21,22]. In addition, because many *Bacillus* strains are regarded as safe and are readily fermented at industrial scale, they are attractive candidates for the development of antitumor agents or functional products for cancer prevention [23]. Cold-adapted *Bacillus* strains from the Antarctic may produce metabolites that differ from those of their mesophilic counterparts, but cytotoxic products from such strains have been little characterized.

**Activity-guided screening strategies**

Efficient discovery from large numbers of isolates requires a screening approach that rapidly identifies strains producing cytotoxic metabolites. The 3-(4,5-dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay is a well-established colorimetric method for assessing cell viability and is suitable for medium- to high-throughput evaluation of crude fermentation products [24]. Used in a cytotoxicity-tracking strategy, it allows active strains to be prioritized at an early stage, and subsequent fractionation, for example by molecular weight cut-off ultrafiltration, can then narrow down the nature of the active components. Evaluating selectivity against a panel of tumor cell lines and a normal cell line, together with stability toward pH and temperature, provides essential information about the therapeutic potential and processing feasibility of the active products [25].

**Aim of the present study**

In view of the large untapped potential of Antarctic microorganisms and the limited information on those from surface water, we isolated microorganisms from surface water samples collected at different Antarctic sites and screened them for cytotoxicity using an MTT-based tracking approach. A strain with potent activity, designated N11-8, was identified by morphological and 16S rRNA gene phylogenetic analyses. The molecular weight distribution of its active fermentation products was then examined, and their inhibitory effects on several human cancer cell lines and on normal human lung fibroblasts were compared. The morphological effects on BEL-7402 cells were observed microscopically alongside mitomycin C, and the pH and thermal stability of the active products were assessed. This work aims to broaden knowledge of Antarctic microbial resources and to provide a basis for developing antitumor agents from polar *Bacillus*.

**Sample collection and microbial isolation**

Surface seawater samples (0–1 m depth) were collected at several sampling stations in the Antarctic during an expedition, using sterile containers. Samples were stored at 4 °C during transport and processed within 24 h. Aliquots (100 µL) of serial dilutions (10⁻¹–10⁻³) prepared in sterile artificial seawater were spread on Zobell 2216E agar and incubated at 4 °C and 15 °C for 7–14 days to recover psychrophilic and psychrotolerant strains [1,2]. Colonies with distinct morphology were picked and purified by repeated streaking until axenic. Pure isolates were preserved in 2216E broth containing 20% (v/v) glycerol at −80 °C.

**Small-scale fermentation and preparation of crude extracts**

Each isolate was inoculated into 2216E broth (50 mL in 250 mL flasks) and cultivated at 15 °C with shaking at 180 rpm for 5 days. Cultures were centrifuged (10,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C) to separate cells from supernatant. The supernatant was filtered (0.22 µm) and used as the extracellular fermented product. Cell pellets were washed with PBS, disrupted by ultrasonication on ice, and clarified by centrifugation to obtain intracellular fractions. All preparations were stored at −20 °C until bioassay.

**Cell lines and culture conditions**

Human hepatocellular carcinoma BEL-7402, glioma U251, colon carcinoma RKO, lung carcinoma A549, breast carcinoma MCF-7, and normal human fetal lung fibroblast HFL1 cells were obtained from a cell bank. Cells were maintained in DMEM or RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. Cells in the logarithmic growth phase were used for all experiments.

**Cytotoxicity screening by MTT assay**

Cytotoxicity was evaluated using the MTT assay [3]. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates (5 × 10³ cells/well) and allowed to adhere for 24 h. Medium was replaced with fresh medium containing fermentation products (10% v/v for primary screening). Mitomycin C served as positive control, uninoculated 2216E medium as negative control, and wells without cells as blanks. After 48 h, 20 µL MTT solution (5 mg/mL) was added to each well and plates were incubated for 4 h. The formazan crystals were dissolved in 150 µL dimethyl sulfoxide, and absorbance was read at 490 nm (or 570 nm) on a microplate reader. The inhibition rate was calculated as (1 − (A_sample − A_blank)/(A_control − A_blank)) × 100%. Each treatment was performed in triplicate in at least three independent experiments. Strains giving inhibition above a predefined threshold (50%) were considered active and selected for further study.

**Identification of the active strain N11-8**

Morphological characteristics were examined by Gram staining and light microscopy, and colony features were recorded on 2216E agar. Genomic DNA was extracted using a bacterial genomic DNA kit. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified with universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCCTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-GGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′) under the following conditions: 95 °C for 5 min; 30 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 90 s; and a final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. Products were checked by agarose gel electrophoresis, purified and sequenced. The sequence was compared with the EzBioCloud and GenBank databases using BLAST [4]. Related sequences were aligned with CLUSTAL W, and a neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree was constructed in MEGA with the Kimura two-parameter model and 1000 bootstrap replicates [5,6].

**Large-scale fermentation and fractionation by molecular weight**

N11-8 was cultured in 2216E broth (1 L) at 15 °C and 180 rpm for 5 days. The cell-free supernatant was concentrated and sequentially fractionated by ultrafiltration through membranes with molecular weight cut-offs of 1, 10 and 30 kDa, yielding fractions of <1 kDa, 1–10 kDa, 10–30 kDa and >30 kDa. Protein concentrations were determined by the Bradford method [7]. Fractions were sterilized by filtration and tested for cytotoxicity at different concentrations against all six cell lines by MTT assay as described above. Half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀) were calculated by nonlinear regression of dose–response curves. Selectivity was assessed by comparing inhibition of tumor cells with that of HFL1 cells.

**Morphological observation of treated cells**

BEL-7402 cells were seeded in 6-well plates (2 × 10⁵ cells/well) and treated for 24 and 48 h with the active fraction, mitomycin C (positive control) or medium alone (negative control). Morphological changes, including cell shrinkage, rounding, detachment and reduced density, were observed and photographed under an inverted phase-contrast microscope. Representative fields were captured from at least three wells per treatment.

**Stability of the fermented active products**

For pH stability, the active fraction was adjusted to pH 2–12 with HCl or NaOH, incubated at 25 °C for 2 h, and neutralized to pH 7.0 before testing. For thermal stability, samples were heated at 40, 60, 80, 100 °C for 30 min (and 121 °C for 20 min for autoclaving), then cooled on ice. Residual cytotoxicity against BEL-7402 cells was determined by MTT assay and expressed relative to untreated samples (100%).

**Statistical analysis**

Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) of at least three independent experiments. Differences among groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance followed by Tukey's or Dunnett's post hoc test using SPSS or GraphPad Prism. Differences with p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

**Isolation and preliminary screening of Antarctic microorganisms**

A total of 129 microbial strains were isolated from surface water samples collected at different Antarctic sites. Colonies differed in morphology, pigmentation, and growth rate on the isolation media. Most isolates grew at 4–15 °C, which is consistent with a psychrotolerant or psychrophilic ecology [1,2]. Crude fermentation extracts of all 129 isolates were tested against BEL-7402 cells in an MTT assay at a single concentration. Twelve strains (9.3%) reduced cell viability by more than 50% relative to untreated controls, and these were classed as potently cytotoxic. Inhibition rates ranged from 52.4% to 89.7%. Strain N11-8 gave one of the highest and most reproducible inhibition values across three independent screening rounds, so it was selected for further study.

**Morphological characterization and phylogenetic identification of strain N11-8**

On solid medium, N11-8 formed opaque, cream-white, slightly raised colonies with irregular margins after 48 h at 15 °C. Light microscopy showed rod-shaped cells that stained Gram-negative in our hands. Because the genus Bacillus is typically Gram-positive, this result was unexpected. Members of the genus can stain variably in older cultures or when the cell wall is damaged [3], and we therefore interpret the staining result with caution.

The nearly complete 16S rRNA gene sequence of N11-8 was amplified and compared with sequences in the GenBank and EzBioCloud databases. The strain showed more than 99% similarity to several Bacillus species. In the neighbor-joining tree, N11-8 clustered within the genus Bacillus, supported by a high bootstrap value, and was separated from the nearest type strains by short branch lengths. The strain was designated Bacillus sp. N11-8. Its position within the genus is clear, but 16S rRNA analysis alone could not resolve it to species level. This is a known limitation within closely related Bacillus lineages [4].

**Cytotoxic activity of fractionated fermentation products**

The fermentation broth of N11-8 was separated by ultrafiltration into fractions of <1 kDa, 1–30 kDa, and >30 kDa. The 1–30 kDa fraction had the strongest inhibitory effect on BEL-7402 cells. The <1 kDa and >30 kDa fractions were considerably less active at equivalent protein or dry-weight concentrations. Subsequent experiments therefore used the 1–30 kDa fraction, referred to below as the fermented active products.

**Antiproliferative spectrum and selectivity**

The fermented active products inhibited the proliferation of all five cancer cell lines tested in a dose-dependent manner: BEL-7402 (hepatocellular carcinoma), U251 (glioma), RKO (colon carcinoma), A549 (lung carcinoma), and MCF-7 (breast carcinoma). Inhibition increased with concentration and incubation time (24–72 h). BEL-7402 and U251 cells were the most sensitive. RKO, A549, and MCF-7 cells were inhibited to a somewhat lesser but still significant degree (P < 0.05 versus control). In contrast, the same concentrations had markedly weaker effects on HFL1 normal human lung fibroblasts, and viability remained high at doses that strongly suppressed tumor cell growth. The selectivity of the fraction for malignant over non-malignant cells is a desirable property for antitumor leads [5]. A full quantitative selectivity index would require IC50 values from additional replicates and non-malignant cell types.

**Morphological changes in BEL-7402 cells**

Inverted phase-contrast microscopy showed clear morphological changes in BEL-7402 cells after treatment. Untreated cells were polygonal, adherent, and grew as a confluent monolayer. After exposure to the fermented active products, cell density decreased markedly. Many cells shrank, rounded up, and detached from the substrate. Cytoplasmic granulation and floating debris were also visible, and these features became more pronounced with higher doses and longer exposure. The changes closely resembled those seen in the mitomycin C positive control, which suggests that the fermented products suppress BEL-7402 growth to a degree comparable to this reference drug under the conditions used. The morphology is consistent with induction of cell death, although these observations alone do not establish the mechanism, such as apoptosis versus necrosis.

**Stability of the fermented active products**
