Co-researchers will receive training in qualitative methods and focus group facilitation, together with payment and supervision in line with INVOLVE guidance. Each focus group will be facilitated by a researcher and a co-researcher where possible.

**Setting and participants**

Participants will be recruited in NHS England through secondary care mental health services, primary care, voluntary sector organisations and service user networks.

*Service users.* Adults (≥18 years) who have received a diagnosis of one of five conditions from a clinician will be eligible: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder or generalised anxiety disorder. They must be able to give informed consent and to participate in English. People will be excluded if they are acutely unwell or lack capacity to consent, as judged by their clinical team or the research team. Two focus groups will be held for each diagnosis, giving ten service user groups.

*Clinicians.* Psychiatrists, general practitioners and clinical psychologists who use diagnostic classification in practice will be eligible. Four clinician focus groups will be conducted, with professional groups mixed or separate depending on feasibility and the need to encourage open discussion.

**Sample size**

Each group is planned to include approximately six to eight participants, a size that allows interaction while giving everyone the opportunity to speak. The total target is about 60–80 service users and 24–32 clinicians. Because of the fixed number of groups, sampling will be purposive, aiming for diversity in age, gender, ethnicity, duration of diagnosis and service setting. The adequacy of the sample will be reviewed during analysis in terms of information power and thematic saturation. Additional groups will be considered if new themes continue to emerge.

**Recruitment and consent**

Clinical teams and partner organisations will identify potential participants and distribute invitation packs containing an information sheet. Interested individuals will contact the research team directly. A researcher will check eligibility and answer questions. Written informed consent will be obtained before each focus group, with consent to audio recording. Participants may withdraw at any point, and data already collected may be retained unless a participant requests otherwise before analysis. Expenses will be reimbursed, and participants will receive a voucher in recognition of their time.

**Data collection**

Focus groups will last approximately 90 minutes and will be held in accessible, neutral community or NHS venues. Before each group, participants will receive a plain-language summary of the proposed ICD-11 criteria for the relevant diagnosis, including changes from ICD-10. A semi-structured topic guide, developed with co-researchers and reviewed by the steering group, will explore: understanding of and reactions to the proposed criteria; whether the descriptions reflect lived or clinical experience; terminology and language, including potential stigma; the clarity, usability and clinical utility of the criteria; perceived effects of diagnosis on identity, access to services and outcomes; and suggested changes. Clinician groups will additionally focus on application in routine practice, ease of use and diagnostic boundaries. The guide will remain flexible so participants can raise further issues. Facilitators will take field notes and a brief debrief will follow each session. Participants will also complete a short demographic questionnaire. A distress protocol will be in place, with a named clinician available for support and signposting if participants become distressed.

**Data management**

Audio recordings will be transcribed verbatim by an approved transcription service under a confidentiality agreement, then checked for accuracy and anonymised. Identifiable information will be removed and participants will be assigned codes. Data will be held on secure, password-protected university servers, with consent forms stored separately, in accordance with the Data Protection Act and Good Clinical Practice. NVivo will be used to manage the data.

**Data analysis**

Transcripts will be analysed using inductive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke’s six phases: familiarisation, generation of initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and reporting. Researchers and co-researchers will independently code an initial subset of transcripts, then meet to compare interpretations, agree a coding framework and resolve discrepancies. The framework will be applied to the remaining transcripts and refined iteratively. Analysis will be conducted within each diagnostic group and then compared across diagnoses and between service users and clinicians to identify shared and divergent themes. Reflexivity will be supported by a reflexive journal and by discussion of how the team’s own backgrounds and experiences shape interpretation. Credibility will be enhanced through multiple coders, input from co-researchers, an audit trail and, where feasible, feedback of preliminary themes to participants.

**Development of recommendations**

Themes will form the basis of draft recommendations for the ICD-11 criteria and associated guidance. These will be refined in co-production workshops involving service users, clinicians and researchers and reviewed by the steering group. The final recommendations will be presented to the WHO in dialogue with those responsible for ICD-11 development, to inform revisions and clinical descriptions.

**Ethics**

The study has been approved by the Coventry and Warwickshire HRA Research Ethics Committee (16/WM/0479) and is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03131505). Confidentiality will be maintained, except where a participant discloses information indicating a risk of serious harm, in which case the risk protocol will be followed.

**Dissemination**

Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences, service user and clinician networks, and summaries for participants. The methodology will be documented to enable replication internationally.

This is a protocol paper, so no empirical findings have yet been generated. The results presented here describe the outputs of protocol development, the anticipated structure of the data, and the planned reporting of findings, rather than outcomes of the focus groups.

**Status of the study**

At the time of writing, ethical approval had been granted by the Coventry and Warwickshire HRA Research Ethics Committee (16/WM/0479), and the study had been registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03131505). Recruitment and data collection had not been completed, and no analysis of focus group data had been undertaken. Accordingly, no thematic findings are reported. The sections below summarise the products of the co-production process that shaped the protocol and describe the results that the study is designed to produce.

**Outputs of co-production in protocol development**

The study team included service users, clinicians and researchers, and all aspects of the design were developed jointly. Through this process, the following protocol elements were agreed.

First, five diagnostic groupings were selected for service user focus groups: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. These were chosen to span common and severe presentations and to include diagnoses that service users and clinicians have often described as contested or stigmatising. Two service user focus groups will be held per diagnosis, giving ten service user groups in total.

Second, four clinician focus groups were planned, drawing on psychiatrists, general practitioners and clinical psychologists, so that professional perspectives from primary and secondary care and from medical and psychological traditions would be represented.

Third, the co-production group developed a topic guide that presents the proposed ICD-11 diagnostic descriptions and criteria for each condition and prompts discussion of the following areas: whether the descriptions match lived or clinical experience; the clarity and acceptability of the language used; perceived omissions or inaccuracies; the potential effects of receiving the diagnosis on identity, service access and treatment; and the usability of the criteria in routine practice. Service user members of the team advised on wording, on the sequencing of questions to minimise distress, and on the provision of breaks and support during sessions.

Fourth, service user members contributed to the design of recruitment materials and information sheets, favouring plain language and emphasising that participants would be consulted as experts by experience. Co-researchers also advised on practical arrangements, including accessible venues, reimbursement for time and travel, and the availability of a named support contact.

Fifth, the analytic approach was agreed: focus groups will be audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and anonymised, then coded inductively using thematic analysis. Coding will be carried out by researchers and service user co-analysts, with a proportion of transcripts double-coded and discrepancies resolved by discussion. Emerging themes will be reviewed in team workshops so that interpretation reflects lived experience as well as clinical and academic perspectives.

**Anticipated data and outputs**

The planned dataset comprises fourteen focus groups: ten with service users and four with clinicians. Findings will be organised by diagnosis, with cross-cutting themes identified across conditions and across the service user and clinician groups. Comparison between the two participant types is intended to highlight where perspectives converge, for example on the need for clear and non-stigmatising terminology, and where they diverge, for example on the balance between diagnostic precision and practical utility.

The principal output will be a set of co-produced recommendations for the refinement of the ICD-11 mental and behavioural disorders chapter. These will be developed in a consensus workshop in which service users, clinicians and researchers review the themes and agree recommendations, which will then be presented to WHO in line with the dialogue established at the outset. Recommendations are expected to address the wording of diagnostic descriptions, the specificity and relevance of criteria, and guidance to reduce unintended negative consequences of diagnosis.

**Dissemination of results**

Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations, and through summaries written in accessible language for participants and the wider service user community. Because the ICD is an international classification, the methods, topic guides and analytic framework will be documented in sufficient detail to allow replication by other groups in different countries and health systems, enabling comparison of feedback across cultural and service contexts.

**Limitations anticipated in reporting**

Findings will be reported with attention to the transferability of qualitative data. The sample will be drawn from NHS England services and so may not represent perspectives elsewhere. Participants will respond to a limited set of diagnoses, and views on other conditions will not be captured. Group dynamics may influence which views are voiced, and the facilitation approach will be described so that readers can judge this. Reflexive notes kept by the team will be used to document how researcher and co-researcher perspectives shaped analysis, and these will be reported alongside the final results.

This protocol describes a co-produced qualitative study that will gather the views of service users and clinicians on the proposed ICD-11 diagnostic criteria for mental and behavioural disorders. It will use focus groups and thematic analysis. The study aims to generate recommendations that can be fed back to WHO to refine the classification before and during its implementation. We expect the findings to show where the draft criteria match lived and clinical experience, where they do not, and where they may have unintended consequences for identity, service access and outcomes.

A main strength of the study is that co-production runs through every stage. Service users and clinicians are involved in designing the topic guides, interpreting the data and formulating recommendations, rather than only supplying data. This approach should improve the relevance and credibility of the questions asked and of the interpretations made. It also responds to long-standing criticism that psychiatric classification systems are developed mainly by professional experts, with limited input from the people to whom diagnoses are applied. Including both service users and clinicians allows comparison across perspectives. Service users may stress the meaning, stigma and personal consequences of a diagnosis, whereas clinicians may emphasise usability, differential diagnosis and the link between diagnosis and treatment decisions. Where the two groups agree, the case for revision is stronger. Where they disagree, the disagreements are themselves informative and may point to tensions that WHO will need to weigh.

Selecting five diagnostic groups is another strength. Personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder cover a wide range of presentations, levels of stigma and care pathways. Personality disorder and schizophrenia are often contested and heavily stigmatised, while depression and anxiety are very common in primary care. Running two service user groups per diagnosis allows some checking of whether themes recur, and it should help the analysis reach a reasonable depth. The inclusion of psychiatrists, general practitioners and clinical psychologists reflects the different ways diagnoses are used across the system: in specialist assessment, in first-contact care and in psychological formulation.

The study also has limitations. Focus groups are well suited to eliciting shared and contrasting views, but some participants may be reluctant to disclose sensitive experiences in a group, and dominant voices may shape the discussion. Facilitators with relevant experience, ground rules and the option of follow-up contact should mitigate this, but it cannot be eliminated. The sample is purposive and drawn from NHS England services, so the findings will not be statistically generalisable, and participants who agree to take part may be more engaged with services or more critical of diagnosis than others. People who have been poorly served by or disengaged from services, and people from minority ethnic or other under-represented groups, may be harder to reach, and diagnostic categories may carry different meanings across cultures. We will monitor recruitment diversity and adapt sampling where possible, but the results should be interpreted with these constraints in mind. In addition, participants will be commenting on criteria and descriptions rather than on the use of the classification in routine practice. Their responses may therefore differ from experiences with the final system, and the study cannot test clinical utility directly. Field testing and quantitative evaluation will remain necessary complements.

The analytic approach also has limits. Inductive thematic analysis is flexible and suited to exploratory questions, but it depends on the interpretive choices of the research team. We will reduce this risk through independent double coding of a subset of transcripts, regular discussion within a team that includes people with lived experience, and transparent records of coding decisions. Reflexivity will be important because team members have personal and professional relationships to diagnosis that may shape interpretation. Moving from themes to recommendations is another step requiring judgement. Recommendations will therefore be developed collaboratively and linked explicitly to supporting data, so that WHO and others can see how each conclusion was reached.

If successful, the study may have several implications. First, it may identify specific wording, thresholds or structural features of the ICD-11 criteria that service users and clinicians find unclear, invalid or potentially harmful, allowing targeted amendments. Second, it may inform guidance on how diagnoses are communicated, helping clinicians discuss them in ways that support understanding, hope and shared decision-making rather than alienation. Third, it may contribute to the broader debate about the validity of categorical diagnosis and the place of dimensional or formulation-based approaches. Because the ICD is an international tool, the methodology has also been designed to be transferable. Other groups could repeat the process in different health systems, languages and cultural settings, producing a body of comparable evidence that would strengthen the legitimacy of future revisions.

Dissemination will include peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations, as well as direct communication with WHO and relevant NHS and professional bodies. Co-producers will be involved in dissemination, and we will also produce accessible summaries for participants and the wider service user community.

In conclusion, the INCLUDE study offers a structured, co-produced way of incorporating lived experience and clinical expertise into the refinement of the ICD-11. By giving those who receive and those who use diagnoses a role in shaping them, it aims to improve the accuracy, acceptability and clinical utility of the classification and to reduce its unintended negative consequences. Despite the inherent limits of qualitative, purposive sampling, the transparent methods and the potential for international replication should make the resulting recommendations a useful contribution to the continuing development of psychiatric diagnosis.

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood coagulation, where it serves as an essential cofactor for the post-translational conversion of specific glutamate residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (GLA) [1,2]. This reaction is catalyzed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) in the endoplasmic reticulum and is coupled to oxidation of the reduced form of vitamin K (hydroquinone) to vitamin K epoxide. The epoxide is recycled by the vitamin K epoxide reductases VKORC1 and VKORC1L1, the target enzymes of the anticoagulant warfarin, to regenerate the hydroquinone [3,4]. γ-Carboxylation confers calcium-binding capacity on GLA-containing proteins, which is required for their conformation and function. The best characterized substrates include coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X, as well as proteins involved in bone and vascular homeostasis such as osteocalcin and matrix GLA protein [5,6]. Additional vitamin K-dependent proteins, including growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) and protein S, signal through TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (TYRO3, AXL and MER), which regulate cell survival, proliferation, migration and immune responses [7,8].

Vitamin K exists in two principal natural forms. Phylloquinone (K1) is synthesized by plants and is the predominant dietary form, found mainly in green leafy vegetables and plant oils. Menaquinones (K2, MK-n) are produced by bacteria and are present in fermented foods and animal products; they differ from K1 in having an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain of variable length [9]. Although both K1 and K2 support GGCX-mediated carboxylation, they differ in their absorption, tissue distribution, half-life and bioactivity. K1 is primarily delivered to the liver, whereas longer-chain menaquinones are redistributed to extrahepatic tissues [10,11]. Menaquinone-4 (MK-4), moreover, can be generated from K1 in tissues by the enzyme UBIAD1, and has been proposed to exert functions independent of carboxylation, including activation of the steroid and xenobiotic receptor (SXR/PXR) and modulation of transcription [12,13].

Interest in vitamin K in oncology has grown from observations that K vitamins influence cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. A substantial body of in vitro work has reported that K2, and to a lesser extent synthetic K3 (menadione), inhibits growth and induces apoptosis, cell cycle arrest or differentiation in leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate, colon, lung, ovarian and breast cancer cells [14–18]. In contrast, K1 has typically been reported to have little or no effect on cancer cell proliferation at comparable concentrations [15,19]. Epidemiological studies have yielded mixed results. Higher dietary intake of K2, but not K1, has been associated with reduced risk of prostate cancer and lower cancer mortality in some cohorts [20,21], whereas associations with breast cancer risk have been inconsistent [22]. Furthermore, clinical studies of K2 in hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence have shown variable outcomes [23]. These disparate observations suggest that the biological actions of vitamin K in cancer are context dependent and may differ by vitamer, tumor type and the expression of the vitamin K cycle machinery.

Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), defined by the absence of estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 amplification, accounts for approximately 15–20% of cases [24]. TNBC is characterized by aggressive behavior, early recurrence, metastasis to visceral sites and a lack of targeted therapies, so that cytotoxic chemotherapy remains the standard of care [25]. A subpopulation of cells with stem-like properties is thought to contribute to therapeutic resistance and relapse in TNBC, and pathways that regulate stemness are therefore of considerable interest as therapeutic targets [26,27]. Notably, AXL signaling, which depends on γ-carboxylated ligands such as GAS6, has been implicated in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness and drug resistance in TNBC [28,29]. This raises the possibility that the vitamin K cycle, by enabling γ-carboxylation, could influence TNBC progression.

Despite these links, little is known about whether breast cancer cells express a functional vitamin K cycle or whether K1 and K2 exert distinct effects in this setting. Most studies of vitamin K in cancer cells have examined antiproliferative effects of K2 without assessing expression of GGCX and VKOR enzymes or the presence of GLA-modified proteins, and K1 has often been used only as a negative control. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the effects attributed to K2 are related to γ-carboxylation or occur through alternative mechanisms, and whether K1 is truly inert in cancer cells or may have its own effects.

In this study, we therefore examined expression of GGCX, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1 across breast cancer cell lines and in clinical breast tumor datasets, and found highest expression in TNBC lines and in advanced-stage disease. We then compared the effects of K1 and K2 on growth, stemness and expression of GLA-modified proteins in TNBC cell lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231 and SUM159PT, using warfarin to probe the role of VKOR activity. Our findings indicate that TNBC cells possess a functional vitamin K pathway and that K1 and K2 elicit divergent phenotypic effects, providing a basis for further mechanistic investigation of this pathway as a therapeutic target.

Cell lines and culture conditions
Human breast cancer cell lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, SUM159PT, MCF-7, T47D, and the non-tumorigenic mammary epithelial line MCF10A were obtained from ATCC or Asterand and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling. Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells were maintained in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), SUM159PT cells in Ham's F-12 with 5% FBS, insulin (5 µg/mL) and hydrocortisone (1 µg/mL), and MCF-7 and T47D cells in RPMI-1640 with 10% FBS [1]. MCF10A cells were grown in DMEM/F-12 supplemented with horse serum, EGF, insulin, hydrocortisone, and cholera toxin [2]. All cultures were kept at 37°C in 5% CO2 and tested negative for Mycoplasma monthly.

Because standard FBS contains vitamin K, experiments used medium supplemented with charcoal-stripped or vitamin K-depleted serum where indicated. Phylloquinone (K1), menaquinone-4 (K2, MK-4), and warfarin (Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved in ethanol or DMSO and protected from light. Cells were treated with K1 or K2 at 1–10 µM, or warfarin at 10 µM, with vehicle-matched controls (final solvent ≤0.1%). Media and treatments were replaced every 48 h.

Gene expression analysis
Total RNA was isolated with TRIzol (Invitrogen) and purified using column-based kits, with DNase treatment. RNA (1 µg) was reverse transcribed using random hexamers and M-MLV reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green master mix on a real-time thermocycler using primers specific for GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, and the stemness markers CD44, CD24, ALDH1A1, SOX2, and NANOG. Reactions were run in triplicate, and relative expression was calculated by the 2^-ΔΔCt method [3] normalized to GAPDH or ACTB. Melt-curve analysis confirmed single products.

To assess expression across disease stage, publicly available datasets (TCGA breast invasive carcinoma and METABRIC) were queried through cBioPortal and UALCAN [4,5]. Tumors were grouped by pathological stage and PAM50/receptor subtype, and expression differences were evaluated by ANOVA with post hoc testing.

Proliferation and viability assays
Cells were seeded at 2–5 × 10³ cells/well in 96-well plates, allowed to attach overnight, and treated with vehicle, K1, K2, or warfarin for 24–120 h. Growth was measured by direct cell counting with trypan blue exclusion, by MTT or CellTiter-Glo assays according to manufacturer instructions, and by real-time confluence imaging (IncuCyte). Growth curves were normalized to vehicle controls. Apoptosis was assessed by Annexin V/propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry, and by immunoblotting for cleaved PARP and caspase-3. Cell cycle distribution was assessed by propidium iodide staining of ethanol-fixed cells followed by flow cytometry.

Detection of γ-carboxyglutamate-modified proteins
Cells were treated for 72 h, washed in PBS, and lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein (30–50 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes, and blocked in 5% BSA in TBST. Membranes were probed with a monoclonal antibody specific for GLA residues (anti-γ-carboxyglutamyl; Sigma/BioMedica Diagnostics), which recognizes GLA-modified proteins independent of protein context [6]. Additional antibodies targeted GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, β-actin, and GAPDH. Bands were visualized with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry in ImageJ. Recombinant or bovine prothrombin-containing samples and lysates from vitamin K-depleted cells served as positive and negative controls, respectively.

Tumorsphere and stemness assays
Stem-like properties were evaluated by mammosphere formation [7]. Single-cell suspensions were plated at 500–1,000 cells/well in ultra-low attachment 24-well plates in serum-free DMEM/F-12 supplemented with B27, EGF (20 ng/mL), bFGF (20 ng/mL), and heparin, with vehicle, K1, or K2. After 7–10 days, spheres larger than 50 µm were counted and sphere-forming efficiency calculated as spheres formed divided by cells seeded. Spheres were dissociated and replated to assess self-renewal in secondary passages. In parallel, the CD44+/CD24- subpopulation was quantified by flow cytometry using fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, and ALDH activity was measured with the ALDEFLUOR assay, using the inhibitor DEAB to define gating [8].

Colony formation
Cells (500 per well) were seeded in six-well plates and treated for 10–14 days. Colonies were fixed with methanol, stained with 0.5% crystal violet, and colonies of more than 50 cells were counted.

Statistical analysis
All experiments were performed in at least three independent biological replicates, each with technical replicates. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation or standard error of the mean, as indicated. Comparisons between two groups used unpaired two-tailed Student's t tests; comparisons among multiple groups used one-way or two-way ANOVA with Tukey's or Dunnett's post hoc correction. Growth curves were analyzed by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
