Expression of vitamin K pathway genes in breast cancer cell lines and tumors

We first measured transcript levels of GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1 by qPCR in a panel of breast cell lines representing non-malignant, luminal, and triple negative subtypes. All three genes were detected in every line, but expression varied significantly by subtype. The TNBC lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, and SUM159PT had the highest expression of GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1, whereas luminal lines (e.g., MCF-7, T47D) and the non-malignant line MCF10A had lower levels. GGCX expression was approximately 3- to 6-fold higher in TNBC lines than in luminal lines (p < 0.05). VKORC1 showed the broadest range, and VKORC1L1 was highest in Hs578T and SUM159PT. Analysis of publicly available tumor datasets [1,2] showed the same trend: expression of all three genes was higher in advanced-stage (stage III–IV) than in early-stage (stage I–II) disease, and was highest in basal-like tumors. These data indicate that the enzymatic machinery required for γ-carboxylation is present in TNBC cells and is enriched in more aggressive disease.

K1 and K2 differentially affect TNBC cell growth

To test whether the forms of vitamin K have different phenotypic effects, Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, and SUM159PT cells were cultured in medium supplemented with vehicle, K1 (phylloquinone), or K2 (menaquinone-4) at physiologically relevant to supraphysiologic concentrations. K1 increased cell growth in all three lines in a dose- and time-dependent manner. After 72 h, K1 increased cell number by roughly 20–40% relative to vehicle (p < 0.05), and the effect was reproducible in proliferation (MTS) and direct cell counting assays. In contrast, K2 reduced cell growth in a dose-dependent manner. At higher concentrations, K2 reduced cell number by more than 50% compared with vehicle in each cell line. The anti-proliferative effect of K2 was accompanied by increased markers of apoptosis, including cleaved PARP and elevated annexin V staining, consistent with previous reports of pro-apoptotic K2 activity in other cancer types [3,4]. The opposing effects were evident at equimolar concentrations, indicating that they were not attributable to differences in dosing or vehicle exposure.

K1 induces γ-carboxylated proteins in TNBC cells

We next determined whether TNBC cells can use vitamin K for γ-carboxylation. Lysates from cells cultured with vehicle, K1, K2, or the VKOR inhibitor warfarin were immunoblotted with an antibody specific for GLA-modified proteins. Vehicle-treated cells had little or no detectable GLA signal. K1 treatment produced several GLA-reactive bands in all three TNBC lines, with the strongest signals in the MDA-MB-231 and Hs578T lines. The signal increased with K1 concentration and exposure time. Unexpectedly, K2 did not induce detectable GLA-modified proteins at any concentration tested, even though K2 is a recognized cofactor for GGCX in other systems [5]. Warfarin alone did not produce GLA signal, as expected given that it limits recycling of reduced vitamin K. Co-treatment with warfarin and K1 reduced the K1-induced GLA signal, supporting the dependence of this modification on VKOR-mediated vitamin K recycling. Equal protein loading was confirmed by total protein staining and β-actin immunoblotting. These findings demonstrate that TNBC cells express a functional vitamin K cycle, and that K1 and K2 are not equivalent in supporting detectable γ-carboxylation in this context.

K1 enhances and K2 reduces stemness features

Because TNBC progression is associated with cancer stem-like populations [6], we assessed whether vitamin K forms altered stemness. In mammosphere formation assays, K1 increased both the number and size of spheres relative to vehicle in all three cell lines (approximately 1.5- to 2-fold increase in sphere-forming efficiency, p < 0.05). K2 had the opposite effect, reducing sphere-forming efficiency by about 40–70%. Flow cytometry for the CD44⁺/CD24⁻ population showed a similar pattern: K1 increased the proportion of CD44⁺/CD24⁻ cells, while K2 decreased it. Aldehyde dehydrogenase activity (ALDEFLUOR assay) was likewise higher in K1-treated and lower in K2-treated cells. Consistent with these functional readouts, qPCR analysis showed that K1 increased expression of stemness-associated transcripts (e.g., SOX2, NANOG, and OCT4), whereas K2 reduced them. Warfarin alone had minimal effects on sphere formation, but it attenuated the K1-induced increase, which is in line with a role for γ-carboxylation or VKOR-dependent processes in mediating K1 effects.

Effects of K1 and K2 on pathway gene expression

Finally, we examined whether vitamin K treatment altered expression of the pathway genes themselves. K1 produced modest changes in GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1 transcripts, with small increases in some lines, whereas K2 did not significantly alter their expression. Thus, the divergent phenotypes were unlikely to result from differential regulation of the carboxylation machinery.

Together, these results show that TNBC cells express a functional vitamin K pathway and that K1 promotes growth, stemness, and GLA-protein accumulation, whereas K2 suppresses growth and stemness without detectable γ-carboxylation.

The present study demonstrates that TNBC cells express the components of the vitamin K cycle (GGCX, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1), that expression is highest in TNBC lines and in advanced-stage disease, and that this pathway is functional, as shown by K1-dependent generation of GLA-modified proteins. Importantly, K1 and K2 produced divergent phenotypes: K1 promoted growth and stemness, whereas K2 reduced stemness and exerted anti-proliferative effects. These findings suggest that the two vitamers, though often considered functionally interchangeable cofactors for γ-carboxylation, are not equivalent in the context of TNBC.

Elevated expression of GGCX and VKOR enzymes in aggressive disease is consistent with reports linking γ-carboxylation machinery and GLA-containing proteins to tumor progression. GGCX has been implicated in the growth and invasiveness of several cancers, and GAS6 and its TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (AXL, MERTK) require γ-carboxylation for activity and are associated with metastasis, drug resistance and stem-like phenotypes in breast cancer [1,2]. Because GAS6 signaling through AXL promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition and survival, one plausible explanation for the pro-growth effect of K1 is enhanced carboxylation and activation of GAS6 or related GLA proteins. The detection of GLA-modified proteins only in K1-treated lysates supports this interpretation, though the identity of these proteins remains to be established. Proteomic identification, combined with GGCX knockdown, would determine whether the K1 phenotype depends on γ-carboxylation.

A notable observation was that K2, and vehicle, did not yield detectable GLA-modified proteins, and neither did warfarin. The absence of signal in vehicle-treated cells likely reflects the low vitamin K content of standard serum-containing media, indicating that carboxylation is substrate-limited in culture. Warfarin's lack of effect is expected in the absence of exogenous vitamin K, since there is little reduced cofactor to deplete. The failure of K2 to induce detectable GLA proteins, despite being a competent GGCX cofactor in other systems [3], is more surprising. Possible explanations include differences in cellular uptake, intracellular conversion, subcellular distribution, or efficiency of reduction by VKORC1 versus VKORC1L1. VKORC1L1 is thought to support vitamin K-dependent processes and protect against oxidative stress, and the two enzymes may differ in substrate preference for K1 versus menaquinones [4]. Alternatively, K2 may be rapidly metabolized or may engage non-carboxylation pathways that predominate over its cofactor role. Sensitivity of the detection method must also be considered, since low-level carboxylation by K2 may have fallen below the threshold of our assay.

The anti-proliferative and stemness-suppressing effects of K2 agree with prior reports of menaquinone-induced growth arrest, apoptosis and differentiation in leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma and other cancer models [5,6]. Many of these effects have been attributed to γ-carboxylation-independent mechanisms, including activation of the nuclear receptor SXR/PXR, modulation of reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial dysfunction and cell cycle regulation [6,7]. Menaquinone-4 also serves as an electron carrier and may alter redox balance in tumor cells. Our data are compatible with such mechanisms, because K2 reduced stemness in the absence of detectable GLA proteins. That K1, which is structurally distinct in its side chain, lacks these effects underscores that side-chain length and saturation may govern interactions with non-canonical targets. Distinguishing carboxylation-dependent from carboxylation-independent actions will be an important next step, for example through use of GGCX-deficient cells or carboxylation-resistant mutants.

These results have potential translational relevance. Dietary vitamin K intake and supplementation are widespread, and K1 is the predominant dietary form. If K1 promotes growth and stem-like properties in TNBC, then caution may be warranted regarding supplementation in patients with this disease, although in vitro findings cannot be directly extrapolated to clinical outcomes. Epidemiological data on vitamin K intake and breast cancer risk are inconsistent, and often fail to differentiate K1 from K2 [8]. Our findings argue that future studies should distinguish between vitamers. Conversely, the anti-proliferative activity of K2 raises the possibility of its use as an adjunct therapy, perhaps in combination with agents targeting cancer stem cells. Furthermore, the pro-tumorigenic role of the carboxylation pathway suggests that targeting GGCX or VKOR enzymes, or the carboxylated effectors such as GAS6-AXL, might be therapeutically exploitable, with the caveat that systemic anticoagulant effects limit warfarin-like strategies.

This study has limitations. Experiments were performed in three TNBC cell lines under in vitro conditions, and physiological concentrations of vitamin K in tissues, particularly of tumor-resident menaquinones, are uncertain. Stemness was evaluated using a limited set of assays, and the molecular mediators were not identified. The contribution of the tumor microenvironment, including stromal and immune cells that also express vitamin K-dependent proteins, was not addressed. In vivo models and analysis of patient samples, including correlation of enzyme expression with survival and subtype, are needed to validate relevance.

In conclusion, TNBC cells possess a functional vitamin K pathway, with expression of GGCX, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1 highest in TNBC lines and advanced disease. K1 increases GLA-protein production, growth and stemness, while K2 suppresses stemness and proliferation without detectable carboxylation. These divergent effects indicate that vitamers should be evaluated separately in cancer biology and nutrition research. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying these differences may reveal new therapeutic strategies for modulating the vitamin K pathway in TNBC.

Fisheries are among the most pervasive human activities in the marine environment, and their expansion over the past century has altered food webs, habitats and the demography of many non-target species [1,2]. Industrial fishing now covers more than half of the ocean surface, and a large and growing proportion of this effort occurs in areas beyond national jurisdiction [3,4]. International waters account for over 60% of the world's oceans, yet they remain the least monitored and least regulated of marine areas. Management relies on regional fisheries management organisations, whose capacity to enforce regulations is limited by the vast scale of the area and by incomplete reporting of catch, effort and bycatch [5,6]. Consequently, how fisheries in these regions shape ecosystem processes is surprisingly poorly understood.

Monitoring of fishing activity at sea has traditionally depended on logbooks, onboard observers and, more recently, vessel monitoring systems (VMS) and the Automatic Identification System (AIS). These approaches have transformed our view of global fishing effort [3,7], but each has limitations. Observer coverage is generally low and biased toward certain fleets, and VMS data are often not publicly accessible. AIS transmissions can be switched off or spoofed, and vessels engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing have a strong incentive to avoid detection [8,9]. Satellite-based radar and optical imagery can detect non-broadcasting vessels, but coverage is intermittent, limited by cloud and resolution, and costly to apply across ocean basins [10]. There is therefore a clear need for complementary methods that can detect vessels irrespective of whether they transmit their position.

Seabirds are among the taxa most affected by fisheries. Many species are attracted to vessels, where they exploit discards, offal and baited hooks, and this behavior brings them into contact with fishing gear [11,12]. Incidental mortality in longline and trawl fisheries is considered the primary threat to albatrosses and large petrels, and it has contributed to the fact that albatrosses are now among the most threatened groups of birds, with most species listed as threatened or near-threatened [13,14]. At the same time, access to fishery waste may provide a food subsidy that influences foraging behavior, diet, breeding success and population dynamics [15,16]. Quantifying the interaction between seabirds and fisheries is therefore essential both for assessing bycatch risk and for understanding the wider ecological consequences of fishing.

Most assessments of this interaction have been based on the spatial overlap between the distributions of tracked birds and the distributions of fishing effort, derived from VMS or AIS data [17,18]. Such estimates of overlap are indirect: they indicate where birds and vessels could encounter each other but not whether encounters actually occurred. Overlap analyses are also constrained by the resolution and completeness of the fisheries data, and they are likely to underestimate exposure in international waters where vessel data are sparse or absent [19]. Furthermore, spatial coincidence at coarse scales provides little information on the behavior of birds in relation to vessels, such as the duration of attendance or the frequency with which individuals follow ships. Direct observations of seabird–vessel interactions are needed to resolve these uncertainties.

Recent advances in biologging provide such an opportunity. Small devices that detect the radar emissions of vessels, in combination with GPS loggers, allow the detection of ships by the birds themselves [20]. Because the marine radars carried by most vessels operate continuously, particularly at night and in poor visibility, such devices can record encounters between birds and vessels, including those from vessels that do not transmit AIS, and can thus reveal the true extent of overlap. Initial deployments on albatrosses and other seabirds in restricted regions have shown that this approach can detect IUU activity and quantify encounter rates [20,21]. Wide-ranging seabirds that cover immense areas may thereby serve as ocean sentinels, sampling the distribution of vessels over scales that are impractical for conventional surveys [22].

The wandering albatross (*Diomedea exulans*) is an ideal model for this approach. It is a wide-ranging, long-lived species that exploits the winds of the Southern Ocean to travel thousands of kilometers during foraging trips, and individuals are known to be attracted to fishing vessels [23,24]. Populations of wandering albatrosses have declined at several sites, partly as a result of bycatch in longline fisheries [13,25]. The Crozet Islands in the southern Indian Ocean hold one of the largest populations of the species, and birds breeding there forage across areas that include both national exclusive economic zones and international waters, where regulatory oversight is weak [24,26]. Despite decades of tracking, how often these birds actually encounter vessels, and where, remains unknown.

Here, we used loggers combining GPS and radar detection, deployed on wandering albatrosses breeding at the Crozet Islands, to measure the true extent of overlap between albatrosses and fishing vessels. Our objectives were to (i) quantify the area patrolled by breeding albatrosses and the distances reached from the colony; (ii) determine the proportion of birds that detected vessels and the frequency of detections; (iii) compare detections with the distribution of vessels broadcasting AIS to estimate the proportion of non-broadcasting vessels; and (iv) generate estimates of the intensity of fishing and the distribution of vessels in international waters. We predicted that encounter rates would be higher than expected from overlap analyses based on AIS and VMS, particularly in areas beyond national jurisdiction. By doing so, we evaluate the potential of seabirds equipped with radar detectors as monitors of vessel presence, with implications for bycatch assessment, fisheries management and the detection of illegal fishing.

Fieldwork was conducted at Possession Island, Crozet Archipelago (46°25′S, 51°45′E), southern Indian Ocean, during the incubation and brooding periods of wandering albatrosses (Diomedea exulans) in 2018–2019. The colony is monitored annually, and the identity, sex, age and breeding status of individuals are known from long-term ringing and nest surveys [1]. Adults were captured by hand on their nests, and all handling was kept to a minimum and carried out under permits issued by the Terres Australes et Antarctiques Françaises and the ethics committee of the Institut Polaire Français Paul-Émile Victor.

**Devices and deployment**

Each bird was equipped with a combined GPS and radar-detector logger (Sextant, Cefas/Toulouse design; mass approx. 60 g, <2% of body mass, below the 3% threshold generally recommended for flying seabirds [2]). The unit has a GPS receiver and a radar detector sensitive to X-band (9.4 GHz) emissions, the frequency used by the marine navigation radars carried by most fishing vessels [3]. The detector records a radar pulse whenever a vessel's radar beam is received, which is possible within approximately 5 km of the bird, depending on sea state and radar power. Detection events were logged with a time stamp and the bird's concurrent GPS position. GPS fixes were taken every 2 min, and radar detection was sampled continuously, with the number of pulses summarised in 1-min bins. Loggers were taped to the dorsal contour feathers with waterproof tape (Tesa) and secured with cyanoacrylate glue [4]. Birds were released at their nests within 15 min of capture. Devices were recovered after one or more foraging trips by recapturing birds at their nests, and the total deployment lasted between 5 and 40 days.

**Data processing**

All analyses were performed in R v4.0 [5]. GPS tracks were examined for errors and resampled at regular 10-min intervals using linear interpolation (package adehabitatLT [6]). Foraging trips were defined as continuous periods at sea beginning when a bird left the island and ending upon return, and trips of less than 1 h were discarded. Behavioural state was assigned from ground speed and sinuosity using a hidden Markov model (package moveHMM [7]) with three states: resting on the water, foraging (area-restricted search) and travelling. Maximum distance from the colony and total path length were calculated for each trip. Utilisation distributions were estimated by kernel density (package adehabitatHR [6]), and the 50% and 95% contours were taken as core and general ranges. The area patrolled was calculated from the cumulative 95% utilisation distribution of all birds, projected onto a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection.

Radar detections were treated as presence of a vessel. Consecutive detections separated by less than 30 min were grouped into a single encounter event, in line with previous work on albatross–vessel interactions [3]. For each encounter we extracted the position, time, duration and the bird's behavioural state before, during and after detection. Detections within 20 km of the colony were excluded because of the research station's radar and local supply and patrol vessels.

**Overlap with fisheries**

To place detections in the context of known fishing activity, we compared radar detections with Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from Global Fishing Watch [8], which provide vessel positions and apparent fishing effort at 0.1° resolution. Each radar encounter was classified as "matched" if an AIS-broadcasting fishing vessel was recorded within 10 km and ±1 h of the bird's position, and "unmatched" otherwise. Unmatched encounters could represent vessels that do not broadcast AIS, either because they are not required to or because transponders were switched off, and were considered potential non-reported or illegal activity [9]. They could also represent non-fishing vessels, so we also compared encounter locations with exclusive economic zone boundaries [10] and regional fisheries management organisation areas. Overlap with legal fisheries was quantified as the proportion of albatross locations within 50 km of AIS-registered fishing effort in the same month.

**Estimating vessel distribution and fishing intensity**

To map vessel distribution, the study area was divided into 1° × 1° grid cells. For each cell, we calculated the proportion of bird GPS fixes with a radar detection, adjusting for variation in bird use (time spent in the cell) by dividing the number of detections by the number of bird-hours. Cells with fewer than 10 bird-hours or fewer than three individuals were excluded to limit pseudoreplication. The resulting index of encounter rate was taken as a proxy for vessel density. We tested its relationship to AIS fishing effort per cell using generalised additive models with a negative binomial error and the log of bird-hours as an offset (package mgcv [11]).

**Statistical analysis**

The proportion of individuals that detected at least one vessel was computed per sex and breeding stage. Differences in encounter rate among sexes and foraging stages were tested with generalised linear mixed models with a Poisson error structure, with individual as a random intercept and log trip duration as an offset (package lme4 [12]). Differences in behaviour before and during encounters were tested with mixed models of speed and sinuosity, again with individual as a random effect. Model selection was based on Akaike's information criterion, and model fit was assessed through residual diagnostics (package DHARMa [13]). Spatial autocorrelation was checked using Moran's I on residuals. Means are reported ± SD, and significance was accepted at α = 0.05.

A total of 169 wandering albatrosses from the Crozet Islands were equipped with combined GPS and radar detector loggers during the breeding season, yielding tracks from both incubation and chick-rearing. Loggers recorded for a mean of 17.4 ± 6.2 days per deployment, and 142 devices (84%) were recovered with complete data. Together, these tracks covered an area of more than 10 million km² of the southern Indian Ocean, extending from subantarctic waters north of the colony to the Antarctic shelf margin and east toward Kerguelen and Australian longitudes.

**Movement and spatial extent**

Birds ranged up to 2500 km from the colony (maximum 2512 km), with the greatest distances reached by incubating individuals and by males and females during long foraging trips. Trip duration differed between breeding stages (incubation: 14.3 ± 5.1 days; chick-rearing: 8.2 ± 4.4 days; linear mixed model, χ² = 41.7, P < 0.001), and maximum distance from the colony declined correspondingly in chick-rearing birds. Sex-related differences in distribution were evident: females tended to use more northerly, warmer waters, whereas males used more southerly waters near the Antarctic shelf margin, consistent with previously described sexual segregation in this species [1,2]. Core-use areas (50% kernel densities) lay mainly in international waters, with only a small proportion inside the exclusive economic zones (EEZs) of Crozet and Kerguelen. Across all tracked birds, 71% of GPS locations fell outside national jurisdictions.

**Detection of vessels**

Of the 142 loggers with complete data, 79.5% (n = 113) detected at least one radar-emitting vessel during deployment. In total, 2,874 radar detection events were recorded, which after clustering by time and space (detections within 10 km and 1 h were merged) corresponded to 1,386 independent encounters. Individual birds encountered a median of 7 vessels per trip (interquartile range 2–16; maximum 61). Detections were not evenly distributed in time: encounters peaked during daylight hours, although a substantial fraction (31%) occurred at night, when visual observation of attendance is not possible. Detection rates were higher during incubation than during chick-rearing (0.74 vs. 0.51 encounters per day), a pattern attributable to the greater distances and wider areas covered by incubating birds rather than to differences in encounter probability per unit distance travelled (P = 0.38).

Detection probability was strongly dependent on location. Within EEZs, encounters were frequent near Kerguelen and Crozet, where licensed longline fleets target Patagonian toothfish (*Dissostichus eleginoides*). However, 64% of all encounters occurred in international waters, including areas beyond the continental shelf where no regulated fisheries are expected to operate at comparable intensity. Encounter rate per 100 km travelled was significantly greater in the high seas than within EEZs (0.46 vs. 0.29; Wilcoxon test, W = 5,812, P = 0.004).

**Overlap with vessels and behavioural responses**

Comparison of radar detections with Automatic Identification System (AIS) data showed that a considerable proportion of detected vessels were not visible in public tracking databases. Only 28% of radar encounters matched an AIS-transmitting vessel within 10 km and 15 min, so that 72% of detected vessels were "dark" with respect to AIS. The proportion of unmatched vessels was highest in international waters (81%) and lowest inside the Crozet EEZ (46%). Matched vessels were mostly identified as longliners and trawlers, while unmatched vessels could not be classified.

Albatross behaviour changed in the presence of vessels. Following detection, birds reduced ground speed and increased path tortuosity (sinuosity index 0.61 ± 0.18 vs. 0.82 ± 0.12 before detection; paired t-test, P < 0.001), and 58% of encounters were followed by a bout of area-restricted search lasting longer than 30 min. Birds approached vessels from distances of up to 30 km, and the median time spent within 5 km of a vessel was 47 min (range 6 min to 9.3 h). Attraction was not uniform: 22% of encounters resulted in no discernible change in movement, suggesting that birds do not respond to all vessels or that some vessels offer little or no discard availability.

**Mapping fishing intensity and vessel distribution**

By interpolating the density of radar detections across the tracked area and correcting for bird effort (number of GPS fixes per cell), we generated maps of relative vessel density at a resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°. High-density cells were concentrated along the Subtropical Front and the edges of the Kerguelen Plateau, with additional hotspots on seamounts and ridges in international waters south-east of Crozet. Several hotspots coincided with known fishing grounds recorded in AIS-based datasets [3], but approximately one-third of high-density cells (34%) had no corresponding AIS fishing effort. Cross-validation, in which detections from a random 25% of birds were predicted from the remaining 75%, showed moderate-to-good agreement (Spearman ρ = 0.63, P < 0.001), indicating that the maps were reasonably robust to individual variation.

**Bycatch risk**

Combining the overlap analyses with the known distribution of vessels, we estimated that the average bird spent 3.1% of its time at sea within 5 km of a vessel (range 0–19%). Overlap was higher in international waters than within EEZs, where bycatch mitigation measures are mandatory, and a considerable proportion of the highest-risk encounters (those with prolonged proximity) occurred in areas lacking regulatory coverage by management bodies. Breeding stage did not significantly affect the proportion of time near vessels (P = 0.21), but individual variation was large, with 12% of birds accounting for 47% of all time spent near vessels.

Our results show that radar detectors deployed on wandering albatrosses reveal a degree of overlap with fishing vessels that is considerably greater than suggested by earlier approaches. Albatrosses breeding on the Crozet Islands ranged over more than 10 million km² and up to 2500 km from the colony, and a large majority of loggers (up to 79.5%) recorded vessel detections. This indicates that interactions with ships are a routine component of the foraging ecology of this species, rather than a rare event restricted to well-regulated, nearby fishing grounds. Because wandering albatrosses forage across both national jurisdictions and the high seas, the exposure of individuals to fisheries is shaped by management regimes over which no single state has control [1,2].

**Overlap between seabirds and fisheries**

Previous assessments of overlap have relied mainly on coupling seabird tracking data with vessel monitoring systems (VMS) or the Automatic Identification System (AIS) [3,4]. These sources are informative but incomplete: VMS data are frequently confidential, AIS can be switched off or is not carried by many vessels, and coverage is particularly poor in international waters, where reporting obligations are weaker [5,6]. Overlap estimates derived from such data are therefore likely to be conservative, especially for longline and trawl vessels that operate without transmitting their positions. By detecting radar emissions directly, our loggers recorded vessels irrespective of their compliance with reporting, giving an independent measure of encounter rather than of potential co-occurrence. The high proportion of devices that detected vessels suggests that the true overlap, and hence bycatch risk, may be underestimated in current risk assessments for albatrosses and petrels [7,8].

The scale of movements also has implications for conservation. Wandering albatrosses are among the species most affected by incidental mortality in longline fisheries, and populations of several Southern Ocean albatrosses have declined as a result [9,10]. Birds that travel thousands of kilometres from their colony during breeding are exposed to multiple fleets and regulatory frameworks, including tuna regional fisheries management organisations whose bycatch mitigation requirements vary in strength and enforcement [11]. Our data support the view that effective protection requires coordinated measures across jurisdictions, and that mitigation at colony-adjacent fisheries alone will be insufficient.

**Behaviour in relation to vessels**

Because loggers also recorded bird position, our approach allows the response of birds to vessels to be quantified, rather than simply assumed. Albatrosses are known to be attracted to vessels by discards, bait and olfactory cues [12,13], and attraction is the mechanism that makes bycatch possible. Detection of radar by a bird does not necessarily imply direct interaction, as the detection range of the loggers extends several kilometres, but it identifies the occasions on which attraction could occur. Subsequent analyses of movement patterns around detections, such as reductions in speed or increased tortuosity, can distinguish between birds that approach vessels and those that merely pass nearby. This distinction is important for estimating the proportion of encounters that translate into risk, and for assessing whether vessel attendance provides a significant energetic subsidy that could influence foraging strategies and breeding success [14].

**Seabirds as ocean sentinels**

A further outcome is that albatrosses can act as sampling platforms for the distribution of vessels. Because they travel widely, fly efficiently and are attracted to ships, they sample large areas of ocean at low cost and with little dependence on satellite or ship-based surveys [15]. Seabirds have previously been used to measure oceanographic variables and detect illegal fishing activity [16], and our results extend this to a direct census of vessel presence. The spatial pattern of detections provides a proxy for fishing intensity in areas with little other information, and may reveal clusters of activity in the high seas or near the boundaries of exclusive economic zones and marine protected areas. Detections that are not matched by AIS or VMS records may point to unreported or illegal fishing, which remains a major threat to Southern Ocean ecosystems and to the efficacy of conservation measures [17,18]. Deployments on a larger number of birds and species with different ranges would increase spatial coverage and temporal resolution.

**Limitations**

Several caveats should be noted. First, the loggers detect only vessels that are emitting radar signals, which excludes small or unlit vessels and those operating with radar off, so absolute vessel numbers are likely to be underestimated. Second, radar detection cannot by itself identify vessel type or fishing activity; combining detections with bird movement, and where available, AIS data, will be needed to separate fishing vessels from transiting cargo ships. Third, deployments were restricted to breeding adults from a single colony and period; birds in other life-history stages, such as juveniles and non-breeders, may differ in range and exposure [19]. Finally, sample sizes limit inference about interannual variation in encounter rates. Estimates of fishing intensity should therefore be regarded as relative indices rather than absolute measures of effort.

**Conclusions**

Radar detectors on wandering albatrosses show that interactions with fishing vessels are widespread and occur at great distances from breeding sites, across areas where monitoring is limited. The method provides a more complete measure of overlap than that obtainable from vessel reporting systems, offers insight into the behaviour of birds around ships, and gives a cost-effective means of surveying vessel presence in remote waters. We suggest that this technology be integrated into bycatch risk assessments and into the surveillance of the high seas, and that it be extended to other wide-ranging species and regions. Such an approach would support more accurate management of fisheries, better targeting of mitigation measures and improved detection of illegal fishing, with benefits for both seabird conservation and ocean governance.

Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is an active microwave imaging system that operates day and night and under nearly all weather conditions, and it has become an indispensable tool for Earth observation, disaster monitoring, marine surveillance, and military reconnaissance [1,2]. Spaceborne SAR systems are particularly valuable because they offer global access and repeatable coverage. As applications have matured, demand has grown for imagery that combines fine azimuth resolution with a wide observation area. Conventional stripmap mode ties the achievable azimuth resolution to the physical antenna length, and ScanSAR trades resolution for swath width by burst-wise beam switching in elevation [3]. Neither mode can deliver high resolution and wide swath (HRWS) at the same time.

**Spotlight and sliding spotlight modes**

Spotlight SAR extends the synthetic aperture time by steering the antenna beam to keep it on a fixed scene center, so the azimuth resolution is no longer limited by the antenna length [4]. The price is lost azimuth coverage, since only a single scene of limited extent is imaged per pass. Sliding spotlight mode relaxes this constraint. The beam is steered about a virtual rotation point located farther from the sensor than the scene, so the footprint moves along the ground at a velocity lower than that of the platform. This yields an intermediate resolution between stripmap and spotlight, together with continuous, longer azimuth coverage [5,6]. Sliding spotlight has therefore been adopted by many spaceborne systems, including TerraSAR-X, COSMO-SkyMed, and TanDEM-X [7,8].

Gaofen-3 (GF-3) is China's first civilian C-band multi-polarization SAR satellite with multiple imaging modes. It offers spatial resolutions from 1 m to 500 m and swaths from 10 km to 650 km, and it includes spotlight, stripmap, ScanSAR, and sliding spotlight modes [9]. Producing well focused sliding spotlight imagery from GF-3 data is both a practical necessity and a useful test of processing methods under real orbital and attitude conditions.

**Challenges in sliding spotlight processing**

Beam steering in sliding spotlight mode enlarges the total Doppler bandwidth of the received signal well beyond the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), which is chosen to match only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth of each target. The raw data are therefore azimuth-undersampled, and the spectrum is folded or aliased. Because the time-frequency relation is also ambiguous, standard frequency-domain algorithms such as the range-Doppler, chirp scaling, and omega-K algorithms cannot be applied directly [10]. Several approaches have been proposed to address this problem. Subaperture methods split the data into pieces whose bandwidths fit within the PRF, but they complicate processing and require subaperture recombination [11]. The chirp scaling and extended chirp scaling variants have been adapted to the steered-beam geometry [12]. Time-domain back projection is accurate but computationally heavy for large scenes [13]. Another class of methods increases the effective sampling rate through zero padding, which raises the memory and computational load.

The two-step processing approach of Lanari et al. offers a more efficient alternative [14]. In the first step, a deramping operation in the azimuth time domain, performed by multiplication with a linear frequency-modulated function, reduces the Doppler bandwidth of the signal to within the PRF. This removes the spectral folding, after which conventional stripmap algorithms can focus the data. In the second step, a further azimuth-scaling or deramping operation restores the correct time-frequency relation and resamples the data onto a proper azimuth grid. Applying this approach to actual spaceborne data requires careful treatment of the curved orbit, the earth rotation, and the range-dependent rotation center, as well as the appropriate choice of deramping reference parameters [15].

A second challenge is the accuracy of the Doppler parameters. Focusing quality depends strongly on the Doppler centroid and the Doppler frequency-rate. Errors in the centroid cause azimuth ambiguity and a loss of signal-to-noise ratio, and errors in the frequency rate degrade azimuth resolution and increase sidelobe levels [16]. In sliding spotlight mode the Doppler centroid varies with azimuth time because of the beam steering, and the effective frequency rate differs from that of stripmap mode, so the standard estimators such as the correlation Doppler estimator and the map-drift or autofocus method cannot be applied without modification [17,18]. Spectral folding adds a further difficulty, since the centroid estimate may be ambiguous by an integer multiple of the PRF. Estimation methods suited to the deramped data are thus required for an automatic, operational processor.

**Contributions and organization**

This paper presents an integrated imaging scheme for GF-3 sliding spotlight data that combines the two-step approach with Doppler parameter estimation. The main contributions are as follows. First, the signal model and Doppler characteristics of the GF-3 sliding spotlight mode are analyzed, and the origin of the azimuth spectral folding is clarified. Second, the two-step approach is incorporated into a complete spaceborne processing chain that removes the folding without oversampling the data. Third, Doppler centroid and frequency-rate estimation algorithms are developed for the sliding spotlight geometry and validated on real GF-3 data. The results are evaluated by image quality and by estimation accuracy.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the geometry and signal model of the sliding spotlight mode and analyzes its spectral characteristics. Section 3 presents the imaging scheme, including the two-step processing and the Doppler parameter estimation algorithms. Section 4 reports the experimental results from GF-3 data and discusses the accuracy and efficiency of the method. Section 5 concludes the paper.

**Signal Model and Imaging Geometry**

In the sliding spotlight mode, the antenna beam is steered in azimuth so that the beam footprint moves on the ground at a velocity lower than that of the sensor. The beam rotates about a virtual point located at a distance R_rot from the flight track, which lies below the scene center in the sliding spotlight configuration. The ratio of the footprint velocity to the platform velocity is defined by the scaling factor A = (R_rot − R_0)/R_rot, where R_0 is the closest slant range of the target. The azimuth bandwidth of the received signal is thereby extended beyond that of the stripmap mode, and the total Doppler bandwidth is the sum of the target bandwidth and the bandwidth produced by beam steering [1], [2]. When this bandwidth exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), the azimuth spectrum of the raw data is folded. The PRF is chosen to exceed only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth, so that the unambiguous processing of the full-aperture signal requires special treatment.

After range demodulation, the baseband echo of a point target is expressed as the product of a range envelope, an azimuth envelope determined by the steered antenna pattern, and a phase term determined by the instantaneous slant range R(η; R_0). The slant range is described by a hyperbolic model with an effective velocity V_r, which accounts for the curved orbit and Earth rotation [3]. The Doppler centroid f_dc and the Doppler frequency rate f_r are the two parameters that govern focusing accuracy and are estimated from the data.

**Two-Step Processing Approach**

To overcome the azimuth spectral folding, a two-step approach combining azimuth deramping and conventional frequency-domain focusing is employed [4], [5]. The procedure is as follows.

*Step 1: Linear-FM deramping and spectrum unfolding.* The raw data are multiplied in the range-Doppler domain or the time domain by a chirp function whose rate is determined by the reference range of the beam rotation center. This convolution-free operation removes the Doppler component caused by beam steering, and the signal bandwidth becomes smaller than the PRF. The data are then represented without aliasing in the azimuth frequency domain. Because the deramping function is applied in the azimuth time domain, the azimuth time axis is subsequently modified, and the azimuth signal is transformed into a frequency-domain representation that is a scaled copy of the target's time-domain envelope.

*Step 2: Range cell migration correction and focusing.* After unfolding, range compression and range cell migration correction (RCMC) are performed using an extended chirp scaling algorithm (CSA) or an omega-K approach with a modified azimuth frequency-rate. The processed signal is multiplied by an azimuth matched filter in the two-dimensional frequency domain. The frequency-rate used in this filter is adapted to the sliding spotlight geometry through the scaling factor A, giving an effective rate f_r' = f_r/A... Following the compensation, an inverse deramping operation is performed. A phase function of opposite sign is multiplied in the azimuth time domain to eliminate the residual quadratic phase generated by the first step, and an azimuth inverse FFT yields the focused image [5], [6].

*Step 3: Azimuth resampling and geometric correction.* The azimuth sampling interval of the focused image is inconsistent across the extended bandwidth, and the azimuth time axis is corrected via an interpolation or a chirp-z transform so that a uniform pixel spacing is obtained. Residual phase errors in range-varying parameters are corrected using a sub-aperture phase compensation.

**Doppler Parameter Estimation**

Accurate Doppler parameters are essential because the sliding spotlight beam steering induces a time-varying Doppler centroid and the focusing is highly sensitive to errors in f_r.

*Doppler centroid estimation.* The fractional part of the Doppler centroid is estimated from the deramped data using the average cross-correlation coefficient (ACCC) method [7], in which the phase angle of the correlation between adjacent azimuth samples is computed and averaged over range. The ambiguity number is determined by the multi-look cross-correlation or the wavelength diversity algorithm [8]. Alternatively, the geometric Doppler centroid derived from the satellite attitude and ephemeris is used to resolve ambiguities and is compared with the data-based estimate for consistency. Because the antenna is steered, the centroid is defined in the deramped domain as the sum of a constant and a time-varying component, and only the constant is estimated from data.

*Doppler frequency rate estimation.* The Doppler frequency rate is estimated by an autofocus technique based on map-drift (MD) or on the sub-aperture correlation [9]. The deramped data are split into two sub-apertures in the azimuth frequency domain, and each is compressed to form a look image. The relative shift between the looks is measured by cross-correlation, and the error in f_r is calculated from the shift as Δf_r = (Δx · f_r)/(kT), where T is the sub-aperture time spacing and k is a geometry-dependent constant. The estimation is performed in several range blocks, and a low-order polynomial is fitted along the range to obtain the range-dependent effective velocity V_r. The process is iterated until the residual shift is smaller than a threshold of 0.1 pixel. Estimation accuracy is evaluated by comparing estimates with those from the orbit-based prediction and by examining the point-target impulse response width and the peak sidelobe ratio.

**Integrated Processing Flow**

The complete scheme integrates the above steps. The raw data are first subjected to range pulse compression and a coarse Doppler centroid estimate from the geometric parameters. The two-step approach is then run, where deramping unfolds the spectrum, the refined Doppler parameters are estimated from the unfolded data, and the CSA-based focusing, inverse deramping and azimuth resampling are applied. Finally, radiometric calibration is performed using the antenna pattern and the range spreading loss. The efficiency of the scheme derives from the exclusive use of FFTs, complex multiplications and one interpolation step, so that the computational load is on the order of N log N for N samples, comparable to that of stripmap processing.

**Experimental Data and Processing Configuration**

The proposed scheme was evaluated using raw sliding spotlight data acquired by the GF-3 SAR sensor in C-band. The scene covers a coastal area containing urban blocks, port facilities, and open water, which provides both strong point-like scatterers and homogeneous distributed regions. The data were acquired at a nominal incidence angle of approximately 40° with a transmitted bandwidth of 240 MHz, giving a slant-range resolution of about 0.6 m. The azimuth beam steering rate yields a steering-induced Doppler bandwidth that exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), so the unprocessed data exhibit azimuth spectral aliasing, as observed in the Doppler spectrum before preprocessing. Processing followed the integrated scheme: Doppler parameter estimation, the two-step azimuth preprocessing, and range-Doppler-domain focusing with residual phase compensation. All results were generated with identical parameters unless otherwise stated.

**Doppler Parameter Estimation Accuracy**

The Doppler centroid was estimated with a combined baseband-centroid and ambiguity-resolution procedure, and the Doppler frequency rate was estimated from the data by a map-drift/autofocus-type method. Because the beam is steered, both parameters vary with azimuth time, so estimates were computed over multiple range blocks and azimuth segments. The estimated Doppler centroid varied smoothly across range, and a low-order polynomial fit left residuals below a few hertz, which is small compared with the PRF. The estimated ambiguity number was consistent across all range blocks, indicating that no ambiguity-resolution errors occurred.

For the frequency rate, the estimates were compared with values computed from precise orbit and attitude data. The relative deviation was below 0.5% across the swath. Residual quadratic phase error produced by such a deviation is well below π/4 over the synthetic aperture, so no measurable defocusing is expected. Repeating the estimation on independent subsets of the data gave a standard deviation of the frequency rate that was a small fraction of the deviation from the geometric reference, supporting the stability of the estimator. These results demonstrate that the estimation accuracy is sufficient for sliding spotlight focusing without iterative refinement.

**Effect of the Two-Step Approach on Spectral Folding**

Before preprocessing, the azimuth spectrum was folded because the total Doppler bandwidth exceeded the PRF. Direct application of conventional stripmap-based focusing to such data produced severe azimuth ambiguities and wrapped targets. After the two-step processing, in which the data were first multiplied by a deramping function in the time domain and then transformed to a spectrum whose bandwidth was contained within the PRF, the spectrum became unfolded and continuous. The azimuth sampling was then extended by zero padding and interpolation, so that the full Doppler bandwidth could be accommodated without aliasing. Following focusing, the azimuth time axis was rescaled and the deramp-related phase removed, yielding an image with uniform pixel spacing. Visual comparison showed that the ghost targets present in the aliased result were eliminated, and that the geometric layout of the harbor structures matched the reference map without azimuth wrap-around.

**Point Target Analysis**

Several isolated strong scatterers, identified as corner-reflector-like structures in the scene, were used for quantitative image quality assessment. Impulse response functions were obtained by oversampling the target neighborhoods by a factor of 16. The measured range resolution was approximately 0.62 m, close to the theoretical value after accounting for the window weighting. In azimuth, the measured resolution was approximately 1.0 m, consistent with the expected resolution from the steering-enlarged synthetic aperture. The peak sidelobe ratio was around −13 dB in both dimensions and the integrated sidelobe ratio was about −10 dB for unweighted processing; these values are typical of the sinc-like response and close to the theoretical values. Applying a Hamming window lowered the sidelobes below −35 dB at the expense of a modest resolution broadening of approximately 1.3 times, in line with theory. Azimuth profiles showed symmetric sidelobes, indicating the absence of significant residual cubic or higher-order phase errors.

**Distributed Scene Evaluation**

For the homogeneous sea and flat land regions, the image exhibited uniform radiometry along azimuth, with no visible scalloping or periodic intensity modulation. This suggests that the deramping and subsequent resampling did not introduce amplitude artifacts. Azimuth ambiguity-to-signal ratios, estimated from the response of bright targets over dark water, were below −20 dB, which is acceptable for operational products. The fine texture of buildings, ship hulls, and quay cranes was clearly resolved, confirming the improvement in azimuth resolution relative to stripmap data acquired over the same region, where the resolution is on the order of several meters.

**Computational Efficiency**

The processing time was measured on a workstation with a multicore CPU. The proposed approach required only additional FFT operations and complex multiplications over a standard range-Doppler workflow, increasing the runtime by roughly 20% relative to stripmap processing of an equivalent number of samples. This cost is much lower than that of methods requiring subaperture division and recombination, which are associated with larger memory requirements. The Doppler estimation stage accounted for less than 10% of the total processing time because it operated on decimated range blocks.

**Discussion**

Taken together, the results confirm that the integrated scheme resolves the azimuth spectral folding problem inherent to sliding spotlight data and achieves near-theoretical impulse response characteristics. The close agreement between estimated and geometry-derived Doppler parameters suggests that the scheme can operate without reliance on precise attitude data, a useful property when attitude uncertainties are present. Remaining limitations include some sensitivity of the frequency rate estimates over low-contrast scenes, where the estimator has little coherent information. Nevertheless, for the scene analyzed, the focusing quality was consistently high across the swath.

**Discussion**

The experiments with Gaofen-3 (GF-3) sliding spotlight data show that the proposed integrated scheme yields well-focused images despite the azimuth spectral folding inherent to this mode. The discussion below covers the factors behind this performance, the practical implications of the Doppler parameter estimation results, and the limitations of the current work.

*Handling of azimuth spectral folding.* In sliding spotlight mode, steering the beam about a point far from the scene center enlarges the Doppler bandwidth of the whole data set well beyond the pulse repetition frequency (PRF). Conventional stripmap algorithms such as range-Doppler and chirp scaling therefore cannot be applied directly [1,2]. The two-step approach resolves this by removing the linear frequency modulation component associated with the beam steering in the time domain, using a deramping operation, before any Fourier transform in azimuth. After this step the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth of each target falls within the PRF, so the signal is unambiguously sampled and standard frequency-domain focusing can follow [3,4]. Unlike methods that interpolate or zero-pad the azimuth data, this approach does not increase the azimuth data volume. This explains its efficiency, which matters for operational processing of the large GF-3 products. The processed point-like targets showed symmetric sidelobes and resolutions close to the theoretical values. This suggests that the residual phase errors from the two-step operations, including the azimuth-variant scaling, are negligible at the resolutions and scene sizes considered.

*Role of Doppler parameter estimation.* The quality of the focusing depends strongly on the Doppler centroid and Doppler frequency-rate estimates. In sliding spotlight mode both parameters are coupled to the continuous antenna steering. The centroid varies with azimuth time, and the effective frequency rate differs from that of the stripmap case by a factor determined by the rotation rate of the beam [2,5]. Errors in the centroid shift the spectrum and may cause azimuth ambiguities, whereas errors in the frequency rate cause defocusing and broadening of the impulse response [6]. Our estimation results were consistent with values derived from the satellite attitude and orbit data, and the images showed no visible ambiguity ghosts or defocusing. This indicates that data-driven estimation, applied after the deramping step, can refine or replace parameters computed from ancillary information, which are limited by attitude measurement and timing errors. Estimating the parameters on deramped data is also better conditioned, because the spectrum is no longer folded and the energy-based or correlation-based estimators operate on a contiguous spectrum [7].

*Comparison with alternative approaches.* Several other approaches to sliding spotlight processing exist, including the extended chirp scaling algorithm, the frequency-domain subaperture method, and time-domain back-projection [8,9]. Back-projection handles arbitrary geometries and avoids spectral folding, but its computational load is prohibitive for large scenes unless fast factorized variants are used. Subaperture methods lower the load but complicate the azimuth stitching of subimages and the geometric correction. The two-step approach strikes a balance: its accuracy approaches that of the more rigorous methods, while its cost is comparable to that of stripmap algorithms. This is the main reason it suits the high-throughput ground segment of GF-3. Its remaining limitation is that the deramping reference function assumes a particular reference point and a straight-line approximation of the geometry. Wide swaths, large squint angles, or very high resolutions could therefore require higher-order corrections.

*Limitations.* The conclusions are drawn from a limited number of GF-3 acquisitions and scene types. Scenes with strong, isolated scatterers allow reliable estimation, but low-contrast regions such as water or desert may degrade the accuracy of the Doppler estimates. In such regions, a scene-adaptive selection of estimation windows or the use of attitude-assisted priors may be needed [7]. Moreover, we did not quantify the radiometric and phase fidelity of the processed images, which matter for interferometric and polarimetric applications. Lastly, the effects of terrain-induced and ionospheric phase distortions were not investigated and may become important at the finest resolutions.

**Conclusion**

This paper has presented an integrated imaging scheme for GF-3 sliding spotlight SAR data that combines a two-step focusing algorithm with Doppler parameter estimation. The two-step processing removes azimuth spectral folding without enlarging the data volume. The subsequent estimation of the Doppler centroid and frequency rate provides parameters accurate enough to produce well-focused images with near-theoretical resolution. Compared with time-domain and subaperture alternatives, the scheme offers a favorable trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, which supports its use in routine production of high-resolution, wide-coverage products.

Future work should address four points. First, the approach should be validated on a larger set of acquisitions covering diverse terrain, resolutions, and squint conditions. Second, estimators should be made more robust in low-contrast scenes, for instance by fusing image-based estimates with attitude and orbit data. Third, the geometric, radiometric, and phase accuracy of the products should be assessed against calibrated targets, and their suitability for interferometric applications evaluated. Fourth, higher-order phase compensation should be incorporated to extend the method to wider swaths and higher resolutions. Such developments would strengthen the role of GF-3 sliding spotlight imaging in applications that demand both fine detail and broad coverage.
